records.title: Warehouse receipt systems: lessons from Niger
records.description:
Description

Since early 1990s the “warrantage system” has been adapted in Niger by local farmer organizations and microfinance institutions (MFIs), becoming a popular financial product.

The principal crops used for inventory credit are:

  • millet
  • rice and
  • peanuts.

However, any crop that can be stored without damage, can be used.

Producer organizations or cooperatives provide:

  • storage facilities; and
  • loan transactions.

The loans enable farmers to:

  • finance their household generating income activities during the storage period;
    • thereby allowing for smoother cash flows.

Revenues from financed short-term activities often enable farmers to:

  • pay back the loan without using revenues from the future sale of the stored production.

The access to the warrantage system phases are:

  • Farmers, after harvesting, meet the head of the cooperative to discuss the amount of each member’s surplus production.
  • The head of the cooperative negotiates a loan from a local bank or microfinance institution using the grain as collateral.
  • Once an agreement is reached, the grain is stored in a secure storage facility owned by the cooperative.
  • The cooperative retains one key while the other is given to the bank or microfinance institution who then issues the loan.
Figure 1. A typical warrantage storage facility

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Negotiating a loan with the bank

©FAO/TECA

1. The benefits

The benefits of the warrantage are:

  • To enable the farmers to sell their grain at a later stage when prices are higher (sometimes after six months).
  • To purchase, with the loan, good seeds for the next season.
  • To engage in other small businesses generating additional revenue helping farmers increase their incomes and wellbeing.
    • Income increase ranged from 19 to 113 percent for participating farmers.
    • Yields increase ranged from 34 and 120 percent, as farmers were able to buy better seeds and fertilizer.

The warrantage system also benefits other participants in the practice including the microfinance institutions. Tanadi, for example, earned 27 percent in interest in 2011. The stock is serving as collateral and the Tanadi loans at 80 percent of the value of the stock. After four to six months the farmers pay back the loan and get back their stored grain from the warehouse (or bank).

Warrantage is promoted by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations with funding from the European Union, Belgium, Luxembourg and Spain.

2. The challenges

However, the system has its challenges depending upon growth condition:

  • During bad harvest seasons, farmers have little or no surplus to put into storage.
  • During good harvest seasons, there is a lot to store but insufficient financing from the banks.

Several conditions need to be met for warehouse receipt financing to work. Some important ones include:

  • lender’s detailed knowledge of agricultural value chain dynamics;
  • stability of agribusiness opportunities faced by borrowers;
  • legal and financial regulatory framework;
  • existence of proper storage management; and
  • facilities and sound governance among producer organizations.

The experience in Niger highlights the relative importance of these conditions. The constant demand for cereal imports from neighbouring Nigeria has created stable business opportunities for farmers in Niger. This represents an effective incentive to build strong producer organizations.

Farmers, through their organizations, have worked steadily to benefit from these opportunities by building storage facilities and making joint loan requests backed by cereal stocks. Lenders understand the worth of these stocks and therefore accept them as collateral. Despite the court system in Niger makes credit contracts difficult to enforce, the combinations of:

  • stable agribusiness opportunities;
  • strong farmer organizations; and
  • lenders familiar with agricultural markets.

All of the above factors make warehouse receipt finance work in the country.

Video: Financing the future: smallholder inventory credit in Niger

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Women-friendly

The above technology is easy to implement and accessible to all.

4.2 Resource use efficiency

The above technology allows for safe crop storage facility and minimise crop losses.

4.3 Pro-poor technology

The above recommendations contribute to agri-food business development and marketing opportunities.

records.title: Commercial scale community bamboo harvesting
records.description:
Description

Bamboo species play a key role in Northern Laos PDR (see map in Figure 1), but traditional production practices are not efficient. These practices entail poor management, low productivity, suppression of the regeneration of permanent tree species, accumulation of biomass creating enormous fuel load, low income for local populations, less information access, and high CO₂ emissions. With this situation, two private companies are being established with contractual agreements with local villagers supported by ForInfo. Local households provide a regular supply of bamboo year-round to the private company at a fair price. It is expected to become a significant contributor to household income either year round or on a seasonal basis.

Figure 1. Bamboo species play a key role in Northern Laos PDR

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Ready for transport: the ForInfo bamboo crawler is loaded with over 350 kg of fresh bamboo

©FAO/TECA

2. Approach

  • Besides private entrepreneurs, the ForInfo project will benefit government officials, community associations and other Non-Govermental Organizations (NGOs), by fostering wide stakeholder ownership and sharing the responsibilities in the role of activities.
    • Activities are:
      • the efficient exact methods to harvest bamboo,
      • the planting of improved species of bamboo,
      • an overall perennial cropping system,
      • the raising of local community awareness of environmental protection, 
      • a reduction CO₂ emission as much as possible, and
      • forest management improvement.
  • ForInfo supports innovative information, education, communication campaigns in partnership with government agencies, local NGOs, and other partners.
  • Ultimately, the project aims to lay the groundwork for a sustainable, efficient and competitive forest-based livelihoods system.
    • This is through the use of innovative approaches and closer collaboration between smallholders, forestry officials, sawmill owners, timber traders and credit associations.

3. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies 

  • Bamboo toothpick manufacturing unit: ID 3888.
  • Bamboo splitting and slivering unit: ID 3865.
  • Bamboo in sericulture: a case study from India: ID 3859.
  • Bamboo treadle pump: ID 3866.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allowed for management practice improvement, participatory decision-making, and a reduction in CO₂ emissions.​

5.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology provided beneficial opportunities for villagers and the private sector through increased income generation.

records.title: Aerobic rice
records.description:
Description

1. What is Aerobic Rice?

Aerobic rice is a production system in which especially developed “aerobic rice” varieties are grown in well-drained, non-puddled (dryland preparation), and non-saturated soils. It is a system, in which the field is not flooded at all any more but just “wetted” like a farmer does with irrigated maize or wheat. With appropriate management, the system aims for yields of at least 4 to 6 tonnes per hectare. 

2. Target area

  • “Favourable uplands."
    • Areas where the land is flat, where rainfall with or without supplemental irrigation is sufficient to frequently bring the soil water content close to field capacity, and where farmers have access to external inputs such as fertilizers.
  • Fields on upper slopes or terraces in undulating, rain-fed lowlands.
    • Quite often, soils in these areas are relatively coarse-textured and well-drained, so that ponding of water occurs only briefly or not at all during the growing season.
  • Water-short irrigated lowlands.
    • Areas where farmers do not have access to sufficient water any more to keep rice fields flooded for a substantial period of time.

3. Management

  • The usual establishment method is dry direct seeding.
  • Aerobic rice also allows practices of conservation agriculture as used in upland crops, such as mulching and minimum tillage.
Figure 1. A dry seeded aerobic rice field

©FAO/TECA 

Figure 2. Dibbling aerobic rice seeds

©FAO/TECA 

  • Aerobic rice can be rain-fed or irrigated.
  • Irrigation can be applied through flash-flooding, furrow irrigation (or raised beds), or sprinklers.
  • Unlike flooded rice, irrigation, when applied, is not used to flood the soil but to just bring the soil water content in the root zone up to field capacity.
  • Site-specific nutrient management (SSNM) can be used to determine the optimal management of fertilizers.
  • In the absence of knowledge on SSNM, 70 to 90 kg N per ha could be a useful starting point to obtain a yield of 4 to 6 tonnes per ha.
  • The first split can best be given 10 to 12 days after emergence, the second at active tillering, and the third at panicle initiation.
  • The application of Phosphorus fertilizer can be more critical for aerobic rice than for flooded rice.
  • Rice fields that are not permanently flooded tend to experience more weed growth and more species of weeds.
  • Appropriate herbicide use, plus additional manual or mechanical weeding in the early phases of crop growth, is therefore needed to control weeds.
  • Soil-borne pests and diseases such as nematodes, root aphids, and fungi are known to occur more in aerobic rice than in flooded rice, especially in the tropics.
  • It is recommended to grow aerobic rice in rotation with upland crops suitable in the area.
Figure 3. A ripening aerobic rice field

©FAO/TECA 

Figure 4. Aerobic rice growing side by side with soya bean

©FAO/TECA 

4. Validation of the practice 

  • Aerobic rice was validated with farmers in Kaifeng, in north-central China along the Yellow River, demonstrated yields of up to 5.5 tonne per ha with as little as 230 mm of irrigation and 340 mm of rainfall in localities where flooded rice required 1 300 mm of water for yields of 6.5 to 9.0 ton per ha.
  • With good management, aerobic rice yield can be 75 to 80 percent of flooded rice yield while using only half as much water or even less.
  • Aerobic rice is now being tested by farmers in northern China on an estimated 200 000 ha and actively researched in the Philippines, India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, and many other countries.
  • In the Philippines, aerobic rice has been tested and adopted by farmers in about 10 provinces.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Rice seedbed preparation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 6973.
  • Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7210.
  • Intensive rice cultivation: ID 7666.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2941.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency

The practice grows “aerobic rice” varieties through the efficient use of irrigation and maintenance of well-drained, non-puddled, and non-saturated soils.

Aerobic rice

Aerobic rice is a production system in which rice is grown under non-flooded, non-puddled, and non-saturated soil conditions. Because aerobic rice needs less water at the field level than conventional lowland rice, the system is targeted at relatively water-short irrigated or rain-fed lowland environments. Irrigation can be applied through flash-flooding, furrow irrigation (or raised beds), or sprinklers. Site-specific nutrient management can be used to determine the optimal management of fertilizers. This growing system experiences more weed growth and more species of weeds, therefore there is a need to control weeds. Soil-borne pests and diseases such as nematodes, root aphids, and fungi are known to occur more in aerobic rice than in flooded rice, especially in the tropics. It is recommended to grow aerobic rice in rotation with upland crops suitable in the area. This practice explains where and how to manage ”aerobic rice”.

2. Target area

  • “Favourable uplands."
    • Areas where the land is flat, where rainfall with or without supplemental irrigation is sufficient to frequently bring the soil water content close to field capacity, and where farmers have access to external inputs such as fertilizers.
  • Fields on upper slopes or terraces in undulating, rain-fed lowlands.
    • Quite often, soils in these areas are relatively coarse-textured and well-drained, so that ponding of water occurs only briefly or not at all during the growing season.
  • Water-short irrigated lowlands.
    • Areas where farmers do not have access to sufficient water any more to keep rice fields flooded for a substantial period of time.

3. Management

  • The usual establishment method is dry direct seeding.
  • Aerobic rice also allows practices of conservation agriculture as used in upland crops, such as mulching and minimum tillage.
Figure 1. A dry seeded aerobic rice field

©FAO/TECA 

Figure 2. Dibbling aerobic rice seeds

©FAO/TECA 

  • Aerobic rice can be rain-fed or irrigated.
  • Irrigation can be applied through flash-flooding, furrow irrigation (or raised beds), or sprinklers.
  • Unlike flooded rice, irrigation, when applied, is not used to flood the soil but to just bring the soil water content in the root zone up to field capacity.
  • Site-specific nutrient management (SSNM) can be used to determine the optimal management of fertilizers.
  • In the absence of knowledge on SSNM, 70 to 90 kg N per ha could be a useful starting point to obtain a yield of 4 to 6 tonnes per ha.
  • The first split can best be given 10 to 12 days after emergence, the second at active tillering, and the third at panicle initiation.
  • The application of Phosphorus fertilizer can be more critical for aerobic rice than for flooded rice.
  • Rice fields that are not permanently flooded tend to experience more weed growth and more species of weeds.
  • Appropriate herbicide use, plus additional manual or mechanical weeding in the early phases of crop growth, is therefore needed to control weeds.
  • Soil-borne pests and diseases such as nematodes, root aphids, and fungi are known to occur more in aerobic rice than in flooded rice, especially in the tropics.
  • It is recommended to grow aerobic rice in rotation with upland crops suitable in the area.
Figure 3. A ripening aerobic rice field

©FAO/TECA 

Figure 4. Aerobic rice growing side by side with soya bean

©FAO/TECA 

4. Validation of the practice 

  • Aerobic rice was validated with farmers in Kaifeng, in north-central China along the Yellow River, demonstrated yields of up to 5.5 tonne per ha with as little as 230 mm of irrigation and 340 mm of rainfall in localities where flooded rice required 1 300 mm of water for yields of 6.5 to 9.0 ton per ha.
  • With good management, aerobic rice yield can be 75 to 80 percent of flooded rice yield while using only half as much water or even less.
  • Aerobic rice is now being tested by farmers in northern China on an estimated 200 000 ha and actively researched in the Philippines, India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, and many other countries.
  • In the Philippines, aerobic rice has been tested and adopted by farmers in about 10 provinces.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Rice seedbed preparation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 6973.
  • Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7210.
  • Intensive rice cultivation: ID 7666.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2941.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency

The practice grows “aerobic rice” varieties through the efficient use of irrigation and maintenance of well-drained, non-puddled, and non-saturated soils.

records.title: Contract farming handbook
records.description:
Description

This guide defines ‘Contract Farming’ (CF) as forward agreements specifying the obligations of farmers and buyers as partners in business. Lawfully, farming contracts entail the sellers’ (farmers’) obligation to supply the volumes and qualities of produce as specified and the buyers’ (processors’/ traders’) obligation to off-take the goods and make payments as agreed. This type of contract already exists in Asia and Latin America since the 19th century. It subsequently spread throughout the United States and Europe in the 20th century and was also introduced to North and Sub-Sahara Africa. Such contracts may be concluded with individual farmers or farmer groups and in a formal or informal manner. The guide states that CF has different business models such as informal, intermediary, multipartite, centralized and nucleus estate models. Aside from the normal agreement, the buyer also provides additional services to assist the farmer to produce better outputs.

1. Contract farming categories

Incentives are classified into two categories:

  • monetary incentives; and
  • non-monetary incentives.

The success and the sustainability of a contract farming scheme is situation-specific,purposely designed based on:

  • market opportunities;
  • product features;
  • suppliers’ and buyers’ capacities;
  • existing business development services; and
  • overall local, national, regional and international framework conditions for agricultural and agri-food business development and private investments.

In short, there is a vast range of conditions for success and failure that need to be taken into consideration when analysing the situation at local level and planning CF arrangements. No aforementioned model is considered to be the overall best option ever for all circumstances. However, six key conditions for successful CF and related success factors have been identified:

  • trust and scope of negotiations;
  • economic viability and incentives;
  • CF arrangements and risks;
  • technology transfer and innovation;
  • investment climate and third party support; and
  • sound analysis, planning and monitoring.

Alongside the successes, there are factors that play in favour of the failure of CF. In order to develop a successful CF, the steps below should be followed:

  • plan initiation;
  • implementation and learning phase of the plan; and
  • sustain and growth within the plan.

It is necessary to follow the steps of the plan, carry out the necessary activities and keep an eye on the projected milestones in order to be able to achieve CF  objectives. The technology is used globally. For example, since 2004, 75 percent of poultry is under CF in Brazil and 36 percent of agricultural productions are under CF in the United States.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Warehouse receipt systems: lessons from Niger: ID 7745.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology helps raising farmers' awareness regarding their obligations and rights as farmers and buyers and partners in business.
records.owner_name: GIZ - Competitive African Cotton Initiative

_annotations.body:
Contract farming handbook

This guide was published by the 'Competitive African Cotton Initiative' (COMPACI) in collaboration with other partners as such as Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), AISP II. It is a powerful tool for linking farmers to buyers, in an increasingly concentrated agri-food sector, and buyers to supply sources in ever-more competitive agricultural markets. The purpose of this guide is to provide a practical and process-oriented approach for a sound planning and implementation of contract farming (CF) schemes. This guide has been developed as a hands-on and process-oriented approach to serve practitioners involved in starting up, managing or supporting the initiation and implementation of contract farming schemes. While giving orientation for a focused approach, the guide remains flexible leaving the selection of tools and sequencing of activities to the discretion of users according to the reality on the ground. The proposed approaches are applicable to any type of product and situation. This depends on whether users are capable of using it in a flexible way, as well as adapting the tools and recommendations to the specific local situation and the ever-faster changing production and market contexts in developing countries.

records.title: Cero labranza
records.description:
Descripción

La comuna de San Ignacio, ubicada en la Región del Biobío (Chile), presenta suelos con una agricultura intensiva producto de un constante laboreo, lo que ha generado procesos de erosión, especialmente durante los meses de invierno. Con el fin de mitigar los problemas de erosión, algunos de los productores de la zona han modificado el uso del laboreo convencional hacia un sistema de cero labranza.

La cero labranza consiste en el establecimiento de un cultivo sin preparar el suelo con arado y volteo, así las semillas se dejan en surcos que tengan el ancho y la profundidad suficiente removiendo el suelo lo mínimo necesario. En la comuna de San Ignacio, las praderas naturales o praderas de alfalfa que han completado su ciclo productivo son sembradas en forma directa con una mezcla de forrajeras usando una sembradora de cero labranza de origen brasileño, que cuenta con una cajón fertilizador que aplica una mezcla de fertilizante en la misma hilera de siembra para apoyar el establecimiento de la pradera que se siembra. No existe aplicación previa de herbicidas como en otros sistema de cero labranza.

Para la implementación de esta tecnología, se debe verificar la presencia de estratos de suelos compactados, espinas o raíces de árboles y retirarlas, ya que dificultan el paso de la sembradora. Además, como parte de las actividades para la preparación del suelo, y si se requiere, se debe adicionar cal con el fin de aumentar el pH. A continuación, se procede a sembrar las semillas de alfalfa y/o forrajeras con la ayuda de la sembradora para cero labranza. Dentro de las actividades recurrentes se encuentran: la fertilización química del suelo, y la adición de cal, además de la resiembra de semilla cada dos años, aproximadamente.

Figura 1. Sembradora de chorro o flujo continuo, de siembra directa de origen brasileño Marca KUHN Modelo SDE 2217/19, que posee un sistema de doble disco desencontrado, que permite cortar la vegetación como una tijera y generar un surco en el suelo donde queda depositada en forma superficial la semilla con el abono

©FAO/TECA

Figura 2. Trabajo del tractor junto con la sembradora sobre una pradera a entrada de invierno

©FAO/TECA

1. Descripción del ambiente donde la estrategia fue aplicada

Las siguientes características describen el ambiente natural y social donde se implementó la práctica de cero labranza. Las condiciones ambientales no son determinantes o excluyentes para el éxito de la práctica, pero deben tenerse en cuenta para implementar o modificar la técnica que sean más apropiada a las condiciones naturales de la zona donde la práctica se quiera replicar.

1.1 Ambiente natural

  • Promedio de precipitación anual: 1 000 a 1 500 mm.
  • Altitud: 100 a 500 m.s.n.m.
  • Pendiente: Casi plana.
  • Profundidad del suelo: 80 a 120 cm.
  • Clima: Templado/mediterráneo.
  • Textura del suelo: Franco arcilloso.
  • Fertilidad del suelo: Media.
  • Contenido de la materia orgánica del suelo: Muy alto.
  • Drenaje del suelo/infiltración: Bueno.

1.2 Ambiente social

  • Tipo del usuario tierra: Individual/gran escala.
  • Tenencia de la tierra: Individual con título.
  • Mecanización: Sí.

El costo total para el establecimiento de la práctica por hectárea es de 1 020 USD e incluye arriendo de maquinaria, semillas, fertilizante y la aplicación de cal.

2. Impactos y resultados

Los beneficios de esta práctica en la zona han sido los siguientes:

2.1 Impactos ecológicos

  • Mejora de la cobertura del suelo.
  • Aumento de la biomasa sobre el suelo.
  • Mejora el ciclo y recarga de nutrientes.
  • Mejora de la resiliencia del sistema agroecológico ante la erosión y desastres naturales.

2.2 Impactos socioeconómicos

  • Incremento de la cantidad y calidad del forraje.
  • Mejora la productividad de los animales.
  • Incremento de la resiliencia del modo de vida de los agricultores ante fenómenos adversos.

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, húmedo/seco.
  • Templado, seco.

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Zero or minimum tillage in rice-wheat system: ID 7715.
  • Mejora de la producción agrícola y optimización del uso del agua mediante la tecnificación del riego: ID 8032.

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Tecnología de ahorro de trabajo

Debido a la práctica de cero labranza que consiste en el establecimiento de un cultivo sin preparar el suelo, se ahorra una labranza intensiva.

5.2 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta práctica de cero labranza contribuye no solo a la mejora ecológica sino también socioeconómica, así como una mayor productividad, resiliencia, fortalecimiento de la compactación del suelo y aumento de la cobertura del suelo.
records.owner_name: The Regional Office of FAO for Latin America and the Caribbean (RLC)

_annotations.body:

En el mismo proceso de trabajo se pueden aplicar fertilizantes y otras enmiendas para mejorar el suelo. En este ejemplo, en la comuna de San Ignacio, la cero labranza se utilizó para establecer praderas. Esta práctica funciona, principalmente, como defensa de la erosión hídrica aumentando la cobertura del suelo, especialmente durante los meses de invierno. La cero labranza está considerada como un sistema económico pero con el riesgo de generar compactación del suelo. La disponibilidad de maquinaria puede ser una limitante para implementar esta práctica.

records.title: Mejora de la producción agrícola y optimización del uso del agua mediante la tecnificación del riego
records.description:
Descripción

El Proyecto de Modernización del Riego a Pequeña Escala, ejecutado por la FAO en convenio con el Gobierno Provincial del Carchi (Ecuador), propone el presente plan, cuyo objetivo es mejorar la producción agrícola y optimizar el uso del agua, con la tecnificación del riego en la comunidad de San Pablo de la Cangahua, para garantizar la producción de alimentos limpios y suficientes para las familias del sector.

Las medidas que se implementaron permitieron:

  • mejorar la captación y conducción del agua en un tramo de 16 km;
  • mejorar la infraestructura de almacenamiento de agua;
  • tecnificar el sistema de distribución del riego parcelario;
  • y mejorar la tecnología de cultivos.

Para lograr el objetivo se implementó un sistema de riego presurizado mediante la aplicación de riego por aspersión y riego por goteo, que permitió alcanzar una mayor eficiencia en el uso y aplicación del agua a los cultivos, asegurando su desarrollo y garantizando la producción, junto con otros beneficios antes mencionados.

Figura 1. Construcción de reservorio con capacidad de 800 m3

©FAO/TECA

1. Descripción del ambiente donde la estrategia fue aplicada

Las siguientes características describen el ambiente natural y social donde se implementó la práctica. Las condiciones ambientales no son determinantes o excluyentes para su éxito, pero deben tenerse en cuenta al implementarla o adaptarla a las condiciones naturales de la zona donde se quiera replicar.

1.1 Ambiente natural

  • Altitud: 500 a 1 000 m.s.na.m.
  • Pendiente: Poco inclinada.
  • Forma del terreno: Parte baja de la ladera.
  • Profundidad del suelo: 20 a 50 cm.
  • Clima: Subtropical.
  • Textura del suelo: Franco.
  • Fertilidad del suelo: Baja.
  • Drenaje del suelo/infiltración: Bajo.

1.2 Ambiente social

  • Tipo del usuario tierra: Familiar/pequeño escala.
  • Tenencia de la tierra: Individual con y sin título.
  • Mecanización: Sí.

El costo total estimado para el establecimiento del proyecto descrito es de 120 000 USD. Es un proyecto bastante grande e incluye costos por la preparación del terreno, implementación en la infraestructura de conducción principal, implementación en la infraestructura de riego por goteo e infraestructura de almacenamiento. El mantenimiento por año se estima en 1 100 USD aproximadamente.

2. Impactos y resultados

Los beneficios de esta práctica en la zona han sido los siguientes:

2.1 Impactos ecológicos

  • Aumentó la cantidad de agua disponible para cultivos.
  • Mejoró la recolección de agua.

2.2 Impactos socioeconómicos

  • Aumentó la diversificación de los productos agrícolas.
  • Se incrementó el área de producción (nuevas tierras útiles).
Figura 2. Evaluación de la producción de cebolla de bulbo bajo sistema de riego por goteo

©FAO/TECA

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Trópicos, cálido.

_annotations.body:
Mejora de la producción agrícola y optimización del uso del agua mediante la tecnificación del riego

Una forma de garantizar la producción de alimentos limpios y suficientes para las familias agrícolas es optimizar el uso del agua, en ese sentido, la modernización del riego es una opción atractiva. Para lograr un mejor uso del agua se debe optimizar su captación y conducción mejorando la infraestructura de almacenamiento y distribución. Estas medidas permiten hacer un uso más eficiente del recurso y reducir las pérdidas de suelo por erosión hídrica. Dado que esta medida tiene un fuerte componente técnico, se requiere una alta inversión y una adaptación a una nueva cultura del riego.

Descripción

El Proyecto de Modernización del Riego a Pequeña Escala, ejecutado por la FAO en convenio con el Gobierno Provincial del Carchi (Ecuador), propone el presente plan, cuyo objetivo es mejorar la producción agrícola y optimizar el uso del agua, con la tecnificación del riego en la comunidad de San Pablo de la Cangahua, para garantizar la producción de alimentos limpios y suficientes para las familias del sector.

Las medidas que se implementaron permitieron:

  • mejorar la captación y conducción del agua en un tramo de 16 km;
  • mejorar la infraestructura de almacenamiento de agua;
  • tecnificar el sistema de distribución del riego parcelario;
  • y mejorar la tecnología de cultivos.

Para lograr el objetivo se implementó un sistema de riego presurizado mediante la aplicación de riego por aspersión y riego por goteo, que permitió alcanzar una mayor eficiencia en el uso y aplicación del agua a los cultivos, asegurando su desarrollo y garantizando la producción, junto con otros beneficios antes mencionados.

Figura 1. Construcción de reservorio con capacidad de 800 m3

©FAO/TECA

1. Descripción del ambiente donde la estrategia fue aplicada

Las siguientes características describen el ambiente natural y social donde se implementó la práctica. Las condiciones ambientales no son determinantes o excluyentes para su éxito, pero deben tenerse en cuenta al implementarla o adaptarla a las condiciones naturales de la zona donde se quiera replicar.

1.1 Ambiente natural

  • Altitud: 500 a 1 000 m.s.na.m.
  • Pendiente: Poco inclinada.
  • Forma del terreno: Parte baja de la ladera.
  • Profundidad del suelo: 20 a 50 cm.
  • Clima: Subtropical.
  • Textura del suelo: Franco.
  • Fertilidad del suelo: Baja.
  • Drenaje del suelo/infiltración: Bajo.

1.2 Ambiente social

  • Tipo del usuario tierra: Familiar/pequeño escala.
  • Tenencia de la tierra: Individual con y sin título.
  • Mecanización: Sí.

El costo total estimado para el establecimiento del proyecto descrito es de 120 000 USD. Es un proyecto bastante grande e incluye costos por la preparación del terreno, implementación en la infraestructura de conducción principal, implementación en la infraestructura de riego por goteo e infraestructura de almacenamiento. El mantenimiento por año se estima en 1 100 USD aproximadamente.

2. Impactos y resultados

Los beneficios de esta práctica en la zona han sido los siguientes:

2.1 Impactos ecológicos

  • Aumentó la cantidad de agua disponible para cultivos.
  • Mejoró la recolección de agua.

2.2 Impactos socioeconómicos

  • Aumentó la diversificación de los productos agrícolas.
  • Se incrementó el área de producción (nuevas tierras útiles).

©FAO/TECA

records.title: Micro-tranque
records.description:
Descripción

1. Construcción de un micro-tranque

  • El primer paso es la construcción de un muro de tierra compactado para acumular agua de lluvias y aguas provenientes de derrames de un predio ubicado aguas arriba.
  • La topografía del terreno es perfectamente adecuada para la construcción de este tipo de obra.
  • En una etapa inicial, se levantó un muro de dimensiones medianas utilizando una retro excavadora pequeña.
  • Además, se construyó el canal de riego utilizando mano de obra, con la ayuda de palas, y buscando de forma cualitativa la pendiente necesaria para trasladar el agua desde el tranque hasta la zona de cultivo (Figura 2).
  • La siguiente etapa consistió en la ampliación de este tranque, levantando el muro de tierra a seis metros en la parte más profunda, utilizando maquinaria de mayor envergadura.
  • Se planea a futuro expandir el largo del muro para aumentar la capacidad de almacenamiento de aguas lluvias.
  • Se debe tener el cuidado de que el agua no rebalse los muros, debido a que la obra se destruiría, por lo que existe un rebalse que permite expulsar el agua en caso de ser necesario para que fluya a otro sector del predio, inundando zonas de poca importancia.
  • Cabe destacar que, para realizar lo anterior, puede ser necesaria la utilización de maquinaria menor que ayude a remover parte del rebalse en forma urgente para proteger los muros.
  • Por otra parte, en caso de que el nivel del tranque disminuya, es necesario utilizar motobombas para extraer el agua del fondo del tranque y así poder levantar el agua y trasladarla hacia los cultivos (Figura 3).
  • El costo total del establecimiento de este micro-tranque es de 4 200 USD aproximadamente, incluyendo un estudio topográfico, la obra gruesa y la construcción del canal de riego.

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Impactos socioeconómicos

  • Aumenta la diversificación de los productos agrícolas.
  • Incremento de área de producción (nuevas tierras).

4. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, frío.
  • Subtropical, frío.

5. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Construcción de lagunas, cisternas y pozos para el abastecimiento seguro de agua: ID 8349.
  • Prácticas de conservación del suelo y el agua para la reducción de la erosión del suelo y reforzar: ID 8689.

Esta práctica conduce a muchos resultados positivos, como una mayor productividad, sostenibilidad, y mejora de recolección y almacenamiento de agua.

La construcción del micro-tranque mitiga los impactos negativos de eventos meteorológicos, ya que ayuda a reducir pérdidas en la producción agrícola, entre otros.

records.title: Siembra de arroz por el sistema de trasplante: una alternativa de producción para el agricultor de subsistencia
records.description:
Descripción

1. Semillero

  • Se promueve el crecimiento de plantas en cama, semillero o almácigo, que pueden ser húmedas o secas, con dimensiones de 5 m a 10 m de largo por 5 m a 10 m de ancho.
  • Para un metro cuadrado de semillero se necesitan 40 g de semilla, lo cual permite trasplantar de 20 a 33 m².
  • Para trasplantar una hectárea de arroz, se necesita preparar de 300 a 500 m² de semillero.
  • Se debe utilizar semilla pregerminada para hacer el semillero.
  • El procedimiento para obtener semillas pregerminadas se detalla a continuación:
    • Se sumerge la semilla en agua por 24 horas (1 día) en bolsas o sacos que permitan la aireación.
    • La semilla se coloca en un lugar húmedo, y a la sombra por 24 a 36 horas (1 o 1,5 días).
    • De 48 a 60 horas (2 a 2,5 días) la semilla está lista para la siembra.

2. Trasplante a tina o melga

  • Con un nivel de hilo se puede nivelar la parcela.
  • Luego se introduce el agua en la parcela y se mezcla la materia orgánica con el suelo (batir) hasta convertirlo en fango.
  • El suelo debe estar bien desmenuzado y húmedo (fangueado).
  • El trasplante debe hacerse cuando la planta tenga de 15 a 20 días de sembrada, de 3 a 4 hojas o 15 cm de altura.
  • La planta debe ser enterrada en el fango o lodo a una profundidad de 3 cm a 5 cm.
    • Distancia entre hilera: 15-20-25 cm.
    • Distancia entre plantas: 15-20-25 cm.
  • La cantidad óptima de plantas por hectárea dependerá de:
    • La variedad utilizada.
    • La fertilidad del suelo.
    • La fertilización y la época del trasplante.

3. Fertilización o abonamiento

  • 90 a 180 kg/ha de (NPK) 12-24-12, 15-30-8 o 10-30-10 al finalizar el fangueo.
  • El nitrógeno se aplica a los 10 días después de trasplante (ddt).

4. Manejo de malezas

  • El mantenimiento de una lámina de cinco centímetros de agua es una de las medidas más efectivas para el control de las malezas.
  • La disminución de los espacios en siembras con variedades enanas aumenta la habilidad del arroz para competir con las malezas.

5. Lámina de agua

  • Se debe mantener una lámina de 5 cm de agua, lo cual permite controlar las malezas en forma efectiva.
  • Esta lámina se debe mantener por los 30 primeros ddt.
  • Se reduce hasta el inicio del macollamiento hasta los 50 días después del trasplante, luego se aumenta de 5 hasta 10 cm hasta la etapa de grano tizoso, y se reduce a 2 cm durante el abonamiento.

6. Cosecha

  • La cosecha se realiza a los 115-130 días.

7. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido. 

8. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Aerobic rice: ID 7941.
  • Intensice rice cultivation: ID 7666.
  • Improving rice quality: video from Africa Rice Center: ID 6976.
  • Alternative seedbed methods for t. aman rice under drought-prone conditions, northwestern Bangladesh: ID 6838.
  • Rice farming: saving water through Alternate Wetting Drying (AWD) method: ID 7939.
  • Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7210.

9. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

9.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta práctica ofrece una descripción alternativa de cómo sembrar arroz de manera más eficiente.

9.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta tecnología conduce a un incremento de los rendimientos, lo que también permite al agricultor aumentar sus ingresos a largo plazo.

records.title: Video on how to defeat the mealy bug
records.description:
Description

The following video explains how to breed Acerophagus papayae and how to carry out the biological control. This practice is more applicable for NGOs or farmer organizations than for individual small-holder farmers.

A laboratory with two rooms is needed to breed the beneficial wasps. The wasps need mealy bugs to reproduce. In a first step the mealy bugs have to be cultivated. Wasps can be provided by bio-laboratories or by plant protection specialists from the Ministry of Food and Agriculture in Ghana. For other west African countries, International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) can be approached: http://www.iita.org/.

Video: How to defeat the mealy bug

Figure 1. Papaya tree infested with the papaya mealy bug (Paracoccus marginatus)

©FAO/TECA

1. Cultivating mealy bugs

  • Potatoes can be used as a breeding ground for the mealy bug.
  • They are left for a week on a flat surface exposed to daylight, so that they sprout.
    • The room should be cooled down to a temperature of 20° C, which is the perfect condition for sprouting potatoes.
  • After one week, plant them in a small plastic bowl containing sterilized river sand.
    • The potatoes must be watered with a fungicide solution to protect them from unwanted diseases.
  • After another seven days the sprouts have grown enough to be a good breeding site for the mealy bugs.
    • Take the potatoes out of the bowl, wash them carefully and cut off the roots.
  • The cleaned potatoes have now to be brought in contact with the mealy bugs for infestation.
    • This is done by covering them with infested papaya leaves collected in the field.
  • After four to five days under the leaves, the potato sprouts are heavily infested.

2. Breeding Acerophagus papayae

  • Transfer the infested potato sprouts into a second room.
    • Here put them in a small rearing cage, which is used to breed Acerophagus papayae.
    • The room is kept at the temperature of 28° C, which is a good temperature for the wasp eggs to hatch.
    • The cage provides a perfect environment for the wasps.
    • Some wasps stored in a test tube are inserted into the cage.
  • They stay in the cage for about 10 to 12 days.
    • During that time, each of the wasps can lay up to 60 eggs in 60 different mealy bugs.
    • By inserting their eggs, the wasps kill the bugs.
    • The cage is covered with a dark cloth, because the wasps feel more comfortable in the shade.
  • To keep off ants and unwanted insects, the feet of the cage are placed in containers filled with water.
  • After 10 to 12 days, take the potatoes out of the cage, cut off the potato sprouts and put them in a container.
    • The mealy bugs on the sprouts are now dead and carry the eggs of the wasps.
  • Close the container with the cut off sprouts and wait for another three to five days.
    • This is about the time period the wasp eggs hatch (the exact timing depends on local conditions).
  • After three to five days, open the container and empty its content on a white paper.
    • This serves to better identify the small wasps.
    • You have to be fast and aspirate all of them in the test tube.
    • Usually about 100 wasps can be aspirated in one test tube.
    • These wasps can be released in the field to control mealy bugs or can be used to start another breeding cycle in the cage.
Figure 2. Rearing cage with infested potato sprouts for Acerophagus papayae

©FAO/TECA

3. Releasing the wasps

  • Farmers need to monitor the crops on a regular basis.
    • As soon as an increase of mealy bugs is detected, the release of the wasps should be initiated.
    • Early releases are essential in achieving effective control.
  • When the wasps are taken to the field, they must be released by walking a diagonal line through the affected field with a test tube open upright, but never shaking.
  • The best release time is early morning or late evening.
    • One test tube with 100 Acerophagus wasps is sufficient to treat 12 acres (or 5 hectares) of affected land.
  • After six weeks, the wasps can travel through a radius of 5 km from the point of release.
    • After the release, the spraying of pesticides should be avoided because it would kill the wasps.
  • After 12 weeks the wasps will have established themselves and beneficial effects should be noticeable.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Video on how to prune a mango tree: ID 8237.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource-use efficiency

This technology is environmentally friendly, as it reduces the use of toxic pesticides and is an organic way to manage pest control. 

5.2 Pro-poor technology

Through pest control, this technology improves crop yield quality and quantity, thereby providing additional sources of food and income

records.title: How to measure soil pH value
records.description:
Description

The following video describes why it is important to know if a soil is acid or alkaline and shows a cheap way to measure a soil’s pH value. The video is available in English language and in Ghanaian language Twi.

Many farmers spend a lot of money on fertilizers, but good soil conditions must be in place for plants to be able to take up nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in an optimal way. Most of the soils in West Africa are too acidic. Under these conditions, plants roots are not able to take up the nutrients optimally, even though a sufficient amount of nutrients is present in the soil. In these cases, buying and applying fertilizers won’t bring much benefit. Most crops grow well in soils with pH values between 5.5 and 6.5. However, most soils used for agriculture in southern Ghana typically have a pH value ranging from 4.5 to 5. They are usually too acidic and limit the nutrient uptake of plants.

Measuring a soil’s pH value allows to see if a soil is too acidic or alkaline. Knowing this, actions can be taken to increase or decrease a soil’s pH value. A pH indicator kit with a pH scale is needed to measure the pH value of a soil. Water, a container and a wooden stick to stir are also needed. Measuring a soils pH value is done through the following procedures.

Video: How to measure soil pH (english)

Video: How to measure soil pH (twi)

1. Taling soil samples

  • Identify several spots on the field from where you would like to take soil samples.
  • Use a spade to remove the first few centimetres of the soil.
  • Dig a hole to take a soil sample.
    • The depth of the hole depends on the type of crop you are going to plant.
    • For shallow crops like chili peppers, tomatoes or lettuce, the depth of the hole should be 0 to 15 cm.
    • For perennial crops like mangos or oranges, the depth of the soil should be 0 to 30 cm or more.
    • Collect the samples in a container.
  • Mix the different samples together and take your sample for the analysis.

2. Measuring the pH value

  • Take the soil sample and add water.
    • The ratio of earth and water should be one to two.
  • Stir the mixture for 30 minutes.
  • Allow the soil mixture to settle for two hours.
  • Pick one stick from the pH indicator kit and dip the tip in the mixture for a few seconds.
  • Compare the colour on your stick with the pH scale.
    • The colour will indicate the pH value of the soil (Figure 1).
Figure 1. pH measurement with indicator paper

©FAO/TECA

3. Improving a soils pH value

  • If a soil is too acidic it can be improved by adding compost, lime or wooden ashes.
  • About ten bags of lime per acre are needed to increase the pH value by one unit.
  • This means, for example, about 5 kg of lime are needed per mango tree.
  • The lime can be applied on a 1 m wide band around the tree (Figure 2).
  • If a soil is too alkaline, compost or sulphur can be added to lower the pH value.
Figure 2. Increasing the soils pH value by applying lime

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Soil nutrient management: ID 7014.
  • Soil and water conservation: ID 7861.
  • Soil cultivation and tillage in organic agriculture: ID 8376.
  • Composting to improve soil fertility: ID 8206.
  • Green manuring in sugarcane production for soil improvement and water efficiency: ID 8768.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for soil quality improving, leading to increases in crop yield. This results in additional sources of food and income.

records.title: Sago plantations on undrained peatland
records.description:
Description

1. Establishing a sago plantation

  • Clear the land and prepare planting holes.
    • It may be necessary to block canals in the peatland.
  • Sago seedlings are inserted in the planting holes.
    • Once sago seedlings are transplanted, they start to grow and produce clusters vegetatively.
    • The clusters are then ready for consecutive, unlimited production cycles.
    • Ten years are needed from planting to continuous harvesting when sago is grown on tidally influenced peatland.
    • Most of the cost for this operation relates to labour and the transport of seedlings.
  • The plantation should be weeded regularly.
  • Dead leaves have to be pruned.
    • If there are too many young sago in a single cluster, some should be removed.
  • Sago grows well on deep peat, even under minimal drainage and maintenance, however, when grown on tidally-influenced deep peat, sago produces less starch and takes longer to mature (more than 12 to 17 years) compared to cultivation on shallow peat, where mature trunks are produced 8 to 12 years after planting.
  • The poor growth of sago palms on deep peat is likely caused by the lack of nutrients in the peat strata rather than a low pH-value.
  • Drainage of peatland for log transport should be avoided.
    • More research is needed to improve sago cultivation. 
Figure 1. Sago plantation on largely undrained deep peatland in Indonesia (Karyanto 2014)

©FAO/TECA

2. Products derived from sago plantations

  • The main product is sago flour.
    • Sago is starch obtained from the trunk by washing the starch kernels out of the pulverized pith with water.
  • About 150 kg to 250 kg of dry sago flour can be produced from one palm tree.
    • The sago flour is used for many food items and chemical products.
    • It is mainly used for sago noodle production, but it can be also used for bioethanol production and other produce (e.g. film, solvents).

3. Environmental advantages

  • After establishing sago plantations on slightly drained peatlands, there is no significant increase in CO₂ emissions compared to secondary forest cover.
    • However, young sago palms require an open canopy, which increases peat temperatures and could increase CO₂ emissions in the first few years.
    • Sago plantations produce much less biomass than secondary peat swamp forest.
    • Cultivating sago increases the resilience and capacity of a community to adapt to climate change.
    • Also, water quality is increased.

4. Validation of the practice

  • Plantations with sago have successfully been established on peatlands in Riau Province, Indonesia.
    • The peatlands of the plantations had a peat depth of over 300 cm, a water table depth between 0 and 0.5 m and no artificial channels.
    • The peatland was a fen receiving water both from groundwater and rainfall.
    • The pH of the water was acidic.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Beje aquaculture and inland fishery in tropical peatland: ID 8619.
  • Illipe nut plantation on undrained peatland: ID 8284.
  • Rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation: ID 3884.
  • Peatland restoration: ID 8278.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency

Small-scale sago cultivation without drainage results in a high sago self-propagation rate, short harvesting cycles and high starch content.

7.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology is low maintenance, which makes it among the most productive plantation systems that can be operated at almost no maintenance cost.

records.title: Peatland restoration
records.description:
Description

1. Establishment of activities

1.1 Blocking drainage canals and gullies

  • For this activity tractors, peat or sand, wooden planks, boulders and bags were needed.
    • In this project, it took five to seven days to accomplish the activity.
    • The cost was USD 116 per dam. 

1.2 Revegetation

  • The grass was reseeded on the bare peat soil.
  • Grass seeds, bags and a truck were needed (the degraded land was levelled for seed growth by a truck).
    • The cost was between USD 50 to USD 80 per ha.
    • To complete the revegetation, one to three days were needed.

1.3 Damming

  • Additionally, during the project, only one peat extraction site was restored by damming.
    • Materials used were concrete, sand, grass seeds and a tractor for levelling the ground.
    • The duration of this specific peat restoration took one week.
    • The cost was USD 5 300 per dam.
    • A 2 m deep pit in the peat extraction site was levelled by a machine for reseeding.
    • Some dams were fenced to prevent trampling by yaks.
    • Polyvinylchloride (PVC) pipes were installed between the peat dams to avoid further erosion.
    • All channels were blocked.
Figure 1. Peatland restoration: blocking canals by (a) wood plank; (b) peat; (c) concrete damming; (d) revegetation (Xiaohong, et al. 2014)

©FAO/TECA

2. Environmental advantages and climate change mitigation potential

  • The limited data presented suggests that rewetted peatlands have enhanced carbon sequestration and may have reduced emissions of N₂O.
  • The restored sites also recreated suitable habitats for endemic amphibians and birds.
  • The water stored in previously dry canals provided water for livestock, which was highly appreciated by local communities.
    • It is urgent to take further action to prevent the continued degradation of these natural peatlands.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Beje aquaculture and inland fishery in tropical peatland: ID 8619.
  • Illipe nut plantation on undrained peatland: ID 8284. 
  • Sago plantations on undrained peatland: ID 8281.
  • Rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation: ID 3884.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology restores rewetted peatlands which enhances carbon sequestration and reduces greenhouse gases. The restored sites also recreated suitable habitats for endemic amphibians and birds. Additionally, the water stored in previously dry canals provided water for livestock.

Peatland restoration

Situated at the headwaters of the Yellow River, the sedge-dominated peatlands in the Ruoergai plateau in China store water and supply it to downstream areas. These peatlands are important grazing lands for local pastoralists and play an important role in Tibetan culture. Other uses from the peatland are fuel, medical plants and honey. From 1960 to 1970s the Ruoergai peatlands, which had been drained for agriculture, began to be badly damaged by overgrazing. Assessments and field observations indicate that over 70 percent of the peatlands were severely degraded. As a result, a large amount of CO2 stored in the peat has been released to the atmosphere and biodiversity has been lost. All of these environmental consequences have had an impact on local livelihoods. With support from the Chinese government, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the European Union (EU), the following activities were tested and demonstrated on 4 733 ha of peatland. These activities can be replicated to restore other peatlands with similar conditions.

Description

1. Establishment of activities

1.1 Blocking drainage canals and gullies

  • For this activity tractors, peat or sand, wooden planks, boulders and bags were needed.
    • In this project, it took five to seven days to accomplish the activity.
    • The cost was USD 116 per dam. 

1.2 Revegetation

  • The grass was reseeded on the bare peat soil.
  • Grass seeds, bags and a truck were needed (the degraded land was levelled for seed growth by a truck).
    • The cost was between USD 50 to USD 80 per ha.
    • To complete the revegetation, one to three days were needed.

1.3 Damming

  • Additionally, during the project, only one peat extraction site was restored by damming.
    • Materials used were concrete, sand, grass seeds and a tractor for levelling the ground.
    • The duration of this specific peat restoration took one week.
    • The cost was USD 5 300 per dam.

TITLE: Integrated Peatland Restoration Technique for Ruoergai Plateau

DESCRIPTION: Comprehensive restoration approach combining canal blocking, revegetation, and damming techniques specifically adapted for high-altitude peatlands, incorporating local pastoral needs and indigenous knowledge.

INNOVATION TYPE: Modified solution in new context, meeting criteria of solving environmental problem while supporting local livelihoods and traditional practices. Combines technical interventions with socio-cultural considerations in unique high-altitude setting.
_annotations.field_shorter_description:
Situated at the headwaters of the Yellow River, the sedge-dominated peatlands in the Ruoergai plateau in China store water and supply it to downstream areas. These peatlands are important grazing lands for local pastoralists and play an important role in Tibetan culture. Other uses from the peatland are fuel, medical plants and honey. From 1960 to 1970s the Ruoergai peatlands, which had been drained for agriculture, began to be badly damaged by overgrazing. 

Assessments and field observations indicate that over 70 percent of the peatlands were severely degraded. As a result, a large amount of CO2 stored in the peat has been released to the atmosphere and biodiversity has been lost. All of these environmental consequences have had an impact on local livelihoods. With support from the Chinese government, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the European Union (EU), the following activities were tested and demonstrated on 4 733 ha of peatland. These activities can be replicated to restore other peatlands with similar conditions.

records.title: Illipe nut plantation on undrained peatland
records.description:
Description

The Illipe species or Shorea spp. (Indonesian name: tengkawang) are Southeast Asian forest trees and are used for nuts and timber. Illipe nuts are an important non-timber forest product with a high commercial value. The fat derived from the nuts is used as a cocoa butter equivalent, in cosmetics and for other products.

The main foreign markets are in Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. The tree also produces quality timber for plywood face-veneer. Plantations with Illipe species have successfully been established on peatlands in West Kalimantan, Indonesia. The area where this practice was applied is located along the Segedong River on a coastal, shallow to moderately deep peatland. The peat depth at the plantation was between 30 cm and 300 cm. The water table depth fluctuated from 0 m to 0.5 m.

1. Establishing an Illipe plantation

Shorea pinanga, S. macrocarpa, S. stenoptera and S. macrophylla are trees species that can be used. A high level of technical knowledge is needed to establish and maintain a plantation with illipe species.

1.1 Key steps

  • Establish a semi-shaded nursery from fruits, wildlings or vegetative propagation. The tree seedlings grow here for three years.
  • The Illipe trees are planted using line planting. The spacing is 3 m by 10 m with a north-south direction and the lane width (line) is 3 m.
  • Open 3 m to 5 m gaps in the forest and prepare planting holes with compost.
  • Weeding has to be done up to three years after planting.

With line planting the annual diameter increment (a parameter for tree growth) is about 1.5 cm. After seven years from the establishment, the plantation starts to fruit. The fruiting usually occurs every three to four years after a period of several rainless weeks. The total establishment cost for three years of maintenance is about USD 1 000 per ha. The costs of establishing a tree nursery are low.

2. Environmental advantages: climate change mitigation potential

  • Illipe species tolerate frequent inundations and do not require drainage, thus lead to conservation of carbon stored in peat soils.
  • The tree species produce additional biomass.
  • Their rapid growth closes the forest canopy and reduces the high temperatures on previously sunlight-exposed peatland. This helps to increase carbon sequestration.
  • The plantation helps to avoid soil losses due to erosion and provides additional income to farmers. These effects improve their resilience against natural hazards and diminish their risk exposure.

3. Validation of the practice

This practice represents the results from a joint programme of GadjahMada University and Inhutani II.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Peatland restoration: ID 8278.
  • Sago plantations on undrained peatland: ID 8281.
  • Beje aquaculture and inland fishery in tropical peatland of Indonesia: ID 8619.
  • Rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation: ID 3884.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology is extreme climate resistant, produces additional biomass, improves soil quality and reduces carbon dioxide emissions.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology provides an additional food source and income. Climate Change Adaptation and Disaster Risk Reduction.

records.title: Banquillo individual para colmenas
records.description:
Descripción

  • El banquillo puede ser construido de madera o bien de metal.
  • Cuando sea construido a base de madera se podrá utilizar fajas de gaucho, trozos de neumáticos o bisagra de metal para articular las bases de este banquillo.
  • Por otro lado, cuando se elabora a base de metal, se recomienda utilizar una base cuadrada en las patas para evitar el hundimiento, deformación o desajuste de las uniones del soporte, producto del peso que va adquiriendo el cajón en la medida que va creciendo la familia.
  • Se recomienda usar tornillos de 4 mm x 25 mm y 4 mm x 35 mm.
  • El banquillo requiere para su construcción cuatro pilares, dos travesaños o listones de madera, dos bisagras o soportes de gaucho o similar, además de dos correas o guinchas de gaucho que puede ser removible.
Figura 1. Fotos de un banquillo sin o con una colmena

©FAO/TECA

  • El banquillo está construido en base a cuatro pilares orientados de forma inclinada para distribuir en peso en forma equitativa y equilibrada sobre toda la base del banquillo.
  • Las medidas del banquillo pueden ser variables dependiendo del tipo de colmena que posea el apicultor, para este caso el banquillo está desarrollado para montar sobre cajones de tipo Langstroth.
  • La medida interna y externa entre las bases es de 42,7 y 52,7 cm respectivamente, (ancho externo del cajón y del piso es de 42 cm).
  • La colmena tipo Dadant también puede montarse sobre este banquillo pues tiene un ancho menor al de la colmena tipo Langstroth, para cualquier fin las medidas del banquillo pueden adaptarse a las dimensiones del cajón que se utilice.
Cuadro 1. Medidas para la construcción de un banquillo para colmenas

©FAO/TECA

  • El ángulo de corte de los listones es 38° en la parte superior y en la parte inferior es 52° para entregar una buena base de soporte.
Figura 2. Medidas del banquillo de una vista lateral

©FAO/TECA

  • El travesaño es el que soporta directamente el cajón y el que determina la distancia desde el suelo a la colmena.
  • Para situar el cajón por sobre los 30 cm, el travesaño de 6 cm de grosor debe ir situado a 27,5 cm de la base del banquillo.
  • Los travesaños deben tener un corte de un diámetro de 2 centímetros a su largo con una inclinación de 52° para permitir un mejor asentamiento del cajón en el banquillo.
Figura 3. Foto del banquillo sin y con una colmena

©FAO/TECA

2. Recomendaciones

  • Siempre es recomendable para retrasar el deterioro del material poder pintar el banquillo o barnizarlo con algún componente protector.
  • Las recomendaciones son pintarlos con un par de días de anticipación, secados y aireados, no se debe usar pinturas con plomo dentro de sus componentes.
  • Otra buena alternativa es proteger las estructuras con barniz de propóleos que se puede obtener de las mismas colmenas.
  • El barniz de propóleos se elabora con una parte de propóleos, una parte de aceite de linaza y 8 partes de alcohol etílico, esto se deja macerar por treinta días y se puede utilizar para pintar alzas, pisos, entretechos e incluso muebles, pues genera una gran impermeabilidad y resistencia a microorganismos dañinos.

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Buenas prácticas apícolas: ID 8217.
  • Alimentador externo e interno para colmenas: ID 8325.
  • Las buenas prácticas en apicultura: ID 8675.

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta práctica ofrece una breve descripción de cómo hacer banquillos de colmenas de manera eficiente para evitar la entrada de agua y humedad.

5.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

El banquillo individual para colmenas conduce a una reducción de plagas que se encuentran en el suelo, lo que entre otras cosas permite un manejo más cómodo para el apicultor.

records.title: Guantes de protección para apicultor
records.description:
Descripción

  • Los guantes de apicultores tienen adheridos en sus extremos una sobremanga de tela algodonada, lona suave, lino o mezclilla o de tipo Drill (tela con alto porcentaje de algodón, muy utilizada para ropa de trabajo) de colores claros, la cual debe de ser de confección holgada para que no se pegue a la piel con la traspiración y así no permite a la abeja picar (Figura 1).
  • Los guantes deben de prolongarse sobre el antebrazo unos 15 a 20 cm y terminar su borde con un elástico para impedir el ingreso de las abejas.
  • Hay diferentes tallas las cuales van desde pequeña, mediana y grande, lo importante es que el elástico de la sobremanga quede sobre el codo para que esta no se baje y se salga el guante.
  • En el mercado podemos encontrar desde la talla número 8 a la 10.
  • Para saber la talla del guante se mide la zona de los nudillos de la mano, desde el dedo meñique hasta el índice y dependiendo de lo que mida tienes una talla u otra.
  • Por ejemplo si mide 8 cm de un nudillo a otro se necesitaría la talla 8.
Figura 1. Guantes de protección para apicultores

©FAO/TECA

1. Materia prima

  • Para la elaboración de los guantes se recomienda usar pieles de contextura lisa y suave de colores claros de tipo Badana flor (cuero de color natural) o Napa (blancos, amarillos, cremas).
  • Se debe de evitar el uso de pieles de gamuza ya que este producto propicia el ataque de las abejas que pierden el aguijón y mueren, aún sin pasar este a picar al apicultor.
  • Tampoco se recomienda el uso de cuerina debido a que es un material de poca durabilidad.
  • El guante es complementado con telas algodonadas, lona suave, lino o mezclilla o de tipo Drill de colores claros (blanco, kaki, amarillo, etc.) material utilizado para la elaboración de la sobremanga el cual en su parte terminal debe de llevar elástico (Figuras 2 y 3).
Figura 2. Partes y medidas del guante

©FAO/TECA

Figura 3. Partes y medidas del antebrazo y manga de tela

©FAO/TECA

Figura 4. Armado y ensamble del guante (cara dorsal y palmar)

©FAO/TECA

2. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Las buenas prácticas en apicultura: ID 8675.
  • Confección de blusa con velo integrado para apicultores: ID 8327.
  • Confección de overol con velo integrado para apicultores: ID 8287.

Esta tecnología también está disponible en inglés: ID 10117 y en francés: ID 10047.

3. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

3.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología ayuda al apicultor a protegerse eficientemente de posibles picaduras de abejas.

3.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta práctica permite al apicultor trabajar mejor al tener protección contra las picaduras de abejas y así un mejor manejo de las colmenas.

records.title: Manejo e identificación de plagas en el almacenamiento del cultivo de frijol
records.description:
Descripción

1. Brúquidos del frijol

1.1 Distribución

  • Los brúquidos del frijol son ampliamente distribuidos en África.
  • Dos especies: Zabrotes subfasciatus (Gorgojo mexicano del frijol) y Acanthoscelides obtectus (Gorgojo común del frijol) son las más conocidas.
  • Esta última es la más común en zonas altas o ambientes fríos, mientras que el gorgojo mexicano del frijol prevalece en ambientes cálidos.
  • En el este de África el gorgojo común del frijol es encontrado más frecuentemente.
  • La larva de ambos gorgojos puede permanecer sin ser vista en la semilla hasta que el adulto emerja.
  • Se pueden esparcir por el movimiento de las semillas.

1.2 Ciclo de vida

  • El ciclo de vida de las dos especies es muy similar pero si hay diferencias importantes muy marcadas.
  • La larva de ambas especies taladran dentro de las semillas de frijol para alimentarse y desarrollarse, dejándolas perforadas con agujeros    (Figuras 1 y 2).
  • Esto hace que las semillas pierdan su viabilidad y no sean útiles para plantar o el consumo humano.
Figura 1. Daño de semillas causado por Acanthoscelides obtectus

©FAO/TECA

Figura 2. Daño de semillas causado por Zabrotes subfasciatus

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Condiciones que predisponen la cosecha a ser atacada

  • Almacenamiento bajo condiciones pobres y antihigiénicas y que las bodegas estén infestada con brúquidos (Figuras 4 y 5).
  • Frijoles secados pobremente.
Figura 3. La infestación del gorgojo común del frijol comienza en el campo y se multiplica en el almacenamiento. Huevos traslúcidos son depositados en las vainas en campo o entre las semillas en bodegas

©FAO/TECA

Figura 4. La infestación del gorgojo mexicano del frijol normalmente empieza y se multiplica en el almacenamiento. Huevos blancos se encuentran pegados a las semillas y sus cubiertas permanecen después de eclosionar

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Estrategias de manejo

  • Cosechas tempranas antes que divisiones aparezcan en las vainas para evitar la infestación por gorgojo común del frijol.
  • Secado profundo de las semillas antes de ser almacenadas.
  • Agitar las semillas en un saco o rodarlas en un barril, aplasta los huevos y detiene que larvas nuevas penetren en las semillas (Figura 5).
  • Usar variedades resistentes de gorgojo mexicano del frijol puede reducir la infestación de esta especie.
  • Hervir los sacos de almacenamiento en agua caliente y secarlos al sol antes de ser usados.
  • Inspeccionar las semillas almacenadas por signos de infestación y tomar acciones para detener su desarrollo.
Figura 5. Cubrir las semillas con aceites vegetales o aceite de semillas de nim a una proporción de 5 ml/kg de semilla. Esto es más adecuado para semillas con propósito de ser plantadas

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Solarización

  • Esparcir semillas en el sol debajo de cubiertas plásticas, permite que la temperatura alta creada mate las plagas que están dentro.
  • ¡Ojo! Este método no es apropiado para las semillas que se pretendan plantar.
Figura 6. Buena higiene de almacenamiento: limpiar la bodega profundamente y quemar toda la basura. Rociar la bodega con insecticida para desinfectar antes del almacenamiento de nuevas semillas. No mezclar la cosecha anterior con la nueva

©FAO/TECA

2. Validación de la práctica

  • La identificación y manejo de estas plagas se llevó a cabo en Uganda.

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Elaboración de pesticidas eco-amigables para el control de plagas y enfermedades: ID 8381.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas en plántulas en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8382.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas en flores en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8383.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas alimentadoras de vainas y semillas en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8385.
  • Manejo e identificación de enfermedades que causan malformaciones y distorsiones de hojas y vainas en el frijol: ID 8387.
  • Manejo e identificación de enfermedades que afectan las raíces en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8389.
  • Manejo e identificación de enfermedades que afectan hojas y vainas en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8392.

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología muestra al productor diversas medidas para reducir eficientemente las plagas.

5.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Este manejo e identificación de plagas en el almacenamiento del cultivo de frijol ayuda a reducir las pérdidas de frijol y así estabilizar la fuente de ingresos.

records.title: Manejo e identificación de plagas en flores en el cultivo de frijol
records.description:
Descripción

1. Escarabajos de flores y polen

  • Diferentes especies de Mylabris y Coryna.
  • Nombres comunes: Escarabajo ampolla, escarabajo “CMR”, escarabajo de polen, escarabajo de flor.

1.1 Biología y naturaleza del daño

  • Los escarabajos de flores y polen que atacan al frijol son largos (1,5 a 3 cm de longitud) y frecuentemente son de colores brillantes con puntos rojos y amarillos sobre las alas negras (Figuras 1 y 2).
  • Se alimentan de pétalos y polen de flores, y una gran infestación puede reducir el llenado de las vainas y la productividad drásticamente.
  • Los huevos son depositados en el suelo y en los primeros instares las larvas se alimentan de huevos de saltamontes; altas poblaciones de esta plaga pueden ser seguidas por altas poblaciones de saltamontes.
  • Los adultos pueden exudar un fluido amarillento que puede irritar o causar llagas en la piel.
Figura 1. Mylabris sp.

©FAO/TECA

Figura 2. Coryna sp.

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Estrategias de manejo

  • Los insecticidas no son conocidos por ser efectivos en el ataque del escarabajo de polen adulto y las formas inmaduras más susceptibles no aparecen en los cultivos.
  • En granjas pequeñas la recogida a mano con un par de tenazas puede ser más práctica.

2. Validación de la práctica

  • La identificación y manejo de estas plagas se llevó a cabo en Uganda.

  • Tropical, cálido.

records.title: Beje aquaculture and inland fishery in tropical peatland of Indonesia
records.description:
Description

The traps allow fish to breed in the pond. Once caught, the fish will stay in the beje throughout the year. The fish are later harvested, without any selection considering the sex or size of the fish, during the dry season when the water recedes from April to October. A schematic representation of the beje practice in peatlands is illustrated in Figure 2. Usually, the peat is laid down between two rivers, and thanks to the soil properties, it forms a kind of water tower or peat dome (Figure 3), with fully diverse vegetation on the top of it. That is why in Figure 2, the peatland is higher than the level of the river. In the rainy season, it collects water and in the dry season, water is slowly released (compare to Figure 3).

Figure 1. Fishing in a peat swamp forest

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Representation of beje system in peatlands of Indonesia, cross-section view. (1) Fluctuation and overflow of the river during the rainy season (Nov-Mar). (2) Fish migrate themselves, by following the flow, from the river bank to the beje (in the back swamp). (3) During the dry season (Apr-Oct), the caught fish stay in the beje where they reproduce and are later harvested 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. 3D representation of the peat dome located between Kahayan and Kapuas rivers, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia  

©Bambang Setiadi, 2015 

Figure 4. Illustrated description of a beje aquaculture system  

©Limin & Bambang Setiadi, 2014

1. Costs of the establishment of a beje

  • Trapping fish using the beje method requires no additional feed and makes use of natural processes.
  • The investment cost of developing the beje fishing method for a size of 812 m², is USD 7 800 / IDR 78 000 000.
    • One US Dollars is equivalent to roughly 10 000 Indonesian Rupiah.
    • One beje can be used for a period of more than 10 years.
    • Table 1 shows the costs of the establishment of a beje.
Table 1. Costs of the establishment of a beje
Elements Associated costs
1. Clearing of the site 
2. Excavation of the pond 
3. Installation of the fence 
4. Wood and wire  
5. Planting plants for fence 
6. Survey beje location 		 Total approx.: 
USD 3 300 / IDR 33 000 000  
Beje construction materials Associated costs
- Wood for fence  
- Special equipment (tools...) 
- Seedling  
- Stationeries 
- Pump machine 
- Wire netting 		 Total approx.: 
 USD 2 000 / IDR 20 000 000
Transportation and maintenance (car and motorboat rental) Total approx.: 
 USD 2 500 / IDR 25 000 000  

Source: FAO 2016

2. Fish production

  • An overview of the composition of fish species caught in a beje, ranges between 5 to 12 types and is dominated by marsh fish (blackfish) from the family Anabantidae and Nandidae.
    • Other types of fish caught in beje are:
      • Sepat siam (Trichogaster pectoralis)
      • Sepat rawa (Trichogaster trichopterus)
      • Gabus (Channa striata)
      • Betok (Anabas testudineus)
      • Tambakan (Helostoma temminckii)
      • Baung (Mystus nemurus)
      • Singgaringan (Mystus nigriceps)
      • Lundu (Mystus Gulio)
      • Lais lampok (Cryptopterus limpok)
      • Lele (Clarias spp.)
      • Singgaringan (Mystus nigriceps)
      • Lundu (Mystus Gulio)
      • Kakapar (Peristolepis fasciatus).
    • Also, because it is highly adaptable and can live in waters with low levels of dissolved oxygen and low pH levels, patin or pangas catfish (Pangasius pangasius) is a fish species that has been selected to reinvigorate the aquaculture sector in Indonesia’s peatlands.
    • This species is known to have a high content of omega-three fatty acids, which are important for nutrition.
  • To cultivate the catfish, ponds are dug 2.5 m deep into the peat until the clay layer is reached.
    • The bottom of the pool is treated with lime to reduce the acidity and avoid fish diseases.
    • Manure, urea and N-P-K (containing nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium) fertilizers are then added to promote plankton growth.
    • For the past two years, the cultivation of tilapia fish (Sarotherodon galilaeus galilaeus), which has also shown commercial promises and success, has been developed in various peatland areas in Indonesia. 
  • Based on data observed in 70 beje locations, the results showed that annual fish production in beje fisheries declined sharply from 500 kg to 2 000 kg per beje before the swampland reclamation in 1996 to 5 kg to 150 kg per beje.
    • The tremendous decline in production (94.6 percent) was mainly due to changes in water fluctuations caused by the construction of irrigation canals and damage to fish habitat.
Figure 5. Patin or pangas catfish (Pangasius pangasius)  

©Ikan Patin (Istimewa) 

3. Patin or pangas catfish (Pangasius pangasius)

  • The beje fishing method contributes to the livelihood and income of communities around peatland areas in Indonesia.
    • Based on identifications by the Ministry of Marine and Fishery of Indonesia, there are 300 potential areas to develop beje in Kalimantan.
    • The beje system also indirectly plays a role in reducing carbon emissions by functioning as a buffer and inhibiting the spread of fires in peatlands, keeping peat wet, thus preventing fires in peat.
    • The beje system also accelerates the development of natural vegetation.

4. Validation of the practice

  • This practice has been tested during two years in the natural tropical peat swamp forest of the East Kalimantan – Indonesia and Rupawan (2004) conducted research in 40 beje sites, randomly chosen from 176 beje located in South Kalimantan.
