Rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation

Bamboo and rattan are ideal resources for development that integrate poverty reduction and environmental sustainability. The International Network for Bamboo and Rattan’s (INBAR) priority is to give people, at all levels, the knowledge and skills they need for long-term development involving bamboo and rattan. Rattan is a natural material and degrades over time. Curing, bleaching and preserving rattan adds value to the raw material, preserves its unique qualities and improves its durability. This technology describes the methods used in several Asian countries to preserve rattan.

Description

1. Rattan oil-curing, bleaching and preservation unit at a glance

1.1 Why cure, bleach and preserve rattan?

  • Rattan is a natural material that degrades over time.
  • It is susceptible to fungal and insect attack, whichthis can seriously affect the quality, usability and price of the canes.
  • Curing, bleaching and preserving the rattan adds value to the raw material, preserves itsunique qualities, and improves its durability.

1.2 How to cure, bleach and preserve rattan?

There is a general process to follow:

  • Grading raw rattan
  • selecting rattan of a specific size
  • boiling in diesel for 10 to 20 minutes
  • cleaning with pressurised water or sawdust
  • air-drying
  • bleaching
  • air drying a second time
  • grading.

1.3 Why is the market for rattan treated in this way?

  • Almost every rattan processing factory requires a supply of preserved rattan and the market is huge.

1.4 What is the role of an oil curing, bleaching and preservation unit in rural development?

  • Establishing a rattan preservation unit creates employment opportunities, adds value to the natural resources, and contributes to the generation of incomes in poor, rural regions.
  • This processing activity benefits harvesters, middlemen, transporters and labourers in processing industries.
  • It raises the standards of living in poor regions in which it is established and contributes to the empowerment of the people living in these regions.

1.5 How to establish an oil curing, bleaching and preservation unit

  • The primary requirements are:
    • a source of start-up funds,
    • a consistent supply of raw materials, and
    • a secured, skilled workforce.
  • Initial costs of fixed assets are expected to be about USD 40 000.
  • The unit should generate net pre-tax profits of over USD 3 500 per month.

2. Development attributes, target groups and benefits of a rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation unit

2.1 Introduction

  • This document presents rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation as a suitable Transfer of Technology Model (TOTEM) for rural development projects in poor regions, where rattan is available as a resource and potentially used in various applications.
    • The document is meant to serve as a guide for local extension workers involved with community-based rattan processing.
    • The document is alsofor those interested in developing a small enterprise for the processing of rattan.
  • The information in this document is based on a detailed inventory of the application of rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation in 38 rattan processing mills in the states of Pahang, Negeri Sembilan, Melaka and Johore.
    • These states are located in the southern parts of Peninsular Malaysia, the focal point of rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation activity in the country.
  • The first part of the report introduces the technology as it is used in Malaysia and discusses the scope for its implementation, its development attributes and its limitations.
  • The second part elaborates in detail on the process of rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation, and as such can be used as a manual for implementation of the technology.
  • For additional illustrative material, the reader can referr to the accompanying demonstration film, the PowerPoint presentation and the poster.

2.2 History of the development of technology in Malaysia

  • The term “primary rattan processing” commonly refers to any activity involving the cooking, drying and processing of rattan into semi-processed products such as peels, cores and skins, either manually or by machines.
    • The technology of rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation (hereafter referred to as primary rattan processing) is a very important part of rattan processing.
    • It adds value to the raw material, preserves its unique qualities and improves its durability.
    • The technology presented here is implemented in Malaysia as well as in neighbouring countries, especially Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines.
  • This technology has made a considerable contribution to the improved quality and benefits of the rattan industry in Malaysia.
    • A decade ago, the Malaysian rattan industry hardly exported processed rattan materials at all.
    • It was characterized mainly by the export of raw material to other furniture manufacturing countries such as Hong Kong and Singapore.
    • At that time Hong Kong and Singapore, which do not possess their own raw materials, already exported rattan products valued at more than USD 53 and USD 23 million respectively.
  • Realizing this discrepancy, the Malaysian government took a drastic measure by banning the export of rattan starting from December 1989.
    • The ban was partly aimed at encouraging the development of in-country manufacturing of rattan products, especially furniture, by ensuring the consistent and affordable supply of raw materials.
    • Another strategy to increase the export value of rattan was the upgrading of technologies used by the primary processing industry.
  • As a result of these policies, the rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation industry in Malaysia has improved and grown significantly in the last decade.
    • The value of rattan furniture exported from Malaysia has increased to about USD 24 million per year.
    • However, the contribution of the rattan-based industry to the country’s’ economy is still very small compared to wood-based industries, which generated about USD 666.1 million in export earnings in 1997.
  • Currently, Malaysia continues to seek ways of improving the output quality of the raw materials used in the rattan industry.
    • The main efforts are focused on increasing the effectiveness of the present oil curing process, bleaching and the application of preservatives.

3. General development attributes and advantages

  • Setting up a rattan processing industry, especially if it is located in a rural area, is a positive move in getting the rural community involved in the business.
    • In forest fringes with abundant rattan, basic processing activities implemented by local people add considerable value to the natural resource and contribute to rural income generation and development.
  • In Peninsular Malaysia, for example, the rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation industry has proved to be of major importance to the social and economic welfare of rural and urban people.
    • As rattan is an important export product for Malaysia, its processing industry benefits a considerable number of rattan harvesters, middlemen, transporters, and laborers in the processing industry.
  • The rattan industry has been one of the mainstays of the small and medium scale forest-based industries in Peninsular Malaysia.
    • It has withstood competition from other substitute materials.
    • Since 1989, the industry has largely increased its export of semi-processed rattans and end products.
    • The industry has greatly contributed to the national economy in terms of employment, capital investment and foreign-exchange earnings.

4. Target groups

  • The target groups for this rattan processing technology are poor rural communities or families involved with rattan harvesting and transport.
    • Other target groups arecommunities who have access to a natural resource-base of rattan, without knowing how to benefit from its processing and commercialization.
    • As has happened in Malaysia, this technology can be taught to people as a way of upgrading their rattan-based activities and their standard of living.
    • This TOTEM can benefit people who are interested in developing a rural village industry and commercialize their rattan resources.

5. Problems faced by the industry

  • Although the rattan primary-processing industry is a successful business, the industry is confronted with several problems.
  • Visits to the processing mills and discussions with plant managers have specific problems:
    • insecure supply of raw material;
    • price fluctuations;
    • a lack of trained workers;
    • technical problems;
    • weak management;
    • a lack of financial resources; and
    • limited market access.

5.1 Supply of raw material

  • The industry is facing problems in securing a continuous supply of rattan of suitable maturity and quality.
    • Rattan resources are rapidly dwindling to a critical level, hindering the expansion of the industry.
    • Logging activities and the conversion of forests to agriculture and settlements have contributed to the rapidly dwindling supply of raw materials.
    • This is happening particularly in more accessible forests where no imperative measures are taken to replace these natural resources.
  • Another problem is the inability to harvest the uppermost part of the plant, which is estimated to consist of about 50 percent of the total length of rattans.
    • It is especially difficult if rattan is entangled with the surrounding canopies.
    • Improved methods of harvesting could be developed to reduce the amount of waste.

5.2 Prices

  • To a great extent, the prices of raw rattan fluctuate depending on demand and supply for the finished products in the export market, since more than 80 percent of rattan production is exported.
    • There is a very large price gap between rattan materials in their raw form to the time they is retailed in the export market.
    • The gap is often up to ten
    • The price of rattan depends on the species, its form, grade, size and colour.
  • Another factor that contributes to the wide fluctuation in prices is the weather.
    • In some areas during the rainy seasons, it is extremely difficult and dangerous to harvest rattan.
    • Rattan easily deteriorates because of its high moisture content.
    • The transport of rattan, especially during this season, also adds to the cost.

5.3 Trained workers and technical problems

  • The industry is labour-intensive but entrepreneurs have difficulty in attracting and recruiting permanent workers or experienced labourer.
    • The workers are either already attached to some already established mills or they prefer to operate their own mills.
  • Despite its long history, the bamboo processing industry in Malaysia is still a backyard industry, which lacks proper technology standards.
    • The level of technology acquired by the industries is very low and relies on traditional skills, resulting in low production volumes.
    • The village industry assistance scheme initiated by the Malaysian government, by providing basic machinery, could not be fully benefited.
    • This is becausethe mills are scattered in rural areas, which lack industrial facilities such as three-phased electricity and telephone services.
  • Entrepreneurs are often slapped with inferior quality products due to various technical problems.
    • The services rendered by various technical agencies usually help to identify and troubleshoot problems.
  • However,oftentimes they are not followed-up by other related governmental bodies.
  • This leaves the entrepreneurs with the same unsolved problems and predicament.

5.4 Management

  • Most of the rattan processing mills visited in Malaysia are either individually or family-operated, with people having a very basic educational background.
    • As such, they have poor accounting practices, inappropriate factory layouts and antiquated production techniques.
    • Thisresults in low productivity levels and poor workmanship.
    • Their activities are usually limited due to a lack of capital and difficulty in obtaining credit and bank loans.
    • These difficulties prevent them from expanding and acquiring a permanent business site.

5.5 Finance

  • The industry also lacks financial resources.
    • The collateral requirement of most lending institutions discourages interested parties from contracting loans.
    • There is also a shortage of long-term financing schemes.
    • The funding of the industry should be given top government priority.
    • There has also been an over-dependence on a few markets.
  • The industry is characterized by a proliferation of small establishments, which are mostly single proprietorships rather than corporations.
    • As a result, most operate on a job order basis, not offering secure jobs nor income to labourers.

5.6 Marketability

  • Most of the rattan processing mills, especially the smaller ones, are unable to compete in the open market due to high production costs.
    • They market their products through direct selling; wholesalers and retailers; and government contracts and subcontracts.
    • Most of them do not have proper areas to exhibit and promote their products.
    • Many do not conduct market surveys to keep abreast of the current popular demand.
    • They rely only on local markets, which often fluctuate.

6. Requirement for success

  • The rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation mentioned in this document is readily applicable in Malaysia,other Association of Southeast Asian Countries (ASEAN ) countries, and other tropical countries such as India and Pakistan, which have their own supply of raw materials.
  • The financial aspects required for operating the rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation industry might be different from one country to the next.
    • For countries such as Indonesia, Vietnam and Laos the labor costs may be cheaper than those in
  • The cost of purchasing machinery and chemicals may also vary depending on the rate of import taxation imposed by the respective governments.
  • This industry can be best run as a small and medium-sized industry (sole proprietorship).
    • It is also suitable as a community cooperative business, since the villagers can be the workforce.
  • Whichever type of business is established, the industry needs a substantial amount of funding, a consistent supply of raw materials and a secured skilled workforce to be successful.

7. Potential improvements and research needs

  • The problems faced by the rattan processing industry need immediate solutions and suggestions in order to improve rattan production in both quality and quantity.
    • Stimulating production through a rural village industry development program is worthwhile.
    • Advocating self-help with government support is very important.
  • Policy changes are needed, such as granting pioneer status to the new factories to provide financial incentives, e.g. reducing the sales tax on rattans and its products.
    • Government agencies could be responsible for overseeing and monitoring the marketing of raw materials, to ensure an adequate supply to local furniture and handicraft manufacturers.
  • Extension of technology to the rural industry should periodically upgrade and improve the traditional skills already in use, safeguarding the full-scale involvement of the rural people.
    • With careful planning and cooperation among the factories, government agencies and the government support to foster the development of the industry, the success of the rattan processing industry is
  • The cultivation of rattan through proper management is essential to ensure a continuous supply of high-quality raw materials.
    • The example of Malaysia shows that government restrictions on the export of raw materials, promote the development of a national rattan industry and benefit national and local economies.
  • The rattan primary processing industry still needs research and development efforts in order to maintain its relevance in the furniture industry worldwide.
    • While the world shows a growing concern for the environment, the rattan oil curing, bleaching and preservation industry should strive to adapt and develop improved and systematic methods for the selection and use of rattan materials.
    • This would be in order to minimize wastage and ensure the highest quality output, both in terms of appearance and in-service strength.
    • Better techniques should be developed to lessen the damage of rattan materials during the processes.
    • Funding needs to be found for research and development activities on rattan primary processing.

7.1 Concluding remarks

  • The setting up of a community-based rattan processing industry, especially in a rural area, offers good potential for local development and income generation.
    • In cases where the raw material is available and local people are interested in upgrading their rattan-based activities, the introduction of the technology presented in this TOTEM for primary processing is a viable option.
    • However, immediate attention should be focused on improving and solving some of the major obstacles that seem to hinder the expansion and development of the industry.
  • Further research and development and training activities need to upgrade the technology and the skills of the labourers.
    • In addition, the success of such development depends on the reliable support of governmental and non-governmental organisations.

    • The rattans start to float in the diesel solution.
  • Immediately after boiling, the canes are either cleaned.
    • They are cleaned withgunny rags and sawdust washed with a spray of pressurized water containing cleaning detergents.
    • They can also be cleaned by being brushed with a broom in a concrete tank containing cleaning detergents.

9.3 Drying of oil-cured rattans

  • After the oil curing and cleaning process, the rattan poles are air-dried in an open ground.

9.3.1 Different methods

  • Leaning them vertically or horizontally on wooden frames (end-racking).
  • Bundling them, loosely tied at one end and placing them in a wigwam-like structure with their upper ends in contact with the ground.
    • This position helps to accelerate the drying process.
  • Small-diameter rattans of about 6 m long are hung over a wooden stand or spread over wooden stackers placed on the ground.
    • The drying period of the oil-cured rattan ranges from 10 to 14 days, depending on the species of rattan and the weather conditions.
    • Scraped (with knives or a splitting machine to remove nodes) rattan dries faster than unscraped and larger size rattan.
    • On the third to the fifth day of drying, the canes are turned over so as to obtain uniform drying.
    • They are considered dry and ready to be transferred to a shed when:
      • the stem surfaces turn yellowish in colour,
      • they are light in weight, and
      • they produce a high-pitched sound when hit on a hard surface or object.
  • The moisture content should be below 20 percent.
  • Studies on Calamus mananboiled in diesel oil showed that the average amount of moisture loss immediately after boiling is about 17 to 54 percent from its green condition of 76 to 98 percent moisture content.
    • The studies also showed that as the rattans reach a position of equilibrium moisture content (20 to 25 percent MC) within 4 to 25 days of drying.
    • The amount of weight loss is between 17 percent and 68 percent.

9.4 Preservation

  • Before used in manufacturing furniture or handicraft items, the rattans should be chemically treated against fungi, insect attacks and deterioration.

9.4.1 Treatment against fungal attack

  • In most cases, fungi infest rattan is stained within 24 hours after harvesting.
    • The cut-ends, abrasions, bruises and the splits are the main points of entry for a fungal attack.
    • Once set in, these blemishes will be deeply rooted up into the core of the rattans.
    • They cannot be eliminated simply by scraping.
    • The only way to conceal the ugliness caused by staining fungi is to paint the product with opaque paint.
  • There are many factors that contribute to fungi infestation.
    • Moisture content in the rattans is above 30 percent.
    • The temperature where the rattans are stored is below 40°C.
    • Presence of food materials like starch, sugar, etc. in the rattans.
    • Very high humidity in storing shed/room.
  • The absence of one of the above factors is enough to restrain the growth of fungi.
    • For example, the fungi will not grow if the moisture content is below 20 percent even if the temperature is below 40°C.
  • Preventive measures against fungi attacks include the proper drying and oil curing of the poles.
    • For this purpose, several chemicals are used in different ratios ((Table 4).
Table 4. Fungicide chemicals and their mixing ratios
Type of fungicide Recommended quantities
Sodium pentachlorophenate powder

3.15 kg in 450 litres of water (Salita,1985).

2 kg in 186 litres

1 kg in 143 litres
Dowicide G powder 3.18 kg in 100 litre water (Ordinario, 1973)
Haipen (liquid). 100 ml in 25 litres water
NP - 1 (liquid).   1 ml in 100 ml water

Source: INBAR-FRIM 2005

  • There is a specific procedure to follow for chemical treatment against fungi.
    • Use a dipping/soaking tank made of concrete/cement or metal (a drum).
    • Prepare the necessary amount of chemical solution (water and chemical) in the dipping tank according to the mixing ratio.
    • Dip two to five rattans (after draining the sap out) at a time in the solution for about 30 to 60 seconds.
    • Take the rattans out of the tank and pile them horizontally.
    • Cover the heap of rattans with a plastic sheet to protect from possible rain.

9.4.2 Treatment of against insect attack

  • Fresh as well as semi-processed rattan poles are susceptible to attack from various boring insects.
    • The most severe are the powder-post beetles that bore holes in the rattan.
    • Chemical treatment largely prevents the attack of such borers.
    • The treatment should be performed on the rattans after oil curing but before manufacturing.
    • Chemicals used for such treatment are:
      • dieldrin,
      • gemaphex,
      • lindane, and
      • zinc chloride.
    • The most widely used ratio is 165 ml of Dieldrin in 10 to 30 litres of water.
    • The procedure for chemical treatment includes the dipping of rattan poles for three minutes in the solution of Dieldrin 30 or one of the other chemicals.

The treatment will remain effective for about six months.

9.5 Bleaching process of oil-cured rattans

  • The bleaching of rattan can be done either by sulphur fumigation, soaking, steeping or dipping.
    • Section 9.5.1 presents the methods that are commonly practiced by the rattan industry in Peninsular Malaysia.
    • Only good quality large-diameter and peeled rattans undergo the process of sulphur fumigation.
    • Those of smaller diameter are only scraped with knives or a splitting machine to remove nodes before further processing.
  • The large diameter rattans are washed and subsequently smoked overnight with sulphur dioxide (SO2) fumes in an enclosed shed or chamber.
    • About one kg of sulphur is required to fumigate approximately 500 poles of rattans overnight.
    • Providing preservative treatment this process will also produce greater uniformity quality in colour of the rattans.

9.5.1 Bleaching methods

  • Fumigation
    • The dried rattan poles are fumigated in closed chambers for 24 hours, with vapours from burnt sulphur dioxide.
    • This produces an ivory colouration on the epidermis of the rattans.
    • About 454 gm of sulphur dioxide is required to fumigate 227 kg of rattan (2 mg:1 kg or, 1:500 kg).
  • Steeping and bleaching
    • Rattans are steeped in a solution of sodium hypochlorite or hydrochlorine in a tank for about one hour
    • 35 kg to 45 kg of hypochlorite is mixed with 3 m3 of water.
    • After repeated usage, more chemicals and water are added.
    • Hydrogen peroxide or chlorine is also sometimes used for the bleaching process.
  • Bleaching
    • Bleaching with sodium hypochlorite produces poles with higher brightness value than with hydrogen peroxide bleach.

9.6 Storage

  • Rattans that have been treated, sorted and graded are straightened manually or by machine before being tied in a bundle of 20 to 30 large poles (depending on the rattan diameter).
    • In the case of rattans of smaller diameter, in bundles of about 30 to 60 kg.
  • They are now ready to be stored, marketed or prepared for further processing.
    • While stored, these rattans are positioned either vertically or horizontally depending on the size of the storage shed.
    • Enough ventilation should be provided to ensure dryness and at the same time to reduce the probability of fungal attack.

10. Capital cost

  • The project costs incurred in setting up a rattan processing mill of medium size are estimated in the following Appendix.
    • The figures are derived from the processing mill survey and present average values.
    • The actual costs involved in setting up the rattan processing industry may vary from one area to another

11. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

12. Related/associated technologies

  • Local tools and equipment technologies for processing bamboo and rattan: ID 3877.
  • Rattan furniture unit: ID 3883.
  • Rattan pole steam bending: ID 3885.

13. Objectives fulfilled by the project

13.1 Resource use efficiency 

The technology allows for the local use of the rattan raw resource. Through its efficient steps on its preparation and preservation, rattan can be used in many ways.

13.2 Pro-poor technology 

The technology allows for the diversified local production of rattan as a raw material and different end products. This leads to additional sources of income.

_annotations.field_shorter_description: Bamboo and rattan are ideal resources for development that integrate poverty reduction and environmental sustainability. The International Network for Bamboo and Rattan’s (INBAR) priority is to give people, at all levels, the knowledge and skills they need for long-term development involving bamboo and rattan. records.description:
Description

1. Rooting of orthotropic stem cuttings under greenhouse conditions

1.1 Semi-hardwood stock plant production

  • Juvenile somatic embryo plants at the sapling stage (at or near jorquette height) should be used as stock plants for generation of orthotropic cutting material.
    • Hard prune the fan branches as this promotes release of dormant axillary orthotropic meristems leading to greater orthotropic shoot production.
    • With the pots remaining upright, arch the plant over so that the main trunk is at a horizontal position and secure the shoot with a metal hook or some rope.
    • Many orthotropic shoots should proliferate in one to two weeks along the top side of the trunk length.
  • Two to three months after bending several orthotropic shoots of 0.7 to 1.0 m height will have proliferated (first 4, then 8 to 12 or more in successive harvests) and be ready for harvest.
    • Harvest shoots at their base at the main stock plant trunk.
    • New shoots are generated at or near the cut, and these may be repeatedly harvested.
  • Harvest hardened and dark green orthotropic shoots from the stock plants early in the morning while leaf water potential is still high.
    • Well-hardened and even material showing beginnings of characteristic browning of the stem works well, so use it all.
  • Prune all leaves to 100 mm.
    • Make single leaf cuttings with stems at least 40 mm long.
    • Stems should be cut such that 5 to 10 mm remains above the leaf axil (so that the axillary bud will not die as the stem is rooting), and 20 to 30 mm of the stem remains below the node.
    • If there are shorter internodes on some portions of the stem, lower leaves may be removed where the petiole narrows (approx. 10 mm.).
  • Dip the stem in the rooting hormone mixture for five seconds.
    • The quick dip method as described by Evans, 1951 has been quite successful for the propagation of single-leaf cuttings under our conditions. Rooting solutions should be prepared beforehand.
    • A 1:1 mixture of Naphthalene acetic acid (NAA) and βIndole-3-butyric acid (IBA) at a total combined concentration of 4 g per litre in 50 percent ethanol should be stored in a dark refrigerator for no more than one month.
    • Rooting mixtures should be used for only one day in the greenhouse and the remainder discarded.
    • If three-leaf cuttings are desired, use a greater concentration of NAA + IBA, 8 to 10 g per litre combined.
  • After dipping, strike the cutting in the rooting media. Any well-draining media can be used for root development.
    • 100 percent silica or sharp sand or a 1:1 mix of sand and soil may be used.
  • Place under mist/fog.
    • Intermittent mist (10 seconds every 10 or 15 minutes) or fogging should be utilized for rooting of cuttings.
    • Relative humidity should be maintained at or near 100 percent, keeping the leaves wet without inundating the cuttings.
    • Light intensity should remain under 1 000 µgmol * m-2 * sec.-1 PAR, or 50 to 60 percent shade.
  • Prop the leaves at an angle with a string or tack on a stick to allow any water droplets to drain off the leaf.
    • Most of the cuttings whose leaves remain wet do none-the-less root.
  • Cuttings should be watered or fertigated every two to three days to keep the media moist and to ensure the stem does not dry out.
    • A complete liquid fertilizer (modified Hoaglund's) at 150 ppm nitrogen works well.
  • Roots will appear in as little as three weeks.
    • By four to five weeks all cuttings that will root will have done so.
    • Any cutting with two or more roots and a live axillary bud of even the smallest size may be transplanted to polythene bags.

1.2 Acclimating, pot establishment, and general cultural management

  • After transplanting, cuttings should remain under 50 percent shade, and RH above 80 percent.
    • Fertilizing will promote bud break.
    • Care should be taken when watering to not damage the many times tender shoots.
  • After the first flush has hardened, the cuttings may be treated as any other material.
    • Light may be increased and RH may be lowered.
  • Orthotropic cuttings have a tendency to jorquette prematurely.
    • To achieve a more standard height of jorquette, the jorquette bud may be removed as soon as it appears.
    • Following removal, an axillary orthotropic shoot from below the cut will release, and the plant will reach a more standard height (1 to 1.5 m) prior to the appearance of the next jorquette.

1.3 Softwood stock plant production

  • Newly acclimatized SE plants may be grown for two to three months and used as stock plants for rooted cuttings.
    • After two months of establishment, orthotropic shoots longer than 0.15 m should be harvested by strong head cuts leaving three to four nodes with leaves of 80 mm long.
  • Successive harvests are then comprised of orthotropic shoots from 0.20 to 0.40 m length and left only two nodes above the previous harvest cut.
    • Multiple orthotropic axillary meristems swell during the first week, and bud break occurs by seven to ten days.
  • Individual shoots are allowed to flush mostly two to three and up to four times prior to harvesting orthotropic shoots depending on shoot morphological characteristics.
    • Stem diameter less than approximately 5 mm was found to be inadequate for rooting.
    • Therefore, shoots are allowed to flush until stem diameter at 40 to 60 mm distance basipedal from apex is at least 5 mm.
  • Softwood cuttings of 40 to 60 mm in length and mostly two leaf nodes were made from the entire harvested orthotropic shoot.
    • Node number varies from one to seven and does not affect rooting success.
    • The bottom 20 mm of each cutting is trimmed of leaves at the petiole base.
    • A maximum of four leaves per cutting remain.
    • These leaf laminae are trimmed to 60 mm length.
  • Rooting of cuttings follows the same method described above.

2. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Producción de semilla mejorada de cacao (Theobroma cacao) ó híbridos comerciales (IMC-67 y UF-296): ID 6471.
  • Uso de sombra en el cultivo de cacao: ID 6475.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2317.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for more efficient use of the cacao crop, increasing yield and profitability. 

4.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for an additional source of income for farmers in developing countries.

records.title: Raising Calliandra tree seedlings
records.description:
Description

Calliandra has many advantages.

  • It grows fast and sprouts after cutting.
  • It reduces soil and water run-off.
  • It has excellent fodder for livestock.
  • It has good fuelwood.
  • It increases soil fertility.

Production of Calliandra seedling will require the following inputs:

  • seeds,
  • sand,
  • forest soil,
  • hoes,
  • spades,
  • pangas,
  • polythene tubing,
  • papyrus mats,
  • watering cans,
  • eucalyptus poles, and
  • nails.

1. Seeds

1.1 Seed collection

  • Collect seed mature Calliandra trees when the pods have started to turn brown in order to avoid shuttering of seed.
  • Dry the pods in the sun in a sack.
  • Thresh the pods and separate the seed from the residue.
  • Store the seeds in tightly closed tins.
  • The seeds can be sown immediately or stored for several months.

1.2 Seed pre-treatment

  • Calliandra seeds have a hard coat, so when sown untreated will germinate after two weeks.
  • For quick germination soak the seeds in cold water overnight.
  • Soaking is complete once most of the seeds have swollen.
  • Sow the seed immediately after pre-treatment.
  • Never boil the seed as this kills them.

2. Stage of seedbed construction

2.1 Seedbed construction

  • Seedbed construction requires the following materials:
    • eucalyptus poles (small size of 4 cm diameter),
    • papyrus mats, and
    • sand.

2.1.1 Stage one

  • Mark area (1 m wide and 8  to 10 m long) where the seedbed will be constructed (see Figure 1).
Figure 1. Stage one

©FAO/TECA

2.1.2 Stage two

  • Erect eucalyptus poles in the marked area (see Figure 2).
Figure 2. Stage two

©FAO/TECA

2.1.3 Stage three

  • Fill the market area with sandy soil up to a height of about 4 cm (see Figure 3).
Figure 3. Stage three

©FAO/TECA

2.1.4 Stage four

  • Erect a shade (1.2 m high at the front and 0.8 m high at the back) over the bed and cover the seedbed with papyrus mats, grass or banana leaves (see Figure 4).
Figure 4. Stage four

©FAO/TECA

3. Seed sowing

  • Sow the pre-treated seed on the seed bed.
  • Cover the sown seed with a thin layer soil but they should not be seen.
  • Water immediately after sowing, thereafter water twice a day (morning and evening).
  • Seed germinate after four to five days.
  • Remove seedling from the seedbed to polythene pots when they reach 3 cm to 4 cm tall (after one and half months).
  • The pots are filled with forest soil.

4. Filling of polythene pots with soil

  • Collect forest soil and leave it for two weeks to allow seeds to germinate from it.
  • Cut the polythene in lengths of 4 inches.
  • Fill the pots with forest soil.
  • Water the pots before transplanting the seedlings from the seedbed.
  • Keep the seedlings in the transplant bed for one and half months.
  • Plant seedling on the field immediately after heavy rain.

5. Advantages/benefits

  • Seedlings are readily available to the farmers.
  • Seedlings raised can be sold to generate money or to increase family income.
    • Each seedling can be sold at 100 UGX, while 1 kg of seed can be sold at 20 000 UGX.
  • When planted in the field and managed properly, they can increase crop yields.
  • Trees planted provide rapidly available fuelwood to the family.

6. Validation of the practice

  • ​​This practice was applied successfully in Uganda.​

7. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • Production of Calliandra seedling will require the following inputs:
    • seeds,
    • sand,
    • forest soil,
    • hoes,
    • spades,
    • pangas,
    • polythene tubing,
    • papyrus mats,
    • watering cans,
    • eucalyptus poles, and
    • nails. 

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Growing fodder for livestock: Calliandra and elephant grass: ID 6989.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

10.1 Women-friendly

​​This practice can be applied as well by women farmers, as it does not require heavy machinery and does not include risks.​

10.2 Pro-poor technology

Planting Calliandra can be a source of income for poor farmers since seedling can be sold at 100 UGX, while 1 kg of seed can be sold at 20 000 UGX.

Raising Calliandra tree seedlings

  • Fill the market area with sandy soil up to a height of about 4 cm (see Figure 3).
Figure 3. Stage three

©FAO/TECA

2.1.4 Stage four

  • Erect a shade (1.2 m high at the front and 0.8 m high at the back) over the bed and cover the seedbed with papyrus mats, grass or banana leaves (see Figure 4).
Figure 4. Stage four

©FAO/TECA

3. Seed sowing

  • Sow the pre-treated seed on the seed bed.
  • Cover the sown seed with a thin layer soil but they should not be seen.
  • Water immediately after sowing, thereafter water twice a day (morning and evening).
  • Seed germinate after four to five days.
  • Remove seedling from the seedbed to polythene pots when they reach 3 cm to 4 cm tall (after one and half months).
  • The pots are filled with forest soil.

4. Filling of polythene pots with soil

  • Collect forest soil and leave it for two weeks to allow seeds to germinate from it.
  • Cut the polythene in lengths of 4 inches.
  • Fill the pots with forest soil.
  • Water the pots before transplanting the seedlings from the seedbed.
  • Keep the seedlings in the transplant bed for one and half months.
  • Plant seedling on the field immediately after heavy rain.

5. Advantages/benefits

  • Seedlings are readily available to the farmers.
  • Seedlings raised can be sold to generate money or to increase family income.
    • Each seedling can be sold at 100 UGX, while 1 kg of seed can be sold at 20 000 UGX.
  • When planted in the field and managed properly, they can increase crop yields.
  • Trees planted provide rapidly available fuelwood to the family.

6. Validation of the practice

  • ​​This practice was applied successfully in Uganda.​

7. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • Production of Calliandra seedling will require the following inputs:
    • seeds,
    • sand,
    • forest soil,
    • hoes,
    • spades,
    • pangas,
    • polythene tubing,
    • papyrus mats,
    • watering cans,
    • eucalyptus poles, and
    • nails. 

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Growing fodder for livestock: Calliandra and elephant grass: ID 6989.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

10.1 Women-friendly

​​This practice can be applied as well by women farmers, as it does not require heavy machinery and does not include risks.​

10.2 Pro-poor technology

Planting Calliandra can be a source of income for poor farmers since seedling can be sold at 100 UGX, while 1 kg of seed can be sold at 20 000 UGX.

records.title: Light attraction method to catch mukene fish on Lake Victoria
records.description:
Description

Fish are a cheap source of fish proteins for both humans and domestic animals. In the lakes, the species the most important as a food source is the Nile perch, the most important export fish in the country. The mukene fish (also called Dagaa or Omena), is fished by light attraction. Compared to gillnetting, light fishing is relatively new in Uganda. Kerosene pressure lamps are floated on water, attracting fishes to light. Mukene thus attracted, is fished out using scoop-nets and nets pulled from the shores (beach seines) and from canoes (lampara nets). Since mukene is a small fish (it grows to an average standard length of 48 mm), the nets used in fishing are meshes 3 mm, 5 mm and 10 mm stretched (see Figure 1).

1. Problems to the fishery

1.1 Fishing grounds

  • Owing to the specialized nature of mukene fishing (light fishing), favourable weather conditions are necessary.
  • Safe fishing grounds consisting of shallow sheltered bays and near-shore waters attract large numbers of fishing boats.
  • These shallow inshore waters and small bays are nursery grounds for immature mukene, Nile perch and Tilapia.
  • The high exploitation rates when added to predation by the Nile perch results in localized mukene over-fishing.
  • In such areas, the fish is harvested before maturity.

1.2 Fishing gears and methods

  • Initially, mukene was fished by beach seines constructed out of 10 mm mesh nets.
  • A more efficient lampara net was later introduced but the mesh size was reduced to 5 mm and in some cases to 3 mm.
  • Nets of small meshes capture mainly immature fishes.

1.3 By-catch

  • Fishing for mukene also captures immature Nile perch and Tilapia as by-catch.
  • The light used in the fishery attracts water insects.
  • Young Nile perch and Tilapia are in turn attracted to the plentiful supply of insect food around the lamps.
  • These fishes are therefore caught as by-catch during fishing for mukene.
  • The mesh size of nets used to fish mukene can catch immature Nile perch and Tilapia.
  • This will affect stocks of fish and will harm the fishery of these two important export fish species (see Figure 2).

1.4 Solutions and recommendations

  • For a regular supply of mukene from Lake Victoria, management measures should be aimed to avoid capture of immature mukene and other fish species that commonly appears as by-catch of the mukene fishing.
    • Control of fishing grounds
      • To avoid capture of immature mukene and by-catch species, fishing should be carried outside the small bays less than 3 km diameter and at least 1.4 km away from the shoreline.
      • This will also solve the conflict with Tilapia fishery that occurs within one-kilometre belt off the shoreline.
    • Control mesh size fishing gear and methods
      • The most popular mesh size of nets in use on Lake Victoria in 5 mm stretched.
      • When this net is operated away from the nursery grounds mentioned above, it captures mainly mature mukene.
      • Nets of meshes smaller than 5 mm capture mainly immature mukene and by-catch and should be discouraged.
      • Likewise fishing for mukene using beach seines (nets pulled from the shore) should be prohibited as these are operated in nursery grounds.
      • Boat (Lampara) seine nets can be operated away from the shoreline and thus are most appropriate for mukene fishing.
      • Mukene fishing depends on the fish being attracted to light; use 5 to10 mm
      • See Figure 3.
    • Fishing seasons
      • Mukene breeds throughout the year but shows two breeding peaks in August and December to January.
      • Mukene produced during these breeding peaks appear in commercial catches as immature fishes in November/December and April/May.
      • These periods could qualify as closed to mukene fishing.
      • However, fishing away from the shore avoids the capture of these immature fishes.

1.5 How to reduce/avoid polluting the water environmental measures

  • The sustainable management of fish in Lake Victoria needs corrective actions to stop water pollution.
  • This requires a combined effort by the water and fisheries managers and grass-root communities.
  • This will involve effective watershed management.
  • Educational programmes aimed at sensitizing the local people about impacts of intense subsistence crop farming and animal husbandry on the atmosphere and water environment and subsequently fish production should be carried out.
  • These practices include:
    • uncontrolled grass and bush burning;
    • tree cutting (deforestation);
    • wetland destruction;
    • shoreline destruction by farming very close to the lake/ river banks; and
    • excessive use of pesticides and herbicides.
  • Pollution control will lead to improved water health that will support high fish yields and sustain high production.
  • It also would contribute to and enhance excess nutrient releases into the water environment.

2. Benefits from the solution suggested above

  • Catching mature fish allows stocks to replenish themselves.
  • These fish will have bred and left offspring for the future.
  • Mukene caught in the open waters far away from the shore are larger than those inshore.
  • They are easier to dry and therefore fetch better prices to the fishers.
  • By avoiding by-catch, the Nile perch and Tilapia are allowed to grow and support the export market which depends on the Nile perch.
Figure 1. Mukene fish

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Mukene cover

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Mukene light fishing

©FAO/TECA

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Small-scale freshwater fish farming: ID 6958.
  • Fish harvesting and post-harvest handling: ID 7024.
  • Fry/seed quality and stocking: ID 7025.
  • Management of fish in the pond: ID 7235.
  • Supplementary feeding for farmed fish: ID 4363.
  • Sustainable fishery on Lake Victoria: exploitation, gears, fishing methods and management: ID 4359.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

This practice allows for the efficient and sustainable harvesting of fish. It also contributes to the prevention of overexploitation of fish in Lake Victoria.

5.2 Pro-poor technology

The practice provides additional sources of food and income.

records.title: Selection of site and water quality testing for fishpond
records.description:
Description

To raise healthy fish, the pond water must be free from diseases, toxic chemicals and other fish enemies. Pond fish should also be supplied with sufficient fresh air and food. Physical characteristics of fishponds affect water quality and influence their production potential. Fish ponds have to be sited where they can be managed well to achieve the highest production potential.

1. Factors to consider when selecting a site and water quality for fishpond

1.1 Land area

  • The area of land required must be large enough to allow for the construction of ponds.
    • The larger the pond, the bigger the area of land required.
    • Extra space is required for water channels, and for walking on or movement of vehicles (e.g. tractor, pickups) (Figure 1).
  • Generally, small ponds can only provide fish for household food and nothing more for sale.
    • The minimum commercial fishpond size starts at 20 m x 25 m (500 m2) can produce 120 kg of Tilapia a year, which can be sold at UGX. 180 000 (about USD 98).
    • This amount of money can be significant in rural areas.
    • Therefore, the pond size of 20 m x 25 m can be regarded as the minimum small-scale commercial size.
    • Larger ponds from 20 m x 50 m to more than 2 ha are recommended for commercial fish production.
    • The larger the pond the more commercial viable it becomes.
  • As far as possible, the land must be fully owned by the farmer who wants to build the fish pond.
    • Often disputes arise when there is no proper agreement on the use of communal land for fish ponds.
Figure 1. Water channels and dykes size

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Dyke size

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Location, wetlands and legal consideration

  • Not only is establishing ponds in wetlands destructive to the environment, but it also is not economical to grow fish in wetlands.
  • Therefore, avoid constructing ponds in the wetlands (Figure 3).
Figure 3. Beyond the wetlands

©FAO/TECA

  • The most suitable location of land for ponds is a land on a slope (Figure 4) next to a flowing stream or river, where a portion of the water is diverted into the pond without disrupting the other uses of the same water downstream.
    • It could be a stream beyond the wetland.
  • The National Environmental Management Authority (NEMA) of Uganda requires anybody who wishes to make a development in the wetland to first carry out an Environment Impact Assessment and seek approval of the plan before the development.
  • An area of open and flat land with a gentle slope that allows water to flow by gravity is ideal.
    • Any land surface that is not flat increases the cost of construction.
    • Constructing a pond on a steep slope involves the expense of removing a lot of earth to level the ground.
    • This is called bad slope and it requires a lot of labour to remove a great amount of the soil, the lower dyke is not firm and it allows only small ponds (Figure 4: Land slope A).
  • Constructing ponds in a very sharp V-valley involves extra costs of widening the valley (Figure 4: Land slope C) as a lot of soil must be removed.
    • To avoid the problem of hidden rocks and stones it is necessary to bore holes down to 1.5 m at various points of the site during the inspection of the site (Figure 5).
Figure 4. Land slope

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Boring holes down

©FAO/TECA

2. The soil type

  • For purposes of aquaculture, soils can broadly be classified as sandy, clay, murrum, humus and loam.
    • The characteristics of these types of soils are given in Table 1. 
  • In general, good soils are those that hold water; sticks and holds together.
    • A sticky soil is good for constructing ponds.
    • It makes firm dykes and walls, which do not collapse and maintains the pond shape.
  • To test this:
    • loosen the soil;
    • add water;
    • mix the soil with the water;
    • roll it in your hand to make a ball and dry the ball for one hour in the shade; and
    • drop the ball from a height of 2 feet (about 61 cm) to the ground.
  • If the ball does not break, the soil is firm and sticky enough to build a pond with strong walls.
  • Many of the negative characteristics of soils can be corrected during construction.
Table 1. Types of soils for ponds
Soil type Positive characteristics Negative characteristics Effect on ponds
Sandy  
  • Has loose grains.
  • Does not hold water well.
  • Has loose grains.
  • Difficult to shape the pond.
Murrum    
  • Difficult to dig.
  • Keeps water dirty brown (unproductive).
Clay
  • Firm and sticks together.
  • Holds water.
  • When pure, cracks in dry season.
  • Grains too fine and do not settle down easily.
  • Maintains shape of pond.
  • Loses water through cracks in dry season.
  • Retains water outside dry season.
  • Keeps pond cloudy (unproductive).
Humus
  • Rich in organic materials.
  • Composed of loose freshly decoying plant parts, hardly any soil.
  • Good source of nutrients for fish.
Loam
  • Firm
  • little loose.
  • Pond shape can be maintained - not for long.
  • Pond shape can be maintained - not for long.
  • Source of nutrients.
Clay/Loam
  • Firm
  • hold water
  • organic material
  • not slity
  • elastic.
  
  • Maintains shape of pond.
  • Retains water.
  • Rich in nutrients.
  • Keeps water not turbid.
  • Doesnot crack in dry season.

Source: NAADS-Uganda 2007

3. Water source, quantity and quality 

  • Leave some distance between the swamp to the pond to allow the grass to filter the water.
    • Water flowing from swamps or a lot of rotting vegetation and other materials tends to contain acid levels that are not suitable for fish.
  • White builder’s lime is used to reduce the acid levels of water.
    • A paper strip (litmus paper) is used to determine the level of acid in the water.
  • A pack of 100 strips costs UGX. 12 000 (about USD 6.54) from a laboratory supplies shop.
  • The use of the water upstream may pose water quality risks for the pond.

3.1 Examples of upstream use of water that can negatively affect the fish in the pond 

  • Garages may be disposing old engine oil into the stream that may find its way into the pond to kill fish.
  • Waragi distillers may be disposing of residues into the stream, which finds its way into the pond to kill fish (Figure 6).
  • Upstream communities may be washing or bathing in the water.
  • Untreated or insufficiently treated sewage may be deposited into the stream.
Figure 6. Discharging Waragi residue into the stream

©FAO/TEC

4. Security

  • Ponds should not be located far from home or from human habitation.
  • They should be near habitation for the security of the fish even though birds may eat the fish from the pond.
  • The pond may leak or flood, and there may be a reduction in fresh air that may not be noticed.
  • Access roads to the ponds should be easy to facilitate transportation of inputs and products.

5. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Fishpond layout and construction: ID 4384.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency

Efficient land-use to construct a fishpond on it. The land can be transformed to generate commercial benefits from the fishpond.

records.title: Sustainable fishery on Lake Victoria: exploitation, gears, fishing methods and management
records.description:
Description

Recent activities in the exploitation of the fisheries, biodiversity and environment of water system in Uganda threaten to reduce fish catches and in some cases fish death.

1. Constraints to increased and sustainable fish production

  • Under capture fisheries, the Fisheries Resources Research Institute (FIRRI) focuses research efforts to generate scientific information on the key constraints.
    • Decline in fish stock and fish species diversity due to excessive fishing.
    • Use of destructive fishing gears and methods.
    • Capture of immature fish.
    • Pollution and degradation of the fish habitat including infestation by aquatic weeds especially water hyacinth.
    • High post-harvest fish losses.
    • Ineffective management of fisheries due to limited community participation.
    • Inadequate investment skills among fishers.

2. Addressing the constraints

  • In order to overcome the constraints mentioned above, FIRRI has developed this technology to empower fisherfolk communities with information to increase and sustain fish production and utilization to overcome poverty.

3. Measures to increase and sustain fish production

3.1 Use recommended fishing gears and methods

  • Some commonly used fishing gears and methods are destructive.
  • Such methods are highly non-selective, catch fish of all types and sizes, disrupt breeding and feeding patterns of the fish and deplete the fish stocks rapidly.
  • Examples of these methods include beach seines, seine nets, cast nets, basket traps and tycooning (beating water).
    • These methods should therefore be avoided.
  • The fisherfolk are encouraged to use recommended fishing gears and methods, like hook fishing and passive gillnetting (use of stationery gill nets).
    • These methods are selective.
    • Bigger nets catch bigger fish.

3.2 Avoid polluting and degrading the fish habitat

  • Communities living around the water system should avoid polluting it.
  • Pollution leads to fish deaths and hence a decline in fish stocks and fish species diversity.
  • If a pollution source is identified within a community, it should be immediately reported to the local or district authorities.
  • There causes of pollution.
    • Wetland degradation.
    • Poor agricultural practices such as exposure of soils and cutting of trees leading to soil erosion.
    • Improper use of farm chemical that may lead to fish poisoning.
    • Industrial pollution.

3.3 Increased community participation

  • Increased community participation leads to increased and sustainable fish production.
  • Communities around water systems should ensure that proper fishing methods are used.
  • They should report observations that may lead to unhealthy and unproductive water environment to Beach Management Units (BMUs) or the Landing Site Committees.
    • See the images: Fisherfolk and Fish production cover and poster.
  • Fish is important for good nutrition, income generation, provision of employment and foreign exchange earning.
  • Uganda earned over USD 80 million in 2001 through the export of Nile perch and other related products.
  • Fishing can also be a social activity.
  • In particular, this technology is to advise the fisher communities and fishery managers on appropriate commercial fish harvesting gears and methods on Lake Victoria, Uganda.
Figure 1. Water hyacinth

©FAO/TECA

4. Problem statement

  • The following are the main problems with fishing in the lake
    • Collapse or decline of important commercial fisheries on the lake.
    • Indiscriminate use of certain fishing gears.
    • Use of small mesh size of gill nets.
    • Uncontrolled fishing methods.
    • The decline of per unit catch (kg per boat yearly) and size of the three major commercial fish species (Nile perch- Mputa, Nile tilapia-Ngege, and Mukene).
      • See the image: Fish market.
Figure 2. Fish market

©FAO/TECA

5. Research statement

  • The size of fish that should be caught is set at first maturity.
  • This is the size at which 50 percent of the fish in a population are allowed to breed before they are caught.
  • The size at the first maturity for Nile perch is 50 cm total length (TL) for male fish and 90 to 100 cm TL for female.
  • For the Nile tilapia it is 23 cm TL for males and 25 cm TL for female.
  • All Nile tilapia are mature at 29 cm TL.
  • The size at the first maturity for mukene is 42 mm standard length.
  • By 45 mm all fish are mature.

6.1 A recent fishing method operated in open waters. Use 6" to 10"

  • Mukene nets
    • Mukene fishing depends on the fish being attracted to light.

©FAO/TECA

  • Beach seine and trawl nets
    • See images: Beach seine net and Trawl nets.
  • Cast nets and tycoon fishing
    • See images: Cast nets, and Tycoon fishing, and Basket traps.

6.3 Some of the recommended fishing gears and fishing methods

  • Gill nets (passive) 5" to 10"
    • See the image: Gill nets.
  • Hooks size 10 to 6 mm
    • See the image: Hooks size.
  • Drift nets.
Figure 4. Tycoon fishing

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Trawl nets

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Basket traps

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Gill nets

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Hooks

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Beach seine net

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10. Cast nets

©FAO/TECA

  • It allows uninterrupted fish breeding and growth.
  • It allows enough female Nile perch to breed.
  • Some organisms that act as food for fish become available.
  • It increases fish catches, resulting in income and improved livelihood among fishing communities.
  • It increases foreign exchange earnings from the export of fish and other fish products.
  • It ensures better food security and increased fish protein availability to people.

©FAO/TECA

Figure 12. Fisherfolk

  • Tropics, warm.

This practice allows for the efficient and sustainable harvesting of fish. It also contributes to the prevention of overexploitation of fish in Lake Victoria.

The practice provides additional sources of food and income.

records.title: Biological control of Armyworm (Spodoptera Exempta)
records.description:
Description

The African armyworm (Spodoptera exempta) is a serious migratory pest of pasture and grain crops in Africa. Outbreaks occur every year in primary outbreak areas of Tanzania. Under favourable conditions the armyworm plagues can sweep across Tanzania and migrate to many parts of eastern and southern Africa. Crop Protection Programme (CPP) projects R6746, R7954 and R8408 aimed to develop and evaluate two novel approaches to replace environmentally damaging and expensive synthetic chemical pesticides to control African armyworm: applying S. exempta nucleopolyhedrovirus (SpexNPV), a naturally occurring biological control agent; and neem, a locally available botanical agent.

1. SpexNPV and Neem as biopesticides

  • Field work confirmed that the candidate technologies worked well in practice, and that SpexNPV could be as effective as chemical insecticides in controlling armyworm.
    • This is when it is applied at rates as low as 1 × 1012 occlusion bodies (OB) per hectare in small-plot trials using ground-based or aerial application (the first use of aerial application for any NPV biopesticide in Africa).
    • The same trials also showed that extracts of neem leaves and seeds could be used to kill armyworm.
  • While these are not as effective as either chemical insecticides or NPV, use of neem should be useful to local communities who lack access to other resources.
    • Scaling-up production of the virus for initial work, SpexNPV was mass-produced under laboratory conditions.
    • However, field trials confirmed that a viable strategy for scaling-up production of the virus in Tanzania would be to spray naturally occurring armyworm outbreaks with an inoculating dose of SpexNPV, and then to harvest the diseased larvae.
  • A Brazilian production model for NPV was identified.
    • Following exchange visits between Tanzanian Pest Control Services (PCS) and the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation (EMBRAPA) with researchers for training and advice on low-cost NPV production techniques, a modified process was developed that is appropriate for the production in Tanzania of SpexNPV at a cost comparable to that in Brazil (USD 1.50 per hectare).
    • This is much lower than the current cost of imported synthetic insecticides (around USD 10 per hectare).
  • Under the protocol modified for use in Tanzania, SpexNPV is produced as a low-cost clay formulation.
    • Simple homogenates of infected insects are filtered, absorbed onto pulverised local china clay then air dried within 12 hours at ambient temperature.
    • These are then ground and stored for use as a bio-insecticide.
    • The system does not require expensive centrifugation, freeze drying or deep freeze storage and gives a stable product (> six months at 20°C, > two years at 4°C), that can be supplied directly by farmers as a substitute for chemical insecticides in all common application systems currently used in Tanzania.
  • The technology and quality control procedures are fully documented in a production manual (Mushobozi et al. 2006a).
  • Its development is reported in published papers (Mushobozi et al. 2006b), and (Grzywacz et al. 2006).
  • The final system and scaling up approach is a product of previous NRI experience.
    • This is with local partners in commercializing NPV in Thailand and India as well as EMBRAPA’s experience at establishing local commercial production of NPV in Brazil.

1.1 Adoption of SpexNPV for armyworm control

  • Tanzania has agreed a national policy, through its National Plant Protection Advisory Committee, to adopt SpexNPV as the replacement for chemical pesticides for armyworm control.
    • PCS will continue to promote the use of SpexNPV through its own channels, and the findings of the project will inform the USAID-funded armyworm control project.
    • Neem leaf can be used in the many areas where neem is already planted as a shade tree.
  • Some 50 to 80 percent of farmers have neem trees, and their leaves and/or berries could be used by smallholder farmers to protect cereal crops.
    • The high bulk of neem needed and high transport costs mean it is not feasible to recommend its use on a large scale.
    • For strategic control on rangelands, NPV is more practical and the use of local neem is currently being promoted to farmers in several trial districts by PCS, as part of the armyworm control project funded by USAID and the Tanzanian government.
  • A consortium of partners, including PCS, NRI, EMBRAPA Brazil, University of Lancaster and CABI ARC was developed to support regional adoption and to set up a pilot production project.
    • DLCO agreed to join in regional scaling up work in East Africa.
    • Several information products, including manuals, publicity and information material have been produced (Mushobozi and Grzywacz 2006a); (Mushobozi and Grzywacz 2006b).
    • Electronic presentations were given to senior policy makers, district pest control officers and farmers groups (Mushobozi et al. 2006c).
  • Posters and leaflets are being used to raise awareness at local level in districts and among national policy makers.
    • In the previous project, longer briefing notes were developed as a briefing tool for the project outputs.
    • In this project more emphasis was placed on the posters and short leaflets that delivered the messages in simple non-technical way.
      • The project staff found this approach to be more effective at attracting interest and getting the message across at all levels.
  • The technology should be of interest to other African countries where armyworm epidemics are a problem (Kenya, Uganda, Mozambique, South Africa, etc.).
    • Kenya now has legislation in place for adoption of biopesticides as a result of other CPP activities.
    • Both South Africa and Kenya have private companies already active in biopesticide products, which could act as national or regional producers of SpexNPV biopesticide.
  • You manipulate and/or use (bio)pesticides?
    • Make inquiries before!
    • Pesticide can be harmful to your health, the health of your family, of the consumers and of the environment.
    • Adopt the right gestures to use pesticides safely: Click on “Reducing risks while manipulating pesticide”

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Crop protection: community-based forecasting of armyworm: ID 4472.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology, through the use of biological and botanical agents, not only controls crop pests but also has a positive impact on the environment.
