records.title: Control of foreign fishing
records.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Distant water fishing fleets may undertake illegal fishing both in the high sea and the exclusive economic zones (EEZ).
    • Coastal states have to protect their fish resources through monitoring and surveillance (MCS).
    • Licensing of foreign vessels can provide the necessary funds for governments to regulate and monitor fishing activities in the EEZ.
  • Control of Foreign Fishing (CFF) enables coastal states to search for and select the optimal combination of fee level, surveillance expenditure, and magnitude of legal penalties, to minimize the risk of illegal fishing and maximize the benefits accruing to the coastal state.
    • This economic model facilitates integration of these complex issues so that costs and benefits of different MCS strategies can be assessed.
    • National case studies indicated that, in the short-term, potential increases to the total state revenue from foreign fishing activity are more likely to occur from increased compliance and the number of licences sold, rather than a direct increase in licence fee.
  • Over the medium to long-term, acquiring additional fishery information should take priority, providing more precise data on the variability and value of the resources taken within the EEZ, by licensed and illegal vessels.
    • Additional surveillance is required to check the veracity of catch reports and make sure there are no unreported incursions at the edge of the zone.
      • Once detection within the EEZ is perceived to be more likely, more licences may be purchased.
    • Lessons Learned Modeling approaches, such as the one described by MRAG (2006), may have value in assisting developing coastal states and in making rational and informed decisions about foreign fishing access to their waters.
  • While each case is undoubtedly different, and optimal decision-making should be based on detailed analyses of specific data, application of the model in a range of examples has provided a number of common lessons learned.
    • It is important to impose large fines for illegal fishing activities.
  • Funds available in developing coastal states to support surveillance activities are often limited.
    • If there were significant potential benefits for foreign fishers within the coastal state’s EEZ, then it is reasonable for the coastal state to set relatively high licence fees.
    • This is only possible, however, provided the expected fine faced by the fishers for fishing illegally considerably exceeds the licence fee.
    • Furthermore, if the amount of surveillance that can be afforded is strictly limited, this can only be assured by imposing very high penalties, potentially including the forfeiture of the catch and vessel.
    • Although high values of maximum net revenue can be obtained from fine proceeds alone, this could lead to unpredictable and unsustainable levels of revenue and put the status of the resource at risk of over-exploitation.
  • While it is important to set penalties as high as possible, the proceeds from fines should not be regarded as a long-term source of revenue in the same way as proceeds from license fee are.
    • Access to a fishery is limited, when necessary, for the purpose of achieving conservation targets;
      • This is not so that revenue can be generated from catching vessels fishing illegally.
    • By basing revenue expectations on the opportunity to impose fines without addressing the central problem of illegal vessels catching too many fish, the stock comes under increased pressure and risk from overfishing.
    • The management aim should therefore be to strongly deter any unlicensed fishing.
    • Only if this is successful, thereby effectively eliminating revenues from fines, will there be a long-term sustainable fishery from which licence revenue can be generated sustainably.
  • Estimates need to be made of the probabilities of detection and successful arrest of unlicensed fishing vessels arising from different levels of surveillance activities.
    • The perceived and actual probability of detecting illegal vessels can be very different.
    • Even though the actual level of surveillance may remain constant, examples indicate that it may be only after a highly publicized and high fine imposed on one vessel caught fishing illegally, that the perceived probability of detection increases and hence licence applications increase.
  • The perceived risk of being detected and fined must rise to a level at which the expected fine exceeds the cost of obtaining a licence, even though the actual risk may not have changed at all.
    • Following a high profile surveillance operation, it is important that the perceived increase in the probability of detection is maintained.
    • This can be achieved, for example, by increasing the number of patrols throughout the year to enhance the appearance of surveillance, thereby maintaining or increasing the perception of the probability of detection.
  • Depending on how the extra surveillance effort is applied, this may also elevate the actual probability of detection.
    • A degree of targeting can be used to increase the chance of detection during surveillance patrols by making use of reports from other sources that illegal fishing activities are occurring (e.g. overflights, or on-board observers).
    • Increasing the efficiency of surveillance can substantially reduce the cost as a proportion of the licence revenue.
    • When the maximum fine is reduced, surveillance can be increased to compensate by increasing the probability of detection and thereby maintaining the level of expected penalty.
  • Under these circumstances, the cost of surveillance can approach the total revenue from licence fees, hence net revenue may be reduced to zero.
    • Where the deterrence of illegal fishing is the primary management issue, affordable surveillance is therefore vital.
    • If the maximum fine must be reduced, and the cost of surveillance must be kept constant, to maintain the perceived level of expected penalty, the efficiency of surveillance must be improved.
    • Very high fines may be impossible to collect in practice.
    • Vessel owners may choose instead to forfeit the vessel, particularly when vessel value is low.
    • The value of the vessel may be the best estimate of the maximum possible fine.
    • It is better to calculate licence fees as a proportion of the marginal benefit arising from fishing inside the EEZ, rather than as a proportion of the catch taken inside the EEZ.
    • This is because the value to the fishers of obtaining a licence arises from the difference between the catches that can be taken inside and those taken outside, rather than just the amount of catch taken from the EEZ.

2. Results

  • Results from the case studies showed that strong inter-annual variability could occur from the expected benefits of fishing inside the zone.
  • In calculating appropriate levels of licence fee, average estimated benefits were mainly used, but this meant that in some years the cost of a licence was greater than the expected benefits.
  • If this were to occur several years in a row, foreign fishers may become reluctant to renew their licences.
  • Under these circumstances, it might be necessary to develop innovative solutions to the problem.
  • Additional benefits can be generated from alternative sources of revenue.
  • In addition to the two sources of revenue commonly used in models.
    • From the sale of licence fees and fines generated from successfully prosecuting illegal vessels, there are a number of other benefits that can be generated from foreign fishing activities such as transhipment fees and port facilities offering goods, services and value added processing.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Management guidelines for Asian floodplain river fisheries: ID 4477.
  • Trainer's guide to control blowfly infestation of traditionally processed fish: ID 4464.
  • Potential yield of south Asian small reservoir fisheries: ID 4474.
  • ParFish toolkit: a participatory fisheries stock assessment approach: ID 4476.
  • Management of flood control, drainage and irrigation (FCDI) sluice gates: ID 4479.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently combines a series of practices of fee level, surveillance expenditure, and magnitude of legal penalties. This leads to optimal risk minimization of illegal fishing and fishermen benefit maximization.

    • Vessel owners may choose instead to forfeit the vessel, particularly when vessel value is low.
    • The value of the vessel may be the best estimate of the maximum possible fine.
    • It is better to calculate licence fees as a proportion of the marginal benefit arising from fishing inside the EEZ, rather than as a proportion of the catch taken inside the EEZ.
    • This is because the value to the fishers of obtaining a licence arises from the difference between the catches that can be taken inside and those taken outside, rather than just the amount of catch taken from the EEZ.

2. Results

  • Results from the case studies showed that strong inter-annual variability could occur from the expected benefits of fishing inside the zone.
  • In calculating appropriate levels of licence fee, average estimated benefits were mainly used, but this meant that in some years the cost of a licence was greater than the expected benefits.
  • If this were to occur several years in a row, foreign fishers may become reluctant to renew their licences.
  • Under these circumstances, it might be necessary to develop innovative solutions to the problem.
  • Additional benefits can be generated from alternative sources of revenue.
  • In addition to the two sources of revenue commonly used in models.
    • From the sale of licence fees and fines generated from successfully prosecuting illegal vessels, there are a number of other benefits that can be generated from foreign fishing activities such as transhipment fees and port facilities offering goods, services and value added processing.

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Management guidelines for Asian floodplain river fisheries: ID 4477.
  • Trainer's guide to control blowfly infestation of traditionally processed fish: ID 4464.
  • Potential yield of south Asian small reservoir fisheries: ID 4474.
  • ParFish toolkit: a participatory fisheries stock assessment approach: ID 4476.
  • Management of flood control, drainage and irrigation (FCDI) sluice gates: ID 4479.

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently combines a series of practices of fee level, surveillance expenditure, and magnitude of legal penalties. This leads to optimal risk minimization of illegal fishing and fishermen benefit maximization.

records.title: Ecologically-based and sustainable rodent control strategies
records.description:
Description

1. Rodent control

  • Rodents are the biggest vertebrate problem in Africa.
  • They consume and damage large quantities of stored grains and food and damage crops in the field.
  • They carry diseases that can be transmitted to humans (e.g. Leptospirosis and Toxoplasmosis).
    • These diseases are responsible for considerable economic loss in terms of decreased worker productivity and health care-costs.
  • Rodents also eat and damage bedding, furniture and other items in the household.
  • Governments tend to control them through the use of rodenticides.
    • However, these conventional methods have remained largely ineffective.
  • Apart from Tanzania, there are few studies which have attempted to develop rodent management strategies for field rodent pests.
    • Therefore, before the technology could be developed, an ecological study of rodent species in the project areas was carried out in the Limpopo province and KwaZulu Natal in South Africa; and the Zambezia province in Mozambique.
  • Eighteen different rodent species were collected.
    • The most common rat species found was the black or house rat Rattus.
    • Other rats found included:
      • Aethomys chrysophilus,
      • Aethomys namaquensis,
      • Aethomys ineptus,
      • Mastomys natalensis,
      • Mastomys coucha,
      • Dasymyus incomtus,
      • Lemniscomys rosalia,
      • Mus musculus,
      • Mus minutoides,
      • Otomys angoniensis,
      • Pelomys fallax,
      • Rhabdomys pumilio,
      • Saccostomus campestris,
      • Steatomys sp.,
      • Tatera brantsii,
      • Tatera leucogaster,
      • Elephantulus sp., and
      • Mysorex sp.
    • The oriental rat Rattus tanezumi was trapped in Africa for the first time ever.
    • Most of these were found in kitchens and storage rooms.
  • An understanding of peoples’ socioeconomic background and knowledge of rodents had to be obtained.
  • In this study farmers identified rodents as both pre and post harvest pests (by both men and women).
  • Post harvest hygiene and waste management were linked to rodents and these issues needed to be dealt with at a community level.
  • Rodents also bite people at night.
  • Farmers were surprised as to how many rodents were caught in traps in a trial and admitted that they knew little about the ecology of the rodents.
  • The rodenticide Rattex® was used by 62 percent of those surveyed but two-thirds of these stated that it was ineffective.
    • Although this might be due to them not seeing evidence of dead rats.
  • People use the name rattex to describe any of a number of rodenticides.
    • Due to the apparent ineffectiveness of rattex, the illegal use of Aldicarb to control rodents has become popular.
    • Aldicarb is normally used on crops to control chewing and sucking insects and nematode worms.
    • Aldicarb is classified by the World Health Organization as a Class Ia 'extremely hazardous' pesticide.
  • Kill traps and glue boards were also available but people complained that the kill trap was difficult to use and “not strong”.
    • However, demand for these traps increased when householders saw the effectiveness of the break-back traps in the demonstrations.
      • Rodent control measures in Mozambique, the effectiveness of the American break-back trap ,and the Indian multi-catch trap was shown and a company agreed to manufacture them locally.
      • In South Africa a pest control company has agreed to modify and manufacture the “Kness” break-back trap.
        • The engagement of a local manufacturer ensures sustainable supply and an appropriate pricing structure.
        • These traps have been proved to be cost effective when compared with alternatives such as rodenticides.
  • Open structure granaries used for maize storage were often less than 1 m from the ground, allowing rodents free access.
    • These can be relatively easily modified to make them rat proof.
    • This was the focus of another project, the details of which can be found in TECA record "Mud plaster and concrete for protection of grain stores from insects and rodents and reduced use of scarce wood construction materials".
  • In a similar manner, dwellings and other buildings can also be made less accessible to rodent entry.
  • Local government improvement to the infrastructure, water provision and waste management also reduce rodent populations and the risk of zoonotic transmission.

2. Awareness raising

  • Due to the ineffectiveness of previous control measures, there was a need for widespread awareness raising before farmers would consider adoption of these technologies.
    • The awareness raising comprised demonstrations to communities and government agricultural extension on the effectiveness of trapping as a management tool as well as the effectiveness of the break-back trap.
    • As literacy amongst the target population was found to be low, regional radio stations were used to promote effective rodent-control management and why it is important.
  • Farmers needed to be aware of the rodent lifecycle, that due to external factors the rodent population will vary and so they should not become less vigilant.
  • The researchers found that many households did not set the traps every night and this led to a reduction in the number of catches.
    • Policy change was required to improve rodent control.
  • In this case, changes were required to the training of government and municipal health and environmental health personnel to the Register: Agricultural remedies and Stock remedies (Act 36 of 1947) and to the Pest Control Service Industries Board.
    • These changes will better inform staff and pest control operators on how best to control rodents through the improved use of rodenticides or through other measures.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour saving technologies and practices: improved storage facilities: ID 7308.
  • Using plants with pesticidal properties to control insects during on-farm grain storage; ID 4506.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

The practice, through rodent control, provides food security and income generation for poor households.

records.title: Disease resistant upland maize varieties validated by and promoted to farmers
records.description:
Description

The Southern Highlands of Tanzania (comprising Iringa, Ruvuma, Mbeya and Rukwa regions) provide the most favourable climatic conditions for the production of maize in the country. They account for almost 50 percent of the total national maize production and up to 90 percent of the annual purchase of maize for the national strategic grain reserve. Maize Grey Leaf Spot (GLS) (Cercospora zeae maydis) was first reported in the Southern Highlands during the 1995/1996 cropping season causing grain yield losses ranging from 15 to 40 percent.

By 1998 this disease had spread to all four regions of the Southern Highlands. All local cultivars, as well as most of the commercial maize varieties under cultivation across the zone during that season, succumbed to the disease. The farmers already had to face the Maize Streak Virus (MSV), which during epidemics can cause up to 80 percent loss in maize grain yield. Instances of complete crop loss are not uncommon.

This disease is a particularly serious problem in irrigated maize and where maize is grown out of season and obtains a premium in the market. In the intermediate altitude maize growing parts of the Southern Highlands, up to 43 percent of sampled farmers identified MSV as a serious constraint to maize production.

1. Resistant varieties of maize

  • Researchers were aware that in other environments, genetic resistance to these diseases had been identified.
    • The Maize Improvement Programme (MIP) at Uyole Agricultural Research Institute commenced a massive screening and evaluation of both local and exotic commercial and pre-commercial maize varieties and inbred lines for GLS tolerance.
  • Evaluation of the GLS-tolerant germplasm, both on-station and on-farm, in these districts confirmed the superiority of several potential new maize hybrids.
    • One of which was officially released during the 2000/2001 season under the name UH615.
    • A further GLS-tolerant hybrid, UH6303, was approved for release in late 2004.
  • The farmers state that, in addition to their disease resistance, they like these varieties and that they produce more than their local varieties.
    • There is now a high demand.
    • Other MSV-tolerant (but not GLS-tolerant) OPVs (Open Pollinated Varieties) were also available, e.g. Staha and TMV1.
    • Variety trials conducted in Mbarali district had found that this tolerance was inadequate under the very early and severe MSV disease occurring irrigated areas, where vectors and disease are maintained year-round.
    • Research is continuing at the MIP to identify suitable resistant OPV lines.

2. Farmer involvement

  • The major constraint the researchers faced was that developing resistant seed does not in itself benefit farmers.
    • Mechanisms need to be in place for the multiplication and provision of seed.
    • This was a major constraint the researchers had to address.
  • Tanzania has been without an organized system for local seed production and distribution since 2000, when the national seed company, TANSEED, collapsed.
    • This situation had severely limited farmers’ access to locally bred, certified and disease-resistant seed, particularly in rural areas.
    • Most of the certified seed, which was marketed through a limited distribution network, had been of questionable purity.
    • In many cases, the seed exhibited unacceptably low rates of germination with, understandably, farmers losing their faith in a certified seed.
  • With respect to seed from improved maize varieties, there has been a significant increase in price and a subsequent decline in returns on the crop.
    • Farmers appear to have adapted their livelihood strategies in response by:
      • growing a larger area of maize to compensate for a decline in fertilizer use,
      • switching to other crops,
      • reducing the amount of improved certified seed purchased, and
      • making greater use of the recycled seed.
    • The returns from the crop have declined and the labour invested in it has increased.
  • The current situation is still associated with a lack of trust or confidence held by farmers in improved crop varieties from seed companies and other institutions dealing with seed distribution.
    • In order to build the farmers’ trust, the project team embarked on a large-scale awareness campaign of roadside trials, published materials and the use of the media to inform farmers of the varieties that had been developed.
    • This was initially done through the public sector and community organizations.
    • It became clear that the private sector was required to generate sufficient quantities of high-quality seed.
  • The team have therefore been working with Highland Seed Growers Limited who have developed a strategy to multiply, promote and market the seed in the Southern Highlands.
    • They are already marketing UH615 and are using small packs, on-farm demonstrations and other marketing tools.
    • They are working in close partnership with the relevant public sector organizations.
    • Details of their involvement can be found in Appendix 3 of (Lyimo, N.G. 2006).
    • There is clear potential for the scaling out of these varieties to highland areas in other countries
    • http://www.fao.org/docs/eims/upload/agrotech/1974/R8406_FTR.pdf.
  • The Ugandan authorities have approved the release of UH615 and UH6303 and FICA Ltd has been licensed to market these varieties.
    • In addition to developing farmer acceptable disease-resistant seed, the research identified the need for and provided farmer training on seed, soil and pest and disease management.

3. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Maize harvesting and post-harvesting handling: ID 7015.
  • Pests and diseases management in maize: ID 7019.
  • Evergreen Agriculture: conservation agriculture in maize production: ID 7846.
  • Well dried maize benefits all: the solar maize dryer: ID 8285.
  • Drought-tolerant maize varieties: ID 8920.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology effectively combats crop diseases, leading to improved cob, higher yields and better resistance. It has also efficiently led to collaborations of farmers with the private sector.

records.title: Development and promotion of wild rice management strategies
records.description:
Description

Rice is the second most important cereal crop in Tanzania, after maize and the majority of rice farmers depend on it both for food and as a cash crop. However, highly competitive annual and perennial wild rice species have been identified as one of the important constraints to rice production on lowlands in southern Tanzania. In addition to competing with the crop, these weed species are the only known alternative hosts for African Rice Gall Midge (ARGM) and are important hosts for Rice Yellow Mottle Virus (RYMV), both of which are major pests of rice in sub-Saharan Africa.

Wild rices contribute to low yields on the large parastatal farms in Tanzania. Due to low profitability, substantial portions of these enterprises have subsequently been handed over to smallholder farmers but the problems of wild rice persist with current agronomic practice and smallholder farmers may abandon these fields leading to severe problems for affected households and a wider impact on the local economy.

Most lowland rice farmers currently use little or no fertilizer or manure and the majority use the photoperiod - sensitive late maturing (160 to 170 days) tall cultivar 'Super India'. This responds poorly under intensive and high input management. When the rains end early there is risk of terminal drought with long duration cultivars. A new lowland rice cultivar TXD 306 (SARO 5), developed in Tanzania, is rapidly becoming popular in Kilombero as it is aromatic (a trait demanded by the market in Tanzania) and high yielding.

However, this non-photoperiod sensitive cultivar, which matures in 130 days is a semi-dwarf that is less competitive with wild rice than the traditional types, thus compounding the need for improved management of wild rice weeds.

1. Control of wild rice species

  • Under CPP project R8198, seven farmer-research groups (128 farm households) undertook demonstration trials on 32 wild rice infested farms.
  • Participatory evaluation during field days and sensitization workshops involved more than 230 rice producers from seven villages within the project areas.
  • Farmers identified the use of glyphosate before planting at the rate of 3 litres per ha for the control of annual wild rice (Oryza punctata on irrigated land) and 4 litres per ha for the control of perennial wild rice (O. longistaminata on rain-fed fields) as the best options for the management of these weeds.
  • Post-emergence application of 2,4-D (2.5 l pro ha) at 21 days after germination was favoured to reduce labour inputs for in-crop weed control.
  • Partial budget analysis undertaken with growers, district agricultural extension staff, village chairmen and ward executive officers demonstrated the benefits of improving wild rice management.

records.title: Green manure for enhancing upland rice productivity on Striga-infested fields
records.description:
Description

Upland rice is an important cash crop in many areas of eastern and southern Tanzania, including Morogoro Rural and Kyela districts. Under continuous cultivation, rice yields have been in decline in recent years. This is associated with falling soil fertility and an increase in infestation by the parasitic witchweed, Striga asiatica. Working with farmers in Kyela since 1996, CPP project R7564 demonstrated that up to 60 percent reduction in Striga numbers and a 45 percent increase in rice yield could be achieved by applying urea fertilizer. However, farmers could not widely adopt the use of urea because they lacked liquidity for fertilizer purchase.

1. Crotalaria ochroleuca as a green manure

The green manure species Crotalaria ochroleuca, (sunn hemp) also called “Marejea” in Kiswahili, presented an alternative approach to managing Striga. This had been grown for many years at St Benedict’s Abbey, Peramiho, southern Tanzania, where it is used to maintain the fertility of organic gardens. At Peramiho, “Marejea” grows up to a height of 2 m and has been found to be fairly drought tolerant, recovering well when rain returns. When broadcasted as a sole crop, growth is vigorous so that weeds are suppressed.

Sunn hemp's many uses include:

  • green manure;
  • nitrogen fixation;
  • weed suppression;
  • livestock forage; and
  • pest control.

Farmers in Tanzania have found tillage easier in fields where sunn hemp has been grown and incorporated into the soil.

  • The improved soil texture facilitates ploughing before the rains, giving crops the benefit of the full rainy season.
  • The plant’s deep root system aerates the soil, increases water infiltration and retards soil erosion.
  • Unlike most nitrogen-fixing legumes, sunn hemp performs well on poor and acidic soils.
  • Under appropriate conditions, it establishes quickly and grows abundantly, thus out competing weeds.
  • If planted densely, sunn hemp prevents weed growth in the first year and reduces subsequent weed growth for the following one to three years.
  • Sunn hemp can outcompete couch grass (Digitaria sp.) but not blackjack (Bidens pilosa).
  • Over the course of three years, sunn hemp eventually outcompetes star grass (Cynodon sp.) in paddies.
  • It is also known from the literature and experimental results from CPP project R7564 that Crotalaria is not a host of Striga but stimulates the “suicide” germination of the seed.
  • Farmers in Tanzania have found that sunn hemp can constitute 60 percent of cattle feed and the unused stems can be mixed with manure to make compost.
  • Chickens will eat any part of the sunn hemp plant except for the seeds.
  • Sunn hemp can also be used to feed tilapia.
  • One acre can yield up to 100 kg to 300 kg of seeds worth Tsh 600 per kilo.
  • Some farmers let their cattle graze sunn hemp for one hour a day if they do not want to harvest the seed.
    • A number of farmers were familiar with “Marejea” from previous projects but viewed these as “just experimental” and there seems to have been limited farmer participation, little reporting of field activities and no follow-up promotion.
  • Under project R7564, seed from Peramiho was planted by two farmer groups in Kyela in 2001 and farmers were very impressed by the growth of these plots, especially on what the community judged to be poor, worked out lands.
    • They observed that no Striga emerged on a rice plot previously sown to “Marejea”, which yielded 2 100 kg-ha-1 rice compared to 1000 kg where no fertilizer was used and 1 600 and 1 900 kg ha-1 respectively where 25 and 50 kg N ha-1 had been applied.
  • Following village seminars, 33 farmers requested seed of Crotalaria to plant in the 2002 season and the process of farmer evaluation of green manure, which was initiated by the research team, subsequently became farmer-driven.
  • A new CPP project (R8194) was designed to promote the use of Crotolaria as a green manure for improving the fertility of Striga-infested upland rice.
    • The project was led by Ilonga Agricultural Research Institute with local partners including district agricultural extension and primary school education staff, the NGO INADES, a soil fertility specialist from Mlingano Agricultural Research Institute, a social economist from Sokoine University of Agriculture, and staff from the Natural Resources Institute, UK.
  • A number of promising new pigeon pea cultivars with resistance to the soil-borne wilt disease, Fusarium udum were included in the legume/rice rotations as an alternative to Crotalaria, as pigeon pea provides an economic grain yield and improves nitrogen and phosphorus availability to the soil.
    • This project, extended by CPP project R8436, developed technologies to promote soil fertility enhancement for control of Striga.
    • The major focus was on participatory evaluation and promotion of Striga management practices with farmer groups, who undertook on-farm demonstrations used as sites for field days.
  • In addition, strategies were developed for the up-scaling promotion of legume rotations through interaction with extension workers, NGO staff, district council policymakers and ward officials, and a primary school programme incorporating knowledge on Striga and improvement of soil fertility in agricultural science classes.

1.1 Cultivation of sunn hemp

  • Experienced sunn hemp farmers mix 10 kg of seed for every 0.5 hectares to be planted with sand or dry soil at the ratio of 1:2 litres to assure a proper planting density (plants spaced 10 cm to 15 cm apart).
  • Above ground, growth is slow initially, as the plants develop deep roots.
  • Eventually, sunn hemp reaches a height of 2 m or more, and flowers appear three to four months later.
  • Sunn hemp does not re-seed itself, since its pods stay closed after the seeds have matured, even protecting them for months into the rainy season.
  • After six months the plants begin to senesce.
    • The stems, however, may persist for as long as eight or nine months and will develop new leaves when cut 30 cm above ground, or when eaten by animals.

2. Participatory evaluation and promotion of Striga management practices

  • On-farm demonstrations were led by groups with a total membership of 239 farmers in 11 villages of Kyela and Matombo districts.
  • Yields recorded from six villages confirmed previous observations from a smaller sample of sites that a one-year break from continuous cereal cropping to plant either the green manure, Crotalaria ochroleuca,  or pigeon pea leads to significantly higher rice or maize yields (p<0.001).
  • Median rice yields were increased by more than 1 000 kg and 800 kg in Kibangile and across Kyela district villages, respectively, by planting rice following the use of Crotalaria as green manure (234 and 81 percent increases respectively over continuous rice).
  • Use of either Crotalaria or pigeon pea increased median maize yield by an average of 188 percent in Kibangile and by 269 percent in Kiswira villages in Matombo.
  • Farmers reported a reduction in Striga abundance with an associated increase in rice vigour on fields where green manures had been planted.
  • By adopting rotations in Kyela, rice yields were boosted on the poorest fields from two to three to seven to eight bags per acre, and farmers believed they were on course to achieve more than ten bags per acre, making rice production very profitable again.
    • Individuals believed that the use of the rotations has reached the stage of sustained adoption with plots of more than one acre on some farms in Kilasilo.

3. Strategies up-scaling promotion of legume rotations

  • Assistance was provided to strengthen the structure of farmer groups and their plans for improving sustainability, including poster and leaflet training materials (Figure 1).
  • Additional extension materials included a training manual, picture set and series of videos.
  • Collaboration between district council agricultural extension and education staff was strengthened.
  • A primary school programme incorporating knowledge on Striga and improvement of soil fertility was supported in 21 villages.
    • Pupils were taught about soil fertility management as the key to reducing Striga abundance and reversing the yield decline.
    • School demonstration plots provided an important source of green manure seed for farmers.
  • Subsequently, a stakeholder workshop drew up plans for up-scaling promotion beyond the life of the project.
    • This led to Kyela district council allocating funds for the promotion of project outputs from 2006.
    • Ten lead farmers will be trained in all villages in the district.
    • A plan to expand promotion in four additional wards in the Uluguru mountains, where both rice and maize are important, have also been formulated by Morogoro District council.
    • CARE International has also initiated promotion work using extension materials developed by the project in four villages in the Uluguru mountains.
  • Policy implications from this work are that farmer group learning approaches including exchange visits and demonstration plots are keys to successful promotion.
  • The partnership between district council agricultural extension and education teams to involve primary schools in the promotion of agricultural knowledge should be expanded.
Figure 1. Poster

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Green manure/cover crops and crop rotation in conservation agriculture on small farms: ID 7250
  • Green manuring in sugarcane production for soil improvement and water efficiency, Tamil Nadu, India: ID 8768

This technology is available in Portuguese: ID 2550.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology uses sun hemp as an alternative for manure, livestock forage, nitrogen fixation and weed suppression. It has multiple benefits, is natural, and increases yield.

6.2 Pro-poor technology 

This technology is pro-poor as it replaces the need to purchase urea fertiliser and increases rice yields simultaneously.

  • Under project R7564, seed from Peramiho was planted by two farmer groups in Kyela in 2001 and farmers were very impressed by the growth of these plots, especially on what the community judged to be poor, worked out lands.
    • They observed that no Striga emerged on a rice plot previously sown to “Marejea”, which yielded 2 100 kg-ha-1 rice compared to 1000 kg where no fertilizer was used and 1 600 and 1 900 kg ha-1 respectively where 25 and 50 kg N ha-1 had been applied.
  • Following village seminars, 33 farmers requested seed of Crotalaria to plant in the 2002 season and the process of farmer evaluation of green manure, which was initiated by the research team, subsequently became farmer-driven.
  • A new CPP project (R8194) was designed to promote the use of Crotolaria as a green manure for improving the fertility of Striga-infested upland rice.
    • The project was led by Ilonga Agricultural Research Institute with local partners including district agricultural extension and primary school education staff, the NGO INADES, a soil fertility specialist from Mlingano Agricultural Research Institute, a social economist from Sokoine University of Agriculture, and staff from the Natural Resources Institute, UK.
  • A number of promising new pigeon pea cultivars with resistance to the soil-borne wilt disease, Fusarium udum were included in the legume/rice rotations as an alternative to Crotalaria, as pigeon pea provides an economic grain yield and improves nitrogen and phosphorus availability to the soil.
    • This project, extended by CPP project R8436, developed technologies to promote soil fertility enhancement for control of Striga.
    • The major focus was on participatory evaluation and promotion of Striga management practices with farmer groups, who undertook on-farm demonstrations used as sites for field days.
  • In addition, strategies were developed for the up-scaling promotion of legume rotations through interaction with extension workers, NGO staff, district council policymakers and ward officials, and a primary school programme incorporating knowledge on Striga and improvement of soil fertility in agricultural science classes.

1.1 Cultivation of sunn hemp

  • Experienced sunn hemp farmers mix 10 kg of seed for every 0.5 hectares to be planted with sand or dry soil at the ratio of 1:2 litres to assure a proper planting density (plants spaced 10 cm to 15 cm apart).
  • Above ground, growth is slow initially, as the plants develop deep roots.
  • Eventually, sunn hemp reaches a height of 2 m or more, and flowers appear three to four months later.
  • Sunn hemp does not re-seed itself, since its pods stay closed after the seeds have matured, even protecting them for months into the rainy season.
  • After six months the plants begin to senesce.
    • The stems, however, may persist for as long as eight or nine months and will develop new leaves when cut 30 cm above ground, or when eaten by animals.

2. Participatory evaluation and promotion of Striga management practices

  • On-farm demonstrations were led by groups with a total membership of 239 farmers in 11 villages of Kyela and Matombo districts.
  • Yields recorded from six villages confirmed previous observations from a smaller sample of sites that a one-year break from continuous cereal cropping to plant either the green manure, Crotalaria ochroleuca,  or pigeon pea leads to significantly higher rice or maize yields (p<0.001).
  • Median rice yields were increased by more than 1 000 kg and 800 kg in Kibangile and across Kyela district villages, respectively, by planting rice following the use of Crotalaria as green manure (234 and 81 percent increases respectively over continuous rice).
  • Use of either Crotalaria or pigeon pea increased median maize yield by an average of 188 percent in Kibangile and by 269 percent in Kiswira villages in Matombo.
  • Farmers reported a reduction in Striga abundance with an associated increase in rice vigour on fields where green manures had been planted.
  • By adopting rotations in Kyela, rice yields were boosted on the poorest fields from two to three to seven to eight bags per acre, and farmers believed they were on course to achieve more than ten bags per acre, making rice production very profitable again.
    • Individuals believed that the use of the rotations has reached the stage of sustained adoption with plots of more than one acre on some farms in Kilasilo.

3. Strategies up-scaling promotion of legume rotations

  • Assistance was provided to strengthen the structure of farmer groups and their plans for improving sustainability, including poster and leaflet training materials (Figure 1).
  • Additional extension materials included a training manual, picture set and series of videos.
  • Collaboration between district council agricultural extension and education staff was strengthened.
  • A primary school programme incorporating knowledge on Striga and improvement of soil fertility was supported in 21 villages.
    • Pupils were taught about soil fertility management as the key to reducing Striga abundance and reversing the yield decline.
    • School demonstration plots provided an important source of green manure seed for farmers.
  • Subsequently, a stakeholder workshop drew up plans for up-scaling promotion beyond the life of the project.
    • This led to Kyela district council allocating funds for the promotion of project outputs from 2006.
    • Ten lead farmers will be trained in all villages in the district.
    • A plan to expand promotion in four additional wards in the Uluguru mountains, where both rice and maize are important, have also been formulated by Morogoro District council.
    • CARE International has also initiated promotion work using extension materials developed by the project in four villages in the Uluguru mountains.
  • Policy implications from this work are that farmer group learning approaches including exchange visits and demonstration plots are keys to successful promotion.
  • The partnership between district council agricultural extension and education teams to involve primary schools in the promotion of agricultural knowledge should be expanded.
Figure 1. Poster

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Green manure/cover crops and crop rotation in conservation agriculture on small farms: ID 7250
  • Green manuring in sugarcane production for soil improvement and water efficiency, Tamil Nadu, India: ID 8768

This technology is available in Portuguese: ID 2550.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology uses sun hemp as an alternative for manure, livestock forage, nitrogen fixation and weed suppression. It has multiple benefits, is natural, and increases yield.

6.2 Pro-poor technology 

This technology is pro-poor as it replaces the need to purchase urea fertiliser and increases rice yields simultaneously.

_annotations.field_innovation_identified:
INNOVATION: Green manure sunn hemp (Crotalaria ochroleuca) for Striga control

DESCRIPTION: Using sunn hemp as green manure to control Striga parasitic weed in upland rice, replacing expensive urea fertilizer. The innovation shows multiple benefits: Striga reduction, soil fertility improvement, yield increase, and additional uses as fodder and food.

CRITERIA MET: Existing solution (green manure) used to solve a new problem (Striga control); pro-poor technology; supports behavioral change from chemical to organic fertilization.
_annotations.field_shorter_description: Upland rice is an important cash crop in many areas of eastern and southern Tanzania, including Morogoro Rural and Kyela districts. Under continuous cultivation, rice yields have been in decline in recent years. This is associated with falling soil fertility and an increase in infestation by the parasitic witchweed, Striga asiatica. Working with farmers in Kyela since 1996, CPP project R7564 demonstrated that up to 60 percent reduction in Striga numbers and a 45 percent increase in rice yield could be achieved by applying urea fertiliser. However, farmers could not widely adopt the use of urea because they lacked liquidity for fertilizer purchase. The following technology promotes using green manure species Crotalaria ochroleuca, (sunn hemp; also called "Marejea" in Kiswahili), to manage Striga asiatica and improve soil fertility in upland rice in Tanzania.

records.title: Development and promotion of quality kale seed
records.description:
Description

The use of quality seeds along with other inputs and appropriate cultural management practices is recognized as the most cost effective way of increasing crop production and productivity. In considering interventions that are likely to reverse the trend of recurring food shortages, seed security has been recognized as having the potential for achieving significant advances in food productivity and production.

Recognising the importance of healthy seed, a previous Crop Protection Product (CPP) project (see Spence 2003) engaged farmers in participatory research on selection criteria for kale plants for seed production. Both suitable (healthy) and unsuitable (diseased) plants were selected by both farmers and researchers for the production of seed, and the resulting seed was grown and evaluated. All of the 19 farmers chose plots with researcher-selected and farmer-selected healthy seeds as their preferred plots. Farmers were very keen to gain knowledge on how to improve the quality of farmer-collected seed.

This research generated great demand from farmers to know good seeds from bad seeds in the local market, because it is not possible to know what type of plants (diseased or healthy) the seeds came from when the seed is being sold. The work also found that farmers in the Kinale region were growing locally adapted landraces of kale (the most important vegetable crop in Kenya in terms of acreage grown), with superior characteristics, including field resistance to several virus diseases.

A subsequent project (see Spence 2005, part 1 and part 2) made progress in understanding farmers’ perceptions and needs with respect to seed purchases. The project identified a strong interest from Kinale farmers in multiplying and marketing seed with improved seed health and quality. An inventory of brassica seeds in Kenya was drawn up from commercial seed companies and local markets. Significant progress was made in analysis of Kinale kale as a distinctive variety, in close collaboration with KEPHIS inspectors using International Union for the Protection of new varieties of Plants (UPOV) guidelines.

Kinale farmers and the project research team selected five kale lines from a trial of 24 lines at the KARI field station at Njabini in the Kinangop for detailed varietal characterisation. These lines (CABI 1, CABI 2, CABI 3, CABI 4, CABI 5) were tested over two seasons for Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS) to carry out trials for distinctness, uniformity and stability (DUS). This gave farmers the option to choose whether to register varieties in a commercial seed business.

1. Seed multiplication

  • Potential models for sustainable seed multiplication of kale were evaluated through on-farm participatory trials in Kinale and on-station at Njabini.
    • This enabled farmers to establish a sustainable kale seed multiplication system that allows smallholders to produce healthy seed of good quality and that has an acceptable market value.
    • The feasibility of a community-based approach to seed multiplication in Kinale and potential for establishing and registering a commercial seed business in Kinale, was been examined.
    • Farmers were keen to pursue this approach.
  • Good seed multiplication practice for kale and seed certification using a preferred model was promoted.
    • However, farmers sought to go beyond this by seeking to formally register Kinale seed varieties under a community-based seed company model and to have a formal release of their varieties.
    • Further work was supported under a follow-up project (see Spence 2006 part 1 and part 2), which included two important activities.
      1. To continue to promote sustainable seed production technologies for farmer-led multiplication of improved kale varieties to smallholder farmers in the Kinale region of peri-urban Kenya.
        • This was in order to improve the quality, health and availability of kale seed to smallholder farmers.
      2. To facilitate the registration and release process of new varieties of Kinale kale whilst also supporting existing informal farmer-to-farmer distribution, under the regulation of KEPHIS and in collaboration with KARI and NGOs.
  • Two particular technologies that resulted from this work.
    1. Evaluation of new kale seed lines.
    2. Promotion of sustainable seed production technologies.

1.1 Evaluation of new kale seed lines

  • Selfed kale seeds from five of the preferred improved kale lines (CABI 1-5) identified by project R8312 were submitted to KEPHIS headquarters, along with documentation detailing their specific characteristics.
    • Trials for DUS were established and seed officers monitored improved kale lines at various developmental stages.
    • Data obtained will enable KEPHIS to decide if the lines are new varieties.
    • DUS trials were completed in December 2005 and the project team was advised informally that improved kale lines did perform significantly better than check varieties.
    • Submission of seeds to National Performance Trials proved unnecessary.
  • Improved kales were planted to evaluate their performance, compared to local varieties, in different agroecological zones in peri-urban Nairobi and Western Kenya.
    • In addition, over one hundred smallholders cultivated improved kales on their farms, and completed evaluation questionnaires.
    • The performances of the five improved kale lines varied considerably between sites, but consistently surpassed the commonly grown commercial variety, 1000 headed kale.
    • In western Kenya, improved lines also out-performed variety Sikuma Siku.
    • Although productivity of improved lines rarely exceeded that of another commercial variety (collards), some improved lines achieved particularly steady leaf yields, indicating their productivity could be sustained after yields decline in other kale varieties.
  • Feedback received from farmers’ participatory trials was overwhelmingly positive.
    • Improved kale lines germinated faster, transplanted better, and provided a longer period for leaf harvesting than the farmers’ own kale varieties.
    • Improved lines were larger, and more resistant to attack by pests and diseases, and farmers perceived the colour and shape of their leaves to be superior to those of local counterparts.
    • They had a shorter cooking time and were also more palatable.
  • The vast majority of farmers ranked the improved kale lines as having a greater consumer appeal than any other kale varieties they normally grow.
    • They were willing to buy the seeds of improved lines for their own use and would recommend these lines to other growers.
  • When the performance of three commercial kales (collards, 1 000 headed and Sukuma Siku) were compared against the five improved varieties in Western Kenya, 1 000 headed kale was found to be particularly susceptible to black rot disease.

1.2 Promotion of sustainable seed production technologies

  • Multiplication plots were established to ensure sufficient seed stocks to meet future demands of farmers for these improved kale lines.
    • Large batches of seed were ready for harvesting just after the project ended.
    • Participatory multiplications provided performance data on the improved kale lines for use, while defending the lines during the KEPHIS variety release committee.
  • A farmer group carried out their own pilot study to scale-up seed multiplication, observing the isolation distance recommended by KEPHIS.
    • This was done in readiness to become seed multipliers in the future.
    • One farmer provided land, and the group paid for a labourer to tend the plot.
  • Following consultations with IPGRI and KARI, seeds of all lines developed, including the five improved kale lines CABI 1-5, were deposited in the KARI genetic resources unit (Muguga), and in the vegetable gene bank (Warwick-HRI).
  • To promote sustainable seed production technologies, on-farm participatory demonstration plots were established with existing farmer groups in Lari division.
  • In preparation for continuous multiplication/commercialisation of the improved kale seeds, Lari Division farmers had extensive discussions amongst themselves and the Community Development Authority.
    • As a result, they obtained official registration and authority from the District Social Development Officer, under the National Community Development Programme in Kenya.
  • Multiple copies of posters (in Swahili) describing self-selection of seeds and its promotion were given to more than 70 farmers for further distribution.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, cool.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Development and promotion of community-based seed production: ID 4551.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology is cost-effective and increases crop production and productivity. Therefore, it prevents recurring food shortages, providing additional sources of food and income.

records.title: Crop protection: early warning systems for improved Quelea bird management
records.description:
Description

Small-grain cereal crops, throughout semi-arid areas of Africa are subject to damage by the Red-billed Quelea bird Quelea quelea of up to USD 45 million per annum. Control of concentrations of thousands of the birds, gathered in breeding colonies or nocturnal roosts, involves the aerial application of organophosphate pesticides or fire-bombs created by the detonation with explosives of mixtures of diesel and petrol. The environmental impact of these activities has not been adequately researched but it is widely recognised that means to minimise the effects are required.

Another researchable constraint is the difficulty of knowing where and when the birds will occur and where they will require control in the extensive semi-arid regions that they live in. This difficulty arises mainly because Quelea is migratory, moving in relation to the timing and distribution of rainfall and the availability of annual grass seeds, the birds’ principal food. Genetically homogenous populations of the subspecies Q. quelea lathamii migrate throughout the southern African region.

In addition to demonstrating their genetic uniformity, CPP projects R6823 (Cheke, 1999) and R7967 (Cheke 2003 Part 1 and Part 2) developed a model for forecasting where and when the birds could breed in southern Africa. The model forecasts the timing and locations of suitable sites where Quelea breeding colonies could require control to prevent the successful fledging of juveniles.

The model uses satellite-derived estimates of rainfall to determine when the threshold quantity of rainfall (60 mm to 70 mm, estimated from the duration of cold cloud at 38°C or below), has been exceeded at any time within a two-week period. This quantity is required to cause grass seed germination and hence to initiate the “early rains migration” by the birds out of their dry season quarters.

When sufficient time (six weeks) has elapsed since the germination of the grass seeds, the satellite data are again used to determine whether sufficient rainfall (240 mm) has fallen to allow the birds to begin breeding.

Another output of these and subsequent projects, R8314 (Cheke, 2005) and R8426 (Cheke, 2006), was to develop and obtain standard protocols or codes of practice to ensure that environmental damage is minimised when birds threatening crops are controlled by aerial spraying their breeding colonies with the avicide “fenthion” or by the use of explosives to destroy nocturnal roosts, and obtain consensus for their adoption in Africa.

Protocols were devised for biodiversity assessment (vertebrates and invertebrates) and evaluation of potential ecological damage. These were to be used before and after Quelea control operations and to enhance the capacity of national organisations to implement the policies.

The projects also investigated the harvesting of Quelea bird nestlings as food for people as an alternative to environmentally questionable sprays and explosions. In parts of Botswana, harvesting Quelea nestlings from breeding colonies, just before they fledge, is a traditional practice for which demand could be further developed through assistance with local transportation, processing and marketing.

1. Model for short-term forecasting of red-billed Quelea breeding

  • The model was created to forecast where and when crops are likely to be damaged so that control teams in southern Africa can identify nesting colonies and target their operations more effectively.
    • Such planning has been difficult, as Quelea birds are long-distance migrants, moving up to 2 500 km in response to the seasonal movements of rain-fronts.
  • Rain causes their main food, grass seeds, to germinate at the start of the wet season forcing birds to move to areas where the seeds have yet to germinate.
    • When rain reaches these areas, the birds are forced to move again, usually returning in “early-rains migrations” in the direction whence they came.
    • By this time sufficient rain needs to have fallen to exceed another threshold within a restricted period for the new grass to have produced fresh seed.
    • Breeding may then commence.
  • Over the following three to four months the birds then undertake further, previously unpredictable, “breeding migrations” to areas elsewhere wherever adequate rainfall will permit them to breed.
    • It is the young, newly fledged, birds that cause the most damage to agriculture.
    • Given the dependence of Quelea activities on rainfall, a model was devised that uses Spatio-temporal information on rainfall throughout southern Africa derived from satellite imagery.
  • The model is intended to provide only short-term predictions using the information on rainfall alone as real-time inputs.
    • The initial spatial scale chosen at the start of the development phase in 2001 was 1° X 1° squares with time steps of one week.
    • During 2002 the resolution of the model was improved to squares of 0.5° X 0.5°.
    • The model accumulates rainfall data throughout a Quelea season (September–May), starting at the beginning of September (calendar week 36, model week one)
    • For each square, the following questions are asked at the end of each week:
      • What was the total rainfall during the current week?
      • What was the total rainfall during the current week plus the previous week?
      • What was the total rainfall during the current week plus the previous four weeks?
  • The rainfall was estimated as one hour of Cold Cloud Duration (CCD cold cloud duration at 38°C or below) being equivalent to 3 mm of rain.
    • The model was programmed in a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet, in which worksheet cells represented every degree square for 2001/2002 or every 0.5 X 0.5 of a degree square, for 2002/2003, of the southern African region.
  • The cell value is given by a formula which implements the model criteria described above.
    • The model was run each week of the 2001/2002 and 2002/2003 seasons and seven days of CCD values were input for every run.
    • The model was originally developed and validated in 2002/2003 and the forecasting system has been disseminated widely to control planners, through the Information Core for Southern Africa Migrant Pests (ICOSAMP, http://icosamp.ecoport.org/) and other routes, and details can be found in (Cheke 2003 Part 1 and Part 2).
  • Regular weekly forecasts were produced and validated in subsequent seasons Cheke (2005) and operation of the model was transferred to the Southern African Development Community (SADC). 
  • Under project R8426, the existing Quelea forecasting model for southern Africa was expanded to include the East African distribution of Quelea quelea aethiopica.
    • In addition to Q. q. lathamii, two other subspecies of Q. quelea are recognised.
    • These are the nominate race (Q. q. Quelea) that inhabits the semi-arid region from Senegal to Chad and Q. q. aethiopica that occurs in Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, eastern parts of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda.
  • As migrations within and between these countries will be governed by the same rainfall thresholds and patterns that have been used to model those of Q. q. lathamii successfully, it was a comparatively simple task to extend the existing model to cover eastern Africa in an extension that has been requested by host countries.

2. Standardised protocols for monitoring effects of Quelea control on non-target organisms

  • Guidelines for standardised protocols for monitoring the effects of Quelea control on non-target organisms were developed based on the monitoring the impacts of Quelea control operations on the environment and non-target organisms under projects R7967 and R8314.
    • An early version of these guidelines was approved by representatives of East African countries at a workshop on Quelea management held in Kenya, 14-22 May 2005.
  • This also led to a proposal for Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) work on Quelea from the Tanzanian Government.
    • EIA is now a requirement for any undertaking in Tanzania that affects the environment under Section 81 (1) of the Environmental Management Act No. 20 of 2004 which came into effect in July 2005
    • See https://www.nemc.or.tz/ and http://www.lexadin.nl/wlg/legis/nofr/oeur/lxwetan.htm for further details.
  • Aerial spraying, including against Quelea, requires an EIA to be conducted as stipulated under Schedule 3 of the Act.

Crop protection: early warning systems for improved Quelea bird management

A short-term forecasting model (now adopted and implemented by the South African Development Community- SADC), predicts the movements and breeding of the Red-billed Quelea bird in southern Africa. This is to enable better mobilization and targeting of control resources by national and regional agencies, and methods for monitoring effects of Quelea control on the environment and non-target organisms agreed and adopted by regional authorities.



Description

Small-grain cereal crops, throughout semi-arid areas of Africa are subject to damage by the Red-billed Quelea bird Quelea quelea of up to USD 45 million per annum. Control of concentrations of thousands of the birds, gathered in breeding colonies or nocturnal roosts, involves the aerial application of organophosphate pesticides or fire-bombs created by the detonation with explosives of mixtures of diesel and petrol. The environmental impact of these activities has not been adequately researched but it is widely recognised that means to minimise the effects are required.

Another researchable constraint is the difficulty of knowing where and when the birds will occur and where they will require control in the extensive semi-arid regions that they live in. This difficulty arises mainly because Quelea is migratory, moving in relation to the timing and distribution of rainfall and the availability of annual grass seeds, the birds’ principal food. Genetically homogenous populations of the subspecies Q. quelea lathamii migrate throughout the southern African region.

In addition to demonstrating their genetic uniformity, CPP projects R6823 (Cheke, 1999) and R7967 (Cheke 2003 Part 1 and Part 2) developed a model for forecasting where and when the birds could breed in southern Africa. The model forecasts the timing and locations of suitable sites where Quelea breeding colonies could require control to prevent the successful fledging of juveniles.

The model uses satellite-derived estimates of rainfall to determine when the threshold quantity of rainfall (60 mm to 70 mm, estimated from the duration of cold cloud at 38°C or below), has been exceeded at any time within a two-week period. This quantity is required to cause grass seed germination and hence to initiate the “early rains migration” by the birds out of their dry season quarters.

When sufficient time (six weeks) has elapsed since the germination of the grass seeds, the satellite data are again used to determine whether sufficient rainfall (240 mm) has fallen to allow the birds to begin breeding.

Another output of these and subsequent projects, R8314 (Cheke, 2005) and R8426 (Cheke, 2006), was to develop and obtain standard protocols or codes of practice to ensure that environmental damage is minimised when birds threatening crops are controlled by aerial spraying their breeding colonies with the avicide “fenthion” or by the use of explosives to destroy nocturnal roosts, and obtain consensus for their adoption in Africa.

Protocols were devised for biodiversity assessment (vertebrates and invertebrates) and evaluation of potential ecological damage. These were to be used before and after Quelea control operations and to enhance the capacity of national organisations to implement the policies.

The projects also investigated the harvesting of Quelea bird nestlings as food for people as an alternative to environmentally questionable sprays and explosions. In parts of Botswana, harvesting Quelea nestlings from breeding colonies, just before they fledge, is a traditional practice for which demand could be further developed through assistance with local transportation, processing and marketing.

1. Model for short-term forecasting of red-billed Quelea breeding

  • The model was created to forecast where and when crops are likely to be damaged so that control teams in southern Africa can identify nesting colonies and target their operations more effectively.
    • Such planning has been difficult, as Quelea birds are long-distance migrants, moving up to 2 500 km in response to the seasonal movements of rain-fronts.
  • Rain causes their main food, grass seeds, to germinate at the start of the wet season forcing birds to move to areas where the seeds have yet to germinate.
    • When rain reaches these areas, the birds are forced to move again, usually returning in “early-rains migrations” in the direction whence they came.
    • By this time sufficient rain needs to have fallen to exceed another threshold within a restricted period for the new grass to have produced fresh seed.
    • Breeding may then commence.
  • Over the following three to four months the birds then undertake further, previously unpredictable, “breeding migrations” to areas elsewhere wherever adequate rainfall will permit them to breed.
    • It is the young, newly fledged, birds that cause the most damage to agriculture.
    • Given the dependence of Quelea activities on rainfall, a model was devised that uses Spatio-temporal information on rainfall throughout southern Africa derived from satellite imagery.
  • The model is intended to provide only short-term predictions using the information on rainfall alone as real-time inputs.
    • The initial spatial scale chosen at the start of the development phase in 2001 was 1° X 1° squares with time steps of one week.
    • During 2002 the resolution of the model was improved to squares of 0.5° X 0.5°.
    • The model accumulates rainfall data throughout a Quelea season (September–May), starting at the beginning of September (calendar week 36, model week one)
    • For each square, the following questions are asked at the end of each week:
      • What was the total rainfall during the current week?
      • What was the total rainfall during the current week plus the previous week?
      • What was the total rainfall during the current week plus the previous four weeks?
  • The rainfall was estimated as one hour of Cold Cloud Duration (CCD cold cloud duration at 38°C or below) being equivalent to 3 mm of rain.
    • The model was programmed in a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet, in which worksheet cells represented every degree square for 2001/2002 or every 0.5 X 0.5 of a degree square, for 2002/2003, of the southern African region.
  • The cell value is given by a formula which implements the model criteria described above.
    • The model was run each week of the 2001/2002 and 2002/2003 seasons and seven days of CCD values were input for every run.
    • The model was originally developed and validated in 2002/2003 and the forecasting system has been disseminated widely to control planners, through the Information Core for Southern Africa Migrant Pests (ICOSAMP, http://icosamp.ecoport.org/) and other routes, and details can be found in (Cheke 2003 Part 1 and Part 2).
  • Regular weekly forecasts were produced and validated in subsequent seasons Cheke (2005) and operation of the model was transferred to the Southern African Development Community (SADC). 
  • Under project R8426, the existing Quelea forecasting model for southern Africa was expanded to include the East African distribution of Quelea quelea aethiopica.
    • In addition to Q. q. lathamii, two other subspecies of Q. quelea are recognised.
    • These are the nominate race (Q. q. Quelea) that inhabits the semi-arid region from Senegal to Chad and Q. q. aethiopica that occurs in Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, eastern parts of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda.
  • As migrations within and between these countries will be governed by the same rainfall thresholds and patterns that have been used to model those of Q. q. lathamii successfully, it was a comparatively simple task to extend the existing model to cover eastern Africa in an extension that has been requested by host countries.

2. Standardised protocols for monitoring effects of Quelea control on non-target organisms

  • Guidelines for standardised protocols for monitoring the effects of Quelea control on non-target organisms were developed based on the monitoring the impacts of Quelea control operations on the environment and non-target organisms under projects R7967 and R8314.
    • An early version of these guidelines was approved by representatives of East African countries at a workshop on Quelea management held in Kenya, 14-22 May 2005.
  • This also led to a proposal for Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) work on Quelea from the Tanzanian Government.
    • EIA is now a requirement for any undertaking in Tanzania that affects the environment under Section 81 (1) of the Environmental Management Act No. 20 of 2004 which came into effect in July 2005
    • See https://www.nemc.or.tz/ and http://www.lexadin.nl/wlg/legis/nofr/oeur/lxwetan.htm for further details.
  • Aerial spraying, including against Quelea, requires an EIA to be conducted as stipulated under Schedule 3 of the Act.
    • Similarly, the National Environment Management Authorities (NEMA) in Kenya and Uganda have, since 2004, required EIAs of any new spray operations requested by commercial farmers.
    • The guidelines were subsequently discussed and approved by representatives of SADC countries attending an ICOSAMP workshop in Pretoria, 11-17 September 2005.
  • The Quelea breeding forecast for Southern Africa has been adopted by the Southern African Development Community (SADC) and is run by the Regional Remote Sensing Unit (RRSU) of the Food, Agriculture and Natural Resources (FANR) Directorate.

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropical, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies 

  • Crop planning and management in organic agriculture: ID 8367.

The technology provides for the efficient control of bird populations which in turn allows for improved and increased crop yields.

records.title: Development of biopesticide legislation in Africa
records.description:
Description

Abuse and misuse of insecticides is common in Africa. Although the use of pesticides in Africa represents less than 5 percent of the global total, misuse is disproportionately high. The use of insecticides is determined largely by export crops, such as cotton and cocoa. Trends are therefore dependent on world prices. The increasingly important peri-urban sector accounts for larger volumes of insecticide use. Products, dose and application frequency are not well regulated. Furthermore, insecticides imported for use in export crops spill over into the peri-urban sector, for which products are not approved.

Without specific measures, a continued increase in insecticide consumption is likely to be matched by continued misuse. Such chemicals are associated with environmental pollution, human contamination, rising costs, and resistance to development. For instance, the appearance of widespread resistance to commonly used insecticides in the Diamondback Moth (DBM) and Plutella xylostella (a widespread pest of brassica crops), is driving farmers to treat their crops more and more frequently, while others abandon their fields or give up brassica cultivation altogether.

Farmers all claim additional pesticides are required for DBM. Many have expressed interest in testing biopesticides. At the same time, there is a need to comply with an increasingly regulated environment imposed by developed countries on import crops, especially on vegetable and horticultural produce (maximum residue limits and Eurepgap standards, see http://www.eurepgap.org/). This threatens the sustainability of export agriculture and fuels demands to reduce chemical pesticides or substitute them with safer alternatives.

1. Biopesticides

  • While there has been substantial technical progress with biopesticides, and increasing public awareness of the need to reduce dependency on chemical pesticides, the uptake of biopesticides has been limited.
  • In Africa, there have been many notable and pioneering studies on the use of viruses for the control of insect pests.
    • However there are few, if any, sustainable examples of their long-term commercial use.
    • Reasons have often included a lack of expertise in the crucial later stages of development and/or pursuit of an inappropriate model of biopesticide development.
  • The early stages of biopesticide research and development, are often undertaken in the public sector using public finances.
    • However many potential biopesticide products fail to go beyond the laboratory or field-trial stage.
  • Commercialization is the key implementation pathway for biopesticides and failure to engage the private sector and a lack of market data may be amongst factors contributing to poor biopesticide uptake.
  • However, the main constraint on progress is probably the lack of a legislative framework for registration and approval of biopesticides in much of Sub-Saharan Africa.
    • This has meant that it is effectively impossible to legally market biopesticide products for commercial use?
    • This is in spit of the fact that these may be based on organisms, and even locally - obtained strains or isolates, that occur naturally within the user countries themselves.
  • Several CPP projects have been concerned with developing biopesticides including:
    • entomopathogenic viruses against DBM and armyworm (Spodoptera exempta);
    • entomopathogenic fungi and bacteria against root-knot nematodes; and
    • phermones against legume pod borers (Maruca vitrata) and cocoa mirid bugs.
  • Project partners have also been concerned with mass-producing predators and parasitoids for horticultural pests.
  • In most of these cases, it was recognized that deficiencies in the existing regulatory environment would present difficulties for commercialization, marketing, and eventual uptake.
    • Efforts were made to help develop and implement the appropriate legislation and approval processes.

2. Legislative structure

  • Recognizing the need for legislative structure to ensure the sustainable development and commercial usage of biopesticides in Kenya, the Kenya Agricultural Research Institute, in collaboration with the Pest Control Products Board and the DFID Crop Protection Programme, hosted a three-day workshop at Nakuru, Kenya in 2003.
  • The full account of this meeting provides useful methodology resource materials for the development and implementation of similar protocols elsewhere.
  • The proceedings include 17 papers arranged in four sessions.
    1. Demand from the horticultural industry
    2. Contribution of research in Africa
    3. Registration in Africa
    4. Registration in other countries.
  • The publication also includes, Annexes finalized for legislation, application documents for the registration of microbial, macrobial and biochemical pest control products.
  • Similar workshops for regulatory authorities were held in Accra, Ghana, in 2005, on the introduction of biopesticide product as well as specific regulations, including provision of model regulations.
  • Presentations made to these workshops are available that complement those produced in East Africa.
    • Biopesticides: a review of active agents. 
    • Biopesticides: a global perspective.
    • Biopesticide registration.
    • Introduction to Ghana’s current pesticides registration framework and requirement for biopesticides regulations in Ghana.
  • Biopesticide registration guidelines were subsequently drafted for the Ghanaian Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
    • The final drafts, together with the draft biopesticides regulations, were to be put before the EPA Board in preparation for consultation with key stakeholders.
  • Observers from Togo, Benin, Ivory Coast and Guinea all expressed interest in developing similar guidelines for biopesticides.

2.1 You manipulate and/or use (bio)pesticides?

  • Make inquiries before!
  • Pesticide can be harmful to your health, the health of your family, of the consumers and of the environment.
  • Adopt the right gestures to use pesticides safely.
    • Click on “Risk reduction while manipulating pesticides”

3. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Integrated pest management: ID 7298.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology reduces environmental pollution, human contamination, costs, and resistance to development.
