records.title: Fish harvesting and post-harvest handling
records.description:
Description

1. Deciding when to harvest

The decision to harvest the fish from a pond is made for two main reasons.

  1. When the fish has attained the right size at which it gives maximum profit in the market and any further waiting may reduce the profit.
  2. When the prevailing market opportunities (like Christmas and Easter) offer the highest profit and the opportunity may be lost with delay.

1.1 Using information from a regular sampling of fish

  • In order for the farmer to decide whether the fish has attained an optimum size for harvest, the farmer must have been sampling and weighing the fish and analysing the data (see Table 1).
    • The example is based on sampling data from Jacob's pond. 
Table 1. The growth of fish in Jacobs pond
Month fish has grown in the pond The average weight of fish each month (g) Increase in average weight each month (g)
1 4.7 0
2 9.0 4.3
3 10.6 1.6
4 12.0 1.5
5 28.9 16.9
6 65.5 36.6
7 121.2 55.7
8 191.8 70.5
9 270.2 78.5
10 380.0 109.8
11 440.0 60.0
12 471.7 31.7
13 504.5 32.8
14 515.0 10.5
15 516.0 1.0
16 517.0 1.0
17 517.5 0.5
18 518.0 0.5

Source: NAADS-Uganda 2011

  • The data shows that the monthly increase in fish weight rises until the tenth month.
    • After month ten, although the fish continues to grow, the rate of growth keeps falling (Figure 1).
  • In the Figure below after month ten, the quantity of food the fish eats increases while the growth rate falls.
    • It is advisable to harvest the fish in the tenth month to avoid losses in profit.
Figure 1. The average of fish weight in kg as a function of months

©NAADS-Uganda

  • Emphasis (impact point): See dotted arrow in the above Figure 1.
    • The figure confirms that delayed harvesting of farmed fish leads to loss of profit and farmers do not necessarily make more profit by growing fish to bigger sizes.

2. Methods and gear for harvesting pond fish

2.1 Definition

  • Method means “ways of harvesting”; gear means “tools used to harvest”.
    • Once the fish has reached the right size for harvest, the pond should be harvested immediately.

2.2 How do we harvest fish from ponds?

  • Common methods and gear for harvesting fish from ponds.
    • Harvesting by draining the pond.
    • Using basket traps.
    • Using hooks and baits.
    • Using cast nets.
    • Using lift nets.
    • Using a seine net.
    • Using gill nets.
  • The methods and gear for harvesting fish ponds depend on the size of the pond.

2.2.1 Harvesting by draining the pond

  • This method of harvesting is the simplest and most effective.
    • Water is let out of the pond by opening the sluices or lowering pipes at the outlet.
    • As the water level drops and the water moves towards the deeper end of the pond, the fish drift with it (Figure 2).
    • All the fish collect at the outlet and are collected by hand or with a net.
  • As the pond drains, the water level falls at the shallower end of the pond.
    • All the fish drift towards the deeper end.
    • When the fish have gathered in a small area at the deep end the farmer then collects the fish in a container.
Figure 2. Harvesting by draining a pond

©FAO/TECA

  • For this method, the pond should have been constructed well with a good slope.
  • Harvesting is made much easier if a depression is made at the point of the outlet as a "harvesting bay".
    • The fish is then scooped or picked from the ditch (harvesting bay).
    • In this way, the fish is picked clean and does not bury in the mud.
  • This method of harvesting is suitable for both small and large ponds.
    • For the larger ponds, it is used in combination with seining.
    • Fish collected from the mud tends to be dirty and dies quickly.
    • Pond fish should be marketed live and clean.
  • During harvesting, there should be two containers with clean water (Figure 3).
    • The first bucket is for washing off the mud from the fish.
    • Then the clean fish are put in another container with clean water to keep alive.
    • The water for washing the fish should be replaced with clean water when it gets dirty.
Figure 3. The fish are put in clean water to keep them alive

©FAO/TECA

2.2.2 Using basket traps

  • The baskets are important in harvesting small ponds where the farmer cannot afford the more expensive gear.
    • The basket is made from twigs, cane or climbing plants (Figure 4).
    • The larger end is the mouth which has a valve that does not allow the fish to escape once it has entered.
    • Some food is put inside the basket.
  • The trap is placed with the open end facing the main pond water. It is given enough time (30 minutes to one hour) for the fish to enter.
  • The gear is simple to make or cheap to buy.
    • It is easy to operate, but it is limited to only small ponds (not suitable for ponds of more than 200 m2).
  • The basket cannot harvest all the fish from the pond.
    • The pond should be drained in order to harvest all the fish.
  • The baskets are cheap and made from local materials.
Figure 4. Farmer setting a basket trap (left), and a basket trap (right)

©FAO/TECA

2.2.3 Using hooks

  • Hooks are bought from shops selling fishing equipment (Figure 5).
    • They vary in sizes from number 1 (the largest) to number 10 (the smallest).
  • A hook is fixed to a rope tied to a handle.
    • The hook and its rope (hook acid line) are very cheap, simple to make and use.
    • However, a hook catches one fish at a time.
    • Therefore, it is not suitable for good scale commercial production.
    • The hook and line cannot harvest all the fish from the pond.
    • Most of the fish still remain in the pond.
    • The pond should finally be drained to completely harvest the pond.
Figure 5. A hook and a line

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. An earthworm used as bait on the hook

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. A farmer using bait and a hook

©FAO/TECA

2.2.3.1 Hook and line attributes

  • It depends on luck; the operator cannot choose the fish to catch.
  • It is not very selective and smaller fish may be caught leaving the larger ones.
  • It injures fish and may not be suitable for sampling fish that will be returned into the pond.
  • It catches a few fish at a time, depends on luck (Figure 8).
    • The pond must be drained to remove all the fish.
  • It is only suitable for small ponds (up to 10 m x 20 m).
Figure 8. Fish caught with a hook. Note to throw the smaller fish away

©FAO/TECA

2.2.4 Harvesting using cast nets

  • A cast net is a net made like an umbrella (Figure 9).
    • It is tied on a rope. It opens out when casting over the pond.
    • As it sinks deep into the pond the mouth is closed, trapping whatever fish that will be in the water space enclosed.
Figure 9. The cast net encloses a space of pond water and traps fish in that space

©FAO/TECA

2.2.4.1 Advantages of the cast

  • A cast net is cheap.
  • It is simple to operate but requires training in the skills.
  • Does not require a large labour force (only one person).
  • Catches by chance and the operator does not have much choice of the fish to catch.
  • It does not harm fish, the fish can be returned into the pond.
  • Its operation is limited to only small ponds (1 m x 20 m) and is time wasting for larger ponds.

2.2.5 Using lift nets

  • The lift net is a net made into a sack with one open end that is dipped into the pond to scoop up fish.
    • The mouth of the lift net is made of a ring made from a cane or a metal rod.
    • The length of the rod or cane is about 1.5 m to 2 m long before bending into a ring (Figure 10).
Figure 10. Two sides of the net are mounted onto a ring

©FAO/TECA

  • The wider ends are tied to the metal ring.
    • The two open edges of the net are seamed together to make an inverted umbrella and the two pieces closed by tying.
  • The lift net can be braided by hand (after training) or are bought and trimmed into a cone with one wider end and one narrow an end.
    • The wider ends are measured to half the length of the ring for each net.
Figure 11. Two sides of the net mounted onto a ring 

©FAO/TECA

  • The lift net can harvest a reasonable quantity of fish, as much as 30 kg at a go, and therefore can be applied for commercial production.
    • The method does not bruise or stress fish, and fish can be delivered to the market very fresh.
    • The lift net, however, is not suitable for ponds larger than 2 000 m2.
    • It cannot harvest all the fish.
    • The pond should be drained so as to complete the harvest.
  • To operate the net it is dipped into the water as shown in Figure 12a.
  • Food is then placed around the net.
    • The net is left for 30 minutes for fish to gather above it while feeding, then quickly, the net is lifted with the fish that was in the water above it (Figure 12b). 
Figures 12a and 12b. a) net is dipped into the water, b)net is in the water left for fish to gather

©FAO/TECA

2.2.6 The seine net

  • The seine net is the conventional pond net.
    • It is like an open curtain made of a net with small meshes.
    • The top side of the net is tied to a rope on which plastic round spheres (floats) are attached at about 1 m interval.
  • The seine net is a large curtain-like net.
    • It has floats on one side that keeps the net above the water surface( Figure 13).
    • It has heavy cement balls on another side that keeps the net at the bottom of the pond.
Figure 13. The seine net

©FAO/TECA

  • Therefore, the net remains open during fishing.
    • One wing of the net metal or wooden ring.
    • 1 m long folded into a ring.
    • The bottom side is tied to another rope on which small stones are attached at about 1 m interval.
    • The length of the net should be longer than the width of the pond by an extra 3 m to 5 m to make a curve when it is operated.
    • Example: a pond with a width of 20 m requires a seine net 25 m long.
  • The seine net at the end of the operation will have trapped fish in the middle.
  • Note the number of people required to operate it (see Figure 13 above).

2.2.6.1 Seine net attributes

  • It makes bulk harvests (harvesting up to 90 percent of the fish stock in the pond when fished four to six times repeatedly).
  • It is expensive (about UGX 10 000 per 1 m length), but it lasts long (up to five years with minor repairs).
  • It requires more labour to operate (ranging from four people for 10 m x 20 m pond to as many as 12 people for a 20 m x 50 m pond).
  • It is most appropriate for large size ponds.
  • If operated carefully, it does not injure fish much and fish can be returned to the pond.

2.2.7 Harvesting using gill nets

  • The gill nets are nets with varying mesh sizes.
    • It is operated by setting it well spread in the pond and left there.
    • It is checked after about an hour or longer.
    • Fish are caught when it pushes its head through the meshes and gets trapped (Figure 14).
    • The gill net is highly selective and the size of fish caught depends on the size of the net.
    • The gill net cannot harvest all the fish in the pond.
Figure 14. A gill net set in the pond

©FAO/TECA

2.2.7.1 Gill net advantages

  • It is easy to operate but the farmer has to enter the pond.
    • Only one person can set it.
  • It may catch many fish, but cannot be used to harvest all the fish. 

2.2.7.2 Gill net challenges

  • The gill net is expensive for small scale farmers (UGX 15 000 for 4" mesh).
  • It harms fish and is not suitable for catching and returning some fish.

3. Displaying fish for marketing

  • Whenever possible it is best to present fish for sale in its freshest form.
    • Live fish are the freshest state.
    • As soon as fish die, they begin to go bad and the longer they stay the smellier they become.
    • When the fish go bad the market price falls.
  • Therefore, fish may be:
    • deep-fried in oil for immediate consumption;
    • sold live or freshly killed;
    • preserved in ice;
    • processed (sun-dried, salted or smoked); and
    • at higher industrial levels, may be filleted and chilled for supermarkets or export.
  • The form in which the fish is marketed depends on:
    • how near the market is;
    • what the market prefers;
    • the amount of fish to be sold; and
    • the need to add value and improve profit.

3.1 Selling deep-fried fish for direct eating

  • Fish may be deep-fried in oil and sold for direct eating at social gatherings (Figure 15).
    • Such opportunities include near schools, at drinking joints and at public functions.
Figure 15. Deep frying fish

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Smoking fish in kilns

  • Fish may also be preserved by smoking in kilns or salting, or by sun-drying thus keeping for a longer time.
    • This makes it possible to sell fish at longer distances.

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Post-harvest fish loss model: ID 4463.
  • Make a living through fish farming: ID 7357.
  • Assessing post-harvest fish losses: load tracking method: ID 4437.
  • Management of fish in the pond: ID 7235.
  • Fry/seed quality and stocking: ID 7025.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for improved pond management and fish health. It has advantageous fish harvesting techniques and fish conservation methods.

records.title: Techniques culturales du manioc
records.description:
La description

REAFOR (Recherche Agricole et Forestière) est un programme visant à contribuer à la réduction de la pauvreté, au renforcement de la sécurité alimentaire et au bien-être des populations de la République Démocratique du Congo, par le renforcement des capacités nationales de la recherche agricole et forestière, en vue de sa relance durable. La fiche technique suivante décrit comment cultiver différentes variétés de manioc. Elle donne des détails sur la préparation du terrain, la sélection des boutures, la plantation, la récolte ainsi que la conservation. Les variétés suivantes ont été choisies pour leur résistance aux maladies et aux ravageurs ainsi que pour leur haut rendement:

  • Zizila,
  • Nsansi,
  • M'vuazi,
  • Disanka,
  • Butamu, et
  • TME 419.

1. Exigences édaphiques du manioc

  • Terrain et type de sol

1.1 Sols

  • Meubles sablo argileux ou argilo-sablonneux, profonds et riches en éléments nutritifs.
  • Éviter le terrain où l’eau stagne ainsi que le terrain avec racines d’arbre hôtes de fomes lignosus établies (le champignon responsable pour les pourritures des racines).

1.2 Précédant cultural

  • Éviter les sols ayant porté une culture avec les mêmes exigences en éléments nutritifs (ex. manioc, patate douce, bananer, taro, etc.).

2. Préparation du terrain

2.1 En forêt

  • Défrichement (bois et sous bois).
  • Coupe de sous-bois trois mois avant l’abattage des futaies.
  • Incinération localisée.
  • Buttage: 1 m x 1 m entre les buttes.
  • Enfouissement: pendant le buttage des débris végétaux décomposables au moins 21 à 45 jours avant la plantation.

2.2 En savane

  • Champ sur buttes, en billons, à plat ou cultivé non labouré.

2.2.1 Labour tracteur

  • 30 à 45 jours avant plantation.
  • Enfouissement des résidus végétaux.
  • Hersage peu avant la plantation.
  • Deux passages croisés.

2.2.2 Préparation manuelle du terrain

  • Enfouissement des résidus végétaux.
  • Création de billons équidistants de 1 m à 1.5 m.
  • 21 à 45 jours avant plantation.
  • Remuer les billons en mélangeant la terre et les débris de décomposition avant de planter.

3. Variété et matériel de plantation

Les variétés à hauts rendements, résistantes aux maladies et aux ravageurs, notamment à la mosaïque africaine sont les suivantes : ZIZILA, NSANSI, MVUAZI, DISANKA, BUTAMU et TME 419. Toutes ces variétés (exceptées la TME 419) sont présentées plus en détail dans le fichier joint à la technologie. Les matériels de plantation doivent provenir d’un champ de multiplication des boutures saines, sur tiges saines de 9 à 15 mois.

4. Mode de plantation

  • Une seule bouture (micro ou petite), longue de 10, 15, 20, 25 cm selon la variété, avec trois à cinq bourgeons.
  • Position
    • Horizontale, couverte complètement (dégâts des termites réduits, faible incidence de la verse).
    • Oblique.
    • Couverte à deux-tiers à un angle de 30 à 45° et verticale.
      • Usages spécifiques: maraîchères, micro propagation, jauge.
  • Plantation avec jauge de préférence pour le regarnissage des champs de multiplication car.
    • Dans ce cas, les plantules ont le même âge.

4.1 Ecartements recommandés

  • 1 m x 1 m, pour la production racines tubéreuses.
  • 1 m x 0.50 m, pour la multiplication des boutures.
  • 1 m x 0.50 m, pour la production des feuilles.

5. Rotation de culture

  • En zone forestière mettre les céréales plutôt que le manioc en tête de rotation.
  • En savane, démarrer avec une légumineuse dans les sols à faible fertilité.

5.1 Époques de plantation

  • Bas-Congo et Kinshasa: Octobre/Novembre et Février/Mars.
  • Bandundu, Ka-saï: Octobre et Mars.
  • Sud – Kivu et Maniema: Octobre/Novembre et Février/Mars.
  • Nord-Kivu: Mars/Avril et Septembre.
  • Equateur, Pro-vince Orientale: Mars/Avril et Octobre.
  • Nord Katanga: Septembre et Février.
  • Sud Katanga: Novembre/Décembre et Février.

5.2  Associations culturales

  • On peut associer le manioc avec plusieurs cultures suivantes.

5.2.1 Arachide

  • Deux lignes de 30 cm x 30 cm ou 40 cm x 20 cm entre deux lignes de manioc.

5.2.2 Soja

  • Une ligne en sol riche aux écartements de 30 à 40 cm.
  • En sol pauvre, deux lignes de 40 cm x 20 cm.
  • Semer deux à trois semaines après le manioc.

5.2.3 Haricot volubile

  • Semis au même moment ou 45 jours après le manioc.
  • Deux lignes aux écartements de 50 cm x 20 cm.

5.2.4 Haricot nain 

  • Semis au même moment ou deux semaines avant le manioc.
  • Deux lignes à 40 cm x 10 cm ou 40 cm x 20 cm.

5.2.5 Maïs

  • Une ligne entre deux lignes de manioc.
  • Deux à trois semaines avant le manioc, au même moment, ou en relais 45 jours avant le manioc à 1 m x 0.5 m d’écartement.

5.2.6 Riz

  • Semis souvent avant le manioc.
  • Deux lignes 40 cm x 20 cm.

5.3 Entretien du champ

5.3.1 Regarnissage

  • Le regarnissage des vides, trois à quatre semaines après plantation.

5.3.2 Mesures phytosanitaires

  • Une fois au regarnissage pour le champ de production des racines tubéreuses, et du regarnissage à la récolte pour le champ de multiplication des boutures saines.

5.3.3 Sarclages (contrôle des adventices)

  • Trois sarclages manuels recommandés en savane.
  • Le premier à partir de trois à quatre semaines de la plantation, avant le regarnissage.
  • Les sarclages sont surtout importants les trois premiers mois de la plantation pour garantir une bonne tubérisation.
  • Buttage appliqué pendant le deuxième et troisième sarclage.

5.3.4 Fertilisation minérale

  • Dose de 50-50-50 ou 75-50-75 (N,P,K) en fonction de l’intensification.
  • Application fractionnée.
    • Tout le P et K à la plantation (dose de fonds).
    • 40 à 46 kg N au redressement appliqué après 30 à 40 jours de plantation.

5.3.5 Fertilisation organique

  • Fumure de ferme à 15 tonnes/ha, enfouissement résidus végétaux et paillage.

6. Récolte

6.1 Feuilles

  • Deux récoltes à trois mois de la plantation.
  • À 45 jours, deux mois après la première.

6.2 Boutures 

  • Entre 9 et 15 mois de la plantation, ou après 9 mois du premier recépage.
  • Le recépage se fait à 20 à 25 cm du collet.
  • Le conditionnement se fait à 50 et 100 tiges d'un mètre de longueur.
  • Conserver en jauge, en meule, verticalement, sous hangars ou sous ombrage, ou près d’un point d’eau.
  • Les racines tubéreuses suivent le cycle (précoce ou tardif) de la variété (entre 9 à 18 mois).
  • L'arrachage complet de la plante à maturité est conseillé.
  • Il n'y a pas de récolte graduelle sur un seul pied.
  • Il est conseillé de cultiver les variétés à différents cycles de maturité pour échelonner la récolte.

Cette fiche technique est disponible en portugais: ID 2140. 

7. Zones agro-ecologiques

  • Tropicale, chaude.

8. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

8.1 L’efficacité d’utilisation des ressources

La pratique permet à la cultivitation plus diverse de différentes variétés de manioc et effectue de manière plus efficace l'utilisation et préparation du terrain, la sélection des boutures, la plantation, la récolte et la conservation. 

8.2 La technologie favorable aux populations pauvres

La pratique permet à la récolte de variétés de haute qualité, résistante aux maladies et aux ravageurs. Cela mène à de plus hauts rendements et une sécurité alimentaire plus élevée.

records.title: Amibiase: une maladie parasitaire des abeilles adultes
records.description:
La description

1. Introduction

L'amibiase est causée par le protozoaire Malpighamoeba mellificae et affecte les abeilles adultes. Les symptômes de l'amibiase - des abeilles avec un abdomen enflé et de la diarrhée – sont très similaires à ceux de la nosémose. En fait, l'amibiase et la nosémose sont fréquemment observées ensemble comme une infection mixte.

Les abeilles sont infectées en ingérant du miel ou du pollen contaminé par les excréments d'abeilles infectées. L'infection provoque une inflammation des intestins des abeilles adultes, qui deviennent progressivement incapables de fonctionner correctement. L'apiculteur peut observer des fèces diarrhéiques au trou de vol et à l'avant de la ruche ainsi que des abeilles incapables de voler, avec des ailes frissonnantes, tremblantes.

La maladie survient principalement au printemps et disparaît ensuite après quelques mois. Dans les cas graves, l'amibiase tue les abeilles adultes et, par conséquent, il n'y a pas assez d'abeilles dans la ruche pour prendre soin du couvain, qui finit par mourir.

2. Symptomes

Les symptômes de l'amibiase (Figure 1) sont similaires à ceux de la nosémose (causée par N. apis):

  • abdomen gonflé;
  • incapacité de voler;
  • ailes frissonnantes;
  • présence de selles diarrhéiques maculées sur les rayons ainsi qu’au trou de vol et à l'avant de la ruche.

L'amibiase et la nosémose sont fréquemment observées ensemble comme une infection mixte. Le diagnostic est confirmé par l'identification en laboratoire des kystes microscopiques dans les tubules et les fèces des abeilles.

Figure 1. Entrée de la ruche maculée de fèces diarrhéiques

©Flickr/D. Broberg

3. Transmission

À l'intérieur de la ruche, les nettoyeuses sont infectées lors du retrait des excréments hors des ruches. Elles transmettent l'infection et la maladie se propage par l'ingestion de miel et de pollen contaminés.

L'amibiase est transmise d'une ruche à une autre par la dérive des abeilles (éclaireuses et butineuses retournant à la mauvaise ruche), le pillage et les points d’eau. L'apiculteur peut également transmettre la maladie entre les colonies en déplaçant les rayons infectés d'une ruche infectée vers une ruche saine et en utilisant du matériel et des outils apicoles infectés.

De longs hivers, un temps froid, des mois d'été et d'automne frais et humides contribuent à propager la maladie. Cependant, l'amibiase affecte une très faible proportion de colonies et est rarement identifiée. Les colonies sont généralement capables de restaurer leur santé naturellement après une infection lorsque les conditions météorologiques s'améliorent.

4. Diagnostic

Il est possible de faire un diagnostic sur le terrain grâce à l'observation des symptômes suivants:

  • abeilles avec un abdomen gonflé et de la diarrhée (Figure 2);
  • fèces diarrhéiques sur les rayons de miel et au trou de vol (Figure 1);
  • abeilles aux ailes tremblantes, incapables de voler.
Figure 2. Abeille avec diarrhée

©IZSLT/Giovanni Formato

Les symptômes de l'amibiase étant très similaires à ceux de la nosémose, ce n'est que par l'examen des abeilles en laboratoire qu'un diagnostic final est possible.

5. Prevention et controle

Les mesures de contrôle de l'amibiase sont similaires à celles de la nosémose. L'adoption des BPA peut aider à prévenir et à contrôler l'amibiase (Tableau 1). 

Tableau 1. Bonnes pratiques apicoles pour la prévention et le contrôle de l'amibiase
Recommandation Avantage ou raison d’utiliser cette pratique
Nettoyez et désinfectez régulièrement le matériel apicole et les outils de la ruche (p. ex. avec de l'eau de Javel), idéalement après chaque utilisation.

Réduit la population bactérienne de la ruche.
Assurez-vous que les ruches sont situées dans un bon emplacement, ensoleillé et sec; évitez l'humidité et le vent. Réduit le stress thermique sur les abeilles.
Renforcez et stimulez les colonies en automne et au printemps en fournissant une alimentation enrichie en substances végétales ou en suppléments vitaminiques spécifiques aux abeilles. Réduit le stress nutritionnel des abeilles.
Contrôlez les autres agents pathogènes (principalement le varroa) pour assurer un bon état de santé de la colonie. D'autres agents pathogènes, en particulier le varroa, provoquent une immunosuppression chez les abeilles.
Retirez les rayons des colonies qui présentent des signes de la maladie (diarrhée). Faites fondre la cire d'abeille. Réduit la transmission de la maladie aux abeilles en bonne santé.
Administrez des suppléments aux colonies infectées. Réduit le stress nutritionnel des abeilles.
Ne nourrissez pas les abeilles avec du miel ou du pollen provenant de colonies infectées. Réduit la transmission de la maladie aux abeilles en bonne santé.
Ne transférez pas de rayons entre les colonies malades et saines. Réduit la transmission de la maladie aux abeilles en bonne santé.

6. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Les principales maladies des abeilles: ID 8714.
  • Varroa (varroase ou varroose): ID 8712.
  • Virus des abeilles: ID 8704.

Cette fiche technique est disponible en anglais: ID 10019. La traduction a été finalisée par Elsa Demoulin, Beekeeping Network North-South.

7. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

7.1 La technologie favorable aux populations pauvres

La technologie, grâce à sa description des causes et des symptômes de l'amibiase, permet à améliorer la santé des colonies d'abeilles. Ceci mène à une production amélorée de produits des ruches, qui fournit des sources d'alimentation et de revenu supplémentaires.

Amibiase: une maladie parasitaire des abeilles adultes

L'amibiase est une maladie qui affecte les abeilles domestiques adultes. Les symptômes de l'amibiase sont similaires à ceux de la nosémose: abeilles avec un abdomen enflé et diarrhée. L'apiculteur peut localiser les au trou de vol et à l'avant de la ruche et observer des abeilles incapables de voler, avec des ailes frissonnantes, tremblantes. En général, l'amibiase est présente dans les régions tempérées des deux hémisphères et semble être absente dans les zones tropicales et subtropicales. Elle affecte une très faible proportion de colonies et est rarement identifiée. Voici une description de cette maladie et de ses symptômes et de la manière de la prévenir et contrôler.

La description

1. Introduction

L'amibiase est causée par le protozoaire Malpighamoeba mellificae et affecte les abeilles adultes. Les symptômes de l'amibiase - des abeilles avec un abdomen enflé et de la diarrhée – sont très similaires à ceux de la nosémose. En fait, l'amibiase et la nosémose sont fréquemment observées ensemble comme une infection mixte.

Les abeilles sont infectées en ingérant du miel ou du pollen contaminé par les excréments d'abeilles infectées. L'infection provoque une inflammation des intestins des abeilles adultes, qui deviennent progressivement incapables de fonctionner correctement. L'apiculteur peut observer des fèces diarrhéiques au trou de vol et à l'avant de la ruche ainsi que des abeilles incapables de voler, avec des ailes frissonnantes, tremblantes.

La maladie survient principalement au printemps et disparaît ensuite après quelques mois. Dans les cas graves, l'amibiase tue les abeilles adultes et, par conséquent, il n'y a pas assez d'abeilles dans la ruche pour prendre soin du couvain, qui finit par mourir.

2. Symptomes

Les symptômes de l'amibiase (Figure 1) sont similaires à ceux de la nosémose (causée par N. apis):

  • abdomen gonflé;
  • incapacité de voler;
  • ailes frissonnantes;
  • présence de selles diarrhéiques maculées sur les rayons ainsi qu’au trou de vol et à l'avant de la ruche.

L'amibiase et la nosémose sont fréquemment observées ensemble comme une infection mixte. Le diagnostic est confirmé par l'identification en laboratoire des kystes microscopiques dans les tubules et les fèces des abeilles.

Figure 1. Entrée de la ruche maculée de fèces diarrhéiques

©Flickr/D. Broberg

3. Transmission

À l'intérieur de la ruche, les nettoyeuses sont infectées lors du retrait des excréments hors des ruches. Elles transmettent l'infection et la maladie se propage par l'ingestion de miel et de pollen contaminés.

L'amibiase est transmise d'une ruche à une autre par la dérive des abeilles (éclaireuses et butineuses retournant à la mauvaise ruche), le pillage et les points d’eau. L'apiculteur peut également transmettre la maladie entre les colonies en déplaçant les rayons infectés d'une ruche infectée vers une ruche saine et en utilisant du matériel et des outils apicoles infectés.

De longs hivers, un temps froid, des mois d'été et d'automne frais et humides contribuent à propager la maladie. Cependant, l'amibiase affecte une très faible proportion de colonies et est rarement identifiée. Les colonies sont généralement capables de restaurer leur santé naturellement après une infection lorsque les conditions météorologiques s'améliorent.

4. Diagnostic

Il est possible de faire un diagnostic sur le terrain grâce à l'observation des symptômes suivants:

  • abeilles avec un abdomen gonflé et de la diarrhée (Figure 2);
  • fèces diarrhéiques sur les rayons de miel et au trou de vol (Figure 1);
  • abeilles aux ailes tremblantes, incapables de voler.
Figure 2. Abeille avec diarrhée

©IZSLT/Giovanni Formato

Les symptômes de l'amibiase étant très similaires à ceux de la nosémose, ce n'est que par l'examen des abeilles en laboratoire qu'un diagnostic final est possible.

5. Prevention et controle

Les mesures de contrôle de l'amibiase sont similaires à celles de la nosémose. L'adoption des BPA peut aider à prévenir et à contrôler l'amibiase (Tableau 1). 

Tableau 1. Bonnes pratiques apicoles pour la prévention et le contrôle de l'amibiase
Recommandation Avantage ou raison d’utiliser cette pratique
Nettoyez et désinfectez régulièrement le matériel apicole et les outils de la ruche (p. ex. avec de l'eau de Javel), idéalement après chaque utilisation.

Réduit la population bactérienne de la ruche.
Assurez-vous que les ruches sont situées dans un bon emplacement, ensoleillé et sec; évitez l'humidité et le vent. Réduit le stress thermique sur les abeilles.
Renforcez et stimulez les colonies en automne et au printemps en fournissant une alimentation enrichie en substances végétales ou en suppléments vitaminiques spécifiques aux abeilles. Réduit le stress nutritionnel des abeilles.
Contrôlez les autres agents pathogènes (principalement le varroa) pour assurer un bon état de santé de la colonie. D'autres agents pathogènes, en particulier le varroa, provoquent une immunosuppression chez les abeilles.
Retirez les rayons des colonies qui présentent des signes de la maladie (diarrhée). Faites fondre la cire d'abeille. Réduit la transmission de la maladie aux abeilles en bonne santé.
Administrez des suppléments aux colonies infectées. Réduit le stress nutritionnel des abeilles.
Ne nourrissez pas les abeilles avec du miel ou du pollen provenant de colonies infectées. Réduit la transmission de la maladie aux abeilles en bonne santé.
Ne transférez pas de rayons entre les colonies malades et saines. Réduit la transmission de la maladie aux abeilles en bonne santé.

6. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Les principales maladies des abeilles: ID 8714.
  • Varroa (varroase ou varroose): ID 8712.
  • Virus des abeilles: ID 8704.

Cette fiche technique est disponible en anglais: ID 10019. La traduction a été finalisée par Elsa Demoulin, Beekeeping Network North-South.

7. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

7.1 La technologie favorable aux populations pauvres

La technologie, grâce à sa description des causes et des symptômes de l'amibiase, permet à améliorer la santé des colonies d'abeilles. Ceci mène à une production amélorée de produits des ruches, qui fournit des sources d'alimentation et de revenu supplémentaires.

records.title: Beekeeping: the Kamara basket hive: an improved traditional hive
records.description:
Description

The Kamara basket hive has been developed by Dr. Kwame Aidoo, International Stingless Bee Centre, University of Cape Coast, Ghana and Pastor John Kamara, Chairman, Musia Beekeepers Association, Koinadugu District, Sierra Leone within the framework of the FAO project "Food Security through Commercialization of Agriculture".

The Kamara basket hive is an improvement over the local hive used by traditional beekeepers of Koinadugu, Sierra Leone. The two-chambered fixed comb hive (brood and honey sections) allows for the removal of mature honey combs leaving the brood camber undisturbed. The honeybee colony is thus managed sustainably and honey and beeswax production is improved substantially.

Figure 1. The Kamara basket hive: an improved traditional hive

©TECA/Kwame Aidoo

1. Materials needed to construct a Kamara basket hive

  • To construct the Kamara basket hive, you need the following items:
    • a sharp knife,
    • midrib of raffia palm /oil palm fronds,
    • dry grass,
    • large leaves (e.g. banana),
    • cow dung (optional), and
    • clay (optional).

1.1 Method of construction

  • To construct the Kamara basket hive, follow the steps as illustrated.
    • Weave two cylindrical baskets using the outer cover of raffia palm fronds (Figure 2).
    • One cylinder should be shorter than the other.
    • The shorter cylinder (brood chamber) should have a lenght of 50 cm and a diameter of about 50 cm.
    • The longer cylinder should have a length of around 80 cm and be slightly wider so that it fits around the smaller basket.  
Figure 2. Strips of the outer cover of raffia palm fronds are arranged and woven into two cylindrical open ended baskets

©TECA/Kwame Aidoo

Figure 3. Two cylindrical baskets are woven to a total length of about 130 cm when put together

©TECA/Kwame Aidoo

  • The shorter cylinder will become the brood chamber.
  • The slightly larger and longer cylinder will become the honey chamber.
  • The brood chamber is closed at both ends with two round disks made up of the inner pith of the raffia frond.
  • They should both have a small hole in the middle.
    • One to serve as a hive entrance and one larger hole (indicated with an arrow in Figure 4) for passage of worker bees to the adjoining honey chamber.
  • The honey chamber is closed to one end with a similar disk, but without hole.
  • The other end is left open to allow for joining the two sections together into a long cylinder of about 130 cm long (Figure 5).
Figure 4. Brood chamber and honey chamber of the basket hive are put together, leaving an opening for the bees to move between the two

©TECA/Kwame Aidoo

Figure 5. The longer honey chamber is 80 cm in length and slightly bigger in diameter to allow the brood section to slot in tightly. It is closed at one end but open at the other end that allow for joining the two sections together into a long cylinder of about 130 cm long

©TECA/Kwame Aidoo

  • The outside of the two cylinders can be coated with a clay-cow dung mixture to seal the holes in the woven basket (Figure 6).
Figure 6. The outside of the baskets coated with a clay-cow dung mixture to close the holes. The hive entrance is left open (red arrow)

©TECA/Kwame Aidoo

  • Cover the coated hive body with a thick layer of dry grass and bound it tightly with raffia bands (Figure 7).
  • This will protect the hive from excess heat.
  • The hive is now ready for mounting on a platform or under a thatch hut.
Figure 7. The coated hive body covered with a thick layer of dry grass and bound with raffia bands

©TECA/Kwame Aidoo

  • Alternatively, the woven basket could be wrapped with two layers of materials.
    • An inner layer composed of large leaves such as banana, and an outer layer of dry grass.
  • This eliminates the use of a clay-cow dung mixture to seal holes in the woven basket (Figure 8).
  • Complete the wrapping with a tight bounding of the outer grass layer with raffia bands (Figure 9).
Figure 8. The woven basket being covered with an inner layer of large leaves instead of the clay-cow dung mixture

©TECA/Kwame Aidoo

Figure 9. The wrapping is complete with tight bounding with raffia bands

©TECA/Kwame Aidoo

  • To finish, trim both ends of the grass cover to expose the hole which serve as a hive entrance (Figure 10).
  • Traditionally, the local basket hives in the Koinadugu district of Sierra Leone are placed high up in trees (Figure 13).
  • During honey harvest the tree must be climbed again to lower the heavy hive that is full of honey and angry bees.
  • The Kamara hive can we easily mounted on a raised platform or arranged under a thatch hut (Figures 11 and 12).
  • Honey harvesting becomes now easy because the honey chamber can be detached from the brood chamber.  
Figure 10. Both ends are trimmed to expose the hive entrance

©TECA/Kwame Aidoo

Figure 11. Kamara basket hives mounted on a raised platform

©TECA/Kwame Aidoo

Figure 12. A thatch hut can protect the hives from excessive heat

©TECA/Kwame Aidoo

  • Protect the mounted hives from wild fires and strayed animals such as cattle if necessary. 
Figure 13. Local basket hives placed high up in trees

©TECA/Charlotte Lietaer

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Good beekeeping practices: ID 8409.
  • Beekeeping in Africa: site selection for bee hives: ID 7323.
  • Beekeeping in Africa: colonization of a bee hive: ID 7324.
  • Beekeeping: how to make a top bar beehive (Kenyan top bar hive model): ID 7274.

This technology is also available in Spanish: ID 8667.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology provides improved apiculture management and better colony health.

Beekeeping: the Kamara basket hive: an improved traditional hive

The re-designing of the original basket hive used by traditional beekeepers of Koinadugu District of Sierra Leone has enabled beekeepers to harvest honey combs in a sustainable way without destroying the entire nest of the bees. Honey and beeswax yields have improved substantially. The new Kamara basket hive has a brood chamber which slots into a second honey section and allows harvesting with little disturbance of the colony. The honey chamber is taken out and all combs are removed after which it is placed back onto the brood chamber which is left untouched. Beekeepers now mount these new hives on platforms or arrange them under thatch huts for easy management of colonies instead of placing them high up in the branches of trees.

records.title: Labour-saving technologies and practices: roof water harvesting
records.description:
Description

Many different systems are used to collect and store rainwater, namely:

  • below ground storage;
    • hanging a plastic sheet across poles collecting water beneath through a hole in the centre;
  • partial below ground;
    • placing a plastic sheet on the ground collecting water beneath through a hole in the centre;
  • above ground storage;
    • placing containers underneath banana leaves, trees and roof eaves.

1. Features of roof water systems

1.1 Basic requirements

The basic requirements are:

  • a roof (preferably rectangular);
    • corrugated iron or tiled roof is preferable, but closely packed thatching also works (do not use asbestos as itis harmful to health);
  • gutters;
    • low cost guttering systems can be made from, for example, split bamboo;
  • down pipe;
  • concrete base; and
  • storage system;
    • ranging from earthenware jars to large tanks of 30 000 litres.

1.2 Below ground storage systems

Below ground storage is a cheap system to construct because of the support of the side walls, however water needs pumping up and this system is more difficult to clean.

1.3 Partial below ground systems

A circular hole is dug into the ground and lined with polyethylene or plaster. It is covered with a roof (from thatch or iron sheets) to protect the water from sunlight, birds and animals.

1.4 Above ground storage

A round tank is constructed from:

  • curved galvanised sheets;
  • ferro-cement; or
  • bricks.

This system does not require a pump, cleaning is easier and leaks can be detected easily. A concrete base is desirable.

Storage systems should prevent:

  • mosquitoes entering and breeding in the water; and
  • sunlight that stimulates algae growth.

Easy access to all storage systems is necessary for periodic cleaning.

A first flush system can be incorporated to flush away the first rainwater, which has dislodged leaves and dirt after a long dry spell.

1.5 Amount of water collected

The amount of water collected depends upon various factors:

  • dimensions of collecting surface;
  • millimetres of rainfall; and
  • storage capacity.

For example, a house with a 7 m x 7 m roof catches 500 litres of water from 10 mm of rainfall. In an area with an annual rainfall of 750 mm and 75 percent efficiency on a well designed and constructed system, yields 28 000 litres per year. If an average family consumes 100 litres per day then that is enough water for 280 days (assuming there is sufficient storage).

Rainwater is clean and can usually be used for drinking and domestic purposes without filtering, depending on the cleanliness of the roof and storage system.

2. Features of runoff collection

Runoff water may be collected:

  • from impermeable surfaces such as granite or rocky outcrops (see figure 1 and 2);
    • stored in a tank and possibly piped downhill to the community; and
    • during heavy rains from any suitable land;
      • lead and directed to uncontaminated pond or subsurface collection area.
Figure 1. Ferro-cement tank

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Reinforced mortar tank

©FAO/TECA

3. Features of simple water filters

Use of water filters is highly desirable to get clean drinking water.

Simple water filters can be made by:

  • filling large containers with graded sands and charcoal; and
  • providing an outlet at the base.

Water filters improve water purity and reduce water borne diseases.

4. Advantages

4.1 Labour saving

The practice saves time by delivering the source of water closer to home.

4.2 Livelihood resilience strengthening

Cleaner water improves the health of community members.

The increase of the volume of available water also:

  • secures supply;
  • eliminates the  strain of looking for water sources during dry periods; and
  • minimises surface runoff and soil erosion.

4.3 Livelihood diversification

If a large amount of runoff water is collected, it can also be used for irrigating vegetable gardens near the house.

The collected roof water can feed directly into a low cost drip irrigation system if the storage tank is located approximately 1.5 m above the area to be irrigated.

Opportunities for earning income can arise by constructing storage tanks.

5. Disadvantages

5.1 Equipment

Roofwater harvesting needs adequate and clean:

  • roof area
  • gutters
  • storage tank.

5.2 Cost

Low cost storage systems are available but have limited storage capacity (around USD 100 for 1 500 litres).

5.3 Skills

Storage tank requires adequate training in terms of:

  • construction
  • maintenance
  • use.

6. Related/associated technologies 

  • Water management in organic agriculture: ID 8366.
  • Rooftop water collection, drip irrigation and plastic mulching in home garden conditions in drought prone areas: ID 8934.
  • Soil and water conservation practices to reduce soil erosion and enhance water conservation: ID 7861.
  • Rooftop rainwater harvesting: ID 7387.
  • Roof top rainwater harvesting: concrete tank: ID 7513.
  • Rainwater harvesting for increased pasture production: ID 7358.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

7.1 Labour-saving technology (LST) 

The practice allows for time-saving provided that the water source is located closer to households.

7.2 Resource use efficiency 

The practice partly eliminates the strain, during dry periods, to water source and prevents soil quality depletion. The water is also used more efficiently for irrigation.​

7.3 Pro-poor technology 

The practice allows for cleaner hence healthier water. Irrigation and water storage increase yields creating additional income.

    • stored in a tank and possibly piped downhill to the community; and
    • during heavy rains from any suitable land;
      • lead and directed to uncontaminated pond or subsurface collection area.
Figure 1. Ferro-cement tank

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Reinforced mortar tank

©FAO/TECA

3. Features of simple water filters

Use of water filters is highly desirable to get clean drinking water.

Simple water filters can be made by:

  • filling large containers with graded sands and charcoal; and
  • providing an outlet at the base.

Water filters improve water purity and reduce water borne diseases.

4. Advantages

4.1 Labour saving

The practice saves time by delivering the source of water closer to home.

4.2 Livelihood resilience strengthening

Cleaner water improves the health of community members.

The increase of the volume of available water also:

  • secures supply;
  • eliminates the  strain of looking for water sources during dry periods; and
  • minimises surface runoff and soil erosion.

4.3 Livelihood diversification

If a large amount of runoff water is collected, it can also be used for irrigating vegetable gardens near the house.

The collected roof water can feed directly into a low cost drip irrigation system if the storage tank is located approximately 1.5 m above the area to be irrigated.

Opportunities for earning income can arise by constructing storage tanks.

5. Disadvantages

5.1 Equipment

Roofwater harvesting needs adequate and clean:

  • roof area
  • gutters
  • storage tank.

5.2 Cost

Low cost storage systems are available but have limited storage capacity (around USD 100 for 1 500 litres).

5.3 Skills

Storage tank requires adequate training in terms of:

  • construction
  • maintenance
  • use.

6. Related/associated technologies 

  • Water management in organic agriculture: ID 8366.
  • Rooftop water collection, drip irrigation and plastic mulching in home garden conditions in drought prone areas: ID 8934.
  • Soil and water conservation practices to reduce soil erosion and enhance water conservation: ID 7861.
  • Rooftop rainwater harvesting: ID 7387.
  • Roof top rainwater harvesting: concrete tank: ID 7513.
  • Rainwater harvesting for increased pasture production: ID 7358.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

7.1 Labour-saving technology (LST) 

The practice allows for time-saving provided that the water source is located closer to households.

7.2 Resource use efficiency 

The practice partly eliminates the strain, during dry periods, to water source and prevents soil quality depletion. The water is also used more efficiently for irrigation.​

7.3 Pro-poor technology 

The practice allows for cleaner hence healthier water. Irrigation and water storage increase yields creating additional income.

records.title: Labour-saving technologies and practices: conservation agriculture
records.description:
Description

1. Features of conservation agriculture

Conservation agriculture is the simultaneous practice of permanent soil cover, minimal soil disturbance and crop rotations. This is achieved by:

  • the maintenance of a permanent vegetative soil cover or mulch to protect the soil surface; direct planting without seedbed preparation through the soil cover to minimise the disturbance of the soil;
  • crop residue management and weed control, to stimulate soil structure formation, improve soil fertility, and to control weeds (with dependence on herbicides); and
  • disease control based on Integrated Pest Management, crop rotations and inter-cropping.

Inputs include cover crops, the use of draught animal-powered knife rollers or herbicides to crush or kill weeds and cover crops, and no-till planters. Farmers require extensive training and change in mindset to shift from traditional practices to conservation agriculture.

No-tillage practices are suited to areas with high rainfall (> 1 000 mm to ensure high levels of biomass production and minimum competition from livestock for crop residues), long growing period (more than six to seven months for biomass production), soils with more than 20 percent clay content (to reduce risk of soil compaction).

Minimum tillage, rather than no-tillage systems are considered to be more appropriate in semi-arid and arid regions with 300 mm to 800 mm annual rainfall.

Conservation agriculture is suitable in areas where there is a capacity to grow cash crops (in order to purchase inputs), markets for a diverse range of crops (to support crop rotation), secure access to land and limited value on crop residues (as livestock fodder and firewood).

It is possible to adopt components of conservation agriculture in a piecemeal manner: for example, inter-cropping cover crops or using conservation tillage equipment or herbicides. These components may act as entry points for moving towards full conservation agriculture.

2. Features of conservation tillage

There is a range of tillage operations that reduces the losses of soil and water, in comparison to conventional tillage, including (in order of reduced soil disturbance):

  • reduced tillage
  • semi-permanent planting basins
  • ridge tillage
  • tined tillage
  • strip tillage
  • zero tillage. 

2.1 Reduced tillage

Tilling the whole surface but eliminating one or more of the conventional tillage operations.

2.2 Semi-permanent planting basins

Known as tassa in Mali, zai in Burkino Faso, demi-lune in Niger, potholing in Zambia, the Matengo pit system in Tanzania.

2.3 Ridge tillage

A system of annual or semi-permanent ridges and furrows, resulting in some residue cover.

2.4 Tined tillage

The land is prepared with implements that do not invert the soil and which cause little compaction, resulting in a good cover of residues on the surface in excess of 30 percent. Equipment used includes chisel plough, vibro-cultivator and draught animal-powered ripper.

2.5 Strip tillage

Strips 5 cm to 20 cm wide are prepared to receive the seed and the intervening bands are not disturbed.

2.6 Zero tillage (or no tillage)

Planting the seed into the stubble of the previous crop without any tillage or soil disturbance. Weed control relies heavily on herbicides. This approach is broadly equivalent to conservation agriculture.

Sub-soiling may be necessary before switching to conservation agriculture to remove hardpans caused by years of hand hoeing or ploughing.

Plough pans are broken up using use ripper tine with draught animals or tractors at the end of the cropping season when the draught animals are in peak condition and before soil hardness increases during the dry season. Alternatively, where time allows, cowpeas may be planted to break up the hard pans.

Excessively uneven land that could lead to waterlogging (possibly resulting from previous poor ploughing practices) are corrected using damscoops or levellers with draught animals or tractors at the end of the cropping season before switching to conservation agriculture.

3. Conservation tillage equipment

3.1 Hand-operated jab planter

The hand-operated jap planter plants through crop residues and crop cover with no tillage and removes the need to prepare the land for planting. It can also be used to apply fertilizer.

3.2 Knife roller drawn by draught animals

The knife roller bends over and crushes crop residues and cover crops prior to planting which then remains on the field as soil cover), saves the removal of crop residues by hand and acts as a cover to suppress weeds.

3.3 Draught animal-powered ripper

The draught animal-powered ripper allows for planting strips in reduced tillage systems by cutting furrows rather than inverting the soil.

A planter attachment places seed directly in ripper furrow. Wings can be attached for ridging and weeding which reduces time by half because do both sides of the row in one pass.

3.4 Draught animal-powered seeder/no-till planter

This equipment helps to plant directly through the cover crop: plant through crop residue and crop cover with no tillage and removes the need to prepare the land for planting.

4. Features of cover crops

  • A cover crop is any crop grown to provide soil cover, regardless of whether it is later incorporated into the soil.
  • Cover crops and green manures can be annual, biennial or perennial herbaceous plants grown in a pure or mixed stand during all or part of the year.
  • They are grown primarily to prevent soil erosion but they also reduce soil surface temperature and water losses, add organic matter to the soil, stimulate soil life, suppress weeds and some fix nitrogen. Examples include dolicos lablab and mucuna.
  • Weed, disease and pest problems need to be addressed before switching to conservation agriculture.
Figure 1. Labour-saving technologies and practices: conservation agriculture

©FAO/TECA

5. Advantages and disadvantages of conservation agriculture

5.1 Advantages

5.1.1 Labour saving

  • Reduced labour inputs for land preparation and weeding once the system becomes established;
  • more even distribution of labour across the year;
  • more timely operations; and
  • a reduction in drudgery.

Changes in draught animal power systems from the mouldboard plough to shallow ripping saves labour.

5.1.2 Livelihood's resilience strengthening

  • Represents a move towards a more sustainable farming system with increased yields.
  • The quality of the environment is improved and the previous degradation reversed.

5.1.3 Livelihood diversification

  • More time is available to undertake off-farm work and hire out services (for example, draught animals).
  • There is the opportunity to move into growing organic produce with payment premiums.

5.1.4 Cost

  • Reduced requirement for herbicides and fertilisers once the system established.

5.1.5 Risk

  • There is a risk in changing land over to conservation agriculture gradually (one plot at a time) in order to minimise risk of using a new farming system.

5.1.6 Agro system’s resilience increased

  • Livelihoods and the agro system are benefited in a way that they are more resilient to adverse weather events and variability.

5.2 Disadvantages

5.2.1 Labour

  • Additional labour inputs are required initially whilst establishing a system for the application of lime, farmyard manure, weeding, breaking hand pans and constructing planting basins.
  • Manual and draught animal-powered minimum tillage systems (without cover crops) increase labour requirements for weeding because they do not bury weeds by inverting the soil during land preparation.
  • An initial investment of time and energy to construct some of the reduced tillage systems is required.

5.2.2 Attitude

  • Other farmers may regard the retention of cover crops and crop residues as a lazy form of farming.

5.2.3 Equipment

  • More complex draught animal-drawn equipment requires skilled local manufacture or import.
  • Farmers require access to seeds of green manure/cover crops, herbicides, liming or farmyard manure to adjust the soil acidity, and fertilisers when crop residues are left on the field until a new equilibrium is reached.

5.2.4 Cost

  • The cost incurred is the purchase of conservation tillage equipment and herbicides.

5.2.5 Skills

  • Farmers need extensive training and changes in the approach to conventional farming systems.

5.2.6 Risk

  • The ability to grow the cover crops is compromised by:
    • the strong demand for crop residues as forage for livestock; in addition, 
    • the communal land tenure system limits the right of land use to the growing season.
  • Higher levels of surface trash may result in higher plant disease and pest infestations, if not managed properly.
  • The system not suited to low precipitation, short growing season, sandy soils and soils at risk of waterlogging.

5.2.7 Infrastructure

  • Access to appropriate inputs and skilled extension service might be constrained.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: improved hand tools for harvesting cereals: ID 7295.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: improved use of hoes for land preparation, planting and weeding: ID 7296.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: integrated pest management: ID 7298.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: raised beds: ID 7299.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: row planting, hand seeders and planters: ID 7301.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: seeds and crops: ID 7302.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: weed wipes and knapsack sprayers: ID 7303.
  • Crop rotation in conservation agriculture: ID 7415.
  • Introduction to conservation agriculture: its principles and benefits: ID 7413.
  • Green manure/cover crops and crop rotation in conservation agriculture on small farms: ID 7250.
  • Conservation agriculture for smallholder farmers in dryland areas: ID 4676.

This technology is also available in Spanish: ID 8684.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

This technology saves labour once the conservation agriculture system is established due to the reduced quantity of labour required to undertake the regular farming tasks. 

7.2 Resource use efficiency

This technology is lower in costs and inputs due to the no-tillage system, and the reduction in the quantity of herbicides and fertilizers required. 

7.3 Pro-poor technology

Due to enhanced livelihoods resilience and resistance, and the reduction in the operational costs of the system, this technology is considered an economic and sustainable practice in the long run.

records.title: Labour-saving technologies and practices: draught animal powered and motorised crop processing
records.description:
Description

1. Features of draught animal-driven equipment

  • Draught animals are occasionally used to drive crop processing machinery such as drive presses and crushers (such as sugar cane crushers) or a Quern (grain milling).
  • Their slow rotational movement around an axis is geared up to provide the much higher rotational speed required to operate machinery.
    • This is either done by converting their motion into rotational motion by pulling a wheel with a driven axle, or through a gearbox on a central pivot.
    • If the latter, shear pins should be incorporated into the system to prevent breakage by the high torque that this system can produce.

2. Features of motorised grain milling

2.1 Plate mills

  • These mills are based on the Quern with two vertical or horizontal iron plates on an axis, one of which rotates.
  • The grain is fed through the central axis and is ground between them.
  • The pressure between the two plates governs the fineness of the product. They are used to grind dry or wetted products, such as wetted maize, tomatoes, peppers and spices.
  • Output is around 270 kg per hour from a 5 kW motor.

2.2 Roller mills

  • Grain is crushed rather than ground for feeding to ruminants.
  • Output is around 400 kg per hour from a 4 kW motor.

2.3 Hammer mills

  • The hammers rotate at around 3 000 rpm in a circular chamber with a perforated screen at the base.
  • The peripheral speed of the hammer tips and their clearance from the bars and screen are critical design parameters.
  • The size of the holes determines the fineness of the flour.
  • Larger sizes are used for animal feed.
  • Output around 240 kg per hour from a 5 kW motor.

3. Features of motorised oil extraction

3.1 Screw-auger press

  • This is the most efficient small-scale press for seeds.
  • The tapered screw-auger rotates in a perforated tapered cylinder through which the oil is expelled.
  • The taper of the screw and the distance of the flights from the cylinder allow adjustment for increased pressure.
  • This and the pre-treatment of the seeds by appropriate heat treatment an important effect on the efficient operation of the press.

3.2 Cage press

  • Motorised operation of the screw or hydraulic press, can be used with several oil seeds, including palm oil, shea nuts, groundnuts, soya and sunflower and on cassava dough.

3.3 Centrifugal cracker for palm oil

  • This breaks the shell from around the palm oil kernel, followed by screening, winnowing and then the screw press.

4. Features of motorised cassava processing

  • A range of motorised root cutters and cassava graters are available.

5. Features of motorised rice hulling

5.1 Engleberg type

  • A ribbed or bladed horizontal cast iron cylinder rotates within a cast housing with a slotted plate in the base.
  • Rice is fed in one end and circulates along the rotor towards the other end where it emerges hulled.
  • Outputs of around 400 kg per hour with a 11 kW motor.

5.2 Rubber roller-huller

  • The hull is sheared between a pair of rubber rollers rotating in opposite directions.

5.3 Disc huller

  • Similar to the plate mills described above.

5.4 Rice polishers

  • They remove the bran after hulling, for example by spinning the rice by means of rotor blades to which are attached leather straps.
  • Some Engleberg hullers have integral polishers and are suitable for small-scale operations.

6. Features of coffee processing

6.1 Coffee pulpers

  • Motorised versions have a roughened drum that rotates to rasp the coffee cherry against a cast iron breast to strip the flesh off the coffee hull.
  • These are then separated from the pulp.
  • Adequate water is required to wash away the flesh.
  • Outputs are around 2 200 kg per hour with a motor of 2 kW.

6.2 Coffee hullers

  • The beans are extracted from their hulls using small hullers of the Engleberg type.
  • Outputs are around 180 kg per hour with a motor of 4 kW.
  • The beans, hulls and dust are then separated by sieves and by winnowing.

7. Advantages

7.1 Labour saving

  • The practice provides higher work rates than traditional methods.

7.2 Livelihood resilience strengthening

  • Crop processing improves the nutritious value of crops and labour saving allows to use time and energy in other activities.

7.3 Livelihood diversification and resilience improvement

  • The practice provides an opportunity for households to engage in small market sales of processed crops.
  • Some may establish crop processing business and hire services to community.

7.4 Equipment

  • The equipment is robust and simple to operate.

7.5 Infrastructure

  • The equipment is relatively easy to fabricate, maintain and repair.

7.6 Risk

  • Financial risks minimised through contractual arrangements.

8. Disadvantages

8.1 Equipment

  • Prior to processing the product should ideally be clean and free of molds, fungal infections and pests.

8.2 Cost

  • There is a high capital cost of equipment, particularly of the motorised power sources, and high operational costs in terms of fuel and maintenance.
  • For much of this processing equipment, the cost of the power source is greater than the cost of the equipment.
    • This is particularly true for diesel or petrol engines as opposed to electric motors.

8.3 Risk

  • There is relatively high financial risk.
  • The practice may fail if hire services are introduced into an area where there is insufficient demand to pay for contractual or community-owned services.

8.4 Infrastructure

  • Substantial infrastructure is required for the supply, maintenance and servicing of the equipment, particularly the power sources.
Figure 1. Hammer mill

©FAO/TECA

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Jab planter user manual: ID 7339.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: row planting, hand seeders and planters: ID 7301.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: seeds and crops: ID 7302.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: conservation agriculture: ID 7294.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: Draught Animal Power (DAP) planters and weeders: ID 7305.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: draught animal power and implements: ID 7306.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: draught animal powered groundnut lifter: ID 7309.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2307 and Spanish: ID 8691.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The technology is labour saving, as well as strengthens and diversifies livelihood resilience.

_annotations.body:
Labour-saving technologies and practices: draught animal powered and motorised crop processing

The following technology provides some examples of the utilisation of animal power as an energy source for post-harvest operations. It details features of draught animal-driven equipment, motorized grain milling (plate, roller and hammer mills), motorized oil extraction (screw-auger press, cage press, and centrifugal cracker for palm oil), motorized cassava processing, motorsing rice hulling (Engleberg type, rubber roller-huller, disc huller, and rice polishers), and coffee processing (coffee pulpers and hullers). It also provides advantages and disadvantages including labour saving, livelihood resilience strengthening, livelihood diversification and resilience improvement, equipment, infrastructure, risk and cost.

Description

1. Features of draught animal-driven equipment

  • Draught animals are occasionally used to drive crop processing machinery such as drive presses and crushers (such as sugar cane crushers) or a Quern (grain milling).
  • Their slow rotational movement around an axis is geared up to provide the much higher rotational speed required to operate machinery.
    • This is either done by converting their motion into rotational motion by pulling a wheel with a driven axle, or through a gearbox on a central pivot.
    • If the latter, shear pins should be incorporated into the system to prevent breakage by the high torque that this system can produce.

2. Features of motorised grain milling

2.1 Plate mills

  • These mills are based on the Quern with two vertical or horizontal iron plates on an axis, one of which rotates.
  • The grain is fed through the central axis and is ground between them.
  • The pressure between the two plates governs the fineness of the product. They are used to grind dry or wetted products, such as wetted maize, tomatoes, peppers and spices.
  • Output is around 270 kg per hour from a 5 kW motor.

2.2 Roller mills

  • Grain is crushed rather than ground for feeding to ruminants.
  • Output is around 400 kg per hour from a 4 kW motor.

2.3 Hammer mills

  • The hammers rotate at around 3 000 rpm in a circular chamber with a perforated screen at the base.
  • The peripheral speed of the hammer tips and their clearance from the bars and screen are critical design parameters.
  • The size of the holes determines the fineness of the flour.
  • Larger sizes are used for animal feed.
  • Output around 240 kg per hour from a 5 kW motor.

3. Features of motorised oil extraction

3.1 Screw-auger press

  • This is the most efficient small-scale press for seeds.
  • The tapered screw-auger rotates in a perforated tapered cylinder through which the oil is expelled.
  • The taper of the screw and the distance of the flights from the cylinder allow adjustment for increased pressure.
  • This and the pre-treatment of the seeds by appropriate heat treatment an important effect on the efficient operation of the press.

3.2 Cage press

  • Motorised operation of the screw or hydraulic press, can be used with several oil seeds, including palm oil, shea nuts, groundnuts, soya and sunflower and on cassava dough.

3.3 Centrifugal cracker for palm oil

  • This breaks the shell from around the palm oil kernel, followed by screening, winnowing and then the screw press.

4. Features of motorised cassava processing

  • A range of motorised root cutters and cassava graters are available.

5. Features of motorised rice hulling

5.1 Engleberg type

  • A ribbed or bladed horizontal cast iron cylinder rotates within a cast housing with a slotted plate in the base.
  • Rice is fed in one end and circulates along the rotor towards the other end where it emerges hulled.
  • Outputs of around 400 kg per hour with a 11 kW motor.

5.2 Rubber roller-huller

  • The hull is sheared between a pair of rubber rollers rotating in opposite directions.

5.3 Disc huller

  • Similar to the plate mills described above.

5.4 Rice polishers

  • They remove the bran after hulling, for example by spinning the rice by means of rotor blades to which are attached leather straps.
  • Some Engleberg hullers have integral polishers and are suitable for small-scale operations.

6. Features of coffee processing

6.1 Coffee pulpers

  • Motorised versions have a roughened drum that rotates to rasp the coffee cherry against a cast iron breast to strip the flesh off the coffee hull.
  • These are then separated from the pulp.
  • Adequate water is required to wash away the flesh.
  • Outputs are around 2 200 kg per hour with a motor of 2 kW.

6.2 Coffee hullers

  • The beans are extracted from their hulls using small hullers of the Engleberg type.
  • Outputs are around 180 kg per hour with a motor of 4 kW.
  • The beans, hulls and dust are then separated by sieves and by winnowing.

7. Advantages

7.1 Labour saving

  • The practice provides higher work rates than traditional methods.

7.2 Livelihood resilience strengthening

  • Crop processing improves the nutritious value of crops and labour saving allows to use time and energy in other activities.

7.3 Livelihood diversification and resilience improvement

  • The practice provides an opportunity for households to engage in small market sales of processed crops.
  • Some may establish crop processing business and hire services to community.

7.4 Equipment

  • The equipment is robust and simple to operate.

7.5 Infrastructure

  • The equipment is relatively easy to fabricate, maintain and repair.

7.6 Risk

  • Financial risks minimised through contractual arrangements.

8. Disadvantages

8.1 Equipment

  • Prior to processing the product should ideally be clean and free of molds, fungal infections and pests.

8.2 Cost

  • There is a high capital cost of equipment, particularly of the motorised power sources, and high operational costs in terms of fuel and maintenance.
  • For much of this processing equipment, the cost of the power source is greater than the cost of the equipment.
    • This is particularly true for diesel or petrol engines as opposed to electric motors.

8.3 Risk

  • There is relatively high financial risk.
  • The practice may fail if hire services are introduced into an area where there is insufficient demand to pay for contractual or community-owned services.

8.4 Infrastructure

  • Substantial infrastructure is required for the supply, maintenance and servicing of the equipment, particularly the power sources.
