records.title: Government-led integrated approach for delivery of services to smallholder poultry farmers
records.description:
Description

Chhattisgarh is a relatively new state in the Indian Union and was formed in 2000. It is broadly divided into three agro-climatic zones, comprising the northern hilly region, the Chhattisgarh plains and the Bastar plateau. The Bastar plateau, situated in south Chhattisgarh, is one of the most backward regions of the country. Seventy per cent of the region’s population is tribal. The region has dense forests, rich in minor forest produce (MFP). Traditionally, tribal communities depend heavily on MFP for their livelihood; they also rear small animals such as goats, pigs and poultry in their backyard in order to supplement income.

Tribal households have been traditionally rearing poultry and women have been the main caretakers of the flock. Poultry rearing, thus, is a key source of supplementary income. It also provides them with nutritional supplements, in the form of valuable animal protein because milk and milk by-products are not part of the tribal diet. The flock sizes are highly variable and range from as low as two hens to ten hens per household. Men usually rear poultry for gaming purposes and champion cockerels are the pride of owners.

1. The problem

  • Backyard poultry in this region is plagued by various problems.
  • Ranikhet disease and fowlpox are endemic throughout the state and cause considerable loss.
  • Moreover, the mortality rate in growing chickens is high due to predation.
  • Parasitic infection is a common problem because both ectoparasites and endo-parasites are found in household poultry.
  • Unhygienic surroundings and kuchcha (temporary) housing aggravates the parasitic infestation, resulting in the death of birds and direct economic losses.
  • The main endo-parasites include roundworms and tapeworms, which compete for food inside the alimentary canal of infected birds and multiply rapidly.
  • All this, in conjunction with lack of access to credit, training and relevant extension information, further complicates the practice of backyard poultry rearing.

2. The good practice

  • Where communities have traditionally reared poultry, as in the Bastar region, a poultry rearing initiative must build on these practices, and at the same time, gradually introduce technical innovations.
  • The project approach was to slowly evolve from step zero through to step three and is explained in Table 1.
Table 1. The gradual change brought about by building upon Indigenous knowledge
Step  Production System
Step 0  Scavenging: No regular water or feed, poor night shelter
Step 1  Offered water and supplementary feed, improved shelter, DOC care in the first week, Newcastle Disease (NCD) vaccination.
Step 2  Practices, as in Step 1, plus better feeding, watering, improved housing, treatment for parasites, additional vaccinations for fowl pox, Infectious Bursal Disease (IBD), etc., though the focus has remained on NCD.
Step 3  As in Step 2, along with the introduction of improved breeds and balanced diets, gradually moving to a semi-intensive system.

Source: SAPPLPP 2012

2.1 Emphasis on low-cost technologies

  • The low-cost, pro-poor technologies introduced in the programme aim at strengthening household poultry production.
    • These include:
      • low-cost;
      • protein-rich feeding;
      • de-worming;
      • vaccination;
      • low-cost housing;
      • egg-candling; and
      • promoting the use of bamboos as feeders and waterers.

2.2 Doorstep animal health service delivery

  • This aimed at improving the risk management capacity of farmers by promoting a doorstep, animal health service delivery on a user-payment basis, and at creating village facilitators (VFs), or para vets, at the village/hamlet level to deliver regular, economically sustainable animal health services within the villages.
  • The BILDP invested significantly in identifying and training VFs, who provided health services to poultry rearers.
  • A modular approach to training (see Figure 1) helped nurture the interest of the facilitators for a sustained period of time.
Figure 1. Modular training programme

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Ethno-veterinary practices

  • The adoption of ethnoveterinary practices to combat common diseases such as cough and cold, diarrhoea, fowl pox, wounds, endo-parasites and ecto-parasites, which contribute to morbidity and mortality in birds, can be adopted easily and costs practically nothing.

2.4 Vaccinations

  • Mass vaccination drives to fight diseases such as Newcastle are unique to Bastar because of the network of VFs, operational in remote villages, to implement the campaign.

2.5 Change in practices

  • A change from traditional scavenging practices to a semi-scavenging system.
    • Low-input, protein-rich feed formulation, using locally available material such as feeding ants and termites through the earthen-pot method has helped save financial resources spent on feed.
    • Checking the fertility of eggs through the candling procedure is another practice that has enabled female farmers to retain only the fertile eggs for hatching, thereby improving the hatchability rate as well as making infertile eggs available for household consumption and sale.

3. Stakeholders and their roles

  • The promotion of rural household poultry is managed by village institutions with support from state departments.
  • The major players in this practice are the self‑help groups (SHGs), model farmers and VFs along with the Block Extension Team and the Project Management Unit.
  • The actors involved and their roles are described in Figure 2.
Figure 2. Stakeholders and their roles

©FAO/TECA

3.1 Outcomes

3.1.1 Health Services

  • Since the VF’s are trained individuals from within the community, there has been better coverage and easier availability of health services.
  • The network of VFs has ensured a regular supply of vaccines and the provision of first-aid services to livestock keepers in remote areas, which in turn has led to a reduction in the mortality rate (from 80 to 90 percent to 20 to 30 percent), thereby contributing to improved flock productivity.
  • The number of poultry birds vaccinated through sustained efforts such as the Pulse Ranikhet drive has almost doubled over the last three-year period.

3.1.2 Employment Opportunities for VFs

  • Over 1 500 facilitators have been trained over a period of eight years.
  • Of these, 813 VFs are currently working.
  • Sixty-four percent are able to earn Rs 500 or more per month as supplementary income.

3.1.3 Strengthening Indigenous Knowledge

  • The use of ethnoveterinary practices to combat common health problems has contributed to strengthening indigenous knowledge systems.

3.1.4 Nutrition and Food Security

  • The low mortality rate in poultry has resulted in the availability of more birds for home consumption.
  • The money generated from the sale of eggs and meat has also contributed to higher food security.
  • The simple practice of egg candling to identify fertile eggs has also made it possible for infertile eggs to be consumed within the home or sold.

3.2 Learning

  • There are key elements that contributed to the success of the project.
    • Full integration of VFs and multi‑disciplinary extension teams for the optimal delivery of health services at the doorsteps of poor tribal farmers.
    • Compared to the more conventional government interventions of introducing improved birds, the approach of providing health and extension services to existing Desi flocks is more effective and cost efficient.
    • Animal health workers/VFs from within the community understand local problems and requirements of the farmers and are more committed to providing their services because they are accountable to the community.
    • The modular training of VFs/animal health workers comprising classroom training, field training and exposure visits, refresher training at regular intervals and being part of referral vet systems helps in sustaining interest and increases the knowledge of the VFs.
    • Focusing on preventive animal health measures such as poultry vaccination drives (Pulse Ranikhet), involving the entire community provides outstanding results in resource-poor areas.

3.3 Suitability and replicability

  • This project has the potential for replication and it has promoted rural household poultry successfully in one of the most inhospitable terrains in the country.
  • The project has now expanded to 16 blocks covering 37 000 farmer families of four different districts of the Bastar region and has created a network of village-level institutions in 435 villages of the region.
  • Its strength lies in building on the traditional knowledge-base and existing farming systems, with minimal introduction of practices that advocate drastic changes.
  • The model demonstrated by the BILDP can be further developed and replicated in other districts of the state, and in the adjoining tribal regions of Madhya Pradesh.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Backyard poultry farming through self-help groups in West Bengal: ID 7675.
  • Women resurrecting poultry biodiversity and livelihoods: ID 7681.
  • Training videos for family poultry production: ID 8148.
  • Making modern poultry markets work for the poor: ID 7678.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Women-friendly

The technology provides women access to new knowledge on poultry rearing given women have been the main undertakers.

6.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for the development, training and support provided to village facilitators, which deliver this knowledge and skills to regular animal health services.

6.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology builds on the traditional knowledge-base and existing farming systems, with minimal introduction of practices that advocate drastic changes. Poultry rearing is a key source of supplementary income in traditional tribal households.

records.title: Agriculture support to nutrition services
records.description:
Description

1. The advantages of using this technology

  • Mothers and caretakers, accompanying malnourished children to Health centers and Nutrition Rehabilitation Units (NRUs), are trained and supported to set up their own vegetable gardens once back in their communities.
    • Reduction of the children relapses in malnutrition after treatment and reinsertion in communities.
    • Low-cost intervention.
    • Women-empowering.
    • Possibility to sell surplus production and increase family incomes.

2. The building process

  • Community mobilizers should be selected and trained in various tasks, such as the training of beneficiaries and the management of nursery beds.
  • Women should be granted priority among beneficiaries as they are the main household stakeholders for nutrition.
  • Identify appropriate land for the setup of nursery beds and demonstration farms.
  • Clear all debris and weeds from a space chosen for gardening.
  • Select seedlings prior to distribution, according to their agronomical particularities and to their nutritional and economical value.
    • Agronomical particularities are: productivity, resistance, maturation length, and compatibility with local conditions.
    • In slums, use vegetable crops which have a short maturity period and long-term benefits.
  • Consider rainwater harvest and storage techniques, to allow watering the gardens even in summer without depending solely on water vendors.
    • Some crops such as bananas, avocado, papaya need a lot of water, so you can plant them close to the water source.
    • There other foods like mango and grapes don’t need so much water.
  • You need to feed your growing plants in order to have a good yield.
    • For this reason you should compost your garden.
      • Every day put waste, grass, fruit skins, animal manure on the pile.
      • Cover it with dirt or ash.
      • Remember to put a fence around the compost to prevent animals or children from scattering it.
      • You can also dig a hole.
      • The compost must be at least 50 steps away from the kitchen.
  • Make sure that beneficiaries have free access to activities and inputs.
  • For monitoring and evaluation, ensure that community mobilizers are adequately trained in data collection interpretation of information received from the beneficiaries.
  • Encourage beneficiaries to collect their own material to assess their motivation and intervene when collection is too difficult or expensive.
  • Ensure that hygiene and good sanitation is practiced especially near the seedbeds to reduce risks of plant contamination.
  • Give priority to vegetables to traditional vegetables which people are familiar with.
    • For the introduction of new vegetables, make sure that people like the taste and know how to use them
      • Cooking demonstrations and basic information on nutrition are necessary.
  • You can use leafy vegetables that keep on growing even after the leaves have been harvested (kale, spinach, leafy onions, etc).
  • You should clear your garden regularly because weeds and unwanted plants are stealing water, nutrients and sunlight.
Figure 1. The establishment of vegetable gardens

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Agriculture support to nutrition service

©FAO/TECA

3. Useful recommendations for facilitators before starting

  • Conduct theoretical lessons on complementary child feeding, nutrition and HIV/AIDS, health and sanitation, basics on low-cost kitchen gardens and on small-scale livestock production.
  • Show practical lessons on:
    • making and using compost manure;
    • planting fruit trees;
    • making seedbeds;
    • transplanting seedlings;
    • producing seeds;
    • watering vegetables;
    • making trenches, etc with hands-on experiences in the NRUs’ and community kitchen gardens.
  • Organize participatory cooking demonstrations and elaboration of locally adapted recipes, ensuring that people like the taste of the dishes.
    • You should involve both elder and young generation in cooking demonstrations thus people can share the experience.
  • Food demonstrations can be conducted in diverse settings and at different events.
      • For example, during agricultural shows, on market days, at religious gatherings, health clinics and schools, and during literacy classes as well as in people’s homes.
    • Try to be creative making different culinary combinations, using the products of the kitchen gardens and henhouses on preparing local dishes (for example cassava tubers with chicken or beans and rape).
      • This creates a good mix of carbohydrate, protein and vitamins/minerals, instead of the nutritionally-poor ones.
  • During the demonstration, the steps and nutritional messages are clearly explained, and all participants should be able to see the tasks that are being performed.
    • Participants join in meal preparation by cutting vegetables, pounding and mixing ingredients and cooking different dishes.
    • This involves learning about combining diverse foods to enhance nutritional value and variety, adding ingredients in the right proportions by using local measures, ensuring correct cooking times and handling and storing foods safely.
  • Once the different dishes have been prepared, participants taste the cooked food and evaluate the taste, appearance, smell and acceptability.
  • In resource poor environments, food demonstrations are most likely to result in positive nutritional benefits if they are combined with a broader range of food production activities targeted to women and the development of appropriate food processing and preservation skills.
    • Examples of activies are home gardens and small-animal raising.

4. Steps to reach successful outcomes

  • The following steps are strongly suggested to be considered to reach successful outcomes
    • Select NRUs according to rates of malnutrition and HIV/AIDS in the area of the NRU, number of admissions, interest of the staff in the project, access to land and water.
      • For each, a Garden Officer and a Garden Monitor should be recruited among local health institutions and trained by specialists on:
        • health and sanitation;
        • nutrition;
        • principles of home gardening;
        • livestock production;
        • and child health.
      • Kits of tools and seeds (vegetables, medicinal and pest control plants) have to be distributed to the beneficiaries at the end of the trainings.
      • For each NRUs, a kitchen garden and a traditional henhouse (kholas) have to be established, fenced with local material and guarded during the day and night.
    • Involve village authorities and self-help groups in community garden activities and management.
    • Recruit project staff within local resources and involve local partners in the selection process.
    • Deliveries of material shall be carried out only if the beneficiaries prove their good will by preparing in advance their kitchen garden, the fenced dimba area for the garden and some compost manure.
    • For areas with water scarcity, suggest:
      • locating the gardens near the community water source;
      • using household waste waters;
      • storing water in containers; and
      • consider solutions that reduce water dispersion in the soil, such as keyhole gardens and container gardens.
    • Distribute the kit only to beneficiaries who have received all trainings and proved their willingness by preparing the grounds for sowing.
      • Preparation of compost manure, construction of fences, keyhole garden or other as relevant.
    • Check that the content of seeds and tools kits is appropriate before distribution.
      • Seeds also can be of non-local plants, to introduce new and more nutrient vegetables in local diets.
    • Monitoring of community gardens’ implementation should be carried out by Garden Monitors through regular visits.
      • Plan accurately the monitoring process and coordinate with the Ministry of Agriculture to rely on national Agricultural Extension Development Officers, usually located in villages, for the monitoring of garden activities in remote areas.

5. Pay particular attention to the following notes

  • Control that the set of kits distributed is complete (tools, seeds are available) because lack of means and staff may hinder the implementation of certain activities and the monitoring of beneficiaries living far from the NRUs.
    • Activities include cooking demonstrations and health trainings.
  • Provision of inputs to NRUs has to be on time.
  • Make sure that all participants, even those who live too far from the NRUs, are monitored and thus receive their kit after the trainings.
  • Monitoring of impact on malnutrition should go through observation of number of relapses at NRUs and through interviews of mothers.
    • The number of relapses at NRUs can also be used as an indicator for the long-term impact of gardens.
  • The mothers and caretakers of recovering children that participate in the project have to be supported by the Garden Monitor.
    • This support is through consultations and refresher trainings.
    • They are expected to setup their own gardens once back in their villages.
    • In communities, training should be carried out by the visiting NRU Garden Officer twice a week.
  • Other beneficiaries, who are not reachable through NRUs and supplementary feeding programmes, may be identified at community level and selected according to their malnutrition rate and to their social status.
    • For example, families living with chronically ill people; with handicapped members; female and orphan-headed households; and elderly members with no family support.

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Farmer field schools on integrated plant nutrient systems: ID 7527.
  • Building life skills for youth: ID 7655.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Pro-poor technology

The establishment of vegetable gardens helps fighting malnutrition at family and community-level.

Agriculture support to nutrition services

Malnourished children are as such because in most cases, their families are not able to feed them properly. Poor families lack the financial means to buy adequate foods in proper quantity, quality and diversity. They consequently adopt diets that lack protein, vitamins and other micro-nutrients in particular. The most affected are those family members whose needs are higher but whose social status is lower. These are women and children. Health centers and Nutrition Rehabilitation Units (NRUs) provide clinical treatment for malnourished children.   • During the demonstration, the steps and nutritional messages are clearly explained, and all participants should be able to see the tasks that are being performed.
    • Participants join in meal preparation by cutting vegetables, pounding and mixing ingredients and cooking different dishes.
    • This involves learning about combining diverse foods to enhance nutritional value and variety, adding ingredients in the right proportions by using local measures, ensuring correct cooking times and handling and storing foods safely.
  • Once the different dishes have been prepared, participants taste the cooked food and evaluate the taste, appearance, smell and acceptability.
  • In resource poor environments, food demonstrations are most likely to result in positive nutritional benefits if they are combined with a broader range of food production activities targeted to women and the development of appropriate food processing and preservation skills.
    • Examples of activies are home gardens and small-animal raising.

4. Steps to reach successful outcomes

  • The following steps are strongly suggested to be considered to reach successful outcomes
    • Select NRUs according to rates of malnutrition and HIV/AIDS in the area of the NRU, number of admissions, interest of the staff in the project, access to land and water.
      • For each, a Garden Officer and a Garden Monitor should be recruited among local health institutions and trained by specialists on:
        • health and sanitation;
        • nutrition;
        • principles of home gardening;
        • livestock production;
        • and child health.
      • Kits of tools and seeds (vegetables, medicinal and pest control plants) have to be distributed to the beneficiaries at the end of the trainings.
      • For each NRUs, a kitchen garden and a traditional henhouse (kholas) have to be established, fenced with local material and guarded during the day and night.
    • Involve village authorities and self-help groups in community garden activities and management.
    • Recruit project staff within local resources and involve local partners in the selection process.
    • Deliveries of material shall be carried out only if the beneficiaries prove their good will by preparing in advance their kitchen garden, the fenced dimba area for the garden and some compost manure.
    • For areas with water scarcity, suggest:
      • locating the gardens near the community water source;
      • using household waste waters;
      • storing water in containers; and
      • consider solutions that reduce water dispersion in the soil, such as keyhole gardens and container gardens.
    • Distribute the kit only to beneficiaries who have received all trainings and proved their willingness by preparing the grounds for sowing.
      • Preparation of compost manure, construction of fences, keyhole garden or other as relevant.
    • Check that the content of seeds and tools kits is appropriate before distribution.
      • Seeds also can be of non-local plants, to introduce new and more nutrient vegetables in local diets.
    • Monitoring of community gardens’ implementation should be carried out by Garden Monitors through regular visits.
      • Plan accurately the monitoring process and coordinate with the Ministry of Agriculture to rely on national Agricultural Extension Development Officers, usually located in villages, for the monitoring of garden activities in remote areas.

    • Activities include cooking demonstrations and health trainings.
  • Provision of inputs to NRUs has to be on time.
  • Make sure that all participants, even those who live too far from the NRUs, are monitored and thus receive their kit after the trainings.
  • Monitoring of impact on malnutrition should go through observation of number of relapses at NRUs and through interviews of mothers.
    • The number of relapses at NRUs can also be used as an indicator for the long-term impact of gardens.
  • The mothers and caretakers of recovering children that participate in the project have to be supported by the Garden Monitor.
    • This support is through consultations and refresher trainings.
    • They are expected to setup their own gardens once back in their villages.
    • In communities, training should be carried out by the visiting NRU Garden Officer twice a week.
  • Other beneficiaries, who are not reachable through NRUs and supplementary feeding programmes, may be identified at community level and selected according to their malnutrition rate and to their social status.
    • For example, families living with chronically ill people; with handicapped members; female and orphan-headed households; and elderly members with no family support.

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Farmer field schools on integrated plant nutrient systems: ID 7527.
  • Building life skills for youth: ID 7655.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Pro-poor technology

The establishment of vegetable gardens helps fighting malnutrition at family and community-level.

Title: Agriculture-Nutrition Integration through NRU-based Garden Training

Description: A social innovation connecting clinical malnutrition treatment with household food production by training mothers/caretakers at Nutrition Rehabilitation Units to establish home vegetable gardens, supported by garden officers, monitoring, and community engagement.

_annotations.field_shorter_description: Malnourished children are as such because in most cases, their families are not able to feed them properly. Poor families lack the financial means to buy adequate foods in proper quantity, quality and diversity. They consequently adopt diets that lack protein, vitamins and other micro-nutrients in particular. The most affected are those family members whose needs are higher but whose social status is lower. These are women and children. Health centers and Nutrition Rehabilitation Units (NRUs) provide clinical treatment for malnourished children. Yet, if the root causes of malnutrition, at family and community level, are not tackled, treated children, once back home, will soon fall back again into malnutrition. Thus, the clinical treatment of malnutrition should be complemented with interventions that support dietary diversification through the establishment of vegetable gardens.

records.title: Improved fallows
records.description:
Description

In western Kenya, farmers are using improved fallows to build up soil fertility. Fallows can be single species or mixed species. A single-species fallow is established with only one plant species in the whole field. Typically, this system is recommended for species that grow fast and develop dense canopies that shade and kill weeds. Such species are Crotalaria grahamiana, Crotalaria paulina and Colopogoniummucunoides (mucuna). On the other hand, planting alternate rows of two or more different fallow species is a mixed fallow system. The species grow together without affecting each other. This practice is particularly good for slow-growing species that will not strongly compete. Figures 1, 2 and 3 are examples of single and mixed species fallows.

Figure 1. Woody single-species fallow of Tephrosia

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. A herbaceous single-species fallow of Colopogonium mucunoides (mucuna)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. A woody mixed fallow of Sesbania and Crotalaria

©FAO/TECA

1. A woody mixed fallow of Sesbania and Crotalaria

  • Not all improved fallow practices are suited to all locations and all farmers.
  • The farmers and extension staff are expected to be active partners in identifying, evaluating and adapting the practices that can address their specific needs and the resources they have at hand.
  • Growing a fallow involves a number of simple steps:
    • obtaining the appropriate seeds of the desired species,
    • seed pre-treatment,
    • establishment,
    • managing pests, and
    • harvesting.
  • These are described in detail below.

1.1 Obtaining Seeds

Seeds for improved fallows species could be obtained by buying or producing on-farm. A good fallow plant must have several of the following characteristics:

  • Its growth is quick, closing the canopy quickly, to suppress weeds and control erosion.
  • It yields much biomass of good quality that decomposes fast and becomes fertilizer for the crops.
  • It is deep-rooted so that it picks up well the nutrients that are leached and deep in the soil.
  • It fixes nitrogen biologically from the atmosphere, building up good nutrients overall.
  • It is easy to establish and manage.
  • It supplies extra products such as stakes, grain and fodder that make its use attractive.
  • It will not spread like a weed into cultivated areas.
  • It easily produces seeds with long viability.
  • It is adapted well to resist pests and diseases in the area.

Examples of improved fallow species:

1.1.1 Woody species

  • Cajanus cajan (pigeon pea)
  • Calliandra calothyrsus (calliandra)
  • Crotalaria grahamiana (crotalaria)
  • Crotalaria mucronata
  • Crotalaria paulina
  • Crotalaria striata
  • Desmodium uncinatum (desmodium)
  • Gliricidia sepium (Mexican lilac)
  • Sesbania sesban (sesbania)
  • Tephrosia candida (tephrosia or fish poison)
  • Tephrosia vogelii.

1.1.2 Herbaceous species

  • Canavalia ensiformis
  • Colopogonium mucunoides (mucuna)
  • Dolichos lablab
  • Macroptilium atropurpureum (siratro).
Figure 4. Calliandra calothyrsus shrub

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Seed pre-treatment

  • Seeds of some fallow species do not germinate quickly or germinate poorly.
    • One such species is Sesbania sesban.
      • Sesbania seeds have a very hard seed coat that requires softening before the seed can germinate.
    • It is recommended that seeds of such species be soaked in hot water at 65° C for 10 to 15 minutes.
    • Do this by leaving boiling water to cool for 15 to 20 minutes before fully immersing the seed in it in a cloth bag.
    • Dry the seed in the sun for 15 to 20 minutes before planting it. Seeds of other plants listed in this guideline germinate easily without pre-treatment.

1.3 Plant density

  • Spacing depends on the size of the seed.
    • The spacing recommended in the table below should give high biomass yield and good canopy cover within six to eight months.
    • The narrow in-row spacing of Crotalaria paulina and Crotalaria striata is because they are short plants when mature.
    • This seed rate can also be used for herbaceous legume cover crops such as mucuna.
  • Table 1 shows recommendations for establishing one hectare of various fallow species.
  • NB: Amounts calculated on seeds being planted two per hole; planting four seeds per hole doubles the seed rate.
  • The germination rate for all seeds is 80 percent, except for Sesbania sesban, which has a rate of 70 percent.
Table 1. Recommendations for establishing one hectare of various fallow species
Species Seeds (per kg) Spacing (cm) Seed rate (kg per ha) Seed rate (g per plot)
Cajanus cajan 7 000 75x30 18.2 1638
Crotalaria grahamiana 18 000 75x30 7.0 630
Crotalaria paulina 64 000 75x10 2.0 180
Crotalaria striata 110 000 75x10 1.2 108
Sesbania Sesban 100 000 75x30 0.3 27
Tephrosia candinda 18 000 75x30 7.0 630
Tephrosia vogelii 18 000 75x30 7.0 630

Source: FAO 2013.

Figure 5. Planting crops on the same field at the beginning of the next season. (A) Maize+trees: fallow species planted in maize plots. (B) Trees: fallow species left to grow alone. (C) Maize: maize planted after improved fallow

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Establishment

For improved fallow species to benefit crops, they must have enough time in the field to grow and accumulate large quantities of biomass and nutrients. Several methods can be used to establish improved fallows:

  • Broadcast the seed in fields among existing crops, for example, with maize after either the first or the second weeding.
    • If intercropping bean with maize, harvest the bean then sow seeds of the fallow plants. This technique is best suited for species with large seeds such as mucuna.
    • An advantage of this practice is that crop husbandry practices such as applying fertilizer and weeding also help the trees to grow better.
  • Plant in rows.
    • Sow seeds of improved fallow trees, shrubs and herbaceous legumes directly between the rows of the food crop after the first weeding or as soon as the food crop has germinated, and cover the seeds with soil.
    • With maize, for example, plant in the furrows between the rows after either the first or the second weeding.
  • Plant the improved fallow trees into existing natural fallows.
    • One way to do this is to dig holes in the natural fallows and sow seeds directly or plant seedlings.
    • If the weeds in the fallow are dense and inhibit digging the holes, first slash them.
    • Crotalaria grahamiana and Tephrosia vogelii can be planted directly into natural fallows.
    • For species like Sesbania sesban that have small seeds or do not grow easily from seed, raise seedlings and plant them either in an existing crop or in natural fallow lands.

1.5 Managing pests

  • Like any plant, fallow species can be attacked by a variety of pests and diseases.
    • When the fallow species share these with the crops to be planted after the fallow, the problem is even more serious and the beneficial effect of the fallow on soil fertility may be lost completely because of a soil-borne pest or disease.
    • It is therefore important to identify pests and diseases and to take appropriate measures to control them.
Figure 6. It is important to identify pests and diseases and to take appropriate measures to control them

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Tephrosia vogelii plant

©FAO/TECA

1.6 Harvesting the fallows

  • After harvesting the food crop, leave the fallow trees in the field to grow.
    • In six to eight months, they form a closed canopy and cast a dense shade on the ground, which helps to suppress weed growth.
    • With fast-growing species such as crotalaria and tephrosia, it is not necessary to weed the fallow.
    • At the end of the fallow period (eight to nine months or longer after planting), cut down the fallow trees and chop off the leaves, twigs and soft branches.
    • Spread them evenly over the field, and then incorporate them into the soil while preparing the land for planting the next crop.
    • Use a jembe or an ox-drawn plough.
    • Remove the woody parts of fallow plants from the field and use them for fuelwood or for stakes for crops such as climbing bean and tomato.
Figure 8. Harvesting the fallows

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. A good maize crop with dark green leaves follows an improved fallow

©FAO/TECA

1.7 Planting crops

  • Planting crops on the same field at the beginning of the next season.
  • At this stage, it is best to add phosphorus fertilizer, especially in phosphorus-deficient soils.

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Fallow cropping garlic after rice: ID 7698.
  • Shortened bush-fallow rotations and sustainable rural livelihoods: ID 4578.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: woodlots, agro-forestry and improved fallow: ID 7320.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The application of this technology helps in restoring soil fertility.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

With restored soil fertility; farmland productivity gets improved and so the farmers' income.

records.title: Cricket farming for human consumption
records.description:
Description

1. Cricket species to be used

Cricket farming has successfully been established with the species shown in Table 1. Acheta domesticus was introduced later to the technology, but is now more popular with farmers in Thailand.

1.1 Life cycle of the crickets

The development from egg to adult cricket is similar for all of the different species mentioned in Table 1 (45 to 60 days). Figure 1 shows a cricket life cycle.

Table 1. Cricket species successfully established in cricket farming

©FAO/TECA

Figure 1. Cricket life cycle

©FAO/TECA

2. Materials for breeding containers

To establish a cricket farm, farmers can choose from a variety of materials to establish breeding containers (Tables 2 and 3).

  • House crickets are bred in various containers described in Tables 2 and 3, sometimes with mosquito nets to keep crickets in and predators out.
  • Tape stripes are attached to the top of the breeding container to prevent the crickets from walking over the edge.
  • The bedding is often made from a layer of rice husks but some breeders do not use any material.
  • Cardboard egg cartons are mainly used in order to resemble a natural environment (Figures 2 and 3).
Table 2. Breeding containers

Source: FAO 2013

Table 3. Breeding containers

Source: FAO 2013

Figure 2. Example of cardboard egg cartons as breeding containers

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Example of cardboard egg cartons as breeding containers

©FAO/TECA

3. How to feed crickets

  • Commercial high protein animal feed, particularly chicken feed, is widely used in cricket farming. Chicken feed with 14 or 21 percent protein content is commonly used.
  • The 21 percent protein feed is used for feeding crickets after hatching until they are 20 days old. Subsequently, they are fed with mixed 14 and 21 percent protein feed until harvesting at 45 days old. The protein content of the chicken feed is described on the package.
  • A few days before harvesting, the high protein feed is replaced with vegetables such as pumpkins, cassava leaves, morning glory leaves and watermelons.
  • Regarding the water supply, water sources should be available either in shallow bowls or other containers which are easily accessible for the crickets. The water source should always be filled and water should be replaced when it starts to become dirty.

3.1 Day to day farming

  • As soon as the male crickets stridulate, bowls containing a mixture of husk and sand are placed in the breeding enclosure in which the females can lay eggs (within 24 hours). Egg-laying duration is seven to fourteen days.
  • The bowls are moved to another breeding tank for incubation and hatching, in which the new colony is established. Hatching occurs usually after about seven to ten days, at a stable temperature. This reproduction cycle can be repeated one to three times for each generation.
  • Production is feasible at temperatures higher than 20° C. The ideal temperature is 28° C to 30° C.
Figure 4. Female crickets laying eggs in husk and rice

©FAO/Christopher Münke

Figure 5. Placing of bowls with nymphs in breeding container

©FAO/Christopher Münke

Figure 6. Nymphs of Acheta domesticus on chicken feed

©FAO/Christopher Münke

4. Harvesting/collection of crickets

  • After the mating period occurs (between days 40 to 45 of the life cycle in normal climatic conditions) the crickets can be collected.
  • Crickets are harvested by lifting the egg cartons out of the container and shaking the crickets into a container.
  • Afterwards, the breeding container is completely emptied and cleaned from all remaining parts and crickets until it can be refilled.

5. Post-harvest handling/processing

Processing can be done at the cricket farm or through a cooperative of farmers or small scale enterprises/wholesalers (Figure 7).

The handling and processing and undertaken as follows:

  • crickets are washed in clean water without added substances;
  • crickets are boiled clean water for a few minutes;
  • second washing in cold clean water;
  • packaging in plastic bags;
  • weighing; and
  • cold storage for transport on ice or in cool unit. Crickets are stored in plastic bags which are then put in plastic tanks on ice. They can only be carried temporarily for two to three days. Long-term storage with -18 to -20° C is possible up to a year. However, most crickets are quickly processed for consumption.
Figure 7. Cricket processing by a wholesale buyer in Maha Sarakham province: (a) first washing, (b) boiling, (c) washing, (d-e) packing, (f) cold storage and delivery to market

7.1 High cost of high protein feed

Approximately half of the production cost is feed, which is commercially produced by the chicken industry. Research is needed to find a low cost or free protein sources to develop into a special feed formula for crickets.

7.2 Disease

Currently, disease risk is almost non-existent. However, in the future, with continuing high-density cricket populations, disease problems are likely to arise. In-breeding is another risk as many cricket farms are closed units using breeding stock produced on the farm. The technique not only produces crickets as means for consumption and sale, but it can also be used for animal feed and animal feed is also used to rear the crickets. 

10.3 Pro-poor technology

Poor farmers can generate income from cricket farming, it can be sustainable if the feeding prices remain low.

_annotations.body:
Cricket farming for human consumption

Cricket farming is a popular activity for farmers in Thailand and started in 1998. Currently around 20 000 farmers raise crickets for human consumption. Cricket farming contributes to the livelihood and nutrition base of farmers and a value chain has been established through which the crickets are marketed around Thailand. The technology presented is aimed at small-scale producers in Thailand and neighboring countries, where these species also live. Small-scale producers can be farmers, but also other people who see a business opportunity in selling crickets. The technology describes some of the common species used, and how a cricket farm is set up. It further describes the daily management of a cricket farm, including processing for sales and important risks to be taken into consideration.

Description

1. Cricket species to be used

Cricket farming has successfully been established with the species shown in Table 1. Acheta domesticus was introduced later to the technology, but is now more popular with farmers in Thailand.

1.1 Life cycle of the crickets

The development from egg to adult cricket is similar for all of the different species mentioned in Table 1 (45 to 60 days). Figure 1 shows a cricket life cycle.

Table 1. Cricket species successfully established in cricket farming

©FAO/TECA

Figure 1. Cricket life cycle

©FAO/TECA

2. Materials for breeding containers

To establish a cricket farm, farmers can choose from a variety of materials to establish breeding containers (Tables 2 and 3).

  • House crickets are bred in various containers described in Tables 2 and 3, sometimes with mosquito nets to keep crickets in and predators out.
  • Tape stripes are attached to the top of the breeding container to prevent the crickets from walking over the edge.
  • The bedding is often made from a layer of rice husks but some breeders do not use any material.
  • Cardboard egg cartons are mainly used in order to resemble a natural environment (Figures 2 and 3).
Table 2. Breeding containers

Source: FAO 2013

Table 3. Breeding containers

Source: FAO 2013

Figure 2. Example of cardboard egg cartons as breeding containers

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Example of cardboard egg cartons as breeding containers

©FAO/TECA

3. How to feed crickets

  • Commercial high protein animal feed, particularly chicken feed, is widely used in cricket farming. Chicken feed with 14 or 21 percent protein content is commonly used.
  • The 21 percent protein feed is used for feeding crickets after hatching until they are 20 days old. Subsequently, they are fed with mixed 14 and 21 percent protein feed until harvesting at 45 days old. The protein content of the chicken feed is described on the package.
  • A few days before harvesting, the high protein feed is replaced with vegetables such as pumpkins, cassava leaves, morning glory leaves and watermelons.
  • Regarding the water supply, water sources should be available either in shallow bowls or other containers which are easily accessible for the crickets. The water source should always be filled and water should be replaced when it starts to become dirty.

3.1 Day to day farming

  • As soon as the male crickets stridulate, bowls containing a mixture of husk and sand are placed in the breeding enclosure in which the females can lay eggs (within 24 hours). Egg-laying duration is seven to fourteen days.
  • The bowls are moved to another breeding tank for incubation and hatching, in which the new colony is established. Hatching occurs usually after about seven to ten days, at a stable temperature. This reproduction cycle can be repeated one to three times for each generation.
  • Production is feasible at temperatures higher than 20° C. The ideal temperature is 28° C to 30° C.
Figure 4. Female crickets laying eggs in husk and rice

©FAO/Christopher Münke

Figure 5. Placing of bowls with nymphs in breeding container

©FAO/Christopher Münke

Figure 6. Nymphs of Acheta domesticus on chicken feed

©FAO/Christopher Münke

4. Harvesting/collection of crickets

  • After the mating period occurs (between days 40 to 45 of the life cycle in normal climatic conditions) the crickets can be collected.
  • Crickets are harvested by lifting the egg cartons out of the container and shaking the crickets into a container.
  • Afterwards, the breeding container is completely emptied and cleaned from all remaining parts and crickets until it can be refilled.

5. Post-harvest handling/processing

Processing can be done at the cricket farm or through a cooperative of farmers or small scale enterprises/wholesalers (Figure 7).

The handling and processing and undertaken as follows:

  • crickets are washed in clean water without added substances;
  • crickets are boiled clean water for a few minutes;
  • second washing in cold clean water;
  • packaging in plastic bags;
  • weighing; and
  • cold storage for transport on ice or in cool unit. Crickets are stored in plastic bags which are then put in plastic tanks on ice. They can only be carried temporarily for two to three days. Long-term storage with -18 to -20° C is possible up to a year. However, most crickets are quickly processed for consumption.

records.title: Banco de forrajes
records.description:
Descripción

  • El sistema de cultivo realiza una rotación entre cultivo de papa (Solanum tuberosum) y el cultivo de pastos para forraje.
  • Posterior al cultivo de papa (cuyo ciclo dura seis meses) se aplica abono verde al terreno y se establece el cultivo de forraje que funcionará como banco gracias a un sistema de cortes sucesivos.
  • Los pastos se mantienen por tres años, cuando se reanuda el cultivo de papa.
  • El forraje se utiliza para la cría de cuyes, y la zona está delimitada por cercas vivas.

1. Descripción del ambiente donde la estrategia fue aplicada

  • Las siguientes características describen el ambiente natural y social donde se aplicó la práctica de bancos de forraje.
  • Las condiciones ambientales son determinantes o excluyentes para definir el tipo de forraje a utilizar, la necesidad de fertilización y estimar el tiempo de crecimiento y programar los cortes del forraje.
  • Por ello, deben tenerse en cuenta para rescatar, implementar o modificar la técnica que sean más apropiada a las condiciones naturales de la zona donde la práctica se quiera replicar.

1.1 Ambiente natural

  • Promedio de precipitación anual: 750 a 1 000 mm.
  • Altitud: 2 500 a 3 000 m.s.n.m.
  • Pendiente: poco inclinada.
  • Forma del terreno: ladera de la colina; parte baja de la ladera.
  • Clima: subtropical.
  • Textura del suelo: franco.
  • Fertilidad del suelo: alta.
  • Drenaje del suelo/infiltración: bueno.
  • Disponibilidad del agua: media.
Figura 1. Áreas destinadas a cultivo de pasto de corte en la región de Municipio de Pasto

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Ambiente social

  • Tipo del usuario tierra: familiar mediana escala.
  • Tenencia de la tierra: familiar con título.
  • Derechos del uso de la tierra: familiar.
  • Derechos del uso del agua: comunal/familiar.

2. Establecimiento de bancos de forrajes

  • En esta práctica se estableció el cultivo de pasto brasilero (Phalaris tuberosa) por esquejes y/o tallos.
  • El clima favorable para su desarrollo es frío y por encima de los 1 800 msnm tolera heladas y requiere suelos de textura franca a franco-arcillosa.
  • La densidad de siembra es de 10 000 esquejes/ha (Figura 2).
  • La fertilización se realiza cada dos cortes con abono orgánico, específicamente compost preparado en la finca con residuos vegetales y estiércol de cuyes, entre otros materiales.
    • Unido a ello, se usa abono foliar en una proporción de 500 ml por 200 litros de agua por hectárea y abono a base de NPK (mayor proporción N), 1 bulto por ha.
    • El primer corte se inicia al cuarto mes de establecido, realizando cortes diarios para la alimentación de aproximadamente 300 cuyes.
    • En promedio, se aprovechan unos 150 kg de forraje verde.
    • Los cortes se realizan por tramos secuencialmente: se empieza por un tramo y se continúa hasta el final del lote, iniciando nuevamente por donde empezó el aprovechamiento.
    • Luego de tres años utilizando el forraje, nuevamente se prepara el suelo para el establecimiento de papa.
  • La práctica se puede alternar con el establecimiento de nabo forrajero, con siembra al voleo.
  • En estado de floración se corta e incorpora al suelo.
  • Al cambio climático una banco forraje está bastante tolerante.
  • Incremento de la temperatura o aumento de episodios de olas de calor, disminución de la temperatura o aumento de episodios de heladas y eventos de precipitaciones intensas o cuantiosas son eventos que la práctica puede aguantar.
  • Los costos totales para el establecimiento de la práctica son de 695 USD y 20 USD por año para su mantenimiento.
Figura 2. Esquema bancos de forraje: los cultivos de cobertura deben considerar una alta densidad, por ejemplo, 10 000 esquejes de pasto de corte por hectárea

©FAO/TECA

3. Impactos y resultados

  • Esta práctica ha tenido los siguientes impactos positivos en el sistema productivo y la comunidad.

3.1 Impactos ecológicos de la práctica

  • Aumento de la biomasa vegetal.
  • Incremento de las especies beneficias.
  • Incremento de la materia orgánica en el suelo.
  • Incremento de la disponibilidad de nutrientes.
  • Aumento de la cobertura del suelo.
  • Mejora de la estructura de la superficie del suelo (formación de costra y sellado).
  • Aumento de la infiltración.
  • Incremento de la humedad del suelo.
Figura 3. Banco de forraje listo para corte en la región de Municipio de Pasto

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Impactos socioeconómicos de la práctica

  • Aumento del rendimiento de los cultivos.
  • Incremento de la cantidad y calidad del forraje.
  • Mejoría de la producción de los animales.
  • Reduce el riesgo del fracaso de la producción.
  • Aumento de los ingresos de la granja.
  • Incremento de la diversificación de los productos.

3.3 Impactos socioculturales de la práctica

  • Mejora de la posición de los grupos socioeconómicos menos favorecidos.
  • Incremento de la seguridad alimentaria.

4. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Subtropical, cálido.
  • Subtropical, fresco.

5. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Conservación de forrajes ante sequías prolongadas e inundaciones: ID 8314.
  • Suplementos sólidos para ganado en pastoreo elaborados con leguminosas forrajeras: ID 6564.
  • Uso de alternativas forrajeras para mitigar las deficiencias nutricionales en rumiantes durante épocas de sequía o inundación: ID 8331.
  • El banco proteínico-energético en el área de Yapacaní y Norte Integrado: ID 7550.

6. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

6.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología conduce a muchos resultados positivos, como una mayor productividad, mejora de la cobertura del suelo y producción de forrajes frescos para el suministro de alimentos de los animales, entre otros.

6.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

El banco de forrajes contribuye a una reducción del riesgo del fracaso de la producción, lo que conduce a un incremento de la seguridad alimentaria.

Banco de forrajes

El establecimiento de bancos forrajes en el área rural de Pasto tiene importancia fundamental, dado que la alimentación de animales y productividad de las fincas tiene un alto costo, que se busca reducir junto con mejorar la productividad. Los bancos forrajeros son cultivos intensivos para la producción de grandes volúmenes de tallos y hojas para alimentación animal. Los objetivos de los bancos forrajeros en esta práctica son:

  • producir forrajes frescos en la finca para alimentación de animales de manera sostenible;                                                                                                   
  • mejorar de la cobertura y estructura del suelo;                                                                                                                                                                           
  • y aumentar la materia orgánica y disponibilidad de nutrientes en el suelo.

_annotations.field_shorter_description:
El establecimiento de bancos forrajes en el área rural de Pasto tiene importancia fundamental, dado que la alimentación de animales y productividad de las fincas tiene un alto costo, que se busca reducir junto con mejorar la productividad. Los bancos forrajeros son cultivos intensivos para la producción de grandes volúmenes de tallos y hojas para alimentación animal. Los objetivos de los bancos forrajeros en esta práctica son:

  • producir forrajes frescos en la finca para alimentación de animales de manera sostenible;                                                                                                   
  • mejorar de la cobertura y estructura del suelo;                                                                                                                                                                           
  • y aumentar la materia orgánica y disponibilidad de nutrientes en el suelo.                                                                                                                                   

La práctica se puede realizar en tierras de cultivos anuales, y se rotan con cultivos para la producción de forraje de corte usados para la alimentación de cuyes. Posterior a la cosecha del cultivo de papas se establece el cultivo forrajero para corte. La fertilización se realiza cada dos cortes con abono orgánico. El primer corte se inicia al cuarto mes desde su establecimiento y el pasto se mantiene por aproximadamente tres años.

records.title: Recuperación de prácticas tradicionales de producción, como estrategia productiva con resiliencia
records.description:
Descripción

En este ejemplo, ambas comunidades (Yavi y Humahuaca) de Jujuy se caracterizan por ser comunidades pequeñas y cultivar superficies relativamente bajas (menores a media hectárea por persona). Los derechos de uso de la tierra y del agua están consignados como de acceso público; en muchos casos la tenencia de la tierra no está bien reglamentada y muchas veces los campesinos cultivan la tierra sin poseer títulos.

1. Impactos y resultados

La reactivación de estas prácticas y tecnologías han tenido los siguientes impactos positivos en las comunidades:

1.1 Impactos socioculturales

  • Mejora de las oportunidades culturales.
  • Fortalecimiento de las instituciones comunitarias.
  • Mejora de la posición de los grupos socioeconómicos menos favorecidos.
  • Incremento de la seguridad alimentaria.

1.2 Impactos ecológicos

  • Mejora de la cobertura del suelo.
  • Mejoramiento del ciclo de los nutrientes.
  • Aumento de la biomasa sobre el suelo.
  • Mejora de la calidad del agua.
  • Aumento de la diversidad vegetal.
  • Incremento de las especies benéficas.

1.3 Impactos socioeconómicos

  • Aumento del rendimiento de los cultivos.
  • Reducción del riesgo del fracaso de la producción.
  • Aumento de los ingresos de la granja.
  • Incremento de la diversificación de las fuentes de ingresos.
  • Aumento de la diversificación de los productos.
Figura 1. Gráfico de los impactos del proyecto por Yavi y Humahuaca

©FAO/TECA

2. Transcurso del proyecto por Yavi y Humahuaca

2.1 En la Zona de Yavi

2.1.1 Recuperación de prácticas tradicionales de producción

  • Se trabajó en la recuperación de estrategias ancestrales con énfasis en la diversificación, tales como biodiversificación de la producción, rescate y mejora de la selección de variedades locales, con énfasis en el cuidado de la diversidad.
  • Se utilizaron abonos compuestos preparados a partir del reciclado de materiales locales y el uso de guanos apagados (estabilizados) de los corrales de llamas y ovejas, y de abonos foliares orgánicos como té de compost y supermagro.
  • Las prácticas ancestrales que fueron rescatadas o reactivadas fueron: barbecho, rotación de terrenos y rotación de cultivos, todas ellas orientadas a la diversificación de la producción en el terreno.
  • Como insecticida biológico se utilizó la especie Beauveria sp. para el manejo de plagas de insectos mediante sistemas “caseros” de multiplicación y uso.
    • Se transfirieron capacidades para la identificación, multiplicación, acopio y aplicación en los cultivos.
    • Un sistema similar se realizó para el uso de Trichoderma sp. (fungicida biológico y promotor de crecimiento de las plantas).
  • Los costos totales del establecimiento de estas prácticas son 500 USD y se requieren 900 USD anuales para actividades de mantenimiento.
Figura 2. Preparación del terreno para la producción tradicional en Yavi

©FAO/TECA

Figura 3. Sistemas productivos de la comuna de Yavi

©FAO/TECA

2.1.2 Descripción del ambiente natural

  • Las siguientes características describen el ambiente natural de la zona de Yavi:
    • Promedio de precipitación anual: < 250 mm.
    • Altitud: 3 000 a 4 000 m.s.n.m.
    • Pendiente: Poco inclinada.
    • Forma del terreno: Existen tres principales:
      • meseta o llanura;
      • valle;
      • y ladera de montaña.
    • Profundidad del suelo: 20 a 50 cm.
    • Clima: Templado/ mediterráneo:
      • Al menos un mes con temperatura media mensual inferior a 5 ºC y cuatro meses o más superior a 10 ºC.
    • Textura del suelo: Franco arenoso.
    • Fertilidad del suelo: Baja.
    • Contenido de la materia orgánica del suelo: Bajo.
    • Drenaje del suelo/infiltración: Bueno.
    • Disponibilidad del agua: Media.
  • Las condiciones ambientales no son determinantes o excluyentes para el éxito de la práctica, pero deben tenerse en cuenta para rescatar, implementar o modificar las técnicas que sean más apropiadas a las condiciones naturales de la zona donde esta estrategia se quiera replicar.

2.2 En la zona de Humahuaca

2.2.1 Recuperación de prácticas tradicionales de producción

  • Recuperación de la tecnología productiva ancestral andina:
    • Las comunidades de la Quebrada de Humahuaca descienden de pueblos insertos en la cultura andina, caracterizada por su gran capacidad para producir en los valles y planicies alto andinas.
    • Siendo estos lugares de poca capacidad natural productiva, requieren estrategias especiales de orden tecnológico para convertirlos en sistemas productivos agropecuarios.
    • Dichas estrategias tecnológicas fueron, entre otras:
      • Organización comunitaria para la construcción y mantenimiento de infraestructura productiva (terrazas, defensas y construcción de parcelas en las riberas de los ríos, sistemas de conducción de agua para riego, entre otras).
      • Biodiversificación de la producción para disminuir el riesgo a heladas, granizos, sequías y plagas (rotación de cultivos, barbechos, rotación de terrenos, diversidad genética, por nombrar algunos ejemplos).
      • Fertilización orgánica de los terrenos.
  • Recuperación de las estrategias comunitarias tradicionales para la gestión y aprovechamiento de los recursos naturales:
    • Recuperación de tecnologías tradicionales.
    • Biodiversificación de cultivos.
    • Rotación de cultivos.
    • Rotación de terrenos para cultivar y para dejar en barbecho.
    • Organización comunitaria para el mantenimiento y gestión de mejoras intra y extraprediales.
    • Utilización de abonos orgánicos (uso de guanos de corral y dormidero de los rebaños).
    • Organización comunitaria para la siembra, la cosecha y el uso del agua.
  • Los costos totales para el desarrollo de estas prácticas son 2 000 USD para establecimiento y 1 500 USD anuales en mantenimiento.
Figura 4. Canal de riego en Humahuaca

©FAO/TECA

2.2.2 Descripción del ambiente natural

  • Las siguientes características describen el ambiente natural de la Zona de Humahuaca:
    • Promedio de precipitación anual: < 250 mm.
    • Altitud: 2 500 a 3 000 m.s.n.m.
    • Pendiente: Poco inclinada.
    • Forma del terreno: Existen tres principales:
      • meseta o llanura;
      • valle;
      • y ladera de montaña.
    • Profundidad del suelo: 50 a 80 cm.
    • Clima:Templado/ mediterráneo:
      • Al menos un mes con temperatura media mensual inferior a 5 ºC y cuatro meses o más superior a 10 ºC.
    • Textura del suelo: Franco arenoso.
    • Fertilidad del suelo: Baja.
    • Contenido de la materia orgánica del suelo: Bajo.
    • Drenaje del suelo/infiltración: Bueno.
    • Disponibilidad del agua: Media.
  • Las condiciones ambientales no son determinantes o excluyentes para el éxito de la práctica, pero deben tenerse en cuenta para rescatar, implementar o modificar las técnicas que sean más apropiadas a las condiciones naturales de la zona donde estas estrategias se quieran replicar.

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Improved practices in rearing indigenous chickens: ID 6921.
  • Small-scale chicken production: ID 6949.
  • Improved chicken breeds raised with vaccination: ID 8941.
  • Replicas of native chicken in rural poultry production: the Satpuda: ID 7680.

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología conduce a muchos impactos positivos, como una mayor sostenibilidad, productividad, resiliencia, diversificación del uso de la tierra, y mejoramiento de la calidad del agua y disponibilidad de nutrientes.

5.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

La recuperación de prácticas tradicionales de producción, como estrategia productiva con resiliencia permite a los agricultores cultivar de forma más sostenible, contribuyendo así a la seguridad alimentaria.

records.title: Uso de enmiendas orgánicas en el suelo
records.description:
Descripción

  • La industria frutícola en Chile es una de las principales actividades agrícolas del país, la cual ha incrementado la superficie plantada en los últimos 20 años, siendo la tecnificación y optimización de los procesos agrícolas el principal soporte de los altos rendimientos de producción.
  • La fertilización en cultivos de uva, requiere principalmente de elementos como N, P, K, Ca, Mg, Fe, Zn, Cu, Mo y Cl, los cuales desempeñan funciones indispensables para generar el balance nutricional adecuado durante el crecimiento vegetal.
  • Sin embargo, en los sistemas tradicionales de producción, el manejo de la fertilización ha generado un consumo irracional de productos químicos, ya que su aplicación es establecida sin un análisis previo del suelo que determine el aporte y la concentración de nutrientes base, siendo así frecuente encontrar cuarteles de uva con niveles de N residual muy altos, indicando una baja eficiencia de recuperación del N en los sistemas productivos, lo cual genera un riesgo ambiental importante y pérdidas económicas significativas al sector agrícola.
  • De esta forma, en los últimos años se han desarrollado alternativas de producción agrícola que se basan en el concepto de que el suelo es un sistema dinámico y vivo, el cual aporta elementos nutricionales a las plantas mediante el ciclaje activo de los nutrientes (C, N, P, S), procesos mediados por la actividad microbiana del suelo, considerada recientemente como parámetro de calidad del suelo.
  • Ante la necesidad de implementar prácticas agrícolas sostenibles que permitan mejorar la calidad nutricional de los parrones y conservar la humedad en el suelo, la adición de materia orgánica es una alternativa útil para el cultivo.
  • En el presente caso, la adición de materia orgánica al suelo se lleva a cabo bajo un sistema de transición de producción tradicional (uso de agroquímicos) a producción orgánica, práctica que se ha realizado en los últimos tres años.
  • La inversión inicial para llevar a cabo esta tecnología consistió en la construcción de pilas de compostaje, que involucra, además de la adquisición de maquinaria como parte del programa de manejo y aprovechamiento de residuos de la empresa, mano de obra para la adición de materia orgánica, deshierbe y cosecha.
  • Ambas actividades, la de compostaje y la de adición de materia orgánica al cultivo, se llevan a cabo anualmente.
  • El proceso de compostaje inicia luego de la temporada de cosecha, en donde se obtienen todos los residuos de escobajo y orujo, que luego son recolectados y compostados durante los meses siguientes, en el que se realiza el monitoreo de la temperatura, humedad, pH y aireación, mediante el uso de maquinaria.
  • Por su parte, la adición de materia orgánica al suelo, se realiza en la temporada de invierno manualmente, adicionando de 15 a 20 ton por ha del compost maduro.

1. Descripción del ambiente donde la estrategia fue aplicada

  • Las siguientes características describen el ambiente natural y social donde se implementó la práctica de uso de enmiendas orgánicas en el suelo.
  • Las condiciones ambientales no son determinantes o excluyentes para el éxito de la práctica, pero deben tenerse en cuenta para implementar o modificar la técnica que sea más apropiada a las condiciones naturales de la zona donde se quiera aplicar.

1.1 Ambiente natural

  • Promedio de precipitación anual: 250 a 500 mm.
  • Altitud: < 100 m.s.n.m.
  • Pendiente: Casi plana.

_annotations.body:
Uso de enmiendas orgánicas en el suelo

La práctica de uso de enmiendas orgánicas en el suelo es una alternativa a los fertilizantes inorgánicos. La adición de materia orgánica es una práctica sostenible y una alternativa útil para el cultivo, que permitan mejorar la calidad nutricional y conservar la humedad del suelo. El aumento de la materia orgánica en el suelo mejora la disponibilidad de nutrientes y la infiltración de la lluvia, controlando la escorrentía y reduciendo la erosión hídrica. La principal ventaja de esta práctica es que la frecuencia de riego puede ser reducida, disminuyendo los impactos negativos de la aplicación intensiva de agroquímicas, no obstante, el uso de enmiendas orgánicas está asociado con altos costos de mano de obra.

Descripción

  • La industria frutícola en Chile es una de las principales actividades agrícolas del país, la cual ha incrementado la superficie plantada en los últimos 20 años, siendo la tecnificación y optimización de los procesos agrícolas el principal soporte de los altos rendimientos de producción.
  • La fertilización en cultivos de uva, requiere principalmente de elementos como N, P, K, Ca, Mg, Fe, Zn, Cu, Mo y Cl, los cuales desempeñan funciones indispensables para generar el balance nutricional adecuado durante el crecimiento vegetal.
  • Sin embargo, en los sistemas tradicionales de producción, el manejo de la fertilización ha generado un consumo irracional de productos químicos, ya que su aplicación es establecida sin un análisis previo del suelo que determine el aporte y la concentración de nutrientes base, siendo así frecuente encontrar cuarteles de uva con niveles de N residual muy altos, indicando una baja eficiencia de recuperación del N en los sistemas productivos, lo cual genera un riesgo ambiental importante y pérdidas económicas significativas al sector agrícola.
  • De esta forma, en los últimos años se han desarrollado alternativas de producción agrícola que se basan en el concepto de que el suelo es un sistema dinámico y vivo, el cual aporta elementos nutricionales a las plantas mediante el ciclaje activo de los nutrientes (C, N, P, S), procesos mediados por la actividad microbiana del suelo, considerada recientemente como parámetro de calidad del suelo.
  • Ante la necesidad de implementar prácticas agrícolas sostenibles que permitan mejorar la calidad nutricional de los parrones y conservar la humedad en el suelo, la adición de materia orgánica es una alternativa útil para el cultivo.
  • En el presente caso, la adición de materia orgánica al suelo se lleva a cabo bajo un sistema de transición de producción tradicional (uso de agroquímicos) a producción orgánica, práctica que se ha realizado en los últimos tres años.
  • La inversión inicial para llevar a cabo esta tecnología consistió en la construcción de pilas de compostaje, que involucra, además de la adquisición de maquinaria como parte del programa de manejo y aprovechamiento de residuos de la empresa, mano de obra para la adición de materia orgánica, deshierbe y cosecha.
  • Ambas actividades, la de compostaje y la de adición de materia orgánica al cultivo, se llevan a cabo anualmente.
  • El proceso de compostaje inicia luego de la temporada de cosecha, en donde se obtienen todos los residuos de escobajo y orujo, que luego son recolectados y compostados durante los meses siguientes, en el que se realiza el monitoreo de la temperatura, humedad, pH y aireación, mediante el uso de maquinaria.
  • Por su parte, la adición de materia orgánica al suelo, se realiza en la temporada de invierno manualmente, adicionando de 15 a 20 ton por ha del compost maduro.

  • Las siguientes características describen el ambiente natural y social donde se implementó la práctica de uso de enmiendas orgánicas en el suelo.
  • Las condiciones ambientales no son determinantes o excluyentes para el éxito de la práctica, pero deben tenerse en cuenta para implementar o modificar la técnica que sea más apropiada a las condiciones naturales de la zona donde se quiera aplicar.

records.title: Construction of raised drying racks for fish - the experience from Burundi
records.description:
Description

Drying is a fish preservation method widely used by small-scale fish operators in Africa. The principle consists of putting the fish in contact with hot and dry air. In this way, water is removed from the surface of the fish and water moves from the deeper layers to the surface.

To ensure an effective drying process, racks should be located in an exposed place with relatively low humidity, Figures 1 and 2. Sites providing good air circulation are recommended. During the whole operation, the fish should remain dry, and recovered with a tarpaulin, or put under shelter at night or during rainy days.

The period of complete drying depends on the method used and the fish species. With the air circulation, the rack sloping system requires an average drying time of eight hours at an ambient temperature of 42 ° C (ten hours for big fish and six hours for smaller ones).

Figures 1 and 2. Raised racks for an effective drying process

©FAO/TECA

1. Why use raised racks?

  • Air movement at ground level is usually very slow.
    • This also slows the drying process and lengthens the drying time.
    • If fish are raised above the ground, even by only one meter, the air movement is greater, and the required drying time shorter.
  • Drying fish at ground level allows air to pass only on the upper side of the fish.
    • The use of raised racks allows drying from the upper, lower and lateral surfaces.
    • With a raised sloping rack, the water trapped in the gill is also easily pulled out.
  • Raised racks allow total protection of the fish (not only from rain by covering fish with plastic sheets), but also against water on the ground.
  • The fish are difficult to reach for animals and insects and are not in contact with dust and dirt.

2. A prototype of metallic raised racks

  • Figure 3 shows the prototype of metallic raised racks promoted by FAO in Burundi.
    • These are drying racks raised 1.10 m above the ground, with metallic or wooden supports.
    • A 12 m long x 2 m large raised rack can receive up to 22 removable trays, with an average capacity of 12 kg of fish per tray.
    • Table 1 illustrates the materials to be used. 
Figure 3. A prototype of metallic raised racks

©FAO/TECA

Table 1. Materials to be used
Material Quantity
Tube 40 x 40 Ten pieces
Wood rod One pack
Cutting disk Two pieces
Rust Two litres
Grinding disk One piece
Cement Three bags of 50 kg each
Sand 2 m3
Gravel 1 m3

Source: FAO 2014

  • For the trays (see Table 2 for material list), the frames are ideally hardwood boards, resistant to heat, fungi, and insect attacks.
    • The base of the frame is made by assembling pieces of wood nailed together.
    • The mesh is placed underneath the frame with small nails.
    • Then the 1.5 cm height batten is mounted from the lower bottom of the frame to maintain firmly the mesh in place.
    • The planks are wider at the level of the frame (10 cm).
    • Dimensions: length 114 cm; width 90 cm; length of the handle 12 cm; the height of the batten 110 cm.
Figure 4. The frame construction including the mesh

©FAO/TECA

Table 2. Materials to be used on the basis of 50 trays

Material 

 Quantity

Beam for the body (width 12 cm, thickness 5 cm, length 3.5 cm)

 60 pieces
Beams for the batten Ten pieces
7 cm nails 10 kg
4 cm nails 5 kg
Netting 55 m
Antitermite liquid 10 litres

Source: FAO 2014

2.1 Building raised racks made with wooden materials

  • Figure 5 shows two sketches of constructed drying racks, based on a 1 m height timber.
    • A taller pole of 1.5 m is used in the centre or on one side of the rack, depending on if a single or a double slope is needed.
    • To make the rack, 160 cm of timber is cut and buried in the ground to a depth of about 60 cm.
    • The distance between the two lines is 1 m, which corresponds to the width of the drying rack.
    • Lighter pieces of wood or bamboo are fixed between the top of the poles, before fixing other materials such as chicken wires, mosquito nets, or old fishing nets to support the fish.
Figure 5. Building raised racks made with wooden materials

©FAO/TECA

3. Validation of the practice

  • Using raised racks for fish drying has ensured a high level of productivity in the sector in Burundi.
    • The level of post-harvest losses has decreased by more than half due to the improved practice. 
    • End-products supplied to consumers are of better quality, and fish prices more than doubled from 4 to 9 Burundian francs (USD 2.5 to USD 6).
  • Racks-dried fish are highly appreciated by consumers, and fish operators and traders reap higher incomes.
    • This positive evolution has also led to an influx of working population towards fish processing and trade activities in Burundi.
  • The Burundi good practice experience could be replicated elsewhere through a participatory approach from all relevant stakeholders.
    • The use of raised racks, which has already been replicated in many neighbouring countries on the shore of Lake Tanganyika, could still be extended to other African fishing countries that suffer from a huge amount of post-harvest losses due to inappropriate processing methods.
  • Raised racks are easily replicable and are not necessarily made with metallic materials, as many women fish operators in Burundi demonstrate.
    • Fish processors who cannot afford the metal racks use racks made with cheaper materials, for example wooden, or nets of different mesh sizes.
    • The latter are usually of lower quality and with a much shorter life span, but they still offer the opportunity for the most vulnerable to benefit from the advantages of this innovation.
  • For some testimonies about the project implementation and results, the factors of the success and the future perspectives, see the video below.
    • An FAO project in Burundi: ‘’Support to post-harvest fisheries technology’’ - Short version

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Preservation of fish and meat: ID 6961.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The use of raised racks has contributed to innovation in the livelihood of men and women fish operators. Their productivity and income have considerably increased. In particular, the role of women in ensuring household food and nutrition security has been enhanced.
