records.title: How to build a fruit fly trap
records.description:
Description

Fruit flies cause damages to fruits such as mangoes, papaya, guavas and citrus fruits and also to vegetables such as tomatoes, pepper and okra. The following video shows a simple way how to reduce a fruit fly population through fruit fly traps. The video is available in English and in Ghanaian language Twi.

  • Video: How to build a fruit fly trap (twi)
  • Video: How to build a fruit fly trap (English)

1. Tools for building a fruit fly trap

The trap uses pheromones to attract male flies. Inside the trap the insects get in contact with an insecticide that kills them immediately.

1.1 Material needed to build a trap 

To build a trap the following items are needed:

  • empty plastic bottle;
  • cotton wool;
  • an insecticide, plan D;
  • a pheromone, methyl eugenol;
  • a sharp knife;
  • pliers;
  • binding wire;
  • a measuring container;
  • a box of matches;
  • rubber gloves.
Figure 1. Tools for building a trap

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Procedure to build a fruit fly trap

This is the procedure to follow:

  1. Cut the plastic bottle at the second ring with a knife. The cut off neck will serve as an entry funnel into the rest of the bottle (Figure 2).

Figure 2. Cutting the bottle

©FAO/TECA

  1. Cut 65 cm of binding wire with the pliers. Then light a match and heat the tip of the binding wire and stick it into the bottom of the bottle. The heating allows the binding wire to penetrate into the bottle easily. At the end 5 cm of wire will remain inside and about 60 cm outside the bottle (Figure 3).

Figure 3. Penetrating the bottle with the binding wire

©FAO/TECA

  1. Then take a piece of the cotton wool and roll it into a ball. Lock it up in the wire at the open side of the bottle. In order to have the cotton wool hanging at the bottom of the trap, slightly bend the wire, so it acts as a hook holding the bottle (Figure 4).

Figure 4. Locking up the cotton wool in the wire at the open side of the bottle

©FAO/TECA

  1. Mix 10 ml of the insecticide Plan D and 40 ml of the pheromone Methyl Eugenol in a container. Use the measuring cup to get the amounts right. Be sure to wear gloves to protect your hands from contamination. Wash your hands carefully after using the chemicals.

  2. Then, being sure that the cotton wool is attached well to the wire, dip it into the mixture. Ensure that the cotton wool is well soaked with the chemicals. The fibres of the cotton will allow the chemicals to be effective for a long time (Figure 5).

Figure 5. Soaking the cotton wool with the insecticide and pheromone mixture

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Soaking the cotton wool with the insecticide and pheromone mixture

©FAO/TECA

2. Positioning of the fruit fly traps

To cover a whole farm five traps per acre are needed. Place the traps in the pattern shown in Figure 7. A trap lasts for six to eight weeks; then the cotton ball needs to be soaked with the insecticide and pheromone mixture again. The traps can be reused over and over again.

Figure 7. Pattern for positioning the fruit fly traps

©FAO/TECA

You manipulate and/or use pesticides? Make inquiries before! Pesticide can be harmful to your health, the health of your family, of the consumers and of the environment. Use pesticides safely. Click here for more information concerning reducing risks while manipulating pesticide.

3. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Risk reduction while manipulating pesticides: ID 8348.
  • Fruit fly control for mango farmers: ID 8471.
  • Controlling mango fruit fly: ID 6920.
  • Crop protection: integrated management of fruit flies: ID 4562.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology helps to reduce the loss in fruits and vegetables and, thus, helps to use resources more efficiently.

5.2 Pro-poor technology

Controlling fruit flies can save the harvest and reduce the risk of harvest loss.

Figure 2. Cutting the bottle

©FAO/TECA

  1. Cut 65 cm of binding wire with the pliers. Then light a match and heat the tip of the binding wire and stick it into the bottom of the bottle. The heating allows the binding wire to penetrate into the bottle easily. At the end 5 cm of wire will remain inside and about 60 cm outside the bottle (Figure 3).

Figure 3. Penetrating the bottle with the binding wire

©FAO/TECA

  1. Then take a piece of the cotton wool and roll it into a ball. Lock it up in the wire at the open side of the bottle. In order to have the cotton wool hanging at the bottom of the trap, slightly bend the wire, so it acts as a hook holding the bottle (Figure 4).

Figure 4. Locking up the cotton wool in the wire at the open side of the bottle

©FAO/TECA

  1. Mix 10 ml of the insecticide Plan D and 40 ml of the pheromone Methyl Eugenol in a container. Use the measuring cup to get the amounts right. Be sure to wear gloves to protect your hands from contamination. Wash your hands carefully after using the chemicals.

  2. Then, being sure that the cotton wool is attached well to the wire, dip it into the mixture. Ensure that the cotton wool is well soaked with the chemicals. The fibres of the cotton will allow the chemicals to be effective for a long time (Figure 5).

Figure 5. Soaking the cotton wool with the insecticide and pheromone mixture

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Soaking the cotton wool with the insecticide and pheromone mixture

©FAO/TECA

2. Positioning of the fruit fly traps

To cover a whole farm five traps per acre are needed. Place the traps in the pattern shown in Figure 7. A trap lasts for six to eight weeks; then the cotton ball needs to be soaked with the insecticide and pheromone mixture again. The traps can be reused over and over again.

Figure 7. Pattern for positioning the fruit fly traps

©FAO/TECA

records.title: Services for marketing animals and milk
records.description:
Description

1. What services do you need?

  • Pastoralists need services to market their animals, milk and hides effectively. 
    • Market information
      • You need to know where to sell and what the price is.
    • Financial services
      • You may need to transfer money, get a loan or insure your animals.
    • Transport
      • You need to get your animals or milk to the buyer.
    • Market facilities
      • You need a marketplace where you can meet the buyers and sell your product.
    • Processing plants
      • You may want to sell your animals to an abattoir, your hides to a tannery, or your milk to a dairy.
  • These services are often provided by the government, the private sector or a development organisation.
  • But you can do some things yourself to get the services you need.
  • You may even be able to provide the services yourself.
Figure 1. What services do you need?

©FAO/TECA

1.1 Market information

  • How much is the price of an animal?
  • Are the roads safe?
  • Will a particular trader be buying next week?
  • Does the abattoir have a big order to fill?
  • Has the ban on exports been lifted?
  • Does the vet store have a supply of vaccines?
  • The answers to such questions may make the difference between a regular day’s herding and a 200 km trek to the nearest market.

1.1.1 What you can do

  • Use your contacts
    • You can get information from friends and relatives or from traders you know and trust.
  • Listen to the community radio.
    • It may broadcast prices and other useful information.
  • Buy a mobile phone and use it to keep in touch with a contact in town who can tell you the latest prices.
  • Set up a small cooperative to obtain, generate and exchange information.
Figure 2. Pastoralists have various ways (traditional and modern) to get marketing information

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Financial services

  • Banks and other financial services are scarce in the drylands.
  • Many people do not have cash;
    • Instead, they barter a goat for a bag of maize or a pot of butter for some sugar.
    • But that is not enough if you want to earn more from your animals.

1.2.1 What you can do

  • Organise a production cooperative.
    • Banks and microfinance institutions do not like to lend to individual pastoralists.
    • But they may be interested in lending to a group.
    • The group takes a loan, then lends out small amounts to its members.
    • If one member cannot repay, the other members agree to do so.
  • Organise a savings and credit cooperative.
    • You can organise your own savings cooperative.
    • A group of people pay a small amount each week into a kitty.
    • The kitty is then lent out to a group member who needs a loan.
  • Insure animals against drought.
    • Drought is the biggest threat to pastoralists’ lives.
    • Check whether there is a drought insurance scheme in your area.
    • In such a scheme, you pay a small amount of money each year to cover your animals.
    • If there is a drought, the insurer pays out to cover your losses.
  • Use mobile money.
    • Get a mobile phone so you can use a mobile-money service (such as Safaricom’s M-Pesa in Kenya and other countries).
    • This lets you send and receive money safely and quickly.
  • Use bus-courier services.
    • Some bus companies offer a courier service to remote communities.
    • Find out if your local bus company does so.
  • Pastoralists and traders find it hard to get loans, insurance and other financial services.
Figure 3. Pastoralists and traders find it hard to get loans, insurance and other financial services

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Transport

  • Roads are bad, and lorries and trucks are few and battered. Many pastoralists herd their animals to market.
  • They arrive thin and exhausted; many pick up diseases or die on the way.
  • Milk is often carried warm, in unsanitary plastic jerry cans.
    • It spoils quickly and can be transported only over short distances.

1.3.1 What you can do

  • Truck, not trek.
    • It may be better to load the animals onto a lorry rather than herding them all the way.
    • That is more expensive, but the animals arrive in better condition and fetch more money.
    • Choose a lorry that has partitions to keep the animals safe on the road.
  • Organise a marketing group.
    • Get together with other herders to sell your animals together.
    • If you have enough animals to fill a lorry, you can bargain for a better price.
    • With enough members, you may be able to hire or even buy your own lorry.
  • Speed up milk delivery.
    • The faster your milk gets to its destination, the better.
    • Use a bicycle instead of carrying it on foot.
    • Better still, use a motorbike instead of a bicycle.
  • Use aluminium cans to transport milk.
    • They are easy to clean.
    • Plastic jerry cans cannot be cleaned properly and the milk will go off more quickly.
  • Move production closer to the market.
    • Keep milking animals close to the milk-collection point.
    • That will cut the cost of transport, speed delivery and improve quality.

1.4 Market facilities

  • There are too few livestock markets and milk-collection centres in pastoral areas, and they tend to have inadequate facilities and be poorly run.
  • Many markets are merely places where producers and traders agree to meet to do business.

1.4.1 What you can do

  • Reorganise markets.
    • Get together with other market users to discuss how to improve the organisation of the market. 
      • Build a fence around the market and post guards to improve security.
      • Build latrines and washing facilities.
      • Build holding pens for each type of animal.
      • Provide troughs for feeding and watering.
      • Build a loading ramp for lorries.
  • Ways to raise money to improve services.
    • Charge an entrance fee for sellers or buyers.
    • Charge a fee for every animal sold.
    • Charge lorries a fee for parking and loading.
Figure 4. To attract buyers and sellers (and to work efficiently) a marketplace needs fencing, water and feeding points, shelter, toilets, and a loading ramp

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Processing plants

  • Dairies pasteurise and chill milk and turn it into products such as butter and ice cream.
  • Abattoirs convert live animals into meat, sausages, fat and hides.
  • Tanneries turn hides into leather.
  • But such processing facilities are scarce in the drylands.
  • The few dairies and abattoirs in pastoralist areas often get erratic supplies of milk and live animals.
  • Production varies hugely from season to season and may fall drastically during a drought.
  • That puts the profitability and viability of the industry in question.
  • It is in the pastoralists’ interest to maintain the industry and keep their business customers.

1.5.1 What you can do

  • Maintain a steady supply of raw materials.
    • Contract to supply a certain number of animals or volume of milk on a regular basis.
    • Agree with the abattoir or dairy on what amounts to deliver in the dry season.
    • To keep up milk production at this time of year, you have to give animals extra feed and water.
  • Attract an investor to set up a processing plant.
    • Together with a group of other producers, you could approach a company, development organisation or the government to set up a processing plant in your area.
    • You will need to show you can deliver a reliable supply of good-quality animals or milk.
  • Start your own processing plant.
    • Your group could set up your own processing plant.
    • You will need to check the potential market, develop a business plan and get the funding, advice and skills required.
    • Start small, a simple processing plant can be a useful outlet for your animals or milk.
Figure 5. Processing facilities do not have to be fancy to be useful

©FAO/TECA

1.6 Getting the government to help

  • You can ask the government to help you get the market services you need.
    • Makes it easier to get market information.
    • Makes it easier to get loans and other financial services.
    • Improves roads, markets and other infrastructure.
    • Builds new markets and feeding and watering facilities on key routes.
    • Improves security in dryland areas and around markets.
    • Encourages the private sector to establish new processing industries.
    • Involves pastoralists in planning and managing services.
    • Provides training in hygiene, marketing and quality control.
  • You can get together with other producers and traders to lobby the government for support.
Figure 6. Individual producers can do little on their own. But together as a group, they can solve their own problems and get support from outside

©FAO/TECA

2. Related/associated technologies

  • Marketing animals and milk: ID 8252.
  • Producing animals and milk for market: ID ​8249.
  • Services for marketing animals and milk​: ID 8248.
  • Organising to market animals and milk: ID ​8243.
  • Ten ways to improve milk marketing: ID ​8240​.

3. Objectives fulfilled by the project  

3.1 Women-friendly

This practice is user-friendly and can be undertaken by anyone.

3.2 Resource use efficiency

The practice allows pastoralists to use services efficiently in order to market their animals, milk and hides effectively. 

3.3 Pro-poor technology

The practice, through improved improved services and market access, increases revenue for poor communities.

records.title: Producing animals and milk for market
records.description:
Description

1. Producing for a market

1.1 Markets for animals

  • Know your market. Most buyers want certain types of animals: a farmer may want bullocks for ploughing or young females for breeding and milk. An abattoir wants young, healthy animals, not those that are old and sick.
  • Buyers may want a certain number of animals at a time - for example, enough to fill a pick-up or a lorry.
  • Buyers may want a regular supply of animals - such as a certain number each month. 

1.2 Markets for milk

  • Buyers may want to buy fresh milk, sour milk, or pasteurised milk. They may want to buy butter, cheese, yoghurt, or other products.
  • Buyers may need a certain volume of milk every day.
  • Milk quality is important: the milk should come from healthy animals and must be fresh and clean.

1.3 What you can do

  • Find out what different buyers want, and how much they want to pay. 
  • Work out how you can supply that sort of animal or product.
  • Supply the amount and type of animals or products that buyers want.
  • Agree to supply at the right time and on a regular basis. 
  • Get together with other producers so you can supply the required amounts.
  • Make sure the animals you sell or use for milking are healthy and well-fed.

Do these things, and you can negotiate for a better price from the buyer.

2. Keep your animals healthy

If an animal is sick, it can be hard to sell or it will fetch a low price.

  • Avoid parasites. Keep the animals away from areas with ticks, tsetse flies and other parasites. Keep the night-enclosure clean and dry. Move the enclosure regularly and move the animals from one pasture to another to prevent the build-up of parasites. 
  • Give animals enough feed and water. Do not expect them to walk too far each day. Make sure they get water frequently. 
  • Treat against ticks. Dip the animals or use a pour-on acaricide to control ticks.
  • Vaccinate the animals against the most serious diseases.
  • If an animal is sick, separate it from the rest of the herd and get advice on how to treat it. 
  • Be wary of fake or expired medicines. Buy only from reputable dealers. 
  • Get organised to buy health inputs and services. As a group, you can get medicines and services more cheaply.
  • Get training in Para veterinary medicine. Many common diseases are easy to treat if you know how. Get people in the community trained, and make sure they have the equipment and drugs they need. 
  • Use traditional medicines. Find out which traditional medicines work against what problems.
  • Comply with quarantine rules and movement bans. These are designed to stop dangerous diseases from spreading.
Figure 1. Buy animal medicines only from a reputable dealer

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Traditional healers know a lot about animals and diseases. Learn from them.

©FAO/TECA

2.1 Feed your animals well

2.1.1 Reduce the need for feed

  • Limit your herd size. Do not keep more animals than the pasture can feed.
  • Sell animals as soon as they reach market weight. Keeping them longer will not always bring more money.
  • Sell animals before a drought. During a drought, the price will fall, and many animals will die. Watch the weather, and sell them before the drought, while prices are still high.
  • Sell underweight animals to a feedlot. Some traders and abattoirs maintain feedlots to fatten up underweight animals. Your community organisation might be able to set up its own feedlot.

2.1.2 Provide extra feed 

  • Move the herd to find grazing and water. Maintain good relations with neighbouring groups. Make agreements with them on sharing the land and water.
  • Give extra feed to pregnant and milking animals, and animals you want to sell.
  • Graze animals on fallow cropland. You can agree with farmers to graze your animals on newly harvested or fallow fields. The animals eat the crop residues and weeds, and fertilise the soil with their dung and urine. You may have to pay rent for using the land.
  • Set aside emergency grazing areas. Your community leaders can designate certain areas for grazing during the dry season or only during a drought. 
  • Grow feed and forage. You may be able to plant improved grasses or legumes for grazing or to cut and feed to the animals. You can make hay or silage and store it until it is needed.
  • Provide supplementary feed. Buy commercial feed or mineral blocks for valuable animals, such as milking cows. You can make your own blocks from molasses, urea, salt, straw or bran, and cement.
Figure 3. Hungry, weak animals fetch low prices (assuming they live long enough to be sold)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. You can make silage in a sealed pit

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Choose the right breed

You need to have the right types of animals, ones that can survive and produce in the drylands.

  • Don’t keep high-yielding exotic breeds. They need special feed, housing and veterinary care. Without these, they will quickly fall ill and die. 
  • Maintain and improve your local breed. Local breeds are hardier and better adapted to the local conditions. You can select the best animals and use them for breeding. If you crossbreed, keep enough animals of the local type to maintain your original breed.
  • Set up a breeding association. Organise a group of breeders to select and promote superior animals. Share the resulting offspring among the group, and use them for breeding.
  • Switch to a superior adapted breed. If you see another breed from a similar area that is better than your own animals, consider buying them. Make sure they thrive in your area before you buy more.
Figure 5. Try buying a superior bull to improve your herd

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Produce good-quality animals and milk

Maintaining quality can be difficult. Problems include poor-quality animals, hides with holes in them, sour or contaminated milk, inadequate hygiene, poor equipment, long transport distances, and a lack of inspection.

Quality has to be appropriate. The highest‑value markets require the best quality and reward it with better prices.

Quality requirements for local markets are not so strict.

Figure 6. Dairies test milk to make sure it is good quality

©FAO/TECA

2.3.1 What you can do

  • Deliver quality animals. Control parasites and diseases, improve feeding and sell only healthy, strong animals.
  • Improve animal handling. Sell to trustworthy traders who do not overload their lorry and who use partitions to support standing animals.
  • Produce quality milk. Do not use milk from diseased cows. Do not dilute the milk, and make sure it is fresh. 
  • Improve milk hygiene. This is the most important! Wash your hands and the animal’s teats before milking. Protect milk from flies and dust. Deliver milk to the collection point quickly - in the morning when it is cool. Use an aluminium container instead of a plastic jerry can.

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Marketing animals and milk: ID 8252.
  • Eleven ways to improve animal marketing: ID 8242.
  • Services for marketing animals and milk: ID 8248.
  • Organising to market animals and milk:ID 8243.
  • Ten ways to improve milk marketing: ID 8240.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Women-friendly

The technology is accessible and easy to use for all.

4.2 Resource use efficiency

Better breed selection and feed usage.

4.3 Pro-poor technology

Additional income thanks to improved market knowledge, healthier livestock and better quality of produce.

1.1 Markets for animals

  • Know your market. Most buyers want certain types of animals: a farmer may want bullocks for ploughing or young females for breeding and milk. An abattoir wants young, healthy animals, not those that are old and sick.
  • Buyers may want a certain number of animals at a time - for example, enough to fill a pick-up or a lorry.
  • Buyers may want a regular supply of animals - such as a certain number each month. 

1.2 Markets for milk

  • Buyers may want to buy fresh milk, sour milk, or pasteurised milk. They may want to buy butter, cheese, yoghurt, or other products.
  • Buyers may need a certain volume of milk every day.
  • Milk quality is important: the milk should come from healthy animals and must be fresh and clean.

1.3 What you can do

  • Find out what different buyers want, and how much they want to pay. 
  • Work out how you can supply that sort of animal or product.
  • Supply the amount and type of animals or products that buyers want.
  • Agree to supply at the right time and on a regular basis. 
  • Get together with other producers so you can supply the required amounts.
  • Make sure the animals you sell or use for milking are healthy and well-fed.

Do these things, and you can negotiate for a better price from the buyer.

2. Keep your animals healthy

If an animal is sick, it can be hard to sell or it will fetch a low price.

  • Avoid parasites. Keep the animals away from areas with ticks, tsetse flies and other parasites. Keep the night-enclosure clean and dry. Move the enclosure regularly and move the animals from one pasture to another to prevent the build-up of parasites. 
  • Give animals enough feed and water. Do not expect them to walk too far each day. Make sure they get water frequently. 
  • Treat against ticks. Dip the animals or use a pour-on acaricide to control ticks.
  • Vaccinate the animals against the most serious diseases.
  • If an animal is sick, separate it from the rest of the herd and get advice on how to treat it. 
  • Be wary of fake or expired medicines. Buy only from reputable dealers. 
  • Get organised to buy health inputs and services. As a group, you can get medicines and services more cheaply.
  • Get training in Para veterinary medicine. Many common diseases are easy to treat if you know how. Get people in the community trained, and make sure they have the equipment and drugs they need. 
  • Use traditional medicines. Find out which traditional medicines work against what problems.
  • Comply with quarantine rules and movement bans. These are designed to stop dangerous diseases from spreading.
Figure 1. Buy animal medicines only from a reputable dealer

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Traditional healers know a lot about animals and diseases. Learn from them.

©FAO/TECA

2.1 Feed your animals well

2.1.1 Reduce the need for feed

  • Limit your herd size. Do not keep more animals than the pasture can feed.
  • Sell animals as soon as they reach market weight. Keeping them longer will not always bring more money.
  • Sell animals before a drought. During a drought, the price will fall, and many animals will die. Watch the weather, and sell them before the drought, while prices are still high.
  • Sell underweight animals to a feedlot. Some traders and abattoirs maintain feedlots to fatten up underweight animals. Your community organisation might be able to set up its own feedlot.

2.1.2 Provide extra feed 

  • Move the herd to find grazing and water. Maintain good relations with neighbouring groups. Make agreements with them on sharing the land and water.
  • Give extra feed to pregnant and milking animals, and animals you want to sell.
  • Graze animals on fallow cropland. You can agree with farmers to graze your animals on newly harvested or fallow fields. The animals eat the crop residues and weeds, and fertilise the soil with their dung and urine. You may have to pay rent for using the land.
  • Set aside emergency grazing areas. Your community leaders can designate certain areas for grazing during the dry season or only during a drought. 
  • Grow feed and forage. You may be able to plant improved grasses or legumes for grazing or to cut and feed to the animals. You can make hay or silage and store it until it is needed.
  • Provide supplementary feed. Buy commercial feed or mineral blocks for valuable animals, such as milking cows. You can make your own blocks from molasses, urea, salt, straw or bran, and cement.
Figure 3. Hungry, weak animals fetch low prices (assuming they live long enough to be sold)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. You can make silage in a sealed pit

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Choose the right breed

You need to have the right types of animals, ones that can survive and produce in the drylands.

  • Don’t keep high-yielding exotic breeds. They need special feed, housing and veterinary care. Without these, they will quickly fall ill and die. 
  • Maintain and improve your local breed. Local breeds are hardier and better adapted to the local conditions. You can select the best animals and use them for breeding. If you crossbreed, keep enough animals of the local type to maintain your original breed.
  • Set up a breeding association. Organise a group of breeders to select and promote superior animals. Share the resulting offspring among the group, and use them for breeding.
  • Switch to a superior adapted breed. If you see another breed from a similar area that is better than your own animals, consider buying them. Make sure they thrive in your area before you buy more.
Figure 5. Try buying a superior bull to improve your herd

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Produce good-quality animals and milk

Maintaining quality can be difficult. Problems include poor-quality animals, hides with holes in them, sour or contaminated milk, inadequate hygiene, poor equipment, long transport distances, and a lack of inspection.

Quality has to be appropriate. The highest‑value markets require the best quality and reward it with better prices.

Quality requirements for local markets are not so strict.

Figure 6. Dairies test milk to make sure it is good quality

©FAO/TECA

2.3.1 What you can do

  • Deliver quality animals. Control parasites and diseases, improve feeding and sell only healthy, strong animals.
  • Improve animal handling. Sell to trustworthy traders who do not overload their lorry and who use partitions to support standing animals.
  • Produce quality milk. Do not use milk from diseased cows. Do not dilute the milk, and make sure it is fresh. 
  • Improve milk hygiene. This is the most important! Wash your hands and the animal’s teats before milking. Protect milk from flies and dust. Deliver milk to the collection point quickly - in the morning when it is cool. Use an aluminium container instead of a plastic jerry can.

3. Related/associated technologies 

  • Marketing animals and milk: ID 8252.
  • Eleven ways to improve animal marketing: ID 8242.
  • Services for marketing animals and milk: ID 8248.
  • Organising to market animals and milk:ID 8243.
  • Ten ways to improve milk marketing: ID 8240.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Women-friendly

The technology is accessible and easy to use for all.

4.2 Resource use efficiency

Better breed selection and feed usage.

4.3 Pro-poor technology

Additional income thanks to improved market knowledge, healthier livestock and better quality of produce.

records.title: Use of stingless bees for pollination
records.description:
Description

1. How to construct a pollination hive: materials needed

1.1 Procedure for the construction of the pollination hive

  • A wooden hive was designed to facilitate colony transport either by land, sea or air for pollination.
  • It has two chambers, one above the other, separated by a division board.
  • The lower chamber (brood chamber) has a single entrance and contains the brood.
  • An elevated brood platform made from a 6.5 cm² piece of plywood is glued to the bottom board and provided with two ventilation holes measuring 1 cm x 1 cm.
  • The bottom board itself is made from a 23 cm x 10 cm x 0.5 cm slab of wood or plywood with four 1 cm x 2 cm x 3 cm cleats nailed at the bottom.
  • Four 1 cm (h) x 1 cm (w) x 3 cm (l) studs are placed on the insides of each corner of the brood chamber to hold the upper chamber during transport.
  • The upper chamber has two entrances, one each in front and at the back.
  • The division board is provided with access points.
  • The hive has a telescoping top cover to protect the hive from the rain and to ensure the cover does not move during transport and a removable bottom board.
Figure 1. Elements and dimensions of the wooden pollination hive

©FAO/TECA

2. What do we need to consider when using stingless bees for pollination

  • Various crops require a different number of pollinator species.
  • When deploying managed pollinators like bees, a good rule of thumb is to saturate, ideally one colony for one plant.
  • However, in large plantations where the number of bees is limited, colony clusters may be distributed in such a way that their foraging radius overlap.
  • For most crops, 15 to 20 colonies per hectare are usually recommended for effective pollination.
  • However, if natural pollinators are scarce, additional hives may be necessary.
  • Computer simulations and modelling of optimal colony distribution for pollination are available at the following link.

3. Transporting colonies for pollination

  • Only established colonies are used in pollination.
  • These are colonies with brood occupying 80 percent of the lower nest chamber (of the wooden hive), surrounded with pollen and honey stores.
  • Food stores should at least occupy a third of the upper chamber.
  • This is to ensure continuous food supply during transport of the bees.
  • The colonies should be certified by the competent authority to be free from pest and diseases.
  • The histerid beetle infests weak colonies and kills the bees by eating the pollen.
  • Colonies may be bundled in pallets of three or four depending on the requirement of the carrier vessel.
  • These are secured with plastic straps, and the hive sections stapled to each other.
  • Entrances are sealed prior to loading.
  • The hives are covered with fine net to prevent the escape of bees.

4. Colony inspection in wooden hive intended for pollination

  • We are now ready to bring our hives to the farm requiring pollination.
  • First, let us ensure that all the colonies are free from pest and diseases.
  • Healthy colonies with complete brood cycle will provide better pollination services than weak colonies.
  • Follow the following procedures.
    • Check entrance
      • Entrance holes of good colonies should be about 1 to 2 cm wide.
      • Flight tube should be moist and pliable.
      • Put aside colonies with very dry and hard flight holes and reduced entrances.
      • These colonies are dead or dying.
    • Observe activities of the colony
      • Open the hive and expose the brood.
      • Check the brood size and or number of brood plates.
      • The brood should be fresh, moist and free from debris.
      • All the brood stages should be present in appropriate proportions.
    • Check pollen and honey stores
      • The colonies should have a ring of pollen and honey pots around the brood area, about 5 cm in all directions.
      • These should extend to third of the upper hive chamber.
    • Check for pest and diseases
      • Weak colonies are prone to the infestation of histerid beetles, flies and mites.
      • Adult beetles and larvae crawl on the top side of the division board, between cerumen sheets and brood area.
      • They feed on the pollen and honey.
      • They also carry mites that infest pollen stores and brood stores.
      • During the rainy season soldier flies lay eggs on the wet cerumen and their larvae feed on wet brood, pollen and honey.
      • Heavy pest infestation results in colony loss or nest abandonment.

5. Placement of colonies in the farms

  • Look around your site and see if there are other plants that are more preferred by the bees.
  • Coconuts and other palms are very attractive to bees.
  • If you have similar plants, or other preferred plants, move hives into the crop at the onset of flowering.
  • If you move them in before the crop blooms, you give bees a chance to forage on another non-target plant.
  • Once bees are trained to such competing flowers, they often ignore the crop when it blooms.
  • With the short flight range of stingless bees, you can spread the colonies evenly within the farm.
  • Make sure that the interior portion of the farm is not neglected.
  • Take note that there are also natural pollinators, and they usually forage in the periphery of the farm and cannot access the interior portion.
Figure 2. Hives of stingless bees for transport to mango farm for pollination

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Colonies off-loaded on site for distribution

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Colonies installed in a mango farm

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Stingless bees on mango flowers

©FAO/TECA

6. How to manage the colonies after pollination

  • After the blooming period, the colonies are removed from the farm and brought back to the apiary site where there are abundant sources of pollen and nectar.
  • The colonies are dispersed to around 20 per site to avoid competition for forage.
  • If the colonies are weakened, super is removed to compress the population inside the hive to facilitate temperature regulation.
  • Supers are added to stronger colonies.
  • When there are already three to four chambers or supers, the colonies may be split anew in preparation for another pollination service.
Figure 6. Colony on stand with entrance plug removed to allow the bees to go out of the hive

©FAO/TECA

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Good beekeeping practices: ID 8409.
  • Beekeeping in Africa: honey harvesting: ID 7329.
  • Beekeeping in Africa: using bees for pollination: ID 7331.
  • Beekeeping in Africa: responding to common bee diseases: ID 7332.
  • Beekeeping in Africa: choosing and rearing a queen: ID 7333.

This technology is also available in Spanish: ID 8669.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Women-friendly

The technology is not labour intensive and can be undertaken by any kind of hand labour.

9.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology explains in detail how to effectively build wooden hives using local resources.

9.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology ensures greater chances of pollination, leading to increases in yields of honey etc. This provides for additional sources of food and income.

records.title: Harvesting honey from giant honey bees
records.description:
Description

There are two known species of giant honey bees in the Philippines. Apis dorsata, is found on the island of Palawan and Apis breviligula is found in the rest of the country. Nests of giant bees abound in forested areas. Giant bees produce 60 to 80 kg of honey per colony which is a source of income of farmers in the community. To conserve giant bees and produce quality products, a honey collection program was developed for each community. The program limits the harvest time from March to May during the dry season when most of the plants produce lots of flowers and nectar. The colonies are mapped by individual gatherers and trees with colonies are marked to allow identification of ownership. Gatherers adhere to guidelines set by the community pertaining to the time of harvest, ownership of the nest and proper harvesting procedure.

1. Preparation

  • At the onset of the honey flow season, the colonies are checked for honey.
    • The honey store is located at the upper front part of the nest.
    • Thickening and extension of this area is a sign that nectar is being collected and stored.
    • When three-fourths of the honeycomb is already sealed, the honey is ready for harvesting.
  • A smoker is made by bundling dry and fresh plant material.
    • The dry leaves and twigs are bundled tightly and fresh leaves are wrapped around until a cigar-like shape is formed.
    • The material is held by vines or twine.
    • Several of these smokers are made.
    • Two of them should be small enough to be carried by the gatherer who climbs up the tree.
  • A clean, food-grade bucket or basket lined with banana leaves is used as a receptacle of honey.
  • A rope is attached to the handle of the bucket or basket and lifted up within the reach of the gatherer.
  • A separate bag is prepared for the brood and pollen. These are harvested only after the honey is removed.
Figure 1. Making a smoker

©FAO/TECA

2. Harvesting honey

  • The smokers are lit prior to climbing the tree.
    • The large smokers are distributed around the tree while the two smaller ones are carried up in the tree and positioned just below the colony to provide a steady stream of smoke.
    • The smoke drives away the bees but leaves the comb intact.
    • With the smoke curtain as a cover, the gatherer climbs onto the branch where the nest is attached and positions the bucket under the nest and secures it in place.
    • The honeycomb is cut in sections starting from the bottom and is allowed to drop into the plastic bag.
    • During cutting, a 1 cm buffer of honey is left between the brood and pollen.
    • This is done to minimize the contamination of the collected honey with pollen.
    • After cutting, the plastic is sealed and tucked into the basket.
    • The basket is covered and lowered to the ground afterwards.
    • The pollen is similarly cut and placed in a separate container.
    • Giant bee has only one comb, and it is totally removed during harvesting.
    • The bees migrate to another tree which is usually close to the original nest.
    • This is the reason why techniques for smoking the nest is important, as it will not cause too much bee mortality.
    • Time of harvest also matters since the broods are minimal during the honey flow season.
    • Since collection expeditions last for two weeks, several plastic bags and baskets are carried by the gatherers.
    • The brood is usually consumed by the gatherers.
    • After harvesting, dispose of the smokers properly.
    • Pile them together and pour adequate water or cover with soil to make sure that it will not cause a forest fire.
Figure 2. A smoker carried by the gatherer

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Smoking the colony from the ground

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Cutting comb

©FAO/TECA

3. Transporting and processing the honey

  • Sealed honey and pollen bags are collected in a community centre and weighed by the buyer.
    • The gatherer is paid according to gross weight.
    • Honey and pollen are paid separately.
    • Afterwards these are taken to a honey house for processing.
  • To extract honey the comb is cut into small pieces and then placed on a straining tray.
    • The bottom of the tray is usually made from stainless steel wire mesh (1 mm x 1 mm).
    • Most of the wax and other debris that may have fallen into the comb during harvest are filtered out.
  • After straining, the moisture content is checked using a refractometer and the honey is kept in a settling tank for about a week for the remaining debris to separate from the honey.
    • If the moisture is above 23 percent, place the honey in a food-grade tank with a wide mouth.
    • Leave the tank open and place it in a clean room with a dehumidifying machine.
    • It takes 8 to 12 hours to reduce the moisture content of honey.
  • Let the honey stand for at least two days to allow it to settle before bottling.
  • It is advisable to pasteurize the honey to inhibit the activity of yeasts that cause fermentation.
    • To pasteurize, place the honey bottle in a saucepan with water and heat to 145 degrees Fahrenheit for 30 minutes (www.beesource.com).
    • While pasteurization inhibits the growth of moulds and yeast, the increase in temperature may denaturize enzymes in the honey.
    • Extreme heat may also cause the honey to caramelize.
  • Store the honey in a dry cool place away from the sun to lengthen its shelf-life.
  • Exposure to sunlight causes photo-oxidation resulting in the discoloration (darkening) of honey.
Figure 5. Bringing the harvest to the village

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Uncapping and chopping honeycomb

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Filtering honey using muslin mesh funnel

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. A honey settling tank with tap

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Bottled and labelled honey ready to be sold

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • How to harvest honey, pollen and propolis from stingless bees: ID 8265.
  • Propagation of stingless bees using coconut shells: ID 8251.
  • Use of stingless bees for pollination: ID 8254.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology/practice supported by the community provides an additional source of honey/income/food substitute from giant bees at no additional costs. The community sets guidelines to be adhered to by the beekeepers, however, bees forage naturally, thus without much external costs

_annotations.body:
Harvesting honey from giant honey bees

Harvesting honey from colonies of giant honey bees, Apis breviligula and Apis dorsata can be a profitable village enterprise. Smoke is used to drive away the bees from their nest. The honeycomb is cut and separated from the pollen and brood. The comb is processed in a honey house to limit contamination. Dehumidification is done when necessary to lower the moisture content to at least 23 percent. Extracted and dehumidified honey is bottled in glass jars.

  • A smoker is made by bundling dry and fresh plant material.
    • The dry leaves and twigs are bundled tightly and fresh leaves are wrapped around until a cigar-like shape is formed.
    • The material is held by vines or twine.
    • Several of these smokers are made.
    • Two of them should be small enough to be carried by the gatherer who climbs up the tree.
  • A clean, food-grade bucket or basket lined with banana leaves is used as a receptacle of honey.
  • A rope is attached to the handle of the bucket or basket and lifted up within the reach of the gatherer.
  • A separate bag is prepared for the brood and pollen. These are harvested only after the honey is removed.
Figure 1. Making a smoker

©FAO/TECA

2. Harvesting honey

  • The smokers are lit prior to climbing the tree.
    • The large smokers are distributed around the tree while the two smaller ones are carried up in the tree and positioned just below the colony to provide a steady stream of smoke.
    • The smoke drives away the bees but leaves the comb intact.
    • With the smoke curtain as a cover, the gatherer climbs onto the branch where the nest is attached and positions the bucket under the nest and secures it in place.
    • The honeycomb is cut in sections starting from the bottom and is allowed to drop into the plastic bag.
    • During cutting, a 1 cm buffer of honey is left between the brood and pollen.
    • This is done to minimize the contamination of the collected honey with pollen.
    • After cutting, the plastic is sealed and tucked into the basket.
    • The basket is covered and lowered to the ground afterwards.
    • The pollen is similarly cut and placed in a separate container.
    • Giant bee has only one comb, and it is totally removed during harvesting.
    • The bees migrate to another tree which is usually close to the original nest.
    • This is the reason why techniques for smoking the nest is important, as it will not cause too much bee mortality.
    • Time of harvest also matters since the broods are minimal during the honey flow season.
    • Since collection expeditions last for two weeks, several plastic bags and baskets are carried by the gatherers.
    • The brood is usually consumed by the gatherers.
    • After harvesting, dispose of the smokers properly.
    • Pile them together and pour adequate water or cover with soil to make sure that it will not cause a forest fire.
Figure 2. A smoker carried by the gatherer

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Smoking the colony from the ground

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Cutting comb

©FAO/TECA

3. Transporting and processing the honey

  • Sealed honey and pollen bags are collected in a community centre and weighed by the buyer.
    • The gatherer is paid according to gross weight.
    • Honey and pollen are paid separately.
    • Afterwards these are taken to a honey house for processing.
  • To extract honey the comb is cut into small pieces and then placed on a straining tray.
    • The bottom of the tray is usually made from stainless steel wire mesh (1 mm x 1 mm).
    • Most of the wax and other debris that may have fallen into the comb during harvest are filtered out.
  • After straining, the moisture content is checked using a refractometer and the honey is kept in a settling tank for about a week for the remaining debris to separate from the honey.
    • If the moisture is above 23 percent, place the honey in a food-grade tank with a wide mouth.
    • Leave the tank open and place it in a clean room with a dehumidifying machine.
    • It takes 8 to 12 hours to reduce the moisture content of honey.
  • Let the honey stand for at least two days to allow it to settle before bottling.
  • It is advisable to pasteurize the honey to inhibit the activity of yeasts that cause fermentation.
    • To pasteurize, place the honey bottle in a saucepan with water and heat to 145 degrees Fahrenheit for 30 minutes (www.beesource.com).
    • While pasteurization inhibits the growth of moulds and yeast, the increase in temperature may denaturize enzymes in the honey.
    • Extreme heat may also cause the honey to caramelize.
  • Store the honey in a dry cool place away from the sun to lengthen its shelf-life.
  • Exposure to sunlight causes photo-oxidation resulting in the discoloration (darkening) of honey.
Figure 5. Bringing the harvest to the village

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Uncapping and chopping honeycomb

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Filtering honey using muslin mesh funnel

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. A honey settling tank with tap

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Bottled and labelled honey ready to be sold

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • How to harvest honey, pollen and propolis from stingless bees: ID 8265.
  • Propagation of stingless bees using coconut shells: ID 8251.
  • Use of stingless bees for pollination: ID 8254.

6.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology/practice supported by the community provides an additional source of honey/income/food substitute from giant bees at no additional costs. The community sets guidelines to be adhered to by the beekeepers, however, bees forage naturally, thus without much external costs

records.title: Production of tree seeds for agroforestry: seed sourcing
records.description:
Description

The availability of tree germplasm (e.g. seeds, seedlings, cuttings) has been identified as one of the crucial elements in scaling up agroforestry technologies by the World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF) and its partner organizations. To respond to this need, a toolkit on agroforestry tree seeds was developed to speed up the adoption of agroforestry technologies and recognize the crucial importance of germplasm especially seeds in scaling up agroforestry. The toolkit was developed as a training tool that collaborating organizations such as non-governmental organizations (NGOs), community based organizations, governmental organizations and other research institutes could use during extension activities involving tree seed and seedlings.

1. What are the best tree seed sources?

  • All seed sources should meet certain standards in terms of the number and quality of trees needed to ensure wide genetic variation and good seed quality.
  • The age and shape of the trees should also be considered when selecting seed source. Other trees that surround them should have good appearance as they could be fathers of the seeds to be collected as so affect the quality of the offspring.
  • They should also match the environmental conditions of where the seeds will be planted to ensure that the trees will be well adapted.
Figure 1. When the seed (mother) tree is surrounded by other good-quality trees, the offspring will most probably demonstrate good quality

©FAO/TECA

2. Seed tree selection criteria differ for various tree types: examples

2.1 Timber trees selection criteria

Timber tree selection criteria could include:

  • a straight stem form;
  • above- average tree height and stem diameter;
  • a long, clear marketable bole;
  • resistance to pests and diseases;
  • good-quality timber; and
  • a mature tree that produces ample quantities of seed.
Figure 2. Examples of good and bad characteristics for mother trees

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Fodder trees and living fences selection criteria

Fodder trees and living fences selection criteria could include:

  • a fast-growing capacity;
  • easy to coppice (tree stems are cut down to near ground level and in subsequent growth years, many new shoots will emerge and which are later harvested and replanted);
  • have many branches;
  • multi-stemmed;
  • high productivity of leaves and pods;
  • high nutritive values of leaves or pods;
  • resistance to pests and diseases; and
  • mature trees that produce ample quantities of seed.

2.3 Fruit trees selection criteria

Fruit trees selection criteria could include:

  • abundant, sweet and big fruits;
  • uniform crown with low branches;
  • fast growing;
  • resistance to diseases and pests; and
  • mature trees that produce ample quantities of seed.

2.4 Firewood, selection criteria

Firewood, selection criteria could include:

  • a high calorific value – meaning it should produce a large amount of heat. Communities can measure it from how effective the fuel is in cooking food, heating water or warming the house;
  • fast growing; and
  • easy coppice (tree stems are cut down to near ground level and in subsequent growth years, many new shoots will emerge and which are later harvested and replanted).

3. Evaluating areas designated as seed source criteria

  1. Is the seed source in a suitable ecological zone for seed production? Seeds from lowland fit well in lowland, while seeds from highlands fit well in highlands.
  2. Will the trees be well pollinated?
  3. Is the size of the source and the number of mother trees adequate? You should ensure that the seed source has at least 100 trees for seed production. The isolation distance from other trees of the same species should be between 200 m and 500 m.
  4. Are the trees healthy and their performance good?
  5. Seed production areas should be easy to access.
Figure 3. Matching the environmental conditions of the collection and planting site

©FAO/TECA

4. Main types of seed sources

  • Farmland: on farms trees that have been planted or retained for the production of other end-products e.g. fodder, timber or other services apart from providing seed.
  • Natural forest: naturally occurring population of trees in forests and woodlands that are used for seed production.
  • Plantations: trees that are planted in blocks to provide services or end products other than seeds.
  • Seed orchards: trees that have been planted in blocks specifically for seed production.
  • Vegetative propagation: this is plant multiplication through cuttings, grafting or micro propagation/tissue culture (a technique where plants are developed from single cells or tissue).
Figure 4. A seed source

©FAO/TECA

5. How to establish and manage seed sources

Seed sources should be managed well to increase seed production while maintaining genetic diversity. The growth condition of the planting site should match the growth condition at the seed collection site. The altitude, latitude, longitude, rainfall, temperature and soils should be appropriate for the target species. Ideally, a seed source should have more than 30 trees producing seed at any one time.

  • Due to the smaller size of most farms, seed production trees establishment should be planned and managed by groups of farmers who occupy adjacent lands, with each farmer having at least four to ten trees of same species for seed production.
  • The seeds should always be bulked before distribution or use. Bulking is putting the same seeds from different mother trees together so as to have suitable levels of genetic diversity.
  • Appropriate spacing differs by species and site. Spacing is done to encourage a large crown development and maximize flowering. The following spacing of seed trees at maturity is recommended: 3 m x 3 m, or 4 m x 2 m, or 3 m x 2 m; for Sesbania sesban, Leucaena spp, Calliandra calothyrsus; and, 5 m x 5 m, or 6 m x 6 m, or 8 m x 8 m, or 8 m x 4 m, for Melia
  • The minimum size of seed unit should be 0.5 ha for species which require a bigger spacing e.g. Prunus africana, Warburgia ugandensis or Melia volkensii, so that a number of 350 trees can be established. These should later be thinned, leaving at least 100 trees. As the trees grow larger, thinning will ensure that the best trees remain to allow free crown growth and exposure to more sunlight. In places with strong sunshine, thinning should be done in early morning or late afternoon.

Note: these guidelines were developed after a review of the available extension materials on tree seed and tree planting was conducted. It was found that extension and training materials had primarily focused on the technical side of seed production. There was limited information on successful seed production and distribution as highlighted by a DANIDA – funded project on the institutional nature of seed production in Kenya, Malawi and Burkina Faso and also the private sector especially those that work with small-scale tree nursery operators and seed dealers. The benefits of collaborating with associations of tree nursery operators were highlighted by a Kenyan DFID funded project in peri-urban Nairobi, Meru and Kisumu. The lessons from the two projects were included to expand the information that was already available on tree seed collection, production and distribution which was basically 90 percent common sense (Soren Moestrup, Forest and Landscape, 2004).

Figure 5. Some examples of different planting schemes and spacing

©FAO/IFSP visual extension material, 2001

Figure 6. Replacement of seedlings

©FAO/IFSP visual extension material, 2001

Figure 7. A seed source

©FAO/TECA

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Strengthening of community seed production groups (CSPG): ID 7707.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for fast-growing healthy, genetically diverse planting material.

8.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for high-quality seeds and superior end products.

Production of tree seeds for agroforestry: seed sourcing

A seed source is a group of trees growing together from which one can collect seed for multiplication. This may be an identified number of trees in a landscape-farmland/natural forest or a group of trees from which you obtain seeds. A good seed source for trees should provide fast-growing healthy, genetically diverse planting material. Selecting good seed sources results in high-quality seeds and therefore superior end products. It is good to note that not every seed source will provide good quality seeds. The genetic quality of the seed source is the decisive factor for the success of any tree planting programme hence seed sources have to be carefully identified and selected. The selection of seed sources is based on the assumption that the characteristics of the seed trees are likely to be transmitted to their offspring. Farmers commonly plant trees on farms or community lands to grow products' that satisfy household needs and market demands. Tree seeds, a key input that determines the success of any tree planting activity, are often in short supply. Smallholders and NGOs collect or produce most of the seed used in their tree planting programs. records.title: Well dried maize benefits all: the solar maize dryer
records.description:
Description

The following video illustrates the function and usage of the solar maize dryer.

Video: Well dried maize benefits all (English)

1. Why dry maize?

After harvesting, maize usually has a moisture content between 21 and 23 percent. At this level, there is a high risk that the grains become moulded or that aflatoxins generate. In such cases, there is a risk for food safety and farmers lose a lot of the initial market price for his or her maize. To avoid losses the maize has to be dried. The perfect moisture level for storage which generates the highest market price is at 12 percent. But, since it takes a long time to dry the maize from above 20 to 12 percent, farmers usually pre-dry their maize to 13 to 15 percent. This is a safe moisture level to store the maize for a while and then complete the drying process. The higher the moisture level of the maize is, the lower the price offered by warehouses, processing companies and open markets becomes.

In many cases, farmers dry their maize in the open. Open drying bears many risks for the grain:

  • Sudden rainfalls can spoil the maize.
  • Animals can access it, eat it, defecate on it and reduce its quality.
  • Open drying involves high labour costs. Somebody has to be around throughout the drying process and keep watch of the maize.

The solar dryer ensures a cost-effective, more hygienic and secure way to dry maize. During the whole drying process, the maize is protected by unexpected rainfalls, or by goats and other animals. Farmers benefit from lower labour costs and less post-harvest losses. Construction costs are low. The drying process works much faster since it continues also at night. The hygienic environment in the dryer ensures a high quality of the maize that brings economic gains to farmers. The dryer is also good for the environment. It doesn’t consume any fossil fuels, unlike those used by commercial warehouses. The solar dryer can be also used to dry other kinds of commodities, such as peppers, all kinds of beans and maybe also fish.

Figure 1. The solar maize dryer improves the quality of your product

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. The maize is spread out on the racks to dry

©FAO/TECA

2. How does the solar dryer work?

The roof is covered by acrylic sheets. The transparent sheets allow sun rays to enter and trap the heat inside the drying chamber. During daytime, the chamber can heat up to a temperature between 50° C and 70° C depending on the weather conditions. The heat in the drying chamber draws moisture out of the maize. Essential in solar drying is constant airflow. Cold air enters the dryer through louvers at the bottom of the dryer. The air is then heated up inside the dryer, absorbs moisture and exists the dryer through a vent placed at the top of the dryer. Before maize is put into the dryer, its moisture content is measured with a moisture meter in order to estimate for how long the maize will stay in the dryer. A small sample of maize is inserted into the moisture meter and the meter will indicate the exact moisture content in percentage. The drying time depends on the weather conditions, but with average weather, a sample with 25 percent of moisture will take about three days to be reduced to the desired level of 14 to 15 percent.

Figure 3. Heat in the drying chamber and a constant airflow through ventilation openings draws moisture out of the maize

©FAO/TECA

3. How is a solar drier constructed?

Basic materials for constructing a solar dryer of 12 m x 7 m are:

  • 35 bags of cement for the foundation;
  • wood;
  • nails;
  • mesh (for the tray tables, 20 pieces);
  • eight roles of net (for the tray tables on top of the mesh as well as for the ventilation openings); and
  • 50 transparent acrylic sheets.

Designs for the building of the drying house can be quite diverse. The important principle is to create airflow through ventilation openings. Detailed sketches on the design used in the MOAP project in Ghana in Figure 4.

Figure 4. Sketches (such as this one) of the design of the solar maize dryer used in the MOAP project in Ghana can be found in the attachment

©FAO/TECA

4. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Except for the transparent sheets, all materials can easily be found locally. The major cost is for the transparent sheets, which currently cost in Ghana about 15 USD per m² (Suntuf polycarbonate clear sheets). The total investment costs are estimated to be between 3 000 and 5 000 USD depending on prices and negotiation power. Between 50 and 60 tonnes of maize can be dried per year in the drying house (two harvests of six weeks each). This maize has a value of about 14 000 USD. The 10 per cent gained from reduced post-harvest losses, therefore, have a value of 1 400 USD. These gains of accrued over about three years would pay for the cash investment cost of the drying house.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Maize harvesting and post-harvesting handling: ID 7015.
  • Maize production: ID 7018.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2285.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Women-friendly

The technology is easy to use and accessible to all.

7.2 Resource use efficiency

All materials to use the technology can be found locally.

7.3 Pro-poor technology

Using the technology leads to a reduction in post-harvest losses and the additional yield accrued leading to additional income and food source. The technology is also low-cost.

During daytime, the chamber can heat up to a temperature between 50° C and 70° C depending on the weather conditions. The heat in the drying chamber draws moisture out of the maize. Essential in solar drying is constant airflow. Cold air enters the dryer through louvers at the bottom of the dryer. The air is then heated up inside the dryer, absorbs moisture and exists the dryer through a vent placed at the top of the dryer. Before maize is put into the dryer, its moisture content is measured with a moisture meter in order to estimate for how long the maize will stay in the dryer. A small sample of maize is inserted into the moisture meter and the meter will indicate the exact moisture content in percentage. The drying time depends on the weather conditions, but with average weather, a sample with 25 percent of moisture will take about three days to be reduced to the desired level of 14 to 15 percent.

Figure 3. Heat in the drying chamber and a constant airflow through ventilation openings draws moisture out of the maize

©FAO/TECA

3. How is a solar drier constructed?

Basic materials for constructing a solar dryer of 12 m x 7 m are:

  • 35 bags of cement for the foundation;
  • wood;
  • nails;
  • mesh (for the tray tables, 20 pieces);
  • eight roles of net (for the tray tables on top of the mesh as well as for the ventilation openings); and
  • 50 transparent acrylic sheets.

Designs for the building of the drying house can be quite diverse. The important principle is to create airflow through ventilation openings. Detailed sketches on the design used in the MOAP project in Ghana in Figure 4.

Figure 4. Sketches (such as this one) of the design of the solar maize dryer used in the MOAP project in Ghana can be found in the attachment

©FAO/TECA

4. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Except for the transparent sheets, all materials can easily be found locally. The major cost is for the transparent sheets, which currently cost in Ghana about 15 USD per m² (Suntuf polycarbonate clear sheets). The total investment costs are estimated to be between 3 000 and 5 000 USD depending on prices and negotiation power. Between 50 and 60 tonnes of maize can be dried per year in the drying house (two harvests of six weeks each). This maize has a value of about 14 000 USD. The 10 per cent gained from reduced post-harvest losses, therefore, have a value of 1 400 USD. These gains of accrued over about three years would pay for the cash investment cost of the drying house.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Maize harvesting and post-harvesting handling: ID 7015.
  • Maize production: ID 7018.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 2285.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Women-friendly

The technology is easy to use and accessible to all.

7.2 Resource use efficiency

All materials to use the technology can be found locally.

7.3 Pro-poor technology

Using the technology leads to a reduction in post-harvest losses and the additional yield accrued leading to additional income and food source. The technology is also low-cost.

records.title: Uso de la harina de ortiga y de aceto balsámico en apicultura
records.description:
Descripción

  • La harina de ortiga es la preparación que se logra del secado y posteriormente desintegrando la ortiga (Urtica sp.).
  • La ortiga es una planta que crece en corrales donde hay animales y es una especie vegetal que en sus estomas posee gran cantidad de ácido fórmico el cual un componente que aumenta la defensa de las abejas frente a enemigos como las avispas (Vespula germanica).
  • El aceto balsámico es un preparado obtenido de las manzanas, el cual se debe estabilizar a un pH=3, el cual es aceptado y consumido por las abejas, con esta variación en el pH interno de la abeja se logra mantener niveles razonables la presencia de Nosema en el tracto digestivo de la abeja, sin producir los daños y mermas propias de esta enfermedad.

1. Harina de ortiga

1.1 Planta de ortiga

  • La ortiga es una hierba (Figura 1) que se encuentra principalmente en suelos ricos y fértiles, o en corrales donde hay animales.
Figura 1. Planta de ortiga

©FAO/TECA

1.2 ¿Qué efectos tiene?

  • En la espinas de las hojas posee ácido fórmico, que hace aumentar el nivel de defensa de las abejas.
  • La ortiga evita el ataque de chaqueta amarilla y evita que prolifere la nosema.

1.3 ¿Cómo se usa?

  • Se usa de dos formas:
    • Harina de ortiga junto a azúcar flor.
    • Hervida con miel.

1.4 ¿Cómo se hace?

  • Se cosecha ortiga madura, a punto de florecer y se saca de raíz.
  • Se lava muy bien y se eliminan las raíces.
  • Secar: Se puede secar de dos formas:
    • Al horno a fuego lento evitando que las hojas pierdan el color.
    • Secar a la sobra en un lugar limpio, hasta que las hojas estén quebradizas (Figura 2).
  • Moler las hojas (en molinillo).
  • Cernir para que quede como harina (muy fina) (Figura 3).
Figura 2. Ortigas secando a la sobra

©FAO/TECA

Figura 3. Hojas de ortiga molidas y cernidas

©FAO/TECA

1.5 ¿Cómo se usa?

  • Se aplica mezclando con azúcar flor (Figura 4) y después se espolvorea sobre los cabezales de la colmena o en el piso de la colmena en un recipiente para que las abejas lo utilicen (Figura 5).
Figura 4. Mezcla de harina de ortiga y de azúcar flor

©FAO/TECA

Figura 5. Mezcla puesta en un recipiente sobre el piso de la colmena

©FAO/TECA

1.6 ¿Cuándo aplicar?

  • La harina de ortiga se utiliza cuando se termina la temporada, después de la última cosecha y últimos manejos, es decir cuando se entra en la invernada, que las familias disminuyen en cantidad de abejas y son más vulneradas por el ataque de las avispas que buscan ingresar a las colmenas en busca de alimento.
  • Se aplica harina de ortiga solamente una sola vez en la temporada.

2. Ortiga hervida con miel

2.1 ¿Cómo se hace?

  • Cosechar ortiga madura.
  • Hervir la ortiga durante 15 min en ½ litro de agua.
  • Cuando esté tibia, mezclar con 1 kg de miel.

2.2 Aplicación

  • 2 a 3 cucharaditas por colmena en una bolsa plástica con un orificio.
  • Ponerla sobre los cabezales de la colmena.
  • No se debe aplicar en periodo de pillaje.

El efecto que produce el aroma del ácido fórmico (uno de los componentes que posee la abeja en su saco de veneno) sobre las avispas es que estas perciben una colmena fuerte y no atacan con tanta ferocidad, a su vez la ortiga genera un aumento en la conducta de defensa de las abejas guardianas, por eso se realiza siempre después de la cosecha, antes de la entrada a invernada, cuando ya no hay fruta en el suelo para las avispas y entonces estas buscan alimento dentro de las colmenas y colmenas débiles no son capaces de soportar estos ataques y mueren a causa de ellos.

3. Aceto balsámico

3.1 Uso del aceto balsámico

  • Es un producto fabricado a partir de la manzana que sirve para mantener bajos niveles de nosema.

3.2 ¿Qué controla?

  • Principalmente controla nosema.

3.3 ¿Cómo se usa?

  • Aplicar el aceto balsámico directamente sobre los cabezales (una cucharada por colmena).

3.4 Materiales

  • 15 kilos de manzana verdes o rojas.
  • Balde plástico de 20 litros.
  • Doble fondo.
  • Un trozo de malla mosquetera.
  • Llave de corte de agua.

3.5 Preparación del material

  • Se debe instalar el doble fondo que es el que nos permite hacer la separación de la parte liquida de la parte solida.
  • Se perfora con un cuchillo caliente el borde de la tacho a la altura de la base, para que poner la llave de paso, que es por donde saldrá el producto (Figura 6).
  • En la tapa de la tacho se hace una perforación para que se ventile el producto (Figura 7).
  • Se pega o funde una doble rejilla de malla mosquetera para que no entren las moscas en el producto (Figura 8).
Figura 6. Ilustración del envase para hacer el aceto

©FAO/TECA

Figura 7. Perforación de la tapa

©FAO/TECA

Figura 8. Malla mosquetera

©FAO/TECA

3.6 Preparación del aceto

  • La manzana se limpia con una toalla absorbente y luego se corta en trozos (una manzana puede dividirse en 8 trozos) utilizando cáscara, pepas y pulpa.
    • Una vez hecho este proceso se llena el balde con manzanas picadas, cubriendo la parte superior con manzanas enteras con el pedúnculo hacia arriba.
    • No se debe añadir agua: El aceto balsámico es sólo con el exudado de las manzanas, puede llegar a obtenerse casi 1 litro para la cantidad de manzanas señaladas, va a depender si estas son más maduras o más verdes.
  • Una vez que ha pasado un tiempo, aproximadamente 15 días se prueba si está listo el producto (Figura 9).
    • Para ello se saca desde la llave inferior algo de aceto balsámico y se deposita en un frasco de vidrio y se mide con papel pH hasta llegar a un pH=3.
    • Este grado es aceptado por las abejas (lo consumen), y cumple la función de acidificar el organismo de las abejas y con ello elimina la nosema.
Figura 9. Foto de la preparación del aceto balsámico

©FAO/TECA

3.7 Aplicación del aceto balsámico

  • Cuando una colmena presenta algún signo de nosema (heces en techo de la colmena, en la piquera, vidrio del automóvil, abdomen distendido, etc.), se le debe aplicar 30 ml de aceto balsámico sobre los cabezales (con una jeringa), así las abejas que están enfermas pueden consumir este producto.
  • Este producto se aplica al entrar a invierno en dos dosis de 30 ml cada una.
    • El aceto balsámico se puede utilizar al inicio y término de la temporada para disminuir la cantidad de nosemosis en un apiario.
    • Si el problema persiste se puede otorgar una tercera dosis, pero si se llega a dar tres veces este producto se debe suplementar con alguna fuente proteica rotándola cada año (poroto de soya o levadura de cerveza).
  • Nota: El aceto balsámico entra en un proceso de oxidación por lo que se torna color amarillo a café oscuro.
    • Este producto mantiene el ph=3 siempre que se introduzcan hojas o ramas de romero (Rosmarinus officinalis) sin flor.
    • El producto no debe quedar expuesto al sol.
Figura 10. Aceto balsámico de diferentes colores y con hojas de rosmero

©FAO/TECA

4. Conclusión

  • Para concluir se señala que la ortiga y el aceto balsámico son estrategias que utilizan los apicultores orgánicos para disminuir los ataques de chaquetas amarillas y la proliferación de la nosema.
    • Ambos manejos se basan en tradiciones de gran data en el tiempo.
  • La harina de ortiga es un método complementario a la eliminación de los nidos de avispas y a otro tipo de trampas con carnada que se utilizan en época invernal, por otra parte hace mucho tiempo los apicultores usan agentes acidificantes del medio de la abeja para combatir la nosema con buenos resultados para las familias que la poseen.
  • Estos manejos no se superponen a las bases nutricionales y sanitarias, y mantener una situación interna en equilibrio y productiva, son elementos complementarios para disminuir estos agentes dañinos.

5. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

6. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Alimentador externo e interno para colmenas: ID 8325.
  • Buenas prácticas apícolas: ID 8217.

7. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

7.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología describe cómo se puede elaborar y usar la harina de ortiga y el aceto balsámico de manera eficiente.

7.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

A través del uso de la harina de ortiga y de aceto balsámico en apicultura, el apicultor puede combatir de forma complementaria los ataques de avispa y los dañinos aumentos de nosema en las abejas, lo que conduce a muchos beneficios.
