records.title: Confección de overol con velo integrado para apicultores
records.description:
Descripción

  • Este equipo de protección o indumentaria está compuesto de dos partes: el overol y el velo, el cual se une mediante el uso de zíperes facilitando el desprendimiento del velo para su lavado.
  • De igual manera permite al apicultor llevarlo hacia atrás permitiendo el descubriendo de la cara en los momentos previos y posteriores a la faena apícola.
  • Asimismo lleva inserto un zíper vertical en la parte frontal que recorre del cuello hasta la entre pierna lo cual permite al apicultor ponerse y sacarse el traje con facilidad.
  • En los extremos de las mangas y de los pies (tobillos) el traje lleva elásticos para ajustar al cuerpo y evitar la entrada de las abejas al interior de este.

1. Material necesario

1.1 Para el overol

  • Tela algodonada/suave: 2,5 m.
  • Zip de 80 cm.
  • Elásticos para puños y tobillos: 50 cm.
  • Tijeras.
  • Hilo blanco.
  • Agujas.

1.2 Para el velo/masquera

  • Dos aros plásticos de 1,2 m de largo cada uno.
  • Malla metálica plastificada: 20 cm x 25 cm.
  • Malla tul cancán/plastificada: 1 m x 1 m.
  • Zip de 80 cm.
  • Tela algodonada/suave: 1 m x 1 m.

 

  • Se recomienda que el traje sea holgado para evitar picaduras, facilitar la movilidad durante su trabajo, sea fresco y que no se pegue con el sudor al cuerpo.
    • El traje debe ser dos tallas mayores a la talla del apicultor.
    • Debe de ser elaborado con tela tipo algodonada de colores claros (blanco, kaki, amarillo, blanco invierno).
  • Para guardar pequeñas herramientas utilizadas en la actividad apícola, es recomendable confeccionarle bolsas o bolsillos al overol en cada una de las piernas en la parte frontal (si se desea un par a la altura del pecho).
  • El velo adherido al overol puede ser elaborado de forma circular o cuadrada según el gusto del apicultor.
    • El circular es confeccionado con cedazo plástico, cancán o cambrellon (punto grueso), reforzado con dos aros plásticos (uno superior y uno inferior) evitando que este se pegue al rostro del apicultor.
    • El velo elaborado de forma cuadrada es confeccionado con malla metálica plastificada en la parte frontal (visor) y malla plástica en los laterales y parte trasera o posterior que garanticen firmeza y eviten la adhesión al rostro del apicultor.
  • La abertura de la trama de la malla más adecuada debe ser de número 12, es decir, que contenga 12 cuadros en línea por cada pulgada (2,5 cm), lo que permitirá obtener una mejor visibilidad al apicultor.
    • Se recomienda utilizar en el visor (parte frontal) una malla de color negro que facilite una mejor visibilidad.
  • El velo elaborado de forma cuadrada tiene las siguientes medidas:
    • Parte media o frontal (frente rectangular):
      • 25 cm de ancho x 20 cm de alto.
    • 2 laterales (izquierdo y derecho) de forma rectangular con borde inferior oblicuo en diagonal:
      • 25 cm de largo x 20 cm de alto parte frontal x 9 cm de alto parte posterior.
      • Se recomienda reducir en un centímetro la longitud del lateral izquierdo para facilitar el pliegue o dobles de la careta.
    • Sección posterior rectangular:
      • 25 cm ancho x 9 cm alto.
      • Los cuatro lados del velo (mallas), van unidas (costuradas) en sus lados mediante cintas de lona, tela gruesa o cuerina, permitiendo doblar las 4 partes rígidas del velo cuando vaya ser guardarlo.
  • En los países centroamericanos se elaboran trajes de diferentes tallas tomando en consideración principalmente la altura del apicultor.
    • Van desde talla S hasta XL:
      • Talla S: 1,70 m - 1,74 m.
      • Talla M: 1,75 m - 1,79 m.
      • Talla L: 1,80 m - 1,84 m.
      • Talla XL: 1,85 m - 1,89 m.
      • Talla XXL: 1,90 m - 1,94 m.

2. Materia prima

  • Elaborado a base de telas algodonadas, lona suave, lino o mezclilla o de tipo drill de colores claros (blanco, kaki, amarillo, etc.), no es recomendable usar colores oscuros pues estos irritan a las abejas, tampoco es conveniente usar colores claros similares al rojo pues la abeja no los visualiza bien.
  • Para la masquera se necesita una malla metálica o plástica, aros plásticos o metálicos, complementados con otros materiales menores como zíperes de nylon o cremalleras, elásticos e hilos (Figura 1).
Figura 1. Overol con velo integrado

©FAO/TECA

3. Partes del overol y del velo

3.1 Piezas del traje

  • Las piezas del traje son completas desde el pie al cuello y se requieren dos piezas delanteras y dos piezas traseras (Figura 2).
  • Cada pieza debe ser la opuesta a su contraparte y de las mismas medidas para que el traje quede correctamente armado y ensamblado para que no existan orificios por donde puedan entrar las abejas.
  • El largo de estas piezas va a depender de la altura del apicultor, siempre se deben considerar un par de tallas a la que usa el apicultor.
  • El largo debe considerar 30 o 40 cm adicionales desde el cuello al tobillo para otorgar la comodidad durante el trabajo, al igual que el ancho de las piezas a la altura del abdomen deben tener 15 a 20 cm más que la circunferencia de la cintura total.
Figura 2. Piezas del traje

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Manga y bolsillo

  • Para la confección de la manga del overol se requieren dos piezas, donde cada una es de igual medidas pero en su contraparte (lado opuesto).
  • En la manga se hace una bastilla para poner un elástico por dentro para que así la manga quede ajustada a la muñeca.
  • La bolsa o bolsillo de pantalón puede ser de las dimensiones señaladas en el esquema o variable según las necesidades del apicultor (Figura 3).
Figura 3. Piezas de la manga del overol

©FAO/TECA

3.3 Sombrero o velo

  • Para la confección del sombrero circular se requieren cuatro tipos de piezas.
    • La copa del sombrero es la parte alta del gorro y se costura al lateral de la copa del sombrero que conforma el gorro del velo.
    • El ala del sombrero es la que determina si el velo es cuadrado o redondo y debe llevar por el borde exterior un soporte de alambre o plástico para mantener la forma del velo y que este no se pegue a la cara.
  • La forma de ensamble y la disposición de cada una de las partes se detalla en la Figura 4.
  • La Figura 5 presenta las formas y medidas de las partes que componen el velo.
Figura 4. Disposición de cada parte del sombrero

©FAO/TECA

Figura 5. Formas y medidas de las partes que componen el velo

©FAO/TECA

3.4 Malla de careta

  • Para la unión de las mallas (Figura 6) entre sí, de las mallas con el ala del sombrero y con la franja que une la careta a la blusa, se deben usar soportes rígidos (metálicos plastificados, plásticos, etc.) que deben ir dentro de un trozo de genero debidamente costurado para no permitir el paso de abejas al interior de la careta, ya que es el lugar más vulnerable y el primer sitio el cual atacan las abejas.
Figura 6. Mallas de careta del velo

©FAO/TECA

4. Unión del overol y del velo

  • La franja que une la careta con la blusa debe ir costurada a un ziper para que se pueda retirar y poner de forma segura y rápida.
Figura 7. Overol con velo integrado durante una visita a las colmenas

©FAO/TECA

5. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Guantes de protección para apicultor: ID 8328.
  • Las buenas prácticas en apicultura: ID 8675.
  • Confección de blusa con velo integrado para apicultores: ID 8327.

6. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

6.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología ayuda al apicultor a protegerse eficientemente de posibles picaduras de abejas.

6.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta práctica permite al apicultor trabajar mejor al tener protección contra las picaduras de abejas y así un mejor manejo de las colmenas.

records.title: The FAO-Thiaroye processing technique: how to use and operate it
records.description:
Description

1. Overview of the comparative advantages of the FTT-Thiaroye

  • The FTT-Thiaroye is an innovative and polyvalent technique with important advantages for each actor of the fisheries supply chain.
  • Firstly, the FTT allows dried and smoked products that better meet food safety requirements.
    • This results in a positive endorsement by the competent authority in charge of certifying products placed on the market, be it at the national, regional or international levels.
    • Consumer confidence is also enhanced with superior quality products that better meet their expectations.
  • Secondly, the FTT allows drying and smoking operations regardless of weather conditions.
    • Consequently, post-harvest losses, which may exceed 50 percent during the rainy season or cloudy days are better controlled.
    • But the FTT-Thiaroye also provides opportunities for additional revenue for fish operators, with the possibility to process by-products.
    • Fat gathered through the fat collection tray allows, for example, the manufacturing of soap, or can be used as cooking or frying oil.
  • Finally, we can say that the FTT-Thiaroye reduces the wood or coal/fish ratio, and it is also adaptable to other fuels such as coconut husks and shells, stems or corncobs, sugar cane bagasse, etc.
    • Overall, the use of the FTT presupposes less deforestation, better protection of mangroves, thus resulting in positive conservation of natural resources.
    • Talking specifically about gender concerns, the use of the FTT-Thiaroye reduces women's fish processors drudgery, including a lower exposure to smoke and heat.
    • At the same time, women spend less time in fish processing, allowing them to simultaneously engage in household chores.

2. The uses of the FTT-Thiaroye

  • Several operations can be carried out thanks to the FTT-Thiaroye.
    • Fish smoking.
    • Fish drying.
    • Fish storage.
    • Fish re-smoking /redrying.
  • For any of these operations, the fish must be cleaned, pre-treated, and be of good quality.
  • All the operations should also be carried out under good hygienic conditions.

2.1 Fish smoking

  • Fish smoking consists of two different phases.

2.1.1 The cooking phase

  • Place the fat collection tray in the cooking compartment.
    • Then place the rack in the kiln cooking chamber, and arrange the pre-treated fish on them.
    • Cover the cooking compartment with the lids to prevent heat loss.
  • Place the fuel in the furnace.
    • Fan it with the forge to obtain red embers, and then push the furnace into the kiln.
    • During the first 30 minutes of cooking, the furnace should only be half full of embers.
    • Turn over the fish from time to time. If using a kiln with stackable racks, these latter are regularly interchanged.
    • Increase the temperature progressively by filling the furnace with red embers and fanning the embers with the forge.
    • When the embers are no longer hot and the fuel almost consumed, remove the furnace and add fuel.
    • Fan the embers before putting back the furnace in the kiln compartment.
    • To save time, small traditional kilns filled with burning embers can be kept aside, ready to be transferred to the large FTT-Thiaroye furnace.
    • The cooking time depends on the size and thickness of the product, as well as on the number of stacked racks.
  • At the end of the cooking, increase the temperature by adding coals.
    • This should significantly reduce the final moisture content.
  • The oil and exudate from the fish fall on the tray.
    • The exudate sticks to the tray and dries while the oil oozes and flows through the pipe welded at the end of the tray to be collected in a container placed at the back of the kiln.
    • The tray has to be cleaned each time fat exudate and crust deposits are significant.

2.1.2 The smoking phase

  • The second compartment of the kiln is used for indirect smoking, and the racks loaded with cooked fish are transferred from the cooking compartment to the smoking one.
  • First of all, prepare the filter casing.
    • Moisten the sponge of plant origin (loofah) with water and lay it onto the filter casing which will be inserted into the metal housing.
  • To start smoking, the barrel of the smoke generator is also loaded with slightly moistened fuel.
  • Humidifying the fuel (at 16 to 20 percent) is desirable to avoid flames from forming and to give good flavour to the product.
    • The smoke is purified and cooled by the smoke generator located 1.5 m from the smoking chamber.
    • Then light the fire, and close the door of the barrel.
  • The smoking process should be finished within an hour at a temperature between 30°C to 34° C. 
Figure 1. Charcoal placed on the furnace

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Inserting the furnace into the oven

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Turning the fish over to prevent them from sticking on the racks

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Switching the trays around during the cooking phase

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Oil oozing and flowing through the pipe

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Collecting oil in containers placed at the back of the kiln

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Humidifying and inserting the filter into the metal housing

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Humidifying the fuel and inserting it in the smoke generator barrel

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Fish drying

  • The whole operation takes place in a single compartment: the one used for cooking.
    • The smoking compartment and the indirect smoke generator system are not needed.
    • The process consists of a single step: drying while avoiding cooking the fish.
  • Lay out the fish to be dried on the rack(s) installed in the hot-air distributor and placed onto the kiln.
    • A furnace equipped with a forge that increases the temperature and the cooking chamber’s air mass heats the drying air.
    • The time and temperature parameters in the chamber must be well controlled to avoid cooking the fish.
    • In the case of drying, the quantity of fuel is very small, and the product should be placed well away from it.
  • This step takes about one hour.
    • After that, the fish is turned over so that the drying may be homogeneous.
    • To accelerate the process of drying, the amount of embers is increased to get a temperature of about 60° C, and the relative humidity to between 60 to 70 percent.
Figure 9. Fish laid out on the racks for drying

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Fish storage

  • The FTT-Thiaroye is an ideal storage room for dried and smoked fish.
  • The side panels of the air distributor serve as a storage chamber.
  • The stacked racks serve as pallets on which the dried or smoked fish has been laid out.

2.4 Fish re-smoking/re-drying

  • This operation is identical to smoking/drying.
  • The only parameters that change are the time and the temperature: the temperature is much lower and the time shorter in this case.

3. Care and maintenance for the FTT-Thiaroye

  • A better shelf-life and good quality of the end product depend on properly maintaining the equipment during and after its use.
    • Yet too often, the equipment is neglected in traditional processing centres.
  • Daily maintenance for the FTT-Thiaroye (kiln, cover, rack, furnace) entails cleaning inside and around the kilns and removing the ashes and the waste stuck on the lids and on the mesh of the removable racks.
  • Remove the smoke generator, clean it with soapy water and then let it dry.
  • Remove the collector containing the mixture of water and exudate located below the metal housing, empty it and put it back into place.
  • Remove the housing and the filter loaded with tar from the smoke and clean it thoroughly.
  • Change the sponge of plant origin (loofah) / filter before each new session, while the used one is washed and left to dry.
  • Remove the fat-collecting tray, and clean the dried exudate and the grease ducts of the tray, and drain the pipe.
  • For regular care and maintenance of the equipment and accessories, a cleaning and disinfection programme should be established and carried out after using the kiln.
    • After cleaning, the material should only be stored once it is completely dry in order to prevent rust forming on the galvanized steel.
  • During the low-production or seasonal rest period, metal accessories need to be protected against rust by keeping them away from adverse weather, such as rain and sun.
    • The mesh and the fins need to be coated regularly with vegetable oil.
    • If rust appears on the metal parts, they will have to be cleaned and repainted with two layers of rustproofing liquid and one layer of food-grade paint at least once a year. Damaged equipment must be repaired.

3.1 Videos

  • The FAO-Thiaroye processing technique (FTT-Thiaroye). Part 1 (English)
  • The FAO-Thiaroye processing technique (FTT-Thiaroye). Part 2 (English)
  • The FAO-Thiaroye processing technique (FTT-Thiaroye). Part 3 (English)

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • How to construct the FTT-Thiaroye and assemble its components: ID 8304.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Women-friendly

The technology alleviates drudgery, is time-saving and therefore allows women to engage in other activities.

6.2 Resource use efficiency

With improved drying and smoking techniques, this technology increases the efficiency and the better use of resources.

6.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for fish to be preserved in different ways thereby providing additional sources of income and food.

    • But the FTT-Thiaroye also provides opportunities for additional revenue for fish operators, with the possibility to process by-products.
    • Fat gathered through the fat collection tray allows, for example, the manufacturing of soap, or can be used as cooking or frying oil.
  • Finally, we can say that the FTT-Thiaroye reduces the wood or coal/fish ratio, and it is also adaptable to other fuels such as coconut husks and shells, stems or corncobs, sugar cane bagasse, etc.
    • Overall, the use of the FTT presupposes less deforestation, better protection of mangroves, thus resulting in positive conservation of natural resources.
    • Talking specifically about gender concerns, the use of the FTT-Thiaroye reduces women's fish processors drudgery, including a lower exposure to smoke and heat.
    • At the same time, women spend less time in fish processing, allowing them to simultaneously engage in household chores.

2. The uses of the FTT-Thiaroye

  • Several operations can be carried out thanks to the FTT-Thiaroye.
    • Fish smoking.
    • Fish drying.
    • Fish storage.
    • Fish re-smoking /redrying.
  • For any of these operations, the fish must be cleaned, pre-treated, and be of good quality.
  • All the operations should also be carried out under good hygienic conditions.

2.1 Fish smoking

  • Fish smoking consists of two different phases.

2.1.1 The cooking phase

  • Place the fat collection tray in the cooking compartment.
    • Then place the rack in the kiln cooking chamber, and arrange the pre-treated fish on them.
    • Cover the cooking compartment with the lids to prevent heat loss.
  • Place the fuel in the furnace.
    • Fan it with the forge to obtain red embers, and then push the furnace into the kiln.
    • During the first 30 minutes of cooking, the furnace should only be half full of embers.
    • Turn over the fish from time to time. If using a kiln with stackable racks, these latter are regularly interchanged.
    • Increase the temperature progressively by filling the furnace with red embers and fanning the embers with the forge.
    • When the embers are no longer hot and the fuel almost consumed, remove the furnace and add fuel.
    • Fan the embers before putting back the furnace in the kiln compartment.
    • To save time, small traditional kilns filled with burning embers can be kept aside, ready to be transferred to the large FTT-Thiaroye furnace.
    • The cooking time depends on the size and thickness of the product, as well as on the number of stacked racks.
  • At the end of the cooking, increase the temperature by adding coals.
    • This should significantly reduce the final moisture content.
  • The oil and exudate from the fish fall on the tray.
    • The exudate sticks to the tray and dries while the oil oozes and flows through the pipe welded at the end of the tray to be collected in a container placed at the back of the kiln.
    • The tray has to be cleaned each time fat exudate and crust deposits are significant.

2.1.2 The smoking phase

  • The second compartment of the kiln is used for indirect smoking, and the racks loaded with cooked fish are transferred from the cooking compartment to the smoking one.
  • First of all, prepare the filter casing.
    • Moisten the sponge of plant origin (loofah) with water and lay it onto the filter casing which will be inserted into the metal housing.
  • To start smoking, the barrel of the smoke generator is also loaded with slightly moistened fuel.
  • Humidifying the fuel (at 16 to 20 percent) is desirable to avoid flames from forming and to give good flavour to the product.
    • The smoke is purified and cooled by the smoke generator located 1.5 m from the smoking chamber.
    • Then light the fire, and close the door of the barrel.
  • The smoking process should be finished within an hour at a temperature between 30°C to 34° C. 
Figure 1. Charcoal placed on the furnace

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Inserting the furnace into the oven

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Turning the fish over to prevent them from sticking on the racks

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Switching the trays around during the cooking phase

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Oil oozing and flowing through the pipe

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Collecting oil in containers placed at the back of the kiln

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Humidifying and inserting the filter into the metal housing

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Humidifying the fuel and inserting it in the smoke generator barrel

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Fish drying

  • The whole operation takes place in a single compartment: the one used for cooking.
    • The smoking compartment and the indirect smoke generator system are not needed.
    • The process consists of a single step: drying while avoiding cooking the fish.
  • Lay out the fish to be dried on the rack(s) installed in the hot-air distributor and placed onto the kiln.
    • A furnace equipped with a forge that increases the temperature and the cooking chamber’s air mass heats the drying air.
    • The time and temperature parameters in the chamber must be well controlled to avoid cooking the fish.
    • In the case of drying, the quantity of fuel is very small, and the product should be placed well away from it.
  • This step takes about one hour.
    • After that, the fish is turned over so that the drying may be homogeneous.
    • To accelerate the process of drying, the amount of embers is increased to get a temperature of about 60° C, and the relative humidity to between 60 to 70 percent.
Figure 9. Fish laid out on the racks for drying

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Fish storage

  • The FTT-Thiaroye is an ideal storage room for dried and smoked fish.
  • The side panels of the air distributor serve as a storage chamber.
  • The stacked racks serve as pallets on which the dried or smoked fish has been laid out.

2.4 Fish re-smoking/re-drying

  • This operation is identical to smoking/drying.
  • The only parameters that change are the time and the temperature: the temperature is much lower and the time shorter in this case.

3. Care and maintenance for the FTT-Thiaroye

  • A better shelf-life and good quality of the end product depend on properly maintaining the equipment during and after its use.
    • Yet too often, the equipment is neglected in traditional processing centres.
  • Daily maintenance for the FTT-Thiaroye (kiln, cover, rack, furnace) entails cleaning inside and around the kilns and removing the ashes and the waste stuck on the lids and on the mesh of the removable racks.
  • Remove the smoke generator, clean it with soapy water and then let it dry.
  • Remove the collector containing the mixture of water and exudate located below the metal housing, empty it and put it back into place.
  • Remove the housing and the filter loaded with tar from the smoke and clean it thoroughly.
  • Change the sponge of plant origin (loofah) / filter before each new session, while the used one is washed and left to dry.
  • Remove the fat-collecting tray, and clean the dried exudate and the grease ducts of the tray, and drain the pipe.
  • For regular care and maintenance of the equipment and accessories, a cleaning and disinfection programme should be established and carried out after using the kiln.
    • After cleaning, the material should only be stored once it is completely dry in order to prevent rust forming on the galvanized steel.
  • During the low-production or seasonal rest period, metal accessories need to be protected against rust by keeping them away from adverse weather, such as rain and sun.
    • The mesh and the fins need to be coated regularly with vegetable oil.
    • If rust appears on the metal parts, they will have to be cleaned and repainted with two layers of rustproofing liquid and one layer of food-grade paint at least once a year. Damaged equipment must be repaired.

3.1 Videos

  • The FAO-Thiaroye processing technique (FTT-Thiaroye). Part 1 (English)
  • The FAO-Thiaroye processing technique (FTT-Thiaroye). Part 2 (English)
  • The FAO-Thiaroye processing technique (FTT-Thiaroye). Part 3 (English)

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • How to construct the FTT-Thiaroye and assemble its components: ID 8304.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Women-friendly

The technology alleviates drudgery, is time-saving and therefore allows women to engage in other activities.

6.2 Resource use efficiency

With improved drying and smoking techniques, this technology increases the efficiency and the better use of resources.

6.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology allows for fish to be preserved in different ways thereby providing additional sources of income and food.

FAO-Thiaroye Processing Technique (FTT-Thiaroye)
An innovative fish smoking and drying technology developed collaboratively by FAO and CNFTPA Senegal. It's an innovation because it modifies traditional fish processing to improve food safety, reduce health risks for women processors, decrease environmental impact, and enable value-addition through by-product utilization, meeting criteria for modified processes that solve multiple problems.
_annotations.field_shorter_description: The FTT-Thiaroye is a technique drawn from the collaborative efforts between the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the National Training Center for Fisheries and Aquaculture Technicians (CNFTPA) training institute in Senegal. Its development addresses the need to improve small-scale fish drying and smoking operations. The key to its adoption rests upon its benefits. Globally, the main condition required for the FAO-Thiaroye to be successfully applied is the know-how of its construction, use and maintenance. This technology describes how to use and operate the FTT-Thiaroye.

records.title: Risk reduction while manipulating pesticides
records.description:
Description

Pesticides, when entering in contact with you and/or the environment, are harmful and can lead to negative effects on human and environmental health and development.

In a short time, contact with pesticides can cause: 

  • poisoning; 
  • skin or eyes irritation/burns; 
  • allergic reactions; and 
  • difficulties to breath, etc.

In the case of long-term exposure, continuous contact with a pesticide can lead to the development of: 

  • cancers; 
  • nervous or neurological disorders (e.g. paralysis, tremors, brain damages, etc.); 
  • diseases of blood, liver, kidneys or lungs (difficulties to breath, asthma, etc.); and
  • infertility, reproductive disorders, fetal malformation, etc.

That is why pesticides always should be used with care!

1. Ways pesticides enter your body

  • Through your skin, this is common and can happen through clothes.
  • By eating, smoking or drinking in contaminated areas.
Figure 1. A man pouring pesticides in a plastic container while the pesticide hits his arm

©FAO/TECA

  • You can be exposed to pesticides by eating food that has not yet passed the recommended amount of days between the application of pesticides on it and its consumption.
Figure 2: Two men smoking and eating in an area contaminated by pesticide

©FAO/TECA

  • Breathing while you are using pesticides, or if you pass near contaminated areas
Figure 3. A woman applying pesticides without facial protection

©FAO/TECA

2. Exposure to pesticides

  • Exposure through spilling, mixing or applying pesticides.
Figure 4. A man pouring pesticides in a plastic container using proper safety clothing and protection and another man after spilling pesticides on the floor in a storage room

©FAO/TECA

  • If you are exposed to pesticides and feel unwell, see a doctor and tell him or her you work with pesticides.
    • Show the doctor the pesticide label.
Figure 5. A woman seeing a doctor after contact with pesticides

©FAO/TECA

3. Precautions to take when buying pesticides

  • Always follow label instructions on use, safety, dose and first aid.
  • Do not buy pesticides without labels or with labels in a language you do not understand.
Figure 6. A man carefully reading the safety instruction of a pesticide

©FAO/TECA

  • Only buy pesticides in the original undamaged packaging.
Figure 7. A man pouring pesticides in a smaller container to sell it

©FAO/TECA

4. Protecting your health when using pesticides

  • Use proper protective equipment that is in good condition and mix pesticides in a well-ventilated area while wearing protective equipment.
Figure 8. A man wearing adequate security clothing to handle pesticides and a woman pouring pesticides correctly using safety clothing and a funnel

©FAO/TECA

  • Do not spray in windy or foggy conditions or against the wind.
Figure 9. A man incorrectly applying pesticides in volatile weather conditions including wind and rain

©FAO/TECA

  • Do not blow into blocked spray nozzles.
Figure 10. A man incorrectly blowing into a blocked spray nozzle

©FAO/TECA

  • After use, thoroughly wash (at least) your face and hands with soap before eating, smoking or going to the toilet.
Figure 11. A woman properly washing and cleaning all body parts that may have been in contact with the pesticide

©FAO/TECA

  • Do not use leaking or defective equipment.
Figure 12. A man applying pesticides using dysfunctional tools

©FAO/TECA

  • Wash contaminated skin and clothing with plenty of water and soap.
Figure 13. A man intensively washing and cleaning body parts and clothing that has been in contact with pesticides

©FAO/TECA

  • Take care to avoid spills or accidents, especially during the transport of pesticides.
Figure 14. Carelessly stored pesticides before transport

©FAO/TECA

  • Never leave pesticides and spray equipment unattended.
Figure 15. Pesticides left unattended and without supervision

©FAO/TECA

  • Contaminated clothing should be washed and stored separately from ordinary clothes.
Figure 16. A woman carelessly storing safety clothing in her wardrobe

©FAO/TECA

  • Place warning signs to alert people to stay out of recently treated crops.
Figure 17. A woman explaining the meaning of a safety instructions sign to a young boy

©FAO/TECA

  • Keep children and expectant or nursing mothers away from pesticides.
    • They are more easily affected by pesticides than men.
Figure 18. A woman staying away from a pesticide-infected field

©FAO/TECA

  • Store pesticides securely well away from foodstuffs and out of the reach of children and animals.
Figure 19. Safely stored pesticides

©FAO/TECA

  • Empty pesticide containers are not safe, even after washing.
  • Never use for foodstuffs or leave within reach of children.
  • Always triple rinse and puncture before disposal so that they cannot be re-used.
Figure 20. A woman falsely using a pesticide container for fruit juice

©FAO/TECA

5. Protection of consumers is key

  • Never use products on food crops that are not registered for that purpose.
Figure 21. A man falsely applying pesticides to a not registered food crop

©FAO/TECA

  • Always observe the correct harvest interval.
  • Respect the recommended amount of time between the date of treatment and the date of harvest/commercialization.
Figure 22. A woman calculating the correct application intervals for pesticides

©FAO/TECA

  • Pesticides should always be used with precaution, and with respect to recommendations mentioned above and specific recommendations mentioned by the manufacturer in the pesticides’ package.
  • Before purchasing and applying pesticides, please make inquiries from an agricultural adviser about alternative solutions, which are less harmful to you, your family, the consumers and the environment.
  • Give priority to eco-friendly and sustainable practices such as crop rotation, biological control of pests, early detection of diseases, etc.
    • It is important to only use pesticides when necessary, but also as prevention!
  • The European Union (EU) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations have invested EUR 7 million to assist countries in Central Asia and Eastern Europe to foster an environment of cooperation and capacity development to:
    • eliminate the risks from obsolete and Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) pesticides; and
    • develop more sustainable agriculture in the future.
  • The project aims at strengthening the capacity of the civil society to contribute to reducing the risks and impacts from pesticide use onto public health and onto the environment.
    • One of the main focuses is the improvement in awareness of the risks of pesticide exposure amongst vulnerable groups, including women, children and seasonal workers in agriculture.
    • Supported by the Secretariat of the Rotterdam Convention and the Pesticide Action Network (PAN) the UK, this project delivers training and technical support to identify particularly hazardous practices and to promote higher safety standards and so reduce risk.
  • This leaflet has been produced with the assistance of the European Union in the framework of the project “Improving capacities to eliminate and prevent recurrence of obsolete pesticides as a model for tackling unused hazardous chemicals in the former Soviet Union”.
    • The contents of this leaflet are the sole responsibility of Pesticide Action Network (PAN) the UK and can in no way be taken to reflect the views neither of the European Union or the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Bonnes pratiques d’utilisation des pesticides: ID 8016.

This technology is also available in French: ID 8353 and Spanish: ID 8354.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

7.1 Women-friendly

The technology is easy to use and accessible to all.

7.2 Resource use efficiency

Avoids contamination of crops and crops, reduces the negative impact on the environment.

7.3 Pro-poor technology

Better quality products, healthier food.

records.title: Mulching in organic agriculture
records.description:
Description

1. Why use mulch?

  • Protects the soil from wind and water erosion: soil particles cannot be washed or blown away.
  • Improves the infiltration of rain and irrigation water by maintaining a good soil structure: no crust is formed, the pores are kept open.
  • Keeps the soil moist by reducing evaporation: plants need less irrigation or can use the available rain more efficiently in dry areas or seasons.
  • Feeds and protects soil organisms: organic mulch material is an excellent food for soil organisms and provides suitable conditions for their growth.
  • Suppresses weed growth: with a sufficient mulch layer, weeds will find it difficult to grow through it.
  • Prevents the soil from heating up too much: mulch provides shade to the soil and the retained moisture keeps it cool.
  • Provides nutrients to the crops: while decomposing, organic mulch material continuously releases its nutrients, thus fertilizing the soil.
Figure 1. Sketch on the effects of mulching

©FAO/TECA

2. Selection of mulch materials

  • The kind of material used for mulching will greatly influence its effect.
  • Material which easily decomposes will protect the soil only for a rather short time but will provide nutrients to the crops while decomposing.
  • Hardy materials will decompose more slowly and therefore cover the soil for a longer time.
  • If the decomposition of the mulch material should be accelerated, organic manures such as animal dung may be spread on top of the mulch, thus increasing the nitrogen content.
  • Where soil erosion is a problem, slowly decomposing mulch material (low nitrogen content, high C/N) will provide long-term protection compared to quickly decomposing material.

2.1 Sources of mulching material

  • weeds or cover crops
  • crop residues
  • grass
  • pruning material from trees
  • cuttings from hedges
  • waste from agricultural processing or from forestry.

2.2 Recommendation while using mulches

  • Mulching has a lot of advantages, but it can also cause problems in specific situations.
    • Some organisms can proliferate too much in the moist and protected conditions of the mulch layer.
    • Slugs and snails can multiply very quickly under a mulch layer.
    • Ants or termites which may cause damage to the crops also may find ideal conditions for living.
  • When crop residues are used for mulching, in some cases there is an increased risk of sustaining pests and diseases.
    • Damaging organisms such as stem borers may survive in the stalks of crops like cotton, corn or sugar cane.
    • Plant material infected with viral or fungal diseases should not be used if there is a risk that the disease might spread to the next crop.
    • Crop rotation is very important to overcome these risks.
  • When carbon-rich materials such as straw or stalks are used for mulching, nitrogen from the soil may be used by microorganisms for decomposing the material.
    • Nitrogen may be temporarily not available for plant growth.
  • The major constraint for mulching usually is the availability of organic material.
    • Its production or collection usually involves labour and may compete with the production of crops.
Figure 2. Potential problems related to mulching (photo of a mulch layer)

©FAO/TECA

3. Application of mulch

  • If possible, the mulch should be applied before or at the onset of the rainy season, as then the soil is most vulnerable.
  • If the layer of mulch is not too thick, seeds or seedlings can be directly sown or planted in between the mulching material.
  • On vegetable plots, it is best to apply mulch only after the young plants have become somewhat hardier, as they may be harmed by the products of decomposition from fresh mulch material.
  • If mulch is applied prior to sowing or planting, the mulch layer should not be too thick in order to allow seedlings to penetrate it.
  • Mulch can also be applied in established crops, best directly after digging the soil.
  • It can be applied between the rows, directly around single plants (especially for tree crops) or evenly spread on the field.
Figure 3. Mulch applied in vegetable fields in the Philippines, with recommendations for the application of mulch in keywords

©FAO/TECA

3.1 A practical example: the Fukuoka system of mulching rice fields

The Japanese organic pioneer Fukuoka developed a system of growing rice which is based on mulching. White clover is sown among the rice one month before harvesting. Shortly thereafter, a winter crop of rye is sown. After threshing the harvested rice, the rice straw is brought back to the field where it is used as a loose mulch layer. Both the rye and the white clover spring up through the mulch which remains until the rye is harvested. If the straw decomposes too slowly, chicken manure is sprinkled over the mulch. This cropping system does not require any tillage of the soil but achieves satisfying yields.

For detailed and compiled information on organic agriculture and farming, please refer to the Training Manual for Organic Agriculture.

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Step by step conversion to organic agriculture: ID 8364.
  • Introduction to organic agriculture: ID 8359.
  • Considerations for conversion to organic agriculture: ID 8363.
  • Water management in organic agriculture: ID 8366.
  • Crop planning and management in organic agriculture: ID 8367.
  • Pest and disease management in organic agriculture: ID 8372.
  • Weed management in organic agriculture: ID 8375.
  • Animal husbandry in organic agriculture: ID 8378.
  • Plant propagation in organic agriculture: ID 8377.
  • Nutrient management in organic agriculture: ID 8368.
  • Soil cultivation and tillage in organic agriculture: ID 8376.
  • Mulching to control soil erosion: ID 8207.

This technology is available in French: ID 8559.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project

5.1 Women-friendly

The technology is easy to use and accessible to all. 

5.2 Resource use efficiency

Improves soil quality leading to improved crop yields.

5.3 Pro-poor technology

_annotations.body:
Mulching in organic agriculture

Mulching is the process of covering the topsoil with plant material such as leaves, grass, twigs, crop residues, straw etc. A mulch cover enhances the activity of soil organisms such as earthworms. They help to create a soil structure with plenty of smaller and larger pores through which rainwater can easily infiltrate into the soil, thus reducing surface runoff. As the mulch material decomposes, it increases the content of organic matter in the soil. Soil organic matter helps create good soil with stable crumb structure. Thus, the soil particles will not be easily carried away by water. Therefore, mulching plays a crucial role in preventing soil erosion. The following describes the technique of mulching in organic agriculture. Details on the benefits and why use mulch are given. The selection and source of mulching materials are also provided as well as recommendations while using mulch and its application. A case study of the Fukuoka system of mulching rice fields highlights the benefits of this technology.

Description

1. Why use mulch?

  • Protects the soil from wind and water erosion: soil particles cannot be washed or blown away.
  • Improves the infiltration of rain and irrigation water by maintaining a good soil structure: no crust is formed, the pores are kept open.
  • Keeps the soil moist by reducing evaporation: plants need less irrigation or can use the available rain more efficiently in dry areas or seasons.
  • Feeds and protects soil organisms: organic mulch material is an excellent food for soil organisms and provides suitable conditions for their growth.
  • Suppresses weed growth: with a sufficient mulch layer, weeds will find it difficult to grow through it.
  • Prevents the soil from heating up too much: mulch provides shade to the soil and the retained moisture keeps it cool.
  • Provides nutrients to the crops: while decomposing, organic mulch material continuously releases its nutrients, thus fertilizing the soil.
Figure 1. Sketch on the effects of mulching

©FAO/TECA

2. Selection of mulch materials

  • The kind of material used for mulching will greatly influence its effect.
  • Material which easily decomposes will protect the soil only for a rather short time but will provide nutrients to the crops while decomposing.
  • Hardy materials will decompose more slowly and therefore cover the soil for a longer time.
  • If the decomposition of the mulch material should be accelerated, organic manures such as animal dung may be spread on top of the mulch, thus increasing the nitrogen content.
  • Where soil erosion is a problem, slowly decomposing mulch material (low nitrogen content, high C/N) will provide long-term protection compared to quickly decomposing material.

2.1 Sources of mulching material

  • weeds or cover crops
  • crop residues
  • grass
  • pruning material from trees
  • cuttings from hedges
  • waste from agricultural processing or from forestry.

2.2 Recommendation while using mulches

  • Mulching has a lot of advantages, but it can also cause problems in specific situations.
    • Some organisms can proliferate too much in the moist and protected conditions of the mulch layer.
    • Slugs and snails can multiply very quickly under a mulch layer.
    • Ants or termites which may cause damage to the crops also may find ideal conditions for living.
  • When crop residues are used for mulching, in some cases there is an increased risk of sustaining pests and diseases.
    • Damaging organisms such as stem borers may survive in the stalks of crops like cotton, corn or sugar cane.
    • Plant material infected with viral or fungal diseases should not be used if there is a risk that the disease might spread to the next crop.
    • Crop rotation is very important to overcome these risks.
  • When carbon-rich materials such as straw or stalks are used for mulching, nitrogen from the soil may be used by microorganisms for decomposing the material.
    • Nitrogen may be temporarily not available for plant growth.
  • The major constraint for mulching usually is the availability of organic material.
    • Its production or collection usually involves labour and may compete with the production of crops.
Figure 2. Potential problems related to mulching (photo of a mulch layer)

©FAO/TECA

3. Application of mulch

  • If possible, the mulch should be applied before or at the onset of the rainy season, as then the soil is most vulnerable.
  • If the layer of mulch is not too thick, seeds or seedlings can be directly sown or planted in between the mulching material.
  • On vegetable plots, it is best to apply mulch only after the young plants have become somewhat hardier, as they may be harmed by the products of decomposition from fresh mulch material.
  • If mulch is applied prior to sowing or planting, the mulch layer should not be too thick in order to allow seedlings to penetrate it.
  • Mulch can also be applied in established crops, best directly after digging the soil.
  • It can be applied between the rows, directly around single plants (especially for tree crops) or evenly spread on the field.
Figure 3. Mulch applied in vegetable fields in the Philippines, with recommendations for the application of mulch in keywords

©FAO/TECA

3.1 A practical example: the Fukuoka system of mulching rice fields

The Japanese organic pioneer Fukuoka developed a system of growing rice which is based on mulching. White clover is sown among the rice one month before harvesting. Shortly thereafter, a winter crop of rye is sown. After threshing the harvested rice, the rice straw is brought back to the field where it is used as a loose mulch layer. Both the rye and the white clover spring up through the mulch which remains until the rye is harvested. If the straw decomposes too slowly, chicken manure is sprinkled over the mulch. This cropping system does not require any tillage of the soil but achieves satisfying yields.

For detailed and compiled information on organic agriculture and farming, please refer to the Training Manual for Organic Agriculture.

  • Nutrient management in organic agriculture: ID 8368.
  • Soil cultivation and tillage in organic agriculture: ID 8376.
  • Mulching to control soil erosion: ID 8207.

This technology is available in French: ID 8559.

5.1 Women-friendly

The technology is easy to use and accessible to all. 

5.2 Resource use efficiency

Improves soil quality leading to improved crop yields.

5.3 Pro-poor technology

Improved crop yields thanks to the mulching technology provide for an additional source of income and food source. In addition, mulching ensures resilience in adverse weather conditions and enhances the overall quality of soil and food products.

records.title: Elaboración de pesticidas eco-amigables para el control de plagas y enfermedades
records.description:
Descripción

  • A continuación, algunas mezclas biopesticidas comúnmente preparadas por agricultores para el control de plagas:
    • Extracto/suspensión del núcleo de semillas de nim (5 por ciento).
    • Extracto de hojas de Tephrosia.
    • Estiércol y orina fermentado de ganado.
    • Extracto acuoso de hojas de tabaco, chile, ajo, etc. en diversas combinaciones.
    • Virus de la poliedrosis nuclear.
  • Todos estos preparados fueron elaborados y aplicados en campos de frijol en Uganda.
  • Biopesticidas disponibles comercialmente:
    • Extracto de nim (polvos y aceites).
    • Bacillus thuringiensis (BT).

1. Preparación de extracto/suspensión del núcleo de semillas de nim

  • El nim, Azadirachta indica, es un árbol perteneciente a la familia Meliaceae, originario de India y Birmania que se le ha atribuido propiedades insecticidas para su uso en la agricultura orgánica.
    • Remojar los núcleos de las semillas de nim maduras (5 kg) en una cantidad mínima de agua por toda la noche.
    • Moler los núcleos de las semillas de nim en un mortero y mantener la pasta obtenida en una bolsa de tela fina por 2 horas.
      • Colocar la bolsa de extracto de semillas de nim en un contenedor lleno de 10 litros de agua, y agitar periódicamente por 30 minutos para extraer la mayor cantidad de ingrediente activo posible.
    • Exprimir la bolsa a fondo o hasta que quede lo más seca posible, remover y filtrar el resultado de la suspensión blanca y añadir pedazos de jabón (100 g) a la suspensión.
    • Diluir la suspensión con agua por 10 minutos (por ejemplo 500 ml len 5 litros) y rociarlo hasta cubrir el cultivo.
  • Usar sólo frutas de nim maduras y separar la semilla de la pulpa, secarla bajo la sombra antes de guardarlas en bolsitas de yute.
    • El secado al sol puede disminuir la calidad de los ingredientes activos.
    • Se deben almacenar en un ambiente bien aireado.
    • El almacenar en áreas confinadas o en bolsas plásticas bien apretadas puede inducir el crecimiento de hongos que pueden degradar el ingrediente activo y la efectividad del producto.
    • Grandes cantidades de núcleos de nim deben ser tratados con polvo de arcilla (en una proporción de 1:10).
  • Los extractos de nim pueden prevenir la puesta de huevos e interrumpir la alimentación y desarrollo de muchas plagas.

2. Preparación de extracto de chile-ajo

  • Moler chiles verdes (3 kg) después de remover el tallo y luego remojar en agua (10 litros) la pasta resultante por la noche.
  • Moler el ajo (0,5 kg) y remojarlo por la noche en 250 ml de kerosene.
  • Disolver jabón (75 g) en un litro de agua.
  • Mezclar las tres soluciones y dejar reposar por 4 horas, luego filtrar a través de una muselina u otra prenda porosa y diluir con agua hasta lograr 80 litros.

Esta preparación sería suficiente para rociar un acre de frijoles.

3. Preparación de extracto de excremento y orina de ganado

  • Diluir el excremento (5 kg) en agua (5 litros) y añadir orina de ganado (5 litros).
  • Fermentar la solución resultante por cuatro días en un contenedor cerrado en un área bajo sombra y luego añadir algún cítrico, como lima (100 g), para neutralizar los fenoles tóxicos y ácidos liberados.
  • Diluir la solución resultante en 80 litros de agua.

Esta preparación es suficiente para rociar un acre de frijoles. Esta solución disuade las polillas hembras de la puesta de huevos de larvas comedoras de hojas (H. armígera y S. litura) y protege de algunas enfermedades.

4. Preparación de virus de la poliedrosis nuclear

  • El virus de la poliedrosis nuclear, pertenece a la familia Baculoviridae.
  • Se trata de un virus entomopatógeno que produce enfermedades infecciosas que se multiplican en los tejidos de los insectos, hasta ocasionar su muerte.
  • La contaminación por el virus se da por vía oral, cuando los alimentos son ingeridos por los insectos.
  • Para producir éste virus, se precisa recolectar o criar las especies hospedantes ya que son muy específicos o especies que hayan muerto por el virus.
    • Recolectar larvas del campo que hayan muerto por el virus (400 de H. armigera ó 200 de S. litura). Puede buscar o pedir información a un experto u organización entrenada para asegurarse de cómo hacer esto.
    • Moler las larvas para una suspensión y filtrado a través de una prenda de poros finos.
    • Diluir en 100 l de agua y luego añadir tinte “Robin Blue” (100 g) para proteger de los rayos UV en el campo.
    • Rociar el cultivo con la solución del virus de la poliedrosis nuclear durante las primeras horas de la noche.
  • El virus de una especie de plaga no afecta a otras especies.
  • Puede tomar algunos días (2 a 5) antes de que las larvas en el campo sean eliminadas por la aplicación de la solución del virus.
  • Sin embargo, dentro de 10 días todas las larvas van a estar afectadas.

5. Bio-pesticidas para el manejo de enfermedades

  • El mejor tratamiento recomendado para la protección de las semillas es cubrirlas con pesticidas, sin embargo, lo mejor es asegurar una producción de semillas limpias y sanas a través de un cultivo sano y el manejo apropiado de enfermedades del frijol así como también la práctica de estrategias de manejo poscosecha adecuadas.
  • Formulaciones de Trichoderma viride y Pseudomonas fluorescens son efectivas para el ataque de un amplio rango de pudriciones de raíces y tallos causados por Rhizoctonia, Sclerotium y Pythium. Estos bio-pesticidas deben ser mezclados en una proporción de 4 g por kilogramo de masa de semilla.
  • Monitorear el cultivo para identificar síntomas iniciales de plagas y enfermedades es una buena estrategia de manejo para evitar problemas y asegurar una mejor producción de semillas en términos de calidad y cantidad.
  • Neemark (Azadirachta indica) 0,5 por ciento es efectiva para la pudrición de la raíz por Sclerotium.

6. Validación de la práctica

  • Todos estos preparados fueron elaborados y aplicados en campos de frijol en Uganda.

7. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

8. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Manejo e identificación de plagas alimentadoras de vainas y semillas en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8385.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas en plántulas en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8382.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas en flores en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8383.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas de almacenamiento en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8384.
  • Manejo e identificación de enfermedades que causan malformaciones y distorsiones de hojas y vainas en el frijol: ID 8387.
  • Manejo e identificación de enfermedades que afectan las raíces en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8389.
  • Manejo e identificación de enfermedades que afectan hojas y vainas en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8392.

9. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

9.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología muestra al productor diversas medidas para reducir eficientemente enfermedades y plagas.

9.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

La elaboración de pesticidas eco-amigables para el control de plagas y enfermedades ayuda a reducir las pérdidas de frijol y así estabilizar la fuente de ingresos.

records.title: Weed management in organic agriculture
records.description:
Description

Weeds have a role to play on the farm. For example, weeds provide cover that reduces soil erosion. In addition, most of the biological diversity in our crop fields comes from the presence of weeds. They provide habitat for both beneficial biocontrol insects and mycorrhiza fungi. Because weeds offer pollen and nectar, they allow biocontrol insects to maintain their populations and, therefore, serve as a valuable instrument in controlling pests.

However, weeds may also alter the environment of the crop in a negative way. Light and air circulation, for example, are reduced between the crop plants. In this darker and more humid environment, diseases find ideal conditions in which to spread and infect plants.

A basic working principle in organic farming is to prevent problems, rather than to cure them. This applies equally to weed management. Good weed management in organic farming includes creating conditions which hinder weeds from growing at the wrong time and in the wrong place, preventing them from becoming a serious problem for crop cultivation. Competition by weeds doesn’t harm the crop throughout the whole cultivation period in the same way. The most sensitive phase of a crop to weed competition is in its early growth stage. A young plant is vulnerable and depends highly on an ideal nutrient, light, and water supply for a good development. If it has to compete with weeds at this stage, the crop may grow weak, which also makes it more vulnerable to pest and disease infections.

Weed competition later in the cultivation period is less harmful. However, some weeds may cause harvesting problems and reduce the crop yield in that way. Therefore, weeds should not be completely ignored after the most critical growth period of the crop, but in general, they become less important.

These considerations should influence the selection and timing of weed management measures. In general, such measures aim at keeping the weed population at a level which doesn’t result in economic loss of the crop cultivation or harm its quality.

1. Preventive practices

  • Several preventive measures may be applied at the same time.
  • The importance and effectiveness of the different methods depend to a large extent on the weed species and the environmental conditions.
  • However, some methods are very effective for a wide range of weeds and are therefore regularly used.

1.1 Choice of crops and varieties

  • Tall crops and varieties with broader leaves will compete better with late occurring weeds than small varieties with narrow leaves.
  • Some varieties will inhibit and suppress weeds while others will tolerate them.
  • For example, there are witchweed (Striga) resistant maize and cowpea cultivars in many countries of Africa, which give better performance at the same level of weeds where other varieties are more affected.

1.2 Mulching

  • The weeds find it difficult to receive enough light to grow and may not be able to pass through the mulch layer.
  • Dry, hardy material, that decomposes slowly, keeps its effect longer than fresh mulch material.

1.3 Living green cover

  • The cover competes successfully against the weeds for light, nutrients, and water and therefore helps to prevent weed growth by winning the competition for resources.
  • The cover crops usually used are legumes, which improves soil fertility on top of suppressing weeds.
  • For example, a ground cover of desmodium (Desmodium uncinatum) or silver leaf, interplanted among maize, reduces striga weed and fixes nitrogen at the same time.
  • Further information on TECA, "How to control Striga and stemborer in maize".

1.4 Crop rotation

  • Rotation of crops is the most efficient measure to regulate seed and root weeds.
  • Changing the conditions of the crop interrupts the living conditions of the weeds, thus inhibiting their growth and spread.

1.5 Intercropping (mixed cropping and under-sowing)

  • Intercropping with fast growing weed-suppressive species (‘smoother crop’ or ‘living mulch’) between rows of main crop species is effective in weed control.
  • There are different examples known to work in Africa.
    • For example, sowing cowpeas and egusi melons or pumpkins as intercrops in cassava to reduce weed occurrence.

1.6 Sowing time and density

  • Optimum growing conditions enhance the optimum crop plant development and their ability to compete against weeds.
  • Proper crop spacing will ensure that minimum space is available for the growth of weeds and will minimize competition with weeds.
  • This will effectively restrict weed development.
  • In order to apply this approach, the limiting weeds must be known and the seasons in which they occur.
  • A weed calendar of the area or region, if available, might be of help.
  • It will be used to manage weeds in a targeted fashion with proper timing and effect.

1.7 Balanced fertilization

  • It can support an ideal growth of the crop, which promotes the growth of the crop over the weeds.

1.8 Soil cultivation methods

  • Soil cultivation methods can influence the total weed pressure as well as the composition of weeds.
  • For example, minimum-tillage systems can increase the weed pressure.
  • Because weed seeds can germinate between soil cultivation and sowing of the crop, weed cures before sowing can be effective at reducing weed pressure.
  • Use of superficial stubble treatment works against persisting weeds.
  • It should be done under dry weather conditions to allow the weed roots, which have been brought to the surface, to dry out.

1.9 Pasturing

  • In perennial crops like coffee, mangoes, avocadoes or cocoa, the use of sheep and goats to reduce rampant weed growth is becoming common.
  • In the case of cattle, broadleaf weeds tend to predominate due to the cattle preference for grasses.
  • Therefore, it is necessary to rotate with sheep and goats which prefer broadleaves to overcome this selective grazing.

1.10 Dissemination of weeds

  • Prevent dissemination of weeds by eliminating them before seed dispersal.

1.11 Seed origin

  • Prevent insemination of crops by weeds by avoiding the introduction of weed seeds into the fields through tools or animals.
  • Another method is also by using only weed free seed material.
Figure 1. Striga on a host plant which shows significant damages

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Cultural practices of managing weeds

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Pasturing for weed control

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. How to prevent weeds

©FAO/TECA

2. Biological control of weeds

  • The soil-borne fungus Fusarium oxysporum (different isolates from Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger) is very effective in reducing the witch weed (Striga hermonthica and S. asiatica) in different cereal crops, leading to yield increases in scientific trials.
  • Other Fusarium species found in Sudan and Ghana are very effective, too (Fusarium nygamai, F. oxysporum and F. solani).
  • This mycoherbicide is on the way to being formulated and registered in different countries in Africa.
  • Rhizobacteria are capable of suppressing germination of witch weed (Striga spp.) seeds or actually destroying the seeds.
    • They are particularly promising biological control agents since they can be easily and cheaply formulated into seed inoculants.
  • Pseudomonas fluorescens putida isolates significantly inhibited germination of Striga hermonthica seeds.
    • However, currently no biocontrol product is available.

3. Mechanical control

  • With the necessary preventive measures, weed density can be reduced, but it will hardly be enough during the critical periods of the crop at the beginning of cultivation.
  • Therefore, mechanical methods remain an important part of weed management.

3.1 Manual weeding

  • This is probably the most important method.
  • As it’s very labour intensive, reducing weed density as much as possible in the field will bring less work later on and should therefore be aimed at.
  • There are different tools to dig, cut and uprooting the weeds; hand, ox-drawn and tractor-drawn tools.
  • Using the right tool can increase work efficiency significantly.
  • Weeding should be done before the weeds flower and produce seeds.

3.2 Flame weeding

  • It is another option: plants are heated briefly to 100°C and higher.
  • This provokes coagulation of the proteins in the leaves and a bursting of their cell walls.
  • Consequently, the weed dries out and dies.
  • Although it is an effective method, it is quite expensive as it consumes a large amount of fuel gas and needs machinery.
  • It is not effective against root weeds.

©FAO/TECA

  • Mulching in organic agriculture: ID 8365.

  • Crop planning and management in organic agriculture: ID 8367.
  • Pest and disease management in organic agriculture: ID 8372.
  • Animal husbandry in organic agriculture: ID 8378.
  • Plant propagation in organic agriculture: ID 8377.
  • Nutrient management in organic agriculture: ID 8368.
  • Soil cultivation and tillage in organic agriculture: ID 8376.
  • Rice seed drying (Africa rice center video on rice advice): ID 7211.
  • Seed propagation of Allanblackia spp.: ID 7793​.
  • How to control Striga and stemborer in maize: ID 7356.
  • Weed management in conservation agriculture: ID 7418. 
  • Rice weed management (Africa rice center video on rice advice): ID ​​7215.

This technology is also available in French: ID 8576.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Women-friendly

The technology is easy to use and is can be undertaken by any kind of hand labour.

5.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for the efficient management of weed growth, thereby balancing removal for good crop cultivation but also maintaing some weed growth for biological diversity and soil erosion prevention.

5.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology prevents crop cultivation economic losses, thereby providing additional sources of food and income.

records.title: Strategy for integrated varroa management: healthier colonies through brood removal
records.description:
Description

The studies in Germany have shown that brood removal at the beginning of the swarming season (20 May) results in a significantly lower yield (average of 7.1 kg compared to 21.5 kg of the control colonies). With a three weeks later brood removal (11 June), an average yield of 16.4 kg was achieved (control group 21.5 Kg) while the highest yield with an average of 27.3 kg was obtained (control group 21.5 kg) with brood removal in early July, exactly 14 days before the final honey harvest. This is explained by the fact that due to the complete removal of brood, the honey consumption of the bees is drastically reduced while the harvesting power remains. The lack of young bees is only noticed after the harvest. There is no danger of robbing and the colony has enough time to repopulate and build up reserves for the winter. This method, however, is less suitable for areas with late harvests (August or later).

This technology is an efficient way to keep varroa infestation under control. The beekeeper should however always check the varroa infestation level in the hive and treat when the infestation is above the threshold (more than five varroa mites per 100 g of bees). See Dietemann et al, (2013) for techniques to control varroa infestation levels.

Figure 1. Hive structure

©FAO/TECA

1. Complete brood removal – process, step-by-step

  1. Remove the honey super and the upper brood box. Assess the honeycombs in the brood nest area of the bottom box (Box A). Move two to four light coloured honey and pollen combs to both sides of the brood box (Box A) (Figure 2).

Figure 2. Beekeepers looking for brood combs

©FAO/TECA

  1. Place one brood comb with eggs and larvae, but without capped cells which will emerge within the next 10 days, in the centre of the brood box.

    • This will be the “catch comb” for the varroa.
    • If available, use a frame with plenty of male bee brood (Figures 3 and 4).
Figure 3. Brood comb without capped cells

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. The "catch comb" for the varroa

©FAO/TECA

  1. Shake or brush the bees of the remaining brood combs back into the brood box.

    • Make sure the queen is in the (bottom) brood box (Box A) (Figure 5).

Figure 5. Beekeeper shaking the bees into the brood box

©FAO/TECA

  1. Fill up the gaps with empty combs or frames with foundation sheets.

    • If there is honey flow, the empty combs will be quickly built up.
    • If there is no strong honey flow, feed the bees if possible with their own honey (Figure 6).
Figure 6. Beekeeper inserting foundation sheets

©FAO/TECA

  1. Place the queen excluder on top of the brood box (Box A) containing the queen (Figure 7).

Figure 7. The queen excluder avoid the queen to go up to the upper part

©FAO/TECA

  1. Replace the honey super on the brood box.

    • Make sure the honey super is replaced in the same position as it was before.
    • After the harvest of the last honey super, a second brood box can be added depending on the strength of the hive.

  1. Collect the removed brood combs with some adhering bees in a separate hive (brood collector hive – Box B).

    • Combs with bees from different colonies can be combined without problems (because there is no queen).
    • At least one comb with honey and pollen on each side of the combs should be provided for the young bees to feed on.
    • Approximately 300 bees on each side of the combs should be enough to care for the further development of the brood.
    • If the bees were completely shaken off the brood combs (to be sure that the queen was included), a suitable number of bees from the honey supers can be added.
Figure 8. Brood collector hive

©FAO/TECA

  1. After seven to ten days, check the colony from which the brood was removed (Box A). The central combs should be rebuilt and the queen should have started laying eggs in the new brood nest (Figure 9).

Figure 9. Brood in the new brood nest

©FAO/TECA

  1. The catch comb in the brood box (Box A), which in the meantime should be mostly sealed, needs to be removed and melted down, including the brood and caught mites.

    • Replace the comb with an empty comb or comb with the foundation sheet.
    • A varroa treatment is not required here (Figure 10).
Figure 10. The catch comb full of varroa must be removed

©FAO/TECA

   10. The brood collector hive (Box B) should be transferred immediately on the day of the brood removal to a separate apiary to prevent the return of bees to the mother colony and the risk of robbery and mite transfer).

    • They only need to be checked after 21 to 24 days.
    • By then the whole brood has emerged and old combs can be replaced with empty combs or combs with foundation sheets.
  • Note: Three weeks after the removal all brood is emerged and the combs are empty.
    • This offers a good opportunity to replace dark or badly constructed combs by freshly build combs or frames with wax foundation.
  • Depending on the size of the colony, the colony will remain on one or two boxes.
    • If unsure whether a new queen has been born, a single comb with an open brood can be added from another hive to allow the bees to build emergency queen cells.
    • If on the other hand, the new queen is not productive enough, she can be replaced as soon as the new brood is available (i.e. new unproductive queen has started laying eggs) (Figure 11).
Figure 11. Beekeeper checking varroa infestation 

©FAO/TECA

11. Thanks to the temporary absence of brood in the collector box (Box B), an effective and simple varroa treatment can now be applied.

  • Suitable treatments include the dripping of oxalic acid, spraying of lactic acid or the use of catch combs (Figure 12).
Figure 12. Varroa treatment in absence of brood 

©FAO/TECA

2. Validation of the practice

  • This technique has been developed with the objective of maintaining productivity while optimizing colony health with minimum treatment.
    • The Bieneninstitut Kirchhain, Germany, has been testing this technique since 2007 to study the effects of the brood removal on colony development, disease infestation and honey yield.
    • No negative effects could be found on the colony development and/or yield and positive effects were observed with regards to the health of the bees and control of disease within the hive. 

3. Related/associated technologies

  • ​​Beekeeping in Africa: responding to common bee diseases:​ ID 7332.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Women-friendly

This technology does not require heavy labour, and can be easily implemented by everyone. 

4.2 Resource use efficiency

This technology of integrated varroa management ensures healthier brood health, free of varroa infestations. This is due to a validated technology that experimented with the right time of brood removal. This ensures an efficient and successful practice. 

4.3 Pro-poor technology

Due to its success, this technology reduces and almost eliminates the risk of varroa infestations with minimum cost, and without jeopardizing the honey yield.

  1. The catch comb in the brood box (Box A), which in the meantime should be mostly sealed, needs to be removed and melted down, including the brood and caught mites.

    • Replace the comb with an empty comb or comb with the foundation sheet.
    • A varroa treatment is not required here (Figure 10).
Figure 10. The catch comb full of varroa must be removed

©FAO/TECA

   10. The brood collector hive (Box B) should be transferred immediately on the day of the brood removal to a separate apiary to prevent the return of bees to the mother colony and the risk of robbery and mite transfer).

    • They only need to be checked after 21 to 24 days.
    • By then the whole brood has emerged and old combs can be replaced with empty combs or combs with foundation sheets.
  • Note: Three weeks after the removal all brood is emerged and the combs are empty.
    • This offers a good opportunity to replace dark or badly constructed combs by freshly build combs or frames with wax foundation.
  • Depending on the size of the colony, the colony will remain on one or two boxes.
    • If unsure whether a new queen has been born, a single comb with an open brood can be added from another hive to allow the bees to build emergency queen cells.
    • If on the other hand, the new queen is not productive enough, she can be replaced as soon as the new brood is available (i.e. new unproductive queen has started laying eggs) (Figure 11).
Figure 11. Beekeeper checking varroa infestation 

©FAO/TECA

11. Thanks to the temporary absence of brood in the collector box (Box B), an effective and simple varroa treatment can now be applied.

  • Suitable treatments include the dripping of oxalic acid, spraying of lactic acid or the use of catch combs (Figure 12).
Figure 12. Varroa treatment in absence of brood 

©FAO/TECA

  • This technique has been developed with the objective of maintaining productivity while optimizing colony health with minimum treatment.
    • The Bieneninstitut Kirchhain, Germany, has been testing this technique since 2007 to study the effects of the brood removal on colony development, disease infestation and honey yield.
    • No negative effects could be found on the colony development and/or yield and positive effects were observed with regards to the health of the bees and control of disease within the hive. 

3. Related/associated technologies

  • ​​Beekeeping in Africa: responding to common bee diseases:​ ID 7332.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Women-friendly

This technology does not require heavy labour, and can be easily implemented by everyone. 

4.2 Resource use efficiency

This technology of integrated varroa management ensures healthier brood health, free of varroa infestations. This is due to a validated technology that experimented with the right time of brood removal. This ensures an efficient and successful practice. 

4.3 Pro-poor technology

Due to its success, this technology reduces and almost eliminates the risk of varroa infestations with minimum cost, and without jeopardizing the honey yield.
