records.title: Dryer construction for solar-dried fruit and vegetables production
records.description:
Description

Experiences in Uganda have shown that there are circumstances where it is feasible to establish solar-drying operations as viable micro-enterprises in rural areas. Such operations require the dedication, patience and basic skills of all those involved. Market channels also need to be developed, product quality controlled and technical assistance provided. An overall and integrated approach is essential if solar-drying activities are to be successful in rural development programmes.

This is part of a series of four related technology records dealing with solar drying, and needs to be considered in conjunction with these other records.

  • Assessing opportunities
  • Dryer construction (this record)
  • Practical aspects of the processing
  • Business profitability.

1. Dryer design

  • The dryer consists of a main frame, with eight supporting legs, incorporating the drying chamber.
    • The drying chamber measures 176 in (4.4 m) length and 60 in (1.5 m) deep x 30 in (0.8 m) height overall.
    • It contains 12 trays to provide a total drying area of 100 ft² (10 m²).
    • Depending upon the fruit or vegetable to be dried and upon the loading density used, it can dry between 20 kg and 35 kg of freshly cut produce over a period of two to four days.
  • The dryer is constructed from 2 in (5.08 cm) x 2 in (5.08 cm) softwood.
    • However, the drying trays, rails and support bars should be made from 2 in (5.08 cm) x 1 in (2.54 cm) hardwood to provide the strength and long-term durability needed.
    • The timber used should be well seasoned, of uniform thickness and straight.
  • There are three hinged doors at the front of the chamber to provide access for loading and unloading of the drying trays.
  • There are two tiers of trays.
    • Each tier can accommodate six trays and these are supported on wooden rails.
  • The trays consist of a hardwood frame across which is stapled plastic mosquito mesh onto which are placed the slices of fruit for drying.
  • The base of the drying chamber is a mat made from papyrus, which is then covered over with mosquito mesh.
    • This arrangement allows air to filter through and enter the chamber from underneath and through the trays of sliced fruit.
    • It also provides a barrier against insects and allows rainwater to easily drain away, which can otherwise collect inside and thereby slow down the drying process.
    • Ventilation slots are built into the top of each of the loading doors and allow the warm moist air created to dissipate through natural convection.
    • These slots are similarly covered with mosquito mesh.
  • To operate effectively, airflow needs to be controlled and there should be no gaps, particularly around the doors, where insects may enter or air escape.
    • The doors should be close fitting and strips cut (using the same material as that used for the main cover) and stapled to the doors to provide seals.
  • To deter termite and insect attack, the legs can be placed inside old cans filled with mineral or vegetable oil.
    • Inverted cones nailed over the top of these will help prevent the cans from being filled with rainwater.
  • In operation, the dryer should be sited in a flat area, unobscured by trees or buildings so that it is fully exposed to the sun throughout the day.
    • If the wind blows predominantly from one direction, the dryer should be placed end-on to the wind.
    • This will reduce the cooling effect of the wind blowing directly into the drying chamber which would increase drying times.
    • It will also reduce the likelihood of dust entering the chamber and contaminating the products.
  • It is likely that as more dryers are built, variations to the design will emerge.
    • For instance, it may be that simpler ways can be found to construct joints, to fit the mosquito mesh or to improve cleaning.
    • Such changes are quite acceptable and should be encouraged if it improves the design, perhaps also by reducing the overall cost of the dryer or increasing its life.
    • However, it is advised not to change the basic design, e.g. the overall dimensions of the dryer; the number of trays used; or the sizes of the air inlet and outlet vents without careful consideration and experimentation.
    • Otherwise, dryer performance, and therefore profitability, could be reduced.
    • The dryer performance could also be affected if a different grade of clear plastic covering is used.
    • Any alterations of this nature require technical assessment.

2. Building the dryer

  • The dryer has four main parts.
    1. Main frame
    2. Drying chamber
    3. Loading doors
    4. Drying trays
  •  The dryer should be built in stages (Figures 1-15).
    • Stage one: Making the main frame structure (Figures 1-5)
    • Stage two: Making the drying chamber base (Figures 6-7)
    • Stage three: Making the rails for the drying trays (Figures 8-10)
    • Stage four: Making the loading doors
    • Stage five: Making the drying trays
    • Stage six: Fitting the plastic cover
    • Stage seven: Checking the completed dryer (Figures 11-15)
  • The timber lengths given are only a guide.
    • The dimensions of timber available are likely to vary and practical account needs to be taken of this when building the dryer.
    • This is why key dimensions only have been given.
    • Joints should be glued and screwed for maximum strength and durability.
    • Whilst steel screws will be cheaper and more available, brass screws would last longer and would not rust.
  • Except for the clear plastic sheet, materials should normally be available locally.
    • The clear sheet is a special heavy-duty plastic sheeting 'Visqueen', which remains reasonably durable under the harmful effects of the relatively high levels of ultraviolet light.
    • It is essential to use this, or other similar, horticultural grade plastic sheeting which does not readily degrade in the tropical sunlight.
    • It is considerably more expensive than the ordinary polythenes normally sold, and may need to be imported.
    • In Uganda, it can be obtained from Fruits of the Nile Ltd as can the mosquito mesh.
Figure 1. Main frame: lower corner joint (such as Figure 4)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Main frame: lower intermediate joint (such as Figure 4)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Main frame: legs and lower cross members

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Main frame: top intermediate joint 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Main frame: completed construction

©FAO/TECA

3. Drying chamber base

  • The base consists of a mat made from papyrus, which is firmly fitted across the width of the dryer and along its length.
  • It is supported by two support rails running along the length of the frame, front and back, which constitute part of the main structure.
  • Mosquito mesh is carefully fitted over the papyrus mat and attached with staples along all edges.
Figure 6. Drying chamber (base): papyrus mat base 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Drying chamber (base): papyrus mat fitted

©FAO/TECA

4. Drying chamber rails

  • The four longitudinal rails' support should be fitted to the main frame structure first.
  • The four sets of double rails and six centre rails next, making sure that they are all square with the frame.
  • The remaining four rails should now be fitted at the ends.
  • In all cases, the gap between each rail needs to be the same.
  • This is important as all 12 trays should be interchangeable and fit into any position.
Figure 8. Drying chamber (rails): tray support rails fitted

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Drying chamber (rails): intermediate cross rails

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10. Drying trays: corner joint

©FAO/TECA

5. Loading doors

  • No dimensions are given since it is important for doors to fit closely into the drying chamber frame as made.
  • The hinges should be fitted to the door only at this stage.
  • The air outlet ventilation gap is 4 in and should be covered with mosquito mesh on the inside.
  • The handle running the length of the door frame should be fitted about 8 in from the bottom.
  • The clear plastic should similarly be fitted to the inside with staples along all edges.

6. Drying trays

  • The trays should be fully interchangeable.
    • All 12 trays should be made exactly the same.
    • Anyone can then fit into any one of the 12 possible positions which will make loading much easier.
    • The trays are fitted with guide blocks which project 4 in (10.16 cm) below the frame.
    • This will make it easier to slide the trays in and out.
  • The length of each tray is intended to be 56 in (142.24 cm).
    • Whatever its length is in practice, it must be identical to the length of the rails inside the drying chamber.
    • This should be checked before any timber is cut to size.
    • Similarly, the width of each tray should be 27.5 in (698.5 cm) such that it will fit neatly on each pair of rails; this width should be 1.5 in (3.81 cm) greater than the distance between the rails and again checked before cutting timber.
  • The trays should be glued and screwed at joints.
    • Plastic mosquito mesh is cut to the size of the tray plus an allowance of 1 in (2.54 cm) overlap on all four sides.
    • It is then stapled in place onto the sides of the frame.
  • A current practice is to put a fabric that lets air pass through the trays.
    • This makes it possible to limit the downtime of the trays at the end of the drying for the collection of dried fruits and necessary washing of the trays.
    • Such fabrics are much easier to wash than the trays themselves.

7. Completing dryer construction

  • The dryer should now be moved to its final position with the traps fitted to the legs to deter termite and insect attack.
  • The clear plastic sheet covering should now be fitted over the drying chamber frame and stapled in position.
    • This should be carried out with care to avoid damaging the plastic.
    • It is better to double - over the edges which are to be stapled by two so as to provide extra strength for fixing.
    • The doors can now be fitted and the hinges screwed to the framework.
    • The top edges of the strips of plastic are stapled to the frame so as to cover over the hinges and provide a form of a seal.
  • The completed dryer should be checked for overall stability, ease of loading and unloading of the trays (which should fit in any position) and the opening and closing of the doors (which must operate freely).
    • The dryer should be fully insect proof before use and any gaps sealed.
Figure 11. Completing the dryer: fitting the plastic cover

©FAO/TECA

Figure 12. Completing the dryer: stapling the cover with the edge doubled-over

©FAO/TECA

Figure 13. Completing the dryer: fitting the loading doors

©FAO/TECA

Figure 14. Completed dryer: rear/side view

©FAO/TECA

Figure 15. Completing dryer: front/side view

©FAO/TECA

8. Using the dryer

  • If properly built, the dryer should last many years.
  • Routine maintenance should be carried out regularly and tears or rips in the plastic covering should be quickly repaired as they will affect performance.
  • The plastic sheeting will probably need to be completely replaced after two or three years.
  • If possible, the dryer should be protected in periods of bad weather or when not in use by using a locally-designed portable thatched cover, as this will help to prolong the dryer’s life.
  • Guidance on using the dryer and processing operations are given in the related technology record:

_annotations.body:
Dryer construction for solar-dried fruit and vegetables production

The preservation of fruit and vegetables by simple sun drying is practiced widely throughout arid and semi-arid areas, for example in Uganda. The use of low cost, solar-drying technologies can significantly improve product quality. This provides practical opportunities for developing small-scale enterprises, particularly in rural areas, and creating employment for women's groups. The specifications and prices detailed below are for the Ugandan context in 1996. Users need to adapt their designs to local situations.

Description

Experiences in Uganda have shown that there are circumstances where it is feasible to establish solar-drying operations as viable micro-enterprises in rural areas. Such operations require the dedication, patience and basic skills of all those involved. Market channels also need to be developed, product quality controlled and technical assistance provided. An overall and integrated approach is essential if solar-drying activities are to be successful in rural development programmes.

This is part of a series of four related technology records dealing with solar drying, and needs to be considered in conjunction with these other records.

  • Assessing opportunities
  • Dryer construction (this record)
  • Practical aspects of the processing
  • Business profitability.

1. Dryer design

  • The dryer consists of a main frame, with eight supporting legs, incorporating the drying chamber.
    • The drying chamber measures 176 in (4.4 m) length and 60 in (1.5 m) deep x 30 in (0.8 m) height overall.
    • It contains 12 trays to provide a total drying area of 100 ft² (10 m²).
    • Depending upon the fruit or vegetable to be dried and upon the loading density used, it can dry between 20 kg and 35 kg of freshly cut produce over a period of two to four days.
  • The dryer is constructed from 2 in (5.08 cm) x 2 in (5.08 cm) softwood.
    • However, the drying trays, rails and support bars should be made from 2 in (5.08 cm) x 1 in (2.54 cm) hardwood to provide the strength and long-term durability needed.
    • The timber used should be well seasoned, of uniform thickness and straight.
  • There are three hinged doors at the front of the chamber to provide access for loading and unloading of the drying trays.
  • There are two tiers of trays.
    • Each tier can accommodate six trays and these are supported on wooden rails.
  • The trays consist of a hardwood frame across which is stapled plastic mosquito mesh onto which are placed the slices of fruit for drying.
  • The base of the drying chamber is a mat made from papyrus, which is then covered over with mosquito mesh.
    • This arrangement allows air to filter through and enter the chamber from underneath and through the trays of sliced fruit.
    • It also provides a barrier against insects and allows rainwater to easily drain away, which can otherwise collect inside and thereby slow down the drying process.
    • Ventilation slots are built into the top of each of the loading doors and allow the warm moist air created to dissipate through natural convection.
    • These slots are similarly covered with mosquito mesh.
  • To operate effectively, airflow needs to be controlled and there should be no gaps, particularly around the doors, where insects may enter or air escape.
    • The doors should be close fitting and strips cut (using the same material as that used for the main cover) and stapled to the doors to provide seals.
  • To deter termite and insect attack, the legs can be placed inside old cans filled with mineral or vegetable oil.
    • Inverted cones nailed over the top of these will help prevent the cans from being filled with rainwater.
  • In operation, the dryer should be sited in a flat area, unobscured by trees or buildings so that it is fully exposed to the sun throughout the day.
    • If the wind blows predominantly from one direction, the dryer should be placed end-on to the wind.
    • This will reduce the cooling effect of the wind blowing directly into the drying chamber which would increase drying times.
    • It will also reduce the likelihood of dust entering the chamber and contaminating the products.
  • It is likely that as more dryers are built, variations to the design will emerge.
    • For instance, it may be that simpler ways can be found to construct joints, to fit the mosquito mesh or to improve cleaning.
    • Such changes are quite acceptable and should be encouraged if it improves the design, perhaps also by reducing the overall cost of the dryer or increasing its life.
    • However, it is advised not to change the basic design, e.g. the overall dimensions of the dryer; the number of trays used; or the sizes of the air inlet and outlet vents without careful consideration and experimentation.
    • Otherwise, dryer performance, and therefore profitability, could be reduced.
    • The dryer performance could also be affected if a different grade of clear plastic covering is used.
    • Any alterations of this nature require technical assessment.

2. Building the dryer

  • The dryer has four main parts.
    1. Main frame
    2. Drying chamber
    3. Loading doors
    4. Drying trays
  •  The dryer should be built in stages (Figures 1-15).
    • Stage one: Making the main frame structure (Figures 1-5)
    • Stage two: Making the drying chamber base (Figures 6-7)
    • Stage three: Making the rails for the drying trays (Figures 8-10)
    • Stage four: Making the loading doors
    • Stage five: Making the drying trays
    • Stage six: Fitting the plastic cover
    • Stage seven: Checking the completed dryer (Figures 11-15)
  • The timber lengths given are only a guide.
    • The dimensions of timber available are likely to vary and practical account needs to be taken of this when building the dryer.
    • This is why key dimensions only have been given.
    • Joints should be glued and screwed for maximum strength and durability.
    • Whilst steel screws will be cheaper and more available, brass screws would last longer and would not rust.
  • Except for the clear plastic sheet, materials should normally be available locally.
    • The clear sheet is a special heavy-duty plastic sheeting 'Visqueen', which remains reasonably durable under the harmful effects of the relatively high levels of ultraviolet light.
    • It is essential to use this, or other similar, horticultural grade plastic sheeting which does not readily degrade in the tropical sunlight.
    • It is considerably more expensive than the ordinary polythenes normally sold, and may need to be imported.
    • In Uganda, it can be obtained from Fruits of the Nile Ltd as can the mosquito mesh.
Figure 1. Main frame: lower corner joint (such as Figure 4)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Main frame: lower intermediate joint (such as Figure 4)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Main frame: legs and lower cross members

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Main frame: top intermediate joint 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Main frame: completed construction

©FAO/TECA

3. Drying chamber base

  • The base consists of a mat made from papyrus, which is firmly fitted across the width of the dryer and along its length.
  • It is supported by two support rails running along the length of the frame, front and back, which constitute part of the main structure.
  • Mosquito mesh is carefully fitted over the papyrus mat and attached with staples along all edges.
Figure 6. Drying chamber (base): papyrus mat base 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Drying chamber (base): papyrus mat fitted

©FAO/TECA

4. Drying chamber rails

  • The four longitudinal rails' support should be fitted to the main frame structure first.
  • The four sets of double rails and six centre rails next, making sure that they are all square with the frame.
  • The remaining four rails should now be fitted at the ends.
  • In all cases, the gap between each rail needs to be the same.
  • This is important as all 12 trays should be interchangeable and fit into any position.
Figure 8. Drying chamber (rails): tray support rails fitted

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Drying chamber (rails): intermediate cross rails

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10. Drying trays: corner joint

©FAO/TECA

5. Loading doors

  • No dimensions are given since it is important for doors to fit closely into the drying chamber frame as made.
  • The hinges should be fitted to the door only at this stage.
  • The air outlet ventilation gap is 4 in and should be covered with mosquito mesh on the inside.
  • The handle running the length of the door frame should be fitted about 8 in from the bottom.
  • The clear plastic should similarly be fitted to the inside with staples along all edges.

6. Drying trays

  • The trays should be fully interchangeable.
    • All 12 trays should be made exactly the same.
    • Anyone can then fit into any one of the 12 possible positions which will make loading much easier.
    • The trays are fitted with guide blocks which project 4 in (10.16 cm) below the frame.
    • This will make it easier to slide the trays in and out.
  • The length of each tray is intended to be 56 in (142.24 cm).
    • Whatever its length is in practice, it must be identical to the length of the rails inside the drying chamber.
    • This should be checked before any timber is cut to size.
    • Similarly, the width of each tray should be 27.5 in (698.5 cm) such that it will fit neatly on each pair of rails; this width should be 1.5 in (3.81 cm) greater than the distance between the rails and again checked before cutting timber.
  • The trays should be glued and screwed at joints.
    • Plastic mosquito mesh is cut to the size of the tray plus an allowance of 1 in (2.54 cm) overlap on all four sides.
    • It is then stapled in place onto the sides of the frame.
  • A current practice is to put a fabric that lets air pass through the trays.
    • This makes it possible to limit the downtime of the trays at the end of the drying for the collection of dried fruits and necessary washing of the trays.
    • Such fabrics are much easier to wash than the trays themselves.

7. Completing dryer construction

  • The dryer should now be moved to its final position with the traps fitted to the legs to deter termite and insect attack.
  • The clear plastic sheet covering should now be fitted over the drying chamber frame and stapled in position.
    • This should be carried out with care to avoid damaging the plastic.
    • It is better to double - over the edges which are to be stapled by two so as to provide extra strength for fixing.
    • The doors can now be fitted and the hinges screwed to the framework.
    • The top edges of the strips of plastic are stapled to the frame so as to cover over the hinges and provide a form of a seal.
  • The completed dryer should be checked for overall stability, ease of loading and unloading of the trays (which should fit in any position) and the opening and closing of the doors (which must operate freely).
    • The dryer should be fully insect proof before use and any gaps sealed.
Figure 11. Completing the dryer: fitting the plastic cover

©FAO/TECA

Figure 12. Completing the dryer: stapling the cover with the edge doubled-over

©FAO/TECA

Figure 13. Completing the dryer: fitting the loading doors

©FAO/TECA

Figure 14. Completed dryer: rear/side view

©FAO/TECA

Figure 15. Completing dryer: front/side view

©FAO/TECA

8. Using the dryer

  • If properly built, the dryer should last many years.
  • Routine maintenance should be carried out regularly and tears or rips in the plastic covering should be quickly repaired as they will affect performance.
  • The plastic sheeting will probably need to be completely replaced after two or three years.
  • If possible, the dryer should be protected in periods of bad weather or when not in use by using a locally-designed portable thatched cover, as this will help to prolong the dryer’s life.
  • Guidance on using the dryer and processing operations are given in the related technology record:
    • Producing solar dried fruit and vegetables for micro- and small-scale rural enterprise development: assessing opportunities for a fruit drying business: ID 4501.
    • Producing solar-dried fruit and vegetables for micro- and small-scale rural enterprise development: business profitability: ID 4504.

records.title: Development and promotion of community-based seed production of groundnut Rosette disease-resistant varieties
records.description:
Description

A needs assessment, funded by DFID in February 1998, identified rosette disease as the most important general or pest and disease problem on groundnuts both by farmers and Serere Agricultural and Animal production Research Institute (SAARI).

1. Rosette disease-resistant groundnut varieties

  • Host-plant resistance is considered to be the most cost-effective management measure against rosette disease because farmers seldom adopt cultural or chemical control practices owing to lack of resources, labour constraints, differing crop priorities and other factors.
    • Rosette resistance was originally identified in groundnut germplasm originating from West Africa.
    • From this material, late-maturing Rosette-resistant genotypes were developed (such as RMP 12 and RG1).
    • However, few farmers adopted these lines because they required a long growing season (150-180 days) to attain maturity, making them sensitive to drought at the end of the season.
    • They also had a spreading growth habit and small pods.
  • Subsequently, rosette-resistance was successfully transferred to short-duration types and several advanced groundnut breeding lines.
    • These had high levels of rosette resistance, acceptable seed size and colour were developed by the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT).
    • Some of these lines were transferred to SAARI, where further improvement and adaptation to farmer and consumer preferences was carried out under an adaptive DFID Crop Protection Programme (CPP) project R7445 (see Chancello, 2002) between NRI, SAARI and ICRISAT.
    • This involved farmer-managed trials and an investigation into the potential for developing village/community seed banks, to ensure adequate high quality seed is passed from one season to the next.
  • Strategic outputs from the earlier project R6811 (see Kimmins, 1999), which focused on the mechanisms of resistance, assisted in the development of breeding lines with combined resistance to both the rosette viruses and the aphid vector.
    • This led to the release of new rosette-resistant varieties of groundnuts, namely Serenut 2, 3, and 4 that conform to the requirements of different local markets.
    • Serenut 3 and 4 are short duration types, allowing two crops to be grown in a single year and thus greatly enhancing the income-earning opportunity of poor farmers.
  • However, owing to the high seed rate requirement for groundnut (low ratio of seed:progeny), seed availability was limited, especially for the rural poor.
    • The new varieties were available at prohibitive prices from research sources.
    • Seed companies found it unattractive to multiply and sell commercially as prices would limit sales volumes.
  • This technology describes ways in which community seed production was promoted and commercialised in Uganda, through CPP projects R8105 and R8442, led by the NGO, AT Uganda.

2. Community seed production

  • Under R8105 starting in 2002 and subsequently extended under R8442, the work was implemented in the 16 sub-counties of the Kumi, Pallisa,Tororo, Mbale and Sironko districts.
    • In each sub-county the project operated in two parishes and worked initially with ten farmer groups with a total membership of 4,317 farmers in the 160 groups.
    • Another 160 groups joined in the second season of 2004.
    • The model for multiplication of seed was an approach practiced with other crops in an earlier project, implemented by AT Uganda with the same farmers.
    • It emphasized participation of the key stakeholders.
      • In this case these were beneficiary farmer groups, Production Committees (PC), Parish Development Committees (PDC) and extension staff sub-county local government authorities in planning, implementing, and monitoring project activities.
  • The project was implemented in collaboration with a groundnut breeder from NARO/SAARI, whose role was the training of trainers, provision of technical advice, and contacts for access to planting material.
    • Field activities with farmers were handled by the sub-county level local government extension staff (FPRA) of the Department of Agriculture.
    • Full details are given in the project reports (see Laker-Ojok 2005a and 2005b).
  • In summary, the process and activities involved were general preparatory activities sensitisation of local government stakeholders from the participating districts and sub-county was done at district level.
    • The main purpose was to discuss and agree on the modalities to be used in implementing the project and to get feedback on the approach.
    • In particular the following categories of people were invited and attended:
      • District Agricultural Officers
      • District Secretaries for production (political leaders in charge of production at district level)
      • Sub-county chiefs
      • Chairpersons of Local Council
      • Secretaries for production at sub-county level
      • Farmers representatives from the participating groups
      • Councillors representing women at sub county level
      • Extension staff in charge of the sub counties.
  • After the sensitisation process, a memorandum of understanding was signed with the leaders of each participating sub-county.
  • In addition to the district level meetings, meetings were held at sub-county for all participating groups and more local leaders were invited to attend.
    • The meetings provided an opportunity to introduce the project and to build support in the community.
    • The basic issues included:
      • each recipient of seed was to return twice the amount received for redistribution to other group members and the community as seed belonged to the community;
      • priority to receive seed given to the able poor and wome;
      • the role of Parish Development Committees (PDCs) in the multiplication and distribution process; and
      • contribution of the beneficiaries in the form of labour, land, inputs for all management practices and peer monitoring.

2.1 Training in groundnut production, multiplication and storage

  • The collaborating groundnut breeder, using the groundnut production manual (http://www.fao.org/docs/eims/upload/agrotech/1998/GroundnutManual.pdf) developed by project R7445, trained extension staff as trainers in groundnut production.
    • This was done together with AT Uganda Programme staff that supervised implementation of field activities.
    • Refresher training on seed quality and storage was done for all staff.
  • Training of beneficiary farmer groups was then organised at sub-county level, facilitated by the extension staff.
    • Later refresher trainings by the Production Committees and Parish Development Committees (PDCs), using the simplified seed production guide (see Appendix 3 in LAKER - OJOK 2005a), were organised at group level at the start of each season to reinforce training under supervision of the extension staff.
  • Sustainability of training called for building of the local capacity to train, and thus the training of PDCs and PCs in place of contact farmers as trainers, to continue with the training of other farmers later as the seed continued to multiply.
  • Providing the beneficiaries and staff with the simple seed production guide as reference material for future use.
    • This equipped them with the necessary knowledge and skills to pass on to others whenever need arose.
  • End of season evaluations were organised both to enable farmers to learn from the experiences of their fellow farmers and to assess and appreciate the varieties and practices promoted.

3. Foundation seed multiplied by farmer group members

  • At the start of the first season of each year, each participating group was given small amounts of seed of the new varieties to multiply for subsequent distribution to the members.
    • In order to multiply seed for redistribution to all targeted beneficiaries in a short period, recipients were required to return more than the amount initially received.
    • The groups were helped to prepare seed multiplication byelaws and regulations to ensure that beneficiaries paid back seed so that the distribution chain was maintained.
    • See Appendix 10 in Laker-Ojok 2005a for a checklist developed by the groups.
    • The byelaws were reviewed to suit emerging situations.
  • Delivery of seed by the project to individuals in groups was based on distribution plans.
    • Each sub-county received new seed at the start of each year.
    • The varieties were introduced gradually, starting with Serenut 2 in the first year, then Serenut 3 and 4 in the second and third years.
    • The first lot of seed of each new variety was procured through the collaborating breeder or bought from the beneficiaries for distribution to other farmers.
  • Acknowledgement of receipt of seed and multiplication terms as contained in the agreement and byelaws.
    • Quantities received and to be repaid was done by all beneficiaries and witnessed by PDCs for accountability, transparency and easy follow-up at the time of repayment.
    • Distribution was done at group or public meetings.
    • The process required PDCs to keep a register of all seed recipients and repayments in the groups and by individuals in the parish.
  • The project facilitated the process by initially providing the books and training on record keeping for PCs and PDCs.

  • Multipliers return twice the amount of planting material received for redistribution and further multiplication.
    • The groups needed to prepare for the large quantities of seeds that became available as pay back to other members.
    • They were assisted by the PCs and PDCs, giving priority to the able poor and women, as well as to members who had shown hard work and commitment, so as to minimise the risk of loss due to poor management.
    • The plans also helped create peer pressure among the recipients thus encouraging them to repay.
    • The process was supported by byelaws.
    • Clear repayment terms and procedures, developed and enforced in a participatory manner, together with group peer pressure arising from community ownership of the seeds, helped to instill a repayment culture in beneficiaries and gave control to the community.

  • A lot of capacity building was needed to promote sustainability of these processes.
    • Roles were identified and assigned to the local leadership structures, e.g. PCs and PDCs, in a participatory manner so as to ensure that seeds zererepaid and given out for further multiplication and that planned activities were completed.
    • The roles included training other beneficiaries on groundnut production; monitoring management of crops in the field; facilitating identification of beneficiaries; distribution and recovery of seed for redistribution and record keeping.
    • This was done in all participating sub-counties and a final checklist was developed.
    • See appendices 1 and 2 of Laker and Okoj, 2005a.

4. General and cross-cutting activities

  • Pre-seasonal planning meetings were held at the beginning of each year at project, sub-county and group level to ensure completion of activities.
    • Payment of the extension staff was based on completion of tasks.
    • Planning and budgeting was done by the extension staff themselves with supervision of project staff and this was seen to increase their commitment.
    • See Appendix 6 of Laker-Okoj 2005a.
  • Review meetings were held with all groups and lessons learnt were used to refine byelaws and other implementation strategies.
    • Joint field monitoring was carried out by PCs, PDCs, and occasionally extension staff and project staff, to assess field performance and adoption of crop management practices and to minimise cases of false reports of crop failure.
    • Joint monitoring of crops in the field was used to remind beneficiaries of their obligation and helped in timely solution of problems.
    • This helped other groups to take precautionary corrective actions as they learnt from each other and helped them to refine their byelaws.
  • End of season evaluations were done at both group and sub-county level each season to assess performance of the varieties and get farmers’ feedback.
    • This motivated others to adopt recommended practices.
    • A competition was organised in 2003 to encourage training, multiplication, distribution and participation of the local leaders.
    • Prizes awarded included peanut butter grinders and groundnut shellers.
    • An impact assessment survey of participating groups was carried out in September 2004 against baseline survey data obtained at the start of the project in 2002.
    • See Appendix 11 of Laker-Okoj 2005a.
  • A control group was also sampled including five people who were neighbours to beneficiaries sampled in each group, in order to test for diffusion outside of the project parishes.
    • Data from field reports indicates that four programme staff, 16 extension staff with their 15 field assistants, 960 community leaders (PCs and PDCs from 320 groups in 16 parishes) and more than 6 000 farmers were trained in groundnut production, storage and multiplication.
    • Foundation seed of Serenut 2 ,3 and 4, sufficient to plant 187.5 ha, was obtained and given to farmers to multiply.
  • The survey, conducted in September 2004, estimated that up to 17,154 people had accessed seeds through the formal project arrangements, sales and gifts by individuals.
    • 3 634 received seed directly from the project.
    • 5 910 purchased seed from farmer multipliers.
    • 7 610 obtained it through gifts or payments in kind.
    • 52 percent of beneficiaries were women.
  • Redistribution of the varieties was continually increasing under the guidance of local leadership.
    • Seeds produced was sufficient to plant 3 275 ha.
    • 1 092 ha was distributed directly from the project and 2 183 ha using seed from sales and gifts.
    • Estimated production from 2004 would be sufficient to plant up to 4 725 ha if all were committed to seeds.
    • Seed availability for the introduced varieties had thus increased substantially and large quantities were being sold, enabling non-participating farmers to benefit from this, thus disseminating the new varieties.

  • Project R8442 expanded the multiplication coverage to neighbouring sub-counties and assisted farmers groups to consolidate into sub-county level marketing associations, in order to be able to capture more lucrative markets by selling in bulk.
    • Foundation seeds of new rosette resistant groundnut varieties were procured and multiplied by an additional 80 farmer groups (five per new sub county).
    • Almost 2 000 additional farmers were trained in seed production, multiplication, distribution management and collective marketing.
  • Multiplication continued among the nearly 8 000 farmers, who were members of the original 160 farmer groups and the 160 partner groups that had already been established, thus bringing the number of total beneficiaries to nearly 10 000.
    • Over 200 ha of Serenut 2, 3, and 4 were multiplied in the 16 new sub counties.
    • In order to foster commercial incentives for sustainable groundnut multiplication, AT Uganda collaborated with SACRED Africa, an NGO based in Kenya, to help the groups form regional marketing initiative associations with sub-county level branches.
  • During its nine months of operation, the project established the foundation and structures on which the marketing groups were to operate.
    • Twenty marketing groups were formed at the sub-county level with a total of 875 members.
    • These marketing groups have been registered at district level.
    • Members have paid shares, elected leadership and advisory committees, and established working sub-committees.
    • They have been trained in record keeping, quality control/management, and market intelligence.
    • Each of the groups has adopted a constitution, opened a bank account, and established a store that acts as a marketing centre for ease of quality control, and bulking.
  • The project engaged a team of field auditors to help the farmers marketing groups to establish a record keeping, a financial management system and to undertake periodic audit of their books.
    • To ensure effective coordination, advocacy, and establish better market linkages, the 20 sub-county Farmers Marketing Groups were consolidated into five District/Regional Marketing Associations, with an elected interim leadership committee.
    • In mid November 2005, SACRED Africa and AT Uganda carried out an evaluation of the Farmers’ Marketing Initiatives, which verified progress achieved to date.
    • They stressed the importance of continued support to these fledgling organizations to achieve full impact and sustainability.
    • See Appendix 11 of Laker, Okoj 2005b.

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Groundnut agronomic and postharvest practices: ID 6991.
  • Groundnuts varieties, management and post harvest: ID 6899.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Pro-poor technology

Through introduced seed varieties, farmers could produce and sell large quantities, enabling non-participating farmers to benefit.

Development and promotion of community-based seed production of groundnut Rosette disease-resistant varieties

    • From this material, late-maturing Rosette-resistant genotypes were developed (such as RMP 12 and RG1).
    • However, few farmers adopted these lines because they required a long growing season (150-180 days) to attain maturity, making them sensitive to drought at the end of the season.
    • They also had a spreading growth habit and small pods.
  • Subsequently, rosette-resistance was successfully transferred to short-duration types and several advanced groundnut breeding lines.
    • These had high levels of rosette resistance, acceptable seed size and colour were developed by the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT).
    • Some of these lines were transferred to SAARI, where further improvement and adaptation to farmer and consumer preferences was carried out under an adaptive DFID Crop Protection Programme (CPP) project R7445 (see Chancello, 2002) between NRI, SAARI and ICRISAT.

_annotations.field_innovation_identified:
INNOVATION: Community-Based Seed System for Groundnut Disease Resistance

DESCRIPTION: Farmer-led seed multiplication model integrating local governance structures, production committees, and development committees for distributing rosette-resistant groundnut varieties. The system combines technological innovation (disease-resistant varieties) with social innovation (community-based multiplication and distribution).

CRITERIA MET: Creates equitable business models, accelerates participatory approaches, facilitates transformative partnerships, and enhances inclusion through community ownership and management of seed systems.

records.title: Fisheries stock assessment using the FMSP stock assessment tool and a simple guide to writing a management plan
records.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • In order to guide responsible management decisions and to achieve sustainable fishery goals, fisheries managers require sound advice based on the application of relevant stock assessment tools.
  • Fisheries assessment can be complex and a large number of tools are available, including those developed by the Fisheries Management Science Programme (FMSP).
  • A number of over-arching principles exist, e.g. the FAO Code of Conduct for Responsible Fisheries (FAO 1995), requires that assessment uncertainties are accounted for in precautionary and adaptive management.
  • However, many managers are constrained in adopting good management practices and in selecting appropriate tools by their limited understanding of the potential benefits and the requirement of the alternatives management strategies available.

2. Fisheries management guidelines

  • A two-part set of guidelines was produced to help fishery managers and those involved in fishery management.
    • These guides have been written for those with a responsibility for monitoring, assessing and managing fish stocks.
  • The aim is to help better collection and use of fisheries data and to support fishery managers in using these data to create better management plans.
  • The concise "Managers Guide" and complementary "Stock Assessment Guide" for fisheries were developed and tested with Indian and Carribean partners.
    • The former describes a simple step by step process for writing and implementing a fishery management plan.
    • The latter shows how stock assessment tools can support fishery managers in designing their management plans and in managing the fishery.
  • The current project has highlighted the importance of fishery managers and stock assessment scientists working together in defining appropriate stock assessment tools, setting relevant indicators for the fishery and developing appropriate management controls.
  • Management and stock assessment activities cannot be carried out in isolation.
  • In addition, stock assessment tools and fishery management guidelines developed through more than 20 previous projects under the DFID Fisheries Management Science Programme (FMSP) were synthesised into a framework guide.
  • This has been published as FAO Fisheries Technical Paper 487 (Hogarth et al. 2006).
  • This framework guide assists fisheries managers in using FMSP stock assessment tools whilst allowing for uncertainty.
    • It also explains how a management plan should be developed.
  • These three packages are introduced below.

2.1 Managers guide

  • The purpose of the Managers Guide is to describe a step by step approach to the development of an effective fishery management plan.
  • The management planning processes recommended are generally compatible with the management framework currently promoted by FAO in the Code of Conduct for Responsible Fisheries and the UN Fish Stocks Agreement.
  • The guide has a number of distinctive features in that it:
    • is aimed at busy fisheries managers;
    • focuses on the need for stock assessment scientists to provide fishery managers with better information about their fish stocks to allow good management plans to be written and action taken;
    • emphasises the need to be able to predict the impact of different management measures through using specific stock assessment tools;
    • stresses the importance of fishery managers working closely with those responsible for data collection, monitoring and data analysis; and
    • provides examples of recently developed tools that will allow stock assessment personnel to make good estimates of fish stocks.
  • At a global scale, many fisheries are in trouble.
  • These fisheries need to be managed more carefully to reverse the current downward trend and to sustain fish production into the future.
  • Fishing can be said to be sustainable when it can be carried out over the long-term at an acceptable level of biological and economic productivity, without leading to ecological changes that reduce options for future generations.
  • If there is too much fishing, the fishery will produce less than its maximum potential.
  • If this continues for too long, the fishery may decline to the point of collapse.
  • In order to manage a fishery in a sustainable manner, three main components or thematic areas need to be considered: ecological, social and economic.
  • Each of these must complement each other for the system as a whole to be sustainable.
  • A fishery management plan is a document that:
    • analyzes the current situation in a fishery;
    • sets out some principles that should be followed in management;
    • details goals and objectives for the fishery;
    • says how they are to be achieved; and
    • says how they are to be monitored.
  • Successful management plans are working documents, constantly referred to by fishery managers, and open to changes in the future.
  • Ideally these should be reviewed and updated on an annual basis.

2.2 Stock assessment guide

  • The Stock Assessment Guide shows how stock assessment tools can support fisheries managers in designing their management plans and in managing the fishery.
    • This Stock Assessment Guide focuses on:
      • where stock assessment tools are needed in fishery management,
      • which tools may be used in which situation,
      • what advice may be provided to managers, and
      • how to allow for the uncertainty in the assessments.
    • To be sustainable, however, we need to make sure that we leave enough stock each year to maintain high levels of spawning and replace those fish that are caught.
    • If we fish too hard or allow the stock to become too small, the potential catch will be reduced.
    • The maximum potential catches will generally be taken by reducing the stock size from its unexploited level, and by fishing at a moderate rate, not too high.
    • The long-term catch should be higher at an intermediate stock size than at the unexploited level because there should be more food available to each fish, so they compete less with each other and grow faster.
  • Stock assessments provide a scientific and quantitative basis to the process of developing and implementing a management plan in several areas.
    • Stock assessments are always based on quantitative data collected from the fishery.
    • Two general categories of stock assessments are the "analytical" and "biomass dynamic" approaches.
    • Both of these approaches model the relationship between fishery inputs (fishing) and outputs (catches).
    • In the analytical approach (also called the "dynamic pool" approach), a number of intermediate processes are also modeled that describe in detail the dynamics of the fish stock and the fishery.
    • Such intermediate processes can include the growth and maturation of the fish and the selectivity of the fishing gears towards different sizes of fish.
  • In contrast, biomass dynamic models are more direct "in-out" approaches in which the productivity of the resource is represented only by the size of the stock and its overall rate of turnover.
    • These models estimate the maximum sustainable yield available from a stock with that size and productivity.
    • Individual processes such as fish growth and gear selectivity are ignored.
    • Models are fitted with a time series of catch, effort and/or abundance data either from the fishery or from surveys.
    • Neither approach is more right or wrong than the other.
    • They are based on different models and assumptions, and use different data.
  • LFDA and Yield are analytical stock assessment approaches whilst the CEDA software and ParFish tool run on the basis of a biomass dynamic model.
    • Analytical models require a reasonable understanding of the population dynamics of the stock.
    • Although several input parameters need to be estimated, most of these can be estimated by a short but intensive period of data collection (e.g. for fish length frequencies and biological data).
    • Biomass dynamic models need less detailed data (only catch and effort) but they need a long time series to give good results.
    • They can be particularly useful for fish species that are hard to age, or for multi-species resources where single-species analytical models are impractical.
      • E.g. where resources are not available to collect data on each of the different species, or for enforcement of species-specific regulations.
    • Since they ignore the size structure of the fish, however, they can not give advice on technical management measures such as mesh size limits or fish size limits, or fishing seasons.
    • They are usually used instead to provide guidance on total allowable catch quotas and/or fishing effort limits (e.g. limits on the numbers of fishing vessels).

2.2.1 The Length Frequency Distribution Analysis (LFDA) and Catch Effort Data Analysis (CEDA)

  • The Length Frequency Distribution Analysis (LFDA) package is a PC-based computer package for estimating growth parameters and mortality rates from fish length frequency distributions.
  • The Catch Effort Data Analysis package (CEDA) is a PC -based software package for analysing catch, effort and abundance index data.
  • For further details on these packages, see TECA record "Length Frequency Distribution Analysis (LFDA) and Catch Effort Data Analysis (CEDA) Software Packages To Aid Fisheries Management".

2.2.2 Yield

  • Yield is a program for calculating fishery yields and stock biomasses, on an absolute or per-recruit basis, and for calculating biological reference points associated with these.
  • Users are asked to enter values of biological parameters (e.g. growth, mortality, age at maturity and stock-recruitment relationship) and fishery parameters (e.g. length at first capture, fishing season) .

2.2.3 ParFish Participatory Fisheries Stock Assessment (ParFish)

  • This software is a PC-based software package that uses Bayesian Statistics and Decision Theory to assess the state of a fishery stock and estimate limit and target control levels.
  • The software supports the overall approach which is described in the accompanying ParFish Guidelines.
  • For further details on ParFish, see TECA record "ParFish Toolkit: A Participatory Fisheries Stock Assessment Approach".

3. Stock assessment for fishery management: a framework guide to stock assessment tools

  • Part one of the framework guide describes key elements of the precautionary approach to fisheries management.
  • A stock assessment process is also outlined that can provide the information needed for such precautionary management.
  • The management process summarized in Chapter 2 is based on recent FAO guidance, including the Code of Conduct for Responsible Fisheries.
    • It emphasizes the need for setting goals and operational objectives.
    • This is needed:
      • for defining these explicitly as reference points for a range of fishery indicators;
      • for adopting decision control rules that include precautionary thresholds allowing for uncertainties and risk tolerances; and
      • that drive fishery management using a set of measures that are pre-agreed with stakeholders.
    • Chapter 2 also stresses the need to integrate use rights and co-management arrangements into the management framework, where appropriate, as key elements for success.
  • Chapter 3 presents the process of stock assessment, underlining the need for quantitative assessment of uncertainties and risks and the provision of advice based on the various goals of the fishery and considering both short and long-term impacts of management strategies.
    • Methods are given to estimate the current status of the fishery either as the stock size, the fishing mortality rate or other ecological or goal-based indicators.
    • Methods are also described for estimating Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY) and other yield-based reference points, as well as some aimed at protecting the spawning capacity of the stock and avoiding recruitment overfishing.
    • For sustainable exploitation, it is recommended that yield-based reference points are used as targets while spawning capacity reference points are used as limits and given the higher precedence.
    • Precautionary thresholds should be set to prevent the limits being exceeded.
  • Chapter 4 provides information on the FMSP stock assessment tools and guidelines, including four FMSP software packages:
    • LFDA,
    • CEDA,
    • Yield, and
    • ParFish
  • These are by which intermediate parameters, indicators and reference points may be estimated.
  • The inputs and outputs and the relative advantages and potential uses of the tools are described.
  • The four chapters in Part two further describe these four software tools, providing guidelines on their use and the fitting of models.
  • Part three then summarizes the guidelines produced by a number of other FMSP projects relating to stock assessment and management approaches that were introduced in Chapter 4.
  • Chapter 10 uses simulation models to compare the performance of length-based and age-based approaches for two tropical fish species.
    • The analysis demonstrates the benefits of using age based approaches where possible, but it is noted that results may differ for other species and their particular life history strategies.
  • Chapter 11 develops simple relationships for the estimation of potential yield and maximum sustainable fishing mortality based on the Beverton and Holt "life-history invariants".
    • These relationships allow sustainable yields and fishing capacity to be estimated from sparse data, which may either be already available, or can be relatively easily obtained.
  • Chapter 12 derives guidelines for the management of multispecies demersal bank and deep reef slope fisheries exploited principally with hooks and lines.
  • Chapter 13 presents a Bayesian stock assessment applied to the Namibian orange roughy fishery.
    • This case study illustrates the benefits and some of the difficulties found in applying the Bayesian approach and draws out some lessons learnt.
  • Chapter 14 describes a number of empirical modelling approaches that can be used to support fisheries management, ranging in complexity from simple methods that only require historical catches through to complex multivariate models based on General Linear Modelling and Bayesian network approaches.
    • These approaches may suit data poor circumstances, or when among fishery comparisons are possible, for example under adaptive approaches to (co-) management.
    • Throughout the framework guide, the use of adaptive learning and feedback approaches are promoted within the general principle of precaution.
    • Complementary use of these approaches should enable uncertainties to be reduced and long-term benefits to be maximized with reduced risks to the resource base.

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Fry Seed quality and stocking: ID 7025.
  • ParFish Toolkit: a participatory fisheries stock assessment approach: ID 4476.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

FMSP stock assessment tools assist fisheries managers in designing their management plans and in managing the fishery.

Fisheries stock assessment using the FMSP stock assessment tool and a simple guide to writing a management plan

Stock assessment tools and fishery management guidelines were synthesised into a framework guide. The guide assists fisheries managers in using Fisheries Management Science Programme (FMSP) stock assessment tools. It describes a process for writing and implementing a fishery management plan and shows how stock assessment tools can support fishery managers in designing their management plans and in managing the fishery.

Description

1. Introduction

  • In order to guide responsible management decisions and to achieve sustainable fishery goals, fisheries managers require sound advice based on the application of relevant stock assessment tools.
  • Fisheries assessment can be complex and a large number of tools are available, including those developed by the Fisheries Management Science Programme (FMSP).
  • A number of over-arching principles exist, e.g. the FAO Code of Conduct for Responsible Fisheries (FAO 1995), requires that assessment uncertainties are accounted for in precautionary and adaptive management.
  • However, many managers are constrained in adopting good management practices and in selecting appropriate tools by their limited understanding of the potential benefits and the requirement of the alternatives management strategies available.

2. Fisheries management guidelines

  • A two-part set of guidelines was produced to help fishery managers and those involved in fishery management.
    • These guides have been written for those with a responsibility for monitoring, assessing and managing fish stocks.
  • The aim is to help better collection and use of fisheries data and to support fishery managers in using these data to create better management plans.
  • The concise "Managers Guide" and complementary "Stock Assessment Guide" for fisheries were developed and tested with Indian and Carribean partners.
    • The former describes a simple step by step process for writing and implementing a fishery management plan.
    • The latter shows how stock assessment tools can support fishery managers in designing their management plans and in managing the fishery.
  • The current project has highlighted the importance of fishery managers and stock assessment scientists working together in defining appropriate stock assessment tools, setting relevant indicators for the fishery and developing appropriate management controls.
  • Management and stock assessment activities cannot be carried out in isolation.
  • In addition, stock assessment tools and fishery management guidelines developed through more than 20 previous projects under the DFID Fisheries Management Science Programme (FMSP) were synthesised into a framework guide.
  • This has been published as FAO Fisheries Technical Paper 487 (Hogarth et al. 2006).

    • stresses the importance of fishery managers working closely with those responsible for data collection, monitoring and data analysis; and
    • provides examples of recently developed tools that will allow stock assessment personnel to make good estimates of fish stocks.

  • These fisheries need to be managed more carefully to reverse the current downward trend and to sustain fish production into the future.
  • Fishing can be said to be sustainable when it can be carried out over the long-term at an acceptable level of biological and economic productivity, without leading to ecological changes that reduce options for future generations.
  • If there is too much fishing, the fishery will produce less than its maximum potential.
  • If this continues for too long, the fishery may decline to the point of collapse.
  • In order to manage a fishery in a sustainable manner, three main components or thematic areas need to be considered: ecological, social and economic.
  • Each of these must complement each other for the system as a whole to be sustainable.
  • A fishery management plan is a document that:
    • analyzes the current situation in a fishery;
    • sets out some principles that should be followed in management;
    • details goals and objectives for the fishery;
    • says how they are to be achieved; and
    • says how they are to be monitored.
  • Successful management plans are working documents, constantly referred to by fishery managers, and open to changes in the future.
  • Ideally these should be reviewed and updated on an annual basis.

      • where stock assessment tools are needed in fishery management,

      • what advice may be provided to managers, and

    • To be sustainable, however, we need to make sure that we leave enough stock each year to maintain high levels of spawning and replace those fish that are caught.
    • If we fish too hard or allow the stock to become too small, the potential catch will be reduced.
    • The maximum potential catches will generally be taken by reducing the stock size from its unexploited level, and by fishing at a moderate rate, not too high.
    • The long-term catch should be higher at an intermediate stock size than at the unexploited level because there should be more food available to each fish, so they compete less with each other and grow faster.

Title: ParFish (Participatory Fisheries Stock Assessment)

Description: A software-based approach combining Bayesian statistics and participatory methods for fisheries stock assessment. It enables data collection from fishers' knowledge and catch data, supporting sustainable fishery management decisions.
