  • Il meurt en dix minutes à 55 à 65 °C et résiste six jours directement au soleil; dans le miel, il perd de sa virulence après cinq à six semaines.
  • Le SBV infecte les jeunes larves d'abeille par voie orale.
  • Les symptômes se manifestent chez les larves dans les cellules operculées (Figure 8), tandis que les adultes sont asymptomatiques.
  • Les cellules operculées sont creux à l'intérieur et les larves deviennent d'abord jaunâtre-brunâtre, puis les organes internes deviennent fluides tandis que le tégument reste intact en prenant le typique aspect "sacciforme" (Figure 5).
Figure 8. Virus du couvain sacciforme (SBV)

©FAO/FERA

5. Virus de la cellule royale noire (BQCV)

  • Ce virus affecte uniquement les cellules royales et est l'une des causes les plus fréquentes de mortalité chez les larves de reine.
  • Le nom du virus vient de la couleur noirâtre des formes larvaires et des parois de la cellule royale (Figure 9).
  • Bien que le couvain de l'abeille ouvrière et des mâles peuvent être infectés par le BQCV, généralement ils ne développent pas de symptômes.
  • L'infection est plus fréquente lorsque les colonies sont affectées par la nosémose parce que les lésions de l'intestin grêle facilitent le passage du virus dans l'hémolymphe.
Figure 9. Virus de la cellule noire de la reine (BQCV)

©FAO/Giovanni Formato

6. Prévention et contrôle des virus

  • Il n'y a pas encore de recours thérapeutiques spécifiques et efficaces pour les maladies virales des abeilles.
  • Dans le cas de symptômes particulièrement graves, le seul remède est la destruction des colonies touchées.
  • Dans d'autres cas, où les symptômes sont moins graves, l'apiculteur peut essayer de remplacer la reine et les cadres infectés, qui seront détruits.

records.title: Supplemental irrigation for improved water use efficiency and productivity of wheat in rain-fed agriculture
records.description:
Description

1. What is supplemental irrigation?

In rain-fed agriculture of semi-arid and arid regions, water is the most limiting factor. That entails the need for additional sources of water in case of lack of rainfall. Irrigation systems can help to solve the problem, but what if the sources for irrigation water are very limited? Usually, wheat crops do have little need for moisture in the early stages of growth (November to January). This is due to a low rate of water uptake when the seedling is young. Hence, during the early stages of crop growth throughout the winter months, there is more water through rainfall available than would be needed by the crop. At later stages of growth (during the dryer months), there usually is less water available than the growth and inflorescence of the crop would require (Figure 1).

Figure 1. Typical soil moisture patterns for the rain-fed wheat growing season in the eastern Mediterranean for wet, normal and dry years (Oweis, T. and A. Hachum, 2012)

©FAO/TECA

An adapted system and technology, to uphold even soil moisture levels and balance the scarcity of soil moisture in later growth stages, could provide the supplemental or additional provision of water to rain-fed agriculture by means of irrigation. This technology is called supplemental irrigation (SI). The technique consists of applying small quantities of water during critical periods to improve and stabilize yields, save water and balance low water availability with a sustainable production level. Supplemental irrigation (SI) is especially effective in very dry years, and it has been shown that it can even triple the yield when applying relatively small amounts of irrigation water.

Three aspects define supplemental irrigation (SI). 

  • Supplemental water is applied to a crop that usually yields without the need for irrigation.
  • Supplemental water is only added when there is a lack of rainfall and the water that usually is provided by rain is missing. It is a supplemental (additive) water provision to the common rainfall water provision.
  • Supplemental irrigation is meant to provide additional water in critical growth stages and not to ensure moisture stress-free conditions for the crop. Rather ensure that the minimum amount of water is available for the critical stages of crop growth. Little water stress to the crop in the early stages might even be beneficial for root formation.

1.1 How much of supplemental water?

Supplemental water is given to the crop in specific amounts during or before different growth stages. There are stages that are more and stages that are less susceptible to water deficits. Thus, it is important to understand how much and at which stage of crop growth supplemental irrigation water should be best applied. In general, one to three supplemental irrigation applications of not more than 100 mm each between late march and early may are recommended.

Research by The International Center for Agriculture Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) has shown that it is recommended to use deficit supplemental irrigation when there is not enough water available for full supplemental irrigation.

  • Applying SI, using 50 percent of the full SI requirements to the whole farm is more efficient than applying full SI to only half of the farm with the other half purely rain-fed. Yields are higher by around one third. 
  • One to two-thirds of the full amount of water that would be used when applying full irrigation is more efficient for water productivity. It is highly recommended to use only 33 to 66 percent of the full amount of irrigation water for a higher yield. Research conducted in Syria has shown these results, indicating that farmers usually tend to overuse their water resources.
Figure 2. Comparison between wheat grown with supplemental irrigation (left) and without additional irrigation (right) (Oweis, T. and A. Hachum, 2012)

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Timing

Applying supplemental irrigation also can help to ensure to sow wheat in early November, when the onset rainfall for sowing is missing. In the lowlands, it is recommended to sow in early to mid November and support it by supplemental irrigation when onset rainfall is missing. Also in the highlands, where the crop is dormant, it is beneficial for yields to proceed with SI, when early rain is missing. Here, only a good early crop stand can ensure survival during dormancy and increase water productivity.

Supplemental irrigation has to be adapted to the needs of the wheat crop. This means that supplemental irrigation should be added at the “right moment”, which is exactly before a critical growth stage and only when direct rainwater is missing or soil moisture is poor. The efficiency of water use with supplemental irrigation is much higher than when using constant irrigation. This saves scarce water resources and helps to increase crop yields at the same time.

1.3 Temporal planning

The exact date of SI application cannot be determined in advance, because it is supplemental in character. SI should be applied when soil moisture drops below critical levels. It is recommended to measure soil moisture on a regular basis, in order to be prepared for applying supplemental irrigation. Usually, farmers rely on their experience related to the crop appearance and the amount of rainfall. When there is water supply, they tend to irrigate more frequent than would be necessary, just to ensure that yields are stabilized. It is recommended to check national weather services for adapting supplemental irrigation to the actual rainfall predictions. A simple visual soil moisture assessment in the field could be appropriate to measure the day-to-day soil moisture.

1.4 Sources of irrigation water

The water used for supplemental irrigation can originate from groundwater sources like rivers and lakes, or surface water reservoirs. Also, water harvesting is a good source for irrigation water. Recently, wastewater has been tested for use in irrigated agriculture and supplemental irrigation.

Figure 3. Water-harvesting in surface reservoirs used for SI (Oweis, T. and A. Hachum, 2012)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Wastewater used for SI with a surface irrigation system (Oweis, T. and A. Hachum, 2012)

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Wastewater used for SI with a surface irrigation system

The general irrigation systems can be used for SI. The main difference with SI is the management of when and how much to irrigate, thus, the exact irrigation planning.

1.5.1 Systems commonly used for SI 

  • surface irrigation techniques, like basin, furrow and border irrigation 
  • sprinkler irrigation methods, for example, set systems, traveling guns and continuously moving systems 
  • trickle irrigation systems, comprising drip irrigation, micro-sprinklers and subsurface systems.

Surface systems are used in areas, where SI is applied only once or twice a year. Investments for these systems are low and if irrigation water is not too expensive, they are economically sound. Sprinkler systems are applied when water is expensive, labour costs high and the surface not suitable for a full irrigation system. Also, water harvesting structures are highly recommended as a water source. Macro- and micro water harvesting systems can be used for collecting water and storing it in surface tanks and or groundwater aquifers.

2. Supplemental irrigation in wheat production in Morocco

In Morocco, the technology of supplemental irrigation is applied during the growing season to overcome lack or delay of precipitation and by this sustain crop water needs. The quality and quantity of the crop is determined by supplemental irrigation since the country has undergone severe droughts since the 1980s.

2.1 Main crop growth stages and water requirements during the single stages

Nearly half of the crop production area of the Tadla region is used for cereals. In the last years, bread wheat production increased, with a concurrent decrease of durum wheat. The dominant rotation is wheat/sugar beet, with some cultivation of vegetable crops and alfalfa after cereals.

Growth periods of wheat occur between planting after the first rains in autumn (60 percent in December and 33 percent in January) and harvesting, which starts in May and can range till mid-June. The moisture in the grain should be around 10 percent, in order to be harvested. The whole cycle of crop growth endures around 160 days.

There are four different stages of crop growth that can be distinguished.

  1. Germination to the beginning of stem elongation: this is the stage from when the plant emerges from the seed until the seedling is established. Usually, the plant has three detectable tillers. The last stage of this main stage is also called the “tillering stage”.
  2. Beginning of stem elongation to the heading stage: this stage ranges from the beginning of the growth of the main stem of the crop to the inflorescence when blossoms are fully developed.
  3. From heading to milky grain stage: this is the period of plant growth, where the plant flowers and develops the fruits (grains). The milky grain stage is the first stage of the ripeness of the fruits (grains).
  4. The grain maturation stage: comprises the ripening, the maturing and the senescence of the fruit (grains).

2.2 Application of irrigation water in different stages of crop growth

  1. Vegetative stage (stage 1: Germination to the beginning of stem elongation): wheat crops are a little susceptible to drought in the first stage (germination to the beginning of stem elongation). The water absorption of the crop is slow and it is limited to the top 40 cm of the soil because the root is in a very young stage and it is not able to uptake the water that is deeper than 40 cm in the soil. The plant can tolerate a bit of water stress because it helps to stimulate root growth. After the root has grown deeper into the soil, it can easily reach water in deeper soil layers. That means that the wheat seedling can well resist drought and could rely on rainfall alone, the crop does not necessarily need supplemental irrigation in this stage.
  2. Reproductive stage (stages 2 and 3: Beginning of stem elongation to milky grain stage): the water requirement of the plant increases during the reproductive stage. This stage lies between the beginning of stem elongation and the flowering (stages 2 and 3). It usually coincides with moisture deficit during the dry springtime. The number of flowers determines the yield and so it is important to maintain a good provision of water for the crop at this stage of growth. Usually, the water is taken up in the top layer of the soil. For keeping the water in the soil and protect it from being evaporated a mulch cover might be of help. Also during the grain maturation stage (stage 4), water stress can have severe consequences for the grain yield. Especially, the first ten days of the grain maturation are important, otherwise, the grain shrivels, affecting the crop yield. Table 1 shows the duration of growth stages of wheat in Ouled Gnaou in Tadla. This is a research station, where the growth stages have been measured over 24 crop cycles. The wheat varieties used were semi to late bread wheat varieties and were planted between November 15 to January 15. Planting dates and the climatic conditions of the site have an effect on the duration of the growth stages. That means that it can take less days or more days for every stage, depending on the weather. In the Tadla region, this might lead to a different length of growth for the four stages:
  • from 54 to 72 days for stage 1 (germination to stem elongation);
  • from 22 to 44 days for stage 2 (beginning of stem elongation to heading);
  • from 24 to 39 days for stage 3 (heading to milky grain); and
  • from 24 to 44 days for stage 4 (grain maturation stage).
Table 1. The duration of different growth stages in wheat in Ouled Gnoua, Tadla, Morocco, in days

Source: Karrou, M., Oweis, T. and A. Bahri, 2011

2.3 How much water to supplement and when?

  • The amount of supplemental water is always dependent on the local average annual rainfall (mm per year) and the water requirements of the respective crop. There are some varieties that are adapted to water shortages by breeding.
  • At 60 mm supplemental irrigation, the best results occurred when irrigating at tillering stage (stage 1). Also at heading stage supplemental irrigation is more effective than when applied at the grain filling stage. 
  • The increase in yield is always very closely related to the growth stages in which the supplemental water is applied. Water that is given before the anthesis (flowering), has more effect on the yield than after anthesis.
  • The best way to apply supplemental water is to target the three critical stages of wheat growth: tillering (during stage 1), heading (end of stage 2) and grain filling (stage 4). 60 mm to 70 mm per stage should be applied.

  • At rainfall deficit early in the season, apply first irrigation at planting or during tillering (when plant is in the vegetative stage 1). To avoid rainfall deficit, plant early. Planting from mid-November to mid-December is recommended. General rule: if there is less than 35 mm rainwater during the first 10 days after planting (DAP), apply supplemental irrigation. 
  • Apply supplemental irrigation during booting-heading (stage 2), when the flowers start to be developed. At this stage, a water deficit could lead to high yield losses (up to 40 percent). 3. Some adapted cultural practices

There are some general practices that are important for improving the efficiency of supplemental irrigation. These practices should be applied additionally to supplemental irrigation.

3.1 Crop variety

Use more water-efficient varieties. Crop varieties should comply with specific criteria:

  • rapid vegetative development, as in a variety grows rapidly so that it can develop early fruits and needs less water in total;
  • high harvest index: Choose a variety that produces a large amount of yield compared with the total biomass produced; and
  • fitting the crop cycle with the rainy season, which means to plant early, in order to align plant growth with the wet months.

3.2 Sowing date

Early application of N-fertilizer is recommended so that it can be utilized with the soil moisture after planting. 4. Validation of the practice

The practice has been tested by farmers in on-farm trials in the context of the research project “Community-Based Optimization of the Management of Scarce Water Resources in Agriculture - Improving water and land productivities in rainfed systems in CWANA” in a benchmark site in Morocco. Complementary research satellite sites were established in Algeria, Syria and Tunisia.

The project was conducted by the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) and the National Institute of Agronomic Research (INRA) of Morocco. Further partners of the project were the Regional Agricultural Development Authority (Office régional de mise en valeur agricole) of Tadla (ORMVAT) and the Directorate for the Development and Management of Irrigation (DDGI). Financial support was provided by the Arab Fund for the Economic and Social Development, the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) and the OPEC Fund for International Development (OFID).

In 2004, an integrated research program was designed with the participation of the local population, institutions and decision-makers, to ensure the integration of new technologies into the local farming systems. During 2005, the selected sites and communities were characterized. The main constraints to the adoption by farmers of efficient water-use options were identified and analysed. Field trials were conducted in 2005, 2006 and 2007 and focused mainly on improving water productivity by introducing new technologies such as high-water-use efficient varieties, supplemental irrigation for some annual crops, deficit irrigation, and drip irrigation in citrus. Satellite sites were selected and used for complementary research in Algeria, Syria and Tunisia.

Morocco relies on a semiarid to an arid climate. Low and highly variable precipitation is one of the main characteristics of a changing climate. More frequent droughts, occurring during recent decades, have led to increased water insufficiency in the country.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Improved rainwater harvesting for fodder shrub production and livestock grazing: the Vallerani micro-catchment system in the Badia of Jordan: ID 8757.
  • Raised beds for improving crop water productivity and water efficiency in irrigated dryland agriculture: ID 8759.
  • Mini ponds for resource poor households to provide supplementary irrigation during drought spells: ID 6847.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology improves soil moisture levels through irrigation during dry periods. It also efficiently uses crop varieties, seeding rate and nitrogen application.

Supplemental irrigation for improved water use efficiency and productivity of wheat in rain-fed agriculture

Supplemental irrigation is used to uphold even soil moisture levels by irrigating the fields during critical and dry periods to balance the scarcity of soil moisture in later growth stages and save the crops. The exact amount of water added and timing are explained in this practice. Additionally, some examples of the application of supplemental irrigation such as in wheat production in Morocco are detailed. Finally, some general practices that are important for improving the efficiency of supplemental irrigation such as crop varieties, seeding rate and nitrogen application are explained.

Description

1. What is supplemental irrigation?

In rain-fed agriculture of semi-arid and arid regions, water is the most limiting factor. That entails the need for additional sources of water in case of lack of rainfall. Irrigation systems can help to solve the problem, but what if the sources for irrigation water are very limited? Usually, wheat crops do have little need for moisture in the early stages of growth (November to January). This is due to a low rate of water uptake when the seedling is young. Hence, during the early stages of crop growth throughout the winter months, there is more water through rainfall available than would be needed by the crop. At later stages of growth (during the dryer months), there usually is less water available than the growth and inflorescence of the crop would require (Figure 1).

Figure 1. Typical soil moisture patterns for the rain-fed wheat growing season in the eastern Mediterranean for wet, normal and dry years (Oweis, T. and A. Hachum, 2012)

©FAO/TECA

An adapted system and technology, to uphold even soil moisture levels and balance the scarcity of soil moisture in later growth stages, could provide the supplemental or additional provision of water to rain-fed agriculture by means of irrigation. This technology is called supplemental irrigation (SI). The technique consists of applying small quantities of water during critical periods to improve and stabilize yields, save water and balance low water availability with a sustainable production level. Supplemental irrigation (SI) is especially effective in very dry years, and it has been shown that it can even triple the yield when applying relatively small amounts of irrigation water.

Three aspects define supplemental irrigation (SI). 

  • Supplemental water is applied to a crop that usually yields without the need for irrigation.
  • Supplemental water is only added when there is a lack of rainfall and the water that usually is provided by rain is missing. It is a supplemental (additive) water provision to the common rainfall water provision.
  • Supplemental irrigation is meant to provide additional water in critical growth stages and not to ensure moisture stress-free conditions for the crop. Rather ensure that the minimum amount of water is available for the critical stages of crop growth. Little water stress to the crop in the early stages might even be beneficial for root formation.

1.1 How much of supplemental water?

Supplemental water is given to the crop in specific amounts during or before different growth stages. There are stages that are more and stages that are less susceptible to water deficits. Thus, it is important to understand how much and at which stage of crop growth supplemental irrigation water should be best applied. In general, one to three supplemental irrigation applications of not more than 100 mm each between late march and early may are recommended.

Research by The International Center for Agriculture Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) has shown that it is recommended to use deficit supplemental irrigation when there is not enough water available for full supplemental irrigation.

  • Applying SI, using 50 percent of the full SI requirements to the whole farm is more efficient than applying full SI to only half of the farm with the other half purely rain-fed. Yields are higher by around one third. 
  • One to two-thirds of the full amount of water that would be used when applying full irrigation is more efficient for water productivity. It is highly recommended to use only 33 to 66 percent of the full amount of irrigation water for a higher yield. Research conducted in Syria has shown these results, indicating that farmers usually tend to overuse their water resources.
Figure 2. Comparison between wheat grown with supplemental irrigation (left) and without additional irrigation (right) (Oweis, T. and A. Hachum, 2012)

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Timing

Applying supplemental irrigation also can help to ensure to sow wheat in early November, when the onset rainfall for sowing is missing. In the lowlands, it is recommended to sow in early to mid November and support it by supplemental irrigation when onset rainfall is missing. Also in the highlands, where the crop is dormant, it is beneficial for yields to proceed with SI, when early rain is missing. Here, only a good early crop stand can ensure survival during dormancy and increase water productivity.

Supplemental irrigation has to be adapted to the needs of the wheat crop. This means that supplemental irrigation should be added at the “right moment”, which is exactly before a critical growth stage and only when direct rainwater is missing or soil moisture is poor. The efficiency of water use with supplemental irrigation is much higher than when using constant irrigation. This saves scarce water resources and helps to increase crop yields at the same time.

1.3 Temporal planning

The exact date of SI application cannot be determined in advance, because it is supplemental in character. SI should be applied when soil moisture drops below critical levels. It is recommended to measure soil moisture on a regular basis, in order to be prepared for applying supplemental irrigation. Usually, farmers rely on their experience related to the crop appearance and the amount of rainfall. When there is water supply, they tend to irrigate more frequent than would be necessary, just to ensure that yields are stabilized. It is recommended to check national weather services for adapting supplemental irrigation to the actual rainfall predictions. A simple visual soil moisture assessment in the field could be appropriate to measure the day-to-day soil moisture.

1.4 Sources of irrigation water

The water used for supplemental irrigation can originate from groundwater sources like rivers and lakes, or surface water reservoirs. Also, water harvesting is a good source for irrigation water. Recently, wastewater has been tested for use in irrigated agriculture and supplemental irrigation.

Figure 3. Water-harvesting in surface reservoirs used for SI (Oweis, T. and A. Hachum, 2012)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Wastewater used for SI with a surface irrigation system (Oweis, T. and A. Hachum, 2012)

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Wastewater used for SI with a surface irrigation system

The general irrigation systems can be used for SI. The main difference with SI is the management of when and how much to irrigate, thus, the exact irrigation planning.

1.5.1 Systems commonly used for SI 

  • surface irrigation techniques, like basin, furrow and border irrigation 
  • sprinkler irrigation methods, for example, set systems, traveling guns and continuously moving systems 
  • trickle irrigation systems, comprising drip irrigation, micro-sprinklers and subsurface systems.

Surface systems are used in areas, where SI is applied only once or twice a year. Investments for these systems are low and if irrigation water is not too expensive, they are economically sound. Sprinkler systems are applied when water is expensive, labour costs high and the surface not suitable for a full irrigation system. Also, water harvesting structures are highly recommended as a water source. Macro- and micro water harvesting systems can be used for collecting water and storing it in surface tanks and or groundwater aquifers.

2. Supplemental irrigation in wheat production in Morocco

In Morocco, the technology of supplemental irrigation is applied during the growing season to overcome lack or delay of precipitation and by this sustain crop water needs. The quality and quantity of the crop is determined by supplemental irrigation since the country has undergone severe droughts since the 1980s.

2.1 Main crop growth stages and water requirements during the single stages

Nearly half of the crop production area of the Tadla region is used for cereals. In the last years, bread wheat production increased, with a concurrent decrease of durum wheat. The dominant rotation is wheat/sugar beet, with some cultivation of vegetable crops and alfalfa after cereals.

Growth periods of wheat occur between planting after the first rains in autumn (60 percent in December and 33 percent in January) and harvesting, which starts in May and can range till mid-June. The moisture in the grain should be around 10 percent, in order to be harvested. The whole cycle of crop growth endures around 160 days.

There are four different stages of crop growth that can be distinguished.

  1. Germination to the beginning of stem elongation: this is the stage from when the plant emerges from the seed until the seedling is established. Usually, the plant has three detectable tillers. The last stage of this main stage is also called the “tillering stage”.
  2. Beginning of stem elongation to the heading stage: this stage ranges from the beginning of the growth of the main stem of the crop to the inflorescence when blossoms are fully developed.
  3. From heading to milky grain stage: this is the period of plant growth, where the plant flowers and develops the fruits (grains). The milky grain stage is the first stage of the ripeness of the fruits (grains).
  4. The grain maturation stage: comprises the ripening, the maturing and the senescence of the fruit (grains).

2.2 Application of irrigation water in different stages of crop growth

  1. Vegetative stage (stage 1: Germination to the beginning of stem elongation): wheat crops are a little susceptible to drought in the first stage (germination to the beginning of stem elongation). The water absorption of the crop is slow and it is limited to the top 40 cm of the soil because the root is in a very young stage and it is not able to uptake the water that is deeper than 40 cm in the soil. The plant can tolerate a bit of water stress because it helps to stimulate root growth. After the root has grown deeper into the soil, it can easily reach water in deeper soil layers.   2. Reproductive stage (stages 2 and 3: Beginning of stem elongation to milky grain stage): the water requirement of the plant increases during the reproductive stage. This stage lies between the beginning of stem elongation and the flowering (stages 2 and 3). It usually coincides with moisture deficit during the dry springtime. The number of flowers determines the yield and so it is important to maintain a good provision of water for the crop at this stage of growth. Usually, the water is taken up in the top layer of the soil. For keeping the water in the soil and protect it from being evaporated a mulch cover might be of help. Also during the grain maturation stage (stage 4), water stress can have severe consequences for the grain yield. Especially, the first ten days of the grain maturation are important, otherwise, the grain shrivels, affecting the crop yield.   • from 22 to 44 days for stage 2 (beginning of stem elongation to heading);
  • from 24 to 39 days for stage 3 (heading to milky grain); and
  • from 24 to 44 days for stage 4 (grain maturation stage).

records.title: Technologie de la ruche Fonge
records.description:
La description

1. Introduction

Les abeilles ont toujours recherché un abri pouvant leur offrir les meilleures conditions de vie. Elles se sont très souvent refugiées tantôt dans des abris (ou ruches) naturels tels que les troncs d'arbres, les cavités rocheuses ou souterraines, les plafonds de maison, et toute sorte d'objets cavitaires abandonnés par l'homme.

Afin de tirer meilleur profit du travail de ces insectes sociaux, l'homme a essayé de reproduire l'habitat naturel des abeilles en fabriquant des ruches de toutes sortes en terre cuite, en raffia, en écorce d’arbre ou encore en bambou et en bois.

Nous pouvons aujourd’hui classer les différents modèles de ruches en trois grandes catégories.

    1. Les ruches traditionnelles ou indigènes.
      • Généralement longiforme, conique ou cylindrique.
      • Les rayons sont fixés par les abeilles aux parois internes de la ruche et ne sont donc pas interchangeable par l'apiculteur.
      • Ces ruches sont généralement en matériaux fragiles (paille, osier, etc.).
    2. Les ruches à barrettes dites améliorées ou «intermédiaires».
      • Les abeilles fixent leurs rayons à des barrettes, qui sont mobiles et interchangeables.
      • La plus connues est la ruche Kenyane qui est horizontale et trapézoïdale, mais l'on retrouve également la «Tanzanienne» ou «La Grande» qui sont de forme rectangulaire.
      • Généralement horizontale, elles se travaillent avec des partitions et l'agrandissement du volume de la ruche durant la miellée se fait en longueur.
      • Elles sont le plus souvent en planche, mais peuvent aussi être confectionnées avec d'autres matériaux tels que les bambous de raphia.
    3. Les ruches à cadres dites « modernes ».
      • Les abeilles fixent leurs rayons à des cadres (quatre côtés), qui sont mobiles et interchangeables.
      • Elles sont de forme carrée ou rectangulaire, et possèdent un corps moins volumineux que les précédentes.
      • L'agrandissement du volume de la ruche durant la miellée se fait alors par le haut via la pose d'une hausse contrairement aux précédents modèles (ruches verticales).
      • Parmi ces ruches, on peut citer entre autres le modèle Dadant et Langstroth.

Chacune de ces catégories présente aussi bien des avantages que des inconvénients, en fonction du biotope, du type d'abeilles, des conditions climatiques, etc.

La ruche Fonge, qui vous est présentée dans cette fiche ne rentre dans aucune de ces trois catégories. C'est une ruche intermédiaire entre le modèle Kenyane à barrettes et le modèle Dadant à cadres.

En passant de la ruche traditionnelle à la ruche Fonge mise sur pied dans le cadre des activités du GIC LUMICAM au Cameroun, le promoteur et ses associés ont bien voulu régler le problème de manipulation des ruches, lié à un environnement climatique très variable d'une zone à l'autre.  Cette ruche hybride est une ruche de synthèse qui intègre les avantages des autres types de ruches, tout en minimisant les inconvénients observés çà et là, tels que présentés dans le tableau ci-dessous.

Tableau 1. Avantages et inconvénients des ruches horizontales et ruches verticales

La ruche Fonge permet dès lors une amélioration du rendement apicole là où les autres types de ruches ont échoué.

2. Presentation de la ruche Fonge

2.1 Description de la ruche Fonge

La ruche Fonge est conçue pour être utilisée sans hausse ou avec une ou plusieurs hausses de type Dadant, le corps étant de forme «Kényane».

Figure 1. La Ruche Fonge sans hausse (A), avec une hausse (B) et avec deux hausses (C)

©FAO/GIC LUMICAM

Cette ruche se présente sous deux modèles:

    1. Le modèle FKm (= Fonge Kenyane modifié), avec des barrettes dans les hausses.
    2. Le modèle FDm (= Fonge Dadant modifié) portant des cadres dans les hausses.

Dans les deux modèles, le corps ne porte que des barrettes.

La ruche Fonge est donc constituée de deux parties:

    1. Un corps de type Kényan.
    2. Une ou plusieurs hausses de type Dadant, avec barrettes ou avec cadres.

Par ailleurs elle est utilisable aussi bien avec un extracteur à centrifugation (Modèle FDm) qu'avec un pressoir (Modèle FKm).

2.2 Comparaison de différents modèles de ruches

Tableau 2. Dimensions comparées de deux ruches horizontales kenyanes (KTBH): KTBH et KTBHm (KTBH modifiée)

Figure 2. Largeur de la ruche KTBH et KTBHm

©FAO/TECA

Nous notons ainsi que dans le modèle KTBH les barrettes reposent sur les parois antérieures et postérieures, alors que dans le modèle KTBHm les barrettes sont encastrées, assurant par le fait même une meilleure étanchéité (Figure 3). 

Figure 3. Position des barettes 

©FAO/TECA

Tableau 3. Dimensions comparées de deux modèles de ruches verticales à cadres 

Tableau 4. Dimensions comparées de deux modèles Fonge

Avec les ruches Fonge, la hauteur ne concerne que les cadres dans le modèle FDm. C'est pourquoi il n’y a pas de données pour la "hauteur" dans les ruches Fonge à barrettes (///).

Il y a une distance très importante à respecter dans n'importe quel modèle de ruche notamment la distance inter-axe des cadres ou des barrettes, c'est- à-dire la distance entre l'axe central d’une barrette (ou d'un cadre) et l'axe central de la barrette (ou du cadre) d'à côté.

Chez les abeilles africaines (Apis melifera adansonii), cette distance est de 33 mm (+/- 1 mm).  Nous préconisons donc une largeur des barrettes (non espacées) de 30 mm, car il y a toujours un petit espace de 1 à 2 mm peu visible. Lorsque vous voyez que la largeur des cadres (ou des barrettes) est de 20 mm, cela signifie que ceux-ci sont espacés de 13 mm.

La figure 4 présente la vérification illustrée de l'espace inter-axes entre les barrettes et les cadres.

Figure 4. Espace inter-axes entre les barrettes et les cadres

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Etude comparée des différentes ruches

Tableau 5. Comparaison des types de ruches par rapport à la production de cire brute, la consommation de cire par la ruche (c'est-à-dire: la quantité de feuilles de cire que l'apiculteur doit intégrer dans la ruche), le coût de production de la ruche, les compétences de l'apiculteur et la fréquence des récoltes.

(*) Sur la fréquence de 1 à 4: c’est possible seulement avec le modèle FDm et Dadant, portant de fortes colonies et situées dans un environnement richement mellifère.  Les prélèvements pourront alors se faire tous les 30 à 40 jours dans les hausses, tout en veillant à laisser une partie de réserves de miel à la colonie pour passer les périodes moins riches en fleurs.

Au Cameroun par exemple, les prélèvements peuvent se faire comme suit:

    • Novembre/décembre
    • Janvier/février
    • Avril/mai
    • Juin/juillet
Tableau 6. Comparaison des types de ruches par rapport à l'équipement d’extraction de miel, la complexité de construction de la ruche, l'utilisation des barrettes ou des cadres, la résistance à la transhumance, la zone géographique d’utilisation et l'utilisation nécessaire des ruchettes.

La Kényane, de même que le corps de la ruche Fonge, sont plus légers, mais ont une faible résistance à la transhumance, à cause de la fragilité des rayons qui sont sur barrettes.  Les rayons de cire chargés de miel ou de couvain peuvent facilement se détacher des barrettes avec les secousses du véhicule. Or les rayons sur cadres sont solidement attachés et ne risquent pas de se briser. Par contre les ruches Fonge avec hausse et Dadant restent plus lourdes que la Kényane.  Notons par ailleurs que le corps de ruche Fonge est parfois directement utilisé comme ruchette. Voire le chapitre 8 – Ruche Fonge et piégeage.

2.4 Spécificités de la ruche Fonge

Les figures 5 et 6 détaillent les spécificités de la ruche Fonge par rapport à la ruche Kényane (Fig. 5) et par rapport à la ruche Dadant (Fig. 6).

Figure 5. Spécificités de la ruche Fonge par rapport à la ruche kényane

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Spécificités de la ruche Fonge par rapport à la ruche Dadant

©FAO/TECA

2.5 Avantages et inconvénients de la ruche Fonge

2.5.1 Avantages

  • Par rapport à la ruche kényane, la ruche Fonge a un meilleur contrôle de la température dans le corps (d'où l'économie d'énergie pour les abeilles).
  • Par rapport à la ruche Dadant, la ruche Fonge n'utilise pas de grille à reine ce qui explique l'économie de temps et d'argent pour l'apiculteur.
  • Les conséquence positives sont un amélioration du rendement!

2.5.2 Inconvéniants

  • Comme ruche mixte, la ruche Fonge présente les inconvénients du corps de ruche kényane, et ceux de la hausse Dadant.
  • Voir le Tableau comparatif de l’introduction.

3. Materiaux et outils necessaires à la fabrication

3.1 Matériaux

Pour la fabrication de la ruche Fonge, nous avons besoin de:

    • bois local non traité, de bonne qualité (bien sec, non toxique et résistant aux intempéries et aux rongeurs), scié en planches de 30 cm sur 500 cm;
    • contreplaqué;
    • tôle lisse; et de
    • clous de 6 ou 7 cm, 4 cm et 2 cm.

Exemples d'essences forestières utilisées au Cameroun sont l’ayus, l'iroko, le fraqué, le sapin, le safoutier, etc.

3.2 Outils

Les outils couramment utilisés ont les suivants:

    • une scie à bois manuelle,
    • un rabot métallique,
    • un marteau,
    • des ciseaux à bois,
    • un crayon,
    • une règle, 
    • un mètre, 
    • equerre,
    • agrafeuse et agrafes.

Remarques :

  • Les clous de 6 ou 7 cm servent à fixer les parois du corps et de la hausse.
  • Les clous de 4 cm servent à la fixation des supports de calle. 
  • Les clous de 2 cm servent à fixer les calles de réglages sur les supports de calle, et les contreplaqués sur le toit.
  • Les tôles sont généralement agrafées, ou fixées avec les clous de 2cm.

4. Fiche technique de la ruche Fonge

Figure 7. Ruche Fonge avec hausse à barrettes (à gauche) et 2 hausses à cadres (à droite).

©FAO/TECA

4.1 Dimensions du corps et de la hausse du modèle FKm

Figure 8. Dimensions du corps et de la hausse - FKm

©FAO/TECA

4.2 Dimensions des barrettes

Figure 9. Dimensions des barrettes 

©FAO/TECA

4.3 Dimensions du corps et de la hausse du modèle FDm

Figure 10. Dimensions du corps et de la hausse - FDm

©FAO/TECA

4.4 Dimensions de la tôle d’espacement des cadres

Figure 11. Dimensions de la tôle d'espacement des cadres (crémaillère) 

La crémaillère ou tôle d’espacement des cadres, permet d’espacer correctement les cadres de la hausse à 1.5 cm entre eux. Les cadres seront « pendus » dans les intervalles comme illustré dans la Figure 12. Elle est généralement fabriquée en tôle, selon les dimensions indiquées ci-dessous. La crémaillère s’installe à l’aide d’agrafes sur les calles de réglage des barrettes.

Figure 12. Tôle d'espacement des cadres (crémaillère) installée sur une ruche

4.5 Dimensions des cadres de la hausse - FDm

Figure 13. Dimensions des cadre de la hausse - FDm

©FAO/TECA

4.6 Dimensions des parois du corps de la ruche

Figure 14. Dimensions des parois de corps de ruche

©FAO/TECA

4.7 Dimensions du support de calle et la calle de réglage des barrettes

Figure 15.  Dimensions du support de calle et calle de réglage des barrettes

©FAO/TECA

Figure 16. Support de calle et calle de réglage des barrettes installés sur la ruche

 

Le support de calle est fixé verticalement par des clous de 5 cm sur les parois antrérieures et postérieures du corps de ruche. La calle est ensuite fixée par des clous de 2 cm sur ces supports, à 1,5 cm du bord (Figure 16).

 

4.8 Dimensions des éléments du toit de la ruche

Figure 17. Compsantes du toit et ses dimensions

©FAO/TECA

5. Fabrication de la ruche Fonge

Les différentes étapes de la fabrication de la ruche Fonge sont les suivantes:

    • Rabotage et découpage des planches
    • Affûtage des côtés
    • Affûtage des barrettes
    • Rangement des différentes pièces
    • Assemblage des pièces
    • Peinture et numérotation éventuelles des ruches

Figure 18 illustre chacune des étapes de la construction de la ruche Fonge.

Figure 18. Etapes de la constructoin de la ruche Fonge

©FAO/TECA

Figure 19. Recapitulatif sur l'assemblage du corps de ruche

©FAO/TECA

6. Installation de la ruche

Pour installer les ruches, il est idéal que l’entrée des abeilles soit dirigée vers l'Est ou vers l’Ouest, afin d'être exposée aux rayons solaires au lever ou au coucher du soleil.

De préférence le rucher sera implanté sous un léger ombrage arboré, non loin d'une source d'eau, et à 20 m au moins des habitations ou des lieux de passages fréquents.  Le cas échéant, une barrière en fils barbelés limitera l'accès des animaux.

Enfin un «PANNEAU DANGER» indiquera clairement la présence du rucher.

Figure 20. Ruche Fonge installée dans un rucher

©FAO/TECA

7. Pose de la hausse

La pose de la hausse se fait comme l'illustre Figure 21. La libération des espaces sur les côtés se fait en recentrant les barrettes, afin de diviser en deux l'espace laissé par la barrette supprimée.  Ce sont ces espaces sur les côtés qui permettent l'accès des ouvrières à la hausse, alors que la reine reste sur les barrettes centrales.  La grille à reine n'est plus nécessaire ici!

Figure 21. La pose de la hausse sur la ruche Fonge

©FAO/TECA

Attention: il faut veilliez à vérifier que la reine ne se trouve pas sur le rayon enlevé.  

8. Ruche fonge et piégeage

Certains apiculteurs utilisent des ruchettes qu'ils accrochent sur des arbustes pour piéger et capturer facilement les abeilles, pour ensuite les transférer dans les ruches de production.

Or la ruche Fonge, par sa taille moyenne, peut être utilisée à la fois comme ruche de capture et ruche de production.  Dans ce cas, elle est accrochée aux branches d'un arbuste, à 2 ou 3 m environ du sol.

Figure 22. Ruche Fonge utilisée comme ruche de capture 

©FAO/TECA

Nous utilisons aussi des ruchettes (cinq à sept barrettes), mais il faut toujours transférer par la suite la colonie de la ruchette à la ruche définitive, ce qui prend du temps, avec en plus le risque de perdre la reine au cours de l'opération.

L'avantage d'utiliser la ruche Fonge en capture (sans hausse) est la suppression de la phase de transfert. Il y a donc moins de manipulations et la colonie capturée a plus de chance de survivre.

Figure 23. Des ruche Fonge avec une hausse prêtes pour leur installation au rucher

©FAO/TECA

Voir les échanges autour de ce modèle dans la discussion lancée le 22/08/2016 intitulée: "Découverte de la ruche FONGE, un modèle intermédiaire entre la KTBH à barrettes et la Dadant à cadres".

9. Récolte du miel

L’extraction du miel de la ruche FKm se fera par pression (à l'aide d'un pressoir) ou par égouttage du miel préalablement broyé, en utilisant un tissu du genre moustiquaire.  

L’extraction du miel de la ruche FDm se fera par centrifugation en utilisant un extracteur centrifuge.  

Après extraction, les cadres bâtis peuvent être retournés à la ruche (en saison) ou bien laissés à nettoyer par les abeilles (lécher le miel) et puis rangés dans la hausse.  Il est conseillé de tasser les hausses avec cadres sur des blocs avec une toile moustiquaire en dessous et au-dessus de la dernière hausse (pour éviter aux insectes ou autres petits animaux de se cacher dans les hausses), dans un endroit ventilé pour éviter l’attaque de la fausse teigne.  Les hausses doivent être protégés du soleil.

Figure 24. Récolte des gâteaux de miel d’une ruche FKm et des cadres d’une ruche FDm.

10. Les zones agro-écologiques

  • Tropiques, chaud.

11. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Fabrication d'une ruche Kenyane trapézoidale à barettes: ID 8707.
  • Comment fabriquer une ruche a barrettes en Nkoko: ID 8745.
  • Comment fabriquer une ruche a barrettes «la grande»: ID 8744.
  • Fabrication d’une ruche traditionnelle Rwandaise longiforme: ID 8750.

12. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

12.1 L'efficacité d'utilisation des ressources

Cette fiche technique présente une comparaison efficace entre différents modèles de ruche et explique les plans et les détails de fabrication de la ruche Fonge.

12.2 Favorable aux populations pauvres

Par la fabrication de ruche améliorée, la technologie permet à une gestion de colonie d'abeilles plus saine et une récolte de produits plus abondante.

_annotations.body:
Technologie de la ruche Fonge

Cette fiche technique présente la ruche Fonge qui est un modèle de ruche intermédiaire entre la ruche à barrettes modèle Kenyane et la ruche à cadres modèle Dadant. Ce modèle a été mis en place et expérimenté sur le terrain par le Groupe d'Initiative Locale Camerounais «Apiculture Lumière du Cameroun» (GIC LUMICAM). Le modèle ayant fait ses preuves, il a commencé à être vulgarisé au Cameroun par le GIC LUMICAM. Christophe Fonge a le plaisir de nous la présenter à travers cette fiche technique. Celle-ci reprend une comparaison entre différents modèles de ruche, les plans et les détails de fabrication de la ruche Fonge. Bonne découverte.



La description

1. Introduction

Les abeilles ont toujours recherché un abri pouvant leur offrir les meilleures conditions de vie. Elles se sont très souvent refugiées tantôt dans des abris (ou ruches) naturels tels que les troncs d'arbres, les cavités rocheuses ou souterraines, les plafonds de maison, et toute sorte d'objets cavitaires abandonnés par l'homme.

Afin de tirer meilleur profit du travail de ces insectes sociaux, l'homme a essayé de reproduire l'habitat naturel des abeilles en fabriquant des ruches de toutes sortes en terre cuite, en raffia, en écorce d’arbre ou encore en bambou et en bois.

Nous pouvons aujourd’hui classer les différents modèles de ruches en trois grandes catégories.

    1. Les ruches traditionnelles ou indigènes.
      • Généralement longiforme, conique ou cylindrique.
      • Les rayons sont fixés par les abeilles aux parois internes de la ruche et ne sont donc pas interchangeable par l'apiculteur.
      • Ces ruches sont généralement en matériaux fragiles (paille, osier, etc.).
    2. Les ruches à barrettes dites améliorées ou «intermédiaires».
      • Les abeilles fixent leurs rayons à des barrettes, qui sont mobiles et interchangeables.
      • La plus connues est la ruche Kenyane qui est horizontale et trapézoïdale, mais l'on retrouve également la «Tanzanienne» ou «La Grande» qui sont de forme rectangulaire.
      • Généralement horizontale, elles se travaillent avec des partitions et l'agrandissement du volume de la ruche durant la miellée se fait en longueur.
      • Elles sont le plus souvent en planche, mais peuvent aussi être confectionnées avec d'autres matériaux tels que les bambous de raphia.
    3. Les ruches à cadres dites « modernes ».
      • Les abeilles fixent leurs rayons à des cadres (quatre côtés), qui sont mobiles et interchangeables.
      • Elles sont de forme carrée ou rectangulaire, et possèdent un corps moins volumineux que les précédentes.
      • L'agrandissement du volume de la ruche durant la miellée se fait alors par le haut via la pose d'une hausse contrairement aux précédents modèles (ruches verticales).
      • Parmi ces ruches, on peut citer entre autres le modèle Dadant et Langstroth.

Chacune de ces catégories présente aussi bien des avantages que des inconvénients, en fonction du biotope, du type d'abeilles, des conditions climatiques, etc.

La ruche Fonge, qui vous est présentée dans cette fiche ne rentre dans aucune de ces trois catégories. C'est une ruche intermédiaire entre le modèle Kenyane à barrettes et le modèle Dadant à cadres.

En passant de la ruche traditionnelle à la ruche Fonge mise sur pied dans le cadre des activités du GIC LUMICAM au Cameroun, le promoteur et ses associés ont bien voulu régler le problème de manipulation des ruches, lié à un environnement climatique très variable d'une zone à l'autre.  Cette ruche hybride est une ruche de synthèse qui intègre les avantages des autres types de ruches, tout en minimisant les inconvénients observés çà et là, tels que présentés dans le tableau ci-dessous.

Tableau 1. Avantages et inconvénients des ruches horizontales et ruches verticales

La ruche Fonge permet dès lors une amélioration du rendement apicole là où les autres types de ruches ont échoué.

2. Presentation de la ruche Fonge

2.1 Description de la ruche Fonge

La ruche Fonge est conçue pour être utilisée sans hausse ou avec une ou plusieurs hausses de type Dadant, le corps étant de forme «Kényane».

Figure 1. La Ruche Fonge sans hausse (A), avec une hausse (B) et avec deux hausses (C)

©FAO/GIC LUMICAM

Cette ruche se présente sous deux modèles:

    1. Le modèle FKm (= Fonge Kenyane modifié), avec des barrettes dans les hausses.
    2. Le modèle FDm (= Fonge Dadant modifié) portant des cadres dans les hausses.

Dans les deux modèles, le corps ne porte que des barrettes.

La ruche Fonge est donc constituée de deux parties:

    1. Un corps de type Kényan.
    2. Une ou plusieurs hausses de type Dadant, avec barrettes ou avec cadres.

Par ailleurs elle est utilisable aussi bien avec un extracteur à centrifugation (Modèle FDm) qu'avec un pressoir (Modèle FKm).

©FAO/TECA

6. Installation de la ruche

Pour installer les ruches, il est idéal que l’entrée des abeilles soit dirigée vers l'Est ou vers l’Ouest, afin d'être exposée aux rayons solaires au lever ou au coucher du soleil.

De préférence le rucher sera implanté sous un léger ombrage arboré, non loin d'une source d'eau, et à 20 m au moins des habitations ou des lieux de passages fréquents.  Le cas échéant, une barrière en fils barbelés limitera l'accès des animaux.

Enfin un «PANNEAU DANGER» indiquera clairement la présence du rucher.

Figure 20. Ruche Fonge installée dans un rucher

©FAO/TECA

7. Pose de la hausse

La pose de la hausse se fait comme l'illustre Figure 21. La libération des espaces sur les côtés se fait en recentrant les barrettes, afin de diviser en deux l'espace laissé par la barrette supprimée.  Ce sont ces espaces sur les côtés qui permettent l'accès des ouvrières à la hausse, alors que la reine reste sur les barrettes centrales.  La grille à reine n'est plus nécessaire ici!

Figure 21. La pose de la hausse sur la ruche Fonge

©FAO/TECA

Attention: il faut veilliez à vérifier que la reine ne se trouve pas sur le rayon enlevé.  

8. Ruche fonge et piégeage

Certains apiculteurs utilisent des ruchettes qu'ils accrochent sur des arbustes pour piéger et capturer facilement les abeilles, pour ensuite les transférer dans les ruches de production.

Or la ruche Fonge, par sa taille moyenne, peut être utilisée à la fois comme ruche de capture et ruche de production.  Dans ce cas, elle est accrochée aux branches d'un arbuste, à 2 ou 3 m environ du sol.

Figure 22. Ruche Fonge utilisée comme ruche de capture 

©FAO/TECA

Nous utilisons aussi des ruchettes (cinq à sept barrettes), mais il faut toujours transférer par la suite la colonie de la ruchette à la ruche définitive, ce qui prend du temps, avec en plus le risque de perdre la reine au cours de l'opération.

L'avantage d'utiliser la ruche Fonge en capture (sans hausse) est la suppression de la phase de transfert. Il y a donc moins de manipulations et la colonie capturée a plus de chance de survivre.

Figure 23. Des ruche Fonge avec une hausse prêtes pour leur installation au rucher

©FAO/TECA

Voir les échanges autour de ce modèle dans la discussion lancée le 22/08/2016 intitulée: "Découverte de la ruche FONGE, un modèle intermédiaire entre la KTBH à barrettes et la Dadant à cadres".

9. Récolte du miel

L’extraction du miel de la ruche FKm se fera par pression (à l'aide d'un pressoir) ou par égouttage du miel préalablement broyé, en utilisant un tissu du genre moustiquaire.  

L’extraction du miel de la ruche FDm se fera par centrifugation en utilisant un extracteur centrifuge.  

Après extraction, les cadres bâtis peuvent être retournés à la ruche (en saison) ou bien laissés à nettoyer par les abeilles (lécher le miel) et puis rangés dans la hausse.  Il est conseillé de tasser les hausses avec cadres sur des blocs avec une toile moustiquaire en dessous et au-dessus de la dernière hausse (pour éviter aux insectes ou autres petits animaux de se cacher dans les hausses), dans un endroit ventilé pour éviter l’attaque de la fausse teigne.  Les hausses doivent être protégés du soleil.

Figure 24. Récolte des gâteaux de miel d’une ruche FKm et des cadres d’une ruche FDm.

10. Les zones agro-écologiques

  • Tropiques, chaud.

11. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Fabrication d'une ruche Kenyane trapézoidale à barettes: ID 8707.
  • Comment fabriquer une ruche a barrettes en Nkoko: ID 8745.
  • Comment fabriquer une ruche a barrettes «la grande»: ID 8744.
  • Fabrication d’une ruche traditionnelle Rwandaise longiforme: ID 8750.

12. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

12.1 L'efficacité d'utilisation des ressources

Cette fiche technique présente une comparaison efficace entre différents modèles de ruche et explique les plans et les détails de fabrication de la ruche Fonge.

12.2 Favorable aux populations pauvres

Par la fabrication de ruche améliorée, la technologie permet à une gestion de colonie d'abeilles plus saine et une récolte de produits plus abondante.

records.title: Raising chicken without grain: the integrated compost and poultry system
records.description:
Description

The system is a modified trailer. The components are a mobile chicken coop with nesting boxes and perches, a movable exterior fence, an automatic waterer, and a dust bath.

The chicken coop is a converted utility trailer, still on its wheels. The trailer is therefore mobile. Surrounding the trailer is a simple, movable fence to keep the chickens confined. Within this confine are four piles of compost. A new pile of compost is built every week. Each week the trailer and mobile fencing are moved forward by four meters, and a new pile of compost is built. Every week, each pile of compost is turned once using a pitchfork or shovel; therefore, each pile is turned a total of four times over a span of four weeks. Between turnings, the chickens are active in scratching and feeding on the food scraps and insects in the compost pile. The total time of creating the compost is four to five weeks. Figure 1 gives an overview of the system.

This diet of chickens is different from that of chickens on many modern farms that have a diet consisting largely of grains, vitamin supplements, and mineral supplements. Pellets are also often used and are synthetically made. Many farmers, especially in developing countries, do not have access to buy these pellets or any commercial feed for their chickens and the cost can be prohibitive, even if such resources are available. In contrast, the approach described here uses materials that may otherwise be discarded as waste. The integrated chicken and compost system is a method both low in cost and environmentally sustainable. Food scraps, manure, and mulch are used for feed and can all be obtained from the farm. Alternatively, if not enough food scraps are generated by the farm, they may be cheaply bought from restaurants or markets

Figure 1. Overview of the system. By the fifth week (four turns total), the compost can be used back into the garden

©FAO/TECA

1. The Trailer

The first step is to build the trailer that houses the hens and contains the nesting boxes. The trailer can be any utility trailer that is worn out or is no longer suitable for the road. A frame is built around the trailer to form the walls of the housing unit, and a roof is constructed over the top. Inside the trailer, an additional movable frame of perches is built. This perch frame can be folded up to the roof to create more space inside to facilitate the cleaning of the trailer. The floor of the trailer, under the perches, is lined with mulch as bedding and to collect the chicken manure. Mulch is any chopped grassy or herbaceous material that can be found; common mulches include straw, weedy grasses, wood chips and old leaves. New mulch is put in the trailer every week, and the old mulch is put into the compost piles, which will be described later in this article.

1.1 The Perches

The perches give the chickens a place to roost and sleep. The perches need to give the chickens adequate space and should be spaced apart by the stretch of a man’s hand, from thumb to pinky, in order for the chickens to perch comfortably. This is usually around 20 cm x 20 cm to 25 cm x 25 cm per bird, but can vary depending on the breed. Depending on the size of the trailer, the number of perches and the length of each perch may vary.

Figure 2. The foldable perch can be pushed up to make more space in the trailer and to facilitate the cleaning of the trailer. The frame consists of 6 perches

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Nesting Boxes

Nesting boxes are where the chickens lay their eggs. In this case they are built on both sides of the trailer. This gives the chicken the freedom to choose which sides she wants to lay her eggs for maximal comfort. The box should have a removable lid so that the farmer can reach in to clean the box and take the eggs out. The bottom of the nesting box needs to be lined with straw, pine shavings, or similar materials for the comfort of the chickens and to keep the eggs laid in place.

The size of the nesting boxes should be just enough space for one chicken to prevent the hens from stepping over each other and potentially breaking the eggs. Generally, a nesting box is a cube with dimensions of 30 cm × 30 cm × 30 cm. This will ensure enough space for one bird to comfortably lay her egg without interruption.

There is a wide range of watering systems. Here we propose two ways to build your own automatic water system for the birds. One is the called the PVC (plastic) Waterer and the other is the Glass Jar Waterer. Both of these methods will work well for any chicken but depending on resources available, one may be easier than the other to make.

Figure 3. The view of inside the trailer from the back

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Glass jar waterer

Supplies:

  • A glass canning jar with an airtight lid (approximately 15 to 25 cm in diameter);
  • glass or plastic bowl: diameter of bowl should be 10 to 15 cm wider than diameter of jar to ensure space for the chickens’ heads, and 5 to 10 cm inches in height; and 
  • an electric drill to make a hole in theglass jar.
Figure 4. Glass jar waterer

©FAO/TECA

The first step in creating the glass waterer is to set the jar in the bowl and make a mark on the glass jar at the height of the bowl top. With a halve inch (13 mm) drill bit, carefully drill one hole on the side of the glass jar below the marked height. When drilling the hole, make sure you wear long sleeves, protective glasses and other protective clothing as necessary as the glass in rare cases may break when drilling.

Once a hole has successfully been made, rinse and clean the jar to get rid of any glass residue. This will make sure that the chickens won’t be harmed by glass shards or sharp edges.

While you fill the canning jar with water, put a thumb where the hole is to prevent water from flowing out. Put the lid on the jar and transport the entire jar to the glass bowl. Once the jar is inside the bowl and set on the bottom, you can release your thumb and water will flow out until the hole is covered.

To clean or refill the bowl, you can simply take the jar directly out of the bowl and tilt it back with the hole facing up to prevent spillage of water. Once the cleaning and refill is done, just put it back into the bowl and it is ready for reuse!

2. PVC waterer

Supplies:

  • a PVC bucket with lid;
  • a flowerpot base (bowl): 7 to 8 cm wider than bucket diameter, and 7 to 10 cm inches in height; and
  • an electric drill (1/2 inch (13 mm) drill bit).

The steps to make a PVC waterer is similar to making a glass waterer, but the bucket (with the lid) is upside down. First, flip the bucket upside down and put the bucket into the flower pot base and make a mark on the bucket at the flower pot base height. Below the line, drill a hole on the side. Once the hole is drilled, rinse the bucket to get rid of any plastic residue.

Take the bucket and fill it up with water before putting the lid on. When the lid is put on tightly, flip the bucket upside down and put it in the flower pot base. The water should fill up and stop once the drilled hole is covered.

When the water level becomes low in the bucket, un-flip the bucket, remove the lid, and refill the bucket again. Once it has been refilled, put the bucket back into the base and it is ready to be used again.

Figure 5. Automatic watering system hanging off the roof of the trailer

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Small gravity pressure keeps the water supply full for the birds

©FAO/TECA

3. Shell grit

Shell grit is an important supplement for all chickens. They use it to help grind their food which improves their digestion. It has a similar function as teeth (which chickens do not have). As the chickens get older, the grit can be coarser. Place a small container of grit near their water. There are many types of grit available and can be: baked and crushed eggshells, crushed snail or oyster shells or even limestone.

4. Dust bath

The dust bath is important for the wellbeing of the animal because it reduces parasites such as mites and lice from living in the chickens' feathers and on their legs. A dust bath is a container, crate, or tray with the dust bath inside, and placed just underneath the trailer for the chickens to have access to it when they want. Keep it out of the rain so that it is clean and dry.

Paddock mulch is used at the Permaculture Research Institute but there are also other ways to make a dust bath for the chickens. For instance, one method of making a dust bath is by combining the builder’s sand, wood ash, soil (make sure it is fertilizer, chemical and vermiculite free), and diatomaceous earth (FOOD-GRADE and not for use in pools). If diatomaceous earth is difficult to obtain, you can mix sand, peat, and wood ashes (optional) to create a dust bath as well.

5. Fence

A fence surrounds the trailer and the four heaps of compost. It prevents the chickens from running into the field, attacking vulnerable vegetable crops and offers limited protection from predators. The fence needs to be easily removable since the trailer is moved once a week. Every week, the last pile of compost (four weeks old) will be left outside the fence for use as a source of organic matter and fertilizer. Just like the movement of the trailer, the fence moves forward by 4 m every week.

6. Compost

Behind the trailer is where the compost is made. A detachable metal cage (2 m x 2 m) with an open top and bottom is used to hold the compost together. The bottom layer is mulch taken from the trailer that has been defecated on by the birds from the week prior. The middle layer is manure, which can be obtained from the farm as well. Finally, food scraps are added to the top to feed the chickens. Each layer should be 0.5 cubic meters in volume to reach a result of 1.5 cubic meters of compost. Every day, food scraps are to be added to the top of the active heap in order to feed the chickens. Below is a photo of how the compost is layered.

Figure 7. The layers of the compost. Mulch on the bottom, manure in the middle, and food scraps on the top. Food scraps are added on top of the active pile each morning

©FAO/TECA

One week later, the cage is disassembled, the trailer moves forward by 4 m, and the cage is reassembled again between the trailer and the newest compost pile. Then each of the four compost piles behind the trailer is turned, including the very last pile that is now outside the fence and ready for use. The average time for a turn is around 20 to 45 minutes for each pile depending on physical abilities and experience in turning. In total, four piles are turned every week, and the last pile is ready to go back into the garden after the last turn.

The process of the composting event repeats itself week by week. With this system, new compost is made weekly and materials within the farm are continuously being recycled.

Note that the compost for the chicken feed needs to be adequately moistened. In wet climates, roofing may be needed to prevent too much moisture, whereas, in dryer climates, it would require regular watering as the decomposition process slows down or can even stop if the pile gets too dry.

No additional feed is required for the chicken as the compost pile provides enough food for the birds in the system. However, it is important to ensure that the food scraps are diverse so they receive the necessary vitamins and minerals.

7. Results

By checking on your chickens every day to make sure that they are getting their food and water and turning the compost piles once a week, there is not much work required to maintain this system. The chickens will continue to grow and produce eggs. Once they are old enough (four weeks or more depending on the breed), you can continue to keep them in the system to produce more eggs or choose to slaughter them for food.

8. Other things to note

  • It may take five weeks to complete the composting process depending on how quickly everything is decomposing and on weather conditions.
  • Some fruits and vegetables are better for chickens than others so it is important to know what kind of food scraps to include in the feed. Examples below:

8.1 Food to feed your chicken

  • corn or other locally available grains
  • apples
  • berries
  • melons
  • oatmeal
  • peas
  • cassava
  • banana
  • bread (in moderation)
  • most cooked or raw vegetables including broccoli, carrots, cabbage, chard, cucumbers, kale, lettuce, pumpkins, spinach, squash, sweet potatoes, and tomatoes.

8.2 Food to avoid feeding your chickens

  • Avocado pits and skin (flesh ok)
  • raw potato peels
  • coffee
  • chocolate
  • anything too salty
  • raw eggs
  • dry or undercooked beans
  • plants from the nightshade family: potatoes, tomatoes, eggplants.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Improved practices in rearing indigenous chickens: ID 6921.
  • Small-scale chicken production: ID 6949.
  • Improved chicken breeds raised with vaccination: ID 8941.
  • Replicas of native chicken in rural poultry production: the Satpuda: ID 7680.

This technology is also available in Spanish: ID 8915.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

  • Women-friendly; and 
  • Pro-poor technology.

Raising chicken without grain: the integrated compost and poultry system

The integrated compost and poultry system is a farming method that combines composting, poultry raising, and egg production. It is a low-cost method to raise chickens while producing good quality compost. Feed costs are almost eliminated because food scraps, manure, and mulch are used for feed – all of which can be obtained from either the same farm or sourced cheaply from nearby restaurants or markets. These birds are fed a zero-grain diet and are comparatively more robust and toned than grain-fed chickens. The number of eggs produced from compost-fed chickens is the same, if not more (by up to a third) than that of grain-fed chickens. The protein content in the chicken feed is high and very good quality compost is made from this system. The system explained in this technology employs a trailer that provides housing for the protection of predators, collection of eggs, and capture of feces of the chicken to enrich the compost. An automatic watering system ensures that there is always enough water for the birds to keep them hydrated. The resulting compost is rich in nutrients and is recycled into vegetable gardens that produce high-quality fruits and vegetables. This system is designed for about 36 adult birds because the chicken coop (a repurposed trailer) has six perches; each perch holds six chickens. The chickens have the option to lay their eggs on two different sides of the trailer where they are housed. Note that the compost for the chicken feed needs to be adequately moistened. In wet climates, roofing may be needed to prevent too much moisture, whereas, in dryer climates, it would require regular watering as the decomposition process slows down or can even stop if the pile gets too dry.

No additional feed is required for the chicken as the compost pile provides enough food for the birds in the system. However, it is important to ensure that the food scraps are diverse so they receive the necessary vitamins and minerals.

7. Results

By checking on your chickens every day to make sure that they are getting their food and water and turning the compost piles once a week, there is not much work required to maintain this system. The chickens will continue to grow and produce eggs. Once they are old enough (four weeks or more depending on the breed), you can continue to keep them in the system to produce more eggs or choose to slaughter them for food.

8. Other things to note

  • It may take five weeks to complete the composting process depending on how quickly everything is decomposing and on weather conditions.
  • Some fruits and vegetables are better for chickens than others so it is important to know what kind of food scraps to include in the feed. Examples below:

8.1 Food to feed your chicken

  • corn or other locally available grains
  • apples
  • berries
  • melons
  • oatmeal
  • peas
  • cassava
  • banana
  • bread (in moderation)
  • most cooked or raw vegetables including broccoli, carrots, cabbage, chard, cucumbers, kale, lettuce, pumpkins, spinach, squash, sweet potatoes, and tomatoes.

8.2 Food to avoid feeding your chickens

  • Avocado pits and skin (flesh ok)
  • raw potato peels
  • coffee
  • chocolate
  • anything too salty
  • raw eggs
  • dry or undercooked beans
  • plants from the nightshade family: potatoes, tomatoes, eggplants.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Improved practices in rearing indigenous chickens: ID 6921.
  • Small-scale chicken production: ID 6949.
  • Improved chicken breeds raised with vaccination: ID 8941.
  • Replicas of native chicken in rural poultry production: the Satpuda: ID 7680.

This technology is also available in Spanish: ID 8915.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

  • Women-friendly; and 
  • Pro-poor technology.
