_annotations.field_innovation_identified:
INNOVATION: Integrated Compost and Poultry System (ICPS)

Description: A low-cost, zero-grain poultry farming method combining composting with chicken raising. Uses a modified mobile trailer housing system where chickens feed on compost materials, eliminating commercial feed costs while producing eggs and high-quality compost.

Criteria met: It's a modified solution solving multiple problems (feed costs, waste management, sustainable farming) and improves existing processes by creating a circular system. Particularly suitable for resource-constrained contexts.
_annotations.field_shorter_description:
The integrated compost and poultry system is a farming method that combines composting, poultry raising, and egg production. It is a low-cost method to raise chickens while producing good quality compost. Feed costs are almost eliminated because food scraps, manure, and mulch are used for feed – all of which can be obtained from either the same farm or sourced cheaply from nearby restaurants or markets. These birds are fed a zero-grain diet and are comparatively more robust and toned than grain-fed chickens. The number of eggs produced from compost-fed chickens is the same, if not more (by up to a third) than that of grain-fed chickens. The protein content in the chicken feed is high and very good quality compost is made from this system. The system explained in this technology employs a trailer that provides housing for the protection of predators, collection of eggs, and capture of feces of the chicken to enrich the compost. An automatic watering system ensures that there is always enough water for the birds to keep them hydrated. The resulting compost is rich in nutrients and is recycled into vegetable gardens that produce high-quality fruits and vegetables. This system is designed for about 36 adult birds because the chicken coop (a repurposed trailer) has six perches; each perch holds six chickens. 

The chickens have the option to lay their eggs on two different sides of the trailer where they are housed. Depending on the breed and the age of the birds, in four weeks’ time, this system will produce a high amount of quality compost, over 200 eggs, and robust chickens that can continue to produce eggs or be processed for food.

records.title: Traditional floating garden practices for seedling production
records.description:
Description

1. Introduction

The floating garden practice is a local indigenous production system most successful in the wetland/submerged areas of selected south and south-western districts (Pirojpur, Barisal and Gopalganj) of Bangladesh. These areas remain submerged for long periods, especially in the monsoon season. Floating garden agricultural practices have been adopted by local farmers for nearly centuries ago. They are amongst the many options developed by local farmers to provide a growing area for poor communities who lack access to land during the period when wetlands are submerged underwater (generally for seven to eight months of the year).

One type of floating beds for floating garden agricultural practices is used mainly for seedling production of different vegetables (bottle gourd, pumpkin, cucumber, bitter gourd, papaya, etc.) and spices (chili, bombai chili, etc.) for marketing during monsoon season (usually from June to October month). This system is traditionally practiced in the wetland/submerged areas of Pirojpur (Nazirpur and Nesarabad sub-districts) and some part of Barisal (Banaripara sub-district) districts. The seedlings produced under this method are generally used for subsequent vegetables/spices production on normal land in the southern and south-western regions of Bangladesh.

Another type of floating bed for floating garden agriculture practices is used as an alternative method for vegetable production during the monsoon season. For a detailed description of this practice please refer to Traditional floating garden practices for vegetable production. 

2. Implementation of the technology

2.1 Construction of floating bed for seedling production

  • The floating bed for seedling production is prepared directly on the water body (water depth 1 m or more) usually by using water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes), dulalilata (Hygroryza aristata) and tapapana (Pistia stratiotes).
    • Matured water hyacinth is the principal component of the floating bed.
    • The size of the bed is generally of 50 to 55 m length, 1.2 m to 1.3 m width and 1.0 to 1.2 m height.
    • Farmers also construct medium-sized floating beds (25 m to 27 m long, 1.2 m to 1.3 m wide and 1.0 to 1.2 m high) for seedling production, particularly in areas where water bodies are scarce.
  • The first layer (0.8 m to 0.9 m height) is made of water hyacinth which serves as the foundation of the bed.
    • The roots of water hyacinth are stacked at the side and the shoot of the plants is kept in the middle position of the floating bed (Figure 1).
  • The second layer (0.2 m to 0.3 m) is made of dulalilata, which is placed on the water hyacinth layer Figure 2).
  • The third and final layer (0.2 m to 0.3 m) is made of topapana (Figure 3).
  • The floating bed material is produced naturally as well as cultivated commercially for marketing in the local floating market (Figure 4).
Figure 1. Farmer preparing foundation layer of floating bed with water hyacinth

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Dulalilata placed on water hyacinth layer and then topapana layer putting on top of the floating bed

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Three-layered (water hyacinth, dulalilata and topapana) floating bed

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Local floating market for different raw materials of floating bed

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Preparation of nursery bed for seed germination

  • Different types of nursery beds are constructed for seed germination.
  • They are usually installed on bamboo made trellis (Figure 5) or on high land (Figure 6) (using banana plant and bamboo platform) at farmers’ homestead areas.
  • Nursery beds can also be constructed at the corner on the floating bed (Figure 7).
Figure 5. Nursery bed on bamboo trellis

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Nursery bed on high land

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Nursery bed at the corner of floating bed

©FAO/TECA

  • The nursery bed (10 to 20 cm height) is prepared using Dulalilata as a first layer and then Topapana as a second layer.
  • Finally, dissected coconut dust is spread on the top and leveled on the bed for making an favorable environment for seed germination.
  • Sometimes, the seed bed is covered by polythene sheet to protect it from damage due to heavy rainfall.
Figure 8. Dulalitata

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Topapana

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10. Coconut dust

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Seed sowing on nursery bed

  • In general, small size seeds of vegetables (e.g. brinjal, cucumber, papaya etc.) and spices (e.g. chili, bombai chili etc.) are sown on the nursery bed and are then covered with coconut dust.
    • The nursery bed should be kept under moist conditions for proper seed germination.
  • Large size seeds (e.g. bottle gourd, pumpkin, country bean, bitter gourd etc.) are primed for three to six hours (depending on the nature of crops/seeds) and then covered with topapana or moist coconut dust for sprouting or germination.
    • The germination of seeds generally takes about five to ten days, depending on the crop variety.

2.4 Preparation of ball as seedling growing media

  • As a seedling growing media, farmers prepare small balls (6 to 8 cm diameter) made of topapana and raped with dulalilata or aquatic algae (Nitella sp.).
  • Locally the ball is known as “Dolla”. Generally women of the farm family make these balls/dolla.
  • A single woman generally can prepare 2 500 to 3 000 ball/dolla in a day.
Figure 11. Woman preparing ball/dolla using topapana that raping with dulalilata

©FAO/TECA

Figure 12. Prepared ball/dolla using topapana and dulalilata

©FAO/TECA

Figure 13. Woman preparing ball/dolla using topapana that raping with algae

©FAO/TECA

2.5 Insert of germinated seeds/young seedlings into the ball/dolla

  • Two to four small holes (2 cm to 3 cm depth) are made on the topapana made ball/dolla with the help of pointed small stick.
  • Afterwards, the root portions of the pre-germinated seeds or young seedlings (vegetables and spices) are inserted into the holes of the ball/dolla.
Figure 14. Germinated seeds of bolle gourd for inserting into the ball/dolla

©FAO/TECA

Figure 15. Germinated seeds inserted into the ball/dolla

©FAO/TECA

Figure 16. Topapana made Ball/dolla containing germinated seeds

©FAO/TECA

2.6. Seedling nursing and placement on the main floating bed

  • The seedling balls are kept under the light shadow and moist conditions at farmers’ home areas for five to seven days for setting pre-germinated seeds or young seedlings into the ball/dolla properly (Figures 17 and 18).
  • During this period watering and other nursing operations are done to make the seedling balls adaptable for growing under floating bed environment conditions (Figure 19).
Figure 17. Nursing of seedling ball/dolla at farmers’ homestead area

©FAO/TECA

Figure 18. Placement of seedling ball/dolla on the main floating bed

©FAO/TECA

Figure 19. Watering and nursing of seedlings on the main floating bed

©FAO/TECA

  • Afterward, the seedling balls are transported to the watershed and placed on the main floating bed maintaining proper spacing (2 000 to 2 200 seedlings per bed).
  • The base of the seedling wall is covered with decomposed water hyacinth to protect them from lodging and any attacks of birds.
  • The times required until the seedling balls can be transplanted to the field is about 25 to 45 days.
  • During the monsoon season (June to October month), local farmers can produce seedlings (vegetables and spices) in three to five times on one floating bed.
  • However, after the completion of each production cycle (25 to 45 days) the floating bed needs to be repaired.

2.7 Intercultural operations

  • The seedlings are irrigated twice a day (in the morning and in the afternoon).
  • A small amount of urea fertilizer (about 400 g per 10 m2) is also applied followed by irrigation to enhance the vegetative growth of the seedlings (Figure 20).
  • The seedlings are harvested or uprooted when they reach the transplanting stage for crop production (Figures 21 and 22).
Figure 20. Urea application and watering on floating bed seedlings

©FAO/TECA

Figure 21. Different stages of vegetable and spices seedlings on floating bed

©FAO/TECA

Figure 22. Vegetable seedlings attaining the transplanting stage for crop production

©FAO/TECA

2.8 Seedling uprooting and marketing at the local floating market

  • Farmers harvest the seedlings when they become suitable for transplanting (25 to 45 days old) for crop production.
  • The seedlings are sold primarily at the local floating market.
  • Afterwards, the seedlings are transported by launch, traller, boat and other vehicles for marketing it in the southern and south-western districts of Bangladesh (Figure 23).
  • The seedlings produced on a floating bed are mainly used for crop production under normal soil conditions in the country.
Figure 23. Marketing of vegetable and spice seedlings at local floating market

©FAO/TECA

2.9 The profitability of seedling production on floating beds

On average, farmers can earn about USD 150 per bed (50 to 55 m long) in one monsoon season by selling their seedlings at the local floating market. Moreover, the decomposed floating beds can be used for succeeding winter crop production as well as for selling (USD 30 per bed) as compost or organic manure to the neighbor farmers.

3. Advantages of the systems

3.1 Resource use efficiency

  • The floating garden agriculture system is a low-input system.
  • First of all, basic and essential materials for preparing floating beds are available in plenty in the region.
  • Second, it needs a minimum amount of fertilizer and chemical inputs.
  • Farmers have no suitable alternative adaptation option of floating garden agriculture practices for the rural livelihoods under the flooded/wetland ecosystem.
    • The floating garden technology can utilize the flooded fallow lands for crop production as well as income generation of the vulnerable local people using the existing natural resources.
    • From the environmental perspective, adequate control of water hyacinth sustainably maintains a good water environment in terms of water-purification and decreased eutrophication.
    • In fact, this system considerably participates to mitigate the risks of natural disasters and climate change.
  • During the winter season, some farmers carry the decomposed floating bed to higher grounds (locally known as Sorjan/Kandi), where they break it and mix it with the soil to enrich the soil fertility.
    • In some cases, the decomposed floating beds are used as compost and incorporated into the soil for growing different winter crops.
    • Adding discomposed floating bed materials into the soil increases soil fertility along with soil organic matter content that ultimately reduces the use of chemical fertilizers for crop production in the winter season.

3.2 Contribution to food security

  • Provides additional space for seedling rising in the wetlands.
  • Early production of seedlings of winter vegetables.
  • Provides primary nutrients (e.g. nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, etc.) and micronutrients (e.g. boron, molybdenum, etc.) in decomposed water hyacinth, comparable with cow-dung and other organic manures.
  • When the water recedes in flooded/wetlands, dismantled floating platforms are used as organic fertilizer.
    • In this way, it enhances eco-friendly agriculture practice in winter seasons to cultivate winter crops.
  • The following video shows how school children in Bangladesh learn about how floating garden practices can contribute to food security: Global Food Security: How can we feed a growing population? This video is produced by from British Council Schools.

3.3 Poverty reduction

  • This system contributes to rural poor people providing equitable access to resources in a sustainable way.
  • Floating agriculture practices have minimal infrastructure and very little capital requirements.
  • This technology can provide a growing area for poor communities who lack access to land, as many wetlands are submerged underwater for six to eight months of the year.
  • In addition, people who are practicing floating-bed cultivation are enjoying a better life, in particular in economic terms, than those in other flood-affected areas who have not yet adopted this practice.
  • As a result, there are various socio-economic, agricultural, environmental, and disaster risk management benefits.

3.4 Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA)

  • Bangladesh is a country vividly affected by the impacts of climate change, e.g. intrusion of soil and water salinity, sea-level rise, heavy rains, flooding, drought, soil submergence, cyclones, etc.
  • Low-lying areas of the southern coastal areas remain submerged for longer periods what makes it difficult to cultivate crops.
  • The floating gardens method has been developed to face these issues because they provide an option for growing crops in flooded areas.
  • This increases agricultural productivity and incomes.
  • Floating gardens are adapted to climate change and have the potential for replication elsewhere.
  • In addition, with no or less agro-chemicals inputs for plant nutrition or pest control, the environmentally friendly floating garden practices can also be regarded as reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

4. Improvements of traditional floating gardens for seedling production in Bangladesh

4.1 Background

  • The quality of the seedlings produced through the traditional floating garden system often does not give satisfactory field performance under normal land conditions due to the application of improper management practices during the seedling growing period on floating beds.
  • For example, farmers generally apply urea fertilizer (as a source of nitrogen) for enhancing the vegetative growth of the seedlings and marketing them quickly.
    • Although the decomposed floating bed is a suitable source of the essential and required amount of plant nutrients for quality seedling production.
  • Excessive application of nitrogen turns the seedling plant into a more succulent and bushy structure what makes them susceptible to normal field conditions.
  • The seedlings are sold in the local floating market just after their uprooting and without doing any hardening process.
  • In some cases, the aged seedlings (after exceeding the optimum stage for transplantation in soil) are uprooted which ultimately decreases the survival rate, growth and development after their transplantation under normal land.
  • Crop production by using these seedlings gives poor yield and less profitability.
  • Another aspect is that farmers generally use traditional/local varieties which do not show good yield potentiality of these crops.
  • Use of high yielding modern varieties will increase the yield and profitability of the crops.

4.2 Improved seed varieties

  • Under these circumstances, research programmes have been conducted at the Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute (BARI) to produce quality seedlings of vegetable and spice crops.
  • In Bangladesh, BARI and other research institutions have developed a good number of improved varieties of crops including vegetables and spices.
  • Farmers can easily collect the seeds from the research intuitions, seed companies and local seed dealers.
  • The seedlings of these crops can be produced on traditional floating beds.
  • Below are listed some of the improved varieties.
    • Bottle gourd (variety: BARI Lau-3, 4)
    • Pumpkin (variety: BARI Mistikumra-2, BARI Hybrid Mistikumra-1)
    • Brinjal (BARI Bt Begun-1, 2, 3, 4)
    • Bitter gourd (BARI Korola-1)
    • Qnake gourd (BARI Chichinga-1)
    • Ribbed gourd (BARI Jhinga-1, 2)
    • Country bean (BARI Seem-6, 7, 8)
    • Yardlong bean (BARI Borboti-1)
    • Okra (BARI Dherosh-1, 2)
    • Kangkong (BARI Gimakalmi-1)
    • Indian spinach (BARI Puishak-2)
    • Chili (as a spice crop) (BARI Morich-1, 2, 3)
Figure 24. Production of brinjal/eggplant seedlings (Variety: BARI Bt Brinjal-2)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 25. Production of chili seedlings (Variety: BARI Chili-1)

©FAO/TECA

4.3. Improved practices

  • Seedlings produced from seeds of improved varieties along with the application of improved management practices give higher yield as well as a net return under normal field conditions.
  • Below are listed some improved practices.
    • Use of quality seeds.
    • Judicious use of natural resources.
    • Application of plant nutrients based on nutrient contents of floating bed/seedling growing media.
    • The uprooting of seedlings at the optimum stage.
    • Hardening of seedlings.
    • Application of improved packaging.
    • Post-harvest technologies.
    • The improved transportation system. 
  • Information obtained from the local farmers revealed that vegetables and spices seedlings produced from improved floating agriculture practices at BARI, provided higher survival rates as well as product yields than that of traditional floating garden system.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • ​Traditional floating garden practices for vegetable production: ID 8867.
  • Improvements of traditional floating gardens for vegetable production: ID 8868.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource-use efficiency

The technology is a low-input system and uses water efficiently in an environmentally friendly way.

7.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology is low-cost, income generating and contributes to food security by increasing yields through improved soil and seed management.

  • During the winter season, some farmers carry the decomposed floating bed to higher grounds (locally known as Sorjan/Kandi), where they break it and mix it with the soil to enrich the soil fertility.
    • In some cases, the decomposed floating beds are used as compost and incorporated into the soil for growing different winter crops.
    • Adding discomposed floating bed materials into the soil increases soil fertility along with soil organic matter content that ultimately reduces the use of chemical fertilizers for crop production in the winter season.

3.2 Contribution to food security

  • Provides additional space for seedling rising in the wetlands.
  • Early production of seedlings of winter vegetables.
  • Provides primary nutrients (e.g. nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, etc.) and micronutrients (e.g. boron, molybdenum, etc.) in decomposed water hyacinth, comparable with cow-dung and other organic manures.
  • When the water recedes in flooded/wetlands, dismantled floating platforms are used as organic fertilizer.
    • In this way, it enhances eco-friendly agriculture practice in winter seasons to cultivate winter crops.
  • The following video shows how school children in Bangladesh learn about how floating garden practices can contribute to food security: Global Food Security: How can we feed a growing population? This video is produced by from British Council Schools.

3.3 Poverty reduction

  • This system contributes to rural poor people providing equitable access to resources in a sustainable way.
  • Floating agriculture practices have minimal infrastructure and very little capital requirements.
  • This technology can provide a growing area for poor communities who lack access to land, as many wetlands are submerged underwater for six to eight months of the year.
  • In addition, people who are practicing floating-bed cultivation are enjoying a better life, in particular in economic terms, than those in other flood-affected areas who have not yet adopted this practice.
  • As a result, there are various socio-economic, agricultural, environmental, and disaster risk management benefits.

3.4 Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA)

  • Bangladesh is a country vividly affected by the impacts of climate change, e.g. intrusion of soil and water salinity, sea-level rise, heavy rains, flooding, drought, soil submergence, cyclones, etc.
  • Low-lying areas of the southern coastal areas remain submerged for longer periods what makes it difficult to cultivate crops.
  • The floating gardens method has been developed to face these issues because they provide an option for growing crops in flooded areas.
  • This increases agricultural productivity and incomes.
  • Floating gardens are adapted to climate change and have the potential for replication elsewhere.
  • In addition, with no or less agro-chemicals inputs for plant nutrition or pest control, the environmentally friendly floating garden practices can also be regarded as reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

4. Improvements of traditional floating gardens for seedling production in Bangladesh

4.1 Background

  • The quality of the seedlings produced through the traditional floating garden system often does not give satisfactory field performance under normal land conditions due to the application of improper management practices during the seedling growing period on floating beds.
  • For example, farmers generally apply urea fertilizer (as a source of nitrogen) for enhancing the vegetative growth of the seedlings and marketing them quickly.
    • Although the decomposed floating bed is a suitable source of the essential and required amount of plant nutrients for quality seedling production.
  • Excessive application of nitrogen turns the seedling plant into a more succulent and bushy structure what makes them susceptible to normal field conditions.
  • The seedlings are sold in the local floating market just after their uprooting and without doing any hardening process.
  • In some cases, the aged seedlings (after exceeding the optimum stage for transplantation in soil) are uprooted which ultimately decreases the survival rate, growth and development after their transplantation under normal land.
  • Crop production by using these seedlings gives poor yield and less profitability.
  • Another aspect is that farmers generally use traditional/local varieties which do not show good yield potentiality of these crops.
  • Use of high yielding modern varieties will increase the yield and profitability of the crops.

4.2 Improved seed varieties

  • Under these circumstances, research programmes have been conducted at the Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute (BARI) to produce quality seedlings of vegetable and spice crops.
  • In Bangladesh, BARI and other research institutions have developed a good number of improved varieties of crops including vegetables and spices.
  • Farmers can easily collect the seeds from the research intuitions, seed companies and local seed dealers.
  • The seedlings of these crops can be produced on traditional floating beds.
  • Below are listed some of the improved varieties.
    • Bottle gourd (variety: BARI Lau-3, 4)
    • Pumpkin (variety: BARI Mistikumra-2, BARI Hybrid Mistikumra-1)
    • Brinjal (BARI Bt Begun-1, 2, 3, 4)
    • Bitter gourd (BARI Korola-1)
    • Qnake gourd (BARI Chichinga-1)
    • Ribbed gourd (BARI Jhinga-1, 2)
    • Country bean (BARI Seem-6, 7, 8)
    • Yardlong bean (BARI Borboti-1)
    • Okra (BARI Dherosh-1, 2)
    • Kangkong (BARI Gimakalmi-1)
    • Indian spinach (BARI Puishak-2)
    • Chili (as a spice crop) (BARI Morich-1, 2, 3)
Figure 24. Production of brinjal/eggplant seedlings (Variety: BARI Bt Brinjal-2)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 25. Production of chili seedlings (Variety: BARI Chili-1)

©FAO/TECA

4.3. Improved practices

  • Seedlings produced from seeds of improved varieties along with the application of improved management practices give higher yield as well as a net return under normal field conditions.
  • Below are listed some improved practices.
    • Use of quality seeds.
    • Judicious use of natural resources.
    • Application of plant nutrients based on nutrient contents of floating bed/seedling growing media.
    • The uprooting of seedlings at the optimum stage.
    • Hardening of seedlings.
    • Application of improved packaging.
    • Post-harvest technologies.
    • The improved transportation system. 
  • Information obtained from the local farmers revealed that vegetables and spices seedlings produced from improved floating agriculture practices at BARI, provided higher survival rates as well as product yields than that of traditional floating garden system.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • ​Traditional floating garden practices for vegetable production: ID 8867.
  • Improvements of traditional floating gardens for vegetable production: ID 8868.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource-use efficiency

The technology is a low-input system and uses water efficiently in an environmentally friendly way.

7.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology is low-cost, income generating and contributes to food security by increasing yields through improved soil and seed management.

Title: Traditional Floating Garden Technology for Seedling Production

Description: An indigenous agricultural innovation from Bangladesh using aquatic plants to create floating nursery beds for vegetable and spice seedling production in flood-prone areas, enabling year-round farming in waterlogged conditions.

Innovation criteria met: It's an existing solution used in a different context (seedling production vs direct cultivation), is pro-poor, climate-resilient, and supports food security in flood-prone regions. The improved version with modern varieties and practices represents technological advancement of traditional knowledge.
_annotations.field_shorter_description: The floating garden practice is a local indigenous production system most successful in the wetland/submerged areas of selected south and south-western districts (Pirojpur, Barisal and Gopalganj) in Bangladesh. Floating garden agricultural practices have been adopted by local farmers for nearly two centuries. This technology describes how to construct and use floating gardens for seedling production of vegetable and spice crops in Bangladesh.

records.title: Consideraciones para disminuir la enjambrazón y migración de abejas
records.description:
Descripción

  • Las abejas como organismo vivo desarrollan acciones, dentro de las cuales se encuentra la reproducción de sus individuos y la multiplicación de sus colonias.
  • Siendo al igual que cualquier organismo, "la reproducción" es un evento resultante de una serie de condiciones favorables, como lo son un buen estatus sanitario y nutricional.
  • En las abejas hay dos formas de multiplicación.
    • Una de ellas es realizada por la reina para aumentar el número de trabajadores dentro de la colmena, con lo cual aumenta la población para la generación de nuevos individuos (obreras y zánganos).
    • Por otra parte, hay una reproducción de colonias (unidades productivas), que se denomina enjambrazón, este proceso corresponde a la salida de una cantidad de abejas de la colonia madre (junto a la reina vieja, si es un enjambre primario) para formar una nueva familia, lo que resulta con la multiplicación de la unidad productiva.

1. Consideraciones para evitar la enjambrazón

  • El apicultor puede disminuir importantemente la posibilidad de que una colonia enjambre aplicando recomendaciones como las siguientes:

1.1 Controlar genéticamente sus abejas, por medio de la selección de reinas europeas que no muestren tendencia a enjambrar, utilizando sus larvas para la producción de reinas

  • Hay ocasiones en que los apicultores rescatan o capturan enjambres silvestres.
  • Si este es el caso además de las consideraciones sanitarias que se debe tener con esta colonia (realizar muestreo y tratar contra varroa), es importante que al pasar unos días se realice el recambio de la reina que viene en el enjambre ya que generalmente es una reina vieja o con mayor tendencia para enjambrar.
Figura 1. Larvas y huevos procedentes de una abeja reina seleccionada para producir nuevas abejas reinas

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Recambiar las reinas viejas de forma periódica

  • Las reinas productivas son aquellas que se encuentran con mayor vigor de generación de hormonas y su potencial de postura.
  • Generalmente es subestimada la importancia de las feromonas en la reina, pues la colmena disminuye su vigorosidad con una reina más vieja, además de la disminución del potencial de postura de huevos.
Figura 2. Inserción de una reina fecundada del año en una familia de abejas huérfana (las obreras están reconociendo a la nueva reina de la familia)

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Utilizar láminas de cera estampada que ocupen todo el marco y si es posible marcos estirados

  • La correcta incorporación de marcos con cera estampada (y mejor aún si es cera estirada, ver Figura 3) facilita la ampliación del nido de cría en épocas de fuerte flujo de néctar.
  • Es importante la utilización de cera de conocida procedencia que otorgue las garantías suficientes para ser utilizada dentro de la colmena.
Figura 3. Cuadro con cera estirada para apresurar el trabajo de las abejas en la cámara de cría

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Proporcionar un amplio espacio a la reina, dejándole dos cámaras disponibles, en los períodos de mayor afluencia de néctar

  • Siempre deben haber uno o más marcos que la colmena pueda trabajar, pues si no hay labores que realizar y se satura de abejas se incentiva la enjambrazón.
  • Este es uno de los principales motivos de enjambrazón, el cual ocurre en los periodos de fuertes flujos de néctar.
  • Fuertes flujos de néctar generan una intensificación en la postura y nacimiento de individuos y con esto se satura de obreras el interior de la colmena, lo cual genera una disminución de la presencia de las feromonas de inhibición de celdas reales (estas feromonas se llaman Footprint y Hormona mandibular) por obrera.
  • Con el aumento de abejas dentro de la colmena estas hormonas no logran llegar a todos los lugares de la colonia y las obreras comienzan a formar celdas reales, interpretando que la reina no produce la cantidad de hormona suficiente para mantener el dominio de la colmena, o también está relacionado a la falta de espacio que no permite expresar el potencial del ambiente y de la colonia.
  • Por estos motivos las obreras generan las condiciones para enjambrar.
  • Esta situación se puede impedir realizando visitas periódicas (entre 7 a 9 días) (ver la ficha técnica: Apicultura: desarrollo de familias a partir de un núcleo (pequeña familia)) y proporcionar el espacio suficiente a las colmenas para que siempre tengan labores que realizar y no comience el proceso de enjambrazón.
Figura 4. Esquema de una colmena con dos cuerpos de cría y un tercer cuerpo para producción de miel

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Mantener la piquera abierta en épocas de calor excesivo, cuando las abejas la cubran totalmente

  • Otro motivo por el cual las abejas en ocasiones enjambran es debido al exceso de calor que se genera dentro de la colmena, esta situación es detectable a la visualización de las piqueras cuando se observan:
    • Abejas ventilando con el abdomen hacia abajo (Figura 5).
    • Abejas colgando desde la piquera hacia afuera (Figura 6).
Figura 5. Abejas ventilando

©FAO/TECA

Figura 6. Abejas colgando desde la piquera hacia afuera, indicando la necesidad de espacio y/o aumento de temperatura

©FAO/TECA

1.6 Remoción de celdas reales emergentes

  • Si las revisiones son irregulares y no se genera el espacio suficiente dentro de la colmena es normal encontrar celdas reales (sobre todo en periferia de los marcos).
  • Siempre antes de remover estas celdas es importante verificar la postura de la reina que se encuentra en la colmena.
  • Si se resuelve que las celdas están formándose por causa de falta de espacio se pueden remover las celdas y utilizarlas en otras colmenas nuevas o huérfanas.
Figura 7. Presencia de una celda real nacida y cuatro celdas reales por nacer

©FAO/TECA

2. Consideraciones para evitar la migración

  • La principal diferencia entre la migración y la enjambrazón es que la migración es generada por la colmena con el propósito de buscar mejoras en las condiciones debido a un estado de estrés de la colmena, ya que si no migra las posibilidades de vida son muy escasas.
  • Las causantes de estrés a las colmenas son todos los imaginables y las vías para evitar la migración son dependientes del agente que las provoque, por ello la interpretación del estado de la familia es importante. Dentro de los manejos a realizar son:

2.1 Alimentar en épocas de escasez

  • Proporcionar alimento en épocas de escases de flores o con muy bajas temperaturas, con fuertes vientos o con lluvias excesivas que impiden que las abejas lleguen a su alimento natural.
  • Se alimenta por medio de azúcar granulada con vitaminas líquidas (compradas en tiendas apícolas), para estimular la postura de la reina.
  • Al existir cría, será menos probable que las abejas abandonen la colmena.
Figura 8. Colmena con alimentador interno

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Proporcionar agua limpia

  • Se aconseja proporcionar agua limpia si esta escasea en épocas de sequía, colocando un recipiente grande con agua limpia junto con algún tipo de flotador (tablas) para evitar que se ahoguen (ver ejemplo en Figura 9).
Figura 9. Imagen de un tipo de bebedero

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Evitar que eventualmente el fuego alcance a las colmenas cortando malezas en el apiario

  • Es buena práctica el control de la maleza circundante el apiario.
  • Es importante que el apicultor lleve ropa adecuada para protegerse contra posibles picaduras de abejas cuando usa la desbrozadora (cortadora de pasto) ya que su ruido puede molestar a las abejas.
Figura 10. Apicultor realizando corte de pasto en los apiarios con protección contra ruidos y abejas

©FAO/TECA

Figura 11. Apiario con manejo de malezas mediante corte

©FAO/TECA

2.4 Controlar a las hormigas y otros enemigos de las abejas

  • Es importante contar con planes de manejo para plagas que atacan a las abejas las cuales varían según la zona geográfica: hormigas, avispas, roedores, etc.
Figura 12. Esquema de una colmena con barrera para hormigas

©FAO/TECA

  • Otros aspectos importantes son realizar la revisión de las colmenas de la manera más breve y simple posible, interviniendo en la colmena de tal forma que se ayude al funcionamiento de la misma, no fomentando el pillaje y el desorden de los marcos en el interior de esta.
  • También es importante evitar el uso excesivo del humo que ahogue a las abejas.

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Subtropical, húmedo.

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Apicultura: desarrollo de familias a partir de un núcleo (pequeña familia): ID 8666.
  • Confección de trampa de cartón para captura de enjambres de abeja africanizada: ID 8658.
  • Apicultura: confección de cajón triple: ID 8907.
  • Alimentador externo e interno para colmenas: ID 8325.
  • Preparación de alimentos para abejas: ID 8393.
  • Buenas prácticas apícolas: ID 8217.

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta práctica le da al apicultor unas consideraciones para disminuir la enjambrazón y la migración de abejas de manera eficiente.

5.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Estas consideraciones conducen a un mejor manejo de la apicultura, lo que conduce a muchos resultados positivos para el apicultor.

Los enjambres son la forma natural mediante la cual las familias de abejas se reproducen y se localizan en un lugar diferente al que habitaban para utilizarlo como nuevo hogar. Este sitio generalmente ha sido inspeccionado por pecoreadoras de avanzada edad para verificar que contemple condiciones para albergar al enjambre. El proceso de enjambrazón de las familias genera una drástica disminución en la cantidad de individuos de la colmena originaria, por lo cual se vuelven muy escazas las posibilidades de obtener producción suficiente para mantener en buenas condiciones económicas el negocio. La multiplicación natural mediante enjambres es una forma de producción que se encuentra en erradicación de las prácticas apícolas debido a los problemas sanitarios y de manejos que genera un enjambre libre. Hay que señalar que no siempre se puede garantizar que no se generen enjambres en una colmena de abejas, pero el apicultor puede realizar ciertas medidas para disminuir su porcentaje considerablemente si considera ciertos manejos en los momentos oportunos. Por otra parte, un fenómeno denominado migración se genera cuando las colmenas se encuentran en condiciones de escases de recursos o en malas condiciones sanitarias lo cual genera estrés en las familias. _annotations.field_shorter_description:
Los enjambres son la forma natural mediante la cual las familias de abejas se reproducen y se localizan en un lugar diferente al que habitaban para utilizarlo como nuevo hogar. Este sitio generalmente ha sido inspeccionado por pecoreadoras de avanzada edad para verificar que contemple condiciones para albergar al enjambre. El proceso de enjambrazón de las familias genera una drástica disminución en la cantidad de individuos de la colmena originaria, por lo cual se vuelven muy escazas las posibilidades de obtener producción suficiente para mantener en buenas condiciones económicas el negocio. La multiplicación natural mediante enjambres es una forma de producción que se encuentra en erradicación de las prácticas apícolas debido a los problemas sanitarios y de manejos que genera un enjambre libre. Hay que señalar que no siempre se puede garantizar que no se generen enjambres en una colmena de abejas, pero el apicultor puede realizar ciertas medidas para disminuir su porcentaje considerablemente si considera ciertos manejos en los momentos oportunos. Por otra parte, un fenómeno denominado migración se genera cuando las colmenas se encuentran en condiciones de escases de recursos o en malas condiciones sanitarias lo cual genera estrés en las familias. Esta conducta también es propia de algunas razas de abejas que tienden a migrar en búsqueda de mejores condiciones. 
Debido a los inconvenientes que se presentan al momento que una colmena enjambra o migra, es importante generar medidas y manejos que disminuyan la posibilidad de que una colmena adquiera estos comportamientos, por lo cual es importante que estos manejos sean conocidos y aplicados por los apicultores. Esta ficha técnica proporciona unas consideraciones para disminuir la enjambrazón y la migración de abejas.

records.title: Construction of a non-recirculation hydroponic unit for commercial lettuce production
records.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • For an introduction to the concepts of hydroponic method please refer to (“Simple non-circulating hydroponic method for vegetables”).
  • The concept of growing vegetables for home-garden use presented in this document can be expanded to commercial-sized grow beds which will be described in the following sections.
  • Hydroponic lettuce is grown in grow beds filled with nutrient solution (water plus a complete hydroponic fertilizer) instead of in soil (Figure 1).
Figure 1. A schematic drawing of a suspended-pot, non-circulating hydroponics system

©FAO/TECA

  • Growbeds are situated in plastic-covered rain shelters or greenhouses with screened ends and sidewalls to protect against rainfall and large flying insects.
  • The grow beds are filled with 5.7 to 7.8 litres of nutrient solution per plant prior to planting.
  • Thus, a grow bed designed to grow 50 heads of lettuce should have a liquid capacity of about 350 litres.
  • The grow bed dimension would be about 1.20 m × 2.40 m, assuming a 12 cm depth.
  • This is a convenient measurement, as many of the materials come in these sizes.
Figure 2. Hydroponic lettuce growing in grow beds of non-circulating nutrient solution

©FAO/TECA

2. Growbeds

  • Common grow bed dimensions are 1.20 m × 2.40 m and 1.20 m × 4.80 m, but other dimensions may be used.
  • The reason is that the polystyrene beadboard is commonly sold in this dimension.
  • Given that most people are unable to reach lettuce plants located more than 1 m away, the use of grow beds wider than 1.80 m is not recommended.
  • Given that grow beds should be leveled to within 2 cm, the grow beds should not be too long if the ground is uneven at all (for example, on a concrete slab).
  • Smaller grow beds are easier to level if the ground is uneven (for example, on stones).

2.1. Materials needed

  • Two wood lengths (5m × 15 cm, 2.40 m length).
  • Two wood lengths (5 m × 15 cm, 1.10 m length).
  • Nails (8 cm) or screws (6 cm).
  • 1.20 m ×2.40 m plywood sheet (1.3 cm or thicker).
    • Or recycled metal roofing, 1.20 m × 2.40 m.
  • Black polyethylene sheeting.
  • Wood pallets (used for grow bed supporting structure).
  • Weed barrier fabric (> grow bed size).
  • As an alternative to wood, you can also use metal profiles (rectangular and cylindrical shaped) for the grow bed support frame.
  • The decision of which material to use can be based on availability and cost, noting that metal has a longer lifespan than wood.

2.2. Step-by-step description

2.2.1 Rectangular frame

  • A rectangular frame of 1.20 m wide × 2.40 m long × 14 cm high is constructed with 5 cm × 15 cm lumber by fastening either with 8 cm nails (or 6 cm deck screws).
Figure 3. Scheme of the rectangular frame

©FAO/TECA

2.2.2 Placement

  • Grow beds can be placed on the floor (Option A) or supported at waist-height (Option B).
  • Option A is cheaper and simpler, but harvesting is less convenient and comfortable.
  • Option A: On the floor
    • Lumber frames (without any additional plywood or metal bottom) may rest directly on the floor (e.g. compacted soil, concrete floor, rooftop, patio, etc.) but make sure that no sharp objects are on the surface of the floor that could puncture the liner.
  • Option B (optional): Grow bed supporting structure
    • Grow beds can be constructed at a convenient working height (75 cm to 90 cm).
    • A full 1.20 m × 2.40 m growbed weighs more than 360 kg.
    • Growbeds should be supported at least every 1.20 m on stacked concrete blocks or have a well-braced lumber frame.
    • You may construct a growbed support structure from cross-braced, upright pallets.
    • Recycled metal roofing is then attached to this framework, making a tabletop (Figure 4).
Figure 4. Growbed support structure from cross-braced, upright pallets with recycled metal roofing as a table top (Waite Farm, Mt. View)

©FAO/TECA

2.2.3 Growbed bottom

  • Fasten a 1.5 cm or thicker plywood sheet to the lumber frame.
  • This becomes the bottom of the grow bed.
  • In place of plywood bottoms you can use recycled metal roofing, but take care to prevent sharp edges from cutting the plastic grow bed liner.
  • Alternatively, lumber frames without the bottom plywood sheet may rest directly on the metal roofing of the supporting structure without any attachment.
  • Lumber frames (without any additional bottom) may also rest directly on level ground.
  • Optionally, weed barrier fabric should be placed under the frame to cushion against rocks and prevent weeds from penetrating the plastic liner (Figure 5).
Figure 5. A lumber frame rests directly on weed barrier fabric placed on a level surface

©FAO/TECA

2.2.4 Black polyethylene sheeting

  • Growbeds are lined with a layer of black polyethylene sheeting with a thickness of 0.8 mm–1.4 mm (Figure 6).
  • It is recommended to use two layers as a failsafe to prevent leakage if the top layer rips.
  • If no black polyethylene sheeting is available, other colours can be used.
  • However, clear plastic is problematic as it allows for algae growth which affects dissolved oxygen (DO) availability.
  • Also, you should avoid clear construction grade polyethylene because sunlight deteriorates exposed plastic not protected by the grow bed cover.
Figure 6. Growbed is lined with two layers of 6 mm black polyethylene sheeting

©FAO/TECA

  • It is easier to lay and fit the two layers consecutively rather than both at once.
  • Polyethylene rolls are typically sold in 3 m and 6 m widths, but it is easier to work with the 3 m width.
  • When cutting the plastic, allow for several inches of overhang on the ends and sides.
  • Lay the polyethylene loosely in the grow bed.
  • Air pockets may develop if the plastic is fastened before water is added, and this often causes leaks.
  • The plastic must be fitted snugly against the sides and bottom of the grow bed because unsupported plastic sheeting is prone to leak.
  • Preliminary fitting is accomplished by using the side of one’s hand (it may be helpful to imagine slow-motion martial art “chop”).

2.2.5 Add some water

  • Add about 5 cm of water.
  • The water may cause the polyethylene to pull away from the sides of the growbed, so it is important to add the water before the polyethylene is stapled in place.
  • The polyethylene is then given a final fitting to the grow bed sides and bottom to ensure that it rests firmly against the lumber.
  • Fold and trim the plastic at the ends of the grow bed.
  • Use a staple gun to fasten the polyethylene to the outside frame rather than to the top of the grow bed.
    • Stainless steel staples are preferred.
  • If a growbed leaks while a crop is growing, add a few handfuls of fine vermiculite to the growbed.
    • Rub the vermiculite between your hands to mill it into very fine particles.
    • The vermiculite can plug small holes and retard the leak.
  • To repair a leaking growbed, a new sheet of plastic can be added over the two existing sheets after the crop is harvested.

3. Grow sheets

3.1 Materials needed

  • Sheets of 5 cm thick polystyrene (white beadboard, 32 kg/m3 density) or extruded polystyrene (StyrofoamTM).
  • Extruded polystyrene should be used preferably to expanded polystyrene, assuming it is available and similarly priced.
  • Over time, expanded polystyrene holds a lot of water which leads to algae growth and makes sheets more susceptible to breaking.
  • Alternative cover materials.
    • Alternative options for grow bed cover materials include plywood and plastic.
    • Thin sheets of plywood (0.6 cm) are easier to cut holes, however, they are susceptible to break more easily under the weight of heavy plants such as tomatoes.
    • Several growers have successfully constructed grow bed covers by covering lumber frames with plastic weed barrier fabric.
      • Holes for the net pots are burned in the fabric with a hot pipe.
    • A coat of white latex paint is recommended for plastic and plywood covers.
    • This is especially true for dark-colored covers, which heat up in direct sunlight.

3.2 Step-by-step description

3.2.1 Sheet size

  • The grow bed cover should be easily removable and fit loosely on top of the grow bed.
  • Sheets of 5 cm thick extruded (or expanded) polystyrene (white beadboard, 32 kg/m3 density) or extruded polystyrene (StyrofoamTM) are preferred because they are lightweight and it is easy to cut holes in them for the net pots.
  • Individual sheets should be cut to 0.60 × 1.20 m to facilitate handling (Figure 7).
  • Larger sheets, such as 1.20 m × 2.40 m, are often broken while handling because they are somewhat fragile.
  • First, score the polystyrene about 0.5 cm deep with a utility knife, then snap the sheet at the score line.
Figure 7. Cutting polystyrene sheets

©FAO/TECA

3.2.2 Mark the sheets

  • Mark the cover sheets according to Figure 8.
  • Equidistant plant spacing is preferred, but this is not always possible if 0.60 m × 1.20 m grow bed cover sheets are used.
  • A suggested plant spacing (density of about 22 plants per square metre) on a 0.60 m × 1.20 m grow bed cover sheet is to first mark three rows along the 0.6 m side (located at 10 cm, 30 cm, and 50 cm) and then mark four plants per row on the 1.20 m side (12 plants per sheet).
  • The suggested layout of the first and third rows will be at the 10 cm, 40 cm, 70 cm, and 100 cm marks.
  • The layout of the middle row will be at the 20 cm, 50 cm, 80 cm, and 110 cm marks (Figure 8).
Figure 8. The layout of marked cover sheets for a density of 22 plants per square metre

©FAO/TECA

  • Additional information regarding plant density.
    • The grower must determine the optimal planting density (the number of plants per square foot or the number of plants per grow bed.)
    • For larger crops, such as tomatoes and cucumbers, a spacing of about 16–20 plants per square metre is recommended.
      • For smaller crops like herbs and lettuce, 20–25 plants per square metre is recommended.
    • Densities greater than two plants per square foot for larger head cultivars grown to mature head stage will often result in slower growth.
      • Higher density plantings are usually done with smaller cultivars of lettuce such as ‘Lollo Rossa’ or when plants are harvested at a younger stage.
    • Growers are advised to compare several planting densities for their growing situation on a small scale before committing to a specific density for commercial-scale production.
      • Parameters to consider include quality, weight, size, shape, diseases and growth rate.

3.2.3 Cut the holes

  • Use an electric drill with a 2-inch hole saw to cut holes at the layout marks (Figure 9).
  • Preferably, cut the holes about three-quarters of the way through from one side, and then complete the operation from the other side of the sheet.
  • This gives a better cut and prevents the plugs from sticking in the hole saw.
Figure 9. An electric drill with a 2-inch hole saw is used to cut holes in the top cover sheets at the layout marks. A template with a suggested plant spacing on a 2 × 4 ft tank cover sheet with a density of 22 plants per square metre is shown.

©FAO/TECA

3.2.4 Arrange the sheets

  • Plastic pots need to be placed on the floor of the grow bed to provide additional support to the middle of the sheets.
  • This prevents bowing or sagging of the polystyrene (Figure 8).
Figure 10. A plastic pot placed on the floor of the grow bed provides additional support to the middle of the sheets, preventing bowing or sagging of the extruded polystyrene.

©FAO/TECA

  • A uniform spacing arrangement in the grow beds can be achieved in a 1.2 m wide grow bed by alternating cover sheets.
  • This means that the first sheet has the 10 cm mark of the first and third rows from one side of the grow bed
  • The adjacent sheet is flipped end-to-end with the 20 cm mark of the first and third rows on that same side of the grow bed (Figure 10).
Figure 11. A uniform spacing arrangement is achieved by alternating the 0.6 m x1.2 m grow bed cover sheets in an end-to-end fashion.

For more information, you can also contact greenercities@fao.org.

©FAO/TECA

5. Validation of the practice 

  • Various leafy vegetables may be grown on a commercial scale with this unique and efficient technique.
  • However, the method is intended only for crops that require less than 8 litres of water per plant for the entire growing season, from transplanting to harvest.
  • Potential crops include leafy, romaine, and semi-head lettuces, cilantro, green onions, kai choy, pak choi, and watercress. 

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Simple non-circulating hydroponic method for vegetables: ID 8825. 
  • Managing a non-recirculation hydroponic unit for commercial lettuce production: ID 8993.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology provides farmers with the steps for the establishment of a hydroponics system for lettuce production. It contributes to providing additional sources of income to farmers utilizing minimum inputs.

Description: A soil-less cultivation method that grows plants without electricity or pumps, using only initial water and nutrients application. It meets criteria of being a modified solution that improves resource efficiency and accessibility, particularly suitable for areas with limited electricity access.
_annotations.field_shorter_description: Hydroponics is the most common method of soil-less culture (growing agricultural plants without the use of soil), which includes growing plants either on a substrate or in an aqueous medium with bare roots. Non-circulating hydroponic methods, importantly, do not require electricity or a pump. With the method presented in this document, the entire crop can be grown with only an initial application of water and nutrients. No additional water or fertilizer are needed. The crop is usually terminated when most of the nutrient solution is consumed. This document provides a detailed description of the construction of the grow beds and grow sheets used in the non-circulating hydroponic unit for commercial lettuce production.

records.title: Bamboo match sticks production
records.description:
Description

1. Synopsis

1.1 Background and introduction

Safety matches are an essential consumer commodity required by all society sections. Wood is the main raw material used for manufacturing matchsticks, but now it is in short supply. Bamboo, which is available in natural forests, is a potential sustainable raw material source for manufacturing matchsticks. Bamboo can be grown in many countries with diverse climatic conditions on a two to four years rotation period.

The use of bamboo for making matchsticks has been constrained by several bamboo characteristics, including poor wax penetration required for good incandescence and burning quality.

Indian Plywood Industries Research and Training Institute (IPIRTI), working in collaboration with and under a project funded by the International Network on Bamboo and Rattan, have developed specific processes for making quality match splints from two widely growing species of bamboo in the Southern India:

  • Bambusa bambos; and 
  • Dendrocalamus strictus.

The manufacturing process developed at IPIRTI  followed standard chemicals and processes adopted for wooden match splints. The process was undertaken at an existing match factory in Tamil Nadu.

Tests carried out at an independent laboratory have shown that the bamboo matchsticks developed at IPIRTI conform to relevant Indian Standard Specifications (IS:2653-1993 and IS:10374-1982).

1.2 Product and use

The match industry is facing problems due to matchwood shortage. Due to certain specific requirements, not many tree species have been found to be suitable for match splints making. While the demand for matches is increasing, there is a gradual reduction in supply of wood logs for matchsticks.

To help the match industries to continue to meet the growing demand, and balance the current and shortfall of wood, several alternative materials including paperboards, have been developed.

However, there is a continuing need for searching/evolving new and cost-effective materials.

Hence, it is apt to use bamboo which:

  • can be grown on short rotation period of two to four years;
  • the leftover lops and tops from the craft sector can be used for making matchsticks (due to the very small dimensions of individual match splints).

1.2.1 General development attributes and advantages

The main advantages of bamboo matchstick technology are:

  • reducing timber use;
  • using a sustainable and renewable raw material resource; (bamboo matchsticks are eco-friendly);
  • reducing soil erosion;
  • enhancing productivity of adjoining agricultural lands;
  • enhancing social and community welfare.

1.3 Market

Demand is increasing along with population growth. The volume of matchbox production is very high. The production capacity is difficult to pinpoint due to mushroom growth of this industry. The Indian consumption is increasing at a rate of about 5 percent per annum. Given the projected demand, bamboo matchsticks, are likely to capture a sizable market share because they are environmentally friendly.

1.4 Target groups

A bamboo matchstick unit can be established near:

  • naturally available bamboos areas; or
  • farmland crops (of any scale).

The technology with bamboo supplying units will be especially advantageous for areas with:

  • soil erosion, (growth can greatly reduce erosion); and
  • land degradation, (growth can gradually restore the land by enhancing productivity).

Four main target groups can benefit from the adoption of the technology:

  • bamboo cultivators;
  • bamboo artisans and handicraft sector;
  • match industry; and
  • forest managers.

1.5 Impact

1.5.1 Environment

In addition to the direct benefits, bamboos have significant environmental benefits, these are:

  • fast growing;
  • annual harvesting;
  • versatile;
  • renewable.

From the point of view of social forestry programmes bamboos aligns well with:

  • soil conservation;
  • afforestation activities;
  • cultivation; and
  • plantations.

1.6 Environment

In addition to the direct benefits, bamboos have significant environmental benefits, these are:

  • fast growing;
  • annual harvesting;
  • versatile;
  • renewable.

From the point of view of social forestry programmes bamboos aligns well with:

  • soil conservation;
  • afforestation activities;
  • cultivation; and
  • plantations.

1.7 Investment

The main requirements to establish a successful bamboo matchstick unit are:

  • capital investment;
  • sustained bamboo supply;
  • trained manpower; and
  • marketing network.

The establishment of bamboo matchstick unit also requires chemicals for:

  • bleaching;
  • carbonization;
  • wax fixing; and
  • head fixing formulation.

In addition to:

  • electricity
  • water
  • labour
  • marketing network.

The cost of machinery required for making bamboo match splints is around 0.6 million Indian Rupees. With other start up cash requirement, the total investment will be 1.0 to 1.2 million Indian Rupees (equivalent to USD 20 000 to 25 000).

1.8 Other requirements

Bamboo matchsticks are a low input-low output product for a factory, but are required in large numbers. All society sectors around the world use matchsticks. To motivate people to switchover to bamboo matchsticks, for marketing purposes, it should be emphasized that the product is:

  • low-cost
  • eco-friendly.

Establishment of a local or regional marketing agency for bamboo matchstick may be beneficial in developing market and thereby ensuring continued growth of the unit.

The renewability of bamboo on a short rotation of two to four years makes it very attractive, even for cottage industries, in terms of cost flow compared to wooden splints.

Cottage industries or small-scale bamboo matchsticks manufacturing may be eligible for development grants or other incentives from the government.

2. Technology assessment

The use of wood for burning is as old as fire itself. The development of matches is just a technological advancement. The match industry combines one of the basic uses of wood with a vital need of humankind. Safety matches are an essential consumer commodity needed by all community sectors. The main raw material for match industry has been and continues to be wood for splints.

Since 1920s, India has been importing aspen logs to make match splints, as the required quantity of aspen wood is not available in the forest reserves. Alternative tree species have been found suitable for the match industry namely:

  • Bombax Ceiba (semul);
  • Populus species (poplar);
  • Hevea Braziliensis (rubber); and
  • Ailanthus (matti).

In recent times, there has been a considerable shortage in the supply of matchwood due to the fact that many of these tree species have found alternative and more profitable application in the composite wood industry.

The demand for matches is increasing along with population growth. There have been several assessments of the demand for matchwood, the latest being a part of demand assessment for wood based industries in India (MoEF, 1999).

While demand for matches is increasing, there is a gradual reduction in wood supplies. The most important raw material for manufacturing matchsticks continues to be wood.

1 000 gross boxes of 50 require about 5 cubic meters of wood for match splints and about 2.5 cubic meters of wood for matchboxes.

Based on reported production, the total requirement of wood is estimated to be 2.3 million cubic meters in 2000, rising to four million cubic meters in 2020. The availability of matchwood presently is only 0.5 million cubic meters.

The short supply of wood is a serious problem for the match industry in the country. In order to balance the current and future shortfall of matchwood, several alternative sources for raw material have been evaluated in the past.

2.1 Evaluation of bamboo suitability

A survey of fast-growing plants focused attention on bamboo. Many species of bamboo are known to grow several centimetres in height daily during the growing season. Strength properties of split bamboo also indicate bamboo as a potential material for the production of match splints.

Bamboo is a fast-growing perennial woody grass of gregarious habit. India is one of the leading countries in bamboo production. Unlike woods that require growing periods of ten years or more, bamboo can be harvested for use at the age of two to four years or even earlier in case of some species. In addition, bamboo is available in many countries.

In India, bamboos are grown throughout the country, except in the Kashmir valley, 125 species belonging to 23 genera are reported to be grown in India. They form an important associate of deciduous and evergreen forests covering both tropical and temperate zones. They grow very well in alluvial plains having good moisture regime and up to 3 000 m in high mountains. Important genera found in India include:

  • Arundinaria
  • Bambusa
  • Dendrocalamus
  • Dinochloa
  • Gigantochloa
  • Melocanna
  • Indocalamus
  • Ochlandra
  • Oxytenanthera
  • Phyllostachys
  • Pleioblastus.

Hence bamboo is a highly suitable alternative material for making match splints.

Another important and highly relevant aspect is the small size of match splints, therefore even lops and tops, which are generally wasted in the bamboo handicraft sector, can be used for match splints.

2.2 Production process

After cross cutting bamboo into required sizes, it is split into slabs of 1.5 mm thickness and then into splints of 1.5 mm x 1.5 mm x 37 mm.

The manufacturing process developed at IPIRTI implies bamboo splints to be:

  • treated with sodium metasilicate;
  • dipped in diluted hydrogen peroxide for 15 to 20 minutes;
  • washed in water;
  • dipped in boric acid solution (with a concentration of 0.5 to 1 percent) or boric acid and borax mixture for around five minutes.
  • dried.

Treated splints are then required to be:

  • dipped in molten wax at 80 °C to 120 °C for 8 to 12 seconds; and
  • heated at around 150 °C for two to three seconds on a hot plate.

Burning heads are fixed to the bamboo match splints using standard chemicals and processes as per wooden match splints.

2.3 Production unit location

The matchstick unit can be set up in any bamboo growing area with a continuous raw material supply, and any country can adopt the technology. One essential condition is:

  • the license for storage and use of explosive materials for the burning heads and striking strips on the matchboxes.

Depending on the availability of raw materials in a particular location, the size of the unit can be:

  • cottage
  • small
  • medium
  • large.

2.4 Socio-economic impact and employment

A bamboo matchstick-manufacturing unit will provide employment and entrepreneurial opportunity to a wide range of people and relevant sectors, such as:

  • bamboo cultivation;
  • bamboo harvesting;
  • primary processing;
  • chemical processing;
  • matchstick marketing; and
  • matchstick retailing.

A cottage unit manufacturing 0.1 million matchboxes per day, can provide regular employment to more than 70 persons. The need for a sustainable supply of raw material will encourage:

  • proper management of bamboo;
  • new plantation establishments; and
  • associated environmental benefits.

The substantial quantity of bamboo plantation required to produce raw material will also increase long-term food security of rural poor in bamboo growing areas. Production of bamboo matchsticks on a small and medium scale is an effective way of utilizing renewable bamboo resources, which not only provides employment for rural people but also gives opportunities for income generation.

The technology will provide employment for a range of people and will generate extra employment in its forward and backward linkages. Its manufacture will benefit a wide range of people involved in all stages of matchstick production, either at the factory or close to the bamboo growing area.

2.5 Role of support services

The technology of bamboo matches can be adopted in the existing matchwood industry, having:

  • same chemical processing; but
  • different mechanical processing, (appropriate training can be organized).

2.6 Analysis of potential transferability issues/constraints

The technology can be adopted by the existing matchstick units using any species of bamboo and in any conditions. Since the anatomical structure of bamboo does not allow the wax to penetrate, pre-treatment of bamboo splints either in sodium hydroxide solution or in sodium metasilicate solution is required. This enhances the bleaching property and improves good wax penetration into bamboo splints.

3. Technology documentation, starting points for adaptation and financial analysis

3.1 Introduction

Research undertaken at IPIRTI in Bangalore, selected two widely grown bamboo species in the southern region of India, namely:

  • Bambusa bambos; and
  • Dendrocalamus strictus.

One important aspect when selecting bamboo species for making matchsticks is:

  • material strength and compliance to wooden match strength as prescribed for splints in relevant Standards.

Both the species selected were found to have the required strength properties.

3.2 Manufacturing processes

Bamboo matchstick manufacture requires two basic steps: 

  • splint making;
  • splint processing.

3.3 Splint making

Splints for making matchsticks have to meet the requirement of size, strength and etc. prescribed in IS:10374-1982 "Specification for Wooden Splints for Safety Matches".

Bamboo splints present the following characteristics:

  • Made from the matured culm of either of the selected species.
  • Dimensions are 37 mm long with a 1.5 mm x 1.5 mm cross section.
    • The cross section is smaller than the prevalent wooden match splints cross section.
  • Strength capacity is higher than the prevalent wooden match splints.
    • The splints of the above dimensions are able to pass the require strength tests.
  • Air-dried balancing moisture content.

3.3.1 Machinery requirements

  • circular saw;
  • splitting machine or machete;
  • splint making machine;
  • cutter and stick cutting machine; and
  • hot air chamber.

3.3.2 Culm sectioning, splitting and splint making

  • Cross cutting of culm into shorter length:
    • by hand; or
    • by using a cross cutting machine.
  • Splitting culm:
    • section is split longitudinally into splits of approximately equal width using the splitting machine.
  • Removing knot:
    • removal of nodes at or very close to either end of a section is necessary as they hinder proper splitting and burning.
  • Splitting culm into slabs with slab machine or slivering machine:
    • each split is passed through a slab-making machine to produce slabs of 1.5 mm thickness;
    • the slab-making machine also removes the epidermal or green outer layer.
  • Sectioning slab into thin splint of 1.5 mm diameter:
    • each slab is passed through stick making machine to produces splints of the same thickness (1.5 mm).
  • Cutting splint into 37 mm length, this is the usual size of matchsticks.

3.4 Splint processing

  • bleaching (optional)
  • carbonization
  • wax fixation
  • head fixing.

3.4.1 Bleaching

The splints are to be bleached in an open tank to ensure:

  • uniformity of colour; 
    • remove the natural colouring matter; and
  • market acceptance;
    • give an acceptable light colour similar to that of wooden match splints.

Prior to bleaching, the splints are:

  • pre-treated with 0.5 percent sodium silicate solution; and
  • bleached in hydrogen peroxide solution diluted with water in the ratio of 1:1 to 1:2.

Ammonia is added to maintain the pH of the bleaching solution in the range of 8 to 8.5.

The pH plays a very important role in bleaching:

  • an increased pH changes the colour of the splints to yellow; and
  • a decreased pH prolongs the time needed for bleaching.

This preliminary step helps to uniform bleaching and it facilitates penetration of wax at a later stage required for proper burning.

3.4.2 Carbonization

Carbonization of match splints imparts the desired level of afterglow properties required while extinguishing the flame of a matchstick.

For safety matches the lesser the period of after-glow the better.

Carbonization is done by:

  • chemical treatment;
    • bamboo match splints are soaked for a minimum period of ten minutes;
  • drying splints at 100 +/- 5 °C.

Though several fire-retardant chemicals are available, boric acid is perhaps the safest chemical in terms of:

  • handling
  • storing
  • transportation
  • cost.

Hence a solution with a concentration of 0.5 percent boric acid is used for carbonization of bamboo match splints.

3.4.3 Wax fixation

Wax fixation is necessary to achieve efficient transfer of flame from the burning head to the matchstick and its continuous burning until it is extinguished.

Wax fixation in the case of wooden splints is generally done by:

  • Bringing splints in contact with molten wax at a temperature of 110 °C to 130 °C for about two seconds.
  • Heating the wax tipped splints to around 150 °C for about two to three seconds on a hot plate to promote wax movement.

As wooden splints have more porosity, wax move into the pores within two to three seconds imparting good burning characteristics.

Anatomical structure of bamboo does not allow the wax to penetrate. Hence, for good wax penetration into bamboo match splints an appropriate formulation was evolved. Bamboo splints are:

  • pre-treated with 0.5 percent sodium metasilicate during bleaching process;
  • dipped in molten wax with a temperature ranging from 80 °C to 120 °C, for approximately ten seconds;
  • the wax treated splints are heated to around 150 °C  for about two to three seconds on a hot plate to promote wax movement.

3.4.5 Head fixing

A matchstick has an inflammable head that ignites only when struck on the friction surface.

The composition of the head plays an essential role in making the wooden splints light effectively when stroked against the friction surface of the matchbox.

The temperature of the flame attained is also one of the major factors that determine the degree of flame transmission from the head to the splint.

After a series of analyses carried out at the Institute laboratory, it was understood that varying percentages of potassium chlorate in the match head would give better results with respect to flame transmission to the splints.

However, two formulations presently used in Indian match industries were tried for bamboo match splints and it was found that the same formulations would also work for bamboo match splints.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Community bamboo harvesting: ID 7948.
  • Bamboo treadle pump: ID 3866.
  • Community bamboo nursery: ID 3868.
  • Bamboo in sericulture: a case study from India: ID 3859.
  • Production of bamboo mat board: ID 3860.
  • Bamboo toothpick manufacturing unit: ID 3888.
  • Bamboo splitting and slivering unit: ID 3865.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

6.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology contributes to resources use efficiency of bamboo, as well as reducing environmental impact and reduces soil erosion.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

Bamboo match sticks production can guarantee an income source for many and help enhance productivity of adjoining agricultural lands.
