Fry/seed quality and stocking

Fry is the young fish that is stocked in ponds to grow; harvested and sold. When the fish is just hatched it is called "fry". When it has grown to a size similar to human finger, it is called "fingerling". This technology describes what good quality fry is and what should be done to ensure good quality.

Description

In commercial aquaculture, the farmer aims at producing fish for profit in the shortest time possible.

The farmers' earnings and profit are reduced under specific circumstances.

  • If the size of the fish harvested is small and is rejected at the market or only sold at a low price.
  • If the harvest is of mixed sizes and only the large fish is selected out for sale and the rest is rejected.
  • If the harvest consists of a mixture of fish types and only one is popular in the market.
    • Only a proportion of the harvest is sold at a good price.
  • If the fish grows so slowly in a particular region, it takes a long time to reach market size.
    • The farmer spends more money in feeding the fish to attain market size.

The type and quality of fry stocked is often the main cause of the above cases, in which case the earnings and profits of the farmer are reduced. It is therefore advisable that the farmers stock good quality fry.

1. What is good quality fry?

  • The good fry is that fry that will produce the most profitable harvest in the shortest possible time.

1.2 Qualities of a good fry

  • Fish grow fast and reach market size quickly.
  • Fish gain the largest weight for every weight of feed given.
  • Fry that is composed of only the fish type popular in the market, not mixed.
  • All the fish, and not only some, will grow at about the same pace to be harvested and sold together.

2. How to differentiate poor quality fry from good quality?

2.1 The characteristics of poor-quality fry 

  • Fry of mixed fish types is not good fry (Figure 1).
    • This often happens when farmers do not get fry from a designated fry producer.
    • Examples: farmer-to-farmer fry supply or from the wild streams, river and lakes.
    • The farmer is sorting out what to sell.
    • Carp may sell at a lower price because Ugandan fish farmers are not familiar with it.
    • The farmer gets less money.
    • Instead of selling 25 kg, the farmer only sells 10 kg.
    • Fry of one fish type at a time is good.
Figure 1. Fry of mixed quality and fish type

©FAO/TECA

  • Fry of mixed ages or size groups is not of good quality.

    • Size normally indicates age. 
    • The bigger fry is older than the smaller ones.
    • Fry of mixed sizes are usually found when fry is collected from ponds not intended specifically for fry production (farmer-to-farmer fry supply), or when it is collected from the wild (streams, river and lakes).
    • Fry of mixed sizes or ages, result in mixed size harvests as shown in Figure 2.
    • In most cases, the older fish start reproducing in the pond and congest the pond much earlier when the majority of the fish are still small.
    • The stunted fish are sold at a reduced price and the farmer loses money.
Figure 2. A harvest from fry of mixed sizes and age groups

©FAO/TECA

  • Fry of uniform size/age is good (Figure 3).
    • Size indicates age, therefore uniform size is also uniform age.
    • In the Catfish ("male") fry, when some individuals are larger than others, the larger fry feed on the smaller ones.
    • When fry of varying sizes is stocked, the overall harvest is low, consisting of few numbers although their sizes may be big.
Figure 3. A harvest from uniform fry groups

©FAO/TECA

  • Stunted fry is not good.
    • Stunted fish is fish that is too old for its size.
    • It is usually a result of inadequate feeding of fry or feeding with poor quality feed.
    • The fry remains small while the age is advancing.
    • The easiest way to recognize stunted fry is large heads with bulging eyes contrasted with its small body size.
  • Any lame (diseased) fry is not good for stocking (Figure 4).
    • There are several types of fish diseases.
    • A diseased fish does not grow well and may die.
    • Fry showing any signs of disease should not be accepted for stocking.
    • Lameness usually affects the skeleton and the fish does not grow well.
    • Fry showing any sign of disease is not good for stocking.
  • Fry may be lame (with deformities) as a result of:
    • serious injuries acquired due to bad handling;
    • feeds that lack certain nutrients (especially minerals and vitamins);
    • a heritable factor (gene); or
    • diseases.
Figure 4. A fish with a diseased mouth

©FAO/TECA

  • Fry that is badly injured.
    • Injury results when fry is badly or roughly handled.
    • The bruised fry may get an infection and die.
    • Or it may take some time for the wounds to cure.
    • During that period, it does not feed, and it grows slowly.
    • It is small at harvest.
  • Fry collected from the wild (stream, river or lakes) is not good.
  • Fry of poor genetic quality.
    • Fry may be of poor quality because of factors inherited from generation to generation (genes).
    • External signs of genetic quality may not be obvious to ordinary people.
    • They may not tell in advance that it is poor fry.
    • They only find that the fish does not grow well.
    • How to identify the poor genetic quality of fry is not in the scope of this manual.
    • The only way to avoid these uncertainties is to get the fry from a certified fish breeder.

2.2 The results of stocking poor quality fry as compared to good quality fry

  • The results of the stocking fry of mixed sizes or fish types.
    • When such fry is stocked in a pond, the harvest will be of mixed fish types, some of which may not be popular in the market and will be sold at a low price.
    • Usually, fry size indicates the age of the fry.
    • Stocking mixed size means some fish are older than others.
    • When fry of different sizes are stocked together, the few older fish mature earlier and start reproducing while the rest are still growing.
    • Because of the increased numbers, all the fish stop growing (get stunted).
    • The harvest consists of very few fish large enough for the market and the rest are too small and are rejected by the market.
    • In Figure 5 the farmer is sorting out the few larger fish to sell at a good price.
      • The rest are sold at a very low price.
      • The market may offer higher price for "Kibaati" and reject Carp.
      • The farmer may get only 30 per cent of what he should have got.
Figure 5. A harvest of mixed fish types (mirror carp, "kibaati" and "lukka") and mixed fish sizes resulting from fry of mixed fish types and sizes

©FAO/TECA

  • The results of the stocking fry of the same fish species and of uniform size.
    • If the farmer stocks only the fish type that the market desires (say, "kibaati") at a uniform size, all the fish will grow at the same pace.
    • All of them attain market size at the same time (see Figure 6).
    • The uniform fry produces uniform size harvest and all the fish are sold at a good price.
    • There is no need for sorting what to sell.
Figure 6. A fish of the same age and size

©FAO/TECA

  • The results of stocking stunted fish.
    • The farmer spends money on feeding, hoping that the fish will grow bigger.
    • The fish does not grow bigger.
    • Instead, it matures and reproduces at small sizes.
    • The result is that the pond gets filled up with many small fish that are difficult to sell at a good price.
    • The farmer loses profit.
  • The results of stocking lame fish.
    • A harvest of lame carp among normal ones dictates that only the normal ones can be sold.
    • Note that the lame fish grow slowly.
  • The result of stocking diseased fish.
    • A diseased fish may not feed comfortably.
    • It does not grow well and if not treated it may die.
    • Nobody would like to buy such a fish to eat.
Figure 7. Lame carp

©FAO/TECA

3. Recommendations on quality of fry

  • Farmers should purchase fry from well-established fry producers.
    • These are the fry producers certified by the Fisheries Department.
    • See the list of the certified seed producer in the Appendix.
  • Complaints about bad fry can be registered with the Commissioner for Fisheries, Department of Fisheries Resources, Entebbe, Box number 4, Entebbe, Telephone 041320563.
  • Farmers should avoid collecting fry from the wild for stocking their ponds.
    • Its quality is not known.
  • Both the fry producers and the farmers collecting the fry to stock are responsible for avoiding injuries on the fry during fishing and handling during transportation.

4. Preparation of ponds for stocking

  • The ponds to be stocked must be prepared adequately before stocking.
  • Pre-stocking preparations include the preparation of a new pond for stocking and the preparation of the pond that previously had fish.

4.1 Preparation of new pond for stocking

  • Final finishing (for new ponds), removal of mud and repairs (old ponds).
  • Liming the pond.
  • Fixing pipes and screens.
  • Fertilizing the pond.
  • Filling the pond with water.
  • Allowing time for the pond to turn green.

4.1.1 How to prepare the new pond

  • Fixing inlet and outlet pipes.
    • The pipe to let water into the pond (inlet pipes) is fixed at the shallowest point of the pond.
    • the drainage pipe is fixed at the deepest end of the pond.
    • The inlet pipes must be screened to keep away wild fish from entering the pond.
    • A netting material with very fine mesh is used.
    • The pond is fertilized first before filling with water.
  • Fertilizing the pond.
    • Pond fertilization is done to allow the growth of natural foods for the fry to be stocked.
    • If fry is stocked before building up the quantity of natural foods, the fry may starve or grow slowly and become stunted.
    • Several materials can be used for fertilizing ponds, including agricultural (also called inorganic) fertilizers and manure (called organic fertilizers).
  • Agricultural or inorganic fertilizers.
    • these include NPK, TSP, SSP, Urea. All these are in powder or granular form, they are available in shops selling agricultural chemicals.
  • Organic fertilizers (manure).
    • The sources of manure include chicken dropping and urine; cow dung and urine; pig dung and urine; compost; sunflower cake.
  • When the pond has developed these organisms (algae) turned green, it is ready for stocking.
    • If fry is stocked before sufficient food has grown in the pond, the fry will not grow well.

4.2 Preparation of pond that previously had fish

  • For the pond in which fish have already been grown, there is no need to go through the whole long process required for the new pond.
  • Important points.
    • Completely drain the pond, remove all the fish (fry or eggs) that may have remained from the previous harvest.
    • Kill off all the germs and other animals that may be at the pond bottom (e.g. tadpoles, frog eggs, insects, etc).
    • Allow the pond to completely dry up so that the mud breaks up).
  • After drying the pond, it may require some repair work before it is ready for re-stocking.

4.2.1 Removing the bottom mud

  • Mud accumulated in the pond comes from two sources:
    • banks that keep collapsing and falling into the pond; and
    • the remains of manure and other feeds that were given to fish and the faeces that fish produce.
  • It is important to remove the mud because it reduces the productivity of the pond.
    • It may also be prone to disease.
    • The mud becomes lighter and easier to remove after drying it.
    • It is simply scraped from the bond bottom using hoes or shovels (see Figure 8).
    • The lighter surface mud, rich in manure, should be carried away and used to fertilize gardens.
    • The firmer mud should be used to build back the pond dyke that has collapsed or is in danger of collapse.
Figure 8. Farmers removing mud from the bottom of the pond

©FAO/TECA

4.2.2 Pond repair

  • A used pond may require some repair as a result of:
    • the banks collapsing to the bottom and accumulating as mud;
    • some fish that dig up the pond banks and dykes, causing leakages; and
    • roots of trees growing bigger and causing cracks through pond dykes.
  • Pond repairs include:
    • building back the collapsed pond banks and re-shaping the pond using the firm soils from the bottom; and
    • sealing off any leakages;
  • After all these repairs the pond is prepared for stocking.
    • The process follows the steps outlined as for new ponds: liming, fertilizing, fixing inlets and outlets and filling the pond with water.
    • In the case of used ponds, however, the lime also helps to kill off germs and eggs or fry from previous harvests.
  • The pond is filled with water through the inlet pipes.
    • The screens prevent the entry of wild fish.
    • The pond is left to stay full for at least two weeks before stocking.
    • During this period sufficient quantities of natural food organisms develop (see Figure 9).
  • In addition to the green plants, the pond water also becomes rich with small animals that are good food for fry.
    • These are the most suitable food items for fry.
    • Farmers would have to be shown by a technical person how to tell that these organisms are present.
    • The pond is now ready for stocking. 
    • Just before stocking, the pond should be fished through with a net twice or three times.
    • This is done to remove any wild fish, frogs or any other animal that may have entered the pond while it was filled with water so that it is free for stocking.
Figure 9. A fertilized pond is green. The green indicates the tiny green plants suitable particularly for Nile tilapia "Kibaati"

©FAO/TECA

5. Collection, good handling, packaging, transportation and stocking of fry

  • There are a number of steps to be followed during the stocking of a fishpond.
    • These steps take time (up to a month) and a schedule needs to be drawn to save time.
    • The following sequence of activities should be followed.

5.1 Identifying the fry producer with the fry required

  • The farmer finds out which nearest fry producer has the right type, size and quantity of fry.
    • If there are many fry producers, which one offers the best price, remember to consider the cost of transportation.
    • It is advisable to keep a list of telephone numbers of as many fry producers as possible.
    • This will always be available at the office of the Commissioner for Fisheries or the Head of Aquaculture Units, Department of Fisheries Resources Entebbe (see Table 7).
  • The farmer should ring and find out the most suitable fry producer.
    • Should there be many fry producers with the right type and size of fry, the farmer should choose the nearest one to cut down on the cost of transportation.

5.2 Making an appointment with fry producers

  • The farmer should make a clear appointment with the fry producer, detailing the number of fry required, type of fish, size of fry and agree on the date for collection.
  • The following steps are followed collecting fry for stocking.
    • The farmer should find out from the nearest fry producers who will be having fry by the time the pond is ready.
      • Find this out at least three weeks in advance.
    • The farmer tells the fry producer exactly when he/she will need the fry.
    • The farmer continues to prepare the pond.
    • The farmer should finally confirm the availability and agree with the fry producer the date for collection at least five days in advance.
    • The confirmation is necessary because the fry producer could have had another buyer and sold off the fry.
    • The five days are necessary to look for an alternative fry supplier in case the original fry supplier sold off his fry.
    • Fry is collected promptly as agreed.
      • Changing the program to collect the fry at the last minute should be avoided at all costs.
      • The fry producer will have removed the fry from the pond intended for that farmers and a lot of the fry may die if not taken as arranged.

5.3 Preparing containers (packaging materials) and means of transport

  • The farmer prepares the containers (packaging materials) for the fry and appropriate transport.
    • The type of container for carrying the fry and the kind of transport to be used depends on the number of fry to be carried and the distance to be travelled.
    • Table 1 shows the types of containers and means of transport commonly used in transporting fry.
Table 1. Types of container used and the number of fry that can be transported
Fry number  Distance  Suitable container  Means of transport
Up to 2 000  Less than 1 km   Open buckets Jerry cans Polythene bags with air Foot, bicycle, motorcycle (see Figure 10)
Up to 2 000  3 km - 20 km  Jerry cans, polythene bags with air Bicycle, motorcycle, taxi, bus (see Figure 11)
2 000 to 10 000 Beyond 50 km Jerry cans, polythene bags with oxygen Motorcycle, taxi, bus (see Figure 11)
More than 50 000   More than 50 km PVC tanks with constant oxygen  Truck

Source: NAADS 2011

  • Note: the catfish fry does not need pumping fresh air into the container.
    • They come to the water surface and breathe in dry air.
  • A few fry, a short distance.
    • An open bucket is suitable for fry up to 2 000 to be taken to nearby ponds, less than 1 km (see Figure 10).
  • A few fry, a long distance.
    • For a distance up to 1 km and beyond (see Figures 11, 12 and 13).
    • Farmer can pack jerry cans and plastic bags of fry into the back of Pick-up. It is wrong to load jerry cans or plastic bags on top of a bus, exposed to direct sunshine. If the only available transport is a bus, put the jerry cans of fry inside the bus in the corridor
Figure 10. A farmer carrying fry in a bucket to a nearby pond, farmer carrying fish in jerry cans on a "boda boda" to some distant village

©FAO/TECA

Figure 11. A farmer carrying fish in jerry can on the head or shoulders on foot for a pond in the next village

©FAO/TECA

Figure 12. A farmer packing jerry cans and plastic bags of fry into the back of Pick-up

©FAO/TECA

Figure 13. Packing fry in poly bags

©FAO/TECA

5.3.1 Packing fry in polythene bags

  • The polythene bags are made from a polythene tube of 500 gauge.
  • The tubes vary in width but commonly they are about 1 foot to 1.5 feet wide when laid flat.
    • They are sold in some hardware shops, displayed as rolls but the farmer can buy in metres.
    • In Kampala, they are found in Owino market the section selling polythene sheets and bags.
  • The tube is cut into 3 feet long pieces.
    • One end is twisted and tied very tight using small strips cut from old bicycle tubes to make a bag.
  • The bag is held vertically upright with the open end up.
    • It is filled with water up to half its length.
    • The same water in the nursing pond or tank is used to avoid causing shock to the fry.
  • If a different source of water is used, this water should be mixed slowly with the water containing the fry to bring it to the same warmth before fry is transferred into the bag.
  • The sudden transfer of fry into water different in warmth from the water containing the fry will shock the fry and cause sudden death.
  • The treated tap water used at home for drinking should not be used for packing fry.
    • The chemicals used to kill fry.
  • The right number of fry as given in the table above is transferred into the bag.
    • The fry must be counted to get an accurate number.
  • The mouth of the poly bags is closed, trapping a sufficient amount of air.
    • The mouth is then twisted tightly until the air pressure makes the bag firm and it can stand without collapsing.
  • For fry that is to be transported a long distance, oxygen can be pumped from an oxygen cylinder into the bags instead of just air.
  • The bag or bags can then be placed in larger boxes made from cardboard.
    • The inside of the cardboard should be inspected to ensure it has no sharp pins.
    • The pins will prick the bags and the water flows out.
  • In the case of many bags, avoid piling many bags on top of each other.
    • The bags at the bottom may burst because of the pressure exerted by the bags on top.
  • It is convenient to pack separately the fry for stocking in different ponds.
    • The bag is opened for a particular pond instead of opening many bags and counting the fry.
    • This saves time during stocking and avoids making the fry exhausted.
  • The clear transparent bags are better because they allow the fry inside to be seen (Figure 13).
    • Place the bag in a horizontal rather than vertical position during transportation.
    • In this way, a wider surface area is available for air exchange with the water for the fry (Figure 14).
Figure 14. Keep the bags in a horizontal position

©FAO/TECA

5.3.2 Packaging fry in jerry cans

  • The jerry can for carrying fry must be very clean.
    • If new, they must not have contained oil or any chemical.
  • Oils can clog the gills of fry and make breathing difficult and can kill the fry.
  • Jerry cans that have contained oils, paraffin, diesel, or any other substance should be washed with soap repeatedly until all traces of smell are finished before use for carrying fry.
    • Better still do not jerry cans.
  • A rectangular opening (about 3 inches x 5 inches) is cut at three sides, leaving it held by the fourth side as a flap.
    • The hole is used to ease packing the fry into the jerry can and it also eases air exchange.
  • The jerry can is filled with good water up to two-third its height, leaving the other one-third containing air.
  • The same water as that in which the fry had been conditioned should be used.
    • If another source of water is used, the new water must be first mixed with some of the water in which the fry had been nursed to equalize their temperatures and avoid shocking the fry.
  • The selected fry is then counted and put into the jerry can through the cut hole.
    • When packed this way, one jerry can contain up to 200 tilapia and Carp fry.
    • Fry can be transported using jerry cans for a distance of not greater than 200 km.
    • Beyond this distance, the number of fry should be reduced slightly'
  • The same jerry can take 300 Clarias ("Male") fry.
  • The "male fry is able to breathe dry air directly from the space while Tilapia and Carp fry only extract air dissolved in the water.
Figure 15. Illustration of jerry cans for carrying fry

©FAO/TECA

5.3.3 Using larger containers

  • Larger containers, such as plastic tanks, are used to transport a large number of fry, as shown in Table 2.
Table 2. The number of fry per volume of water used in the package is given in the table below
Volume of water in package (litres)  Number of fry in package 
1  15  
10  150
20 300

Source: NAADS 2011

  • The most commonly used are the crest tanks volumes 300 to 500 litres (see Figure 16).
    • It is difficult to handle fry in tanks much larger than this size range.
  • Metallic tanks should be discouraged because they may heat up on a hot day.
  • The tanks with larger mouths are better than those with smaller mouths.
    • They make it easier to put the fry in and taking the fry out, it also eases the exchange of water during transportation.
  • The water should be the same water that had been used to nurse the fry.
    • Or the new water should first be mixed with the old water before fry is introduced.
  • The tank must be filled up to two-third their height, the top one-third being left to allow air exchange.
    • The prepared fry is counted and packed into the tanks.
  • The maximum number of fry that can be safely carried by the different tanks sizes are given in Table 3.
    • In each case the number of fry of the Catfish is higher than that of Tilapia and Carp.
  • For shorter distances that take up to two hours, the air in the space above the water is adequate for the fry.
  • For distances that take longer than two hours, an oxygen cylinder should be fixed to provide continuous supply of oxygen throughout the journey.
  • For Clarias ("male") fry, the oxygen cylinder is not required.
    • The fry breathes dry air directly from the space above the water.
Figure 16. Illustration of crest tanks for carrying fry

©FAO/TECA

Table 3. The number of fry of different fish species that can be carried in tanks of different size (litres)
Tank size (litres)    Maximum number of Tilapia fry Maximum number of Carp fry Maximum number of Catfish fry 
50       
100  1 000  1 000   1 500
200  2 000  2 000  3 000 
300  3 000  3 000   6 000 
500  5 000 5 000 10 000

Source: NAADS 2011

5.3.4 Care for fry on transit

  • Fry is a living and delicate thing.
    • It should not be handled like goods.
    • If not handled well it may die before reaching the pond for stocking.
  • The trip for collecting fry should not be combined with other activities that may cause delays.
    • If it is not avoidable, then the other activities must be completed and the fry is loaded last.
  • Young fish cannot tolerate starvation for long, they die easily.
    • Therefore, ensure that there is sufficient food in the pond before collecting the fry to stock.
  • The source of fry may be far and transportation costs high.
    • Yet ample time must be given to the fry producer to prepare the fry for collection.
    • Therefore, it is important to make an appointment with the fry producer before collection to avoid disappointment or delay.

5.4 Fry transportation and pond stocking

  • Preparation of fry for collection is the responsibility of the fry producer.
    • But the farmer needs to know the process because he/she will lose the fry if not prepared well.
  • The fry to be transported the following day should be harvested from the pond a day before.
    • During harvesting, fry get tired and needs to rest for at least a day before they are transported.
  • The fry to be transported should not be fed for that day. 
    • They should be allowed to empty their gut and remain with an empty gut throughout the journey.
  • When the gut has food, the fry will be emptying their gut into the containers and the excreta will pollute the water and kill the fry.
  • If the farmer waits to complete pond preparation and to fill with water and then starta looking for fry, a lot of time can be wasted.
  • The following schedule of these activities can help save time.
    • Tables 4 and 5 showing the schedule for stocking fish pond can be of great help.
    • The following two tables summarize the arrangements for collecting and stocking the fry.
Table 4. Activities for stocking your pond with fry
Activity number  Activity
1 Find out from a fry producer when fry can be available then allow three weeks to prepare for stocking
2 Drain pond and allow to dry (if had been with fish)
3 Repair pond bottom, banks and dyke and water channels
4 Lime then enter a little water to the depth of 2 inches at inlet end
5 Fix screens on outlet and inlets
6 Add manure
7 Fill pond with water to maximum level
8 Allow pond to become green (at least five days)
9 Confirm date for collecting fry, leaving at least five days for preparation
10 Collect fry and stock

Source: NAADS 2011

Table 5. A schedule of activities for stocking a fish pond

Source: NAADS 2011

  • It takes normally a minimum of two and a half weeks from completing pond construction or harvesting to stocking with new fry.
    • Note: do not stock fry in the pond to starve to death.
  • When fish are stocked in a pond that has not yet developed enough natural food, the fish may starve and die.
    • The pond to be stocked must be prepared to develop a sufficient quantity of natural food for the fry before stocking.
  • A summary of steps followed in fry collection, transportation and stocking.
    • Preparation of the pond to be stocked.
    • Making an appointment with the fry producer (agreeing date for collection, type and number of fish, items required).
    • Prepare packaging materials.
    • Packaging fry.
    • Care during transit.
    • Introducing (stocking) the fry into the new pond.
    • Inspect stocked pond for any dead fry for at least three days after stocking.
    • If many fry die, arrange for restocking.

5.5 Preparation of fry for collection

  • The farmer should collect the fry promptly according to the appointment.
    • Failure to collect the fry on the date agreed may result in some fry dying.
    • For this reason, fry producers may demand an advance payment (a percentage cost of the fry).
    • The fry producer harvests the fry and prepares it for collection.
  • Fry should be collected on an appointment with the fry producer, specifying the date, time, fish type and quantity of fry, to allow adequate time for preparation.
  • The main activities from collecting fry to stocking fry in the pond and the time required are outlined in this sector.
  • Fry must be harvested from the nursery pond and allowed to rest for one full day before transporting.
    • During rest, the fry should not be fed at all.
    • Therefore, do not keep fry resting for more than three days otherwise it starves.
    • The reasons.
      • The rest period allows the fry producers to sort out the fry that was injured or exhausted to die out.
      • The survivors are those that are strong and healthy enough for sale.
      • The rest period also allows the fry to empty their gut before transportation because fry is not fed.

5.5.1 Packaging fry for transportation

  • The type of containers required for carrying fry and the type of transport depend on a number of factors. 
    • The travel distance.
    • The quantity of fry to be carried (see Figure 17).
    • Fry is packaged and transported in appropriate containers depending on the travel distance and the quantity of fry.
    • When fry are transported with full gut, they release their excreta into the container during the journey.
      • The excreta, mainly ammonia, is poisonous and may cause mass death of the fry along the way.
  • Table 6 gives the disadvantages and loss of benefits that may arise from collecting fry from the wild.
Table 6. Advantages and disadvantages of using fish hatcheries compared to wild sources
Source of seed      Fish Hatcheries Wild sources
Advantages 
  • Lower risk of obtaining fish of the wrong species.
  • Seed supply not influenced by seasons.
  • Quality assurance (size, age, species, health).
  • In case of problems, one can follow up the source.
  • Greater guarantee of obtaining farmers required a number for stocking of required quality.
  • Sources may be closer to farmers, hence often more accessible.
  • May be cheaper.
Disadvantages
  • Sources often far for the majority of farmers which increases transport costs for farmers.
  • Seed costs may be higher.
  • Supply influenced by seasons.
  • Difficult to obtain larger numbers of the same quality at the time a farmer requires them.
  • In order to collect required numbers, fish often collected and stored over a period of time by fishermen which is more stressful for fish. This results in heavy losses (high death rates) at stocking.
  • Cannot guarantee age of fish.
  • It is illegal to fish undersized fish from the wild.

Source: NAADS 2011

Figure 17. Picking up the adequate quantity of fry to be carried

©FAO/TECA

5.5.2 Care for fry during transportation

  • As much as possible avoid transporting fry during very hot hours of day.
    • Very late evening or night are the most ideal times.
  • Do not expose fry in direct sunlight.
  • The rains help to keep the fry cool.
  • Avoid stopping on the way.
    • But if you must stop, keep it very short and park the fry under the shade.
  • Stop at intervals during travel to inspect the fry in the containers.
    • Fry may get exhausted, some may die and dissolved oxygen may be depleted.
  • The simplest sign that the fry is in need of fresh air is when most of the fry come to the top of the water in the container and start gulping for air (see Figure 19).
  • At this point, the water in the containers need to be changed (completely or partial replacement).
    • Find the nearest stream with water that you have no reason to suspect that it is polluted or dirty.
  • Stop at the stream and open the containers.
    • Carefully reduce the water in the containers (by siphoning or pouring out, depending on the type of container).
    • Take care not to pour out the fry.
  • As water is pouring out, add the stream water very slowly to avoid shocking the fry.
    • The temperatures of the water carrying fry and the stream water may be very different.
    • When the replacement is sudden, the sudden change in temperature may kill the fry.
  • Any dead fry must be removed immediately from the container to avoid rotting and polluting the water.
  • Note: the steps outlined above shows the need to have certain basic containers during fry transportation.
    • These include buckets with handles for collecting water and extra polythene bags, in case one develops a leakage.
Figure 18. Caution

©FAO/TECA

Figure 19. A picture of fish gulping for air

©FAO/TECA

5.5.3 Introducing the fry into the pond

  • If not done properly the fry may arrive at the pond having travelled a long distance and then die at the pond edge.
    • What usually kills fry at stocking is the sudden introduction into the new pond whose water temperature may be very different from the water that the fry came in.
    • The fry must be introduced very slowly to allow it to get used to the new conditions. 
    • This is done as follows.
      • Get the fry for each pond into a container.
      • Fry to be stocked must be counted.
      • Get some water from the pond to be stocked and slowly add into the container with the fry.
      • Mix the waters slowly until about 50 percent of the water with the fry has been replaced (see Figure 20).
Figure 20. Releasing fry into the pond

©FAO/TECA

  • Place the container with the fry in the water at the edge of the pond.
    • Tilt the container slowly into the pond water until the two waters are in contact.
    • Slowly pour the container water with the fry into the pond.
    • Watch that the fry swims into the new water voluntarily.
  • The stocking process will last as long as 20 minutes for a small pond.
  • Some fry may become too exhausted during transportation and may not recover fully.
    • To ensure the exact number of fry that was successfully stocked, the farmer should inspect the pond for any fry that may die.
    • The number of fry that died at stocking is recorded each day for up to three days.
  • The inspection recording of the dead fry should be done very early before birds come and pick out the dead fry.
  • The total number of fry that died at stocking is added up and subtracted from the total fry that was collected.
  • If the number of fry that died does not exceed 20 percent, the growth of the remaining stock continues.
    • If the number exceeds 20 percent, a trip is made to collect and replace the dead number.
    • The fry should be collected from the same farmer and the same stock to avoid mixing fry of different age groups.
  • For the moment a stocking rate of two fish per m² of pond area is recommended for all the three commonly farmed fish types (Nile tilapia, Carp and Catfish).
  • For the more intensive production systems, where the farmer is able to feed intensively, higher stocking rates are calculated for the farmer on a case-by-case basis. Seek expert advice from Kajjansi or a qualified service provider.
  • Note: because of the elaborate steps taken during transporting and stocking fish fry, it is strongly recommended that, if more than one pond is to be stocked, fry for each pond should be packed separately to minimize the effects of handling.
    • Stocking becomes a lot easier.

5.5.4 Recommendations

  • Avoid collecting fry from the wild (lakes, rivers/streams or swamps).
  • Fry should be purchased from well-known and certified fry producers.
    • These fry producers keep production records make it easier to follow up sources of poor fry.
Table 7. The list and contact addresses of certified fry producers as at 2004 (this list may keep changing with time as informed by Fisheries Department Entebbe)

Source: NAADS 2011

6. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Make a living through fish farming: ID 7357.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The technology allows for the growth of fry that will produce the most profitable harvest in the shortest possible time.

8.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology provides efficient guidance in terms of preparation, stocking, quality check, handling, pond management and transportation amongst others.

The text describes a detailed technical guide for fish fry quality assessment and pond management, but it presents standard aquaculture practices rather than introducing any new or innovative solutions or technologies for agrifood systems transformation.
_annotations.field_shorter_description: Fry is the young fish that is stocked in ponds to grow; harvested and sold. When the fish is just hatched it is called "fry". When it has grown to a size similar to human finger, it is called "fingerling". This technology describes what good quality fry is and what should be done to ensure good quality.

records.title: Rice-fish Culture System (RFC)
records.description:
Description

Rice-fish culture has great potential for being developed in countries with vast areas of irrigated rice fields. Standing water in rice fields promotes the development of a teeming ecosystem with aquatic animals such as fish, ducks, freshwater prawns, marine shrimps, crayfish, crabs, turtle, bivalve, frogs, snails and even insects.

Although cultivating fish reduces the area available for planting rice, the integrated system leads to higher returns than those of rice monoculture. This is due to the fact that within the Rice-fish Culture System (RFC), the rice yield is higher, the farmers receive an additional income from the fish sales and in most of the cases, they save on fertilizers and pesticides. In addition, rice-fish farming presents a more efficient use of water. However, it is not recommended for areas with limited water supply as it requires about 26 percent more water than rice monoculture.

1. Benefits of the integrated system

  • The benefits of the integrated system are related to nutrition quality and to the interactions between fish and rice systems.

1.1 Nutrition

  • The combination of different plant and animal species makes rice-fish systems nutritionally rich.
  • The rice-fish agroecosystem supplies a wide range of micronutrients, proteins and essential fatty acids that are especially important in the diets of pregnant women and young children.
  • While rice is the main dietary source of carbohydrates, the fish supplies protein, being an important source of cheap and easily digestible animal protein.

1.2 Interactions between fish and rice systems: pest control

  • Equally important are the interactions among plant and animal species, which improve the:
    • sustainability of production;
    • reduce the use of pesticides, herbicides and fertilizers; and
    • improve soil fertility.

1.2.1 Soil fertility

  • The rice paddies offer protection, shade and organic food for the fish.
    • As fish swim in the paddies, as reciprocity, they soften the soil, bring the oxygen to the water and provide nutrients for the rice crop.
  • The interactions between plant and animal species in rice-fish fields also improve soil fertility.
    • The nutrients in fish feed are recycled back into fields through excreta and made immediately available to the rice crop.
    • Reports from China, Indonesia and the Philippines indicate that rice-fish farmers’ spending on fertilizer is lower.

1.2.2 Pest control

  • Fish are biological control agents for weeds, insect pests and vectors of serious diseases, such as mosquitoes.
    • The fish eat insects and weeds maintaining a perfect ecological balance that improves biodiversity while limiting problems caused by insects and plant diseases.
  • In China, by using fish for integrated pest management, rice-fish systems achieve yields comparable to, or even higher than, rice monoculture, while using up to 68 percent less pesticides.
    • Weed control is generally easier in rice-fish systems because the water levels are higher than in rice-only fields.
    • Studies in China found that the presence of rice stem-borers was around 50 percent less in rice-fish fields.
    • As examples, a single common carp can consume up to 1 000 juvenile golden apple snails every day.
    • The grass carp feeds on a fungus that causes sheath and culm blight.
  • Rice-fish farming is practiced in many countries in the world, particularly in Asia.
    • While each country has evolved its own unique approach and procedures, there are also similarities, common practices and common problems.

2. Infrastructure

  • There are two types of rice-fish production systems.
    • Concurrent culture
      • The most common is concurrent culture, where fish and rice are raised in the same field at the same time (Figure 1).
    • Rotational culture
      • Rice and fish are produced at different times.
      • This type of culture is less common.
  • In general, rice fields to be used for rice-fish culture have to be modified to varying degrees to make them favourable for fish growth, by the application of low-cost appropriate technology for the production of fish in irrigated rice fields.
  • The physical renovation includes the excavation of ditches and sumps as a shelter for fish and building of higher and wider dikes to prevent the escape of cultured fish, and at the same time to prevent flooding.
  • There are four physical improvements that are commonly made to prepare rice fields for fish culture.
    • Increase the height of the dike or bund to allow deeper water inside the field and/or to minimize the risk of it being flooded.
    • Provide weirs or screens to prevent the fish from escaping as well as keeping predatory fish from coming in with the irrigation water.
    • Not always practiced but often recommended, provide proper drains.
    • Provide deeper areas as a refuge for the fish.
Figure 1. Excavation of ditches

©FAO/TECA

2.1 Increasing dike (bund) height

  • Rice field embankments are typically low and narrow since the usual rice varieties do not require deep water.
  • To make the rice field more suitable for fish, the height of the embankment needs in most cases to be increased.
  • Reports on rice-fish culture from various countries show embankments with a height of 40 cm to 50 cm (measured from ground level to crown).
  • Since the water level for rice does not normally exceed 20 cm, such embankments will already have a freeboard of 20 cm to 30 cm (Figure 2).
  • This is sufficient to prevent most fish from jumping over.
  • The height of the embankments cannot, of course, be increased without a corresponding increase in the width.
  • There are no hard and fast rules as to the final width, but generally, it is within the range of 40 cm to 50 cm.
  • In China, rice farmers raise fish in trenches up to 100 cm wide and 80 cm deep, which are dug around and across the paddy field and occupy about 20 percent of the paddy area.
Figure 2. Dike construction to prevent the escape of for cultured fish and prevent flooding

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Provision of weirs or screen

  • Once the fish are inside the rice field, efforts are made to prevent them from escaping with the water, regardless of whether it is flowing in or out.
  • To prevent loss of the fish stock, farmers install screens or weirs across the path of the water flow.
  • The screens used rely on the local materials available.
  • There are three types of screens: bamboo slats, a basket, and a piece of fishnet material (even a well-perforated piece of sheet metal).
  • In China, bamboo screens or nets are used to prevent fish from escaping.

2.3 Provision of drains

  • In general rice fields are not equipped with gates for management of water levels.
  • The common practice is to temporarily breach a portion of the embankment to let the water in or out at whatever point is most convenient.
  • This is understandable since typically dikes are no more than 25 cm to 30 cm high with an almost equal width.
  • Using a shovel, a hoe or bare hands, water can be made to flow in or out.
  • Repairing the dike afterwards is just as easy.
  • The larger dike required for rice-fish culture makes it more difficult to breach, and it will also take more effort to repair.
  • It is therefore advisable to provide a more permanent way of conveying water in or out just like in a regular fish pond, although this may incur an extra cost.
  • Generally, reports do not contain enough detail on the type of water outlets installed, but among these are bamboo tubes, hollowed-out logs, metal pipes or bamboo chutes.

2.4 Fish refuges

  • A fish refuge is a deeper area provided for the fish within a rice field.
  • This can be in the form of a trench or several trenches, a pond or even just a sump or a pit.
  • The purpose of the refuge is to provide a place for the fish in case of water in the field dries up or is not deep enough.
  • It also serves to facilitate fish harvest at the end of the rice season, or to contain fish for further culture whilst the rice is harvested.
  • In conjunction with the refuge, provisions are often made to provide the fish with better access to the rice field for feeding.
  • There are various forms of refuges ranging from depressions in a part of the rice field, to trenches to a pond adjacent to the field connected with a canal. A multitude of systems have been reported (trenches, ponds, pits, sumps), but they all follow the same principles.
  • It is common to combine them as well.
  • The trenches have three main functions.
    • Be a refuge should water levels drop.
    • Be a passageway providing fish with better access for feeding in the rice field.
    • Be a catch basin during harvest.
  • There are several ways the trenches could be dug (Figure 3).
    • The simplest way involves just digging a central trench longitudinally in the field.
  • The common width of the trenches is between 40 cm and 50 cm and as suggested minimum depth is 50 cm, measured from the crown of the bund to the bottom of the trench resulting in the bottom of the trench being 25 cm to 30 cm to below the field level.
  • However, there are several variations according to the fish for the culture and the country.
  • For fingerling production, the ditches are dug together with 50 cm to 70 cm deep 1 m² pits or sumps at the water inlet and outlets.
  • Rice seedlings are planted along both sides of each ditch and three sides of each pit to serve as “a fence”.
  • A variation, reported from China, is a “wide ditch” (referred to as a trench) measuring 1 m wide and 1 m deep, placed laterally along the water inlet side of the rice field with a ridge rising about 25 cm above the field level.
    • It is constructed along the side of the ditch that is away from the embankment.
    • To allow the fish to forage among the rice plants, 24 cm wide openings are made along the ridge at 3 m to 5 m intervals.
    • These ditches occupy around 5 to 10 percent of the rice field area.
  • In coastal areas with poor drainage in West Java - Indonesia, producers use the “surjan system” (Figure 4).
    • In this system, the dikes are raised to function as beds for dryland crops.
    • The trenches, the rice area and the dikes form three levels for the fish, rice and dryland crops.
Figure 3. Designs and construction of fish trenches in Indonesia (Koesoemadinata and Costa-Pierce, 1992). 1) Peripheral trench. 2) Diagonal trench. 3) crossed trenches. 4) Y-shaped trench. 5) Peripheral with one central longitudinal trench. 6) Peripheral with two equidistant transverse trenches. 7) Latticed trenches

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Design of Indonesian rice-fish-vegetable farm or “surjan system” (Koesoemadinata and Costa-Pierce, 1992)

©FAO/TECA

2.5 Ponds in rice fields

  • Another approach to providing a relatively deeper refuge for fish in a rice field is the provision of a pond at one side of the rice field.
    • In Indonesia, the payaman or lateral pond is used in rice fields that are located right beside a river.
    • The pond is constructed here so that water from the river has to pass through the pond to get into the rice planting area.
    • A dike separates the pond from the rice planting area (Figure 5).
  • Openings are made along the dike to enable the water to flow freely to the rice and allow the fish to forage within the rice field.
    • When the rice field is drained, the pond serves as a refuge for the fish, making it possible to catch them after the rice harvest.
  • This model makes it possible to take advantage of the mutualism between rice and fish while desynchronizing the fish culture cycle from that of rice.
    • With the lateral pond, farmers have the option of making temporary breaches along the partition dike separating the pond from the rice field to interconnect the fishpond with the rice field, therefore allowing the fish to graze among the rice plants.
    • Water for irrigating the rice has to pass through the fishpond.
    • By draining the rice field and repairing the breach, the fish are made to congregate in the pond compartment and their culture continues independently of the agronomic cycle of the rice.
    • Thus the fish, if still under-sized, can be cultured through the succeeding rice crop if necessary.
  • Another option is to include two ponds, one pond at each end of the rice field (Figure 6).
    • The design of the West Bengal State Fisheries Department in India refers to ponds of a top width of 18 m and pond bottom width of 1.5 m.
    • They are 1.5 m deep measured from the field level.
    • The rice field has a total length of 125 m (inclusive of 3 m dikes).
    • Thus the ponds actually cover 28 percent of the gross rice field area and the dikes about 4.8 percent.
Figure 5. Design and construction of Indonesian rice-fish farm with lateral pond or payaman (Koesoemadinata and Costa-Pierce, 1992)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Rice-fish system with two ponds

©FAO/TECA

2.6 Rice fields in ponds

  • The sawah-tambak rice field - fish pond combination (Figure 7) – in Indonesia is unique to the low-lying (1 m to 2 m above sea-level) coastal areas of East Java.
    • These areas are flooded throughout the wet season but lack water during the dry season.
    • Farmers construct 1.4 m to 2.0 m high dikes around their land with a 3 m wide peripheral trench parallel to the dike.
    • A second dike is built around the rice field that is low enough to be flooded over.
  • Milkfish (Chanos chanos) and silver barb (Barbodes gonionotus) are the main species raised in the polyculture system, although the common carp and the giant freshwater prawn (Macrobrachium rosenbergii) may be grown together with both species.
    • These are adaptable for either concurrent or rotational systems of rice-fish culture.
Figure 7. Design and construction of Indonesian coastal rice-fish farm or sawah-tambak

©FAO/TECA

3. Development of a fish-rice system in a pond

  • Rice-fish culture is one component of aquaculture which has great potential for development in regions with vast areas of irrigated rice fields.
    • Adoption of proper techniques in rice-fish culture is expected to help improve food security in these regions and increase the profit of rice farmers
  • The full guideline of how to build, manage and evaluate a fish rice system could be found in "Farmer Field School (FFS) curriculum for aquaculture in rice-based farming systems for Guyana and Suriname": link

3.1 Preparation of the pond

3.1.1 Area

  • The area to be utilized for implementing the fish-rice system is 2 000 m² (less than half of an acre for easy management).
  • One-fourth of it would be used to develop it into a fishpond.
  • The fishpond is located at the lowest portion of the rice plot.
  • A rice field comprising three-quarters of the total plot area is modified by raising and widening the bunds to hold enough water during the culture period of the fish.
  • A centre trench is constructed lengthwise of the rice field, one end connecting directly into the opening in between the rice field and the pond.
  • The trench does not occupy more than 10 percent of the total rice field area.

3.1.2 Resources needed

  • A fish pond.
  • A rice field.
  • Animal manure.
  • One PVC pipe 5-foot length and 3-inches diameter with a fine mesh screen at one end.
  • One PVC pipe elbow 3-inches diameter with a fine mesh screen at one end.
  • A seed paddy.
  • Fish fingerlings.

3.1.3 Activities

3.1.3.1 Good pond rice field management

  • Apply the right amount of fertilizer (see more information in section 6).
  • Use appropriate fish stocking density (start at two fish per meter square).
  • Eliminate and control weeds.
  • Prevent entry and control of predatory animals and competitors of fish.
  • Practice proper water management.
  • Use supplemental feeds (see more information in section 5).
  • Apply the correct harvesting technique.

3.1.3.2 Pond/rice field preparation

  • For an old fish pond, dry the pond bottom under sunlight to kill fish predators and organisms that may cause fish diseases. 
  • In a new pond, apply lime (if available) to pond bottom and dikes at 5 kg per 100 m² to neutralize the soil, making it suitable for the production of natural food for the fish and to kill bacteria harmful to the fish to be stocked.
    • Apply animal manure to the pond at the rate of 50 kg per 100 m².
    • Let the water in gradually to allow the production of natural food for the fish until the desired water level is attained.

3.2 Transporting and stocking of live fish

  • The transport of live fish from the hatchery to any unit of water plays an important role in aquaculture management.
  • Transporting fish involves the hauling of large quantities of fish in a small quantity of water.
  • Unless this is done properly, the length of time involved can quickly deteriorate the water quality which can cause fish mortality.

3.2.1 Resources needed

  • Happa net for holding fingerlings.
  • Plastic bags.
  • Pandan bag.
  • Prepared fishpond or rice field with rice 21 DAS (days after seeding/sowing).

3.2.2 Activities: stocking of fish

  • Upon arrival, float the fish container into the pond water surface for 15 minutes to balance water temperature between the container and pond water (Figure 8).
  • Let the pond water come inside the fish container and allow the fish to swim outside into the pond (Figure 9).
Figure 8. Float the fish container to balance water temperature

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. Let the fish swim into the pond

©FAO/TECA

3.3 Nets construction

  • Nets are among the basic gears and equipment in fish culture and are indispensable in the rice-fish culture operations.
  • For ease of use, without harming the fish, it is important for a fish farmer to have knowledge on how to make the right net and its proper use.
  • The types of nets most commonly used in the rice-fish culture:
    • Hapa net
      • It looks like an inverted mosquito net.
      • It is used to nurse fry until fingerling size (fine mesh hapa net) or used to hold or keep large-sized fish alive before stocking or marketing (larger mesh size hapa net).
    • Lift net
      • It is an assembly consisting of a plain net cut in a square shape measuring 2 m x 2 m seamed with a rope along the edges of its four sides.
      • It is made ready for lift netting operation by stretching it, through the use of two bamboo splits measuring 3 cm wide by 8 m long, tied at the net’s opposing corners forming a crossed arc position.
      • It is very effective in catching fishes with no injuries sustained.
    • Scoop net (dip net)
      • It is a device made of a fine netting material with all openings at the sides and bottom stitched together forming a purse and the upper opening stitched into a round or square-shaped iron rod.

3.3.1 Materials needed

  • Bamboo splits measuring 3 cm width by 8 m long.
  • One bamboo pole 6 m long.
  • Fine nylon twine for stitching the seam of nets.
  • An 8 m of fine mesh net, 1 m wide (for making hapa net of size 1 m x 1 m x 2 m).
  • An 8 m long small size rope for edging the hapa net.
  • A 4 square meters of quarter-inch mesh size net for making lift net.
  • A 0.5 m x 1.0 m of quarter-inch mesh size net for making scoop net.
  • A 0.5 m x 1.0 m of fine mesh net for making fry/fingerlings scoop net.
  • One piece of three- quarter inch iron rod 1.5 m long each, for ring and handle of scoop nets.

3.3.2 Activities

3.3.2.1 Construction of a hapa net

  • From the netting material measuring 1 m width x 8 m long, cut out a piece measuring 2 m long.
  • Stitch the remaining 6 m of the net into the just cut 2 m length by joining their sides together until both ends met for final joining by stitching (Figure 10).
  • After an inverted mosquito net shape is formed, fold one inch of the edges of the opening and stitch it all around.
  • Insert a small size rope into the folded edges of the assembled hapa net and leave knots at each of the four corners for tying into wooden posts upon installation into the fish pond (Figure 11).
Figure 10. Stitching the nets

©FAO/TECA

Figure 11. A hapa net cage

©FAO/TECA

3.3.2.2 Construction of a lift net

  • Prepare a quarter-inch mesh size net measuring 2 m x 2 m (Figure 12).
  • Reinforce four sides of the net by inserting a small size rope all-around at its edging mesh.
    • Stretch the rope and distribute its length equally into four sides of the net.
    • Make a knot in every corner of the net with the rope (Figure 13).
  • To assemble the lift net, connect opposing corners of the net to each opposing ends of the bamboo split measuring 3 cm width by 8 m long.
    • The remaining two corners are also tied to another bamboo split of the same measurement the same way as the previous one, making the net stretched out by the bamboo splits formed in a crossed arc position (Figures 14 and 15).
  • After this assembly, the lift net is made ready for lift netting of fish operation by submerging it inside the pond.
    • It is lifted by using an extended bamboo pole of 6 m length hooked into the crossing portion of two bamboo splits (Figure 16).
Figure 12. Prepare the net size

©FAO/TECA

Figure 13. Reinforce the sides of the net with the rope

©FAO/TECA

Figure 14. Prepare the bamboo splits

©FAO/TECA

Figure 15. Stretching the net with the bamboo splits

©FAO/TECA

Figure 16. A lift net

©FAO/TECA

3.3.2.3 Construction of a scoop net (dip net)

  • Make a circular or square frame out of a three- quarter inch iron rod having a length of 1.5 m.
  • From the netting material measuring 0.5 m x 1.0 m, join together by stitching its side and bottom to form like a purse.
    • The upper opening is also stitched into a round or square-shaped iron rod (Figure 17).
Figure 17. Parts and types of dip nets

©FAO/TECA

3.4 Fish feeds and feeding

  • Fish cultured in ponds or rice fields get their initial source of food from the natural food present in the water.
  • The natural food consists mainly of planktons, which are produced after a thorough pond or rice field preparation.
  • As the fish grow, their food-needs increase, to the point where the natural food present in the water may not be enough to sustain them.
  • It may then be necessary to supply additional feed.

3.4.1 Resources needed

  • A fishpond.
  • A rice-fish field.
  • Fish fingerlings.
  • On-farm feeds (rice bran, termites, leftover foods, wheat bran, sliced papaya leaves, vegetable wastes, crushed snail meat, etc.).
  • Compound artificial feeds.
  • Feeding box or pan.
  • One hapa net.
  • Scoop nets.
  • A gram scale (Figures 18, 19, 20).

3.4.2 Activities

  • Feed on-farm feeds to the fish in the pond by using a feeding box or pan at a quantity of 5 percent of the fish total biomass.
    • Adjust the amount of feeds monthly based on the result of the latest fish sampling conducted.
    • If the floating type of on-farm feeds (like termites) is applied, observe the fishes’ daily consumption and make adjustments for the right quantity that the fishes are able to consume (Figure 21).
  • Make another feeding trial by using a hapa net suspended in the same pond using compound artificial feeds.
    • The stocking density of the hapa net should be the same as of the pond.
    • Feed the fish regularly at the same time of feeding the fish in the pond.
  • Sample the fishes cultured in the pond using lift net, and those in the hapa net using scoop net, on the same day every month to determine growth rate.
    • Make adjustments of the fish feeds for the next one-month feeding ration.
  • Compare the results after a six month culture period.
Figure 18. Vegetable waste

©FAO/TECA

Figure 19. Sliced papaya leaves

©FAO/TECA

Figure 20. Compound artificial feeds in a feeding box or pan

©FAO/TECA

Figure 21. Preparing the feeding box for the pond

©FAO/TECA

3.5 Pond and rice field fertilization

  • Fertilizers stimulate the growth of plankton, which is the natural food of the fish.
  • When the fish are still small, they rely on the natural food present in the water to sustain their growth.
  • Therefore, since fertilization increases the availability of natural foods in the water, fertilization is a key factor for increasing fish yields.

3.5.1 Resources needed

  • Animal manure.
  • Chemical fertilizers (Urea and TSP).
  • Sample plankton inside a transparent plastic bottle.

3.5.2 Activities

  • Initial organic fertilization of the pond is done by applying animal manure at 50 kg per 100 m² while the rice field is undergoing preparation.
  • For maintenance fertilization, chemical fertilizer (TSP or Urea) could be applied at a rate of 0.6 kg per 100 m² weekly.
    • It should be dissolved in a few litres of water using a bucket.
    • Or, animal manure could be used, at a rate of 50 kg per 100 m² every other week.
  • Adjust the quantity of maintenance fertilizer applied (increase or decrease) depending on the greenness of the pond water.
  • To measure the water quality to determine if there is enough natural food, submerge your hand under the pond water until at elbow level with palm facing upward.
    • If the palm is seen very clearly, there is not enough natural food in the water; therefore, apply more animal manure or chemical fertilizer.
    • If the palm is not visible, there is an overproduction of natural fish food, that may lead to bad pond water; reduce the application of animal manure or chemical fertilizer and remove about 6 inches of the pond water and add 6 inches of clean water. 
    • If the palm is slightly visible, there is enough natural fish food present in the pond water, maintain the current amount of animal manure and/or chemical fertilizer.
  • For the rice field, apply the first dose of fertilizer to the rice on the 21st D.A.S. and the second dose of fertilizer on the 48th D.A.S.

3.6 Water management

  • Water is the only medium that makes the culture of fish with rice possible.
  • Too little or too much of it would be detrimental to the fish.
  • Therefore, proper water management in rice-fish culture is essential to make both rice and fish co-exist harmoniously in the same field.

3.6.1 Resources needed

  • A fishpond connected to a rice field.
  • One 5-inch diameter PVC pipe with a fine mesh screen at one end.
  • One PVC elbow attached to the PVC pipe with a fine mesh screen at one end.

3.6.2 Activities

  • Install the screened PVC pipe into the dike of the rice field with the rotating elbow located inside of rice-fish plot.
    • The elbow should be tilted at an angle that would enable water to be maintained at the depth desired for the rice-fish plot.
  • Water management starts at the point of letting water into the pond or rice field, and its preparation for the growth of natural food.
    • At this time (the pond and the rice field are still separated by a dike), gradually let the water come inside to the pond and maintain to the level of the rice field bed.
  • During sowing of pre-germinated seeds in the rice field, irrigate water into the pond at 3 inches higher than the water level in the rice field.
  • In the second week after sowing, irrigate water into the rice field.
    • As much as possible, maintain the pond water level at 3 inches higher than the water in the rice field.
  • In the third week after sowing, when the rice is fertilized, stock the fish at a rate of twp fish per square meter.
  • On the 25th day after sowing open the dike/blockade in-between the pond dike and rice field and let fishes swim out from the pond into the rice field through the centre trench.
  • On the 45th day after sowing raise water level in the rice field 5 to 8 inches deep (water level in the pond rises at the same level as the rice field).
  • On the 60th day after sowing raise the water level in the rice field from 8 to 12 inches deep (water level in the pond also rises at the same level with the rice field).
  • On the 80th to 85th day after sowing drain the water gradually and let fishes inside the rice field go back into the fishpond through the centre trench.

3.7 Pond and rice-fish field maintenance

  • To be able to do effective maintenance of a rice-fish farm, it is a must for a farmer to regularly visit his farm site.
  • By having the farmer’s regular presence on his farm he can immediately take remedial actions to whatever problems he could see before the problem gets serious.

3.7.1 Activities

  •  Major maintenance and operational activities to be done by farmers.
    • Always maintain the desired water depth of the pond and rice field and make sure both ends of water inlet and outlet pipes (if any) are properly screened.
    • Maintain the desired greenness of pond water.
    • Change the pond water when it is smelling bad, or when fishes are seen gulping at the water surface due to a lack of oxygen.
    • Feed fish daily at 5 percent of the total body weight.
      • Adjust daily feeding ration monthly, based on the latest sampling of the fish stock conducted after every thirty days.
    • To maintain the growth of plankton and other natural food for the fish present in the water, apply fertilization into the pond at a rate of 50 kg of animal manure per 100 m² every two weeks, or 0.6 kg of inorganic fertilizer per 100 m² per week.
    • Remove floating and submerged weeds growing inside the pond, as they compete with the stocked fish for space and nutrients necessary for the production of natural food in the water.
    • To prevent poaching of cultured fish, stakes or barbed wires can be installed underwater inside the pond.
    • Grow and maintain crawling grass on top and slope of the dikes to help in maintaining compaction and preventing soil erosion.
    • Always repair any damage to the dike, such as leakages or seepages, before it becomes big and causes serious damage to the pond.
    • Check for any foreign objects in the screens of the pond pipes and clean regularly to avoid screens from becoming clogged.

4. Potential threats

4.1 Fish predators and other pests

  • Fish production in ponds and rice fields is commonly affected by some pests and predators.
  • Predators are organisms that prey on the fish being cultured.
  • The animals that compete for food or space are called competitors.
  • To protect the field, farmers should:
    • install traps within the vicinity of the rice-fish plot located at a passageway of the fish predators; and
    • control the entry of unwanted fish competitors and some predatory fish species, at the same time preventing the escape of cultured fishes inside the pond, by the installation of a fine mesh screen at both ends of the water irrigation/drainage PVC pipe.

4.2 Fish stocking density

  • The growth of fish depends on the number of fish stocked and the number of fishes present in the pond or rice field.
    • This is due to several factors that include density and competition.
  • Fish stocking density is one of several factors that affect fish growth.
    • At low stocking density, the amount of natural food in the pond is higher for each individual fish and the excess food is not utilized.
    • However, at higher stocking density the growth of fish will be slow because the capacity of the natural food to support the fish population will be limited to a certain extent.
    • The maximum physiological growth of tilapia is attained at low stocking density.

5. Cost and return analysis of rice-fish culture

  • The primary purpose of culturing fish with rice is to get additional income derived from fish, as a secondary crop, in addition to rice, which is the main crop.
  • However, in order for fish to live in harmony with the rice, there needs to be an additional input for the construction of ponds with higher and stronger dikes to keep fish at a certain period of time, before they are released into the rice field, and for heightening of the rice field perimeter dikes.
  • With all the expenses entailed in developing the rice-fish culture site, coupled with operating and maintenance expenses, it is important to analyse its cost of production and return of investment after a one-year operation to be able to know whether the rice-fish farming venture is giving the farmer his desired profit or not.

6. Some benefits experienced in China 

  • The price for fish produced in a rice-fish system is about 70 Yuan per kg, higher than the price of fish from non- fish rice systems.
    • The price could increase even more if the systems are designated as Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems (GIAHS).
    • As an example, the fish produced in the paddy fields of Longxian village was sold for 20 Yuan (USD 2.5) per Kg.
    • Today, with the designation of GIAHS site, fish from the rice-fish system in Longxian village are sold for 120 Yuan (USD 19).
  • High yields, fish sales and savings on inputs produce income up to 400 percent higher than income from rice monoculture.
  • In China with good management, a one-hectare paddy can yield from 225 kg to 750 kg of finfish or crustaceans a year, while sustaining rice yields of 7.5 to 9 tonnes.
  • In China, profit margins may be more than 400 percent higher for rice farmers culturing high-value aquatic species.
  • The information in this practice has been compiled by Laura Angulo thanks to the collaboration of GIAHS - Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System.

7. Validation of the practice

​​This practice has been used along continental Asia extending from eastern India through Myanmar, Thailand, the Lao PDR, northern Vietnam, and into southern China. While each country has evolved its own unique approach and procedures, there are also similarities, common practices and common problems. This practice includes experiences from China, Indonesia, Philippines, Guyana and Suriname. In China, the main example is Longxian, which is a traditional rice-fish culture system village located In Qingtian Country, Zhejiang Province in China. Besides, part of the information is presented on the document: a curriculum for farmer field school on integrated pest management and aquaculture, applied by farmers in Guyana and Suriname.​ 

8. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm; and
  • subtropics, warm/mod cool.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Fish pond lay out and construction: ID 4384.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology improves land usage and allows for the efficient stocking of fish in rice fields which provide fish crops in addition to the main rice crop.

10.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology increases the rice farmer’s production and the income derived from rice and fish.
