Bamboo in sericulture: a case study from India

Traditionally, bamboo equipment has been used in sericulture. The main uses of bamboo in sericulture are baskets for gathering mulberry leaves, trays for feeding leaving to larvae, mountages for production of cocoons, trays for cocoon storage, stifling baskets for steaming of cocoons and some woven mats. The present study is targeted to find out quantities of bamboo used, their sources, employment generation, economics and problems in the whole chain from raw bamboo resources through to the use as equipment in silk production.

Description

Use of silk originated in China in 2 200 BC and went to India through Tibet around 140 BC. Mulberry leaves form ideal food for the silkworm larvae, they spin the cocoon through glands and these forms silk.

Approximately 17 000 tonnes of mulberry are used for annual silk production in India, about 87 percent is produced in the three South Indian States of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamilnadu. Over 330 000 farm families cultivate about 28 000 hectares of mulberry to make a living by selling cocoons reared by them.

Traditionally bamboo equipment has been used in sericulture. The main uses of bamboo in sericulture are:

  • baskets for gathering mulberry leaves;
  • trays for feeding leaves to larvae;
  • mountages for the production of cocoons;
  • trays for cocoon storage;
  • stifling baskets for steaming of cocoons; and
  • woven mats.

There are also other minor uses of bamboo in silk production.

Bamboo available in the Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh natural forests are the main sources of the bamboo supply. Shortages are offset by purchasing from private sources in Maharashtra, Goa and Assam. Substitute equipment is used to overcome shortages of bamboo, but is not very popular. Manufacture of bamboo equipment required for sericulture, engages hundreds of thousands of traditional weaver families and provides their means of livelihood.

The present study is targeted to establish:

  • quantities of bamboo used;
  • bamboo sources;
  • employment generation;
  • economics; and
  • problems in the entire chain from sourcing bamboo to its use as equipment in silk production.

A large number of artisans, farmers and reelers were appraised to study the sources of bamboo supply, economics of the manufacture of equipment, sale or hire of such equipment to silkworm-rearing farmers and silk reelers. The results of the study are summarized.

All aspects of silk production and marketing are properly studied, documented and have been subjected to research as a result of the importance of silk in the economics of the country. However, the importance of bamboo in silk production and the problems of artisans engaged in weaving and fabrication of equipment, have not been properly documented, studied or remedied.

The present study aims at identifying the importance of the bamboo supply to sustain sericulture as an industry. The study also identifies the necessity of overcoming problems in terms of quality, quantity and sustainability of the smooth supply chain of raw material for manufacture of equipment for the silk industry disclosing ways and means to overcome the difficulties of the artisans, silk farmers and the reelers.

To improve the socio-economic conditions of a large number of rural families in this economically important industry, the following conditions are necessary:

  • the scientific management of bamboo forests;
  • improvement of harvesting tools;
  • reduction of transportation time;
  • reduction of wastage during storage;
  • improvement of production quality and quantity; and
  • creation of agencies to coordinate between supplies and markets.

1. Background

1.1 History of silk

According to early authentic references in the chronicles of Chou-King, the use of silk has been known in China since 2 200 BC, in which silk figured prominently as a symbol of homage to emperors in public ceremonies. The silk industry originated in the province of Chang-Tong in China over 3000 years ago. As a result of the commercial relations between China and Persia, silk goods travelled to markets in Southern Europe in the first century BC. Korea was the first country to adopt sericulture after acquiring the knowledge from Chinese immigrants.

Japan learned about sericulture in the third century BC when Semiramus, a general in the army of Empress Singu-Congo of Japan, invaded Korea. A Chinese princess, who married the King of Khotan in Tibet, is said to have taken silkworm eggs and mulberry seeds with her. Mulberry cultivation came to India from Tibet around 140 BC and started spreading along the banks of the Brahmaputra and the Ganges. There is mention of use of silk obtained from wild natural cocoons in old Sanskrit literature. The popularity of silk in India was enhanced when the East India Company started trading in silk.

Arab traders took silkworm eggs and mulberry seeds from India in the early part of the Christian era. Though sericulture spread to other parts of India, its use for the cottage industry was widely adopted in the princely State of Mysore in Southern India and by the weavers in Kashmir. In the fourth and sixth century AD, raw silk from India and Central Asia was exported to Persia, Rome and Athens and then the silk spread from there to other European countries. In the nineteenth century, an epidemic of pebrine, a destructive disease, spread in France and gradually wiped out sericulture in Southern Europe. In 1870, Louis Pasteur discovered that the disease could be diagnosed and cured, helping to partially revive the silk trade. Fabulous silks were traded from China and India to the west, establishing a 6 000 mile long silk route.

1.2 Silk production in India

Major silk production in India is through mulberry cultivation and feeding the leaves to the worms. There are other natural silks of which Tassar, Moga and Eeri have some commercial significance. During the last three decades, efforts have been made by the state governments to develop sericulture as an industry because  it generates rural employment and alleviates poverty. The climate and soil suited to economic mulberry cultivation play a major role in its popularity in the states of India.

Statistics on silk production are available at the Central Silk Board, according to which the major states producing mulberry silk in South India are:

  • Karnataka
  • Andhra Pradesh
  • Tamilnadu.

In North India, the States of:

  • West Bengal
  • Manipur.

In East India:

  • Himachal Pradesh
  • Kashmir.

In India the production of mulberry silk averages 17 746 tonnes per year, whereas production of non-mulberry silk is an average of 120 tonnes per year, i.e. less than one percent.

  • Karnataka State accounts for 63 percent of Indian silk production;
  • Andhra Pradesh State accounts for 22 percent; and
  • Tamilnadu State accounts for 5 percent.

Silk production from these three states is 90 percent of the production in India and hence the present study, undertaken to evaluate the use of bamboos in sericulture in South India, becomes significant for India as a whole.

Other types of silk are not produced in South India, except for about 2.5 tonnes of Tassar in Andhra Pradesh.

Assam State leads with over 100 tonnes of Moga and Eeri silk.

Manipur State and Meghalaya State produce about 20 tonnes each per annum of Eeri silk.

Southern India dominates in the mulberry silk production.

1.3 Popularity of silk industry

Silk is a very popular natural fabric around the world. It is important in religious activity, in fashion and in all-important functions in India and abroad. Silk is used both in pure form and in blends with cotton, wool, viscose, gold, silver and artificial fibres in all kinds of apparel. Many states have an independent Ministry for Sericulture and a fully-fledged department with branches in all corners of the state. The Union Government has created the Central Silk Board, with the headquarter in Bangalore and branch offices in most states. There are silk marketing agencies, silk cooperative societies at all stages of silk production, processing and marketing.

Similarly, research institutes have been established to take care of the continuous development of disease-free egg mulberry production, for fashion design silk produced in India. Statistics of farmers and the extent of land occupied for producing mulberry, the number of villages, families and people engaged in rearing of worms, production of cocoons, processing and marketing of silk at all stages are being gathered annually both by the State Departments of Sericulture and the Central Silk Board. Credit requirements for the industry through all production and marketing stages  are reviewed from time to time. The financial institutions take care of the credits, recoveries, etc. with refinancing by the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD).

In all main silk producing states, the importance of sericulture in rural employment, poverty alleviation, sociological and economical aspects has been acknowledged. The necessity of all inputs for irrigation, fertilization, plant protection, harvesting, transportation, storage, processing and marketing have been recognized in all important silk producing states and have been documented.

However, the importance of bamboo in the sericulture industry has not been studied or documented properly, in particular:

  • its sustainable supply to artisans producing and supplying bamboo equipment required for the harvesting the mulberry leaves:
    • leaves transport;
    • leaves storage systems;
    • rearing of worms;
    • cocoons production in filatures, reeling and looms; and
    • cocoons transport.

Due credit has to be given to the International Network of Bamboo and Rattan (INBAR) for recognizing the socio-economic aspects of the role of bamboo in the silk industry in India and initiating a comprehensive field study through systematic sampling to highlight the importance of bamboo in sustaining the silk industry in India.

2. Different uses of bamboo in sericulture

Bamboos form the backbone of all agricultural products in tropical India through agricultural implements, in particular:

  • tool handles;
  • fencing;
  • transport;
  • storage; and
  • processing equipment.

Similarly, bamboo has multifarious uses for:

  • mulberry leaves collecting baskets;
  • mulberry leaves harvesting;
  • mulberry leaves storing;
  • silkworms rearing;
  • silkworms production;
  • silkworms transport;
  • silkworms storing; and
  • processing of cocoons:
    • silk filatures
    • silk reeling
    • silk weaving.

Among the different uses of bamboo in sericulture the largest quantity is used in:

  • chandrikes
  • trays
  • baskets
  • mats.

3. Advantages of bamboo use in sericulture

Bamboo is a renewable natural ligno-cellulosic resource with the advantage of annual production and growth. The rhizome, i.e. the underground stem of bamboos that spreads in the soil, annually produce culms or poles from the axillary bud. Emergence of culms takes place in the early part of the monsoon in South India, which is June to August.

The food material, stored by the woody grass in its rhizome, is used to activate the axillary bud during early rains, when the climatic and soil moisture conditions are the best for the growth. Emerging from the soil as a conical shoot covered by whorls of leaf sheath, the elongation of the shoot is rapid. The maximum height and girth of the shoot is attained within a short period of 8 to 12 weeks.

The number of culms thrown out annually depends on the age of the rhizome, from the time it has developed from either seed or propagule, as well as from the soil moisture and fertility conditions. Similarly, the height and diameter of a culm for a given species or provenance, depends on the age of rhizome, food stored by it during the previous year’s growth and the conditions of climate and soil.

It is the annual productivity of culms that can provide the sustained supply of bamboos to end users.

  • The culms or poles can be split easily with knives.
  • The split bamboo can be cut into slivers of required thickness to facilitate weaving. Since the slivers can easily bend without breaking, it is possible to use them in weaving into flat mats, duly strengthened by splits, or into baskets of different shapes and sizes.
  • After evaporation of excess moisture, the air-dry bamboos, splits, or slivers absorb some atmospheric moisture, depending on the relative humidity. This does not cause any major changes in the products such as mats, baskets, trays etc. either in shape or in size.
  • Air-dry bamboo splits and slivers are absorbent, therefore the secretion from silk glands dries quickly and provides a good surface and support for the strands of silk.
  • Being locally available from natural forests and from farms in South India, bamboos become the ideal material for various equipment ranging from silkworm rearing to silk production.
  • Bamboo is light, compared to metals and is a cheap resource for use in the silk industry. Since the equipment in worm-rearing and silk production requires human labour, the advantage of volume to weight ratio makes it popular in Southern India.
  • Besides, bamboo has very good insulation properties and is not much affected by heat and cold, it is a bad conductor of electricity.

4. Bamboo resources and management issues

4.1 Bamboo resources

The forest area containing bamboo in India is 8.962 million hectares, which is 11.71 percent of the recorded forest area. The growing stock is estimated as 80.5 million tonnes. Seven states of northeast India contain 66 percent of the growing stock. Madhya Pradesh accounts for 12 percent of the growing stock. The states in South India have fewer stocks.

The bulk of bamboo is available on the government land and mainly in the moist deciduous forests. Dowga is prevalent in the moist valleys of deciduous forests.

Marihal bamboo is grown on private lands, including homesteads in the Konkan belt from Ratnagiri district in Maharashtra, through to Goa up to South Kanara district in Karnataka.

These species are the entire resources for uses in sericulture. In the Kerala State, both the major species of bamboo are grown in homesteads. According to one report, made for Kerala forest resources, the annual output of bamboo from homesteads is 10 000 tonnes per year.

Recent studies (2000) made by the author, have revealed that about 15 000 tonnes of bamboo, mostly of Marihal variety, are brought to markets in the Belgaum district by the farmers of Konkan in Goa and Maharashtra and sold annually to weavers in Karnataka and neighbouring districts of Andhra Pradesh and Tamilnadu.

Apart from weaving into baskets, this bamboo is used for making equipment used in sericulture. Small quantities of Medri bamboos comes in from Andhra Pradesh to the southern districts of Karnataka, either as poles or in the woven form for use in trays and Chandrikes. The quantity brought in is about 1 000 tonnes per year and is less significant in comparison with production in Karnataka and supply from private land in Konkan.

4.2 Species in use

Naturally grown species of bamboo mostly used in South India are:

  • Medri/Dendrocalamus strictus, which is common in the deciduous forest zone dominant in the state.
  • Dowga/Bambusa bambos which grows in the wetter zone of peninsular India.
  • Marihal or Shame/Pseudoxytenanthera stocksii, which grows on farms and homesteads in Konkan region.

Two other commercially available species are:

  • reed bamboo/Ochlandra travancorica in Kerala State; and
  • reed bamboo/Ochlandra talbotti available in the moist pockets in Western Ghats.

These two species are also used in weaving, but have little application in the sericulture industry. Along with these local species, some mats are brought from northeast India for use in Chandrike. These mats are woven from Dendrocalamus hamiltonii and Melocanna baccifera.

4.3 Composition of species

Karataka has a larger area of Medri (Dendrocalamus strictus) than Dowga (Bambusa bambos). However, the volume or weight of the growing stock between the two species can be equal, as each culm of Dowga is nearly three times in weight.

In Tamilnadu and Kerala, the proportion of Dowga is higher. In Kerala, reed bamboos are not often used for sericulture equipment.

In Andhra Pradesh Medri is over 90 percent of the growing stock. Due to higher availability in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh States, Medri is used more in sericulture and is estimated at 70 percent by volume.

4.4 Bulk uses

Medri forms the bulk species in use in the silk industry, followed by Dowga (Bambusa bambos) and Marihal (Pseudoxytenanthera stocksii). Medri (Dendrocalamus strictus) is used in the round, split and sliver forms for various applications in the industry.

Due to bulk availability and the presence of traditional weavers in the wet zones, Dowga is mainly used in weaving mats and baskets, much less as splits and not in the round form, except in frames constructed to support rows of trays stacked vertically.

Shortages of the above two species are made up by using Marihal, both in weaving and as sticks. Annually, some bamboo mats are brought from northeast India, mainly from Assam. These mats are 2 m x 1.2 m suited for the construction of Chandrikes. These mats are superior in quality to the locally woven mats, due to the bamboo species used and to the superior skills of the weavers. An average of 100 M tonnes of such mats are transported by lorries over a distance of nearly 2 500 km for use in Karnataka. Each lorry transports 3 500 to 4 000 mats, which are formed in bundles of 35 each in the size of 2 m x 1.2 m.

4.5 Storage

Immediately after extraction, the bamboos are stacked in the forest on accessible roadsides for few days, before arranging:

  • inspection
  • accounting  
  • transport.

This system applies to bulk removals either to designated forest depots or to the end users, such as pulp mills and artisans/cooperatives. Local villagers and artisans manage to get licenses for headload or cart load removal by obtaining prepaid permits, either from the Forest Department or from the village forest committees. In all the states, the artisans have formed cooperative societies. These societies are allotted bamboos at concession rates at quotas fixed per family.

Generally, 50 bamboos per family are allotted per month. The rates for supply are different for:

  • cooperatives
  • market users
  • industries.

Industries buy bamboos either stacked in the depots or are permitted removal of dead bamboos upon payment of a fixed rate per tonne. The tonnage is decided either on weight recorded at the weighbridge or on average volume (cum) fixed per metric tonne. Sometimes, bamboo extracted departmentally and stacked in depots remains without disposal for months.

No arrangement is made by the Forest Department or by the Forest Corporation or the end users including the pulp industries, to provide preservative treatment during storage. Fungus and insects cause damage to extracted bamboos and thereof loss is neither cared for nor remedied.

4.6 Bamboo market centres

As for timber and fuelwood, there are bamboo merchants in most cities and towns of the southern states. Large cities have traditional marketing centres, called "Bamboo Bazaars".

Permits for transportation of extracted bamboo are granted from the Forest Department, to:

  • bamboo merchants; and
  • leaders of artisans’ cooperatives.

Before storage and sale, the bamboos are graded according to:

  • species
  • lengths
  • sizes.

The sale price at the market end is three to four times the standing value of bamboos.

As most artisans are not rich enough to buy bamboos in bulk and store them for use, they are at the mercy of bamboo depot owners and merchants for their daily or weekly requirement for making of bamboo products for sale.

Though there is an effort by the Sericulture Department to establish service centres for the supply of bamboo equipment, these centres are also dependent on traditional bamboo merchants for supply.

4.7 Agency for felling

Until 1990, the contracts for the removal of bamboos were awarded by the Forest Department.

  • Pulp mills engaged their own extraction contractors on a tender basis.
  • Some cooperative societies of Buruds (community engaged in the profession of bamboo weaving named Buruds or Medars) were engaging their own felling contractors.

Since the extraction rates were decided based on the lowest tender, either on stacked volume, i.e. cum or on rates per 100 bamboos extracted, the bidders were looking to extract from less congested clumps and easily accessible areas.

This system resulted in:

  • unscientific removals;
  • clumps congestion.

Hence, the Forest Department switched over to departmental extraction. However, no improvement has been noted in the growing stock as a result of this approach in any of the states.

Grazing and fire are common in bamboo forests, consequentially both these factors:

  • damage regeneration;
  • affect recruitment; and
  • congest standing clumps.

No serious effort has been made by the Forest Department to arrange either for scientific extraction or for proper clump care to improve their condition, which is the key to higher recruitment and improve culms shape and size available for extraction.

The State Governments, issue orders annually or biennially to fix the rates for bamboo supply both for the industries and the artisans. Rates for the supply to the artisans involve some concession.

4.8 Apathy of government agencies

It is over 10 years since the Forest Department has done away with the contract system of extraction of forest produce. Forest Development Corporations have been established in all major states and they are also taking up extraction of bamboos.

However, neither the Forest Department nor the Forest Development Corporation has established strategies necessary for conservation of this important resource, such as:

  • scientific bamboo management;
  • preservative treatment; or
  • organized rational utilization.

The artisans and users, including the pulp industries, are constantly suffering as a result of the disorganized supply and continuous shortages in terms of both quality and quantity for proper end users.

It is an irony that no studies have been initiated to quantify the needs of various end users of bamboo or the sources of these supplies. The main reason for this being that there is no accurate data available on the utilization of bamboo in the silk industry. Even the Department of Sericulture has not made efforts to organize the supply of bamboos and their products for the sericulture farmers.

Substitutes for bamboo equipment have been attempted with no tangible success. Substitutes are neither practical, biodegradable nor energy efficient.

5. The study

An early attempt at assessing the quantities of bamboos for different uses in Karnataka was made and results were published in an article in the National Seminar on Bamboos held in Bangalore during December 1990.

The quantity of bamboos used in the silk industry was given as 550 000 tonnes for the production of 7 052 tonnes of silk. Based on the average silk production in Karnataka over the previous three years, an assessment of the bamboo requirement each year for the main three items such as leaf baskets, trays and mountages used in Karnataka was given as 40 000 tonnes.

INBAR took the initiative to take up a detailed field study in India on:

  • quantities and source of bamboo supply;
  • stakeholders chain involved in manufacture; and
  • silk sale and production and its contribution to the national economy.

The field study work for South India was entrusted to Bamboo Society of India, Bangalore.

5.1 Approach

The society created a core team to initiate the study, formed by the society executives consisting of the Chairperson, Executive Director and the Treasurer, all of whom are experienced foresters. An economist, who had previous exposure to practical sericulture, was taken into the team to advice on statistical and economic approach to the field study for gathering data through a set of designed questionnaires.

These data forms were then handed over to a number of field officers who visited a samples selection of:

  • mulberry farms;
  • silkworm-rearing farmers;
  • bamboo equipment manufacturers;
  • intensive worm-rearing villages;
  • cocoon markets; and
  • silk filatures and reeling centres.

Baseline data for sampling was gathered through the Department of Sericulture in the States of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamilnadu.

However, the sericulture data in Kerala State had to be obtained from the Office of Sericulture Federation (SERIFED) based in Trivandrum. State silk production data during the last five years was readily available from the Office of Central Silk Board in Bangalore.

Data on the extent of mulberry cultivation, egg-producing centres, quantity of Disease-Free Laying (DFL) used raw silk, produced, etc. was also available from the Board.

District data on the extent of silk production and mulberry cultivation was obtained from the Directorate of Sericulture in the three states and from SERIFED in Kerala.

Data on bamboo resources, harvest and sale were obtained from the forest department statistics, from bamboo cooperatives and traders.

Lists of manufacturers of bulk equipment using bamboos procured was obtained from the district officers in the Department of Sericulture, district offices of the Forest Department and from traders.

Using the baseline data obtained, it was possible to draw stratified samples of:

  • mulberry farmers;
  • bamboo harvesters;
  • purchasers; and
  • groups of artisans engaged in the manufacture of bamboo articles for sale to users.

The mulberry farmers, officials of the Sericulture Department, manufacturers, owners of silk filatures, etc. were then visited for interaction to gather information on the whole chain of production and supply of bamboo articles, to evaluate:

  • costs;
  • extent of use of each product;
  • average life;
  • cost of replacements; and
  • sources from which the materials are either hired or bought.

The data gathered was collated to arrive at averages of bamboo articles and cocoons, in terms of:

  • requirements of products;
  • products life;
  • products costs;
  • socioeconomics of production.

5.2 Major production area

It was found that the nucleus of silk production occurs in few districts situated in the South Central part of the Deccan Plateau belonging to the States of:

  • Karnataka
  • Andhra Pradesh
  • Tamilnadu.

These districts are in the tropical zone having the advantage of annual rainfall of about 750 mm, spread over seven to eight months in the year and have tropical red loam as the main soil type. This zone has the advantage of both southwest and northeast monsoons bringing pre-monsoon showers in April-May and precipitation between June and November. The area enjoys light rains, long sunshine and mild temperatures ranging between 15 ºC in December-January and touching 34 ºC in midsummer of May-June. Mulberry farming is sustained by light irrigation to supplement the number of rainy days ranging from 100 to 125 days between March and November of each year. Groundwater is recharged repeatedly as a result of the prolonged rainy season, though the intensity of rain is low. The red loam assists in percolation and moisture retention to sustain a good mulberry crop for eight to ten months in the year, which permits leaf harvests of at least six cycles at an average interval of six weeks.

Districts in Karnataka form the core of the mulberry farmers, namely:

  • Kolar
  • Tumkur
  • Bangalore
  • Mysore and
  • Mandya.

Neighbouring districts in Andhra Pradesh and Tamilnadu supplement mulberry and cocoon production. Naturally, filatures, reeling and weaving are situated around the centres of large scale cocoon markets.

5.3 Organizing fieldwork

The field officers engaged in data collection, using the forms prepared by the core team, gathered state-wide data. The heads of sericulture Departments in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh are based in Bangalore and Hyderabad respectively. However, the Directorate of Sericulture in Tamilnadu is based in Salem, which is 200 km away from Bangalore and is not based in the State Capital at Chennai (Madras). This is proof that the zone bordering Karnataka is a cocoons production area.

Similarly, Andhra Pradesh districts bordering Kolar district in Karnataka, are intensive mulberry farming centres. There is too little silk production in Kerala hence it is administered by the State Sericulture Federation. Since a major part of Kerala State is under the strong influence of the southwest monsoon, which brings heavy precipitation between June and September, there is very little mulberry farming in the state, except for Palakkad district, which borders the Coimbatore district of Tamilnadu. To gathered data in the structured forms, the field officers were sent to visit:

  • silk farmers;
  • bamboo cooperative societies;
  • district service centres which service small-scale industries;
  • bamboo market centres;
  • equipment manufacturers; and
  • cocoon markets.

5.4 Concession to artisans

Available government orders and data on supply of bamboos to the Burud cooperative and individuals were obtained from the offices of the Forest Department in the respective states. It is seen that an average of 400 societies have gathered between 3.8 million to 7.7 million bamboos. It is likely that part of market supply has gone into making sericulture equipment, just as part of artisan supply is used for the purpose.

Exhaustive forms for data collection through the field officers were prepared to gather information on:

  • bamboo sale centres or outlets both in Government and outside government;
  • manufacturers of bamboo equipment for sericulture either in societies or individuals;
  • units providing equipment on a hire basis; and
  • cocoon-rearing profession.

The field officers were given copies of the forms to use in the field survey to gather all physical and socioeconomic data on use of bamboos in sericulture.

5.5 Field experience

Experience has shown that:

  • production and control of bamboo is with the State Forest Departments;
  • bulk of the trade is with bamboo extraction contractors and traders who have now joined the Buruds, SC and ST groups to participate in one or more cooperative venture;
  • contractors or traders control the production and sale of equipment for sericulture. This includes enlisting themselves with the concerned government departments;
  • traders have established production centres where they engage skilled and unskilled workers for production of equipment.

Contractors and traders form bulk suppliers to:

  • service centres created by government;
  • farmers;
  • cocoon producers;
  • reelers.

Contractors and traders have:

  • experience and information on the bamboo extraction policies and programmes of the departments, artisans and groups who can supply components of bamboo to fabricate equipment, such as trays and Chandrikes.
  • knowledge and access to the bamboo market, mat suppliers, etc. from all over India, which they use to keep up their trade. They form the core group controlling bamboo equipment:
    • production
    • supply
    • hire
    • price.

Since there are many such traders, it is safe to assume that:

  • the prices of equipment are competitive and vary according to market forces of demand and supply;
  • minor variations in the unit cost are controlled by seasonal variations in the cost of labour;
  • the quality of the product is reflected in the sale price; and
  • the policy and efficiency of the Forest Department is a major factor governing supplies of raw material and prices. It was found that the intervention through the orders of the Honourable Supreme Court in 1997-1998 and the constraints of forest management due to restraints by the provisions of the Forest Conservation Act, upset smooth extraction and supply of bamboos mainly in Karnataka. Yet the traders managed to establish contacts with private suppliers in Maharashtra and Goa, mat manufacturers in northeast India and were able to keep up production and supply to the sericulture farmers.

There are some government schemes in the Forest Department, Sericulture Department, tribal welfare, etc. in which there is a provision to provide equipment to the rural poor free of cost. The production of cocoons is subsidized.

There is governmental assistance at different stages from supply of disease-free laying, mulberry farming and supply of equipment to fillip marketing of cocoons.

The establishment of service centres, under the Ministry of Small Scale Industries, has not changed the mode of production and supply of bamboo equipment to the sericulture industry. These district service centres have listed the bamboo traders/societies to whom they pass on equipment supply orders at negotiated prices and keep two percent of the cost of supply as their service charge.

5.6 Mulberry farming

Mulberry farming is an essential part of sericulture. Few large farms cultivate over four hectares of mulberry. Over 96 percent of mulberry farming is done by small farmers. Most farmers in the traditional silk production zone set aside for mulberry cultivation 0.25 to 0.5 hectare out of their average holding of one to four hectares.

In over 90 percent of such farmers, the work is done by family members, without distinction between age, sex, physical or mental skills. Duties consist of:

  • harvesting leaves;
  • chopping leaves;
  • feeding to larvae; and

transfer of larvae to and from trays or to Chandrike. The cocoons gathered from Chandrikes are carried as headload, cartload, on buses or by stage carriers for sale in the government-supported cocoon market or to private traders.

The business of handling cocoons and separating silk thread and waste after steaming the cocoons, is sticky and smelly. This is done in filatures, which is a domestic or tiny scale industry, traditionally run mostly by Muslims. Here again the whole family and some casual local labour is involved.

5.7 Extent and number

The Department of Sericulture has maintained annual statistics of the area under mulberry cultivation, number of families and villages involved, the quantities of Disease-Free Laying (DFL) supplied for rearing of worms, quality and quantity of cocoon production, production of silk and silk waste in the states under study.

It is found that the districts having large mulberry cultivation are:

  • Bangalore, Kolar, Mysore and Mandya districts, which account for 77.3 percent in Karnataka.
  • Anantpur, Chittoor, Kurnool and Cuddapah districts, which account for 85 percent in Andhra Pradesh.
  • Dharmapuri, Salem, Erode and Vaniyambadi districts, which account for 70 percent in Tamilnadu.
  • Cannonore, Idukki and Palakkad districts, which account for 70 percent in Kerala.

6. Bamboo uses in sericulture

Bamboo thorns and splits are used for fencing on farms. This practice is limited to natural bamboo zones, which are at some distance from the sericulture farms. No assessment is made for the use of bamboo thorns, as this is common practice only in high rainfall areas where paddy and sugarcane are cultivated.

6.1 Leaf collection basket

The baskets are woven with 1 cm to 3 cm wide bamboo slivers, between 0.4 cm thick strips and strengthened at the top by similar strips. It has a small opening on top and a wide middle section, sloping again towards the bottom to form the shape of a compressed sphere.

Two kinds of baskets are used in mulberry farming:

  • Manuring basket for collecting the manure of the crop;
    • circular in shape approximately 60 cm diameter and 25 cm deep.
  • Leaf collection basket for collecting plucked mulberry leaves;
    • circular in shape approximately 55 cm middle diameter, tapering to about 20 cm at the bottom with a 20 cm opening at the top.

The average weight of both these baskets is 1.5 kg each and they have an average life of:

  • three years for manuring baskets; and
  • one year for collecting baskets.

The average market price is Rs 30/- each. The number of baskets needed was calculated during field studies at ten per hectare for the application of manure and six per hectare for leaf collection.

The manure basket can hold 8 kg to 10 kg of manure and leaf basket can hold 12 kg of fresh mulberry leaves for easy carriage.

About 80 percent of farms use bamboo baskets. Leaves are harvested up to nine times year. Leaves harvested amount to nearly 35 tonnes/hectare for irrigated mulberry and half this quantity for rain-fed crop.

6.2 Mats

Bamboo mats are regularly woven by traditional weavers for various end uses. The most common being for:

  • partitions;
  • fencing for cash crops (i.e. betel-leaves);
  • dunnage in stores; and
  • sun drying of sugar and grains.

In addition, the mats are used for:

  • chopping mulberry leaves to feed the worms; and
  • storing steamed cocoons after these are stifled by steam in woven baskets;

Normal size of woven mat is 1.8 m x 1.2 m. The average air-dry weight of a mat is 1.5 kg.

The weaver sells such mats at Rs 22/- to Rs 25/- each. The market price is Rs 35/- each. Mats are rolled into bundles of ten and sold in the market in South India.

Such mats from Assam come in bundles of 35 in each roll. About 3 500 mats are transported over 2 000 km to consumption centres in South India. Assam mats are superior. They are sold in retail market at Rs 45/- each and are mainly used for fabricating mountages.

The average life of a mat is two years. Farmer/family uses five mats per annum. Taking account of these considerations, the requirement of mats, quantity of bamboos and their market value are worked out. In addition to use of mats by sericulture farmers, they are used by silk filatures.

6.3 Mats in filature

After steaming the cocoons in the stifling basket, the hot, soft cocoons are unloaded onto a bamboo mat. The average number of mats used is equal to the number of stifling baskets in use.

number of mats = number of stifling baskets

The mat has an average life of two years because of the contact with heat and rough usage. The requirement of mats and baskets is calculated at 10 kg of cocoons per basket as holding capacity and at 80 percent for filatures.

Production of reeling cocoons in the four states under study is 108 380 tonnes per annum. At one mat for 10 kg of cocoons, the mats requirement is 0.86704 million for 80 percent of farmers using such mats. Mats in filature are used for an average life of 200 times. Each mat is 1.5 kg in weight and the market value is Rs 25/- each.

6.4 Rearing trays

Woven, round bamboo trays are generally used to feed worms. The trays are usually 0.9 m to 1.3 m diameter with a rim 5 cm to 7 cm high. The requirements of such trays increases as the worms grow in size after every moult.

This equipment is also called "Tatte", are vertically placed one above the other on frames, which are made of wood or bamboo. Generally, the outer frame is wood and the partitions are either wooden reepers or round bamboos. Each frame is generally two metres in height and can hold 20 trays in two rows. This is meant to save rearing space in the village homes. Either a part of the dwelling house is used for these frames or rearing houses, protected from ants, are specially constructed in areas where cocoon production is a repeating annual feature.

Each tray weighs from 2 kg to 4 kg, with an average dry weight of 3 kg. Trays are woven from 1.5 cm to 2 cm wide slivers of both Medri and Dowga bamboos and strengthened by splits of 1.5 cm to 3 cm.

The rim of the trays requires special strengthening using thick splits. Bamboo trays are not used for branch feeding, which is resorted to by some large farms to save on the cost of labour required in leaf harvesting, chopping and feeding. Branch feeding is done on large frames 3.5 m x 1.5 m made of wood or bamboo frames, on which coir ropes or plastic ropes are tied to hold the branches.

From field studies, it is estimated that 82 percent of farmers use bamboo trays. Bamboo trays are preferred as they absorb the excretions of the worm and are easy to clean. The number of mulberry leaf crops harvested varies from five to nine per year depending on moisture and growth conditions. The average number of crops is eight in the traditional zones under irrigated cultivation and five under rain-fed cultivation.

The trays are used repeatedly approximately five to six times each year and have an average life of three years. The trays are smeared with a mud-and-cow-dung mixture and are disinfected with sprayed insecticides. Trays are priced at Rs 40/- to Rs 60/- each depending on diameter and season. The number of trays required has been assessed by contacting samples of farmers.

The data collected from the field officers was used to find the average requirement of bamboo trays and mountages needed by farmers, as these two items comprise the largest use of bamboos in sericulture. There have been accurate research studies on the use of the number of trays, number of times used annually and average life of trays. These studies have produced data on the number required for 100 DFL as well as per acre, per hectare. Such data compares favourably with the data generated from our field studies. The requirement of bamboos on the basis of average number needed per hectare of cultivation is given in the following paragraph. The number of trays per year will be one-third of the total number as the average life is three years.

6.4.1 Sources of supply

Some manufacturers and traders in the traditional mulberry zone are major suppliers of trays. The manufacture of trays is done by artisan families who procure the bamboos mainly from government sources and supplemented by private purchases.

One large bamboo (Dowga) can provide for making two trays. Conversely, two thin Medar may be needed per tray. The circular portion, as mats, is sometimes made in one place (i.e. Nandyal in Andhra Pradesh, Shimoga in Karnataka) and the trays are fabricated near the farm centres such as Chintamani in Kolar district, Vijayapura and Kanakapura in Bangalore rural district, Maddur and Malavalli in Mandya district, Sira in Tumkur district.

An average of four trays are made per day for which the total value is Rs 200/- and the wages earned by a pair of workers is Rs 100/- to Rs 120/- per day. The market price varies from Rs 40/- to Rs 60/- each depending on size, quality and season. On the basis of Rs 50/- per tray as the average price, the average labour required for the manufacture of trays, employment generation and value of production of trays every year, is given in the previous paragraph.

6.5 Mountage (Chandrike)

This equipment is also called “Chandrike" and is used for rearing cocoons it is of great importance in cocoon production. Mature larvae that are about 23 days old are transferred to the mountages in the circular thin frames between which cocoons are spun. It provides anchorage to the silk thread as the larvae weave the nest around them for the pupal stage. The spinning process takes 48 to 60 hours, after which the cocoons are removed for sale. The remnant waste silk is removed, the mountages cleaned and disinfected before reuse. Bamboo provides the best absorbent surface for quick drying of secreted silk to become a strand.

A mountage is made of 1.8 m x 1.2 m mat strengthened with solid bamboo at the back tied with coir rope. On the front side of the mat, 45 cm to 50 cm long woven bamboo ribs 5 cm to 6 cm high are fixed concentrically by coir rope. The mat is strengthened on the rear side with 3 cm bamboo strips or rounds on all four edges and crisscross by coir rope. These are called "flowers" (Hoovu in Kannada) and are either locally prepared or brought from bamboo production centres such as Shimoga and Nandyal. The mats are locally woven or bought in bundles from Shimoga and Gauhati in Karnataka and Assam respectively.

Thrissur and Trivandrum districts in Kerala manufacture large quantities of mats of reed bamboo, however these are not used in sericulture, though the prices are competitive. Kerala State Bamboo Corporation is the main manufacturer of mats through many cooperative societies in Kerala using the supply of reed bamboo given free of royalty to the corporation by Kerala Government.

A mountage weighs from 10 kg to 20 kg depending on the weight of bamboos used. The average weight of the mountage is 13 kg of which 12.5 kg is the weight of the bamboo and the balance is that of coir rope.

Field studies have assessed the requirement of mountages per hectare, per crop and for every 100 DFL. 80 percent of farmers use bamboo mountages, which are priced at Rs 160 to Rs 250/- each depending on quality and season.

Mountages are bought by large farms and are often hired during peak production for the three days of pupation. Hire charges are Rs 5/- to Rs 6/- each per use, these are needed for three to four days at a time, until the cocoons are removed after completion of the spinning, which takes around two days.

It noted that 40 percent of farmers in Andhra Pradesh own mountages and 60 percent hire them. It is used repeatedly and has an average life of three years even after some repairs. Research studies have also been conducted on the requirement of mountages per 100 DFL or per hectare of mulberry cultivation, which is Rs 250 per hectare. On the basis of average numbers needed, average weight per mountage and average life, the requirement of bamboos is worked out and given.

Labour and value: two mountages are made per day if the whole manufacture includes:

  • splitting
  • slivering
  • weaving
  • fabrication at the place of manufacture.

However, mats and flowers are bought in bulk and fabricated at the manufacturing place in which case five to six mountages are made ready per day by one pair of workers. The average wage is Rs 40/- per day for women and Rs 60/- per day for men respectively. The cost of bamboos is on average Rs 6/- per metre.

6.6 Cocoon storage trays

Cocoon storage trays are similar to rearing trays and are woven from bamboo slivers and splits with a diameter of about 75 cm to 100 cm and a depth of 5 cm to 7 cm. These trays are filled with steamed cocoons and mounted on stands vertically for air-drying of cocoons.

The average number of trays used for storing cocoons produced from 100 DFL is 15. The trays are priced in the market at Rs 40/- each. The average weight of the tray is 2.5 kg and it can hold 12.5 kg of cocoons. The average life of these trays is five years.

The requirement of cocoon storage trays is worked out on average DFL. The study reveals that trays are used each year calculated for only 80 percent of cocoon production, as wooden trays are also used. One pair of weavers can prepare five trays per day. Two Medri bamboos are needed per tray. Rectangular trays of 1.2 cm x 60 cm are also in use.

6.7 Steam stifling baskets

Most of the conversion of cocoons to silk is carried out in the filatures on a cottage industry scale. The filatures are located near the cocoon markets. A filature processes about 300 kg cocoons per day and works for about 250 days in a year.

The basket has a wide top and narrowing bottom and is used to gather cocoons and stifle them on steam baths. This allows to loosen the strands for separation of the silken threads from the pupae. The basket is about 75 cm tall, 55 cm to 60 cm in diameter at the top and 35 cm to 40 cm at the bottom.

Each basket weighs about 1 kg, can hold 12 kg of cocoons and can last from18 to 24 months.

As shown earlier, average production of cocoons in the four states is 108 380 tonnes/year; 10 kg of cocoons are stifled in steam per batch in a basket. The requirement of baskets per year is 43 352 based on 200 times usage for each basket.

Since the average weight per basket is 1 kg, the total weight of the baskets is 43 352 tonnes or approximately 45 tonnes of air-dry bamboo. At six baskets woven per day per weaver, the labour used is 7 225 working days per annum. The value of baskets at Rs 20/- each comes to Rs 0.867 million per annum. The wages earned at Rs 50/- per day comes to Rs 0.722 million per annum.

6.8 Bamboo sticks in rearing stand

Where rearing stands are used, round bamboos support the rearing trays placed one above the other. Ten trays in two rows are placed on such stands in the village houses to save space. It is seen that the stands are made of wood, whereas partitions are created by round bamboo sticks in 80 percent of such stands. The round bamboo sticks are 1.5 m long each. Every stand needs 20 sticks, which can be obtained from five bamboos. The average life of sticks is three years. As 200 rearing trays are used per hectare per year, the number of stands per hectare is ten.

6.9 Chawki sticks

The requirement of Chawki sticks is small. Only five sticks are used per hectare of mulberry cultivation. The sticks have an average life of three years. Since each stick is about 1 m long and 3 cm to 4 cm in diameter, the number of bamboos at five sticks per bamboo works out to bamboo numbers equal to the area of mulberry per annum divided by three years of average life. 1 m long 3 cm thick bamboo split or small rounds cost Rs 2/- each.

6.10 Reeling sticks

0.5 m long splits of bamboo are used in reeling silk thread around them for later use in twisting into yarn or in weaving. Six sticks are needed per hectare per annum for which the cost will be Rs 6/- per hectare.

6.11 Chopsticks

20 cm long, chopstick size are used to pick up the delicate worms for shifting or transfer as they are not handled by fingers, to prevent infection. However, their use is too little and not of significance.

6.12 Related bamboo uses

Besides the direct uses in sericulture, there are many other uses by harvesters and weavers. The bamboo felling labour has to stay in temporary sheds constructed from bamboo, mats and leaves. The yearly bamboo felling operation in South India takes place between December of one year to the end of May of the following year. Felling is suspended during the rainy season between June and November. Since the bamboos are extracted for various end uses, including pulp mills, its use for temporary dwellings cannot be accurately assessed for sericulture use. Residues of felling are available as fuelwood for such labour in the forest.

Bamboo is also used as a common household material in:

  • agriculture
  • horticulture
  • sericulture
  • housing
  • packaging
  • transport
  • storage.

Industrial uses of bamboo consist of pulping, matboards and as core-sticks in Agarbathis (scented sticks).

Generally, green and straight bamboos are used in the domestic sector and in weaving.

Slightly defective, bent and dry bamboos are used for pulping. Weaving and core sticks of Agarbathis are possible from green bamboos or after soaking dry bamboos.

Dry bamboos are used for strengthening the back of mats in Chandrikes and splits are used for similar purposes in baskets, mats and trays. Dry bamboos are used to construct frames to support a series of trays in silkworm rearing.

6.13 Sheds for weavers

Most large-scale manufacturers create bamboo-made workshops for storage of bamboos, shelters for workers and storage of articles manufactured. Such sheds are used for weaving of other bamboo products such as vegetable baskets, agricultural needs for grain storage bins and winnows. Hence it is not possible to assess bamboo requirement exclusively connected to the silk industry.

7. Bamboo extraction management

Bamboos are extracted on a selection basis in a felling cycle of three or four years. Bamboo forests are divided into felling series each is divided into three or four equiproductive coupes for felling.

Generally, all three year old and older culms and part of second year-old culms are extracted during the year of felling. The clumps are rested for two to three years for recuperation.

The method of extraction has been unscientific, causing deterioration in the extent and quality of bamboo growing stock.

Extraction of bamboos from forests was prescribed as an overlapping working circle on a three to four year cycle in the working plans drawn up for forests.

Irregularity of extraction and supplies are mainly attributed to:

  • neglect of normal forestry operations;
  • rigid conservation policies;
  • reservation of bamboo areas as wildlife preserves;
  • stoppage of green felling due to lobbying by ill-informed environmental activists;
  • diversion of attention of forest staff to social forestry;
  • interventions of the Honourable Courts lengthening of the red-tape in approval of management schemes; and
  • periodic flowering and death of clumps.

It can be said that the famine of bamboos in the market and related miseries to artisans and users, can be attributed to lack or neglect of forest management and more so in the last five years. Even the bamboo plantations raised under different planning schemes have remained neglected, resulting in very poor yields and no improvement in yields.

Bamboo equipment artisans and manufacturers suffer from:

  • uncertainty of supplies;
  • irregularity of supplies; and
  • fluctuation in prices.

As a result of:

  • neglect of management;
  • apathy of government departments to the artisans needs; and
  • legal and administrative hurdles in extraction and supply.

All these factors cause problems to:

  • workers
  • sellers
  • users.

8. Employment for bamboo extraction

Extraction of bamboos in the forest from thorny intertwined branches in the clumps is both difficult and time consuming. The approach to the base of clumps also requires clearing of basal thorny branches. Even after cutting the base with a long handled axe or billhook, the culms have their branches intertwined with others at the middle and top of clumps.

The current requirement of labour for bamboo extraction is worked out on averages. The felling contract is granted based on 100 bamboos, for better culms used in weaving and tonnage or volume for industrial uses. In addition, labour is used for loading, unloading, storage, etc. The present average requirement for felling and extraction of bamboos from forests consists of six working days per tonne. Loading, unloading and stacking require one working day per tonne. Average wage rate now is Rs 75/- day.

9. Economic importance of silk beyond silk production

After the silk threads or silk waste is produced, several stages are required up to the end use of silk, which has great significance in the gross national product and employment generation. Spinning, colouring, blending, weaving of silk into fabric or sarees and manufacture of apparel are all the downstream activities. The bulk of weaving is in the rural sector on handlooms or power looms. Though some components in such weaving can be made from bamboo, no further study for such uses is deemed necessary since wood, plastics and metals have been progressively used in place of bamboo.

10. Competition between bamboos and substitute materials in sericulture equipment

Cardboard trays, plastic trays and mountages have been devised and introduced in silkworm rearing. The traditional cocoon rearing farmers in South India use bamboo trays and mountages in preference to other equipment.

During the field sampling, almost all farmers have been unanimous in their opinion, that bamboo equipment is still the best and, rather than looking for substitutes, they have suggested removal of bottlenecks in the bamboo:

  • supply;
  • transport;
  • products standardization; and
  • costs standardization.

11. Problems in supply

Almost the entire supply of bamboos as raw-material for manufacture of equipment comes from government forests. Bamboos are defined, under the Forest Act, as "forest products [….] whether brought in from the forests or not". Therefore, transportation of bamboos has to be covered by a permit duly issued by an authorized Forest Officer. Procurement of transit permits involves delay in movement of the harvested bamboo, resulting in losses from drying out, pilferage and decay caused by fungi and insects.

During the last ten years, harvesting of bamboo has been taken over by the Forest Department. This has introduced more red-tape which must be borne by users, such as:

  • delays;
  • corruption; and
  • higher costs of extraction.

Weavers of mats, trays and manufacturers of mountages have to put up with these problems.

Billhooks tied to long bamboo poles used to cut the obstructive branches higher up. The culm is then dragged by holding the butt-end either by a set of labourers, by hand or by tying a rope around the butt-end. The felling operation has become cumbersome because of unscientific harvests, resulting in congestion of clumps and intertwining of culms through the clump while attaining heights. Heavy grazing compacts on the forest soil, which is also responsible for congestion of clumps. These factors can be remedied, if the bamboo forests are scientifically managed.

The weavers, traders and other artisans have to accept the quality, quantity and age of culms as handed over to them, without selection. A certain percentage of material sold to them cannot be used.

Weavers would like green and soft bamboos for ease of weaving, quality of product and minimum wastage through residues. Since users have no control on selection, harvest and transportation of bamboos, they suffer in both quality and cost of the products.

There are instances when the supply of bamboo is made long after their felling, resulting in drying, decay and total loss of the produce for use in sericulture. The situation is no better when extraction is done by the Forest Development Corporations.

It is an irony that there is neither improvement in quality or quantity of bamboo production in all the states, even after introduction of the departmental harvest.

There has been no attempt to introduce silvicultural management of clumps or scientific harvesting. No modernization in tools and methods for harvesting, transport, storage, grading and no preservative treatment is resorted to.

The policy of governments on concessional supplies to artisans and their societies has been misused for an unhealthy nexus between politicians, officials and traders. Traders backed by the politicians control the societies.

Although the Ministry of Textiles, Sericulture and the Departments of Sericulture as well as Central Silk Board, have been trying to find substitutes to traditional bamboo equipment, they have not given adequate thought to improving bamboo quality or its smooth and adequate supply, which traditional farmers would prefer to use instead of substitutes. Only in cases of non-availability and unreasonable high prices, farmers use substitutes such as cardboard and plastics.

Branch feeding is resorted to by large farms to save on cost of labour and not for better results. The agencies promoting mulberry cultivation and sericulture have not looked into supply improvement of much needed bamboo equipment. A suggestion made to introduce useful bamboo species as a border-crop around mulberry farms, has no takers (consensus).

12. Private sources of supply

The fall in yields from forest extraction and obstacles with availability have resulted in homesteads in Kerala and Goa growing bamboos on their own holdings because of the ease of cultivation and a ready market.

Konkan districts of Maharashtra, along the border of Karnataka, have taken up cultivation of bamboos. Species grown in Kerala is Bambusa bambos.

Species grown in Goa and Maharashtra are Pseudoxytenanthera stocksii in bulk and Dendrocalamus strictus in smaller numbers.

An estimated annual production of 10 000 tonnes is recorded from private sources in Kerala and about 30 000 tonnes between Goa and Maharashtra. Tanjore district in Tamilnadu has taken up bamboo cultivation on private land, but the produce is locally used as props for banana cultivation.

The artisan groups dealing in equipment for sericulture buy private bamboos in bulk at markets in Sankeshwar and Belgaum and transport them to destinations in drier districts in Southern Karnataka, neighbouring Andhra Pradesh and Tamilnadu for their use.

They have managed to solve problems of permits, checkpoints and transport obstacles on their own at some additional cost, which is a fraction of the cost of purchase and transport. It was revealed to our field staff that the average cost of purchase of one lorry load of about 2 500 small bamboos at Sankeshwar is Rs 25 000/-, transportation cost to Denkanikota and Dharmapuri in Tamilnadu is Rs 30 000/- and additional costs for overcoming obstacles of different departments involved is an average of Rs 5 000/- per lorry load. The landed cost of such bamboo comes to Rs 20/- to Rs 25/- each or Rs 4 000/- to Rs 5 000/- per tonne.

13. Manufacturing at site

Except for the few wholesale contractors in different towns in Karnataka and bordering Andhra Pradesh and Tamilnadu, hundreds of artisans live in hutments. There are streets in the towns where the Buruds are concentrated. Each household either buys a headload of 20 to 30 bamboos, depending on the size, at Rs 30/- and the family members do the splitting and weaving.

There are many instances, where the wholesaler supplies the raw material and pays fixed wages for the products made to order. Some villagers situated near bamboo forests collect bamboo on headloads, with or without a permit and sell products to wholesalers.

Individual families are always needy because of the irregular availability of raw material resulting in many idle hours and days or related to the time required to get back the value of bamboos and their maintenance costs, which comes after sale of the produce. This is one reason for which they depend on traders:

  • to obtain advance amounts, for which they commit quantity and rate for supply; or
  • for supply of raw material.

The larger manufacturers or traders have been in this business for 15 to 30 years and know the tricks of the trade. They also have knowledge of alternative sources of supply of raw material or semi-finished products used in fabrication of trays and mountages at different centres in Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Assam for the supply of mats.

They buy bamboos, mats, flowers (used inside Chandrike), coir-ropes, etc. in bulk and supply the same to individual families for manufacture or hire artisans on a wage per unit of manufacture. In the latter case, they construct a large shed or pandal mostly out of bamboos, mats and plastic sheets. These sheds and pandals are used for storage of raw material up to one or two lorry loads and storage of finished products until they are sold. Weaving and fabrication is done either outside or inside these pandals.

These traders buy mats at Tarikere and around Shimoga in Karnataka or from Nandyal and Rajamundry in Andhra Pradesh and shortages are obtained from Assam. The cost of purchase of mats sized 1.8 m x 1.2 m varies from Rs 25/- to Rs 35/- for wholesale and Rs 40-45 for retail. Bamboos are bought in the districts of Belgaum, Shimoga, Rajamundry and Kurnool, from:

  • forest department sources;
  • bamboo cooperative societies;
  • forest development corporations; or
  • bamboo merchants.

Flowers of about 45 m length are bought at Rs 65 to Rs 80/- each and its length is tailored to fabrication of one mountage. Coir rope bundles come from Kerala or Coastal Karnataka.

The field study revealed that the experienced traders succeed because of their skills to overcome problems in procurement of raw material and their ability to make investments up to about Rs 200 000 during the peak season to sustain their trade.

In cases where there is a lack of ready demand for mountages for sale, they hire them to small farmers at Rs 5 to Rs 6/- for a three days requirement and keep recycling them.

In Karnataka, about 40 percent of rearing farmers own the mountages and 60 percent hire them. Those depending on hired mountages number 75 percent in Andhra Pradesh and Tamilnadu. The annual production of larger bamboo traders varies from 3 000 to 10 000 trays and 2 000 to 6 000 mountages per annum. Trays are generally bought and not hired. Many small-scale farmers take both mountages and trays on loan from neighbours or on barter to avoid purchase.

14. Improvement in resources

The Department of Sericulture should promote bamboo plantations along with mulberry in the zones where artisans need supply of fresh bamboos. Such bamboo planting can be on:

  • homesteads;
  • boundaries of mulberry fields; or
  • block planting on common property resources.

Service societies should be encouraged to motivate farmers to grow bamboos on assurance of:

  • purchase at support price;
  • easy credit facilities;
  • supply of quality planting stock; and
  • technical and extension services.

Such societies should help in:

  • bamboo planting;
  • bamboo harvesting;
  • contacting agencies having technical competence in:
    • bamboo planting;
    • bamboo harvesting ;
    • preservative treatment; and
    • market information.

User groups should be attracted by the Forest Department and the Forest Development Corporations in joint forest management of extended bamboo plantations for mutual benefit.

Information technology should be harnessed for dissemination of market information between producers, traders, processors and users for proper linkages.

Forest and Sericulture Research Institutes should undertake applied research on continuous improvement of equipment in use to reduce:

  • cost of purchase;
  • maintenance; and
  • replacement.

Service societies manufacturing and supplying of improved tools for:

  • splitting
  • slivering
  • strengthening
  • joinery.

These can help in reducing:

  • labour cost;
  • wastage; and
  • improve product quality.

Storage of bamboo equipment during this idle period has not been given attention and deserves educating the users on this matter.

Promotion of a multiplicity of products and their ready sales for reasonable returns to the artisans will help to:

  • reduce bamboo wastage;
  • avoid idle time; and
  • improve wages for the poor families of artisans.

15. Socioeconomic conditions of Buruds

15.1 Weaving communities

Bamboo weaving is a traditional centenary old cottage industry. A large section of weavers belong to a defined community in South India and are known as Buruds. Karnataka alone has a population of 50 300 Burud families and Andhra Pradesh has 2 900 families. In addition to Buruds, bamboo weaving is a domestic profession among several families in the low-income group of rural communities.

Since villagers situated near natural bamboo forests enjoy the privilege of bringing headloads of bamboos for their weaving profession, there is no exact record of quantities removed on headloads. Woven bamboo is used in several sectors, of which sericulture is quite important and compares equally with these used in the agricultural sector in South India.

The silk industry in South India is a large user of bamboo, next only to the pulping sector. Weaving is an art passed down through the generations in the poor rural communities, therefore the employment evolving from this type of application is much higher than that for bamboo use as raw material as such as the pulp and paper industry.

15.2 Caste

The growing of mulberry and production of cocoons are activities taken up by farming communities belonging to all castes, mostly Vokkaligas and Lingayats. Manufacture of bamboo components for use in mulberry growing and rearing of silk worms for cocoon production is invariably taken up by families belonging to Medar and Korama castes which belong to a scheduled category. This is a traditional occupation of these communities. There is little occupational mobility in these groups.

15.3 Family size

The general impression is that the poorer sections of the society are characterized by larger family size. This notion is endorsed by the families engaged in manufacture of components for sericulture. Based on case studies the findings are as follows:

  • Average family size: 6.2
  • Number of male adults: 2.2
  • Number of female adults: 1.1
  • Number of male children: 1.7
  • Number of female children: 1.2.

15.4 Housing

The families are poorly housed. Most often their houses are made of bamboo and thatch. Some portions of the houses are made of mud-plastered brick walls, mud flooring and tiled roofs. The dwelling house, working place, place for storing raw materials and manufactured components are the same. The sanitary and other conditions are typically not good, even in a village where they live in a colony or on their own lane.

15.5 Education

Education receives minimum attention by elders and attracts few children. All children are enrolled in the schools, but attendance is not regular. Among adults, the literacy is only 18 percent for males and 6 percent for females. The highest qualification acquired is Secondary School Leaving Certificate (SSLC equivalent to O level), i.e. tenth standard (matriculation) for males and seventh standard for females.

It is appropriate to mention here that the environment for children’s education is not conducive. Starting from the age of five, the children have to assist the elders in their work. Initially they do so before and after school hours. They start receiving tips for their assistance. This will make them familiar with handling money. By the time they are tenor twelve years old, they are used to handling money and start needing it most and, by then, they would have acquired some skills in manufacturing the bamboo components. In a way, they become adults both in occupation and handling money. This distracts them from education. The parents will not be able to force the children to study and incur their displeasure because they will be asking children to assist them in their work.

15.6 Health

Health conditions are not satisfactory due to living conditions and to a fair extent due to other habits. Whilst children are attracted to eating roadside foods and even smoking, adults resort to drinking liquor. Conditions of the aged persons are pathetic. The economic conditions force them to work. This is forced upon them since they stay where there is work. Drinking country-made liquor of dubious source is their habit and this is one reason for their poverty.

15.7 Economic status

The families engaged in the manufacture of bamboo components make  their living mainly by their labour. The average earning per adult is Rs 60/- day, for children between five and ten years old Rs 30/- day and for children between eleven and fifteen years old it is Rs 45/-. This is after accounting for varying conditions in the supply of bamboo and demand for components. The supply of bamboo will not be regular throughout the year. The sale of bamboo components will generally increase during January to March because the farmers will have cash to buy them. Their possessions are, apart from the house, transistor, cycle, tools for their jobs and wrist watches, savings are negligible.

15.8 Working hours

There are no regular working hours. The male adults start their work at about 7 a.m. in the morning and continue until 7 p.m. in the evening with breaks for food and brief rest. The female adults support male members after the domestic work. The children will work between 7 a.m. and 10 a.m. in the morning and 5 p.m. and 7 p.m. in the evening whenever possible and necessary. Except for the cinema, some religious functions and fairs, they do not have any other entertainment, transistors and radios are their main sources of entertainment.

15.9 Organizational support

There are societies formed for the manufacturers of bamboo components. These are formed mostly due to external (like government departments) pressure. In most cases these societies are defunct and most of the members are defaulters. The bamboo is supplied by a few individuals or sometimes a few manufacturers join to obtain bamboo by truck loads. Individually, they are dependent on the bamboo contractors and wholesale dealers of components.

  • Forest and sericulture research institutes should undertake applied research in continuous improvement of equipment in usage to reduce on cost of purchase, maintenance and replacement.
  • Manufacture and supply of improved tools for splitting, slivering, strengthening and joinery by service societies can help in reducing labour costs, wastage and improve quality of the product.
  • Storage of bamboo equipment during the idle period has not been attended to and deserves education of the users on the same.
  • Promotion of a multiplicity of products and their ready sales for reasonable returns to the artisans will help to reduce bamboo wastage, avoid idle time and improve wages to poor families of artisans.
  • The Department of Small-scale Industries and the Handicrafts Development Board should have special cells at the district level to study, identify and remove bottlenecks in the chain of activity from resource to the marketing of the products.
  • Help and advice from voluntary agencies engaged in bamboo development should be continuously taken by the producers of bamboo such as the Forest Department, Forest Corporations, joint forest management committees, on one hand and on the other, service centres and wings of development departments to improve coordination.

16. Policy interventions needed

Scientific management of forests by introducing all known silvicultural practices for improvement of yields and improved technologies and tools in harvesting, storage including prophylactic treatment has to be introduced. Guidelines for such management can be introduced immediately in consultation with scientific institutions, based on which the entire bamboo growing stock is regularly treated and available increments harvested. After the prophylactic treatment, bamboos should be graded to suit end uses. Such graded bamboo should be sold to artisans, farmers on priority and the balance sold to markets and industries without much delay in storage.

  • Wet storage facilities should be created at chosen centres, either by the Forest Department or the Forest Corporations, for the supply of green bamboos to rural artisans for retail sale.
  • Transit of bamboos and products should be freely permitted on production of certificates of origin by prescribed authorities consisting of Forest Department, Forest Corporation offices, joint forest management committees, cooperative societies of growers and harvesters, on the basis of maintenance of accounts and submission of periodical returns to a single central authority, in an office nearest in range or forest division.
  • Credit cooperatives should be created to assist artisans with short-term cash credit near the villages having a concentration of bamboo artisans.
  • The service societies in each district with a suitable number of branches should open depots for storage and sale of raw material such as bamboos, ropes, purchase of equipment at predetermined unit prices and sale of such equipment to needy users.
  • Service societies can also store equipment for hire and maintain them for improving their service life. These service societies should also ensure continuous supply of raw material, purchase of prepared goods, their quick disposal or ready hire and wage disbursement to artisans without delay. A development fund created by such societies should take care of social, educational, health and other basic needs of the families of artisans.

17. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

18. Related/associated technologies

  • Community bamboo harvesting: ID 7948.
  • Bamboo treadle pump: ID 3866.
  • Community bamboo nursery: ID 3868.
  • Bamboo match sticks production: ID 3862.
  • Production of bamboo mat board: ID 3860.
  • Bamboo toothpick manufacturing unit: ID 3888.
  • Bamboo splitting and slivering unit: ID 3865.

19. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

19.1 Resource use efficiency

This technology contributes to resources use efficiency of bamboo, as well as reducing environmental impact and improving storage.

19.2 Pro-poor technology

Bamboo equipment production related to sericulture can guarantee an income source for many and help enhance productivity of adjoining agricultural lands.
