records.title: Practices for occupational health and safety in forestry
records.description:
Description

Workers may be subject to extreme heat and cold. High temperatures reduce work capacity and may lead to heat stress and dehydration. The risk can be reduced by, for example, the provision of sun shelters, the regular intake of water, the judicious use of rest periods, and by undertaking the heaviest work in the coolest work hours. Cold weather can reduce dexterity, blood flow, muscle strength and balance. Regular food intake, adequate clothing and sufficient facilities for drying clothes can reduce the risk to human health posed by cold weather.

Terrain and site factors, such as slope and soil type, influence work safety. Forestry activities often occur on steep slopes, with a consequent high risk of machinery accidents and rock falls. Finely textured soils (e.g. clays) are slippery when wet, increasing the risk of accidents involving heavy machinery. Training and proper tool selection and maintenance can help reduce risks. Training should include planning, risk assessments and precautionary measures.

Bad examples of forest harvesting without protection are illustrated in the Figures below.

Figure 1. No protection

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Manual loading

©FAO/TECA

1. Protective equipment

A wide range of personal protective equipment is available to help minimize the risk of injury to forest workers. Protective clothing can reduce the risk of chainsaw injury. For example, the padding in “chaps” (worn over trousers) and chainsaw trousers comprise hundreds of polyester, polypropylene or nylon fibers that work by clogging the chainsaw chain and thereby preventing it from cutting through to the worker’s skin. Protective clothing that resists cutting such that the chain “glides” over the surface is also available.

Protective rubber footwear with a cut-resistant lining on the upper part of the boot and metallic toecaps can protect against chainsaw cuts and other hazards. In hot climates, since rubber boots could be uncomfortable, leather boots or ankle-high shoes with cut-resistant linings and toe caps can be used. Boots and shoes should also be designed to reduce the risk of slipping and falling, and chemical- resistant soles may be necessary, especially for forest operations involving the application of pesticides.

The chainsaw is the most dangerous tool in forestry. Its operator is the most exposed worker. Trees falling and crosscutting activities are also incidents where serious and fatal accidents are also likely to occur. Work involving hung-up trees and wind-thrown stands is particularly risky. Training in safe practices and the use of adequate safety equipment can reduce such risks.

Another hazard is chainsaw kickback, which occurs when the upper quarter of the bar nose comes in contact with an object, resulting in an instantaneous “kicking” of the chainsaw, potentially towards the operator. The risk of kickback can be minimized by avoiding contact between the bar nose and the tree, and by always operating the chainsaw with two hands on the saw handles, not using it above the shoulders, and always keeping it in front of the body.

Helmets protect against falling objects and chainsaw kickbacks. They should be comfortable and as light as possible without compromising their strength and durability. The strength of both plastic and alloy helmets decreases as they age, and therefore they should be replaced regularly. Headbands must be correctly adjusted. Helmets should have in-built devices for attaching visors and earmuffs.

A good example of protective clothes is depicted in the following picture.

Figure 3. A well-equipped worker

©FAO/TECA

The face and eye protectors fitted to helmets are normally made of aluminum or fiberglass mesh. Although the mesh reduces incoming light, most operators prefer it to Perspex shields and goggles, which fog easily. Hearing protectors should be certified and fitted tightly against the head.

Tree bole crosscutting is often done close to the ground, placing a strain on the operator’s back, but the ideal work height is hip level, and this can be achieved by using other fallen trees as “benches”. The chainsaw should be partly rested on the tree bole during de-limbing. Repetitive work patterns over extended periods can lead to repetitive strain injuries and should be avoided.

Noise from chainsaws and brush cutters can lead to hearing loss if hearing protection is not used. The use of hand-held power tools such as chainsaws and brush cutters can also cause hand-arm vibration, which can affect blood circulation in the hands and forearms and damage nerves, tendons, muscles, bones and joints. The risk of injury due to chainsaw vibration has been reduced by the introduction of vibration-damping chainsaws; although still available in some countries, chainsaws not equipped with this feature should be avoided.

Operators of machines such as skidders and loaders may be subject to whole-body vibrations, which can cause lower back pain as well as repetitive strain injuries. Whole-body vibrations can be reduced by the use of vibration-damping seats in machinery and decreased exposure through job rotation.

Loading and unloading wood is a hazardous operation in forestry. Risks can be reduced through the use of safe working routines and adequate personal protective equipment. The transport of wood on narrow roads, possibly in poor weather conditions, is another hazardous activity, the safety of which can be improved through good practices. Log trucks suitable for the job should be well maintained and operated by trained and properly licensed drivers. Overloading should be avoided, and binders should be used to secure loads.

2. Chemical and biological hazards

The forestry sector has a range of chemical hazards, including the potential for exposure to fumes associated with chainsaw use and to pesticides, and biological hazards such as the potential for allergic reactions to plants, pollen, wooden products and insect bites. Biological hazards also include snakebites and diseases that can be contracted from, for example, mosquitos and ticks. Chainsaws and brush cutters are sources of exhaust emissions, which include the suspected carcinogens benzene and formaldehyde. Aerosols from the oils used in chainsaws and brush cutters can cause irritation to skin, eyes and the respiratory system, which can be reduced by the use of goggles and gloves and by regular washing.

Exposure to herbicides and pesticides in forestry can lead to a variety of health problems. Personal protective equipment, such as overalls, boots, gloves, and, for toxic agents, respiratory devices, should be used. Smoking and eating should be avoided when working with chemicals.

The risks posed by many biological hazards can be reduced through adequate training, effective management (e.g. by reducing mosquito breeding grounds in the vicinity of camps and the use of mosquito nets), and an adequate level of personal hygiene.

2.1 Other hazards

Non-wood forest products are often harvested by individuals in remote locations, and help may be far away if accidents occur. Tree-climbing, cutting, digging, gathering, picking and manually transporting products are all common non-wood forest products-harvesting activities, and all have associated risks. Other hazards include heavy repetitive or static work, the use of inappropriate tools, difficult terrain, and contact with poisonous plants and venomous animals. Accidents associated with cutting are the most common hazard. Training and proper tool selection and maintenance can help reduce risks.

Many rural people collect forest products alone in remote locations and may be exposed to a range of biological hazards as well as to extreme weather, accidents, and – especially for women, children and the elderly – assault.

3. Skills and training

Many forestry workers receive their training “on the job”, and often such training does not involve much more than imitation or trial and error. Even in industrialized countries, many forest owners, self-employed workers and contractors do not receive proper training. For some jobs, mobile training – in which trained instructors travel to workplaces – is an efficient and effective alternative to schools and training centres.

4. Codes of practice

Many countries have codes of practice – sets of rules, prescriptions and recommendations – for health and safety in the forest sector, although they vary greatly in scope and coverage. Such codes can be a useful complement to safety laws and regulations that are not necessarily forestry-specific.

At least two international codes of practice relevant to health and safety in the forest sector have been developed: the FAO Model Code of Forest Harvesting (1996) (crosslink), and the International Labour Organization’s Safety and Health in Forestry Work (first published in 1969, revised in 1998). National codes of practice vary in their legal status; for example, they may be legally binding or voluntary. Forest management certification schemes also normally have components that are relevant to worker health and safety.

5. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Traditional floating garden practices for seedling production: ID 8869.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Pro-poor technology

The practice allows for increased security to risky forestry activities, thereby ensuring greater yield and added source of income.

Other hazards include heavy repetitive or static work, the use of inappropriate tools, difficult terrain, and contact with poisonous plants and venomous animals. Accidents associated with cutting are the most common hazard. Training and proper tool selection and maintenance can help reduce risks.

Many rural people collect forest products alone in remote locations and may be exposed to a range of biological hazards as well as to extreme weather, accidents, and – especially for women, children and the elderly – assault.

3. Skills and training

Many forestry workers receive their training “on the job”, and often such training does not involve much more than imitation or trial and error. Even in industrialized countries, many forest owners, self-employed workers and contractors do not receive proper training. For some jobs, mobile training – in which trained instructors travel to workplaces – is an efficient and effective alternative to schools and training centres.

4. Codes of practice

Many countries have codes of practice – sets of rules, prescriptions and recommendations – for health and safety in the forest sector, although they vary greatly in scope and coverage. Such codes can be a useful complement to safety laws and regulations that are not necessarily forestry-specific.

At least two international codes of practice relevant to health and safety in the forest sector have been developed: the FAO Model Code of Forest Harvesting (1996) (crosslink), and the International Labour Organization’s Safety and Health in Forestry Work (first published in 1969, revised in 1998). National codes of practice vary in their legal status; for example, they may be legally binding or voluntary. Forest management certification schemes also normally have components that are relevant to worker health and safety.

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Pro-poor technology

The practice allows for increased security to risky forestry activities, thereby ensuring greater yield and added source of income.

records.title: How to collect the raw wax from the hive
records.description:
Description

1. The procedure of wax production by bees

  • Young bees in the hive, after feeding the young brood with royal jelly, take part in the construction of the hive.
  • Engorged with honey and resting suspended for 24 hours together with many other bees in the same position, eight wax glands on the underside of the abdomens of the young bees secrete small wax platelets.
  • These are scraped off by the bee, chewed and masticated into pliable pieces with the addition of saliva and a variety of enzymes (Figure 1).

1.1 Bees species that produce wax

  • Many bee species produce wax but unless otherwise mentioned, only the wax of the honeybee species Apis mellifera will be referred to in this technology.
  • The wax from other honeybee species (ghedda wax) is very similar but has characteristics sufficiently different for it not to be used by the cosmetic industry.
    • Even the wax produced by A. mellifera is not always the same.
Figure 1. The white flakes on the picture are wax scales that fell on the bottom board

©FAO/Daniele Olivotti

1.2 Reasons why bees produce wax

  • Once chewed, attached to the comb and re‑chewed several times, the wax scales finally form part of this architectural masterpiece, a comb of hexagonal cells.
    • This is a 20 g structure that can support 1 000 g of honey.
  • Wax is used to cap the ripened honey and when mixed with some propolis, also protects the brood from infections and desiccation.
  • Together with propolis, the wax is also employed for sealing cracks and covering foreign objects in the hive (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Honeycomb with propolis

©FAO/Charlotte Lietaer

2. Physical characteristics of beeswax

  • Virgin beeswax, immediately after being secreted by the bees, elaborated and formed into a comb, is white (Figure 3).
  • Wax becomes darker with use inside the hive and as pollen, propolis and larval debris are inadvertently incorporated.
  • Sometimes, brood combs are completely dark (Figure 4). Rendered, but untreated beeswax comes in varying shades of yellow (Figure 5).
Figure 3. Newly constructed white comb in a traditional log hive

©FAO/TECA

3. Collecting wax

  • Old combs, honeycombs and capping wax can be melted for further use.
  • However, dark old combs should not be melted together with fresh honeycombs or capping wax.
  • Wax melts between 61°C and 66°C.
Figure 4. Dark brood comb (top part)

©FAO/Charlotte Lietaer

Figure 5. Cakes of rendered wax

©FAO/Charlotte Lietaer

4. Methods for wax extraction from the combs

4.1 Using a solar wax melter

  • The beekeeper can put the empty combs inside a box with a glass cover to melt the wax (Figures 6 and 7).
  • The heat of the sun accumulated in the box will make the combs melt.
  • The melted wax can be stored and processed later.
    • Before processing, all comb or wax pieces should be washed thoroughly to remove honey and other debris.
    • Soaking combs in water for several hours, or up to two days for older brood combs will be the best.

4.2 Melting wax by boiling with water

  • It is also possible to melt the wax using fire.
    • In that case, the beekeeper uses a stainless steel, aluminium or glass container.
    • Fill the container with water, add the pieces of comb and bring the water to boiling.
    • The combs will melt.
    • Once the wax is melted, remove the container from the fire and let the water and wax cool down.
    • Because the wax is lighter than water, it will stay on the surface of the container.
    • When the wax is cold (solidified), warm a little bit the container again only to melt the wax in contact with the container walls to remove the block of wax (wax cake) from the container very easily.
    • Debris will deposit on the bottom of the wax cake.
    • The beekeeper should scrape off the layer of debris.
    • The wax can be melted again to remove more debris.
  • Wax should never be heated above 85° C. If the wax is heated directly (without water) or above 85° C discolouration occurs.
  • Therefore, wax always needs to be processed in water or in a water bath.
  • Wax should not be processed in iron or copper containers since it will discolour from reaction with these metals.

4.3 Storing wax

  • Beeswax should only be stored in its rendered, clean form.
  • Uncleaned wax will quickly be attached by wax moths, which are able to destroy large quantities of wax in a short period of time.
  • Clear wax in large blocks not attached by wax moths.
  • Wax should be stored in cool dry places and never in the same room with any kind of pesticide.
  • Wax will slowly crystalize over time and as a consequence become harder, but this process is reversible without any damage, just as with crystallized honey.
  • The white bloom, (for example dust), that sometimes appears on the outside of a wax cake or candle consists of small wax crystals.
  • The crystals will disappear when the wax is melted again.
Figure 6. Solar wax melter

©FAO/Charlotte Lietaer

Figure 7. Melted wax in solar wax melter

©FAO/Charlotte Lietaer

5. Related/associated technologies 

  • Beekeeping in Africa: honey and beeswax extraction: ID 7330.
  • How to process the raw beeswax into value added products: ID 8776.

This technology is also available in French: ID 10036.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Women-friendly

The technology is easy to use and accessible to all.

6.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently collects raw beeswax which can be diversely used in a multitude of applications including the food process, textile and pharmaceutical industries.

6.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology informs beekeepers how to collect and prepare wax for further processing for sale since it can be an additional source of income.

records.title: Fish powder
records.description:
Description

In Uganda, fish is an important food commodity since it provides the main source of protein for some 34.5 million Ugandans. Fish exports are the second largest income earner after coffee in Uganda and thus fillets of Nile perch (Lates Niloticus) and other fish species are mostly exported leaving the remaining parts of the fish, which often go to waste. Thus, they present an opportunity to utilize these by-products that are not commonly eaten and otherwise go to waste, to create a unique product such as fish powder.

Simultaneously, iron deficiency among Ugandan children and women is unacceptably high and many interventions, including bio-fortification of staple foods, have been implemented to combat anaemia, stunting and malnutrition amongst Ugandans. In Uganda, the production of fish by-product powder high in calcium, phosphorous, zinc, iron and vitamin A was initiated to contribute to reducing malnutrition. Staple foods enriched with by-product powder are suitable as a weaning food, high in calcium and phosphorous and other minerals and vitamins supporting skeletal development and rich in omega-3 contributing to cognitive development during the first 1 000 days of life.

1. Benefits of fish by-product powders

Fish by-product powders can be used to enrich staple foods such as grains, rice, maize and wheat, and tubers such as cassava. In Uganda, maize and cassava are staple foods. Maize is deficient in the essential amino acids lysine and tryptophan and cassava is low in protein and fats and where these are staple foods, protein deficiency frequently prevails in children. Enrichment of maize and cassava with by-product powder can increase the protein quality of the diet but also enhance the diet with essential omega-3, fatty acids and particularly micronutrients. Fish and by-product powders can be incorporated into school feeding programs and made available to purchase from local markets to help combat anaemia, stunting and general malnutrition among vulnerable groups such as women, infants and children. Table 1 shows the micronutrients of tuna backbone powder.

Table 1. Chemical composition, mineral content and amino acid and lipid profiles in bones from tuna species
Nutritional information mg/100mg RDI for kids (mg/day)
Calcium 10 200 700
Zinc 8.6 5.6
Iron 36 8.9
Selenium 0.03 0.02
EPA+DHA 3,080 150

Source: FAO 2016

Compared to the mukene powder, tuna bone powder has less flavour and more nutritional value (five times higher - calcium, four time higher - iron and two times higher - omega-3). It could be good replacement for tuna backbone powder. Table 2 shows a comparison between mukene powder with tuna bone powder.

Table 2. Comparison of mukene powder with tuna bone powder
Nutritional information mg/100 g Mukene fish powder Tuna bone powder
Calcium 1,650 10 200 
Zinc 10 8.6
Iron 9.5 36
EPA+DHA 1,650 3,080

Source: FAO 2016

Fish by-products intended for human consumption must be handled and treated the same way as the main parts of the fish. To ensure that by-products are both safe and nutritionally rich, prerequisites such as Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) and Good Hygiene Practices (GHP) should be applied and where possible, Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP) too (for more information click on the following link). Compositional analysis of the final product must be carried out to ensure that levels of microbiological contaminants and heavy metals such as lead, mercury and cadmium are below the safety limit. A food grade mill should be used to create a fine powder from dried by-products. Lastly the product is vacuum packed to reduce spoilage and maximize the shelf life of the powder.

2. Production of powder from Nile perch by-products

The following steps can be adjusted depending on the species of fish and by-products that are being used. Steps three to five may be skipped if the by-products are clean and have not been contaminated in the production process. Washing might remove some of the nutritious parts of the fish. Table 3 shows the steps to process nutrient rich fish powder from Nile perch (Lates Niloticus) by-products in Uganda.

A similar process is being used in Ghana where they are producing fish by-product powder from tuna by-products, specifically bones, gills and trimmings. In this case, the by-products are not pre-cooked. Furthermore, efforts are being made in both Ghana and Uganda to produce fish powder from small indigenous species, underutilized, not commonly eaten or discarded, which are particularly high in micronutrients when processed whole.

Figure 1. Dried fish bones

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Milling of the dried fish by-products

©FAO/TECA

3. Fish by-product powder recipes

In addition to the recipes below, fish and fish by-product powders can be used as a flour composite and as a condiment for adding flavour to soups, stews and leafy vegetables.

3.1 Fried cassava balls, Ghana

3.1.1 Ingredients

  • cassava dough 285 g;
  • blended onion 60 ml;
  • by-product powder 15 g; and
  • salt half teaspoon.

3.1.2 Instructions

  • Peel and grate the cassava.
  • Squeeze the liquid from the grated cassava using a cheesecloth to make cassava dough. 
  • Mix the cassava dough with salt and blended onion (if not possible to blend, finely chop the onion). 
  • Add the by-product powder and mix well. 
  • Mould the dough into small rounds balls.
  • Deep fry for eight minutes until golden. See Figure 3.
Table 3. Production of powder from Nile perch by-products

Source: FAO 2016

Figure 3. Enriched cassava balls

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Baked corn dough cakes, Ghana

To make corn dough, mix two cups of maize flour with one to two cups of warm water and a quarter teaspoon of baking powder.

3.2.1 Ingredients

  • fish by-product powder 15 g; 
  • sweet potato flour 50 g; 
  • corn dough 235 g;
  • baking powder a quarter teaspoon; and 
  • sugar one and a half teaspoon.

3.2.2 Instructions

  • Mix Fish by-product powder, sweet potato flour and corn dough together.
  • Add the sugar and baking powder and continue mixing.
  • Mould with plantain leaves into dough cakes.
  • Bake in an oven heated to 177°C for 15 minutes. See Figure 4.
Figure 4. Baked corn dough cakes

©FAO/TECA

3.3 Vegetables cooked with by-products powder served with posho maize flour bread, Uganda

3.3.1 Ingredients 

  • one medium size cabbage;
  • two medium onions;
  • 5 ml of vegetable oil;
  • 50 g fish by-product powder; 
  • half a teaspoon of iodized salt;
  • one teaspoon of curry powder; and 
  • two teaspoons of mixed spices.

3.3.2 Instructions 

  • Slice the cabbage and onions into thin strips.
  • Add the oil to a frying pan and gradually heat.
  • Fry the onions in the oil, stir continuously until soft.
  • Once the onions are soft, add the cabbage and stir for five minutes.
  • Add the fish by-product powder, salt, curry powder and mixed spices and continue to stir.
  • Allow the mixture to simmer for two minutes and then remove from the heat.
  • Serve with posho maize flour bread.

3.3.3 Ingredients for the posho maize flour bread

  • maize flour 500 g; and 
  • water (1 litre).

3.3.4 Instructions for the posho maize flour bread 

  • Sieve the maize flour into a fine powder. 
  • Heat the water to boiling point before adding maize flour.
  • Mingle into hard bread for 30 minutes at 90 °C.

4. Validation of the practice

In 2012, a school feeding program in Ghana incorporated different fish powders into local school lunches. The powders were made from locally available raw materials; tuna frames, flying gurnard, woevi, and anchovies and were used to prepare four local dishes that were given to school children to test their acceptability. The full information about the results could be found under: GloverAmengor, M., Atikpo, O., MA, A., Ayin, J., & Toppe, J. (2012). Proximate composition and consumer acceptability of three underutilized fish species and tuna frames. World Rural Observ, 4(2), 65 - 70.

In addition, the “Securing the nutritional value of freshwater fish products in the East, Central and Southern African region Report” registered the production of fish powder using species caught from different lakes in Uganda in order to stabilize the nutritional value and ensure food safety.

5. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies 

  • Fish and their by-products: ID 8717. 
  • Preservation of fish and meat: ID 6961.
  • Construction of raised drying racks for fish. The experience from Burundi: ID 8215.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Women-friendly

The technology is easy to use and accessible to all.

7.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology uses all parts of fish efficiently and avoids waste.

7.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology produces fish powder used from remaining fish parts that are not eaten and that are usually wasted. Incorporating fish powder improves micronutrient levels in diets, preventing malnutrition. Fish powder can also be a product to sell, providing additional income.

  • half a teaspoon of iodized salt;
  • one teaspoon of curry powder; and 
  • two teaspoons of mixed spices.

3.3.2 Instructions 

  • Slice the cabbage and onions into thin strips.
  • Add the oil to a frying pan and gradually heat.
  • Fry the onions in the oil, stir continuously until soft.
  • Once the onions are soft, add the cabbage and stir for five minutes.
  • Add the fish by-product powder, salt, curry powder and mixed spices and continue to stir.
  • Allow the mixture to simmer for two minutes and then remove from the heat.
  • Serve with posho maize flour bread.

3.3.3 Ingredients for the posho maize flour bread

  • maize flour 500 g; and 
  • water (1 litre).

3.3.4 Instructions for the posho maize flour bread 

  • Sieve the maize flour into a fine powder. 
  • Heat the water to boiling point before adding maize flour.
  • Mingle into hard bread for 30 minutes at 90 °C.

4. Validation of the practice

In 2012, a school feeding program in Ghana incorporated different fish powders into local school lunches. The powders were made from locally available raw materials; tuna frames, flying gurnard, woevi, and anchovies and were used to prepare four local dishes that were given to school children to test their acceptability. The full information about the results could be found under: GloverAmengor, M., Atikpo, O., MA, A., Ayin, J., & Toppe, J. (2012). Proximate composition and consumer acceptability of three underutilized fish species and tuna frames. World Rural Observ, 4(2), 65 - 70.

In addition, the “Securing the nutritional value of freshwater fish products in the East, Central and Southern African region Report” registered the production of fish powder using species caught from different lakes in Uganda in order to stabilize the nutritional value and ensure food safety.

5. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies 

  • Fish and their by-products: ID 8717. 
  • Preservation of fish and meat: ID 6961.
  • Construction of raised drying racks for fish. The experience from Burundi: ID 8215.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Women-friendly

The technology is easy to use and accessible to all.

7.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology uses all parts of fish efficiently and avoids waste.

7.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology produces fish powder used from remaining fish parts that are not eaten and that are usually wasted. Incorporating fish powder improves micronutrient levels in diets, preventing malnutrition. Fish powder can also be a product to sell, providing additional income.

records.title: Intensive stall-fed system for rearing goats
records.description:
Description

1. Construction of a goat shed

  • In the case of an existing tree crop garden, a goat shed of about 1.2 m (4 ft) above the ground level is constructed under the canopy. For roofing, galvanised corrugated sheet is used (Figures 1 and 2). 
  • The dimension of the shed is approximately 30 m x 3 m (100 ft x 10 ft) and the height is 3.6 m (12 ft) from the ground level. The pillars supporting the shed and the floor of the shed should measure 1.2 m (4 ft) in height from the ground. For easy understanding see the picture with the arrows below. The thickness of the pillars is 15 cm to 20 cm. 
  • There are ten sections inside the shed, each section is 3 m (10 ft) in length and 3 m (10 ft) in width. In each section has the ability to house ten adult animals. 
  • Buck and doe are kept separately so that breeding can be controlled. The young are kept in separate rooms for feeding them with a special feed/fodder.
Figure 1. Side view of goat shed with feeding throughs fixed outside the shed

©FAO/TECA

  • The floor of the shed is laid out with wooden planks at a gap of 2 cm (three‑fourths of an inch) in between the planks. This facilitates smooth descent of the goat droppings and urine onto the soil below the shed. The droppings can be collected at a six months interval and used as manure for the cultivation of vegetables and fodder crops.
Figure 2. View of top of the roof which is covered with galvanized sheet at the centre

©FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Inside view of the goat shed with 3 m x 3 m sections separated through wooden poles

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Top view of goat shed showing wooden poles roofed with galvanised corrugated sheets

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Construction steps

  • Erect cement, stone or wood pillars of 4 m (12 ft) in height at a 3 m distance along 30 m of total length. In total, 20 main pillars of 4 m (12 ft) in length are needed.
  • In between the main pillars, erect shorter pillars of 1.50 m (5 ft) height. Entrench them at a 30 cm (1 foot) depth. The pillars are erected at 150 cm (5 ft) intervals, in between the main pillars. In total, 37 pillars of 1.5 m (5 ft) in height are required. 
  • The shed is formed at the height of 1.2 m (4 ft) from the ground level, anchored over the (cement) pillars.
  • The shed is constructed with wooden poles roofed with galvanised corrugated sheets.
  • The floor of the shed is laid with wooden planks at a gap of 2 cm spacing between planks.
  • Nails are used for fixing the planks over the wooden poles. Usually the poles are obtained from casuarinas trees that are prevalent throughout the Indian subcontinent.
  • Both sides of the shed are closed with a wire grid to prevent the escape of goats.
  • The shed is divided into sections of 3 m x 3 m by erecting wooden poles and reapers with provision to let goats out conveniently.
  • The wooden reapers are manufactured in factories artificially using powdered wooden materials.
Figure 5. Erecting cement pillars for constructing the goat shed

©FAO/TECA

2. Steps to construct the feeding trough

For each room fix separate troughs. For the stall of 30 m x 3 m this would mean building ten troughs, each of which is fixed for the ten separated 3 m x 3 m sections. The feeding trough dimension is 2.75 m (9 ft) in length and 0.45 m (1.5 ft) in width.

  • Purchase tin sheets of 4 mm thickness of required length and width.
  • The feeding trough is made up of galvanised metal sheet of 4 mm thickness. At both ends of the trough semi‑circled wooden planks are fixed. The depth of the tough is 15 cm (half feet). For each room one feeding trough is fixed to facilitate ten goats to take feed when standing inside the shed.
  • Bend the tin sheet by placing a wooden plank of 3.6 m (9 ft) in length and 30 cm (1 ft) in width so as to make a frame for the feeding trough.
    • At each end, semi‑circular wooden planks of 45 cm (one and a half ft) in length are fitted as indicated in the picture with an arrow. Nails are used to fix both wooden planks and the tin sheets together.
    • The trough is then fixed using nails at the same height as the bottom of the wood planks of the floor.
    • The whole installation can be designed easily with the local carpenter by showing and interpreting the pictures.

This structure is easier to clean from the outside without entering the animal shed. It is convenient to deliver feed into the feeders from outside. The trough also avoids wastage of feed materials.

Figure 6. A rear view of goat shed made up of wooden poles covered with wire mesh

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Below the goat shed. The distance between the soil and the wooden planks is 1.2 m

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. The goat shed along with the feeding trough attached externally. The arrow shows the width of the feeding trough (45 cm)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9. The goat shed along with the feeding trough attached externally

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10. Feeding trough view along with feeding materials

©FAO/TECA

Figure 11. Feeding trough view along with feeding materials

©FAO/TECA

3. The cost of constructing a goat shed

Table 1 shows the cost of construction of a goat shed for housing 100 goats.

Table 1. Costs for constructing a goat shed in Tamil Nadu, India (cost bases on rates in 2012 and is subject to changes in prizes)

Source: SEVA

Figure 12. The goat keeper is standing near the main entrance of the goat shed (SEVA)

©FAO/TECA

Figure 13. Inside view of the goat shed with different sections along with outlet gates (SEVA)

©FAO/TECA

4. Validation of the practice

This practice has been adopted by 16 farmers in the Coimbatore district of Tamil Nadu. The NGO SEVA documented and shared this local innovation, set up by a farmer in Tamil Nadu state of India.

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Improvement of livestock production: community based goat production: ID 4495.
  • Goat raising in controlled areas and vaccination: ID 8937.
  • Rearing dairy goats: ID 6925.
  • Herbal de-worming for lower goat mortality: ID 7690.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project

7.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for the efficient construction of livestock stalls which can fulfill a variety of functions.

7.2 Pro-poor technology

Improved stalls can lead to healthier and better quality livestock, which in turn provides for an improved source of food and additional income.

records.title: Video on how to prune a mango tree
records.description:
Description

1. How to prune a mango tree

  • The following video shows what is needed and how it is done. The video is available in the English language and in Ghanaian language Twi.
  • There are two types of pruning.
    • The first is formative pruning, which is conducted on young trees.
    • The second is maintenance pruning, which is continuously done every year after harvest. This practice focuses on maintenance pruning.

1.1 Tools for pruning

  • Tools for pruning include:
    • hand shears,
    • long shears,
    • a pruning saw, and
    • a pruning pole.
  • While pruning, it is important to:
    • wear safety clothes and wear a helmet,
    • gloves,
    • safety boots, and
    • a protective jacket.

1.2 Pruning steps

  • A well-pruned tree has evenly distributed branches and no branches growing into the centre of the canopy.
  • In pruning, it is very important to know where to cut the branches.
  • Look for branches with a V shape.
    • All the branches which haven’t developed a V shape should be cut off.
  • Figure 1 shows yellow bars indicating where the branches should be cut.
Figure 1. Yellow bars mark the places where the pruning should take place

©FAO/TECA

  • Make sure not to cut off the well-directed buds or young branches.
    • The aim of pruning is to help the tree to develop new good branches.
    • This is why the shoots should be selected carefully.
    • For example, a shoot like in Figure 2 should never be cut off.
    • It is well directed and does not prevent sunlight to enter in the canopy.
Figure 2. This branch should not be cut off

©FAO/TECA

  • Figure 3 shows an example of a shoot that should be cut off.
    • The shoot grows towards the centre of the canopy.
    • If not removed, this new branch will grow into the tree, but this is something that should be avoided.
    • When cutting a branch, the cut should not be horizontal, but rather slanted.
    • This ensures that water drips off the cut.
    • If water stays on the cut, it can lead to disease infestations and also to rot.
Figure 3. This branch needs to be cut off

©FAO/TECA

  • Video: How to prune a mango tree (twi)
  • Video: How to prune a mango tree (english)
Figure 4. Cuts have to be slanted

©FAO/TECA

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Routine tree management practices: pruning and cutting tree tops: ID 4653.
  • Fruit fly control for mango farmers: ID 8471.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project

4.1 Resource use efficiency

The practice enhances flowering and is effective against pest and diseases, leading to higher tree health and higher quality fruits.

4.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology is not costly and leads to improved quality fruit which can provide for as an additional source of income and food.

records.title: Introduction to organic agriculture
records.description:
Description

Organic agriculture follows the principles and logic of a living organism, in which all elements (soil, plant, farm animals, insects, the farmer, local conditions) are closely linked to each other. This is accomplished by using, where possible, agronomic, biological and mechanical methods, following the principles of these interactions, using the natural ecosystem as a model.

Organic agriculture shares many techniques used by other sustainable agricultural approaches (e.g. intercropping, crop rotation, mulching, integration of crops and livestock). However, the use of natural inputs (non-synthetic), the improvement of soil structure and fertility and the use of a crop rotation plan represent the basic rules that make organic agriculture a unique agricultural management system.

According to the Guidelines of Organically Food Produce of the Codex Alimentarius (2007), an organic production system is designed to:

  • enhance biological diversity within the whole system; 
  • increase soil biological activity; 
  • maintain long-term soil fertility; 
  • recycle wastes of plant and animal origin in order to return nutrients to the soil, thus minimizing the use of non-renewable resources; 
  • rely on renewable resources in locally organized agricultural systems; 
  • promote the healthy use of soil, water and air as well as minimize all forms of pollution that may result from agricultural practices; 
  • promote the careful processing methods agricultural products in order to maintain the organic integrity and vital qualities of the product at all stages; and 
  • become established on any existing farm through a period of conversion, the appropriate length of which is determined by site-specific factors such as the history of the land, and type of crops and livestock to be produced.

In addition, the International Federation of Organic Agriculture Movements (IFOAM), a non-governmental organization internationally networking and promoting organic agriculture, has established guidelines that have been widely adopted by the organic community for organic production and processing.

Figure 1. Using the natural ecosystem as a model

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Overview of organic production in 2003

©FAO/TECA

1. Principles of  organic agriculture practices, according to IFOAM (2002)

According to IFOAM (2002), organic agriculture practices are based on certain principles.

1.1 Principle of health

  • The role of organic agriculture, whether in farming, processing, distribution, or consumption, is to sustain and enhance the health of ecosystems and organisms from the smallest in the soil to human beings.
  • In view of this, it should avoid the use of fertilizers, pesticides, animal drugs and food additives that may have adverse health effects.

1.2 Principle of ecology

  • Organic agriculture should be based on living ecological systems and cycles, work with them, emulate them and help sustaining them. Organic management must be adapted to local conditions, ecology, culture and scale.
  • The reduction of inputs by reuse, recycle and the efficient management of materials and energy will contribute to improve environmental quality and will conserve resources.

1.3 Principle of fairness

  • This principle emphasizes that those involved in organic agriculture should conduct human relationships in a manner that ensures fairness at all levels and to all parties‑farmers, workers, processors, distributors, traders and consumers.
  • It also insists that animals should be provided with the conditions and opportunities of life according to their physiology, natural behaviour and well-being.
  • Natural and environmental resources that are used for production and consumption should be managed in a socially and ecologically fair way and should be held in trust for future generations.
  • Fairness requires systems of production, distribution and trade that are open and equitable and account for real environmental and social costs.

1.4 Principle of care

  • This principle states that precaution and responsibility are the key concerns in management, development and technology choices in organic agriculture.
  • Science is necessary to ensure that organic agriculture is healthy, safe and ecologically sound.
  • However, it must consider valid solutions from practical experiences, accumulated traditional and indigenous knowledge and prevent significant risks by adopting appropriate technologies and rejecting unpredictable ones, such as genetic engineering.

2. Why organic agriculture?

The goal of organic agriculture is to contribute to the enhancement of sustainability. But what does sustainability mean?

  • In the context of agriculture, sustainability refers to the successful management of agricultural resources to satisfy human needs while at the same time maintaining or enhancing the quality of the environment and conserving natural resources for future generations.
  • Sustainability in organic farming must, therefore, be seen in a holistic sense, which includes ecological, economic and social aspects.
  • Only if the three dimensions are fulfilled an agricultural system can be called sustainable. But how are they achieved? Some examples are described in the following sections.
Figure 3. The three dimensions of sustainability

©FAO/TECA

2.1 Ecological sustainability

Organic agriculture techniques are known to be ecologically sustainable: 

  • Improving soil structure and fertility through the use of crop rotations, organic manure, mulches and the use of fodder legumes for adding nitrogen to the soil fertility cycle. 
  • Prevention of soil erosion and compaction by protecting the soil planting mixed and relay crops. 
  • Promotion of biological diversity through the use of natural pest controls (e.g. biological control, plants with pest control properties) rather than synthetic pesticides which, when misused, are known to kill beneficial organisms (e.g. natural parasites of pests, bees, earthworms), cause pest resistance, and often pollute water and land. 
  • Performing crop rotations, which encourage a diversity of food crops, fodder and under-utilized plants. This, in addition to improving overall farm production and fertility, may assist the on-farm conservation of plant genetic resources. 
  • Recycling the nutrients by using crop residues (straws, stovers and other nonedible parts) either directly as compost and mulch or through livestock as farmyard manure. 
  • Using renewable energies, by the integration of livestock, tree crops and on farm forestry into the system. This adds income through organic meat, eggs and dairy products, as well as draught animal power. Tree crops and on-farm forestry integrated into the system provide food, income, fuel and wood.

2.2 Social sustainability

  • Sustainability is also about equity among and between generations.
    • Organic agriculture contributes to social well‑being by reducing the losses of arable soil, water contamination, biodiversity erosion, GHG emissions, food losses, and pesticide poisoning. 
  • Organic agriculture is based on traditional knowledge and culture.
    • Its farming methods evolve to match local environments, responding to unique biophysical and socioeconomics constraints and opportunities.
    • By using local resources, local knowledge, connecting farmers, consumers and their markets.
    • Economic conditions and rural development are improved.
  • Organic agriculture stresses diversification and adaptive management to increase farm productivity, decrease vulnerability to weather vagaries, and consequently improves food security, either with the food the farmers produce or the income from the products they sell.

2.3 Economic sustainability

  • Organic farming appears to generate 30 percent more employment in rural areas and labour achieves higher returns per unit of labour input.
    • By using local resources better, organic agriculture facilitates smallholders’ access to markets and thus income generation; and re-localizes food production in market-marginalized areas.
  • Generally, organic yields are 20 percent less as compared to high-input systems in developed countries but could be up to 180 percent higher as compared to low‑input systems in arid/semi-arid areas.
    • In humid areas, rice paddy yields are equal, while the productivity of the main crop is reduced for perennials, though agroforestry provides additional goods.
  • Operating costs (seeds, rent, repairs and labour) in organic agriculture are significantly lower than conventional production, ranging from 50 to 60 percent for cereals and legumes, to 20 to 25 percent for dairy cows and 10 to 20 percent for horticulture products.
    • This is due to lower input costs on synthetic inputs, lower irrigation costs, and labour cash costs that include both family labour and hired workers.
    • Total costs are, however, only slightly lower than conventional, as fixed costs (such as land, buildings and machinery) increase due to new investments during conversion (e.g., new orchards, animal houses) and certification.

2.4 Market opportunities

  • The demand for organic products creates new export opportunities.
    • Organic exports are sold at impressive premiums, often at prices 20 percent higher than the same products produced on non-organic farms.
    • Under the right circumstances, the market returns from organic agriculture can potentially contribute to local food security by increasing family incomes.
  • Entering this lucrative market is not easy.
    • Farmers require hiring an organic certification organization to annually inspect and confirm that their farms and businesses adhere to the organic standards established by various trading partners.
    • During the conversion period to organic management, which lasts two to three years, farmers cannot sell their produce as “organic” and thus, tap price premiums.
      • This is because consumers expect organic produce to be free of residues. However, according to the Codex Guidelines on Organically Produced Food (2007), products produced on land under organic management for at least one year, but less than the two-three year requirement could be sold as “transition to organic”; but very few markets have developed for such products.
  • While most developing country producers have historically targeted international export markets in the European Union and North America, domestic market opportunities for organic food are emerging worldwide. Acknowledging the role of domestic organic markets in supporting a vibrant organic sector, alternative systems to certification have emerged worldwide.
  • In developed countries, consumers and organic producers have built direct channels for home delivery of non-certified organic produce (e.g. Community Supported Agriculture).
    • In the United States of America (USA), farmers marketing small quantities of organic products are formally exempt from certification.
    • Increasingly in developing countries, Participatory Guarantee Systems (PGS) are recognized as substitutes to third party certification (e.g. India, Brazil, Pacific islands).
Figure 4. Definition of some farming systems

©FAO/TECA

  • More recently, organic agriculture has become an option to improve household food security or to achieve a reduction of input costs. With the economic crisis, this phenomenon is seen also in developed countries.
    • Produce is used by farmers for their own consumption or it is sold on the market without a price distinction as it is not certified. Economic objectives are not the only motivation of organic farmers.
    • The goals are often to optimize land, animal and plant interactions, preserve natural nutrient and energy flows and enhance biodiversity while safeguarding the human health of family farmers and contributing to the overall objective of sustainable agriculture.

_annotations.body:
Introduction to organic agriculture

Organic agriculture is an integrated production management system that promotes and enhances agroecosystem health, including biodiversity, biological cycles and soil biological activity. It emphasizes the use of natural inputs (i.e. mineral and products derived from plants) and the renunciation of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides.

Description

Organic agriculture follows the principles and logic of a living organism, in which all elements (soil, plant, farm animals, insects, the farmer, local conditions) are closely linked to each other. This is accomplished by using, where possible, agronomic, biological and mechanical methods, following the principles of these interactions, using the natural ecosystem as a model.

Organic agriculture shares many techniques used by other sustainable agricultural approaches (e.g. intercropping, crop rotation, mulching, integration of crops and livestock). However, the use of natural inputs (non-synthetic), the improvement of soil structure and fertility and the use of a crop rotation plan represent the basic rules that make organic agriculture a unique agricultural management system.

According to the Guidelines of Organically Food Produce of the Codex Alimentarius (2007), an organic production system is designed to:

  • enhance biological diversity within the whole system; 
  • increase soil biological activity; 
  • maintain long-term soil fertility; 
  • recycle wastes of plant and animal origin in order to return nutrients to the soil, thus minimizing the use of non-renewable resources; 
  • rely on renewable resources in locally organized agricultural systems; 
  • promote the healthy use of soil, water and air as well as minimize all forms of pollution that may result from agricultural practices; 
  • promote the careful processing methods agricultural products in order to maintain the organic integrity and vital qualities of the product at all stages; and 
  • become established on any existing farm through a period of conversion, the appropriate length of which is determined by site-specific factors such as the history of the land, and type of crops and livestock to be produced.

In addition, the International Federation of Organic Agriculture Movements (IFOAM), a non-governmental organization internationally networking and promoting organic agriculture, has established guidelines that have been widely adopted by the organic community for organic production and processing.

Figure 1. Using the natural ecosystem as a model

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Overview of organic production in 2003

©FAO/TECA

1. Principles of  organic agriculture practices, according to IFOAM (2002)

According to IFOAM (2002), organic agriculture practices are based on certain principles.

1.1 Principle of health

  • The role of organic agriculture, whether in farming, processing, distribution, or consumption, is to sustain and enhance the health of ecosystems and organisms from the smallest in the soil to human beings.
  • In view of this, it should avoid the use of fertilizers, pesticides, animal drugs and food additives that may have adverse health effects.

1.2 Principle of ecology

  • Organic agriculture should be based on living ecological systems and cycles, work with them, emulate them and help sustaining them. Organic management must be adapted to local conditions, ecology, culture and scale.
  • The reduction of inputs by reuse, recycle and the efficient management of materials and energy will contribute to improve environmental quality and will conserve resources.

1.3 Principle of fairness

  • This principle emphasizes that those involved in organic agriculture should conduct human relationships in a manner that ensures fairness at all levels and to all parties‑farmers, workers, processors, distributors, traders and consumers.
  • It also insists that animals should be provided with the conditions and opportunities of life according to their physiology, natural behaviour and well-being.
  • Natural and environmental resources that are used for production and consumption should be managed in a socially and ecologically fair way and should be held in trust for future generations.
  • Fairness requires systems of production, distribution and trade that are open and equitable and account for real environmental and social costs.

1.4 Principle of care

  • This principle states that precaution and responsibility are the key concerns in management, development and technology choices in organic agriculture.
  • Science is necessary to ensure that organic agriculture is healthy, safe and ecologically sound.
  • However, it must consider valid solutions from practical experiences, accumulated traditional and indigenous knowledge and prevent significant risks by adopting appropriate technologies and rejecting unpredictable ones, such as genetic engineering.

2. Why organic agriculture?

The goal of organic agriculture is to contribute to the enhancement of sustainability. But what does sustainability mean?

  • In the context of agriculture, sustainability refers to the successful management of agricultural resources to satisfy human needs while at the same time maintaining or enhancing the quality of the environment and conserving natural resources for future generations.
  • Sustainability in organic farming must, therefore, be seen in a holistic sense, which includes ecological, economic and social aspects.
  • Only if the three dimensions are fulfilled an agricultural system can be called sustainable. But how are they achieved? Some examples are described in the following sections.
Figure 3. The three dimensions of sustainability

©FAO/TECA

2.1 Ecological sustainability

Organic agriculture techniques are known to be ecologically sustainable: 

  • Improving soil structure and fertility through the use of crop rotations, organic manure, mulches and the use of fodder legumes for adding nitrogen to the soil fertility cycle. 
  • Prevention of soil erosion and compaction by protecting the soil planting mixed and relay crops. 
  • Promotion of biological diversity through the use of natural pest controls (e.g. biological control, plants with pest control properties) rather than synthetic pesticides which, when misused, are known to kill beneficial organisms (e.g. natural parasites of pests, bees, earthworms), cause pest resistance, and often pollute water and land. 
  • Performing crop rotations, which encourage a diversity of food crops, fodder and under-utilized plants. This, in addition to improving overall farm production and fertility, may assist the on-farm conservation of plant genetic resources. 
  • Recycling the nutrients by using crop residues (straws, stovers and other nonedible parts) either directly as compost and mulch or through livestock as farmyard manure. 
  • Using renewable energies, by the integration of livestock, tree crops and on farm forestry into the system. This adds income through organic meat, eggs and dairy products, as well as draught animal power. Tree crops and on-farm forestry integrated into the system provide food, income, fuel and wood.

2.2 Social sustainability

  • Sustainability is also about equity among and between generations.
    • Organic agriculture contributes to social well‑being by reducing the losses of arable soil, water contamination, biodiversity erosion, GHG emissions, food losses, and pesticide poisoning. 
  • Organic agriculture is based on traditional knowledge and culture.
    • Its farming methods evolve to match local environments, responding to unique biophysical and socioeconomics constraints and opportunities.
    • By using local resources, local knowledge, connecting farmers, consumers and their markets.
    • Economic conditions and rural development are improved.
  • Organic agriculture stresses diversification and adaptive management to increase farm productivity, decrease vulnerability to weather vagaries, and consequently improves food security, either with the food the farmers produce or the income from the products they sell.

2.3 Economic sustainability

  • Organic farming appears to generate 30 percent more employment in rural areas and labour achieves higher returns per unit of labour input.

  • Operating costs (seeds, rent, repairs and labour) in organic agriculture are significantly lower than conventional production, ranging from 50 to 60 percent for cereals and legumes, to 20 to 25 percent for dairy cows and 10 to 20 percent for horticulture products.
    • This is due to lower input costs on synthetic inputs, lower irrigation costs, and labour cash costs that include both family labour and hired workers.
    • Total costs are, however, only slightly lower than conventional, as fixed costs (such as land, buildings and machinery) increase due to new investments during conversion (e.g., new orchards, animal houses) and certification.

    • Organic exports are sold at impressive premiums, often at prices 20 percent higher than the same products produced on non-organic farms.
    • Under the right circumstances, the market returns from organic agriculture can potentially contribute to local food security by increasing family incomes.

  • While most developing country producers have historically targeted international export markets in the European Union and North America, domestic market opportunities for organic food are emerging worldwide. Acknowledging the role of domestic organic markets in supporting a vibrant organic sector, alternative systems to certification have emerged worldwide.
  • In developed countries, consumers and organic producers have built direct channels for home delivery of non-certified organic produce (e.g. Community Supported Agriculture).
    • In the United States of America (USA), farmers marketing small quantities of organic products are formally exempt from certification.
    • Increasingly in developing countries, Participatory Guarantee Systems (PGS) are recognized as substitutes to third party certification (e.g. India, Brazil, Pacific islands).

records.title: La gestion des ravageurs et des maladies en agriculture biologique
records.description:
La description

1. Introduction

1.1 Les conditions favorable à la bonne santé d’une plante

  • Une plante en bonne santé est moins vulnérable aux ravageurs et à l’infestation de la maladie.
  • À partir de ce principe, l’un des objectifs majeurs de l’agriculteur biologique est de créer et de maintenir les conditions favorables à la bonne santé des cultures (Figure 1).

1.2 Les principes de la gestion des ravageurs et des maladies en agriculture biologique

  • L’interaction entre les organismes vivants et leur environnement est très importante pour la santé de la plante.
    • La diversification des espèces, des milieux, des habitats, etc., présentes sur une exploitation permet une interaction équilibrée entre les cultures et les ravageurs/maladies.
    • On comprend alors que la santé des plantes est gravement mise en danger dans les systèmes agricoles qui ne produisent qu’une seule et même culture.
    • Un écosystème bien géré, qui fait intervenir les bonnes espèces au bon moment, peut être un moyen efficace de réduire le niveau de ravageurs ou de maladies.
      • Par exemple, certaines variétés de cultures possèdent des mécanismes de défense plus efficaces que d’autres en raison de leur nature adaptative à l’environnement et elles ont donc un risque d’affectation plus faible.
Figure 1. Les facteurs qui influencent la santé d’une plante

©FAO/TECA

  • L’état de santé d’une plante dépend en grande partie de la fertilité du sol.
    • Lorsque le pH et les teneurs en élément nutritifs sont bien équilibrés et correspondent aux exigences de la plante, cette dernière devient plus vigoureuse, peut pleinement se développer et elle est donc moins vulnérable aux parasites.
  • De bonnes conditions climatiques, telles que des températures appropriées et la disponibilité en eau, jouent également un rôle important pour la santé des cultures.
  • Si l'une de ces conditions n’est pas remplie, la plante peut alors entrer en état de stress.
    • Le stress affaiblit les mécanismes de défense des plantes qui deviennent ensuite des cibles faciles pour les ravageurs et les maladies.
    • Un des points les plus importants pour un agriculteur biologique, est donc de cultiver des plantes saines et de diversifier les espèces.
    • Cela évite de nombreux problèmes d’infestation des cultures et des récoltes (Figure 2).
Figure 2. Les bases de la gestion des ravageurs et des maladies en agriculture biologique

©FAO/TECA

2. Les pratiques de prévention et de surveillance

2.1 Les pratiques de prévention

  • Les connaissances sur la santé des plantes et sur l’écologie des ravageurs et des maladies aident l’agriculteur à choisir des mesures efficaces de prévention et de protection des cultures.
  • Étant donné que de nombreux facteurs influencent le développement des parasites et des maladies, il est essentiel d’intervenir sur les paramètres les plus sensibles.
  • Une bonne stratégie de prévention s’appuie sur le choix de la période d’intervention, sur la combinaison appropriée de différentes méthodes ou le choix d’une seule et efficace méthode.
  • Les points suivants décrivent les mesures de protection préventives les plus efficaces.

2.1.1 La sélection d’espèces et de variétés adaptées et résistantes

  • Choisir les variétés qui sont adaptées aux conditions environnementales locales (températures, disponibilité en éléments nutritifs, précipitations, résistances, etc.), car cela assure un bon développement des cultures qui sont alors en bonne santé et luttent mieux contre les infections de parasites et de maladies.

2.1.2 La sélection de semences et de plants sains ainsi que d’outils de plantation propres

  • Utiliser des semences et des plants sains, qui ont été certifiés sans pathogènes et sans contamination par des mauvaises herbes lors de leur production et de leur transport.
  • Utiliser des outils de plantation propres, provenant d’une source sûre.

2.1.3 Planifier une rotation des cultures cohérente et appropriée (voir 6. La gestion et la planification des cultures en agriculture biologique) 

  • Système de cultures associées.
    • Cela peut limiter la pression des ravageurs et des maladies étant donné qu’il y a moins de plantes hôtes et qu’il y a plus d’espèces bénéfiques (ennemies des ravageurs et des maladies). 
  • Rotation des cultures.
    • Cela réduit les risques de maladies transmises par la terre et améliore la fertilité des sols. 
  • Engrais verts et cultures de couverture.
    • Ces pratiques augmentent l’activité biologique dans le sol et encouragent la présence d’organismes bénéfiques.
    • Par contre elles augmentent également la présence des ravageurs, donc une sélection rigoureuse des espèces appropriées est nécessaire.

2.1.4 La gestion équilibrée des nutriments

  • Fertilisation modérée.
    • Une croissance continue et progressive rend la plante moins vulnérable aux organismes nuisibles.
    • Une fertilisation trop abondante peut accroître fortement la teneur en sel du sol et endommager les racines des cultures, ce qui offre de nouvelles voies d’infection. 
  • Veiller à une teneur équilibrée en potassium dans les sols contribue à la prévention des infections bactériennes et mycorhiziennes (par les champignons).

2.1.5 L’apport de matière organique 

  • La matière organique augmente la densité et l’activité des micro-organismes dans le sol, et réduit ainsi la densité des populations de champignons pathogènes présents dans les sols.
    • Elle permet de stabiliser la structure du sol et d’améliorer l’aération et l’infiltration de l’eau. 
    • Elle apporte des nutriments qui permettent de renforcer les mécanismes de défense de la plante.

2.1.6 La pratique des méthodes adaptées de préparation des sols

  • Faciliter la décomposition des plantes infectées.
  • Contrôler les mauvaises herbes qui sont souvent des hôtes propices au développement des espèces nuisibles.
  • Protéger les micro-organismes qui permettent de réguler les populations de maladies présentes dans le sol.

2.1.7 La pratique d’une bonne gestion de l’eau 

  • Éviter l’engorgement.
    • Cela provoque un stress pour la plante, ce qui favorise les infections pathogènes. 
  • Éviter d’asperger d’eau les feuilles.
    • Cela facilite la colonisation des plantes par les maladies et surtout par les champignons présents dans l’eau.

2.1.8 Protéger et stimuler les ennemis naturels 

  • Créer et maintenir un habitat approprié pour le développement et la reproduction des agents de lutte biologique (c’est-à-dire les ennemis naturels des espèces nuisibles). 
  • Éviter d’utiliser des substances qui détruisent les ennemis naturels.

2.1.9 La sélection des périodes et des densités de plantation idéales 

  • La plupart des ravageurs ou des maladies attaquent la plante seulement pendant un certain stade de son développement.
    • Par conséquent, il est crucial que cette étape vulnérable de la vie des cultures ne corresponde pas avec la période de forte densité de l’espèce nuisible et donc que le moment de plantation soit adéquatement choisi. 
  • Planter/semer les plants à une distance raisonnable les uns des autres permet de diminuer les possibilités de propagation des ravageurs et des maladies au sein de la parcelle. 
  • Une bonne aération des cultures (surtout au niveau des feuilles) permet à la plante de sécher ses feuilles plus rapidement.
    • Cela fait obstacle au développement des espèces pathogènes.

2.1.10 La pratique des bonnes mesures d’hygiène 

  • Enlever systématiquement les parties infectées de la plantes (feuilles, fruits, branches, etc.) et ne pas les laisser au sol.
    • Cela diminue les possibilités de propagation des maladies.
  • Éliminer les résidus des plantes infectées après la récolte.

2.2 Les pratiques de surveillance

  • Le suivi régulier des quantités de ravageurs, de maladies et de mauvaises herbes constitue la base d’une gestion efficace des cultures.
    • Pour être en mesure de contrôler ces espèces nuisibles, il faut tout d’abord obtenir des informations sur les espèces qui sont spécifiques à la région, au climat et aux cultures de l’exploitation et connaître les dégâts qu’elles peuvent causer.

2.2.1 Les signes typiques de l’attaque des cultures par les ravageurs

  • La plupart des ravageurs des cultures sont des insectes, des acariens et des nématodes.
    • Cependant, en Afrique, les mammifères (par exemple les éléphants, les singes ou les campagnols) et les oiseaux (par exemple les moineaux, les étourneaux ou les corneilles) peuvent également endommager les cultures.
    • Les dégâts causés par les insectes peuvent être catégorisés selon le type de blessure sur les plantes y compris les cultures mordues et/ou mâchées (par exemple chenilles, charançons), les percées et sucées (par exemple pucerons, psylles) ou forées (par exemple pyrales, mineuses des feuilles).
    • Certains insectes sont lents (par exemple chenilles), rapides (par exemple mouches des fruits), cachés (par exemple pyrales, sésamies), ou faciles à observer (par exemple chenilles, charançons).
  • Les dégâts causés par les ravageurs sont souvent spécifiques à une (ou plusieurs) espèce(s) d’insecte caractéristiques.
    • Les feuilles perforées par des trous ou en partie dévorées sont le signe de la présence de chenilles ou de charançons.
    • Les feuilles enroulées indiquent l’attaque de pucerons.
    • Les fruits endommagés ou pourris sont souvent infestés par des larves de mouches des fruits.
    • Le flétrissement des plantes peut être dû aux larves de noctuidés ou de foreurs de tige.
    • Les branches ou les troncs perforés de galeries indiquent la présence d’insectes lignivores (qui mangent la  lignine, c’est-à-dire le bois). 
  • Les acariens sont très petits et ne peuvent pas être vus à l’œil nu.
    • Cependant, certaines espèces d’acariens (telles les tétranyques ou araignées rouges) tissent sur les plantes infestées un tissu typique et peuvent, par conséquent, être facilement détectés.
    • Souvent, si les acariens sont présents sur les plantes, les feuilles et les fruits deviennent jaunâtres. 
  • Les nématodes (ou vers ronds) sont aussi très petits et difficilement observables à l’œil nu.
    • Ces minuscules vers attaquent principalement les racines des plantes qui deviennent alors jaunes, se flétrissent et meurent.

2.2.2 Les signes typiques de l’attaque des cultures par les maladies

La majorité des maladies des cultures sont causes par des champignons, des bactéries ou des virus.

  • Les champignons provoquent la grande majorité (environ deux tiers) des infections végétales.
    • Les pathologies telles que les rouilles, les caries, le brun des aiguilles, les cloques (enroulement des feuilles), les moisissures, la fumagine et l’anthracnose sont des maladies fongiques (c’est-à-dire causées par des champignons).
    • Ils sont aussi à l’origine de la plupart des taches observées sur les feuilles, sur les fruits, et sur les fleurs, et sont responsables des chancres, des fusarioses, des flétrissements, du mildiou, des gales, etc., et du pourrissement prématuré des racines, des tiges, des fruits et des fleurs.
    • Dans le meilleur des cas, seule une partie de la culture est touchée, mais parfois la totalité de la parcelle est à éliminer.
  • Les bactéries sont à l’origine de quatre problèmes.
  1. Certaines bactéries produisent des enzymes qui détruisent toutes les parois cellulaires des plantes.
    • Les parties détruites pourrissent et la plantes finit souvent par mourir.
  2. Certaines bactéries produisent des toxines qui endommagent les tissus végétaux, entraînant la mort précoce de la plante.
  3. D’autres produisent de grandes quantités de sucres très gluants et peu fluides.
    • En circulant à travers les tissus de la plante, ces sucres bloquent les vaisseaux étroits et empêchent l’eau de pénétrer dans les racines et d’atteindre les feuilles, provoquant la mort rapide de la plante par déshydratation.
  4. D’autres bactéries produisent des protéines qui imitent les hormones végétales.
    • Le déséquilibre hormonal provoque une prolifération anarchique des tissus végétaux et conduit à la formation de tumeurs cancéreuses.
  • Les virus provoquent souvent des maladies systémiques (qui touchent l’ensemble de la plante).
    • Généralement, leur présence peut être observée par le changement de couleur des feuilles et/ou des parties vertes (par exemple décoloration, chlorose).
    • Sur les feuilles infectées, on observe la formation de taches vert clair ou jaune de différentes nuances, et de formes et tailles variées.
    • Ces taches forment des motifs en mosaïque caractéristiques, qui sont signe de réduction de la croissance et de la vigueur de la plante.

2.2.3 La surveillance en temps réel

  • Une surveillance attentive et continue des niveaux de ravageurs et de maladies, notamment pendant les périodes critiques de croissance d’une culture, est la clé de réussite de la gestion sanitaire des cultures.
    • Le suivi de l’état de santé des cultures s’appuie sur l’inspection régulière et méthodique par l’agriculteur de ses parcelles cultivées (Figure 3).
    • Grâce à ses connaissances, ses expériences et ses observations, l’agriculteur doit être en mesure d’établir à tout instant un diagnostic de ses cultures (i.e. y-a-t-il présence d’espèces nuisibles dans les cultures? Lesquelles? etc.) et d’intervenir avant que les cultures ne soient endommagées par les ravageurs ou les maladies.
  • La surveillance en temps réel permet d’éviter l’utilisation inutile de pesticides naturels (par exemple extraits de plante).
    • L’utilisation de ces substances naturelles (par exemple pyrèthre, derris, tabac) n’est pas réglementée, mais limiter leur usage permet également d’éviter l’éloignement des espèces bénéfiques (prédateurs et parasites des ravageurs).
    • L’utilisation trop fréquente de ces produits peut conduire au développement de résistances chez les ravageurs ou les maladies, qui ne sont alors plus sensibles aux pesticides naturels.
    • Par conséquent, la surveillance doit être planifiée et réalisée selon un parcours prédéfini, le même pour toute les parcelles.
    • Il est important d’obtenir des échantillons relevés aléatoirement, qui seront représentatifs de la situation générale d’une parcelle.
    • Par conséquent, l’agriculteur doit parcourir ses parcelles fréquemment et enregistrer (de préférence dans un carnet de suivi des cultures) toutes les observations qu’il aura faites, afin de pouvoir au final prendre les bonnes décisions.

2.2.4 Contrôler les populations de ravageurs

  • Pour constater et contrôler les populations d’insectes ravageurs, de différents pièges peuvent également être utilisés (Figures 4 et 5).
    • Ce type de piège permet d’évaluer rapidement la densité d’individus nuisibles sur les parcelles, notamment pour les espèces très mobiles et rapides (par exemple mouches des fruits, lépidoptères, etc.).
  • Les mouches des fruits peuvent être capturées à l’aide de pièges alimentaires (aussi appelés pièges à appâts).
    • Des pièges simples peuvent être élaborés.
      • Par exemple il est possible de percer des trous dans la partie supérieure d’une bouteille en plastique et de la remplir à moitié d’un mélange d’eau, d’urine de bétail, de morceaux de fruits ou de petits poissons morts et de quelques gouttes de détergent ou d’eau savonnée.
      • La bouteille est ensuite accrochée dans un arbre et vérifiée tous les trois jours par l’agriculteur.
  • Les cartons adhésifs jaunes sont efficaces pour surveiller les populations de pucerons et de cicadelles qui viennent s’y coller.
    • Les cartons jaunes-orange sont plutôt appropriés pour les mouches blanches (ou aleurodes), tandis que les  bleus attirent les thrips (thysanoptères).
  • Les pièges lumineux sont particulièrement contre les noctuidés, c’est-à-dire les insectes qui sont attirés par la lumière (par exemple mites, vers gris, chenilles défoliantes, ver de la capsule du cotonnier, etc.).
    • Pour les cultures susceptibles d’être attaquées par les vers gris, des contrôles visuels de présence des chenilles sont à faire à l’aube.
