records.title: Drought-resistant aquaculture fish species
records.description:
Description

Resistant aquaculture species were introduced in small farms in Lao PDR as part of the project Consolidating capacities for DRR in Agriculture in South East Asia.

1. Step by step description

1.1 Step one: releasing and stocking of fingerlings

  • Common carp and silver barb should be combined in the same pond, as each species eats different feeds.
  • They should be stocked at a ratio of one to two fingerlings per square meter of the pond.
    • Exceeding this ratio would slow down the growth rate of fish and require regular supplemental feeds.
  • Fingerlings should be released when the temperature is not too high, i.e. either in the early morning or late evening.
  • Before releasing fingerlings, leave the fingerling plastic bags on the surface of the fishpond around 5 to 10 minutes, in order to allow fingerlings to adjust to the temperature of the fishpond.
    • When opening the bags, let the fingerlings gradually flow out by themselves.

1.2 Step two: feeding 

  • Fishponds should be fenced with bamboo.
  • After that, put grass or straw and animal compost into the pond at a ratio of about 0.5 kg to 1.5 kg per 10 m2 of pond per day.
  • One week later, throw a mix of fertilizers and water in the fishpond at a ratio of about 1.7 g per square meter of pond per day.
    • Do not exceed this quantity, and dissolve the fertilizer tablets in a bucket before adding to the pond.
  • Throw animal composts and fertilizers into the fishpond every day until the colour of water in the fishpond becomes light greenish (similar to the colour of green tea).
  • Throwing supplemental feeds every morning and evening will accelerate fish growth.
    • Supplemental feeds could be leaves from cassava, sweet potatoes, water glory, grasses, termites, earthworms, snails, rice bran, broken rice and others that can be locally found within communities.
    • Supplemental feeds should be thrown in a specific area of the fishpond at a fixed time.
      • Before throwing supplemental feed, make noise by hitting two pieces of woods, so that the fish will gather in the same location.

1.3 Step three: maintenance 

  • Monitor the dikes and drainage, and remove the grass surrounding the fishpond in order to avoid the presence of snakes, which are the main predator of fish.
  • Control water quality by putting your hand in the fishpond to the depth of half arm.
    • If your palm lines are clearly visible, it means that feed content is inadequate and additional compost and fertilizers are needed.
    • If the colour of the water is too dark, it means that the water lacks oxygen and the pond needs additional water.
  • If less fish comes during feeding or too many fish appear on the water surface for breathing in the morning or when it is cloudy, it means that the water lacks oxygen, and the pond needs additional water.
  • Farmers should keep records on fish raising such as expenses, incomes from selling, weight, amount of fish consumed in the household, problems encountered, etc.

2. Major costs and resources involved 

  • Pond construction: about kip 90 000 per m2 (including labour). 
  • Labour: one person for about two hours per day for feeding and maintenance of the pond.
  • Common carp fingerlings: between kip 200 and 700 per kg. 
  • Common carp fish market price: between kip 25 000 and 35 000 per kg. 
  • Rice bran (feed): between kip 1 500 and 2 000 per kg.
  • The costs mentioned in this technology refer to the time of writing.

3. Benefits

  • In large well-fed ponds, common carp grows faster and therefore brings additional food and income to fish farmers.
  • It also has a lower mortality rate under stress conditions, especially during dry spells, as it can survive in shallow waters.

3.1 Cost-benefit analysis of the practice

  • The performance of drought-resistant species was monitored in aquaculture farms during the 2015 wet season and the 2016 dry season.
    • All monitored farms are located in Savannakhet Province.
    • During the wet season, all farms experienced dry spell conditions due to delayed rainy season.
    • On the other hand, no hazards affected the farms during the dry season.
  • The net benefits obtained from drought-resistant species such as common carp were measured through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA) and compared to the net benefits of tilapia and mrigal farming.
    • The CBA projects the cumulative net present value of benefits obtained from 1 m2 of pond over a period of 11 years (10 percent discount rate), as well as the benefit-cost ratio (BCR), which is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
  • Figure 1 and Figure 2 provide an overview of the outcomes of the CBA in the wet and dry season, respectively. In particular, they show that:
    • in farms affected by a dry spell (delay in 2015 wet season), the net benefit from drought-resistant species is 46 percent higher than that of fish species such as tilapia and mrigal (Figure 1); 
    • in farms not affected by hazards (2016 dry season), the net benefit from drought-resistant species is still 25 percent higher than that of fish species such as tilapia and mrigal (Figure 2); and
    • the BCR of the good practice is higher than the BCR of the local practice in both seasons and under both hazard and non-hazard conditions.
  • The observed absolute increase in net benefits in the dry season, as compared to the wet season, could be mainly due to the delay in the rainy season, which caused the drying up of ponds and consequent fish losses.
  • The newly introduced fish species have proved to be more resistant to dry spell, yet overall fish production suffered from such climate extreme.
  • Another factor contributing to the increase in absolute net benefits in the 2016 dry season might be the improved capacity of fish farmers in applying this good practice.
Figure 1. Cumulative Net Benefits and Benefit-Cost Ratios of Good Practice and Local Practice in farms affected by dry spell (USD per m2 of pond per year) – 2015 Wet Season

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Cumulative Net Benefits and Benefit-Cost Ratios of Good Practice and Local Practice in farms not affected by hazards (USD per m2 of pond per year) – 2016 Dry Season

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Added benefits

  • Under non-hazard conditions in the dry season, drought-resistant species yield 25 percent more benefits than the traditional fish species.
    • This makes the DRR good practice technology a “no-regret” measure.

3.3 Avoided losses

  • In fish farms affected by dry spell (delay in rainy season) during the wet season, fish production losses are reduced by 46 percent, corresponding to about USD 0.2 per m2 of pond yearly.

3.4 Co-benefits

  • Rapid fish growth implies lower input requirements for common carp aquaculture, making production more sustainable.

3.5 Climate change adaptation related benefits

  • Common carp fish species are more resistant to stresses, especially to dry spells.
    • These species are therefore adapted to face unreliable rains and rainfall variability induced by climate change.

3.6 General recommendation

  • For operating aquaculture in drought and flood-prone areas:
    • the selected location should be easily accessible to allow maintenance; and
    • dikes should be wide enough and well compacted.
  • Their level should be higher than the annual flooding level.
  • Upper dikes should be installed with a bamboo net or any type of nets to prevent destruction from flooding.
    • In case of floods, fingerlings should be fed in a nursery cage until the flooding has ended, and then released into the fishpond.
    • The cage used for nursery must be strong and floated at the same water level.

4. Validation of the practice

4.1 Geographical area of practice validation

  • The performance of resistant aquaculture species was monitored in aquaculture farms in Lao PDR. All monitored farms are located in the Savannakhet Province.

4.2 Context of implementation

  • Drought-resistant species were introduced in small aquaculture farms (average size of about 500 m2) in Lao PDR as part of the project Consolidating capacities for DRR in Agriculture in South East Asia.

4.2.1 Environmental and climatic (period/season) context

  • The good practice was monitored during the 2015 wet season and the 2016 dry season.
  • In the wet season, all farms experienced dry spell conditions due to delayed rainy season.
    • On the other hand, no hazards affected the farms during the 2016 dry season.

4.2.2 Social - target group

  • Smallholder aquaculture farmers.

4.2.3 Farmer’s perceptions 

  • Sustainability
    • All fish farmers interviewed said they would replicate the good practice in the coming years.
    • They found the good practice particularly effective in the face of hazards such as dry spells and delays in the rainy season. 
  • Socio-economic benefits.
    • During the dry season, almost all farmers found that drought-resistant species such as common carp grow up faster than other species (e.g. malican, tilapia).
    • Rapid fish growth led to higher income and reduced cost of inputs.

5. Constraints (limiting factors) for the implementation of the technology

  • Some fish farmers raised the need to get more training on aquaculture technologies and practices, especially on how to keep water longer in the pond.

6. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Tropics, warm.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Integration of aquaculture into the farming systems: ID 4590.
  • Management of self-recruiting species in aquaculture: ID 4581.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Resource use efficiency

This practice introduces the use of drought-resistant fish species such as common carp that have shown much higher yield in drought-affected seasons and normal seasons than the previously used fish such as tilapia. This shows that farmers can make use of the drought-resistant species to mitigate the negative effects of losing drought-related yields.

records.title: Straw mushroom (Volvariella volvacea) cultivation for livelihood diversification
records.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Straw mushrooms (Volvariella volvacea) are suitable to be planted in flood and drought risk areas.
    • In flooded areas, they should be grown in baskets that can be moved. In drought-prone areas, containers should be used. If growing in a growing house, a high location should be found, so that flooding does not affect it and there is no water flowing through the area. 
    • In order to save water during the growing phase, a basin should be available. Soaking rice straw to make the rice straw wet will save more water than sprinkling.
    • Materials for straw mushroom growing are rice straw, banana leaves or dry banana trees that have not been sprayed with pesticides or herbicides.
    • Straw mushrooms can be grown in both the rainy and dry seasons and can improve the living conditions of farmers affected by such risks.

1.1 Choosing a suitable location

Mushrooms can be grown indoors or outdoors. The procedure for growing the mushrooms is the same.

  1. As a first step, it is necessary to find a suitable place that is easy to access and to ensure that there is no impact from flooding and/or drought.
    • In areas affected by dry spells, the location should be near the water or near a pond.
    • The location should be easily accessible so that the mushrooms can be moved when there is a disaster.
    • A clean location should be selected that is free from chemicals and other substances.
  2. The arrangement of a location for straw mushroom growing depends on the growing method.
    • If growing indoors there should be shade, not much sunlight, no harm from animals, and the ability to maintain and water easily when needed.
    • In the dry season, a location near water sources should be found, or a water storage vessel should be made.
    • For growing straw mushrooms, per 100 kg of rice straw, materials in Table 1 are required.
Table 1: Materials

Source: FAO 2017

1.2 Collecting the mushroom spores

  • Collect mushroom spores that are ready to be planted, considering that the young and older spores should not be planted.
  • Mushroom spores are the seedlings that can be cultivated and grown in the dry season at high temperatures and low moisture.

1.3 Growing method and preparation of materials

  • Bring the amount of straw from rice or banana leaves or dry banana tree as needed.
  • After that, soak the rice straw in water for about 24 hours.
    • Instead of soaking for 20 hours, the straw can also be sprayed with water until the straw is completely wet, then stacked to be the plot as appropriate.

1.4 Preparation of the location to make the stack and plot for rice straw mushrooms: stack growing form (plot)

  • Bring the prepared rice straw to stack into plots with a width of 40 cm to 80 cm, and the length as needed.
    • The stacking in the first layer requires spreading the rice straw out to the outer edge of each side flatly.
  • When the rice straw is spread out higher than 10 cm, use the hands to push it down or trample upon it.
  • After stacking on the floor for 10 cm, take the dung and husks to spread on the top and spray water as in a vegetable bed, then take the thrush to spread thinly and spray water again.
  • After that, construct the second layer and then the third and fourth.
  • After finishing the fourth layer, cover with the rice straw and water it until it is completely wet.

  • Growing the mushrooms in troughs will make it easier to move them compared to the plot in case of a flood.
  • Make the mushroom grow in structure by taking wood to make a pattern, of which the width is 40 cm, the length 120 cm and the height 40 cm, to facilitate easy lifting.
  • After putting the prepared rice straw in the pattern higher about 10 cm, use the hands to push it down or trampling upon it.
  • After the stack on the floor is about 10 cm, take dung and husks to spread on the top and spray water to wet it, then take the thrush to spread thinly and spray water again.
  • After making stack number 4, apply the thrush and spray the water, adding more rice straw and spraying water again that completed the stack 1.
  • The second stack should be about 25 cm from the plot 1 for the gap of mushroom growing and to be able to harvest the mushrooms.
  • If the stacks are too far from each other, the areas will be wasted.

1.6 Growing the baskets

  • Growing the mushrooms in the baskets is an appropriate way in flood-prone areas because it will be easy to move if there is a disaster.
    • The baskets may be plastic baskets or wooden baskets that have plaiting similar to a net or coop to have gaps for the mushroom to grow through.
    • The baskets to plant should have a centerline of 60 cm to 80 cm and a height of 60 cm.

    • After tightly stacking for 10 cm, use dung and husk to spread thinly and then repeat for the third.

  • Basket 2 and basket 3 can stand near each other to facilitate the covering with the plastic sheets.
    • By doing this, they can be moved and watered as needed.

  • The thrush is the most important part that is used to evaluate if the mushroom will grow well or not, so it should be observed that the thrush growing in the bags has full fibers beforehand and avoid using the old thrush because it can have yellow or coffee-colored fibers.
  • Thus, farmers should observe and pay attention to this point.

  • After inoculation, the wet straw will start to decompose which causes heat production.
  • Three to four days after planting, it is important to check the humidity and temperature in the stacks or plots to see whether they have sufficient temperature and humidity.

    • If the nearby temperature is too hot, open the plastic cover for ventilation.
    • If the temperature is too low, moisture them and thoroughly close them.

    • Do not leave the small mushrooms because they might become palely dry.

  • Straw mushroom production was introduced in small-scale farms in Lao PDR as part of the projects “Consolidating Capacities for DRR in Agriculture in South East Asia” and “Institutionalizing Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) in Agriculture for Enhanced Resilience Programming and Integrated Implementation Across Sectors”.
  • Straw mushrooms can be grown at very low cost, using locally available material (e.g. rice straw, cow dung).
  • It requires little work effort and the first mushrooms can be harvested two weeks after preparing the straw beds.
  • It is a DRR good practice technology for small-scale farmers during the dry season when lack of water often prevents them to grow rice.
  • Indeed, straw mushroom production requires a little amount of water, thereby reducing vulnerability to dry conditions.
  • During the 2016 dry season, the performance of this DRR good practice technology was monitored in 42, 24 and 26 farms in the Khammouane, Champasak and Savannakhet provinces respectively.
  • None of the farms experienced hazard conditions during the monitoring period.
  • The results of the qualitative and quantitative analyses conducted based on field demonstration data are summarized hereafter.

2.1 Cumulative net returns over 11 years

  • The net benefits obtained from the good practice were valued through a cost-benefit analysis (CBA) based on quantitative data collected during the monitoring period in the 2016 dry season.
  • The CBA projects the cumulative net present value of benefits obtained from an average mushroom house in the analysed area (six straw beds) over a period of 11 years.
  • A 10 percent discount rate is applied to express the future value of costs and benefits in present terms.
  • The benefit-cost ratio (BCR) is the ratio between total discounted benefits and total discounted costs over the appraisal period.
  • Since straw mushroom cultivation was not previously practiced in the monitored farms, control plots were not available to conduct a comparative analysis.
  • As an alternative, the opportunity cost of agricultural labor was used, i.e. the income foregone by not employing the labor used for straw mushroom production elsewhere.
  • Results from the dry season show that net benefits from straw mushroom production under non-hazard conditions are about 98 percent higher than the opportunity cost of labor under non-hazard conditions.

Figure 1 and Figure 2 provide an overview of the outcome of the CBA. In particular, it shows that:

  • in the dry season and under non-hazard conditions (Figure 1), the net benefits of mushroom growing in an average mushroom house (6 straw beds) over 11 years are about two times higher than the opportunity cost of labour.
    • The BCR is 1.74.
  • Figure 2 shows the breakdown of costs and benefits accounted for in the analysis.
Figure 1. The cumulative net benefit of good practice (straw mushroom production) and the opportunity cost of labour in farms not affected by hazards – 2016 Dry Season

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Costs and benefits of mushroom production, as compared to the opportunity cost of labour (USD per year) - 2016 Dry Season

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Benefits and losses

2.2.1 Economic

  • Under the condition of the absence of natural disasters, the net yield of straw mushroom production doubles compared with the opportunity costs of other agricultural activities.
  • When the production is not affected by natural disasters, approaches to avoid losses cannot be measured nor analyzed.

2.2.2 Environmental

  • Growing straw mushroom needs less water compared with some other crops.
  • This approach improves the flexibility in the dry season and sustainable water management.

3. Validation of the practice

3.1 Geographical area of practice validation

  • In the dry season of the year 2015 to 2016, there were appropriate pilot activities in three target provinces:
    • 42 families in the Xebangfai district, Khammouane Province;
    • 24 families in the Xaybouly district, Savannakhet Province; and
    • 26 families in the Sanasomboun district, Champasak Province.
  • While following up and inspecting, the results of qualitative and quantitative analyses were conducted according to the data from the diagnostic site.

3.2 Additional benefits of growing mushrooms

3.2.1 Sustainability

  • 100 percent of the 92 farmers that tested straw mushroom growing are planning to continue the activity during the next dry seasons.
  • 72 percent say that straw mushrooms are “easy to grow”.

3.2.2 Socio-economic benefits

  • 80 percent of farmers found that mushroom cultivation required a low amount of inputs and less labor effort.

3.2.3 Environmental/natural resource management co-benefits

  • 60 percent of farmers affirmed that mushrooms can be grown using limited amounts of water.

3.2.4 Additional needs

  • 93 percent of farmers raised the need to receive more training on mushroom cultivation, as well as to visit other villages to exchange knowledge and practices.

3.3 Farmers reactions

  • All farmers interviewed declared that they would be willing to replicate this disaster risk reduction (DRR) good practice technology in the next seasons.
  • 72 percent of the farmers explicitly mentioned that straw mushrooms are “easy to grow”.
    • They reported that growing straw mushrooms is a good practice because of low investment needs (inputs and labor), and they are able to have a production and income during the dry season.
  • Furthermore, 79 percent of all farmers noted that mushrooms need less water than other crops, and about 80 percent appreciated the reduced labor efforts required.
  • Finally, about 60 percent of farmers stressed that mushrooms contributed to diversifying their diets.
  • None of the farmers highlighted any unintended effect of this DRR good practice technology.
    • However, some farmers raised the need to get additional training on how to effectively commercialize mushrooms.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies 

  • Indoor oyster mushroom cultivation for livelihood diversification and increased resilience: ID 8933.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

Straw mushrooms cultivation requires a limited amount of water compared to other crops, thereby enhancing resilience during the dry season and sustainable water resources management.

records.title: Small Hive Beetle (SHB)
records.description:
Description

1. Introduction

The SHB, Aethina tumida, is native to sub-Saharan Africa and is currently present in North America, Central America, the Caribbean, Brazil (South America), Australia, the Philippines (Asia) and Italy (Europe). Able to cause serious damage to the environment and the beekeeping economy, the SHB is considered an invasive alien species (IAS). Such species are animals and plants that are introduced accidentally or deliberately into a natural environment where they are not normally found, with serious negative consequences on their new environment. They represent a major threat to native plants and animals, causing extensive financial damage every year.

The SHB affects honeybee colonies and other pollinating insects of the Apoidea family, such as the bumblebee (genus: Bombus). The beetles are attracted by the smell of live bees and combs containing pollen and/or larvae. They enter beehives through the entrances or cracks in the hives. Once inside a hive, adult beetles spend the winter season feeding on pollen, honey and bee brood.

The SHB can adopt attack or defence behaviours when bees try to damage them. They assume the typical “turtle position” – retracting legs and head under their bodies. They can fool the bees through antennal contacts, which ask for food transfer by trophallaxis (a bee behaviour consisting of sharing collected nectar among worker bees through mouth-to-mouth transfer). This means that the bees will actually feed honey to the SHB. Bees can ignore the parasites, try to move them away from the hive, or try to confine them to small closed spaces in the nest with propolis (as a kind of prison).

Adult beetles (Figure 1) mate in the colony, and the females oviposit hundreds of eggs in clutches, preferably in capped brood cells, which they perforate to deposit their eggs. Alternatively, they deposit their eggs in cracks, interstices and small gaps in the hive where it is difficult for bees to access and remove the eggs. One single female may oviposit 1 000 to 2 000 eggs in her lifetime (four to six months). Many species of bees are able to identify and remove the more accessible beetle eggs from the hive. However, when eggs are laid in cracks in the hive where bees cannot reach, the bees cannot remove the eggs and the larvae can develop freely.

Figure 1. Small hive beetle (Aethina tumida) adult (dorsal and ventral view)

©IZSMe/Giovanni Federico

The SHB larvae emerge from the eggs after one to six days (most within three days), depending on the temperature and relative humidity conditions. They feed on the pollen, honey and bee brood they find in the hive. Larval development takes one to four weeks (usually about two weeks), depending on food availability and temperature. At the end of their development, when they are about 1 cm long, the mature larvae reach the “wandering phase” where they congregate at the bottom of the hive and leave the colony (usually through the hive entrance), dropping on the ground to pupate (Figure 2) in the soil surrounding the hive. Here, they penetrate into the soil down to 5 to 60 cm deep in order to begin the process of metamorphosis. Pupation in the ground may take 2 to 12 weeks (usually three to four weeks), depending on the temperature and the soil properties. Pupation is a stage characterized by high mortality because the SHB is very vulnerable in this phase. Soils that are too hard or too muddy greatly reduce the birth rate of adults. This is why the SHB prefers sandy soils for pupation.

Figure 2. Small hive beetle (Aethina tumida) pupa

©University of Florida/Lyle J. Buss

Emerging adults leave the soil and fly to search for new host colonies, thereby completing their life cycle.

External factors condition the damage done by the parasite to the beehive:

  • Environmental factors, especially temperature (development of any stage of SHB stops below 10 °C, and temperatures above 35 °C cause high mortality of all SHB life stages) and rainfall (the soil moisture should be above 5 percent for pupation of SHB).
  • Genetics and bee behaviour (the species and race of the bees) affect the number of beetle cycles. For African honeybee subspecies, SHB is not a serious threat because they can defend themselves very well from the parasite by adopting different behavioural strategies, such as more efficient fighting and trapping of the beetles. However, European bees do not show the same aggressiveness towards SHB.

2. Morphology of the small hive beetle

2.1 Morphology of the adult small hive beetle

Adult SHBs are flat, oval-shaped (0.5 to 0.7 cm long and 0.3 to 0.45 cm wide) beetles ranging in colour with increasing age. The colours range from yellow-reddish, to brown, dark brown and eventually to black when they reach sexual maturity. Their antennae are club-shaped, and their long legs enable them to move easily and rapidly inside the hives. The armour on their back and the characteristic “turtle position” (retracting head and legs under the body) they assume when attacked protect them from honeybee bites and stings. They are very good flyers, and can easily fly from one apiary to another.

2.2 Morphology of small hive beetle larvae

The larvae of the SHB are cream-coloured and about 11 mm long at the end of their development stage. The larvae can be recognized by four rows of dorsal spikes along their backs, three pairs of legs, and two rear spines (Figure 3). These are three characteristics that distinguish SHB larvae from larvae of the wax moth (Galleria mellonella) (Figure 4).

Figure 3. Small hive beetle (Aethina tumida) larva, dorsal view (bottom) and ventral view (top) view. A larva of the small hive beetle can be distinguished from that of the wax moth larvae by its four rows of dorsal spikes along the back, three pairs of legs and two rear spines

©IZSMe/Giovanni Federico

Figure 4. Wax moth (Galleria mellonella) larva on the bottom tray of the hive

©FAO/Daniele Olivotti

2.3 Morphology of small hive beetle eggs

The eggs of the SHB are white-pearly with a shape quite similar to those of bees but smaller (about two-thirds of the size) (Figure 5). They are 1.4 mm long and 0.26 mm wide.

Figure 5. The eggs of the small hive beetle are white-pearly with a shape similar to those of bees but smaller

©WUR/Bram Cornelissen

3. Symptoms

The larvae of the SHB are responsible for the greater damage inside the hive. They dig tunnels among the cells of the combs (Figure 6) to feed on pollen, honey and bee brood. They can also move up to the honey super when it is not well populated. By defecating, they increase the humidity of the honey, causing its fermentation. In the worse cases, this may destroy an entire hive or induce the colony to swarm. Typically, SHB infestation leads to the death of weak colonies already affected by other diseases (such as varroa). ©Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services/Jeffrey W. Lotz

©BNNS/Elsa Demoulin

5.1 On-site diagnosis

Adult SHBs have a dark colour and can move very quickly. They are not easily identified among the bees within the hive, particularly when the number of adult beetles in the hive is low. Moreover, SHBs avoid light, hide in crevices or cavities of the hives, or fly away from combs when the beekeeper opens the hive for inspection. When it is possible to collect the whole body of the parasite, the best way to identify SHB is through morphological identification. The specimens collected in or near honeybee hives should be killed before submission (for example, by freezing them or putting them in ethanol).

Recommendation Advantage or reason for practice

Recommendation Advantage or reason for practice

For areas where SHB is not present, it is important for beekeepers to have a good knowledge of the morphology of SHB eggs, larvae and adults, as well as hive inspection methods, and to periodically monitor the possible presence of SHB by sampling debris or honey.

  • Amoebiasis: a parasitic disease of adult honeybees: ID 10019.
  • Tropilaelaps: a parasitic diseaseof the brood: ID 10021.
  • Stonebrood (aspergillosis): a fungal disease of the brood and adult honeybees: ID 10031.
  • European foulbrood (EFB): a bacterial disease of the brood: ID 8418.

8.1 Resource use-efficiency

Small Hive Beetle (SHB)

The small hive beetle (SHB), or Aethina tumida, is an external parasite that affects honeybee colonies and other pollinating insects. It is a pest native to sub-Saharan and has spread into various regions of the world in the past few decades. The SHB can cause serious economic damage to the beekeeping sector because it can destroy entire colonies as well as stored unextracted honeycombs in the honey house.



Description

1. Introduction

The SHB, Aethina tumida, is native to sub-Saharan Africa and is currently present in North America, Central America, the Caribbean, Brazil (South America), Australia, the Philippines (Asia) and Italy (Europe). Able to cause serious damage to the environment and the beekeeping economy, the SHB is considered an invasive alien species (IAS). Such species are animals and plants that are introduced accidentally or deliberately into a natural environment where they are not normally found, with serious negative consequences on their new environment. They represent a major threat to native plants and animals, causing extensive financial damage every year.

The SHB affects honeybee colonies and other pollinating insects of the Apoidea family, such as the bumblebee (genus: Bombus). The beetles are attracted by the smell of live bees and combs containing pollen and/or larvae. They enter beehives through the entrances or cracks in the hives. Once inside a hive, adult beetles spend the winter season feeding on pollen, honey and bee brood.

The SHB can adopt attack or defence behaviours when bees try to damage them. They assume the typical “turtle position” – retracting legs and head under their bodies. They can fool the bees through antennal contacts, which ask for food transfer by trophallaxis (a bee behaviour consisting of sharing collected nectar among worker bees through mouth-to-mouth transfer). This means that the bees will actually feed honey to the SHB. Bees can ignore the parasites, try to move them away from the hive, or try to confine them to small closed spaces in the nest with propolis (as a kind of prison).

Adult beetles (Figure 1) mate in the colony, and the females oviposit hundreds of eggs in clutches, preferably in capped brood cells, which they perforate to deposit their eggs. Alternatively, they deposit their eggs in cracks, interstices and small gaps in the hive where it is difficult for bees to access and remove the eggs. One single female may oviposit 1 000 to 2 000 eggs in her lifetime (four to six months). Many species of bees are able to identify and remove the more accessible beetle eggs from the hive. However, when eggs are laid in cracks in the hive where bees cannot reach, the bees cannot remove the eggs and the larvae can develop freely.

Figure 1. Small hive beetle (Aethina tumida) adult (dorsal and ventral view)

©IZSMe/Giovanni Federico

The SHB larvae emerge from the eggs after one to six days (most within three days), depending on the temperature and relative humidity conditions. They feed on the pollen, honey and bee brood they find in the hive. Larval development takes one to four weeks (usually about two weeks), depending on food availability and temperature. At the end of their development, when they are about 1 cm long, the mature larvae reach the “wandering phase” where they congregate at the bottom of the hive and leave the colony (usually through the hive entrance), dropping on the ground to pupate (Figure 2) in the soil surrounding the hive. Here, they penetrate into the soil down to 5 to 60 cm deep in order to begin the process of metamorphosis. Pupation in the ground may take 2 to 12 weeks (usually three to four weeks), depending on the temperature and the soil properties. Pupation is a stage characterized by high mortality because the SHB is very vulnerable in this phase. Soils that are too hard or too muddy greatly reduce the birth rate of adults. This is why the SHB prefers sandy soils for pupation.

Figure 2. Small hive beetle (Aethina tumida) pupa

©University of Florida/Lyle J. Buss

Emerging adults leave the soil and fly to search for new host colonies, thereby completing their life cycle.

External factors condition the damage done by the parasite to the beehive:

  • Environmental factors, especially temperature (development of any stage of SHB stops below 10 °C, and temperatures above 35 °C cause high mortality of all SHB life stages) and rainfall (the soil moisture should be above 5 percent for pupation of SHB).
  • Genetics and bee behaviour (the species and race of the bees) affect the number of beetle cycles. For African honeybee subspecies, SHB is not a serious threat because they can defend themselves very well from the parasite by adopting different behavioural strategies, such as more efficient fighting and trapping of the beetles. However, European bees do not show the same aggressiveness towards SHB.

2. Morphology of the small hive beetle

2.1 Morphology of the adult small hive beetle

Adult SHBs are flat, oval-shaped (0.5 to 0.7 cm long and 0.3 to 0.45 cm wide) beetles ranging in colour with increasing age. The colours range from yellow-reddish, to brown, dark brown and eventually to black when they reach sexual maturity. Their antennae are club-shaped, and their long legs enable them to move easily and rapidly inside the hives. The armour on their back and the characteristic “turtle position” (retracting head and legs under the body) they assume when attacked protect them from honeybee bites and stings. They are very good flyers, and can easily fly from one apiary to another.

2.2 Morphology of small hive beetle larvae

The larvae of the SHB are cream-coloured and about 11 mm long at the end of their development stage. The larvae can be recognized by four rows of dorsal spikes along their backs, three pairs of legs, and two rear spines (Figure 3). These are three characteristics that distinguish SHB larvae from larvae of the wax moth (Galleria mellonella) (Figure 4).

Figure 3. Small hive beetle (Aethina tumida) larva, dorsal view (bottom) and ventral view (top) view. A larva of the small hive beetle can be distinguished from that of the wax moth larvae by its four rows of dorsal spikes along the back, three pairs of legs and two rear spines

Figure 4. Wax moth (Galleria mellonella) larva on the bottom tray of the hive

©FAO/Daniele Olivotti

records.title: Producción de pollos sin grano: el sistema integrado con aves de corral y compost
records.description:
Descripción

  • El sistema es un remolque modificado.
    • Los componentes son un gallinero móvil con cajas y perchas de anidación, un tabique móvil exterior, un bebedero automático, y un baño de polvo.
  • El gallinero es un remolque de utilidad convertido, aún sobre sus ruedas, y por lo tanto móvil.
  • El remolcador es rodeado con una valla simple y móvil para mantener a los pollos confinados.
  • Dentro de este confín hay cuatro pilas de compost.
  • Una nueva pila de compost se construye cada semana.
  • Cada semana, el remolque y las vallas móviles se mueven hacia adelante por cuatro metros, donde se construye una nueva pila de compost.
  • Cada semana, cada pila de compost se voltea una vez usando una horquilla o una pala.
    • Por lo tanto, cada pila se gira un total de cuatro veces en un período de cuatro semanas.
  • Durante los cambios las gallinas están activas buscando y alimentándose de los restos de comida y los insectos en la pila de compost.
  • El tiempo total de crear el compost es de 4-5 semanas. La figura 1 ofrece una visión general del sistema.
  • Esta dieta de las gallinas es diferente de la de los pollos en muchas granjas modernas que tienen una dieta que consiste en gran parte de granos, suplementos vitamínicos, minerales y suplementos.
    • Los pellets son también de uso frecuente y se hacen sintéticamente.
  • Muchos agricultores, especialmente en los países en desarrollo, no tienen acceso a comprar estos concentrados o cualquier alimento comercial para sus pollos y el costo puede ser prohibitivo, aún cuando se disponga de ellos.
  • En contraste, el método descrito aquí utiliza materiales que de otro modo se puede desechar como residuos.
  • El sistema avícola y compost integrado es un método de bajo costo y ambientalmente sostenible.
    • Los restos de comida, estiércol y mantillo se utilizan para la alimentación y todos se pueden obtener de la granja.
    • Como alternativa, si no hay suficientes restos de comida que son generados por la granja, se pueden comprar a bajo precio en los restaurantes o mercados.
Figura 1. Descripción general del sistema. Por la quinta semana (4 vueltas en total), el compost se puede utilizar de nuevo en la huerta

©FAO/TECA

  • El sistema avícola y compost integrado permite a las gallinas correr libremente dentro de la valla que rodea el remolque y las cuatro pilas de compost.
  • Por la noche, las gallinas vuelven al remolque gallinero y se bloquea para su protección contra los depredadores.
  • Lo que sigue es la descripción paso a paso sobre cómo construir este sistema a su granja.

1. El remolque

  • El primer paso es construir el remolque que alberga las gallinas y contiene los nidales.
  • Se puede usar cualquier remolque en desuso o que ya no es adecuado para el transporte.
  • Una trama se construye alrededor del remolque para formar las paredes de la unidad del gallinero, y un techo se construye sobre la parte superior. En el interior del remolque se construye un bastidor móvil adicional de perchas.
  • Este marco de percha se puede plegar hasta el techo para crear más espacio en el interior y facilitar su limpieza.
  • El suelo del remolque, debajo de las perchas, se cubre con mantillo como cama y para recoger el estiércol de pollo.
  • El mantillo es cualquier cubierta de hierba picada o material herbáceo que se puede encontrar; las coberturas comunes incluyen paja, hierbas maleza, viruta de madera y hojas secas.
  • Cada semana se cambia un nuevo mantillo dentro del tráiler, y el viejo se pone en las pilas de compost, como se describirá más adelante en este artículo.

1.1 Las perchas

  • Las perchas dan a las gallinas un lugar para descansar y dormir.
  • Las perchas deben dar los espacios adecuados, y deben estar separadas por el tramo de la mano de un hombre, desde el pulgar al meñique, a fin de que las gallinas se posen cómodamente.
  • Esto es por lo general alrededor de 20 cm x 20 cm a 25 cm x 25 cm por ave, pero puede variar dependiendo de la raza.
  • Dependiendo del tamaño del remolque, el número de perchas y la longitud de cada percha pueden variar.
Figura 2. La percha plegable puede ser empujada hacia arriba para hacer más espacio en el remolque y para facilitar su limpieza. El marco es de 6 perchas

©FAO/TECA

1.1.1 Las cajas de anidación

  • Los nidos son lugares donde las gallinas ponen sus huevos.
  • En este caso se construyen en ambos lados del remolque.
  • Esto le da a las gallinas la libertad de elegir en qué parte quieren poner sus huevos para su comodidad máxima.
  • La caja debe tener una tapa removible para que el agricultor pueda llegar a limpiar la caja y recoger los huevos.
  • La parte inferior del nido debe ser cubierta con paja, virutas de pino, o materiales similares para la comodidad de las gallinas y para mantener los huevos en su lugar.
  • El tamaño de los nidales debe ser sólo suficiente para una gallina, para evitar que las gallinas pasen por encima de otra y potencialmente rompan los huevos.
  • En general, un nido es un cubo con unas dimensiones de 30 cm × 30 cm × 30 cm.
  • Esto asegurará suficiente espacio para que una gallina ponga cómodamente sus huevos sin interrupción.
Figura 3. La vista del interior del remolque de la parte posterior

©FAO/TECA

1.1.2 Agua

  • Hay una amplia gama de sistemas de bebederos.
  • Aquí proponemos 2 maneras de construir su propio sistema automático de agua para las aves.
  • Uno de ellos es el llamado el bebedero de PVC (plástico) y el otro es el bebedero de frasco de cristal.
  • Ambos métodos funcionan bien para cualquier gallina, dependiendo de los recursos disponibles, uno puede ser más fácil de construir que el otro.
  • Bebedero de frasco de vidrio Suministros:
    • Frasco de vidrio tapa hermética (aproximadamente 15 a 25 cm de diámetro).
    • Recipiente de vidrio o plástico:
      • Diámetro del tazón debe ser de 10-15 cm más ancho que el diámetro del frasco para asegurar el espacio para las cabezas de las gallinas, 5 a 10 cm de altura.
    • Taladro eléctrico para hacer agujero en el frasco de vidrio.
Figura 4. Bebedero de frasco de vidrio

©FAO/TECA

  • El primer paso en la elaboración del bebedero de vidrio es fijar el frasco en el recipiente y hacer una marca en el frasco de vidrio a la altura de la parte superior del tazón.
  • Con una broca de 1⁄2 pulgada (13 mm), perforar cuidadosamente un agujero en el lado del frasco de vidrio por debajo de la altura marcada.
  • Al taladrar el agujero, asegúrese de usar mangas largas, gafas protectoras y ropa de protección cuando sea necesario ya que el vidrio en raras ocasiones puede romperse durante la perforación.
  • Una vez que se ha realizado con éxito el agujero, se debe enjuagar y limpiar el frasco para eliminar cualquier residuo de vidrio.
    • Esto asegurará de que los pollos no se verán perjudicados por los fragmentos de vidrio o bordes afilados.
  • Mientras se llena el frasco con agua, poner el dedo pulgar en el agujero para evitar que el agua fluya hacia fuera.
  • Ponga la tapa en el frasco y lleve el frasco de vidrio al tazón o plato.
  • Una vez que el frasco está dentro del recipiente y situado en la parte inferior, se puede soltar el dedo pulgar y el agua fluirá hasta que el agujero está cubierto.
  • Para limpiar o rellenar el recipiente, puede simplemente tomar el frasco directamente de la taza e inclinarlo hacia atrás con el orificio hacia arriba para evitar el derrame de agua.
    • Una vez hecha la limpieza, se realiza la recarga con agua.
    • Sólo hay que poner de nuevo en el recipiente y ya está listo para su reutilización.

2. Bebedero de PVC Suministros

  • balde de PVC con tapa;
  • base de macetas (tazón): 7 a 8 cm más ancha que el diámetro de cubo o 7 a 10 cm de altura;
  • taladro eléctrico (broca de 1⁄2 pulgadas -13 mm).

 

  • Los pasos para hacer un bebedero de PVC es similar a hacer un bebedero de vidrio, pero el balde (con la tapa) está boca abajo.
  • En primer lugar, dar la vuelta al balde boca abajo y ponerlo en el fondo de la base de maceta y hacer una marca en el balde a la altura de la parte superior de la base de maceta.
  • Debajo de la línea, perforar un agujero en el lateral.
    • Una vez que se perfora el agujero, enjuague el balde para deshacerse de los residuos de plástico.
  • Tome el balde y llénelo con agua antes de poner la tapa.
    • Colocar la tapa con firmeza, voltear el balde boca abajo y ponerlo en el fondo de la base de maceta.
    • El agua debe llenarse y parar una vez que cubra el agujero antes perforado.
  • Cuando el nivel del agua es bajo en el balde, se debe dar la vuelta al balde, quitar la tapa y volver a llenarlo.
    • Una vez que se ha rellenado, poner el balde de nuevo en la base y ya está listo para ser utilizado de nuevo.
Figura 5. Sistema de bebedero automático que cuelga del techo del remolque

©FAO/TECA

Figura 6. La pequeña presión de la gravedad mantiene el suministro permanente de agua para las aves

©FAO/TECA

3. Conchas molidas

  • Las conchas molidas son un suplemento importante para todas las aves.
  • Lo usan para ayudar a triturar su alimento y mejorar su digestión.
  • Tiene una función similar a los dientes (que los pollos no tienen).
  • A medida que los pollos crecen, se pueden usar partículas más gruesa.
  • Coloca un pequeño contenedor cerca de su agua.
  • Hay muchos tipos de grano disponibles, y pueden ser:
    • cáscaras de huevo cocidas y machacadas;
    • caracoles o conchas de ostras trituradas;
    • o incluso piedra caliza.

4. Baño del polvo

  • El baño de polvo es importante para el bienestar del animal, ya que reduce los parásitos como los ácaros y piojos que viven en las plumas de los pollos y en las piernas.
    • Un baño de polvo es un contenedor, cajón o bandeja con polvo en el interior, y se coloca justo debajo del tráiler para que los pollos tengan acceso a ella cuando lo deseen.
    • Mantenerlo fuera de la lluvia para que esté limpio y seco.
  • El mantillo dentro del corral se utiliza en el Instituto de Investigación de Permacultura, pero también hay otras maneras de hacer un baño de polvo para las gallinas.
    • Por ejemplo, un método es mediante la combinación de la arena de construcción, ceniza de madera, el suelo (asegúrese de que sea de vermiculita, libre fertilizantes y productos químicos), y la tierra de diatomeas (grado alimenticio y no para su uso en piscinas).
    • Si la tierra de diatomeas es difícil de obtener, se puede mezclar arena, turba, y las cenizas de madera (opcional) para crear un baño de polvo, también.

5. Cerca

  • Una valla rodea el remolque y los cuatro montones de compost.
  • Evita que las gallinas se escapen al campo, atacando los cultivos vegetales vulnerables y, ofrece una protección limitada de los depredadores.
  • La valla tiene que ser fácilmente extraíble desde el remolque, dado que éste se mueve una vez a la semana.
  • Cada semana, la última pila de compost (4 semanas de edad) se quedará fuera de la valla para su uso como fuente de materia orgánica y fertilizantes.
  • Al igual que el movimiento del remolque, la valla se mueve hacia adelante 4 m cada semana.

6. Compost

  • Detrás del remolque es donde se hace el compost.
  • Una caja metálica desmontable (2 m x 2 m) con una parte superior abierta y la parte inferior se utiliza para acumular el compost.
  • La capa inferior es mantillo tomado del remolque y, que se ha sido defecado por las aves durante la semana anterior.
  • La capa intermedia es estiércol, que se puede obtener de la finca también.
  • Por último, los restos de comida se añaden a la parte superior para alimentar a los pollos.
  • Cada capa debe ser de 0,5 m³ de volumen para llegar a un resultado de 1,5 m³ de compost.
  • Cada día se añaden los restos de comida a la parte superior de la pila activa con el fin de alimentar a los pollos.
  • A continuación se muestra una foto de cómo se acomoda el compost.
Figura 7. Las capas de compost. El mantillo en la parte inferior, el estiércol en el medio, y los restos de comida en la parte superior. Los restos de alimentos se añaden en la parte superior de la pila activa cada mañana

©FAO/TECA

  • Una semana más tarde se desmonta la jaula, el remolque se desplaza hacia adelante 4 m, y la jaula se vuelve a montar de nuevo entre el remolque y la pila más nueva de compost.
  • A continuación, cada una de las 4 pilas de compost detrás del remolque se giran, incluyendo la última pila que ahora está fuera de la cerca y listo para su uso.
  • El tiempo medio de un giro es de alrededor de 20-45 minutos para cada pila en función de las capacidades físicas y experiencia en el giro.
  • En total, cuatro pilas se voltean todas las semanas, y la última pila está lista para volver a entrar en el jardín después de la última vez.
  • El proceso del compostaje se repite semana a semana.
  • Con este sistema, el nuevo abono se hace semanalmente y se reciclan continuamente los recursos dentro de la granja.
  • Tenga en cuenta que el compost para la alimentación de gallinas necesita ser humedecido adecuadamente.
  • En climas húmedos pueden ser necesarios los techos para prevenir el exceso de humedad, mientras que en climas más secos, se requeriría el riego regular de lo contrario el proceso de descomposición se reducirá o incluso se puede detener si la pila se seca demasiado.
  • No se requiere alimentación adicional para las aves ya que la pila de compost proporciona suficiente alimento para ellas en el sistema.
  • Sin embargo, es importante asegurarse de que los restos de comida sean diversos, de modo que reciben las vitaminas y minerales necesarios.

7. Resultados

  • Revisar sus aves cada día para asegurarse de que están recibiendo su comida y agua y, abrir las pilas de compost una vez por semana, no necesario mucho trabajo para mantener este sistema.
  • Las aves seguirán creciendo y produciendo huevos.
  • Una vez que están lo bastante mayores (4 semanas o más dependiendo de la raza), puede continuar manteniéndolas en el sistema para producir más huevos o, elegir el sacrificio de ellas para su alimentación.

8. Otros datos a tener en cuenta

  • Se puede tomar cinco semanas para completar el proceso de compostaje dependiendo de la rapidez de todo lo que se está descomponiendo y de las condiciones climáticas.
  • Algunas frutas y verduras son mejores para las aves que otros, por lo que es importante saber qué tipo de restos de comida se debe incluir en la alimentación. Ejemplos a continuación:

8.1 Los alimentos para alimentar a su pollo

  • Maíz u otros granos disponibles localmente.
  • Manzanas.
  • Bayas.
  • Melones.
  • Harina de avena.
  • Chícharos (arvejas).
  • Mandioca (yuca).
  • Plátano.
  • Pan (con moderación).
  • La mayoría de vegetales cocidos o crudos, incluyendo brócoli, zanahorias, repollo, acelga, pepino, col rizada, lechuga, calabaza, espinaca, calabaza, patatas dulces (camote), y los tomates.

8.2 Alimentos que debe evitar en la alimentación de las gallinas

  • Semillas y cáscara de aguacate-palta (la carne está bien).
  • Cáscaras crudas de papa.
  • Café.
  • Chocolate.
  • Cualquier cosa demasiado salada.
  • Huevos crudos.
  • Los frijoles secos o poco cocidos.
  • Las plantas de la familia de las solanáceas: papas, tomates, berenjenas.

9. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Improved practices in rearing indigenous chickens: ID 6921.
  • Small-scale chicken production: ID 6949.
  • Improved chicken breeds raised with vaccination: ID 8941.
  • Replicas of native chicken in rural poultry production: the Satpuda: ID 7680.

Esta tecnología también está disponible en inglés: ID 8863.

10. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

10.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología trae muchos resultados positivos, como por ejemplo una buena calidad del compost, que no sólo es sostenible sino también rico en nutrientes.

10.2 Atiende a las necesidades de la mujer

Esta práctica no requiere un trabajo físico pesado, por lo que puede realizarla cualquier persona.

10.3 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

El sistema integrado con aves de corral y compost conduce a un bajo costo de alimento para los pollos.

Producción de pollos sin grano: el sistema integrado con aves de corral y compost

El sistema integrado de producción avícola y compost es un método que combina el compostaje, la cría de aves de corral, y la producción de huevos. Es un método de bajo costo para criar pollos, mientras se produce compost de buena calidad. Los costos de alimentación son casi eliminados debido al uso de restos de comida, estiércol, mantillo que se utilizan para la alimentación - los cuales se pueden obtener ya sea de la misma finca o se consiguen a bajo precio en los restaurantes o mercados cercanos. Estas aves se alimentan con una dieta cero granos y son comparativamente más robusto que los pollos alimentados con granos. El número de huevos producidos a partir de pollos alimentados con compost es el mismo, o incluso más alto (hasta 1/3), que la de los pollos alimentados con granos. El contenido de proteína en la alimentación de los pollos es alta y muy buena por el compost de calidad que se produce en este sistema. El sistema que se explica en esta tecnología emplea un remolque que proporciona alojamiento para la protección contra los depredadores, recolección de huevos y la captura de las heces de los pollos para enriquecer el compost. Un sistema de riego automático garantiza que siempre haya suficiente agua para que las aves se mantengan hidratadas. El compost resultante es rico en nutrientes y se recicla en huertas que producen frutos y verduras de alta calidad. Este sistema está diseñado para un total de 36 aves adultas porque el gallinero (un remolque reutilizado) tiene seis perchas; cada percha tiene seis gallinas. Las gallinas tienen la opción de poner sus huevos en dos lados diferentes del remolque donde se alojan. Dependiendo de la raza y la edad de las aves, dentro de cuatro semanas, este sistema va a producir una gran cantidad de compost de calidad, más de 200 huevos, gallinas robustas que pueden continuar produciendo los huevos o ser procesados en la comida.

Descripción

  • El sistema es un remolque modificado.
    • Los componentes son un gallinero móvil con cajas y perchas de anidación, un tabique móvil exterior, un bebedero automático, y un baño de polvo.
  • El gallinero es un remolque de utilidad convertido, aún sobre sus ruedas, y por lo tanto móvil.
  • El remolcador es rodeado con una valla simple y móvil para mantener a los pollos confinados.
  • Dentro de este confín hay cuatro pilas de compost.
  • Una nueva pila de compost se construye cada semana.
  • Cada semana, el remolque y las vallas móviles se mueven hacia adelante por cuatro metros, donde se construye una nueva pila de compost.
  • Cada semana, cada pila de compost se voltea una vez usando una horquilla o una pala.
    • Por lo tanto, cada pila se gira un total de cuatro veces en un período de cuatro semanas.
  • Durante los cambios las gallinas están activas buscando y alimentándose de los restos de comida y los insectos en la pila de compost.
  • El tiempo total de crear el compost es de 4-5 semanas. La figura 1 ofrece una visión general del sistema.
  • Esta dieta de las gallinas es diferente de la de los pollos en muchas granjas modernas que tienen una dieta que consiste en gran parte de granos, suplementos vitamínicos, minerales y suplementos.
    • Los pellets son también de uso frecuente y se hacen sintéticamente.
  • Muchos agricultores, especialmente en los países en desarrollo, no tienen acceso a comprar estos concentrados o cualquier alimento comercial para sus pollos y el costo puede ser prohibitivo, aún cuando se disponga de ellos.
  • En contraste, el método descrito aquí utiliza materiales que de otro modo se puede desechar como residuos.
  • El sistema avícola y compost integrado es un método de bajo costo y ambientalmente sostenible.
    • Los restos de comida, estiércol y mantillo se utilizan para la alimentación y todos se pueden obtener de la granja.
    • Como alternativa, si no hay suficientes restos de comida que son generados por la granja, se pueden comprar a bajo precio en los restaurantes o mercados.
