L’apiculture doit faire face aujourd’hui à de nombreux problèmes, principalement en relation avec le changement climatique et la perte d’habitat. A cause de tous ces changements, les abeilles souffrent de malnutrition ainsi que des effets des pesticides, des nouveaux agents pathogènes et des espèces invasives telles que le petit coléoptère des ruches et le frelon asiatique (Vespa velutina).

Les bonnes pratiques apicoles et les mesures de biosécurité dans l’apiculture sont des outils utiles que l’apiculteur peut adopter dans le rucher afin de garantir la santé des abeilles, des humains (p.ex. les consommateurs) et de l’environnement.  Cette fiche technique offre un aperçu général des bonnes pratiques apicoles et des mesures de biosécurité dans l’apiculture.



La description

1. Introduction

L’apiculture se définit comme la conduite des abeilles dans une ruche en vue de la pollinisation et de la production de miel et d’autres produits, comme la cire, la gelée royale, la propolis et le pollen. En outre, la production de matériel vivant tel que les abeilles et les reines, peut également être considérée comme un produit de l’apiculture. Enfin, les abeilles offrent d’autres services comme l’api-tourisme, l’apithérapie, et la surveillance de la pollution environnementale.

L’apiculture inclut les activités qui portent sur la conduite pratique des espèces d’abeilles sociales.  Les espèces utilisées en apiculture sont :

  • L’abeille naine comme Apis florea et Apis andreniformis;
  • L’abeille géante comme Apis laboriosa et Apis dorsata;
  • L’abeille domestique et ses proches parents comme Apis cerana, Apis mellifera, Apis koschevnikovi, Apis nigrocincta et Apis nuluensis;
  • L’abeille sans dard (genus Melipona);
  • Les bourdons (genus Bombus).

Les abeilles mentionnées ci-dessus peuvent offrir un moyen de subsistance et/ou une source de revenu pour beaucoup de familles en zone rurale et pour de petites fermes à travers :

  • La production et la vente de produits de la ruche, comme des abeilles vivantes (en fournisant des reines ou des essaims à d’autres apiculteurs), du miel, du pollen, de la cire, de la propolis, de la gelée royale et du venin. Les produits des abeilles peuvent être consommés en tant que nourriture pour les humains ou pour les animaux, utilisés dans des produits cosmétiques ou en médecine (en médecine conventionnelle, p.ex. pour le traitement d’allergies au venin des abeilles ou en apithérapie) ou comme composants de produits industriels tels que des vernis et édulcorants;
  • Les services offerts par les abeilles tels que la pollinisation, la surveillance de la pollution environnementale, l’apithérapie, l’api-tourisme et les ruches pour la conservation génétique. 

En même temps, la valeur des abeilles pour l’environnement est souvent sous-estimée.

Dans les dernières décennies, le secteur apicole a dû faire face à un nombre croissant de facteurs externes qui affectent la santé et la productivité des abeilles. On peut citer, entre autres, le réchauffement global, la propagation de nouveaux agents pathogènes, l’urbanisation et la perte de biodiversité parmi les plantes. Ce sont des facteurs que l’apiculteur ne peut pas contrôler et donc il doit adopter des pratiques et mesures de conduite des ruches qui l’aident à limiter l’impact de l’environnement en changement dans lequel il travaille.

Une approche moderne de l’apiculture s’oriente vers un système agricole de plus en plus durable. Cependant, une agriculture durable demande toujours de bonnes connaissances de la conduite des abeilles afin d’optimiser les systèmes naturels et les ressources dont dépend l’apiculteur.

Les bonnes pratiques apicoles (BPA) et les mesures de biosécurité en apiculture (MBA) décrites dans cette fiche technique traitent des Apis mellifera et visent à offrir aux apiculteurs des outils qui aident à maintenir des colonies saines et fortes.

2. Les bonnes pratiques apicoles

Les bonnes pratiques apicoles (BPA) sont un ensemble cohérent d'activités que les apiculteurs appliquent afin d’obtenir une santé optimale pour l'homme, les abeilles et l'environnement.  C’est pour cela que l’adoption des BPA aura un effet positif sur la santé de la colonie et de la société tout en garantissant des standards de production élevés. Il s'agit de mesures générales valables pour les activités apicoles et qui sont mondialement acceptées. Elles ne concernent pas des maladies spécifiques ; l’apiculteur est censé les adopter pour la production primaire des produits de la ruche. Elles constituent un outil permettant aux apiculteurs de relever avec succès les défis auxquels ils sont confrontés dans la conduite quotidienne de leurs ruchers.

Les BPA constituent la base d’un secteur apicole durable et résilient. Leur adoption quotidienne dans la conduite apicole offre plusieurs impacts positifs:

  • Des bénéfices économiques tels que la réduction des coûts, une production plus importante par ruche et des revenus supérieurs pour les apiculteurs ;
  • Des mesures de sécurité meilleures grâce à une manipulation plus sûre des médicaments vétérinaires ;
  • Un impact positif sur les consommateurs grâce à des produits apicoles de meilleure qualité ;
  • Un impact positif sur la santé publique grâce à la réduction des résidus de produits vétérinaires dans les produits apicoles suite à une manipulation plus sûre des médicaments ;
  • Un impact positif sur la performance générale des abeilles en améliorant leur santé et leur productivité, ainsi que l’efficacité des traitements ;
  • Des bénéfices sur la santé de l’environnement en améliorant sa protection grâce à l’utilisation de traitements biologiques et à la protection de la biodiversité.

Voici quelques BPA pertinentes. (Pour une liste plus complète de BPA, voir la fiche technique « Bonnes pratiques apicoles: liste non-exhaustive des bonnes pratiques apicoles répertoriées selon les principes généraux de conduite du rucher » [ID 10100]).

  • Sélectionner un endroit approprié pour l’emplacement du rucher. Un endroit approprié se trouve éloigné des sources de pollution telles que l’agriculture intensive et les industries, et offre suffisamment de nourriture pendant toute l’année. De même, les ruches ne devraient pas être exposées à l’humidité et aux vents froids (figure 1).
Figure 1. Ruchers situés dans un endroit approprié

©IZSLT/Giovanni Formato

  • Sélectionner soigneusement les fournisseurs d’abeilles et d’équipements apicoles et contrôler l’état de santé des essaims, colonies et reines nouvellement acquis. Pour des maladies spécifiques, adopter des mesures de quarantaine afin d’éviter leur introduction dans le rucher.
  • Identifier chaque ruche par l’application d’un code numérique unique (figure 2).
Figure 2. Identification de ruches avec un code numérique et des signes graphiques

©IZSLT/Giovanni Formato

  • Garder un registre des visites de chaque ruche, de la productivité de chaque ruche et de sa résistance aux maladies.
  • Vérifier régulièrement pendant l’année l’état sanitaire des colonies (figure 3). La fréquence des inspections dépend du moment de l’année.  Pendant l’hiver et quand les conditions climatiques sont défavorables, l’ouverture des ruches doit être limitée au strict minimum nécessaire.
Figure 3. Inspection des ruches

©IZSLT/Giovanni Formato

  • Renouveler les cadres (tous les deux ans) et remplacer régulièrement les reines (tous les un à deux ans). Donner la préférence aux reines qui montrent une résistance aux maladies, un comportement hygiénique, de la docilité, une faible tendance à essaimer et une productivité élevée.
  • Garder dans le même rucher des colonies avec une force égalisée; décourager l’essaimage en assurant que les abeilles aient assez d’espace dans la ruche; prévenir le pillage en retirant du rucher les colonies fortement malades ou affaiblies et plus susceptibles aux attaques ou au pillage.
  • Effectuer un entretien régulier des ruches.
  • Adopter des techniques appropriées afin d’assurer le bien-être des colonies,  en particulier les colonies jeunes/faibles; nourrir les colonies qui ne disposent pas de réserve alimentaire ou lors de conditions météorologiques défavorables, comme l’automne, l’hiver et les printemps trop froids ou pluvieux; assurer un bon hivernage; fournir des sources d’eau adéquates, surtout en période de chaleur.
  • Eviter de nourrir les abeilles avec du miel si l’on n’est pas sûr qu’il ne contient pas de spores de la loque américaine ou européenne. Dans ce cas, fournir du sucre candi ou du sirop de glucose/fructose. Vérifier l’origine et la salubrité de l’alimentation fournie aux abeilles.
  • Assurer une utilisation appropriée de l ́enfumoir en respectant le bien-être des abeilles et en évitant d’utiliser des matières toxiques qui peuvent contaminer le miel et nuire aux abeilles.
  • Eviter l’utilisation de substances toxiques telles que des désinfectants ou des traitements chimiques et peintures toxiques pour les ruches.
  • Eviter le tranfert de cadres entre ruches si l’état de santé des colonies n’est pas connu. Les ruches malades doivent être enlevées du rucher et détruites si nécessaire.
  • Utiliser uniquement des médicaments enregistrés pour les abeilles et respecter stictement les instructions et les directives d’utilisation. Enregistrer l’utilisation de médicaments dans le registre du rucher. L’utilisation abusive et intempestive de produits chimiques pendant la production de miel peut provoquer sa contamination.
  • Entretenir régulièrement le rucher, par exemple, en coupant l’herbe devant les ruches.
  • Conserver le matériel apicole en bon état et propre; si nécessaire, le renouveler.
  • Consulter un expert en cas d’anomalie.

Notez que l’adoption de bonnes pratiques apicoles dans le rucher ne veut pas dire que les abeilles ne tomberont pas malades mais cela réduira l’apparition de maladies.

3. Mesures de biosécurité en apiculture

Les mesures de biosécurité dans l'apiculture (MBA) sont toutes les activités opérationnelles mises en œuvre par les apiculteurs afin de réduire le risque d'introduction et de propagation d'agents pathogènes spécifiques des abeilles. Cependant, les MBA ne peuvent apporter des bénéfices que si l’apiculteur applique systématiquement les bonnes pratiques apicoles. Les mesures de biosécurité peuvent varier d'une région à l'autre en raison de facteurs locaux tels que les conditions climatiques, le matériel apicole utilisé ou les races d'abeilles, ainsi que la prévalence, la virulence et l'importance des maladies des abeilles. L'adoption des MBA est le fondement de tous les programmes de contrôle des maladies, quelle que soit l'espèce animale. Si les mesures de biosécurité sont correctement appliquées, il est possible de réduire l'incidence des maladies et, par conséquent, la nécessité d'appliquer des traitements, jusqu’à un minimum absolu.

La fiche technique « Mesures de biosécurité dans l'apiculture concernant les principales maladies des abeilles » (ID10101) offre une liste non-exhaustive des MBA.

4. Les zones agro-écologiques

  • Régions couvertes par Apis mellifera.

5. Les technologies associées/relatives

  • Fabrication d’un enfumoir metallique à soufflet: ID 8871.
  • Comment récolter la propolis brute d’une ruche: ID 8826.
  • Comment récolter la cire d'abeille: ID 7580.

Cette fiche technique est disponible en espagnol: ID 8675, et en anglais: ID 8409.

6. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

6.1 Favorable aux femmes

Cette fiche technique est conçue et a le potentiel de répondre aux besoins et aux demandes de main d’œuvre des femmes. Par exemple, la fiche technique est facile à utiliser, abordable, légère et gérable, supportant des tâches spécifiquement assignées aux femmes; les services de conseil ciblent les besoins des femmes et leur disponibilité en temps.

6.2 L’efficacité d’utilisation des ressources

Cette fiche technique permet une meilleure gestion de l’apiculture et une meilleure santé des colonies.

6.3 La technologie favorable aux populations pauvres

Grâce à une gestion améliorée et à une meilleure santé des colonies d’abeilles, cette fiche technique permet la production de produits de meilleure qualité.

records.title: Fabricación de muestreador para varroa en alcohol
records.description:
Descripción

El muestreo de doble tamiz es uno de los metodos con el cual se puede medir en terreno el nivel de infestación de varroa de una colmena. Con el método de muestreo de abejas mediante doble tamiz se mide la cantidad de varroa adulto presente en la colmena, tomando una muestra de por lo menos 200 abejas jóvenes. Para instrucciones sobre cómo aplicar el método de muestreo con con doble tamiz, véase la ficha técnica.

1. Construcción del doble tamiz

Para la construcción del muestreador de doble tamiz se requieren los siguientes materiales:

  • Frasco de plástico de 0,5 litros con tapa;
  • malla mosquetera (diámetro de 2 a 3 mm);
  • malla metálica fina (diámetro de 0,5 mm) o tela de genero; y
  • corchetes, tijeras, cuchillo cartonero, tijera para cortar metal y pegote o guincha aisladora.

El primer paso (Figura 1) es cortar el frasco en su parte inferior y luego desprender una franja de 1,5 centímetros de grosor (que será el soporte de la malla mosquetera) que retendrá a las abejas. Una vez realizado esto, se debe colocar la malla mosquetera en el interior del frasco.

Figura 1. Primer paso

©FAO/TECA

Luego (Figura 2) de posicionada la malla mosquetera en la mitad del frasco ya cortado, donde se fija mediante corchetes a la franja ya cortada. Posteriormente se corta el excedente de malla mosquetera y se recubren con la guincha las puntas salientes de los corchetes por la cara externa del frasco.

Figura 2. Segundo paso

©FAO/TECA

El último paso (Figura 3) es cortar el fondo de la tapa de plástico de forma circular e instalar en ella la malla metálica fina o tela de género que será la encargada de retener las varroas y permitir el paso del agua jabonosa con la que se extraerá la muestra.

Figura 3. Tercer paso

©FAO/TECA

2. Utilización del muestreador de doble tamiz

Para la utilización del doble tamiz se puede revisar la ficha técnica “Método para determinar niveles de varroa en terreno“ que describe paso a paso cómo utilizarlo, así como el método alternativo de muestreo con azúcar flor (véase enlace abajo). Este último no requiere matar las abejas para evaluar el nivel de infestación de varroa.

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, fresco.

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Método para determinar niveles de varroa en terreno: ID 8663.
  • Varroa (Varroosis): ID 8694.

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Esta práctica describe cómo se puede confeccionar doble tamiz para evitar pérdidas de abejas y determinar el nivel de infestación de varroa en etapa forética.

records.title: Organising to market animals and milk
records.description:
Description

To market animals or milk successfully, pastoralists need certain skills, and they need to get organized! This practical guide tells you how.

1. Organize in a group

1.1 Advantages of groups

  • You can sell in bulk as you have enough milk to fill a can or enough animals to fill a pick-up or lorry, which saves your time and the trader’s time. Traders normally pay more if they do not have to waste time looking for animals to buy.
  • You can negotiate higher prices as you can approach two or more buyers and sell to the one who gives you the best price.
  • You can specialize as one person can deliver the animals; another takes care of negotiations and another does the paperwork.
  • You can process the product. For example, together, the group may have enough milk to make and sell butter and cheese, which brings in more money than milk.
  • You can learn from one another since group members can share ideas and experiences.
  • You can get services from the government or other organizations. For example, a group can ask a government extension worker for advice or it can approach a bank and ask for a loan.
Figure 1. Belonging to a group has many advantages

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Types of groups

  • Milk-collection groups collect milk from their members and sell it to consumers, collection centres or dairies.
  • Livestock marketing groups market their animals collectively.
  • Processing groups add value to the raw product. For example, small-scale tanneries turn hides into leather. Dairies turn milk into butter and other products. Processed products are more valuable and less perishable than raw items.
  • Savings and credit groups save money and lend it to members in turn.
  • Cooperatives are formal organizations that enable their members to collaborate on marketing and processing.
Figure 2. Members of savings and credit groups save a small amount of money each week. When they need cash, they can borrow from the group

©FAO/TECA

2. How to organize?

  • Begin with those who are interested.
  • Find other people who are interested in working together, for example, to sell their animals or milk as a group. They should live close together and have approximately the same number of animals.
  • Decide what you want to do.
  • Agree with the group members what they want to do. For example, maybe you all want to sell some goats each month.
  • Find out about the market, the prices, potential buyers and the type of product they want.
  • Decide on the rules:
    • In a savings group, how much money should each member save? How often should you meet? Who can borrow money? How much interest must they pay?
    • In a marketing group, how much milk or how many animals should each member supply? Who will negotiate with buyers? Who will manage the deliveries? Who will handle the money?
  • Elect leaders for the group. A group will need at least:
    • a chairperson to call the meetings and lead them;
    • a secretary to keep records; and
    • a treasurer to look after the money; and other leaders, such as a marketing coordinator or a transport manager.
  • Get advice on several topics:
    • find out where you can get the information and skills you need. Possibilities include government extension workers, development organizations, traders and people in other successful groups.
Figure 3. Begin with those who are interested in improving their production and marketing

©FAO/TECA

3. Do some market research

Interested in selling to an abattoir or dairy? Organize a visit for your group to find out what their requirements are. Want to sell to traders in town? Get some contacts, then arrange to meet them. Find out what you can about each buyer’s needs and decide where you will get the best deal.

3.1 Things to ask

When you meet a potential buyer, ask about the things listed in Table 1.

Table 1. Market research: things to ask

Source: IIRR 2015

4. Make a business plan

If you form a marketing group, you will need a business plan. Write down what you plan to do, and work out whether it will be worthwhile. If so, make sure all the group members agree, and put your plan into action.

4.1 Things to include in the business plan

4.1.1 The product

What do you want to sell? Live animals: cattle, camels, sheep, goats...? What age and sex? How many animals at a time? Milk: from what type of animal?
What quantity and quality will be needed? Can the group reliably deliver these amounts and quality?

4.1.2 The buyers

  • Who do you want to sell to? A travelling trader, a market trader, a shop, an abattoir, a butcher...? What type of animal or product do they want?
  • How can you identify potential buyers? How can you contact them?
  • How can you get the animals or milk to the buyer? Will the buyer pick them up, or will you have to deliver them?
Figure 4. Do some market research to find out where and to whom you might sell

©FAO/TECA

4.1.3 Income

  • What price can you realistically expect for your animals or milk?
  • Will you get the money straight away, or will you have to wait?

4.1.4 Production

Organising to market animals and milk

Pastoralists need certain skills and have to be organized to market animals or milk successfully. This practical guide tells you how to do so by explaining strategies for doing good market research, writing professional business plans and organizing effectively with fellow farmers.

Description

To market animals or milk successfully, pastoralists need certain skills, and they need to get organized! This practical guide tells you how.

1. Organize in a group

1.1 Advantages of groups

  • You can sell in bulk as you have enough milk to fill a can or enough animals to fill a pick-up or lorry, which saves your time and the trader’s time. Traders normally pay more if they do not have to waste time looking for animals to buy.
  • You can negotiate higher prices as you can approach two or more buyers and sell to the one who gives you the best price.
  • You can specialize as one person can deliver the animals; another takes care of negotiations and another does the paperwork.
  • You can process the product. For example, together, the group may have enough milk to make and sell butter and cheese, which brings in more money than milk.
  • You can learn from one another since group members can share ideas and experiences.
  • You can get services from the government or other organizations. For example, a group can ask a government extension worker for advice or it can approach a bank and ask for a loan.
Figure 1. Belonging to a group has many advantages

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Types of groups

  • Milk-collection groups collect milk from their members and sell it to consumers, collection centres or dairies.
  • Livestock marketing groups market their animals collectively.
  • Processing groups add value to the raw product. For example, small-scale tanneries turn hides into leather. Dairies turn milk into butter and other products. Processed products are more valuable and less perishable than raw items.
  • Savings and credit groups save money and lend it to members in turn.
  • Cooperatives are formal organizations that enable their members to collaborate on marketing and processing.
Figure 2. Members of savings and credit groups save a small amount of money each week. When they need cash, they can borrow from the group

©FAO/TECA

2. How to organize?

  • Begin with those who are interested.
  • Find other people who are interested in working together, for example, to sell their animals or milk as a group. They should live close together and have approximately the same number of animals.
  • Decide what you want to do.
  • Agree with the group members what they want to do. For example, maybe you all want to sell some goats each month.
  • Find out about the market, the prices, potential buyers and the type of product they want.

©FAO/TECA

When you meet a potential buyer, ask about the things listed in Table 1.

Table 1. Market research: things to ask

Source: IIRR 2015

What quantity and quality will be needed? Can the group reliably deliver these amounts and quality?

records.title: Intensive rice cultivation
records.description:
Description

The system of intensive rice cultivation (or SRI – Système de Riziculture Intensive in French), developed in Madagascar in 1983 by Fr. Henri de Laulanié, is an innovative cultivation method that can increase yields considerably without the need for inputs that are often costly and hard to access for small scale farmers. The great discovery was that rice is not an aquatic plant; rather it develops with an alternating system of watering. A further discovery was that the earlier the rice is replanted, the greater the production of tillers (presence of stalks or tillers from a seedling). A single seedling can produce up to 80 stalks, or even more. In the course of a single year, depending on soil and climate conditions, it is possible to produce three harvests of rice, as well as vegetables during the off-season. Compost used for vegetable production also benefits rice.

Figure 1. Rice crop

©FAO/TECA

This technical guide outlines the basic ideas and practices in order to obtain good yields.

  • Choice and sorting of seeds.
  • Pregermination of seeds.
  • Preparation of the dry seedbed and sowing.
  • Widely spaced replanting of seedlings with two leaves.
  • Preparation of the rice paddy and water control.
  • Paddy maintenance.
  • Harvesting.
  • Controlling soil fertility.

1. Choice and sorting of seeds

  • Choose quality seeds for your nursery, improved seeds or just the seeds from the previous harvest.
  • Next, sort the seeds by throwing them into a bucket of water.
  • The good grains sink and remove the empty husks as they float to the surface.
Figure 2. Choice of seeds

©FAO/TECA

2. Pregermination of seeds

  • Pregerminating can save time during sowing.
  • For a good pregermination, put the rice in a well-ventilated sack (e.g. cloth or hessian) and place it in a stream or a bucket filled with lukewarm water (30°C) for 24 hours.
  • Then take the sack out of the water and put it in a pre-warmed hole (it must be warm) for another 24 hours.
  • Sow the seed sparsely in order to produce stronger plants.
  • On days when it does not rain, give seedbeds plenty of water in the morning and/or the evening.
Figure 3. Pre-germination

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Preheated hole

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Low density seeding

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Watering the sowing

©FAO/TECA

3. Replanting

  • Replanting can begin in the paddy when  seedlings have two leaves, that is, about five to ten days after sowing, depending on the soil and climate conditions.
  • It is important to replant seedlings with not more than two leaves because the more the seedling grows before replanting, the less it tillers and the lower the yield.
  • Replant the seedlings on a grid using knotted string, with a minimum space of 25 cm x 25 cm between plants (more if the paddy is fertile) to produce good tillering and easy hoeing.
Figure 7. Plantula

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Transplantation

©FAO/TECA

4. Preparation of the rice paddy and water control

  • Intensive rice cultivation requires a good control of water (irrigation and drainage).
  • Dig irrigation channels (about 30 x 30 cm) around each plot.
    • It is normal to leave a shallow puddle of water in the paddies (muddying)
  • The evening before hoeing, flood the fields slightly, so hoe can be used more easily.
  • After hoeing, drain the paddies completely for a day or so.
    • Draining improves tillering during this phase of their growth.
    • As the rice grains develop, leave a thin layer of water on the paddies for 15 to 20 days, before completely draining them eight to ten days before the harvest.
Figure 9. Digging watering channels

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10. Draining the flowerbed after weeding

©FAO/TECA

Figure 11. Monda

©FAO/TECA

5. Paddy maintenance

  • It is important to eliminate weeds and to aerate the soil by hoeing three to four times per season.
  • Flood the paddies slightly before hoeing so hoeing tools can be used more easily.
  • First hoe (in both directions) eight to ten days after replanting, and then two to three times every eight to ten days.

6. Harvesting

  • To avoid losing any grains through accidental shedding, harvest the rice even if some grains are not yet completely ripe.
  • During harvesting, make sure to select the most beautiful stalks and keep them carefully for next year’s seed.
Figure 12. Harvest

©FAO/TECA

7. Controlling soil fertility

  • Spread compost when preparing my paddy field, and grow off-season vegetables (especially leguminous plants such as peas and beans) because they enrich the soil.
  • Alternating dry cultivation with rice growing is very important to maintain good aeration and soil fertility.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Aerobic rice: ID 7941.
  • Rice seedbed preparation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 6973.
  • Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7210.

This technology is also available in Portuguese: ID 1666.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Pro-poor technology

The technology increases yields without the need for inputs that are often costly and hard to access for small-scale farmers.

Intensive rice cultivation

Demand for rice on the global market is on a constant rise. Yet despite the Green Revolution, production levels are unable to keep up with demand. Irrigated rice production is practised by millions of farmers around the world. The technique is based on an almost permanent flooding of the paddy-fields, which is an enormous source of methane production. As a result of population pressure and frequent shortages of land and water, other methods of cultivation should be used in order to improve rice yields. records.title: Evergreen agriculture: conservation agriculture in maize production
records.description:
Description

1. Introduction

Conservation agriculture (CA) employs the judicious use of conservation tillage, mulching and integrating of main crop with legume crops and/or trees to conserve natural resources of soil and water for improved and sustainable production. Conservation tillage is the core principle of conservation agriculture as it portrays the new tillage system from the predominant ridge based tillage system. It is so crucial in the social dynamics of tillage practices because burning of crop residues and ridging is strongly engraved in the social fabric of smallholder agriculture in Malawi. It requires a systematic transformation of the mindset of smallholder farmers to conservation tillage as economically viable, ecologically sustainable and smallholder friendly. Conservation agriculture enhances natural ecological processes to conserve moisture, enhance soil fertility and improve soil structure. CA also reduces soil erosion and emergence of pests and diseases.

Conservation agriculture is a combined application of three non-negotiable principles.

  1. Minimum soil disturbance.
  2. Maximum soil cover.
  3. Crop associations and rotation.

2. Minimum soil disturbance

  • The tendency of splitting the old ridges and forming new ridge year by year is so dominant among the smallholder farmers in Malawi.
  • This type of tillage disturbs the soil so much that it encourages soil erosion and loss of soil fertility.
  • This key principle stipulates that a farmer should till the soil as little as possible.
  • The numerous on-farm research works indicate that maize and other crops can still grow well in less tilled or un-ridged fields.
  • This principle encourages farmers to disturb the soil where strategic inputs such as the seed, fertilizer and manure are to be placed.
  • CA promotes the minimum soil disturbance to 12 to 15 percent.
  • Under conventional agriculture, soil tillage is 100 percent.
  • Minimum tillage overcomes many of the disadvantages of ridging.
  • Ploughing and hoe ridging disturb soil layers and thereby destroying the structure of soil.
  • When the soil structure is destroyed, water infiltration and soil organic matter are disturbed.
  • Low levels of organic matter render soil less capable retaining nutrients and water in the soil.
  • In conventional tillage, ridges are seldom constructed across the slopes as recommended hence promoting soil erosion and land degradation.

2.1 Benefits of conservation tillage

  • Conservation tillage entails reducing tillage operations to the minimum required to plant crops.
  • In Malawi, this tillage would involve scratching or ripping out the soil where the crop is to be planted and leaving the rest of the land untilled until weeding is required.
  • Alternatively, conservation tillage can be done by constructing planting basins where seeding would take place.
    • Maintains soil structure.
    • Reduces soil erosion.
    • Improves water infiltration.
    • Retains and enhances build-up of soil organic matter.

2.2 Forms of conservation tillage

  • This is a very important cultural practice in conservation agriculture and it varies from one place to another and one farmer to another.
  • In Malawi, in the first year to practice conservation tillage, farmers have difficulties to plant maize in old ridges which are usually infested with weeds.
  • There is a chronic problem of weed infestation due to poor weeding practices farmer do.
  • When the main crop has reached physiological maturity, they let the weed to flower and shed off seeds on and in the soil.
    • This breeds fear by smallholder farmers of increased labour in weeding when they intend to practice conservation tillage.
  • Despite extensive extension messages on the recommended ridge spacing to obtain recommended plant population for maize system, farmers have tended to construct either closer or wider planting ridges at 50 to 60 cm apart or 80 to 90 cm apart, respectively.
    • This also predisposes difficulties among farmers in using right spacing during demonstrations.
    • The planting of next maize becomes difficult because the planting stations become both on the ridges and on the furrows.
  • Since labour is generally a problem during land preparation and CA is promoted as labour saving, it would not be wise to advice farmers to break the old ridges to start practicing CA.

2.2.1 Use of old ridges

  • Since no agro-ecological suitability studies have been conducted on conservation tillage in Malawi, the rule of thumb would be that farmer should be encouraged to use old ridges of previous ridge spacing to avoid breaking old ridges as such would be considered as conventional tillage.
  • There are many NGOs that promote the use of old ridge in the early years in CA.
    • These include Total LandCare (TLC), National Smallholder Farmers Association of Malawi (NASFAM), Concern Universal, Development Aid from People to People (DAPP), Farm Income Diversification Programme (FIDP) and many others.
    • ICRAF in collaboration with NASFAM, CRS and TLC have been active in scaling up Evergreen Agriculture (agroforestry based conservation agriculture) in Kasungu, Mchinji and Chiladzulu districts and also with NASFAM, Government of Malawi and Lake Malawi Basin project in implementing an AGRA project on CA in Kasungu, Lilongwe and Salima districts.
    • Farm demonstrations were set up on the use of old ridges and other CA practices and farmers showed interest in the practices.
      • Farmers indicated that the use of old ridges is easy to follow and is labour saving.
  • During planting period, the farmers should plant maize and agroforestry tree seeds in rows as recommended in specific areas.
    • However, the rule of thumb is that maize should be planted one seed per planting station spaced at 15 cm apart and the row should be made across the slope spaced at 75 cm apart.
    • It should be emphasized that row spacing was previously at 90 cm apart and this has been stopped because the current maize varieties do quite well at 75 cm apart.
  • The old ridge would die off as years go by.
  • The rain splash and human activity play a great role in levelling the maize field down.
Figure 1. Maize field under “old ridge” tillage or flat tillage in Nkhota kota under MACC project of TLC in 2009

©FAO/TECA

2.2.2 Permanent planting basins

  • Climate change has affected the smallholder agriculture with increased temperature, change in rainfall pattern, erratic rainfall and drought.
  • CA proves to be adaptive to climate change when permanent planting basins used as water conservation structures.
    • It has been witnessed that farmers across the country during CA field days organized by CA practitioners that CA plots with permanent planting basins retained enough soil water for crops to survive three to four day dry spells.
    • This could be a potential investment in water shadow areas and dry areas.
  • The permanent planting basins also act as focal points for strategic application of nutrients such chemical fertilizer, manure and biomass from agroforestry.
  • Under conventional tillage, nutrients are not specifically directed to micro environments accessible by the crop roots.
    • Year by year under conventional tillage, farmers change points for nutrient application because the ridge keep on changing.
    • It then becomes cost effective when all strategic nutrients are precisely applied within the proximate root radius which is the farmers‟ area of concern.
    • All other land preparation operations will be carried out in the planting basins and these include weeding, fertilizer application, tillage, manure application and others.
  • The permanent planting basins also have recommended row and basin spacing depending on different agro-ecological zones.

3.1 Preparing the basins

  • It is very important for extension worker to get acquainted with the practical steps in constructing plantings basins.
  • It is noted that a lot NGO partners have disseminated confusing messages on planting basins.
    • These basins are meant to be permanent in the sense that the following years the farmer would not be required to construct new basins.
    • It is encouraged that the farmers should prepare the basins during land preparation from June to October.
    • Digging planting basins only requires few tools.
      • A Malawian standard hoe or a chaka hoe.
      • Strings to mark out planting rows.
      • Measuring sticks or tape measure.
      • Pegs.
      • Bottle tops.

3.2 Weeding in cropped land and virgin land

  • If the family labour is not a problem and the field is relatively flat or a farrow, farmers should be encouraged to take time to re-align or dig basins correctly (as indicated in Table 1) so that in future years the same basins can be used.
  • If the farmer would like to use virgin land for CA, it is encouraged to cut down the stumps, roots and trees.
    • Ploughing is discouraged to till the virgin land to be used for CA.
    • Weeding is encouraged on previously cropped land prior to constructing basins.
  • Famers are encouraged to start on a small area for them to learn from.
    • Expansion of area will take place as farmers get more skilled and convinced.
    • Farmers can start with 0.5 ha (2 acres) of land.
    • This would require a total of 8888 basins using the current recommended plant population (Table 1).

Basin spacing (cm)

3.3 Marking out Basins

  • Mark out a straight line at the end of the field across and along the slope to easily mark the basins spacing and row spacing, respectively.
  • Use Table 1 (above) for spacing dimensions.
  • Calibrate the strings with bottle tops clipped to mark the row spacing and basin spacing.
    • For example, following the current recommended plant population 53 333 per hectare, basin strings and row strings will be clipped with bottle tops at 75 cm.
    • This will change with different configurations and plant population.
  • Tie the calibrated strings to the peg at the end of the field and stretch the strings across the slope to the other peg to mark out the planting row where to dig the basins.

3.4 Constructing basins

  • Starting at the first bottle clip at one end of the string, stand facing across the slope (the way farmers were standing in making ridges) and construct each basin about 30 cm long, 15 cm wide and 20 cm deep.
    • The width of the basin is determined by the blade of the type of hoe used.

    • The rows of basins can be constructed in linear or staggered format.
    • Some NGOs promote the use of staggered basins over linear basins in order to capture water and reduce run off.
    • This should be encouraged in running slopes.
    • Well-constructed basins will allow farmers to use correct amounts of seed, fertilizer and manure at the right place.
    • This reduces wastage of resources, money and time.

4.1 Retaining residues

  • Conventional tillage system encourages the clearing of crop and weed residues during land preparation.
  • The cleared residues are burnt to control weeds, pests and diseases. However, the residues go away with residual nutrients in their stalks rendering nutrient cycling impossible and difficult.
  • This burning of residues also predisposes the clear soil to run off by early heavy rains leading to soil erosion and land degradation.
  • Due to continuous clearing of residues and rain splash for a number of years coupled with continuous hoeing, hoe hand pan is created rendering root penetration and water infiltration difficult.
  • It is against this background that conservation tillage encourages the incorporation or spreading of crop residues.
    • The residues are supposed to come from the same crop field unless otherwise.
    • For instance, cotton and tobacco residues are commanded to be burnt to avoid sustaining pest and disease build up.
    • However, the fields which can be spread with tobacco and cotton residues can be rotated with other crops (See crop association section).

4.2 Residue management and challenges

  • In the maize-based system, the multiple uses of maize stover render them scarce and unavailable for farmers to cover their field.
  • In the southern region, maize stover is so scarce that farmers spread old grass thatch or combed grass on their crop fields.
    • The maize stover is used for cooking and construction of fences due to the scarcity of firewood.
  • In the central region, farmers use maize stover for fumigating tobacco seedbed nurseries and feeding livestock.
    • They usually burn them when hunting for mice.
  • In northern region, the maize stover is also used for feeding livestock and fumigating tobacco seedbed nurseries.
  • These are potential challenges for scaling up conservation agriculture in Malawi.
    • There is a tendency that a farmer only possesses ownership rights on crop produce and losses them on crop residues.
    • This attitude predisposes crop residues as open-access resources that can be utilized by any member of the community.
    • It is a common practice in Malawi to see farmers feeding their livestock on other farmers’ field without any form of reciprocity.
  • ICRAF mobilized farmers through traditional leadership and extension workers to develop livestock bylaws to control the free-roaming of livestock during and after the growing season.
    • Communities willing to practice CA should be encouraged to manage their livestock properly because CA is still compatible with livestock systems.
    • The livestock when well managed would provide manure and draught power to CA farmers.
  • The culture of heaping maize stalks with cobs for drying up and harvesting makes the work of spreading maize stover laborious to farmers.
    • The CA farmers usually tend to take back the stover to where the practice is being done and find this work tedious.
    • Some farmers have commended the heaping practice because it makes their stover secure at one place and protected from mice hunters and roaming livestock.
  • Farmers can harvest their maize from the standing stalks and the harvested stalks can be cut and laid down whilst harvesting the field.
    • This reduces the double operation of taking away and bringing back of maize stover.
  • The only challenge with this early spreading of stover is roaming livestock and lack of tenure over residues.
    • If this improves farmers find this practice doable and time and labour saving.

4.3 Spreading of soil cover

  • Farmers can use soil cover materials such as crop residues, old thatch grass and combed grass (flower heads removed).
    • Caution should be made when farmers want to retain weed residues in the early stages of CA.
    • Most weed residues have seeds that will infest the field because tillage will be minimized.
  • The crop residues should be spread systematically around the planting basins and planting stations.
    • It is a little bit tasking for farmers in the first year of doing CA.
    • In the subsequent years, farmers will mark where the old maize stumps are and crop residue will be spread around them.
    • Studies are currently being conducted to determine the recommended amount of stover or soil cover at the smallholder scale.
    • It is really envisaged that maize stover will soon be an economic commodity.

4.4 Benefits of maximum soil cover

  • Well placed residues reduce the impact of rain splash and runoff.
    • This checks soil erosion and land degradation.
  • The residues promote biological activity by the soil fauna and flora.
    • These activities facilitate the breakdown of residues into small participles that turn into humus or soil organic carbon.
    • The increased fauna activity improves nutrient cycling from sub soil to top soil.
  • In termite infested areas, the residues divert the attack on green growing maize to the decomposing stover or residues.
  • Residues retain soil moisture by reducing evaporation and evapotranspiration.
    • One farmer noted during ICRAF field days that CA plots with maximum mulch had turbid leaves whilst non-mulched plots had withered leaves.
  • Crop residues release trapped mineral nutrients in the stalks through mineralization and are made available to the roots of the main crop.
    • This is cost-effective as the amount of fertilizer to be applied will reduce.
  • Soil temperature is regulated by the crop residues which as heat insulators.
    • This promotes biological activity and reduces the volatilization of mineral compounds from the soil.
  • Soil aggregates stability and porosity increases.

4.5 Cover crops

  • Alternatively, cover crops are intercropped with main crop to serve the physical attributes of soil cover, biological nitrogen fixation and mineralization from the N rich biomass.
    • Although this could be classified as following the third principle of crop association or intercropping, it however needs to be emphasized that farmers who have problems of scarcity of maize stover and crop residues due to their multiple uses can use cover crops to attain maximum soil cover.
    • The cover crops include cowpeas, velvet beans, soya beans, common beans. A
    • fter harvest of the main crop, the cover crops should be well managed against livestock and fire.
  • Care should be observed when intercropping with cover crops.
    • Recommended spacing for cover crops under intercrop should be followed to avoid light, space and nutrients competition with crops.

4.6 Dealing with livestock problems

  • Livestock problem has been cited as one of the challenges of the adoption of CA by farmers in Malawi and other areas with agro-pastoral systems.
  • It has to be emphasized that livestock and CA are still compatible but proper management system has to be put in place.
  • Currently, in Malawi after crop harvest, livestock are let loose to forage on.

Evergreen agriculture: conservation agriculture in maize production

Evergreen Agriculture is a combination of conservation agriculture and agroforestry practices within the same spatial and temporal dimensions. In other circles, evergreen agriculture is referred to as agroforestry based conservation agriculture or Conservation Agriculture With Trees (CAWT). Evergreen agriculture is being tested by The World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF) in conjunction with partners in Malawi and across Africa as the means for enhancing soil fertility, increasing crop productivity and increasing food production. This section will focus on the principles and practices of Conservation Agriculture (CA) as applied in maize production in Malawi. Conservation agriculture also improves the soil health and productivity as well as improves the crop production. ICRAF envisages that a combination of these two technologies together with other technologies will improve soil health and improve crop production and finally improves food security in Malawi.

Description

1. Introduction

Conservation agriculture (CA) employs the judicious use of conservation tillage, mulching and integrating of main crop with legume crops and/or trees to conserve natural resources of soil and water for improved and sustainable production. Conservation tillage is the core principle of conservation agriculture as it portrays the new tillage system from the predominant ridge based tillage system. It is so crucial in the social dynamics of tillage practices because burning of crop residues and ridging is strongly engraved in the social fabric of smallholder agriculture in Malawi. It requires a systematic transformation of the mindset of smallholder farmers to conservation tillage as economically viable, ecologically sustainable and smallholder friendly. Conservation agriculture enhances natural ecological processes to conserve moisture, enhance soil fertility and improve soil structure. CA also reduces soil erosion and emergence of pests and diseases.

Conservation agriculture is a combined application of three non-negotiable principles.

  1. Minimum soil disturbance.
  2. Maximum soil cover.
  3. Crop associations and rotation.

2. Minimum soil disturbance

  • The tendency of splitting the old ridges and forming new ridge year by year is so dominant among the smallholder farmers in Malawi.
  • This type of tillage disturbs the soil so much that it encourages soil erosion and loss of soil fertility.
  • This key principle stipulates that a farmer should till the soil as little as possible.
  • The numerous on-farm research works indicate that maize and other crops can still grow well in less tilled or un-ridged fields.
  • This principle encourages farmers to disturb the soil where strategic inputs such as the seed, fertilizer and manure are to be placed.
  • CA promotes the minimum soil disturbance to 12 to 15 percent.
  • Under conventional agriculture, soil tillage is 100 percent.
  • Minimum tillage overcomes many of the disadvantages of ridging.
  • Ploughing and hoe ridging disturb soil layers and thereby destroying the structure of soil.
  • When the soil structure is destroyed, water infiltration and soil organic matter are disturbed.
  • Low levels of organic matter render soil less capable retaining nutrients and water in the soil.
  • In conventional tillage, ridges are seldom constructed across the slopes as recommended hence promoting soil erosion and land degradation.

2.1 Benefits of conservation tillage

  • Conservation tillage entails reducing tillage operations to the minimum required to plant crops.
  • In Malawi, this tillage would involve scratching or ripping out the soil where the crop is to be planted and leaving the rest of the land untilled until weeding is required.
  • Alternatively, conservation tillage can be done by constructing planting basins where seeding would take place.
    • Maintains soil structure.
    • Reduces soil erosion.
    • Improves water infiltration.
    • Retains and enhances build-up of soil organic matter.

2.2 Forms of conservation tillage

  • This is a very important cultural practice in conservation agriculture and it varies from one place to another and one farmer to another.
  • In Malawi, in the first year to practice conservation tillage, farmers have difficulties to plant maize in old ridges which are usually infested with weeds.
  • There is a chronic problem of weed infestation due to poor weeding practices farmer do.
  • When the main crop has reached physiological maturity, they let the weed to flower and shed off seeds on and in the soil.
    • This breeds fear by smallholder farmers of increased labour in weeding when they intend to practice conservation tillage.
  • Despite extensive extension messages on the recommended ridge spacing to obtain recommended plant population for maize system, farmers have tended to construct either closer or wider planting ridges at 50 to 60 cm apart or 80 to 90 cm apart, respectively.
    • This also predisposes difficulties among farmers in using right spacing during demonstrations.
    • The planting of next maize becomes difficult because the planting stations become both on the ridges and on the furrows.
  • Since labour is generally a problem during land preparation and CA is promoted as labour saving, it would not be wise to advice farmers to break the old ridges to start practicing CA.

2.2.1 Use of old ridges

  • Since no agro-ecological suitability studies have been conducted on conservation tillage in Malawi, the rule of thumb would be that farmer should be encouraged to use old ridges of previous ridge spacing to avoid breaking old ridges as such would be considered as conventional tillage.
  • There are many NGOs that promote the use of old ridge in the early years in CA.
    • These include Total LandCare (TLC), National Smallholder Farmers Association of Malawi (NASFAM), Concern Universal, Development Aid from People to People (DAPP), Farm Income Diversification Programme (FIDP) and many others.
    • ICRAF in collaboration with NASFAM, CRS and TLC have been active in scaling up Evergreen Agriculture (agroforestry based conservation agriculture) in Kasungu, Mchinji and Chiladzulu districts and also with NASFAM, Government of Malawi and Lake Malawi Basin project in implementing an AGRA project on CA in Kasungu, Lilongwe and Salima districts.
    • Farm demonstrations were set up on the use of old ridges and other CA practices and farmers showed interest in the practices.
      • Farmers indicated that the use of old ridges is easy to follow and is labour saving.
  • During planting period, the farmers should plant maize and agroforestry tree seeds in rows as recommended in specific areas.
    • However, the rule of thumb is that maize should be planted one seed per planting station spaced at 15 cm apart and the row should be made across the slope spaced at 75 cm apart.
    • It should be emphasized that row spacing was previously at 90 cm apart and this has been stopped because the current maize varieties do quite well at 75 cm apart.
  • The old ridge would die off as years go by.
  • The rain splash and human activity play a great role in levelling the maize field down.

_annotations.field_innovation_identified:
Conservation Agriculture with Trees (CAWT) / Evergreen Agriculture

Description: An integrated approach combining conservation agriculture principles with agroforestry practices, specifically adapted for smallholder farmers in Malawi and across Africa. It combines minimum tillage, permanent planting basins, maximum soil cover, and strategic integration of trees.

Innovation criteria met: It's an existing solution (conservation agriculture) modified and used in a new context (integration with agroforestry), creating an improved system that enhances soil fertility, water conservation, and crop productivity while supporting climate adaptation for smallholder farmers.
_annotations.field_shorter_description:
Evergreen Agriculture is a combination of conservation agriculture and agroforestry practices within the same spatial and temporal dimensions. In other circles, evergreen agriculture is referred to as agroforestry based conservation agriculture or Conservation Agriculture With Trees (CAWT). Evergreen agriculture is being tested by The World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF) in conjunction with partners in Malawi and across Africa as the means for enhancing soil fertility, increasing crop productivity and increasing food production.

This section will focus on the principles and practices of Conservation Agriculture (CA) as applied in maize production in Malawi. Conservation agriculture also improves the soil health and productivity as well as improves the crop production. ICRAF envisages that a combination of these two technologies together with other technologies will improve soil health and improve crop production and finally improves food security in Malawi.

records.title: A guide to construct and maintain net tunnels to protect quality sweet potato planting material from viruses carried by insects
records.description:
Description

1. Net tunnel

One of the major yield-limiting factors in sweet potato production is the lack of clean planting material owing to infection by sweet potato virus disease (SPVD). Viruses are diseases spread by insects (vectors such as whiteflies and aphids) that build up over time in the plants, reducing yields with each season. Some sweet potato varieties are more resistant to virus infection than others, showing less yield loss, and breeding programs in Africa focus on selecting for this very important trait. So-called susceptible varieties can disappear completely in one or two seasons in areas with high virus pressure. Research stations produce disease-free starter or pre-basic cuttings (vines) and protect them in expensive, large-screen houses. The much smaller net tunnel uses the same quality netting as the screen house, but is an affordable size for smallholder farmers wanting to maintain their own high-quality starter “seed”.

2. Net tunnel construction

2.1 Size of the tunnel

  • Height of the tunnel:1.40 m in the middle.
  • Length: Up to 3 m. 
  • Width:1.8 m wide at each side.

Larger tunnels can be built if the netting can be afforded.

  • Some farmers have made tunnels 10 m long.
  • But we highly recommend that each tunnel only has one variety to avoid mixing.

2.2 Material requirements per tunnel

  • Netting material.
    • For the top and long sides:4 m x 3.20 m.
    • For the front end: 2 m x 1.7 m.
    • For the back end: 2 m x 1.7 m.
    • Total amount of netting per tunnel: 19.6 m2
  • About 16 elastic wooden sticks, each 3.6 m long with a diameter of 4 cm.
  • Binding wire 5 m long; or, alternatively, sisal twine can be used, but the sisal twine has to be replaced every time you harvest the vines.

The most cost-effective way to purchase netting is in rolls.

  • We recommend the equivalent of OPTINET 50 mesh size netting sold in Kenya. 
  • One roll can make 15 net tunnels, measuring 3 m x 100 m, or 20 net tunnels, each measuring 4 m x 100 m.

3. Choosing the site for the construction of the tunnel

  • The site selected for rapid multiplication of planting material in a net tunnel should have fertile, easy-to-work, well-drained soils and be near a perennial source of water.
  • Avoid old sweet potato fields as these are potential sources of diseases and pests.

3.1 Size of the plot under one tunnel

  • The size of the bed should be 1.8 m x 4.8 m with a plant population of 360.
  • When soils are poor (e.g. sandy soils), plow in manure at a rate of one wheelbarrow load per square meter of bed space.

4. Construction steps

4.1 Step one: construction of the tunnel frame

  • Use seven 3.6 m long elastic wooden sticks (Figure 1).
  • Bend them and push them into the ground about 20 cm deep (Figure 2).
Figure 1. Choice of elastic wooden sticks

©FAO/TECA

  • As shown in Figure 2, the distance between the sticks on the sides should be 50 cm.
    • If you increase the tunnel length, reduce the distance between the sticks.
  • Put one vertical 1.7 m wooden sticks at each end (front and back) and one 3 m long stick on the top.
Figure 2. Putting up the structure using the elastic wooden sticks

©FAO/TECA

  • Use iron wire or sisal twine to connect the end sticks and all of the bent sticks to the 3 m long central stick to increase stability (Figure 2).
  • Figure 3 shows how four additional 3 m long sticks should be placed lengthwise on the sides and tied with iron wire at all of the joints with the bent sticks.
    • If such long sticks are not available, two shorter sticks can be joined, but they should overlap by at least 50 cm to be able to make a strong joint.
Figure 3. Improving the stability of the structure by reinforcing with more sticks

©FAO/TECA

4.2 Step two: sourcing and preparing the sweet potato cuttings

  • Source your cuttings from mother plants that have been tested and are known to be virus-free.
    • The most likely source will be the research station.
  • Note that on each vine you will see bumps.
    • These are called nodes, and each node can generate roots.
    • To get the most cuttings possible, cut up each vine into pieces that are two to three nodes in length (Figure 4).
    • Note that different varieties have different distances between their nodes.
Figure 4. Cutting showing leaves emerging from each of 3 nodes

©FAO/TECA

4.3 Step three: planting inside the tunnel

  • Within a row, leave 10 cm between each plant (Figure 5).
  • If using three-node cuttings, two nodes should go under the soil.
  • If you plan to cut every 80 days, leave 15 cm between the rows.
    • Then you will have 12 rows, 30 plants per row (plant population total of 360).
  • If you plan to cut less frequently, you can leave 20 cm between the rows and have nine rows with 30 plants per row (plant population total of 270).
Figure 5. Planting inside the tunnel

©FAO/TECA

4.4 Step four: covering the tunnel with the quality netting

  • Put the netting on top of the tunnel frame (Figure 6).
Figure 6. Covering the tunnel with the quality netting

©FAO/TECA

  • If you have a good tailor, have a heady duty zipper installed on one side of the tunnel.
    • Use a lock on the zipper to prevent theft (Figure 7).
Figure 7. Net tunnel with zipper to facilitate access

©FAO/TECA

  • Fix it to the structure with iron wire (Figure 8).
  • If the wire is covered in plastic, that will help prevent putting holes in the netting.
Figure 8. Using iron wire, seal the front and back netting pieces onto the frame

©FAO/TECA

  • Cut the netting so that there is an extra 20 cm extension of the netting beyond that which reaches the ground on all sides.
  • Leave at least a 10 cm allowance of extra netting at the front and back to connect with front and back cover.
  • Fix the net pieces at the front and back onto the netting on the top and the frame itself (Figure 9).
  • On each side, where the net tunnel touches the earth, place an elastic wooden sticklong the length of the respective side and then cover it with 20 cm of soil, to make it stormproof (Figures 9 and 10 )
  • Further support the structure’s stability by placing stakes in each outside corner.
    • Each of the four stakes (50 cm long; 20 mm diameter) should run horizontally through the net into the soil 40 cm deep.
    • The stakes should run through the net allowance which has been covered by soil. (Figure 10)
Figure 9. Construction of the net tunnel, including placing the supporting poles before adding the soil cover to make it stormproof

©FAO/TECA

Figure 10. A completely sealed net tunnel

©FAO/TECA

5. Care/cultural management practices of the tunnel beds

An integrated control strategy for effective insect management includes many features.

  • Preparing tunnel beds where the soil has been worked to be fine, without lumps.
  • Applying and incorporating mature farmyard manure or compost into the tunnel bed before planting, at a rate of 30 kg or 45 liters for one standard tunnel.
  • Removing weeds around the tunnels, since weeds serve as hosts for the insects.
  • Irrigating twice a day (early morning and late afternoon) with a 20 litre watering can without opening the tunnel-pour from the top through the net.
    • Note that watering is not necessary when it is raining.
    • You want to avoid waterlogged conditions caused by excessive watering;
  • Using mulching material to control weeds by spreading dried grass before planting on the prepared beds.
  • Ensuring that the beds do not become dry, especially during the first five days after planting.
  • Labelling each bed with the name of the variety and date of planting.
  • Ensuring that farm animals, such as goats and pigs, do not have access to the nursery.

6. Harvesting of cuttings from the tunnel

  • Depending on the growing conditions, harvesting can be done about 80 to 100 days from the time of planting or last cutting.
    • Be careful when opening the netting, so as not to damage it.
  • Cut apical (top) portions of vines (25 to 30 cm long), at least 10 cm above the soil level, leaving some nodes on the remaining stems (Figure 11).
    • These remaining stems will grow again.
  • If any type of NPK fertilizer is available, after each harvest of vine cuttings apply N:P:K (e.g. 17:17:17) fertilizer at a rate of 200 grams per net tunnel (which is equivalent to a level teacupful of fertilizer).
    • To apply, make a 2 cm deep furrow between the lines by using a stick, and apply the fertilizer evenly in the furrows.
  • After the fertilizer application, cover the furrows with soil.
  • After harvesting, spray the tunnel with an insecticide (against aphids and white-flies) before covering again.
    • You can apply insecticides based on organophosphorus, synthetic or natural pyrethroid active ingredients at the recommended rates on the package.
    • For example, the Duduthrin brand is a 1.75 EC synthetic pyrethroid, that you would apply at a rate of 10 g per 20 litres of water using a spray pack or hand sprayer.
Figure 11. Women harvesting vines inside the tunnel

©FAO/TECA

7. Economic benefits of using th etunnel

  • Using insect-proof netting attached to a simple tunnel far outweigh its cost. In 2011 in Kenya, the cost of one net tunnel (to build and maintain it), as described in this guide, was about USD 120.
  • To determine the benefits of the tunnel, we calculated the total number of vine cuttings produced from the tunnel and the yield of sweet potato roots from three different varieties planted with the planting material from the tunnels.
  • Then the total production was multiplied by the value of sweet potato roots in dollars.
  • This resulted in an average benefit of USD 839 (Table 1) obtained by using the insect-proofed net tunnel.
    • This was done by combining the accumulated effect of higher yields per unit area of planting material and root yields when using healthy vines from the net tunnel compared to vines not protected by the net tunnel.
Table 1. Dollar value of sweet potato roots from vines derived from 6 cuttings (over 33 months) from vines in net tunnels compared to vines outside the tunnels
Variety Exposed Net Tunnel Difference
Kemb 37 1054 2070 1016
SPK 004 924 1853 929
Zapallo 266 839 572
Average 748 1587 839

Source: CIP 2016

  • Note that among these three varieties, Zapallo is considered to be more virus susceptible than the other two.
Figure 12. Another way to close the tunnel is with manila string (shown on the right) which prevents holes being put in the net, but requires an extra 1.2 m of netting to construct 

©FAO/TECA

Figure 13. A very long net tunnel constructed at Umudike research station in Nigeria with more expensive metal poles. Note use of zipper

©FAO/TECA

8. Validation of the practice

  • Research conducted by the International Potato Center (CIP) and the Kenya Agriculture Research Institute (KARI) at Kakamega from 2009 to 2012 proved that the use of a properly managed net tunnel is very effective in maintaining virus-free planting material for at least 33 months.
  • Results showed, from the second cutting onwards, a significantly higher production of vine cuttings from material from the net tunnel when compared to planting material from the equivalent area that was not under the net tunnel.
  • Vines produced under tunnels produced much higher yields of roots than vines not protected under tunnels.
  • The technology has subsequently been tested by farmers in Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Mozambique and Nigeria with good results.
  • Key to success is assuring that any small hole in the netting is patched immediately, as the insects spreading viruses are very small.

9. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm.

10. Related/associated technologies 

  • Making sweet potato chips and flour: ID 6904.
  • Production of orange-fleshed sweet potato: ID 4373. 
  • Working with farmers to control sweet potato virus disease in East Africa: ID 4557.
  • Most serious insect pests affecting sweet potato: ID 6936.
  • The most serious sweet potato diseases in sub-Saharan Africa: ID 6937.

This technology is also avialble in Portuguese: ID 2650 and Spanish: ID 8651.

11. Objectives fulfilled by the project

11.1 Women-friendly

Sweet potato production in Africa is usually a woman's activity.

11.2 Resource use efficiency 

The practice allows for high-quality planting material with limited infection, and material multipliers, which continually renew planting material.

11.3 Pro-poor technology

The practice allows for the maintenance of sweet potato yields over time with positive financial benefits.

Description: An affordable, small-scale insect-proof net structure for smallholder farmers to maintain virus-free sweet potato planting material, consisting of a simple frame covered with specialized netting that protects plants from virus-carrying insects.

Innovation criteria met: It's a modified solution making an expensive technology (screenhouses) accessible to smallholder farmers, supports improved business models, and enhances inclusion by enabling women farmers to maintain crop yields and generate income.

records.title: Groundnut agronomic and postharvest practices
records.description:
Description

The groundnut is widely grown in Uganda as a food and cash crop. It is one of the highest paying crops with fairly stable prices. It is grown in nearly all parts of the country but especially in eastern Uganda and Northern regions. Household consumption is quite high with preferences to the brown/red-kenneled varieties because of their reputed taste. In addition, there is a huge informal trade at the borders. The Kenyan market demands small-white and big-white varieties.

It is a useful rotation crop. Being a legume, it can fix atmospheric nitrogen. It has the advantage of generating residual nitrogen in the soil which benefits subsequent crops, especially when groundnut residues are incorporated into the soil during ploughing. Thus maintains soil fertility. It also controls soil erosion.

All parts of the plant can be put to use. The plant stalks are fed to cattle in the form of green, dried and silage. The groundnut shell, haulms and hay are good fodder. Groundnut cake is a good feed for livestock and it is also used as manure

Because of the importance of groundnut, the demand far exceeds output. Thus the need to increase yields and acreages. Well managed plots and high yielding varieties could go a long way to achieve this.

1. Improved groundnuts varieties and the recommended practices

The National Agricultural Research Organization (NARO), whose mandate institution is the Serere Agricultural and Animal Research Institute (SAARI) based in Soroti, released a number of groundnut varieties. These are shown in the table below. 

Table 1. Improved varieties of groundnuts

Source: FAO 2010

Table 2. Recommended agronomic practices

Source: FA0 2010

Table 3. Recommended agronomic practices continued

Source: FAO 2010

 2.  Postharvest handling processing practices of groundnut

2.1 Timing for harvesting

  • It is very important to harvest groundnuts at the correct time.
    • If harvested too early, the seeds will shrink when drying which lowers the oil content and quality of the seed.
    • Delays in harvesting will result in poor quality seed due to mould infections and subsequent aflatoxin contamination of the seeds/pods.
    • Late harvesting also reduces yield because higher proportions of pods are left in the ground due to the pegs being weak and the pods breaking off.
    • If harvested late, some non-dormant varieties will begin to sprout in the field resulting in yield losses. 

2.2 Indicators for harvesting time

  • A proper time to commence the harvest is when a good number of pods are fully developed and are fairly intact.
    • The maturity of pods is normally achieved when the vine begins to turn yellow and leaf shedding starts.
    • It is recommended that a few plants (three to five) should be pulled up and the pods removed and shelled.
    • The insides of the shells should be examined.
    • If the majority of pods (70 percent upwards) have dark markings inside the shell and the seeds are plump and the correct colour for that variety, then the groundnuts are mature and ready for harvest.
    • The estimated period of maturity for each variety can be used as a rough guide.
  • A proper time to commence the harvest is when a good number of pods are fully developed and are fairly intact.

2.3 Other considerations for harvesting

  • If leaf spots or other diseases are a problem in the field, do not delay harvest.
  • If there is a weather forecast that would delay the harvest, this must be taken into account.
  • Harvest must be done when sufficient labour and adequate equipment are available.
  • Failure of peg strength and well-filled pods with pink seed coat indicate maturity in large-seeded Virginia type.
  • Signs of weakening peg strength indicate an immediate need for harvest if excessive losses are to be avoided.
  • Check groundnut crop closely as the average number of days to maturity approaches. Shells with dark interior indicate harvest maturity.

2.4 Harvesting

  • The actual method of harvest employed depends upon the type of groundnut grown.
  • Harvesting by hand only is more suitable for erect groundnut varieties in sandy, loam soils that are well-drained.
  • In bunch types, pod development is confined to the base of the plant and the pegs carrying the pods into the soil are thick and strong.
  • Almost all the pods are recovered with the plants when they are pulled out of the soil.
    • That is why the bunch type of groundnut is mostly harvested by pulling out the plants with manual labour.

  • It is important to shake the plant after lifting to remove excess soil from the pods, particularly when the soil is wet or heavy.
  • Soil stuck to the pods will lengthen drying times and produce better conditions for the development of unwanted fungal growth.

2.6 Drying

  • The correct drying or curing of the harvested groundnuts is very important as poor curing can help induce fungal growth (producing aflatoxin contamination) and reduce seed quality for consumption, marketing and germination for the following seasons planting.
  • For good storage and germination, the moisture content of the pods should be reduced to 6 to 8 percent.
  • There are different ways of drying the pods, some of which are better than others.
  • It is particularly important to note that if the pods are exposed to the sun for too long the seed quality can deteriorate considerably and germination can be affected.

2.7 Drying in windows

  • If the harvested groundnut plant is left to dry on the soil surface where they have been lifted, the pod are likely to be in contact with the soil, which can contain moisture and be at a higher temperature.
    • This method can easily affect the quality of the seed, particularly if there is rain during the drying period.
  • If field drying is used, it is better to use windows, where plants are laid in rows to catch the wind and dry more quickly.
  • The drying of pods in windows (three to five days) should produce the required level of moisture before the pods are picked or stripped.
    • Excessive exposure to the sun can affect the quality of the seed.

  • The plants can be picked/plucked from the window and then laid out in a thin layer in the sun on dry ground, matting or other dry surfaces for a further two to five days which would normally dry the pods to the required moisture content for storing.
  • Pods should be covered or taken indoors during wet weather.

  • Ideally, pods should be dried with plenty of air circulation and in the shade.
  • Two principal methods are used elsewhere in Africa, both of which can produce good quality seed with reduced levels of fungal infection. After two to three days of wilting in the field in windows, the plants should be dried using one of the following. 
    • Cock
      • Plants are laid, with foliage, directly on the ground in a circle 1-2 m in diameter, the pods placed towards the inner part of the circle.
      • Layers of plants are built up, gradually reducing the diameter of the circles as the cock gets higher until there is a small opening left at the top of the cock.
      • Foliage (e.g. banana leaves) can be used to cover the top of the cock.
      • The cock should be built on the raised ground so that the lower parts do not get waterlogged if it rains during drying.
      • Polythene should not be used for the base of the cock as this reduces drainage in the case of rain, and also should not be as a cover as a built-up of condensation can occur. 
    • A-Frame
      • The wilted plants are gathered and stacked on an A-frame with the pods facing inwards and away from the soil.
      • A-frames are easy to construct using three thick poles as a base with thin poles attached to either side of the main poles of the A-frame forming shelves on to which the wilted plants can be placed.

  • In both cases, the groundnut should normally be left to dry for three to four weeks before the pods are picked.
    • After picking do not dry further by putting the pods into the sun as this could result in over-drying or a reduction in seed quality.

  • After proper curing and drying, the pods are separated from the plants.
  • This operation is called stripping or plucking.
    • Stripping of pods is done manually by the small farmers.
    • Also, groundnuts meant for seed purpose are stripped manually.
    • The hand removal of pods from the plants (plucking) can be labour intensive.

3. Storage

  • It is best to store groundnuts in their shells.
  • Good drying of the pods to 7 to 8 percent moisture content will help to ensure that the seeds remain in good condition during storage.
  • Never bag groundnuts for storage when the pods are still dump.
  • Before storing, poor, damaged shrivelled, rotten, or fungus-infected pods should be removed.

      • When pests damage the pods/seeds, they create the condition for the build-up of fungal infection.
      • Insect storage pests can be controlled using pirimiphos-methyl (Actellic super) applied as a dust to the pods before bagging.

  • Shelling should be done as and when groundnut seeds are required for consumption, marketing or for planting as the storage life of the seed outside the shell is short and the quality can reduce rapidly.

      • Hand shelling is labour intensive but is effective for small quantities of groundnuts.
      • It is particularly good for the selection of seed for planting the following season as there is less damage to the seeds, thus avoiding fungal infections. 
  • The practice of putting pods into sacks and beating them to break them up is not recommended as this can produce a high level of damaged seeds.
    • Mechanical shellers
      • There are a number of mechanical hand shellers on the market that can shell groundnuts at a rate of up to six bags an hour.
      • The rotary types have the advantage of continuous operation (rather than shelling in batches) and new designs produce very little wastage in terms of damaged seed.

5.  Aflatoxin problem in groundnut

5.1  What are aflatoxins?

Aflatoxins are toxic substances produced by certain fungi called Aspergillus flavus and Apergillus parasiticus. The word “ aflatoxin” derived as:

  • "A" stands for aspergillus; 
  • ''fla" for flavus; and 
  • "toxin" for poison.

5.2.1 Pre-harvest

During pre-harvest, there are many factors contributing to contamination.

  • End of season moisture stress to the crop for more than 20 days.
  • Growth cracks and mechanical injury to the pod.
  • Insects damage to pods by termites or pod borers.
  • Death caused by diseases (stem, root, and pod rots) at pod maturity stage.
  • Nematodes damage to the pod.

5.2.2 Post-harvest
