records.title: Improvements of traditional floating gardens for vegetable production
records.description:
Description

1. Introduction

  • Floating garden agriculture (locally known as vasoman/dhap chash) is a local innovative crop production technology for the submerged ecosystems of the southern region of Bangladesh.
    • Traditionally, farmers of the Gopalganj, Pirojpur and Barisal districts have been practicing the farming technology for about two centuries as an adaptation to the flooded/submerged conditions.
  • For a detailed description of the traditional practice please refer to the TECA technology: "Traditional floating garden practices for vegetable production", technology ID 8867.
  • In the traditional system, farmers generally cultivate only a limited number of crops like red amaranth, Indian spinach, okra, turmeric and aroid crops on floating beds during monsoon season (generally from June to November month).
    • The traditional floating beds are not suitable for cultivating cucurbits or different creeper type of vegetable crops because it is not wide enough but rather narrow shaped (breadth 1.1 m to 1.3 m).
  • Vegetables, particularly cucurbits and creeper/vine types of vegetable crops, generally need sufficient space due to their large canopy size and vigorous growth habit.
    • The crops grown on the traditional floating beds do not have the required space for their proper growth and development.
    • Hence, only a few numbers of plants can be grown on the bed due to lack of required space on the floating bed.
  • In addition, the fruits are grown next to the floating beds and they often fade in colour but the opposite side remains green due to uneven absorption of sunlight.
    • This also deteriorates the market value of the agro-products.
    • Moreover, there is more rat infestation in cucurbits or creeper vegetables grown on floating beds which damages the flowers as well as fruits of the crops severely.
  • Considering the above facts, research programmes were undertaken at the Regional Agricultural Research Station, Rahmatpur, Barisal of Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute (BARI) to improve the traditional floating garden agriculture practices for growing cucurbits or creeper type of vegetable crops successfully.
    • Recently improved, technology-based, floating garden practices for cultivating cucurbits or different types of creeper vegetable crops are termed as Floating Bed cum Trellis (FBT).
  • The FBT system constructs alternate floating beds and trellis.
    • With the FBT method, cucurbits or creeper vegetables can be planted on the floating beds but they grow and develop on wide trellises (width 3 to 6 m) constructed just next to the floating beds (Figure 1 and Figure 2).
    • Therefore, as per the requirement for the optimum crop growth, 3 m to 6 m distance is kept between two floating bed for making the trellis.
    • This ultimately also reduces the usage of water hyacinth for floating garden practices.
    • The trellis is generally made with bamboo, nylon net and dhaincha (Sesbania sp.)
Figure 1. Bottle guard cultivation on Floating Bed cum Trellis (FBT) in the research area for Floating Agriculture

©BARI

Figure 2. Fruits of cucumber (a), bottle gourd (b), and pumpkin (c) hanging under the trellis

©BARI

2. Improvements 

2.1 Increased production and higher yields 

  • Under this system, it is possible to grow a number of plants on the floating bed which increases the yield of the crops.
  • Besides, fruits of vegetable plants get uniform shape and colour due to an adequate supply of nutrients and sunlight.
  • In an experiment, hybrid cucumber gave the fruit yield of about 45 to 50 tonnes per ha under FBT method.
    • The same crop generally gives the yield of about 25 to 35 tonnes per ha under normal land condition.
    • This indicated that hybrid cucumber cultivated through FBT technology provided about double yield as compared to that of normal land condition.

2.2 ​Increased land-use efficiency​ 

  • In the FBT method, different short duration vegetables like red amaranth, spinach, radish, coriander leaf can be grown on a floating bed at the early stage of the cucurbits (Figure 3).
  • This increases the production of vegetables as well as cropping intensity over the traditional practices. 
Figure 3. Cultivation of red amaranth (a) and spinach (b) at an early stage of bottle gourd cultivation

©BARI

2.3 Reduced amount of water hyacinth 

  • The availability of water hyacinth is decreasing day by day in Bangladesh due to various reasons (salinity, lack of conservation, etc.).
  • However, the improved FBT technology utilized 50 to 60 percent less amount of water hyacinth as compared to the traditional floating garden system. 

2.4 Contribution to food and nutritional security of the poor 

  • The total area of medium-low to the very low type of land in Bangladesh is about 3.0 million hectares (21 percent of the total country) and a remarkable amount of the land remains fallow particularly in the monsoon season due to flooding or submerged conditions.
  • Generation of floating agriculture-based suitable modern technologies like Floating Bed cum Trellis (FBT), through intensive research programmes and extension/dissemination of the technologies, can utilize the wet/flooded lands for crop production.
    • This would improve the food and nutritional security of the vulnerable poor people in wetland/flooded areas of Bangladesh.
  • Currently, a good number of research programmes are going on at Regional Agricultural Research Station, Rahmatpur, Barisal of BARI cultivation of pumpkin, bottle gourd, potato, cole crops (cabbage, cauliflower, knolkhol, broccoli etc.), carrot, watermelon, strawberry, chili, bush bean etc. on floating bed (Figure 4).  
Figure 4. Cultivation of potato (a), carrot (b), cabbage (c), cauliflower (d) and bushbean (e) on floating bed

©BARI

3. Validation of the practice 

  • The FBT system has been tested during two cropping seasons, under the on-station condition at Regional Agricultural Research Station, Rahmatpur, Barisal of Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute (BARI). 

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies 

  • ​​Traditional floating garden practices for vegetable production: ID 8867.
  • ​Traditional floating garden practices for seedling production: ID 8869​.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

6.1 Resource-use efficiency

This innovative crop production technology allows for crops to be effectively grown in submerged ecosystems, where they wouldn't be able to do so under normal circumstances.

records.title: Increasing yield of mango with selective harvest
records.description:
Description

1. Introduction

Harvesting of mangoes at incorrect timing results in a loss of yield of mangoes: the mangoes are either too ripe or not ripe enough. This loss is further increased due to the damages caused to the mango while plucking. The farmers usually pluck all the mangoes when most of the fruits are ready for harvest. However, the mango flowers grow at different times and hence the fruits also do not mature at the same time. Hence at the harvest, nearly 50 percent of the fruits are at the right maturity level while the remaining 50 percent are either over-ripened or under-ripened. As a consequence, the farmers lose nearly half the income due to rejection of the fruits which are not at the correct maturity level. The fruits which are not matured yet will never ripen since they lack the nutrients from the mother plant while the over-ripened mangoes will spoil very quickly. In addition, leaving over-ripened mangoes on the trees is dangerous; they attract birds, fruit flies and diseases onto the farm. Using selective harvest techniques, the mango harvest can be done in different stages in an organized way which is very promising in increasing the yields of the harvest. The fruits can be classified roughly into three different maturity levels; the farmer can mark the branches with different colour tags where flowers appear at the same time for convenience during harvest. At the beginning of the flowering season, the farmer can attach red flags to branches with the first flowers. Branches with the next batch of flowers can be marked yellow and the last batch with green flags. The dates of flowering needs to be recorded by the farmer.

Figure 1. Farmer recording the dates of the flowering of buds and marks the branches with different colour tags 

©GIZ

The mangoes can be harvested in three different sessions by judging the maturity of the fruits, e.g. selectively harvesting only matured fruits in a session. For the first session, the farmers can harvest the fruits from the branches marked red depending upon the type and date of planting. For the second session, the fruits on the branches marked yellow can be harvested after seven to ten days depending upon the maturity level. For the last session of the harvest, the branches marked with green flags can be harvested seven to ten days after the second harvest. The fruits on the branches with similar colour tags will mature roughly at the same time. Although maturity tests should be performed for a good harvest. 

 ​2. Assessing the right harvesting moment by carrying out the maturity test​ 

  • The maturity level of the mangoes can be assessed by two methods.
    1. The preliminary
    2. The destructive analysis
  • The preliminary check can be performed using visual aid while the destructive check requires cutting open the fruit.
  • After a preliminary non-destructive maturity test, a few samples from the similar batch are checked for destructive assessment of matured fruits. 
Figure 2. Image depicting panicle drop in matured mangoes 

©GIZ

  • On the fruit skin, there are tiny spots present known as lenticels.
  • These lenticels are brown for a matured fruit.
  • For un-ripened fruits, these lenticels are either white or yellow. 
Figure 3. Image depicting brown lenticels of the ripe mango 

©GIZ

After reaching maturity, the stalk (hanging point of the fruit) begins to dry since it no longer requires nutrients from the mother plant. 

Figure 4. Image depicting dried up stalk of the ripe mango 

©GIZ

 2.2 Destructive maturity assessment 

  • The destructive maturity assessment consists of two tests.
    1. To check the Brix level (e.g. sugar content)
      • To check the Brix level of the mango, a refractometer is required.
      • The fruit needs to be cut into three parts as shown below. 
Figure 5a. Mango cut in three equal parts (a) through the seed 

Figure 5b. Mango cut in three equal parts (b) middle of edge and the seed

©GIZ

The juice of the part cut in Figure 5(b) is poured on the refractometer and directed towards the sun.

Figure 6. The mango juice being tested on a refractometer for sugar content 

©GIZ

The refractometer scale gives the Brix level of the fruit. Higher values indicate more sweetness. Usually, for a Brix level of greater than 9 degrees, the fruit is considered mature. 

Figure 7. Brix scale inside the refractometer. Meter indicates a Brix level of 6: the mango is not ripe 

©GIZ

2.3 To check the internal colour

A colour chart ranging from white to deep yellow is often used to determine the different growth stages of the fruit. The remaining part of the mango (cut to check the Brix level) is matched against the chart to determine the exact state of the maturity of mango. The colour of the matured fruit varies depending upon the variety of the mango. 

Figure 8. A typical colour chart to check the maturity of mango 

©GIZ

Brix level and colour chart value help to determine the exact maturity level of your fruits. The specific values of brix level and colour chart indicator differ depending upon the requirement of the buyers (for local consumption, import or for the manufacture of fruit juices or dry fruits). Hence, the requirements of the buyer need to be checked before the harvesting season arrives and harvest should be planned accordingly. 

3. Reduce damage by using the right picking pole 

  • Once the fruits to be picked are selected, they should be plucked without causing any harm to the fruit.
  • Many farmers currently use a hook on the end of a stick to hook the mango and pull it so that the mangoes are dropped from the tree into the ground.
  • The fruits dropped from above 2 m of height suffer internal cracks often unnoticed by the farmers from the outside.
  • Upon coming in contact with the ground, the chances of fungal infections in the fruit also increase.
  • Hence proper picking poles that are able to hold the mangoes should be used. 
Figure 9. A man using a picking pole for mango harvest

 

©GIZ

  • The mangoes should then be gently transferred into a plastic crate. 
Figure 10. Women in Ghana carrying mangoes in a plastic crate 

©GIZ

  • The mangoes stored in such crates have proper ventilation and thus there are fewer chances of damage.
    • The picking poles should be disinfected with spirit or alcohol before use to avoid spreading diseases.
    • These practices improve the hygienic standard of the harvest. 
  • The selective harvesting technique is labour-intensive and requires an initial investment on correct harvesting tools but this limitation can be easily defeated by the added benefits of the higher yields.
    • This method of harvesting allows the farmer to harvest mangoes at the right time of maturity.
    • This increases the yield of mangoes to nearly twice which is a major economic benefit to the farmers in terms of increased income.
  • Also increased quality of the fruit through improved picking practices can receive a higher price for the fruit sold to the suppliers.
  • This technique also reduces the chance of spreading diseases through an over-ripened mango.
  • Farmers growing mangoes in every part of the world can benefit from this technique to harvest the mango.

4. Validation of the practice 

  • ​This improved harvesting technique has been tested with mango farmers in Ghana. 

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Intercropping drought-tolerant fruit trees (Mango and Jujube) in rice based farming systems: ID 6854.
  • Controlling mango fruit fly: ID 6920.
  • Processing mango and guava nectar: ID 7150.
  • Video on how to prune a mango tree: ID 8237.
  • Anthracnose control for mango farmers: ID 8466.
  • Bacterial Black Spot (BBS) identification and control for mango farmers: ID 8470.
  • Fruit fly control for mango farmers: ID 8471.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

7.1 Resource-use efficiency

The technology provides efficient methods to improve mango harvesting properly and reduce post-harvest losses. 

7.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology, through the reduction of post-harvest losses, increases yield, thereby providing additional sources of food and income.

records.title: Soya and other leguminous crops
records.description:
Description

1. Cultivation requirements for legumes

1.1 Suitable areas

Legumes and soya can be grown under a wide range of agroclimatic conditions. 

1.1.1 Upland river terraces and hills where shifting cultivation takes place

Shifting cultivation is a system in which farmers cut down an area of trees, burn the remaining vegetation and use the land they have cleared for agriculture. The ash from the burned material contains a lot of nutrients, so the soil is fertile and in the first season crops with high nutrient requirements can be grown. In the following seasons other crops are grown.

Figure 1. Example of shifting cultivation where not all trees have been felled

@CTA

1.1.2 Lowland along rivers and coastal areas where rice is often grown

The soils in these areas are surrounded by rivers. Coastal areas where mangroves used to grow are often not suitable for legumes as they are too acid once they have dried out after the rice harvest. Other soils in these areas which are not subjected to salt water are less acid and more suitable for agriculture. If these areas are submerged under water during the rainy season, rice is the only crop that can be grown. If the water recedes after the rice harvest, legumes can be grown as a second crop, making use of the moisture that remains in the soil. If it is possible to irrigate, the land can also be used in the dry season.

1.1.3 Highland areas

Many legume food crops are grown at altitudes above 1 000 m. Highland areas are characterized by low temperatures, dryness and a relatively short growing season. The fields are often small, which makes it difficult to use machines. Farmers work the land by hand or using animal traction. Legumes are grown on their own or in combination with other crops such as maize. The yields are often low, but the beans are an important source of protein for many families. Legumes such as chickpeas, peas, broad beans and lentils are grown in areas where the soils are poor because they are resistant to drought, and the crop remains can be used as animal feed.

Erosion is a common problem in these marginal areas. In some areas farmers work the land in such a way as to ensure that the ridges run horizontally as far as possible, following the contour lines. Rainwater is caught by the ridges and so seeps down slowly into the soil. If the ridges are made that follow the slope, rainwater runs off quickly, taking soil with it and causing erosion. If the rainfall is very heavy the soil cannot always absorb the water quickly enough. The water will then flow over the ridges, breaking them and causing serious erosion. In areas where this is a problem it is better to build the ridges diagonally over the slopes, so that some of the water is caught and can seep into the soil, and the rest can run off.

In the Bolivian highlands, where the amount of rainfall varies a lot, traditional methods are used to try and predict how much rain is likely to fall. If a lot of rain is expected the ridges are dug so that they run more in the direction of the slope; if less rain is expected the ridges are made so that they run more or less parallel with the contour lines.

1.2 Climate

1.2.1 Cool climates with cold periods at high latitudes or in higher areas of the tropics

Beans grown in moderate climates come from western Asia and the Mediterranean, where they have been grown for thousands of years. These include lentils (Lens culinaris), peas (Pisum sativa), kidney beans (Phaseolus sp.) and chickpeas (Cicer arietinum). The cultivation of these crops spread over time to the Indian subcontinent and China. Peas and broad beans (Vicia faba) also spread northwards to the cooler areas of northern Europe, and later were also taken to North and South America, Australia and South Africa. They are also found in highland areas of African countries such as Ethiopia and Kenya.

1.2.2 Humid tropical climates

Soya (Glycine max) and pigeon peas (Cajanus cajan) are suitable for warm, humid climates.

1.2.3 Hot arid climates

Cowpea (Vigna inguiculata), green gram (Vigna aureus), black gram (Vigna mungo) and groundnut (Arachis hypogaea) can tolerate extreme dryness and high temperatures. Groundnuts, for example, are grown in semi-arid and low-humid tropical areas of Africa, Southeast Asia and Central America between 30° North and 30° South.

1.2.4 Adaptation to cold

Much soya is grown in areas with temperatures around 25°C to 30°C. It seems that night-time temperature has a greater influence on the crop than daytime temperature. If the night-time temperature falls below the critical level of 10°C the crop will undergo more damage than if the night-time temperature stays above 10°C, regardless of the optimal daytime temperature range of 25°C to 30°C.

1.2.5 Water requirements

Soya has two critical periods concerning water requirements: from sowing to germination, and the period during which the beans grow in the pods. Before a seed can germinate it needs to absorb 50 percent of its weight in water. Nevertheless during the germination phase too much water causes more damage than too little water. The soil needs to be between 50 percent and 85 percent saturated with water. The amount of water needed increases as the crop grows, reaching its maximum as the beans develop in the pods (7 to 8 mm per day), and then decreases again. To be sure of a good yield, soya needs between 450 and 800 mm water each day during its whole growth cycle, depending on the climate. In high temperatures more water evaporates, so more rainfall is needed to provide the crop with enough water.

1.3 Varieties and cultivars

Farmers often know a lot about local varieties and the conditions under which they grow well. They often grow different varieties of the same crop in order to spread their risks. If a field sown with one variety suffers damage in the form of disease, pests or bad weather, it is still possible that a field with a different variety will suffer less from the problems.

Day-length sensitivity will determine the choice of legume made, not only the type but also the variety.

1.3.1 Soya

Soya is a short-day plant, and is sensitive to day length. It flowers when the day length is shorter than 16 hours. Short-cycle varieties flower 30 to 35 days after sowing and ripen within 75 to 105 days. These varieties have low yields. The middle-length varieties also flower 30 to 35 days after sowing and mature within 110 to 140 days. These have good yields. The long-cycle varieties produce a large amount of leaf material.

In integrated farming systems where livestock are raised this soya leaf material is an attractive form of animal feed; it is easily digestible and contains a lot of protein. In Ivory Coast (West Africa) short-cycle varieties do better because the rainy season is short.

1.4 Soil

1.4.1 Soil conditions

Legumes grow in different soils, even very acid soils (up to pH 3.8).

  • Groundnuts and Bambara groundnuts (Vigna subterranea) grow in poor sandy soils and loamy soils, but also in clay soils such as vertisols, although harvesting the pods from under the ground is difficult. While groundnuts grow well in chalky soils, Bambara groundnuts do not. Good drainage is important, especially for Vigna and Phaseolus types.
  • The butterbean (Lablab purpureus) has deep roots, which enable it to grow better on badly draining soils than most legumes. The butterbean however does not do well in saline (salty) soils. Generally speaking, legumes do not do well on salty soils, although there are a few exceptions: pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan) and pea.
  • Soya:
    • grows best in soils that are not too light and not too heavy in texture;
    • grows well in soils with high organic-material content;
    • prefers a pH of between 5.8 and 7.8, and does not like alkaline or acid extremes; and
    • does not tolerate saline soils.
Figure 2. If the soil has the correct degree of acidity (pH) the crop and its root nodules will develop well

@CTA

Figure 3. Examples of different types of soils and their effects on the growth of soya

@CTA

1.4.2 Improving soil fertility

Figures from Bolivia show that maize and wheat grown after soya can have an increase in yield of up to 22 percent. Where legumes are used as green manure, maize yields are clearly higher than maize grown after a short fallow period where nothing is grown. If soya is grown for use as green manure, where the whole crop is dug under, it can increase soil fertility by up to 200 kg nitrogen per hectare. Soya dug in in this way also improves the texture of the soil because the crop residue contributes organic material.

If soya is grown as part of a mixed cropping system it is important to ensure that nitrogen given to the other crop in the form of artificial fertilizer does not come into contact with the roots of the soya. Soya will not fix nitrogen (or only very little) if there is nitrogen present in the soil (in this case from the artificial fertilizer).

When the remains of the soya and other crops are dug into the soil together, the nitrogen-rich soya remains will ensure that the organic material in the soil is broken down quickly. This will increase the amount of nutrients in the soil by more than if the remains are dug in separately.

2. Integrating legumes into existing farming systems

2.1 Livestock keeping

Two ways of integrating legumes with livestock keeping.

  • When the beans have been harvested the crop residue is used as animal feed for the livestock kept in the village, e.g. cattle or buffalo. The dung from the animals is used to fertilize the land together with the crop remains left in the soil, which increases the nitrogen content of the soil.
  • You can also let livestock graze in a mixed crop of a legume and grain. For example, you let the animals eat half of the legume crop. Animals will first eat legumes because they contain a lot of protein, which means they will leave the grain crop undisturbed. As they eat the legumes, nitrogen will be released which is good for the grain crop, such as maize. The animals convert the nitrogen in the soya into urine and dung. The nitrogen in the urine is immediately taken up by the grain crop.

2.2 Mixed/rotational cropping systems in Asia

The main leguminous crop in Asia is soya, so the examples below all refer to this crop. Soya is usually sown in the dry season, after rice, wheat or maize while the soil still contains sufficient moisture, or where irrigation is possible. Soya is also often intercropped with maize or sorghum.

Figure 4. Example of rotational cropping: in the first year fields 1 and 2 are cultivated (A). In the following year all crops move round one field, so fields 2 and 3 are cultivated (B).

@CTA

In Indonesia a similar system at 6°N yields 700 kg soya per hectare. The soya is sown at the end of the rains in February or March, or just after the rains have stopped in April. If the rains are to be used for the legume crop, then sowing is done in July/August just before the first rains start, so that the seed is ready to benefit from the rains that start in September. The harvest takes place at the end of the rainy season, between December and April or in the dry season at the end of June, depending on when the soya was sown. If the seed is sown in the dry season, the crop starts to grow during the rains and it takes one or two months longer before it can be harvested.

In Thailand yields up to 1 200 kg per hectare are harvested at a latitude of 15°N. In this area most soya is sown during the rains between April and July. Where there is irrigation, soya is sown at the beginning of the dry season in December. In Taiwan a similar system of cultivation is used at 23°N and yields of 1 500 kg per hectare are achieved. Here the dry season is from November to May and the rains fall between May and October.

2.3 Mixed/rotational cropping systems in Africa

In Uganda legumes are grown in various shifting cultivation systems. A number of crop systems in which different legumes are grown are listed in Table 1.

Table 1. Crop systems used in Uganda (from: Grain Legumes in Africa, FAO 1966: 61)

The legumes in this example are not cultivated on ridges, and they are not irrigated. Reading the table it can be seen that groundnuts are grown as sole crop, but are also grown between other crops (intercropping), usually maize or cotton. Groundnuts are the first or second crop grown after a fallow period. Optimal spacing has also been calculated: if the groundnuts are the sole crop and the soil is worked using animal traction it is best to allow 40 to 60 cm between the rows and 15 cm between plants within the rows. If the work is done by hand it is better to have crop spacing of 30 cm x 30 cm.

2.4 Labour requirements

Table 2 below gives an indication of the amount of time in hours needed to cultivate one hectare of soya (monoculture).

Table 2. Labour required (in hours) to cultivate one hectare of soya

Sowing soya by hand is very labour intensive. The sowing density must be very high to ensure a good yield. The only way to keep weeds down is by letting the soya plants cover the whole of the ground. Most other leguminous crops have a wider branching pattern, which means that the sowing density is lower. Other legumes therefore take less time to sow.

3.1 Storage of beans and seed selection

  • Storing seeds in ash of the neem tree and treating seeds with a neem tree solution had good results.
  • Plastic bags which can be hermetically sealed (made airtight) can be used to store soya beans (at least those to be used as seed material). The beans must be well dried (less than 11 percent water in the bean) and the plastic bags must be carefully sealed.
  • To ensure 90 percent germination capacity then it is a good idea to keep seed in cool storage places.
    • Experiments in Senegal and Cameroon show that seed stored under these conditions for nine months retains 90 percent of its germination capacity.
    • In Guyana seeds can only be stored for six months before they lose their germination capacity.
    • In all three countries seeds which are kept in cold storage places maintain 90 percent of their germination capacity for nine months.
    • In the high lands of Madagascar it is not necessary to store seed in cool houses because the temperatures are low enough anyway. Plastic bags are also not necessary for storing the seed.

3.2 Plant density

Plants spaced not too far apart will grow less tall, are less likely to be flattened by wind or rain and will have more branches. They also form more pods with heavier beans, which means a bigger yield per plant. Where the plant density is low and plants are far apart, the yield for the whole field will be relatively low. If there is a lot of space between plants, weeds will be a problem. It is important to find the optimal plant density. This can vary even for the same place, depending on the season. The sowing density has to be adjusted in areas where day length varies depending on the time of the year.

Figure 6. Optimal planting distance: 15 to 18 plants in a row one metre long. Too few plants: 6 tp 8 plants in a row. Too many plants: 20 to 30 plants in a row. The distance between the rows is 30 to 60 cm.

@CTA

3.3 Sowing period

The following climate requirements must be taken into account for deciding when to sow:

  • temperature required for the seed to germinate
  • period when water will be available
  • correct day length during the flowering period.

The table below shows how the time at which soya is sown determines the crop yield.

Table 3. Sowing date and yield obtained

Source: ICARDA/IFPRI Report, 1990

3.4 No-tillage cropping

Using a stick or a knife holes are made in the ground at the foot of the mounds upon which the previous crop grew. The soya seeds are planted in the holes. Soya is planted in this way after a rice crop.

In Taiwan the same field is used for two rice crops and one soya crop. The soya yield varies between 1.5 and 2 tons per hectare. The soya takes 85 to 100 days to ripen.

3.5 Weed control

The most critical period is between the 15th and the 35th day after sowing. If you only start weeding after the 35th day, the yields will be lower.

The best way to fight weeds is by encouraging the growth and develop- ment of the crop as much as possible so that it does better than the weeds. Below is a list of ways to do this.

  • crop rotation; i.e. do not grow crops of the same family on the same piece of land after each other;
  • use ground cover plants;
  • prepare the soil well before planting;
  • sow at the right time; and
  • make sure the sowing density is correct.

It is also possible to control weeds using machinery. Often it is enough to do this two or three times during a crop cycle: the first time should be from two weeks after the crop has germinated and the last time up to 45 days after germination or just before the crop flowers. A machine should not be used during or after flowering as it can pull the flowers off the plant, which will lead to lower yields.

In countries where weeding is done by hand, such as in Senegal, it is best to weed five times during the first six weeks. The importance of weeding is easy to see in the table below, which is based on trials done in Senegal.

Table 4. The effect of good weeding on yield

Source: ICARDA/IFPRI Report, 1990

3.6 Pests

3.6.1 Insects

Insects damage leads to reduced yields, however the use of insecticides is not recommended. It is only worth using insecticides if you can reduce your crop losses by more than the costs of using insecticide. In order to be able to estimate accurately whether this is possible you have to inspect your crop regularly. You can do this by laying down a sheet measuring 100 cm x 70 cm between the rows and then shaking the plants on both sides so that the insects fall off.

  • If more than 30 to 40 caterpillars fall onto the sheet or if more than 35 percent of the plants are seriously damaged it is worth fighting the caterpillars.
  • Insects that attack leaves with their mouthparts should be controlled if there are more than two adults found per metre of a row.
  • Caterpillars that bite through stems of the plants must be controlled if 20 to 25 percent or more of the plants are damaged.

3.6.2 Nematodes

Nematodes are small worms that damage the roots. The effects of nematode damage are yellow leaves, stunted growth even though soil fertility is good, and wilting even though there is enough water in the soil. The best way to control nematodes is to plant resistant varieties and to use crop rotation.

3.7 Diseases

Most diseases are transferred through the seed. It is therefore very important that you use seed that is free of disease pathogens, or treat seeds chemically so that they become free of disease. This way you can prevent losses or reduce them to a minimum.

3.8 Harvesting legumes

Harvesting must be done at the correct time.

  • If harvesting is done by hand, when the leaves first start to turn yellow, it is best to cut down the plants and spread them to dry in a place where it is easy to collect the beans as they fall out of the pods. Once the plants have dried they can be threshed. Where not all plants ripen at the same time the beans should be harvested from the plants that ripen first, while the other plants are left standing to ripen further. This spreads the harvesting work out over a longer period, which also means there are no peaks in labour requirements which can be a difficult problem.
  • If you harvest with a machine you have to be very careful that it does not cause damage. Damaged beans cannot be kept for long, sell for less money and are less suitable for seed material. The optimal moisture content during harvest for soya that is going for industrial processing is 13 to 15 percent. For seed material the optimal moisture content during harvest is 13 percent.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Suptropics, warm/mod cool.
  • Temperate cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Improving fodder by incorporating legumes in the cropping system: ID 4370.
  • Participatory varietal selection: short duration legume crops for rainfed rabi: ID 4584.
  • Cover crop species, with a special focus on legumes: ID 7414.
  • Introduction of fodder legumes into rice-based cropping system to use as a supplement for dairy cattle: ID 4494.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

Legumes take up nitrogen from the air and pass it on to the soil, thereby improving soil fertility.

6.2 Pro-poor technology

The yields of crops grown on the same land after the legume crop will increase. In addition legumes are nutritious, and may provide income opportunities. Products made from soya and other legumes can be eaten or sold.

_annotations.body:
Soya and other leguminous crops

Plants that belong to the legume family (Leguminosae) have pods in which beans grow. Legumes absorb nitrogen from the air. Many crops that are unable to do this are dependent on the nitrogen that is present in the soil. Most soils in tropical areas do not contain sufficient nitrogen, an important nutrient. For this reason growing legumes (in addition to other staple crops such as potatoes, maize and rice) is a good way for farmers in tropical areas to enrich the soil. The legume crops also provide extra food for the daily diet of both humans and animals. Legumes must never be eaten raw. Nevertheless, they have so many advantages that it is worthwhile growing and processing them. Soya beans are a legume that is very rich in nutrients and there are a number of products that can only be made from soya. Soya beans and soya products can also be sold and can therefore be a source of extra income.



Description

1. Cultivation requirements for legumes

1.1 Suitable areas

Legumes and soya can be grown under a wide range of agroclimatic conditions. 

1.1.1 Upland river terraces and hills where shifting cultivation takes place

Shifting cultivation is a system in which farmers cut down an area of trees, burn the remaining vegetation and use the land they have cleared for agriculture. The ash from the burned material contains a lot of nutrients, so the soil is fertile and in the first season crops with high nutrient requirements can be grown. In the following seasons other crops are grown.

Figure 1. Example of shifting cultivation where not all trees have been felled

@CTA

1.1.2 Lowland along rivers and coastal areas where rice is often grown

The soils in these areas are surrounded by rivers. Coastal areas where mangroves used to grow are often not suitable for legumes as they are too acid once they have dried out after the rice harvest. Other soils in these areas which are not subjected to salt water are less acid and more suitable for agriculture. If these areas are submerged under water during the rainy season, rice is the only crop that can be grown. If the water recedes after the rice harvest, legumes can be grown as a second crop, making use of the moisture that remains in the soil. If it is possible to irrigate, the land can also be used in the dry season.

1.1.3 Highland areas

Many legume food crops are grown at altitudes above 1 000 m. Highland areas are characterized by low temperatures, dryness and a relatively short growing season. The fields are often small, which makes it difficult to use machines. Farmers work the land by hand or using animal traction. Legumes are grown on their own or in combination with other crops such as maize. The yields are often low, but the beans are an important source of protein for many families. Legumes such as chickpeas, peas, broad beans and lentils are grown in areas where the soils are poor because they are resistant to drought, and the crop remains can be used as animal feed.

Erosion is a common problem in these marginal areas. In some areas farmers work the land in such a way as to ensure that the ridges run horizontally as far as possible, following the contour lines. Rainwater is caught by the ridges and so seeps down slowly into the soil. If the ridges are made that follow the slope, rainwater runs off quickly, taking soil with it and causing erosion. If the rainfall is very heavy the soil cannot always absorb the water quickly enough. The water will then flow over the ridges, breaking them and causing serious erosion. In areas where this is a problem it is better to build the ridges diagonally over the slopes, so that some of the water is caught and can seep into the soil, and the rest can run off.

In the Bolivian highlands, where the amount of rainfall varies a lot, traditional methods are used to try and predict how much rain is likely to fall. If a lot of rain is expected the ridges are dug so that they run more in the direction of the slope; if less rain is expected the ridges are made so that they run more or less parallel with the contour lines.

1.2 Climate

1.2.1 Cool climates with cold periods at high latitudes or in higher areas of the tropics

Beans grown in moderate climates come from western Asia and the Mediterranean, where they have been grown for thousands of years. These include lentils (Lens culinaris), peas (Pisum sativa), kidney beans (Phaseolus sp.) and chickpeas (Cicer arietinum). The cultivation of these crops spread over time to the Indian subcontinent and China. Peas and broad beans (Vicia faba) also spread northwards to the cooler areas of northern Europe, and later were also taken to North and South America, Australia and South Africa. They are also found in highland areas of African countries such as Ethiopia and Kenya.

1.2.2 Humid tropical climates

Soya (Glycine max) and pigeon peas (Cajanus cajan) are suitable for warm, humid climates.

1.2.3 Hot arid climates

Cowpea (Vigna inguiculata), green gram (Vigna aureus), black gram (Vigna mungo) and groundnut (Arachis hypogaea) can tolerate extreme dryness and high temperatures. Groundnuts, for example, are grown in semi-arid and low-humid tropical areas of Africa, Southeast Asia and Central America between 30° North and 30° South.

1.2.4 Adaptation to cold

Much soya is grown in areas with temperatures around 25°C to 30°C. It seems that night-time temperature has a greater influence on the crop than daytime temperature. If the night-time temperature falls below the critical level of 10°C the crop will undergo more damage than if the night-time temperature stays above 10°C, regardless of the optimal daytime temperature range of 25°C to 30°C.

1.2.5 Water requirements

Soya has two critical periods concerning water requirements: from sowing to germination, and the period during which the beans grow in the pods. Before a seed can germinate it needs to absorb 50 percent of its weight in water. Nevertheless during the germination phase too much water causes more damage than too little water. The soil needs to be between 50 percent and 85 percent saturated with water. The amount of water needed increases as the crop grows, reaching its maximum as the beans develop in the pods (7 to 8 mm per day), and then decreases again. To be sure of a good yield, soya needs between 450 and 800 mm water each day during its whole growth cycle, depending on the climate. In high temperatures more water evaporates, so more rainfall is needed to provide the crop with enough water.

1.3 Varieties and cultivars

Farmers often know a lot about local varieties and the conditions under which they grow well. They often grow different varieties of the same crop in order to spread their risks. If a field sown with one variety suffers damage in the form of disease, pests or bad weather, it is still possible that a field with a different variety will suffer less from the problems.

Day-length sensitivity will determine the choice of legume made, not only the type but also the variety.

1.3.1 Soya

Soya is a short-day plant, and is sensitive to day length. It flowers when the day length is shorter than 16 hours. Short-cycle varieties flower 30 to 35 days after sowing and ripen within 75 to 105 days. These varieties have low yields. The middle-length varieties also flower 30 to 35 days after sowing and mature within 110 to 140 days. These have good yields. The long-cycle varieties produce a large amount of leaf material.

In integrated farming systems where livestock are raised this soya leaf material is an attractive form of animal feed; it is easily digestible and contains a lot of protein. In Ivory Coast (West Africa) short-cycle varieties do better because the rainy season is short.

1.4 Soil

1.4.1 Soil conditions

Legumes grow in different soils, even very acid soils (up to pH 3.8).

  • Groundnuts and Bambara groundnuts (Vigna subterranea) grow in poor sandy soils and loamy soils, but also in clay soils such as vertisols, although harvesting the pods from under the ground is difficult. While groundnuts grow well in chalky soils, Bambara groundnuts do not. Good drainage is important, especially for Vigna and Phaseolus types.
  • The butterbean (Lablab purpureus) has deep roots, which enable it to grow better on badly draining soils than most legumes. The butterbean however does not do well in saline (salty) soils. Generally speaking, legumes do not do well on salty soils, although there are a few exceptions: pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan) and pea.
  • Soya:
    • grows best in soils that are not too light and not too heavy in texture;
    • grows well in soils with high organic-material content;
    • prefers a pH of between 5.8 and 7.8, and does not like alkaline or acid extremes; and
    • does not tolerate saline soils.
Figure 2. If the soil has the correct degree of acidity (pH) the crop and its root nodules will develop well

@CTA

Figure 3. Examples of different types of soils and their effects on the growth of soya

@CTA

1.4.2 Improving soil fertility

Figures from Bolivia show that maize and wheat grown after soya can have an increase in yield of up to 22 percent. Where legumes are used as green manure, maize yields are clearly higher than maize grown after a short fallow period where nothing is grown. If soya is grown for use as green manure, where the whole crop is dug under, it can increase soil fertility by up to 200 kg nitrogen per hectare. Soya dug in in this way also improves the texture of the soil because the crop residue contributes organic material.

If soya is grown as part of a mixed cropping system it is important to ensure that nitrogen given to the other crop in the form of artificial fertilizer does not come into contact with the roots of the soya. Soya will not fix nitrogen (or only very little) if there is nitrogen present in the soil (in this case from the artificial fertilizer).

When the remains of the soya and other crops are dug into the soil together, the nitrogen-rich soya remains will ensure that the organic material in the soil is broken down quickly. This will increase the amount of nutrients in the soil by more than if the remains are dug in separately.

Two ways of integrating legumes with livestock keeping.

  • When the beans have been harvested the crop residue is used as animal feed for the livestock kept in the village, e.g. cattle or buffalo. The dung from the animals is used to fertilize the land together with the crop remains left in the soil, which increases the nitrogen content of the soil.
  • You can also let livestock graze in a mixed crop of a legume and grain. For example, you let the animals eat half of the legume crop. Animals will first eat legumes because they contain a lot of protein, which means they will leave the grain crop undisturbed. As they eat the legumes, nitrogen will be released which is good for the grain crop, such as maize. The animals convert the nitrogen in the soya into urine and dung. The nitrogen in the urine is immediately taken up by the grain crop.

Figure 4. Example of rotational cropping: in the first year fields 1 and 2 are cultivated (A). In the following year all crops move round one field, so fields 2 and 3 are cultivated (B).

records.title: Traditional feeding of cattle with intercropped forage sorghum
records.description:
Description

1. Sorghum as forage

  • Sorghum is a genus in the grass family (Poaceae), native probably from Ethiopia.
    • It has been grown in India for more than 2000 years.
    • A prominent species of this genus is Sorghum bicolour, whose different varieties are used for grain production for human consumption or utilized as forage for animals.
    • Some of the varieties have a dual-purpose.
  • Most of the sorghum varieties are drought- and heat-tolerant, due to their root system.
    • This makes them important staple crops in arid regions.
    • They can replace maize as a staple crop in stress-prone semi-arid areas.
    • Generally, sorghum is tolerant of soil salinity (which usually is the case in semi-arid and arid areas).
    • However, it is sensitive to frost and sustained flooding.
  • The plant is tall and erect, reaching up to 5 m height.
    • The culms can be around 4 m long and are used as forage.
    • If grains are not utilized for human consumption, they are frequently used as forage.
    • Forage sorghum can be grazed, cut fresh as green feed, dried into hay or ensiled as silage.
  • The following practice is appropriate for farms that have a small number of animals to feed.
    • It involves feeding entire sorghum plants to cattle with all parts attached (head with grains, stems and leaves).
    • Traditionally, it is taken for Thattu Koduthal (e.g. “feeding fodder sorghum by administering it orally one by one using our hands”).
  • Make sure to use only dried sorghum for this form of feeding, because freshly cut sorghum may contain toxic levels of HCN (feedipedia/Sorghum forage: http://www.feedipedia.org/node/379).

1.1 Growing sorghum as forage

Figure 1. Sorghum field

©FAO/TECA

  • Forage sorghum is grown as an intercrop or in hedgerows together with finger millet (also known as ragi, Eleusine coracana), groundnut (Arachis hypogaea) or red gram (Cajanus cajan) during the rainy season Adipattam (July-October).
  • It is exclusively sown for the purpose of animal fodder in drylands.
  • In July before sowing, the field is ploughed three times.
  • Usually, ten rows of fodder sorghum are raised in one acre (25 rows in 1 hectare) with one meter (3 ft.) space within the rows.
  • After sowing, the seeds germinate within a week by the moisture obtained through rainwater.
  • Water harvesting facilities may help to prevent moisture deficits during the main stages of crop growth.
  • From October to November, two and a half months after sowing the forage, sorghum attains the flowering stage.
    • This period is the right time for cutting and storing it.

1.2 Harvesting the sorghum forage

  • At the flowering/panicle initiation stage (about 1.5 m to 2 m height), the forage sorghum is usually cut.
  • Take care to cut it 30 cm above the ground, so that ratoons appear in one to one and a half months after cutting.
  • Ratooning ensures that the sorghum can be cut up to three times during the cropping season at about 30 days of interval.

1.3 Harvesting own forage sorghum seeds

Figure 2. Harvesting sorghum seeds at flowering stage

©FAO/TECA

  • For saving your own seed, it is important to leave a few plants without using them as fodder.
  • After flowering, the fodder sorghum will bear an ear head with greyish coloured grains (locally called: “vellaicholam”).
  • Some harvested seeds could be used for sowing during the following growing seasons.
  • Appropriate storing technology should be used, in order to conserve the germination potential of the seed, when stored before seeding.
  • Generally, about 50 kg of seeds is sown in one hectare for fodder purposes.
Figure 3. Sorghum seeds

©FAO/TECA

Figure 4. A farmer after harvest

©FAO/TECA

2. Feeding cattle (“ThattuKoduthal”)

  • Usually, “Thattu Koduthal” is performed in the afternoon/early evening (between 6 and 7 p.m. local time) by tying the bullocks in front of the house.
    • Family members sit on the “Thinnai” (traditional sitting bench) and feed the fodder to the cattle.
    • Many villagers in Northern Tamil Nadu who own cattle perform this practice.
  • Attention is paid to give the sorghum plant one by one, with the stalks first (e.g. the part nearest to the roots).
    • If the head of the fodder is fed first then there are chances of wastage, as cattle relish the ear head portion, which is more palatable.
  • During Mondays, special care is taken while feeding the animals in the morning (between 5-6 a.m.), as Mondays are considered as birthdays of the cattle.
  • About 15 kg to 25 kg of fodder sorghum is fed to a bullock per day and approximately 10 kg to a cow.
  • During the off-season (November to April) when the green fodder sorghum is not available, it is possible to produce concentrate feed.
    • Mix finger millet (ragi), horse gram (kollu) and sorghum seeds and grind them to a powder together.
    • Half a kilo of the flour is fed to one animal per day.
Figure 5. Local farmer feeding sorghum to the cattle

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Local farmers feeding the cattle with sorghum

©FAO/TECA

  • This practice can substantially reduce the wastage of fodder while feeding.
  • The whole culm with the ear head is fed to the cattle, starting with the other end of the culm.
  • Animals gain higher weight due to timely feeding of the right amount of fodder.
  • On Mondays, cattle are not taken for any work (including ploughing).
  • Weekly rest also increases the body condition of animals.

4. Limitations of this practice

  • The practice is time-intensive, due to hand feeding of the cattle.
  • Only a small number of cattle can be fed.
  • The practice cannot be used for high-yielding intensive livestock production.
  • The practice is best suitable for family farms, where family labour can be used to keep costs of feeding low.

  • About 2000 farmers in Northwestern Tamil Nadu practice this way of feeding cattle “Thattu Koduthal” (hand feeding of fodder for animals).

  • According to SEVA, the same method is practised in the neighbouring state of Karnataka by some 5000 thousand farmers.

The intercropping of the forage sorghum between other crops additionally improves the land-use efficiency, providing diversified yields within a specified area of cropping. records.title: Manejo e identificación de enfermedades que causan malformaciones y distorsiones de hojas y vainas en el frijol
records.description:
Descripción

1. Virus del mosaico común del frijol (VMCF) y virus del necrosamiento del mosaico común del frijol (VNMCF)

1.1 Distribución

  • Estas son las dos enfermedades virales más importantes que afectan los cultivos de frijol en África.

1.2 Síntomas

  • Los síntomas típicos de VMCF (Figura 1) y VNMCF (Figura 2) son un mosaico entre verde claro o amarillo y verde oscuro sobre las hojas (Figura 3) acompañada usualmente por arrugamiento, distorsión y enrollamiento de las hojas.
    • Otros síntomas que se pueden apreciar en hospederos susceptibles incluyen: moteado, rizado y mal formación de las hojas, como también enanismo de las plantas (Figura 4).
  • Una infección severa puede causar distorsiones en las hojas y flores, ampollas, enanismo y vainas pequeñas.
  • Las plantas infectadas en estadíos iniciales de crecimiento o crecidas por semillas infectadas pueden sufrir un retraso en la maduración y tener menos vainas y semillas por vainas que las plantas sanas.
  • VNMCF (Figura 5) causa la enfermedad de raíz negra en variedades susceptibles, que ocurre como una necrosis sistémica apareciendo primero en las hojas trifoliadas jóvenes como áreas difusas de color café rojizo con venas que se pueden tornar negras.
    • Los tallos, semillas, vainas y raíces pueden oscurecerse también.
    • Luego se da el marchitamiento apical, caída y necrosis (Figura 6). 
Figura 1. Infección de VMCF

©FAO/TECA

Figura 2. Infección de VNMCF

©FAO/TECA

Figura 3. Patrón del mosaico sobre las hojas

©FAO/TECA

Figura 4. Enanismo general de plantas

©FAO/TECA

Figura 5. Enfermedad de la raíz negra por VNMCF

©FAO/TECA

Figura 6. Marchitamiento apical, caída y necrosis

©FAO/TECA

1.3 ​Fuentes de infección​

  • La mayor fuente de infección es la semilla infectada.
  • Otras leguminosas y hierbas hospederas sirven como el principal inóculo.
  • La infección es diseminada por diferentes especies migrantes de áfidos.

1.4 ​Estrategias de manejo​

  • Plantar variedades resistentes es la mejor medida de control para VMCF.
    • Por ejemplo: OAC Rex (OAC 95-4), BelMiNeb-RMR-8, -9, -10, -11, -12 -13, etc.
  • Minimizar plantar las variedades susceptibles en áreas conocidas de ser atacada por VNMCF.
  • Plantar semillas limpias, libres de enfermedad.
  • Plantar en estadíos tempranos para ayudar a aislar las poblaciones altas de áfidos.
  • Destruir otras leguminosas y hierbas hospederas antes de establecer un cultivo y durante el período de crecimiento de la plantación de frijol.

2. Validación de la práctica

  • La identificación y manejo de estas enfermedades se llevó a cabo en Uganda. 

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido. 

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Producción artesanal de semilla de frijol para el pequeño agricultor: ID 6496. 
  • Manejo de la babosa del frijol: ID 7231.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas en plántulas en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8382.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas en flores en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8383.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas de almacenamiento en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8384.
  • Multi-stress tolerant bean varieties: ID 8919.

5. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología muestra al productor diversas medidas para reducir eficientemente enfermedades.

5.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Este manejo e identificación de enfermedades que causan malformaciones y distorsiones de hojas y vainas en el frijol ayuda a reducir las pérdidas de frijol y así estabilizar la fuente de ingresos.

Algunas plagas de insectos también afectan la calidad de las semillas y la germinación de las plantas debido al daño que causan en la semilla en campo y el almacenamiento. records.title: Manejo e identificación de enfermedades que causan crecimientos anormales en hojas y vainas en el cultivo de frijol
records.description:
Descripción

1. ​Mildiu polvoso: Erysiphe polygoni​ 

1.1 ​Distribución​

  • La enfermedad es escasamente distribuida en África y no tiene tanta importancia.
  • Es favorecida por temperaturas cálidas (20 °C-24 °C), baja humedad y sombra.

1.2 Síntomas

  • Mildiu polvoso puede ser confundido con manchas harinosas sobre las hojas causadas por Mycovellosiella phaseoli, sin embargo a diferencia de éste último, los primeros síntomas aparecen en la parte superior de las hojas como pequeños, circulares, mildiu blanco polvoso (Figuras 1 y 2).
  • El área bajo el hongo se convierte en café oscuro (Figura 3) y consecuentemente el hongo blanco puede cubrir toda la superficie de la hoja.
  • La planta puede marchitarse, mal formarse, tornarse amarilla y las hojas pueden caer prematuramente.
  • Las vainas también pueden marchitarse, mal formarse o morir.
  • Las semillas se infectan a través de la infección de la vaina y pueden llevar la infección al siguiente cultivo si se plantasen.
Figura ​1​. ​Pequeñas manchas circulares de hongos en la superficie de la hoja

©​FAO/TECA

Figura ​2​. ​Hongos blancos cubriendo la superficie de la hoja

©​FAO/TECA

Figura ​3​. ​Estadío tardío de infección

©​FAO/TECA

1.3 ​Fuentes de infección​

  • La mayor fuente de infección son las semillas contaminadas y los rastrojos de plantas infectadas.
  • La enfermedad se disemina por viento, lluvia e insectos.

1.4 Estrategias de manejo

  • Rotación de cultivo con cultivares no hospederos, como maíz y otros cereales.
  • Arado profundo de residuos de plantas enfermas después de la cosecha.
  • Uso de variedades resistente, donde estén disponibles, por ejemplo: ESAL 686.
  • Uso de semilla limpia y libre de enfermedades.
  • Espaciamiento amplio entre plantas para incrementar la aireación.

2. ​Mancha harinosa de la hoja: Mycovellosiella phaseoli​

2.1 ​Distribución​

  • La enfermedad es ampliamente distribuida en el este de África, en altitudes medias y altas con temperatura fresca a moderada y altos niveles de humedad relativa.

2.2 Síntomas

  • Los síntomas iniciales son manchas blancas, redondas de hongos sobre la superficie de las hojas.
  • Las manchas se juntan y se tornan irregulares y harinosas (Figura 4).
  • Sobre el haz de las hojas, los síntomas aparecen como manchas amarillas o verdes y café que pocas veces contienen hongos (Figuras 5 y 6).
  • Infecciones severas pueden causar defoliación prematura.
  • La clorosis ocurre sobre la superficie de la hoja, correspondiendo a una lesión en el envés de la hoja.
Figura ​4​. ​Plantas de frijol presentando síntomas iniciales de mancha harinosa de la hoja

©​FAO/TECA

Figura ​5​. ​Síntomas de la mancha harinosa sobre el haz de las hojas

©​FAO/TECA

Figura ​6​. ​Síntomas de la mancha harinosa en el envés de las hojas 

©​FAO/TECA

2.3 ​Fuentes de infección​

  • La mayor fuente de infección es la semilla contaminada.

2.4 Estrategias de manejo

  • Plantar semillas sanas y libres de enfermedad.
  • Hacer aplicaciones oportunas de fungicidas, preferiblemente orgánicos, en el cultivo.

3. ​Hongo blanco: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum​

3.1 ​Distribución​

  • Extendido pero solo importante estacionalmente bajo condiciones templadas y de humedad en altitudes intermedias.

3.2 Síntomas

  • La enfermedad ataca los tejidos de plantas adultas como flores, cotiledones, semillas, vainas y hojas o tejidos lastimados de la planta.
  • Los síntomas aparecen inicialmente como lesiones de agua de color verde – grisáceo, seguidas por el crecimiento de un hongo blanco parecido al algodón y acompañado de una pudrición blanda sobre la parte afectada de la planta (Figuras 7 y 8).
  • Los esclerocios negros se forman en y sobre el tejido infectado.
  • El tejido infectado luego se torna seco y de colores claros como si hubiese sido blanqueado.
  • En el dosel de la planta se puede observar marchitez.
  • Debido a la infección de las vainas, las semillas están deterioradas (Figura 9).
Figura ​7​. ​Vaina y tallo dañado por el hongo blanco

©​FAO/TECA

Figura ​8​. ​Vaina y tallo dañado por el hongo blanco

©​FAO/TECA

Figura ​9​. ​Vainas maduras y tallos muertos por el ataque del hongo blanco

©​FAO/TECA

3.3 ​Fuentes de infección​

  • Las mayores fuentes de infección son el suelo infectado, semilla infectada o contaminada y rastrojos o residuos de plantas infectadas.
  • La enfermedad también es diseminada a través del riego en surco.

3.4 Estrategias de manejo

  • Enterrar los residuos del cultivo u otras plantas infectadas.
  • Plantar variedades resistentes, por ejemplo, USPT-WM-1.
  • Espaciamiento amplio entre las plantas para incrementar la aireación.
  • Aplicar mulch para evitar el contacto de las vainas con el suelo.
  • Exponer los rastrojos de las plantas enfermas al sol para que se sequen y maten los esclerocios.

4. ​Óxido de la hoja: Uromyces appendiculatus​

4.1 ​Distribución​

  • El óxido de la hoja se presenta en cualquier lugar donde el frijol crece.
  • Es favorecida por temperaturas frescas a moderadas con condiciones de humedad que resultan en largos períodos de humedad sobre la superficie de la hoja por más de 10 horas.
  • Las plantas infectadas durante los estadíos iniciales de crecimiento sufren más pérdidas en el rendimiento.
  • Cualquier factor que retrase la maduración de la planta, como establecimiento tardío, daño por herbicida, exceso de nitrógeno o daño por granizo; puede incrementar el potencial de disminución de rendimiento cuando una epidemia de roya ocurra. 

4.2 Síntomas

  • Las esporas de las manchas de las hojas se pegan en los dedos, mientras que la roya no.
  • Estas manchas se alargan hasta formar pústulas de color café rojizo (Figuras 10, 11, 12) y da una apariencia de oxidado a cualquier cosa que tienen cerca.
  • Una infección severa puede causar que las hojas se tornen café, se enrollen hacia arriba, se sequen y aborten prematuramente.
  • Las vainas verdes, y ocasionalmente los tallos y ramas, pueden también infectarse y desarrollar pústulas típicas de la roya (Figura 13).
  • El establecimiento y llenado de las vainas, junto con el tamaño de las semillas puede reducirse si la infección inicial es severa.
  • Un campo de frijol severamente afectado luce como si hubiese sido quemado (Figura 14). 
Figura ​10​. ​Óxido en el haz de la hoja

©​FAO/TECA

Figura ​11​. ​Óxido en el envés de la hoja

©​FAO/TECA

Figura ​12​. ​Las manchas se tornan a color café rojizo

©​FAO/TECA

Figura ​13​. ​Vainas infectadas

©​FAO/TECA

Figura ​14​. ​Plantación severamente afectada

©​FAO/TECA

4.3 Fuentes de infección 

  • Las mayores fuentes de infección son los rastrojos de plantas infectadas y las plantas infectadas voluntariamente.
  • La enfermedad es principalmente propagada por el viento. 

4.4 Estrategias de manejo

  • Practicar la rotación de cultivos cada 2 o 3 años con cultivos no hospederos como los cereales.
  • Arado profundo del rastrojo de plantas infectadas.
  • Remoción  de  fuentes  potenciales  de  esporas  de  la  roya,  por  ejemplo  alternar  hospederos  y  plantas  voluntarias.
  • Plantar  durante  los  períodos  recomendados  para  reducir  la  exposición  tardía  a  niveles  altos  de  patógenos. 
  • Plantar variedades resistentes a la roya como ABCP-8, BelMiNeb-RMR-8, -9, -10, -11, -12 y -13.
  • Monitorear  las  plantas  frecuentemente  durante  la  floración  y  desarrollo  temprano  de  vainas  para  detectar signos tempranos de roya. 

5. Validación de la práctica

  • La identificación y manejo de estas enfermedades se llevó a cabo en Uganda.

6. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

7. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Elaboración de pesticidas eco-amigables para el control de plagas y enfermedades: ID 8381.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas en plántulas en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8382.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas en flores en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8383.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas de almacenamiento en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8384.
  • Manejo e identificación de plagas alimentadoras de vainas y semillas en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8385
  • Manejo e identificación de enfermedades que causan malformaciones y distorsiones de hojas y vainas en el frijol: ID 8387.
  • Manejo e identificación de enfermedades que afectan las raíces en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8389.
  • Manejo e identificación de enfermedades que afectan hojas y vainas en el cultivo de frijol: ID 8392.

8. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

8.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología muestra al productor diversas medidas para reducir eficientemente enfermedades.

8.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

Este manejo e identificación de enfermedades que causan crecimientos anormales en hojas y vainas en el cultivo de frijol ayuda a reducir las pérdidas de frijol y así estabilizar la fuente de ingresos.

records.title: Manejo e identificación de enfermedades que afectan hojas y vainas en el cultivo de frijol
records.description:
Descripción

1. ​Roya bacterial común: Xanthomonas phaseoli​

1.1 ​Distribución​

  • La enfermedad está ampliamente distribuida a lo largo de las regiones cultivadoras de frijol y es favorecida por temperaturas de templadas a altas y altos niveles de humedad.

1.2 Síntomas

  • Los primeros síntomas aparecen como puntos de agua en el envés de las hojas.
  • Los puntos de las hojas se alargan y se unen hasta formar largas lesiones irregulares de color café rodeadas por una zona amarilla angosta (Figura 1).
  • Los puntos pueden comenzar a juntarse, y el amarillo de las hojas se puede convertir más generalizado en las hojas (Figura 2).
  • El tallo puede podrirse en el primer nudo donde los cotiledones estaban adheridos y la planta puede quebrarse.
  • Las vainas en este punto, han hundido los puntos circulares donde inicialmente eran de agua (Figura 3) pero luego se secaron, con un borde angosto color café rojizo (Figura 4).
  • Bajo condiciones húmedas, un exudado bacterial amarillo con apariencia babosa, sale de las lesiones y forma una costra.
  • Las vainas pueden marchitarse y las semillas infectadas (Figura 5) pueden podrirse.
  • La bacteria también invade la semilla (Figura 6) y puede permanecer dormida hasta la germinación.
  • Incluso, un rastro de semilla infectada cuando fue plantada, puede iniciar una infección severa en todo el campo.
Figura ​1​. ​Lesiones en hojas

©​CIAT

Figura ​2​. ​Amarillo generalizado sobre hojas

©​CIAT

Figura ​3​. ​Puntos circulares hundidos en vainas 

©​CIAT

Figura ​4​. ​Puntos en vainas que luego de ser secados desarrollaron un borde angosto color café rojizo

©​CIAT

Figura ​5​. ​Vainas se pueden marchitar y las semillas infectadas se pueden podrir

©​CIAT

Figura ​6​. ​Semilla infectada por bacteria


​​ ​©​CIAT

1.3 ​Fuentes de infección​

  • La mayor fuente de infección es la semilla.
  • Otras fuentes de infección incluyen escombros de frijol secos o residuos de suelo en la superficie, y plantas infectadas voluntariamente.
  • La enfermedad se propaga por salpicadura de agua, lluvia con viento, irrigación aérea, insectos y equipo y vestimenta contaminada.

1.4 Métodos de prevención de la enfermedad

  • Usar semilla libre de enfermedad.
  • Rotación de cultivos: evitar plantar frijoles en parcelas contaminadas por los próximos tres años para eliminar el riesgo de infección.
  • Arado profundo para asegurar la destrucción del patógeno en escombros infectados.
  • Suspender las operaciones en campo cuando las hojas estén húmedas para reducir la propagación de la enfermedad.
  • Utilizar variedades de plantas resistentes donde estén disponibles, como por ejemplo: ABCP-8; USDK-CBB-15 (GP-244, PI 639867); OAC Rex (OAC 95-4); BAC-6; etc.

2. ​Halo de la roya: Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. phaseolicola, Pseudomonas syringae pv. Phaseolicola​

2.1 ​Distribución​

  • Esta enfermedad es ampliamente distribuida pero más predominante en áreas de media a baja altitud.
  • Es favorecida por temperaturas frescas (16 °C a 20 °C), humedad y condiciones nubladas.
  • Se multiplica rápidamente en presencia del rocío.
  • No es muy común en regiones o estaciones de altas temperaturas.
  • Los síntomas más característicos de esta enfermedad, ocurren en las hojas de los frijoles (Figura 7).

©​CIAT

2.2 ​Síntomas​

  • Los primeros síntomas aparecen como pequeños puntos de agua sobre el envés de las hojas.
  • Los tejidos que rodean las manchas, gradualmente se convierten en un halo verde-amarillo (Figura 8), por eso el nombre de halo de la roya.
  • Los peciolos y ramas infectadas soportan puntos grasosos que desarrollan una decoloración rojiza.
  • El tallo puede podrirse en el primer nódulo donde los cotiledones estaban adheridos y pueden causar que la planta se quiebre.
  • Las manchas pronto cambiarían a un café rojizo (Figura 9).
  • Las vainas infectadas muestran lesiones de puntos de agua que también desarrollan una decoloración rojiza (Figura 10).
  • Bajo condiciones de humedad, exudados bacteriales blancuzcos amarillos aparecen en las lesiones.
  • La semilla se puede marchitar y decolorar o podrir (Figura 11).
  • Pero algunas veces no se pueden ver síntomas de enfermedad alguna.

​​

©​CIAT

Figura ​9​. ​Manchas se convierten en café rojizo

​​

©​CIAT

Figura ​10​. ​Vainas infectadas muestran lesiones de puntos de agua

©​CIAT

Figura ​11​. ​Las semillas pueden marchitarse y decolorarse o podrirse

2.3 Fuentes de infección 

  • Las mayores fuentes de infección son las semillas infectadas y las plantas de rastrojo o escombros.
  • La enfermedad se disemina por salpicadura de agua, lluvia con viento y contacto entre plantas debido al movimiento de equipos y/o trabajadores, especialmente cuando el follaje está húmedo.

2.4 Estrategias de manejo

  • La prevención de la infección puede ser a través de una combinación de las siguientes estrategias: 
    • Rotación de cultivos con un cultivo no hospedero por al menos de dos a 3 años.
    • Arado profundo para enterrar y destruir el patógeno infectado en los escombros.
    • Uso de semillas sanas y limpias.
    • Plantar variedades resistentes donde sea disponible, por ejemplo, Redtoke, Almonga, GLP 92.
    • Evitar el movimiento de trabajadores en el campo cuando esté húmedo.
    • Remover todas las plántulas infectadas del campo inmediatamente cuando sean detectadas.

3. ​Mancha angular de la hoja: Phaseoriopsis griseola​

3.1 ​Distribución​

  • La mancha angular de la hoja es una importante enfermedad ampliamente distribuida en África.
  • El desarrollo de la infección y la enfermedad se favorecen por condiciones húmedas y temperaturas moderadas (20 °C a 25 °C).

3.2 ​Síntomas​

  • La enfermedad puede afectar todas las partes de la planta de frijol sobre el suelo (Figura 12).
    • Los síntomas son más notorios durante el florecimiento tardío y los estadíos tempranos de formación de vainas.
    • La enfermedad forma lesiones circulares que usualmente aparecen como manchas de color café con un centro café claro o plateado.
    • Las manchas inicialmente se encuentran confinadas al tejido entre las venas mayores, dándole una apariencia angular (Figura 13).
  • En algunas variedades un halo amarillo puede rodear las lesiones y eventualmente la hoja entera se torna amarilla antes de abortar prematuramente.
    • Las lesiones pueden ser observadas en el envés de la hoja y es ligeramente más pálida que las del haz de las hojas (Figuras 14a, 14b).
    • Las lesiones sobre los tallos y peciolos se muestran alargadas y de color café oscuro.
    • Las lesiones sobre las vainas son de hundidos irregulares a manchas negras circulares con centros de color café rojizo y puede ser similar a los que causan antracnosis (Figura 15).
    • Vainas infectadas pueden contener semillas pobremente desarrolladas, marchitas o decoloradas (Figura 16).

©​CIAT

©​CIAT

©​CIAT

Figura ​15​. ​Lesiones en vainas

3.3 Fuentes de infección

  • Las principales fuentes de infección son rastrojos de plantas o residuos y plantas voluntariamente infectadas.
  • La enfermedad es diseminada por equipos contaminados y vestimenta, rocíos de agua y lluvia con viento.

3.4 Estrategias de manejo

  • La enfermedad puede ser manejada por una combinación de las siguientes estrategias:
    • Rotación de cultivos con un cultivo no hospedero, por ejemplo maíz por lo menos dos años.
    • Remover o arar profundamente los rastrojos o residuos del cultivo.
    • Evitar el movimiento en las parcelas del cultivo cuando las plantas estén húmedas.
    • Plantar cultivares resistentes donde sean disponibles, por ejemplo: AND 277, AND 279 y CAL 143 (en Malawi, Sudáfrica, Tanzania y Zambia) pero éstas son susceptibles en Uganda. Variedades resistentes para Uganda incluyen: Mex 54, BAT 332 y G 5686.
    • Plantar mezclas de variedades resistentes de frijol para reducir la diseminación de la infección.

4. ​Antracnosis del frijol: Colletotrichum lindemuthianum​

4.1 ​Distribución​

  • La antracnosis es ampliamente distribuida, muy común y una de las enfermedades del frijol más importantes en el mundo (Figura 17).
  • Especialmente es común en regiones con lluvia frecuente y más destructiva en temperaturas frescas y moderadas con humedad relativamente alta.
Figura ​17​. ​Campo de frijol afectado por la Antracnosis

​​

©​CIAT

4.2 ​Síntomas​

  • La enfermedad puede afectar cualquier parte de la planta, dependiendo de la época de la infección y la fuente de inóculo.
  • Los síntomas iniciales de antracnosis aparecen como una lesión café oscuro a negro a lo largo de las venas en el envés de las hojas (Figura 18).
  • Los peciolos e incluso los tallos pueden mostrar estos síntomas.
  • Chancros hundidos también ocurren en los hipocotilos en desarrollo.
  • El síntoma más notable de la antracnosis del frijol aparece en las vainas (Figuras 18, 19, 20).
  • Las lesiones de las vainas típicamente están hundidas y son rodeadas por un anillo negro de ligero relieve alrededor de un borde rojizo        (Figura 20).
  • Bajo infecciones severas, vainas jóvenes pueden marchitarse y secar prematuramente.
  • El hongo puede penetrar a través de la vaina causando decoloración y distorsión de la semilla (Figura 21).
  • También puede penetrar la cubierta de la semilla y llegar a establecerse dentro de la semilla.
  • Cuando esta semilla sea plantada, será fuente de infección segura para el cultivo.

©​CIAT

Figura ​19​. ​Antracnosis del frijol en vainas

©​CIAT

Figura ​20​. ​Lesiones unidas de antracnosis en vaina de frijol​

​​

©​CIAT

Figura ​21​. ​Antracnosis del frijol en semillas​​ ​ 

©​CIAT

4.3 Fuentes de infección

  • Las principales fuentes de infección son a través de semillas infectadas y rastrojos de cultivo.
  • La enfermedad es diseminada por el rocío de la lluvia, lluvia con viento y movimientos de insectos, animales y el hombre, especialmente cuando el follaje de las plantas está húmedo.

4.4 Estrategias de manejo 

  • Una combinación de las siguientes estrategias puede ayudar a reducir la infección y la propagación de la enfermedad:
    • Usar semilla libre de enfermedades.
    • Rotación de cultivos con no hospederos de la enfermedad (como cereales) por al menos 2 años.
    • Remover o enterrar el rastrojo de las plantas del campo antes de la cosecha.
    • Plantar variedades resistentes donde estén disponibles, por ejemplo: G 2333, NAT 002, NAT 003 y AB 136. 
    • Actividades de campo como siembra o aplicaciones de pesticidas químicos, restringidos cuando las hojas estén húmedas por lluvia o rocío.
    • Limpiar los lugares de almacenamiento de las semillas para evitar la contaminación.

5. Mancha de hoja Ascochyta: Phoma exigua var. exigua, Ascochyta phaseolorum

5.1 Distribución

  • La enfermedad se presenta ampliamente a lo largo de África, particularmente bajo condiciones frescas y húmedas.

5.2 Síntomas

  • Los primeros síntomas aparecen en las hojas como manchas largas de color gris a negro.
  • Luego el área infectada se llena de anillos concéntricos alrededor de la mancha contenida de picnidios negros (Figuras 22 y 23). 
  • El oscurecimiento de los nódulos es característico de la infección en los tallos (Figura 24); esto puede rodear el tallo y matar la planta.
  • Bajo infecciones severas, caídas de hojas prematuras pueden ocurrir (Figura 25).
  • La infección de la flor puede llevar a la pudrición de las vainas y causar chancros extensivos (Figura 26).
  • Las infecciones de las vainas pueden resultar en infección de semillas, que pueden ser transmitidas al siguiente cultivo.
