records.title: Growing maize and soybean in rotation
records.description:
Description

The practice is done in stages broken down in years.

Figure 1. Year one grow soybean

@FAO/TECA

1. Steps for the first year

1.1 Apply fertilizer

  • Apply SSP fertilizer to the prepared land, the application rate is usually based on the level of fertility of the soil in case a soil test has been done (recommended).
  • On average apply six bags of SSP per hectare. 
Figure 2. Apply fertilizer

@FAO/TECA

1.2 Make ridges

  • Make ridges 50 cm apart either by hand, animal traction or by tractor.
Figure 3. Ridge making  

@FAO/TECA       

1.3 Planting

  • Plant after a good rain. Make shallow grooves (1 to 2 cm deep) on ridges and drill soybean seed (one seed every 5 cm) and cover lightly with soil.
Figure 4. Planting

@FAO/TECA

1.4 Bird watching

Scare birds the first two weeks after planting, this can be done manually or with the use of a scarecrow.

Figure 5. Manual scaring of birds 

@FAO/TECA

1.5 Weed control

  • Control weed manually or by use of a herbicide recommended by the extension officers that is good for soybean.
Figure 6. Weed control

@FAO/TECA

1.6 Pests and insects control

  • In instances when the crop is infested with pests or insects, spray with the recommended pesticide or insecticide.
Figure 7. Spraying insecticide

@FAO/TECA

1.7 Harvesting

  • Harvest by cutting at ground level with sickle when leaves turn yellow.
  • Do not harvest by uprooting the plants.

1.8 Threshing

  • Thresh the soybean in the field so that the haulms can be retained in the field, when the haulms is used to feed livestock collect the manure and spread it in the field.
Figure 8. Threshing

@FAO/TECA

2.  Year two plant maize on the same field

Figure 9. Maize on the same plot

@FAO/TECA

2.1 Purchasing maize seed

  • Farmers should buy improved maize seed only from a certified input supplier.
Figure 10. Farmer purchasing maize seed

@FAO/TECA

2.2 Break old ridges

  • Break the ridges from the old crop in order to make new ones for the maize crop, since spacing for two crops differ.
Figure 11. Breaking old ridges

@FAO/TECA

2.3 Planting of maize

  • Plant after a good rain.
  • Use a stick to make planting holes 5 cm deep at every 25 cm on the ridge.
  • Plant one seed per hole and cover lightly with soil.
Figure 12. Maize planting

@FAO/TECA

2.4 Weed control

  • Spray a recommended herbicide to control against weeds or manually control the weeds.
Figure 13. Controlling for weeds in the maize field manually

@FAO/TECA

Figure 14. Spraying herbicide

@FAO/TECA

2.5 Application of fertilizer

  • Apply three bags of Urea when plants are at the knee height.
  • Use a stick to make a hole at 5 cm away from plants. Place the fertilizer in the hole using a coca-cola cap (one cap full) and cover the hole.
Figure 15. Top-dressing with Urea

@FAO/TECA

2.6 Bend crops

  • Bend cobs downward at maturity to hasten drying and to minimize spoilage.
Figure 16. Bending cobs downward

@FAO/TECA

2.7 Dehusking

  • Harvest the maize by dehusking.
Figure 17. Harvesting

@FAO/TECA

2.8 Drying

  • Dry the cobs properly before storage to avoid contamination with bacteria.
  • Store in a dry place.
Figure 18. Drying the harvested maize

@FAO/TECA

3. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • Good weather conditions for growing both maize and soya.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Crop rotation in conservation agriculture: ID 7415.
  • Green manure or cover crops and crop rotation in conservation agriculture on small farms: ID 7250.
  • Soya and other leguminous crops: ID 6954.
  • Maize production: ID 7018.
  • Drought-tolerant maize varieties: ID 8920.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Resource use efficiency

The same piece of land can be used for production of both maize and soybean. In this way the soil is enriched with nitrogen and specific crops are controlled.

records.title: Cassava brown streak disease: control measures
records.description:
Description

1. How does Cassava Brown Stake Disease (CBSD) affect cassava?

  • Cassava Brown Streak Disease (CBSD) is a devastating disease that causes loss of cassava root (tuber) production and quality.
  • It can render susceptible varieties unusable if cassava roots are left in the ground for over nine months.
  • CBSD is now occurring in areas that were believed to be unsuitable for the disease, such as high altitude areas away from the Indian coastal belt in Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique.
  • CBSD causes substantial root yield loss of up to 100 percent particularly in worst affected areas.
  • This is worsened by the fact that the symptoms are elusive, e.g. cannot be recognized easily by untrained or inexperienced people, and may not appear until the cassava plant has stayed longer than nine months.
  • Worse still, some farmers even confuse the symptoms with those caused by the more familiar Cassava Mosaic Disease (CMD).
  • The gravity of the situation is that almost all varieties bred or selected for resistance to CMD are susceptible to the “new strain” of CBSD occurring in Uganda, inland areas of Tanzania and Western Kenya.
  • Additionally, the disease causes loss in both quality and quantity of storage roots (tubers).
  • Storage roots showing CBSD symptoms are not fit for human and animal consumption. 

2. Main symptoms caused by CBSD

  • Symptoms of CBSD can be observed on leaves, stems and cassava roots as described below.
  • However, some cassava plants or varieties do not show symptoms on leaves nor tubers.
  • Other varieties may only express symptoms on leaves and not on roots.
  • Others do not show symptoms on leaves but on roots only.
  • However, the typical response of cassava plants is the one in which plants reveal symptoms on leaves, stems, and roots.
  • The symptoms may appear and disappear in young plants, but appear again in cassava plants at a later stage.

2.1 Symptoms of CBSD on leaves

  • Symptoms of CBSD appear as patches of yellow areas mixed with normal green colour (see Figure 1).
    • This phenomenon is commonly referred to as chlorosis.
  • It produces characteristic yellow or necrotic vein banding on leaves which may enlarge and join to form comparatively large yellow or necrotic patches
  • The yellow patches are more prominent on mature (bottom) leaves than younger ones.
  • Chlorosis is often also associated with secondary veins; veinal chlorosis is on mature cassava leaves.
  • The infected leaves do not become distorted in shape as occurs with leaves infected by CMD.
  • Advanced symptoms on the leaves become an irregular yellow blotchy chlorosis, that is most pronounced in the periphery (margins or edge) of lower leaves.
Figure 1. Advanced CBSD symptoms on leaves (arrows)

@FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Mild CBSD symptoms on leaves (arrows)

@FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Early CBSD symptoms on leaves (arrows)

@FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Variable CBSD symptoms on leaves

@FAO/TECA

2.2 Symptoms of CBSD on stems

  • The disease appears as dark brown “streaks” and “spots” (see pictures below) on stems, with dead spots on leaf scars.
  • These streaks are most prominent on upper, green portions of the stem.
  • Streaks appear as scratch-like wounds on stems.
  • The diseased plants may show shoot tip death, which may progress into cassava stem die-back.
  • In severe cases there may be leaf drying and shoot die-back.
Figure 5. CBSD symptoms on stems (arrows showing streaks and spots)

@FAO/TECA

Figure 6. CBSD symptoms on stems (arrows showing streaks)

@FAO/TECA

2.3. Symptoms on storage roots

  • The disease may cause cracks and discoloration in the storage roots.
  • It often causes root constriction and malformation (see pictures below).
  • The harvested roots have corky, yellow-brown necrotic spots.
  • Root rot becomes evident (roots start rotting).
  • In the roots of a susceptible variety, the disease causes a dry, hard rot which is irregular, yellow blotchy chlorosis (see pictures below).
  • Necrosis is most pronounced in the edges of the root when the root/tuber is cut across with a knife.
Figure 7. CBSD symptoms on cassava roots (black arrow showing root constriction; red arrow showing dry hard rot when the root is cut)

@FAO/TECA

2.4 Notes

  • CBSD symptoms vary from variety to variety, and from one geographical location to another.
  • Some varieties show more symptoms on above ground parts (foliar), while others show symptoms only on below ground parts (roots).
  • Not all symptoms have been shown in these resource material.
  • Careful inspection of cassava plants and consulting agricultural extension and research officers is necessary to confirm presence of CBSD.

3. How does CBSD spread?

  • Planting cassava cuttings from infected cassava plants is the major way CBSD spreads.
  • This also explains the rapid spread of the disease in areas where it is re-emerging, such as Uganda.
  • Additionally, sharing and distribution of infected planting materials is responsible for rapid spread of the disease.
  • It is also believed to be spread by insects called white flies and by infested farm implements such as knives used for cutting cassava stems but research is still on-going in this area.
  • Below is a detailed outline of how CBSD is spread.
    • The disease is spread through planting of stem cuttings from CBSD infected plants.
    • The virus also spreads from plant to plant by white flies (Figure 8).
    • Planting of susceptible varieties helps build up CBSD in the affected countries.
    • CBSD also spreads through multiplication centres if the original source of cassava materials were infested or if the planting materials being distributed are not checked for the presence of CBSD?
    • Farm implements such as knives used in cutting cassava sticks into cuttings can spread CBSD to healthy planting materials when the infested knife is used on them 
Figure 8. White fly manifestation on cassava leaves – White flies are vectors of CBSD

@FAO/TECA

4. Management of CBSD

  • Planting of clean (symptomless) cassava cuttings is the main way of controlling CBSD.
  • Use of resistant varieties is the most sustainable way of controlling CBSD.
    • However, research in developing or selecting resistant varieties is currently on-going in several countries, with some promising results in Tanzania, Uganda and Mozambique.
  • At the moment planting tolerant varieties is being encouraged in most cassava growing countries.
  • Integrated management of CBSD is the best way forward.
  • Management options for integrated management of CBSD are discussed in detail below.

4.1 Field hygiene

  • Field hygiene is one of the most important ways of managing CBSD and other diseases, which are spread through cassava cuttings and insects.
  • Field hygiene involves uprooting and destroying all cassava plants which are showing disease symptoms, and this helps in reducing the source of the disease.
  • However, this approach is not practical in farmers’ fields.
  • It should be practised in cassava multiplication plots or blocks.
  • The following need to be done in order for field hygiene to be effective.
    • Cassava plants in multiplication plots/blocks should be regularly checked for the presence of CBSD.
    • Checking for CBSD should involve checking mature (lower) leaves, stems and storage roots for CBSD symptoms as shown above.
    • All infected cassava plants should be uprooted and destroyed to avoid disease build up and spreading CBSD from the multiplication blocks.
    • All farm implements need to be sterilised over fire, especially when cutting cassava stems into planting materials (cuttings) in multiplication blocks.

4.2 Use of disease free planting materials

  • This strategy is interlinked to the field hygiene strategy/option.
  • Since CBSD spread mostly through planting cuttings from diseased cassava plants, it is important that farmers should select cuttings from healthy cassava plants. 
    • Farmers should use clean planting materials.
    • Farmers should only plant cassava from reliable multiplication sources.
    • Farmers should plant resistant/tolerant varieties when available.
    • Farmers involved in community multiplication of cassava planting materials.
      • All those involved in such exercises should be trained in proper identification, on how to reduce spread, on how to manage and on how to avoid spreading CBSD through cuttings.

4.3 Use of CBSD resistant/tolerant cassava varieties

  • Tolerant cassava varieties exist in some countries even though some of them have not been consistent in showing tolerance to CBSD.
    • Unfortunately all improved cassava varieties which were bred or selected for resistance to CMD are susceptible to CBSD.
      • This is reversing most of the gains made in breeding cassava in the Eastern and Southern Africa Region.
    • Farmers were even used to the improved varieties.
  • In order to win farmers’ acceptance of any new improved varieties resistant/tolerant to CBSD, CMD and other diseases, deliberate efforts will need to be made.
    • These include creating awareness on CBSD, and the fact that all previous improved varieties are susceptible.
    • Also involve farmers in breeding/selecting new improved and disease resistant varieties in order to make sure that the varieties meet farmers’ preferences.
  • Participatory breeding/varietal selection will need to be employed.
    • However, some tolerant varieties exist.
    • In Uganda two varieties are showing tolerance, these are MH97-2961 and 00061 (AKENA).
    • Resistance to CBSD is also reported in Tanzania, Malawi and Mozambique.
    • List of tolerant cassava varieties in the region (Kenya).
      • Kaleso
      • Shibe
      • Nzalauka
      • Siri
      • Tajirika
      • Karibuni
  • The following should be followed in order to manage CBSD using resistant/tolerant varieties.
    • Farmers should only plant resistant/tolerant cassava varieties where present.
    • Distribution of CBSD-tolerant varieties should be accompanied by information for raising farmers’ awareness about CBSD, and where farmers can get tolerant varieties in each country.
    • Arrangements should be made to share and test new CBSD resistant/tolerant varieties against CBSD in areas of new outbreaks.
  • This will need to be overseen by a reputable organisation such asthe Association for Strengthening Agricultural Research in Eastern and Central Africa (ASARECA).
  • Quarantine regulations should be followed when sharing resistant varieties across countries to avoid introducing of new strains of CBSD.

5. Propagation of clean materials 

  • Vegetative propagation of cassava planting materials is a crucial component of cassava improvement in all cassava growing regions.
  • A number of organisations and individuals are involved in propagating cassava planting materials, vegetatively.
  • In most cases this is done as a food security measure.
  • However, due to the high demand for planting materials, some organisations or individuals may take short cuts, thus increasing the risk of spreading CBSD and other diseases which are spread through cuttings.
  • Planting infected cuttings is the major avenue for spreading CBSD to a wider area and even across countries.
  • Propagators of cassava planting materials should therefore follow specific guidelines.
    • Be trained in proper identification of symptoms of CBSD and other diseases which are spread through cuttings.
    • Where possible, particularly where international organisations are involved in propagation of cassava planting materials, molecular techniques, such as PCR, should be used in testing elite cassava materials for propagation.
      • This however raises the question of sustainability due to the high costs involved in running PCR based tests.
      • It would compell nvestigation in the development of easy to use field kits for detecting CBSD.
      • However, more research will be required to develop these even though some kits are in existence for other diseases.
    • Only resistant/tolerant cassava varieties should be propagated and distributed when confirmed healthy by trained inspectors.
    • Multiplication of varieties known to be tolerant to CBSD should be fast tracked with proper backing on rigorous inspections by trained inspectors for CBSD.

6. Quarantine and legislation

  • Farmers living along borders between countries should be targeted for awareness, raising the importance of avoiding moving cassava plant materials across borders without following quarantine procedures.
  • Restrict the movement of cassava cuttings from CBSD infested areas in the country.
  • Movement of cassava germplasm between countries should only be done through virus-indexed tissue culture form.
    • Only virus-tested tissue culture materials should be used for inter-country germplasm movements.
  • Countries neighbouring CBSD infested countries should follow specific guidelines.
    • Create awareness of CBSD through print, radio and TV media channels, in particular through distribution of leaflets and posters on CBSD symptoms.
      • This should also be carried out in countries with CBSD already.
      • Survey all introduced cassava materials being grown in the country to determine whether or not CBSD is present.
    • Assess the health status, with respect to CBSD, of all cassava multiplication blocks (even in countries with CBSD).
    • Governments should tighten surveillance of border points to prevent illegal crossing of cassava materials.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Participatory breeding of superior, mosaic disease-resistant cassava: ID 4536.
  • Participatory breeding of superior, mosaic disease resistant cassava for Africa: ID 4513.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Women-friendly

This practice benefits women farmers in saving their cassava harvest.

9.2 Resource use efficiency

Mitigating Cassava diseases saves the harvest, which can be sold and rescue the farmers’ income.

9.3 Pro-poor technology

Being aware of CBSD symptoms helps poor farmers in identifying the affected plants and taking the appropriate action to managing and mitigating the disease.

Figure 1. Ravageurs du coton et leurs dégâts sur les plants

1.2 Les ravageurs du feuillages: phyllophages

  • Les phyllophages sont responsables pour la destruction des feuilles qui s'enroulent sous forme de "cigares" (une courbure du bord des feuilles vers le bas) et qui finissent par se crisper et se déchirer.
  • Quand les haritalodes sont responsables de la défoliation quasi-totale des plants (Figure 2), les acariens déchirent les feuilles rendant ainsi la vie difficile aux plants (Figure 3).
  • Tandis que les piqueurs-suceurs s’alimentent de la sève des plants et les injectent avec leur salive (Encadré 4), le phénomène qui provoque la crispation des feuilles et empêchant ainsi le développement des plants.
Figure 2. Dégâts causés par les haritalodes: les feuilles s'enroulent sous forme de "cigare"

@FAO/TECA

Figure 3. Dégâts causés par les acariens: les feuilles sont trouées

@FAO/TECA

Figure 4. Dégâts causés par les piqueur-suceurs: les feuilles sont vidées de leur sève et se dessèchent

@FAO/TECA

1.3 Les ravageurs des organes reproducteurs

  • Les ravageurs des organes reproducteurs s’attaquent à ceux-ci et les détruisent.
  • Tandis que le ver rose pénètre la capsule tout juste après l’éclosion et s’alimente des graines dans cette dernière où il effectue son développement (Figure 5), l’Helicoverpa armigera se nourrit lui de tous les organes reproducteurs du cotonnier (squares, boutons floraux, la fleur et la capsule) (Figure 6).
  • Ce type de ravageur peut aussi se nourrir des folioles et des feuilles après avoir fini de manger les organes reproducteurs.
  • Tout comme l’Helicoverpa, le Diparopsis watersi se nourrit aussi des mêmes éléments (les boutons floraux, les fleurs et les capsules) (Figure 7).
  • Alors que l’Helicoverpa peut s’attaquer à d’autres plantes comme le gombo, le maïs, la tomate, le tabac, le tournesol etc., le Diparopsis watersi se nourrit exclusivement du plant de coton.
  • Un autre ravageur du cotonnier est Earias spp.
    • Ces chenilles, en plus de la consommation des boutons floraux, des fleurs et des capsules, forent le sommet des tiges des jeunes plants sans organes de reproduction qui se dessèchent et se brisent (Figure 8). 
Figure 5. Dégâts causés par le ver rose: les boutons floraux ne s'ouvrent pas et il s'alimente des graines une fois les capsules arrivées à maturité

@FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Dégâts causés par l'helicoverpa: tous les organes reproducteurs sont attaqués par cette chenille qui s'en nourrit

@FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Dégâts causés par le diparopsis: les boutons floraux sèchent et se dissèquent après avoir été vidés par cette chenille

@FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Dégâts causés par l'earias: les boutons floraux sont consommés par ces chenilles qui essiment aussi les jeunes plants

@FAO/TECA

2. Lutte contre les ravageurs du cotonnier

2.1 Echantillonnage des plants

  • Un bon échantillonnage des plants est nécessaire.
  • Ce dernier est basé sur une définition appropriée de l’unité parcellaire à observer en tenant compte de la forme, de l’homogénéité en âge et du développement des plants.
  • Ensuite le producteur choisit les deux diagonales de son unité parcellaire et les matérialise par un piquet à chaque extrémité des diagonales (Figure 9).
  • Le producteur doit veillez à ce que les 40 plants à observer soient pris au hasard sur les deux diagonales.
  • Ceci doit être fait tout en évitant d’échantillonner les plantes proches des bordures ainsi que les plants nettement plus grands ou plus petits que la moyenne du champ.
Figure 9. Illustration de l'échantillonnage des plants avec la méthode des diagonales

@FAO/TECA

2.2 Observation des plants

  • Une observation attentive des organes des plantes échantillonnées est effectuée du bas vers le haut, tout en tenant compte des types de dégâts de chaque ravageur (Figure 10).
  • Il faut aussi prendre en considération le calendrier cultural pour pouvoir commencer l’observation le 31ème jour après levée et à une fréquence d’une semaine jusqu’au 101ème/106ème jour après levée.
  • Au cas où la date de l’observation coïncide avec la date d’un traitement de base, on réalise l’observation avant le traitement ou la veille du traitement afin d’éviter que l’observateur circule dans un champ récemment traité.
  • Lors des observations, il faut prêter attention aux différents seuils ravageurs pour pouvoir planifier un traitement approprié.
  • On distingue plusieurs seuils, voir ci-dessous.
Figure 10. Observation d'un plant du bas vers le haut pour détecter la présence de ravageurs

@FAO/TECA

2.2.1 Le seuil "pucerons"

  • Les plants considérés comme attaqués présentent une déformation du feuillage (feuilles recroquevillées vers le bas) et les nouvelles feuilles terminales portent de nombreuses colonies de pucerons.
  • Ce seuil est atteint lorsque 33 plants au moins sur 40 plant observés sont attaqués.
  • Toutefois, si les nouvelles feuilles terminales sont saines et sans pucerons, le plant n’est plus compté comme plant attaqué. 

2.2.2 Le seuil "Haritalodes derogata"

  • Un plant est considéré comme atteint lorsqu’il présente des feuilles enroulées avec la présence de chenilles vivantes d’Haritalodes derogata (Figure 11).
  • Ce seuil est atteint lorsqu’au moins 10 plants sur 40 observés sont attaqués.
Figure 11. Reconnaissance du seuil haritalodes

@FAO/TECA

2.2.3 Le seuil "acariens"

  • Un plant est considéré comme attaqué lorsqu’il présente des feuillages infestés avec des feuilles déformées, crispées, aux bords enroulés et présentant des déchirures sous formes de ‘coups de couteau’ (Figure 12).
  • Ce seuil est progressif lorsque un, deux ou trois plants sur 40 plants observés sont attaqués lors des 1er, 2ème et 3ème traitements.
  • Toutefois, si les nouvelles feuilles sont saines ou s’il n’y a pas de forme mobile d’acarien sur la face inférieure des feuilles, le plant n’est plus considéré comme attaqué. 
Figure 12. Reconnaissance du seuil acariens

@FAO/TECA

2.2.4 Le seuil "Helicoverpa"

  • Ce seuil est atteint lorsqu’on dénombre au moins quatre chenilles sur les 40 plants observés (Figure 13).
  • Cette observation s’applique aussi aux autres carpophages tels que Diparopsis watersi, Earias spp., Pectinophora gossypiella et Thaumatotibia leucotreta.
Figure 13. Reconnaissance du seuil helicoverpa

@FAO/TECA

2.4 Prise de décision: traitement ou non?

  • Un outil de travail, ‘la planchette d’observation’ est conçu pour servir de guide au cours de la pratique.
  • Les différentes étapes d’utilisation ont été décrites dans la Figure 14.
  • A la fin de chaque observation, il s’avère nécessaire au producteur de prendre une décision de procéder ou non à un traitement.
  • Cette prise de décision se fait en comparant le résultat des observations par type de ravageur au seuil critique leur correspondant.
  • Ainsi, deux produits complémentaires ou plus peuvent être appliqués en mélange le même jour si deux seuils différents sont atteints.
  • Procéder au traitement le plus rapidement possible après un comptage est important car plus un traitement est retardé, moins il sera efficace.
  • Il faut aussi garder à l’esprit que les dégâts des ravageurs s’intensifient de jour en jour.
Figure 14. Illustration de la planchette d'observation

@FAO/TECA

3. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Lutter contre les parasites du mouton: ID 7661.
  • Comment lutter contre la mouche des mangues: ID 7650.
  • Comment lutter contre Striga et les foreurs de tige du maïs: ID 7535.
  • Bonnes pratiques d’utilisation des pesticides: ID 8016.

4. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

4.1 La technologie favorable aux populations pauvres

La technologie mène à une diminution des dégâts causés par les ravageurs. Ceci améliore les cultures en terme de quantité et de qualité, fournissant des sources supplémentaires d’alimentation et de revenu.

_annotations.field_innovation_identified:
Title: Targeted Sequential Control (LEC - Lutte Étagée Ciblée)

Description: An integrated pest management approach for cotton farming that combines systematic field observation methods with targeted pesticide application based on pest-specific thresholds. It reduces pesticide use through precise monitoring and intervention.

Innovation criteria met: This is a modified process that helps solve pest management problems more efficiently, reducing chemical inputs while maintaining crop protection. It supports behavioral change in farmers' pest control practices.

records.title: Good practices for the establishment of a new cashew farm
records.description:
Description

The block of pictures is meant to facilitate the training sessions with cashew farmers for the establishment of their new cashew orchards. It is instructive in form. The picture on the front and the text on the overleaf  help the animator to get the key messages across, with the aim of improving practices. The animator should ask questions and not read the answers. The questions help to discover the "correct” answer with the help of the pictorial. The animator will need almost one hour to communicate the key messages contained in this block of pictures. Questions and answers act as a guide for the animator and should not be read continuously during the session with the farmers. Suggestions for modifications by the farmers are welcome for the improvement of this block of pictures.

The following questions and answers should help farmers identifying a good site for a cashew farm:

  • Question one: Which areas are the most suitable for cashew cultivation?
    • Answer: The savanna and transitional zones are the most suitable areas for cashew cultivation. In Ghana, cashew trees can grow and produce well in some districts in the Northern, Brong-Ahafo, Volta, Upper West and Central Regions.
  • Question two: What types of soils are suitable for Atta for cashew farming?
    • Answer: Almost all types of soils from sandy to laterite, deep, fertile and well-drained soils.
  • Question three: What types of soils are not suitable for cashew farming?
    • Answer: Heavy clay soils with poor drainage condition and also excessive alkalinity and salinity soils, as well as areas prone to waterlogging and hardpan, are not suitable for cashew growing.  
Figure 1. Site selection 

©FAO/TECA

1. Land clearing

1.1 Bushes

  • All the bushes and undergrowth with machetes needs to be cleared.
  • In addition all cut woods and twigs need to be removed because the cashew trees do not tolerate shade.
  • Long sticks need to be collected.
    • They will be used for the staking and the shorter one for fencing to protect the young plantings.
  • The clearing should be done in the dry season, during March. 
Figure 2. Land clearing 

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Fallow land

  • The farm needs to be weeded with a hoe.
  • Cleared weeds will be left on the ground to decompose.
  • Weeding of the farm should be done in the dry season, during March.
Figure 3. Land clearing

©FAO/TECA

2. Land preparation

2.1 Line and pegging

  • The plant holes will be marked with sticks using a rope.
  • The plant spacing is 10 m by 10 m (100 trees per ha).
  • The lining of the farm should be done in the dry season before the rains start.
    • This is between the end of March and the beginning of April.
Figure 4. Line and pegging 

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Digging holes

  • Digging the plant holes can be done with the dribbler, machete and hoe.
  • Farmers should start by measuring a stick of 30 cm to be used for the width and the depth of the hole.
  • Then they dig the hole with dribbler and remove the soil with a hoe.
  • They should separate the soil into two parts because they put the topsoil on one side and the lower layer on the other side because the topsoil is more fertile.
  • During the planting, he will put the topsoil in the hole first.
  • Digging holes should be done after the first rains, mid-April.
Figure 5. Digging holes 

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Refilling the planting holes

  • Farmers should refill the plant holes by put the topsoil first and the lower layer second.
  • If the soil of the farm is very poor, they could add some manure by mixing the soil with compost or well-decomposed cow dung at the rate of one bucket (size 34 = 10 kg) per tree.
  • This should be applied two to four weeks after the digging, in May. 
Figure 6. Refilling the planting holes 

©FAO/TECA

3. Planting process

3.1 Planting

  • Farmers have two options to obtain plant material for his new cashew farm.
    • Sowing with cashew seed nuts.
    • Using grafted plants.
  • For a grafted plant for example, farmers should make a hole with depth according to the size (7 cm by 10 cm) of the seedling poly bag.
    • Then with a knife, the polybag can be cut at the base, and placing the seedling in the hole, and pulling up carefully the poly bag.
    • Then the plant can be covered with the soil but the collar can be left free of soil.
    • Planting is usually done after a rainfall, at the beginning of June until mid-July.
Figure 7. Planting 

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Fertilization

  • The soil on the farm can be poor, due to a lack of nutrients.
  • The farmer can apply compost or manure if these are not available then they can apply to chemical fertilizer to improve nutrients in the soil, as the third option.
  • For chemical fertilizer, Sulfate of Ammonia (SA) and Triple Superphosphate (TSP) can be used.
  • The application can be done one month after transplanting.
    • 70 g of SA (two-third of milk tin).
    • 100 g (1 full milk tin) of TSP per plant.
    • That means 10 kg of TSP per ha and 7 kg of SA per ha.
Figure 8. Fertilization 

©FAO/TECA

3.3 Seed nuts selection

  • Farmers have two options to obtain plant material for their new cashew farm.
    • Sowing with cashew seed nuts.
    • Using grafted plants.
  • If the seed nuts option was chosen, they will obtain the seeds from the elite mother trees of mature farms.
  • These trees are characterized by high yield, large nuts/good apples, and consistency in fruiting. 
  • The observation for a mother tree starts during the fruiting period over two to three years.
  • Farmers must mark the identified trees, record the yield, nuts count (100 kg to 170 per kg), tree age, and farm sanitation.
  • The seed nuts harvested by picking the nuts under the mother trees by detaching the nut properly from the apple, sundry and sort (discarding small, shriveled, diseased or damaged).
  • Seed collection can be harvested during the harvest period (January to March) after choosing the mother trees in the past seasons. 
  • To know whether the seed nuts are good quality for sowing, farmers conduct a water test to establish the seed nuts density before sowing, by following specific steps.
    • Prepare a salt solution by dissolving one tablespoon of salt (10 g) in six and a half bottles of the big mineral water (10 litres) in a bucket.
    • Soak the seed-nuts in the salt solution for about five minutes.
    • Select seed-nuts which have sunk.
    • The selected seed-nuts are then soaked in clean-salt water for eight hours to obtain good germination.
    • The seed nuts will be air-dried before the next rainy day for sowing.
Figure 9. Seed nuts selection

©FAO/TECA

3.4 Sowing of seed nuts

  • Farmers sowing two seed nuts in the planting hole (mole-shaped) at 3 cm to 5 cm depth and 15 cm apart.
  • The stalk end of the seed nut is positioned pointing upwards and slightly inclined.
  • Sow the seed nuts is done after a rainfall, at the beginning of June until mid-July.  
Figure 10. Sowing of seed nuts

©FAO/TECA

3.5 Protecting young plants

  • Young plants should be fenced using the small sticks which were collected during the clearing of the land.
  • The fence is prepared one week after the sowing, at the end of July.
Figure 11. Protecting the young plants 

©FAO/TECA

3.6 Weeding and establishment of intercrops in the new cashew farm

  • Farmers need to weed the cashew farm and sow maize between the rows of cashew plants.
  • This intercrop:
    • increases crop production per unit area;
    • reduces maintenance cost of the cashew farm;
    • improves soil fertility when the leguminous crop is grown;and
    • reduces weed infestation and risk of bush fire.  
  • Intercrops are planted at 1 m from the main trunk of the young cashew plants.
  • Food crops like groundnuts, soybean, sorghum, yam, pepper or pineapple can be used as intercrops.
  • Intercrops can be established until the cashew trees develop their crown/canopy, until the canopy closes and the crowns touch one another.

_annotations.body:
Good practices for the establishment of a new cashew farm

The application of good practices is an essential foundation for the establishment of a new functional and thriving cashew farm. This flip-chart (picture bloc), with its very comprehensive pictures as well as a question and answer section, describes how to better prepare an area for the establishment of a thriving cashew farm. It is designed to help introduce novice cashew farmers to this kind of farming or those who want to expand their cashew farming endeavors. It is used as training material by the African Cashew Initiative and is intended to be used by extension agents to animate group sessions to train such farmers. It can also be consulted by someone who has the intention of establishing a cashew plantation. This picture-based extension material is part of a series which covers the establishment phase; good agricultural practices of cashew plantation management; harvest and post-harvest operation as well as quality issues.

Description

The block of pictures is meant to facilitate the training sessions with cashew farmers for the establishment of their new cashew orchards. It is instructive in form. The picture on the front and the text on the overleaf  help the animator to get the key messages across, with the aim of improving practices. The animator should ask questions and not read the answers. The questions help to discover the "correct” answer with the help of the pictorial. The animator will need almost one hour to communicate the key messages contained in this block of pictures. Questions and answers act as a guide for the animator and should not be read continuously during the session with the farmers. Suggestions for modifications by the farmers are welcome for the improvement of this block of pictures.

The following questions and answers should help farmers identifying a good site for a cashew farm:

  • Question one: Which areas are the most suitable for cashew cultivation?
    • Answer: The savanna and transitional zones are the most suitable areas for cashew cultivation. In Ghana, cashew trees can grow and produce well in some districts in the Northern, Brong-Ahafo, Volta, Upper West and Central Regions.
  • Question two: What types of soils are suitable for Atta for cashew farming?
    • Answer: Almost all types of soils from sandy to laterite, deep, fertile and well-drained soils.
  • Question three: What types of soils are not suitable for cashew farming?
    • Answer: Heavy clay soils with poor drainage condition and also excessive alkalinity and salinity soils, as well as areas prone to waterlogging and hardpan, are not suitable for cashew growing.  
Figure 1. Site selection 

©FAO/TECA

1. Land clearing

1.1 Bushes

  • All the bushes and undergrowth with machetes needs to be cleared.
  • In addition all cut woods and twigs need to be removed because the cashew trees do not tolerate shade.
  • Long sticks need to be collected.
    • They will be used for the staking and the shorter one for fencing to protect the young plantings.
  • The clearing should be done in the dry season, during March. 
Figure 2. Land clearing 

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Fallow land

  • The farm needs to be weeded with a hoe.
  • Cleared weeds will be left on the ground to decompose.
  • Weeding of the farm should be done in the dry season, during March.
Figure 3. Land clearing

©FAO/TECA

2. Land preparation

2.1 Line and pegging

  • The plant holes will be marked with sticks using a rope.
  • The plant spacing is 10 m by 10 m (100 trees per ha).
  • The lining of the farm should be done in the dry season before the rains start.
    • This is between the end of March and the beginning of April.
Figure 4. Line and pegging 

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Digging holes

  • Digging the plant holes can be done with the dribbler, machete and hoe.
  • Farmers should start by measuring a stick of 30 cm to be used for the width and the depth of the hole.
  • Then they dig the hole with dribbler and remove the soil with a hoe.
  • They should separate the soil into two parts because they put the topsoil on one side and the lower layer on the other side because the topsoil is more fertile.
  • During the planting, he will put the topsoil in the hole first.
  • Digging holes should be done after the first rains, mid-April.
Figure 5. Digging holes 

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Refilling the planting holes

  • Farmers should refill the plant holes by put the topsoil first and the lower layer second.
  • If the soil of the farm is very poor, they could add some manure by mixing the soil with compost or well-decomposed cow dung at the rate of one bucket (size 34 = 10 kg) per tree.
  • This should be applied two to four weeks after the digging, in May. 
Figure 6. Refilling the planting holes 

©FAO/TECA

3. Planting process

3.1 Planting

  • Farmers have two options to obtain plant material for his new cashew farm.
    • Sowing with cashew seed nuts.
    • Using grafted plants.
  • For a grafted plant for example, farmers should make a hole with depth according to the size (7 cm by 10 cm) of the seedling poly bag.
    • Then with a knife, the polybag can be cut at the base, and placing the seedling in the hole, and pulling up carefully the poly bag.
    • Then the plant can be covered with the soil but the collar can be left free of soil.
    • Planting is usually done after a rainfall, at the beginning of June until mid-July.
Figure 7. Planting 

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Fertilization

  • The soil on the farm can be poor, due to a lack of nutrients.
  • The farmer can apply compost or manure if these are not available then they can apply to chemical fertilizer to improve nutrients in the soil, as the third option.
  • For chemical fertilizer, Sulfate of Ammonia (SA) and Triple Superphosphate (TSP) can be used.
  • The application can be done one month after transplanting.
    • 70 g of SA (two-third of milk tin).
    • 100 g (1 full milk tin) of TSP per plant.
    • That means 10 kg of TSP per ha and 7 kg of SA per ha.
Figure 8. Fertilization 

©FAO/TECA

3.3 Seed nuts selection

  • Farmers have two options to obtain plant material for their new cashew farm.
    • Sowing with cashew seed nuts.
    • Using grafted plants.
  • If the seed nuts option was chosen, they will obtain the seeds from the elite mother trees of mature farms.
  • These trees are characterized by high yield, large nuts/good apples, and consistency in fruiting. 
  • The observation for a mother tree starts during the fruiting period over two to three years.
  • Farmers must mark the identified trees, record the yield, nuts count (100 kg to 170 per kg), tree age, and farm sanitation.
  • The seed nuts harvested by picking the nuts under the mother trees by detaching the nut properly from the apple, sundry and sort (discarding small, shriveled, diseased or damaged).
  • Seed collection can be harvested during the harvest period (January to March) after choosing the mother trees in the past seasons. 
  • To know whether the seed nuts are good quality for sowing, farmers conduct a water test to establish the seed nuts density before sowing, by following specific steps.
    • Prepare a salt solution by dissolving one tablespoon of salt (10 g) in six and a half bottles of the big mineral water (10 litres) in a bucket.
    • Soak the seed-nuts in the salt solution for about five minutes.
    • Select seed-nuts which have sunk.
    • The selected seed-nuts are then soaked in clean-salt water for eight hours to obtain good germination.
    • The seed nuts will be air-dried before the next rainy day for sowing.
Figure 9. Seed nuts selection

©FAO/TECA

3.4 Sowing of seed nuts

  • Farmers sowing two seed nuts in the planting hole (mole-shaped) at 3 cm to 5 cm depth and 15 cm apart.
  • The stalk end of the seed nut is positioned pointing upwards and slightly inclined.
  • Sow the seed nuts is done after a rainfall, at the beginning of June until mid-July.  
Figure 10. Sowing of seed nuts

©FAO/TECA

3.5 Protecting young plants

  • Young plants should be fenced using the small sticks which were collected during the clearing of the land.
  • The fence is prepared one week after the sowing, at the end of July.
Figure 11. Protecting the young plants 

©FAO/TECA

3.6 Weeding and establishment of intercrops in the new cashew farm

  • Farmers need to weed the cashew farm and sow maize between the rows of cashew plants.
  • This intercrop:
    • increases crop production per unit area;
    • reduces maintenance cost of the cashew farm;
    • improves soil fertility when the leguminous crop is grown;and
    • reduces weed infestation and risk of bush fire.  
  • Intercrops are planted at 1 m from the main trunk of the young cashew plants.
  • Food crops like groundnuts, soybean, sorghum, yam, pepper or pineapple can be used as intercrops.
  • Intercrops can be established until the cashew trees develop their crown/canopy, until the canopy closes and the crowns touch one another.
Figure 12. Weeding and establishment of intercrops in the new cashew farm 

©FAO/TECA

3.7 Gap filling

  • The gap should be filled with some seedlings at the beginning of the rainy season in the second year (May-June).
Figure 13. Gap filling 

©FAO/TECA

3.8 Pruning the young cashew tree

  • The lower branches should be pruned with a bow saw at the height of 1 m (50 percent of the height of the young tree), at the beginning of the rainy season in the second year (May-June).
Figure 14. Pruning the young cashew tree

©FAO/TECA

4. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropical, warm. 

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Guide to harvesting and post-harvest handling of cashew nuts: ID 7467.
  • How to estimate the quality of cashew nuts (RCN): ID 7475.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology facilitates training and knowledge on how to establish a cashew farm, leading to more sources of food and income for farmers.

records.title: Mitigating diseases and saving valuable assets - poultry vaccinators delivering services to the poorest
records.description:
Description

1. ​Background​

  • Smallholder poultry production has a strong correlation with poverty reduction and women's empowerment.
    • With about 89 percent of rural households rearing poultry in Bangladesh, the sector has a GDP share of 9 percent in the country.
    • There are about 183 million indigenous chicken and 37 million ducks reared mainly in scavenging conditions on household waste and crop residue.
    • Poultry in Bangladesh is also more equitably distributed compared to land.
    • With just 9 percent population owning more than 1 ha of land and over 59 percent owning less than 0.20 Ha of land, rearing poultry provides a ready source of income and nutrition.
    • Women in particular, who suffer impediments like illiteracy, poor health and mobility, find poultry rearing an extremely viable occupation.
  • However, mortality from preventable diseases like Newcastle, Fowl Pox, Fowl Cholera, Fowl Typhoid, Coccidiosis, Gumborro, deficiency diseases, and worm infestations are often very high (ranging from 35 to 80 percent) within scavenging systems.
    • Although four types of major vaccines (Ranikhet, Pox, Cholera and Duck Plague) have been produced by the Government, traditional service delivery mechanisms have been unable to serve all parts of the country.
    • With only four field staff and one Government Livestock Officer deployed at each sub-district having to provide livestock services to about 200 000 poultry and 50 000 cattle and sheep, the system suffers obvious limitations of human power and outreach.
  • Furthermore, while commercial poultry has been patronized and serviced by the private sector and continues to grow at 20 percent annually, the rural scavenging system and some small scale commercial farms neither had their own vaccination program nor access to Government's vaccination services, creating high-risk conditions for rearers.
    • To address this gap, in 1983 the Non-Governmental Organisation (NGO) Bangladesh Rural Advancement Committee (BRAC), initiated a poultry vaccinator programme with an aim to prevent poultry from contracting common diseases through vaccination and dissemination of information to rearers. 
Figures ​1 and 2​. ​Women poultry vaccinators​

​​

©​FAO/TECA

2. ​How did good practice work?​

  • This good practice grew out of a semi-scavenging poultry programme initiated in the 1970s by the Department of Livestock Services (DLS) and BRAC as well as other NGOs.
    • There was support from both bilateral and multilateral donors that aimed to use poultry as a tool to reduce poverty among landless women.
    • Through implementation and trying to turn problems into opportunities, the erstwhile programme evolved into the now famous 'Bangladesh poultry model'.
    • The common feature of this poultry system of production, supply and services is that the requirements for services and inputs have turned into opportunities for people.
  • One of the key impediments of the earlier programme phase was high poultry mortality caused by a lack of capacity to provide timely vaccination services.
    • BRAC thus initiated the first poultry vaccinator pilot in Manikganj district to test the feasibility of a decentralised service delivery model based on building local capacities.
    • This pilot was later up-scaled to all 50 districts of Bangladesh.
    • Herein, BRAC integrated the poultry vaccinator component within its pre-existing organisational structure.
    • Activities were thus coordinated through functional linkages between the head office in Dhaka, regional offices and field offices.
    • At the field level, BRAC staff worked directly with Village Organisations, which provided them the administrative link to identify and monitor women vaccinators.
  • Based on experiences from the pilot at Manikganj, where men and unmarried women largely dropped out from the programme, BRAC field staff have now adopted a participatory approach for selection.
    • The Village Organisation, widows, abandoned women and married women between the age group of 25 to 45 having basic level of literacy are selected democratically as poultry vaccinators.
    • To note, as part of BRAC's work, communities are organized into Village Organisations (VOs) comprising 30 to 40 members.
    • The mandate given to all selected, is to function as an interface between BRAC field offices and the rearers by procuring and administering vaccines at fixed prices and schedules; to vaccinate at least 500 birds per month at 1 TK per vaccination.
      • The vaccinations are to be conducted before 8 am.
    • This averages to about two hours of work per day and to provide first aid and advisory support to rearers.
  • In the beginning, these vaccinators are inducted into a five-day training followed by monthly refresher training.
    • The induction training focuses on many topics.
      • Poultry vaccination
        • Cold chain maintenance and appropriate vaccination techniques,
      • Poultry management
        • Information on feed and brooding.
        • Disease control including identification of Ranikhet, Pox, Gumborro, Coccidiosis, Cholera, worms, parasites and malnutrition.
    • Each vaccinator is also provided a free of cost vaccination kit comprising a bag, thermos and syringes.
    • The refresher training serves as an important interface between BRAC field offices and vaccinators and creates a platform to address emerging issues of importance such as building awareness about bio-security, sharing problems experienced in the field, and sharing knowledge of extension tools.
    • BRAC estimates that it takes approximately TK 750 to capacitate each vaccinator for their future roles.
  • BRAC manages a streamlined supply of equipment, vaccines and medicines to the vaccinators.
    • Female poultry vaccinators provide vaccination service (on a cost basis) in groups by dividing each village into four parts and administering vaccines in rotation.
  • Rearers are informed of the vaccination dates and spots where they bring their birds on a routine basis.
    • The DLS on its behalf, which used to earlier administer vaccines free of cost now supplies vaccines in smaller vials to BRAC field offices on a cost basis.
    • These are then picked up by poultry vaccinators for administration.
    • BRAC also purchases basic medicines for de-worming in bulk and supplies it to vaccinators at the lowest rates.
    • The cold chain and financial sustainability of the model are thus maintained through an interplay between the DLS-BRAC-poultry vaccinators and rearers.
    • The vaccinators are held responsible for their services by both the BRAC field staff and the VO on a routine basis through monitoring of outputs.
Figure 2​. ​Stakeholders and their interactions​ 

Source: Dhamankar et.al, 2008

2.1 ​Key learnings​

  • This practice effectively showcases a workable Government-NGO cooperation wherein the combined strengths of the Government, in terms of resources and technology, human-power and networks available to an NGO were used in a sustainable and cost-effective manner to provide vaccination and information services to the remotest areas of Bangladesh.
  • Further, the poultry vaccinator also served as a critical link between rearers and animal health authorities by contributing to epidemiological surveillance.
    • As an example, during bird flu, the vaccinators were given specialised training to equip rearers to prevent and respond to outbreak conditions.
  • A critical element emerging from this practice is also the importance of mass vaccination to reduce mortality to a minimum.
  • Here the introduction of payment for vaccination services, the maintenance of cold chain, the improved biosecurity awareness, and the easy access to technical back-up support all proved vital for the success and sustainability of the model.
  • Another remarkable aspect was the selection criterion adopted.
    • Drawing from BRAC's integrated agenda of reducing poverty and empowering women, the tireless efforts put in to select widows as well as abandoned and married women as vaccinators gave women a chance to overcome societal resistance, become financially strong professionals, and become skilled entrepreneurs. 

3. ​What and where next?​

  • This practice is worthy of replication because it highlights that decentralised vaccinations and health care delivered by trained poultry vaccinators with access to technical back up support provide a strong foundation for mitigating diseases.
    • The Government of Bangladesh is convinced by the positive outcome of this practice and has encouraged NGOs and the private sector to upscale the activity.
    • To this end, BRAC’s attempts to introduce standardisation in selection criteria, training content, duration, and frequency of training have served as a strong base to build the skills of vaccinators.
    • Thus, while a definitive legal framework that fully safeguards the ethics and encourages professional fair play for such semi-skilled professionals to dispense simple services is not yet streamlined in Bangladesh, it does set an example of how far openness on behalf of the government can go in mitigating diseases.
    • It requires a persuasive and integrated approach to empower women as vaccinators.
  • In this case, it took strong selection, motivation, supervision, and monitoring to encourage women to break stereotypes and become vaccinators.
    • Women now also benefit from other BRAC programmes related to sanitation, adult education, legal awareness, and health promotion.
    • The easier the access of poultry vaccinators to technical support, the better the performance.
    • The distance to and quality of the (veterinary) support are also decisive factors. 

4. Validation of the practice

  • This model today reaches out to 2.47 million women poultry rearers in the farthest regions of Bangladesh and has been successful in reducing mortality levels and increasing incomes for the poorest.
  • It has also created an invaluable opportunity for self-employment for rural women with over 19 900 vaccinators delivering services in the country.
  • Recent studies conducted by DLS and BRAC reveal that knowledge of balanced feed and timely vaccination has taken strong root in the villages.
  • Women vaccinators, who earlier had to struggle for livelihoods are well respected and have developed strong skills in handling all disease prevention procedures and are aware of protocols to respond to outbreaks like bird flu. 

5. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropical, warm. 

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Replicas of native chicken in rural poultry production: the satpuda: ID 7680.
  • Women resurrecting poultry biodiversity and livelihoods: ID 7681.

7. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

7.1 Women-friendly

The technology allows for women to play a greater role in poultry rearing, leading to an improved in their skillset, education, social status and livelihoods.

records.title: Building fodder security in rural areas
records.description:
Description

1. Background 

  • In order to document this critical knowledge, a comprehensive action research program was initiated by Anthra.
    • The key focus was on conducting an appraisal of local feed and fodder used in the past and present; the seasonal differences in feeding practices. the traditional evaluation or assessment of a feed by farmers; its palatability and availability (both temporal and actual quantity over time) of fodder, storage of feed and fodder; and special feeding practices during disaster situations.
    • Mapping grazing routes and associated watering practices was also an integral component of the research.
  • Anthra, the implementing agency, took the lead in conceptualising the parameters for this participatory research process.
    • This was done with the active participation of key community members such as farmers, barefoot documenters, researchers, healers, and elders from different sections of the community.
    • They took up the responsibility for training the community researchers to document the oral traditions. 
Figure ​1​. ​Building fodder security in rural areas​ 

©​FAO/TECA

Figure ​2​. ​Building fodder security in rural areas​ 

©​FAO/TECA

2. ​Innovation in the good practice​

  • Scientists trained in the formal paradigms of “western science” were able to engage with “peoples science” and helped give validity to this body of knowledge, which goes beyond the narrow and limited definitions of “monetary value' being placed on traditional knowledge systems.
  • Participatory documentation of the wealth of traditional knowledge across different agro-ecological regions; communities and ethnic groups; genders; and age-groups ensured that the “sum of the whole” was much greater than the individual pieces of information.
  • It stimulated a process of self-analysis and reflection by the participating communities, which in turn, led to an increase in the dignity of their own heritage and re-integrating some of these practices into their ongoing livelihoods.

2.1 ​The methodology​

  • A network comprising of various key stakeholders was formalised through a process of dialogue.
    • There were continuous and close interactions between all the different members of this network throughout the entire period.
    • The process included informal interviews, participatory visualisation exercises (like resource mapping and problem ranking), observational walks, identifying plant specimens (making herbariums of these), and photo-documentation were some of the tools applied for generating the requisite outputs.
    • This information was then analysed by the team of Anthra and key community members.
    • Local NGOs and CBOs assisted in selecting barefoot researchers, villages and most importantly assisted in establishing critical linkages with knowledgeable farmers and community leaders.
  • Farmers representing different sections of the community (e.g. caste, landholding, gender, age-group) participated in sharing their knowledge with respect to:
    • fodder species,
    • their seasonal availability,
    • palatability,
    • nutritional content,
    • medicinal value,
    • effects on animals, and
    • the reasons for their disappearance.
  • Scientists from research institutions, experimental fodder farms, researchers, and academics provided technical guidance for the research.
    • Laboratories helped in testing the nutrient content of traditional fodder varieties.
    • Conscious efforts were made to include women in the process of documenting since traditionally it is the women who play an active role in rearing livestock and as such are custodians of a wealth of knowledge which is not recognised.
  • The participatory action research process was carried out over three phases.
    1. Documentation (1996-1998)
    2. Validation and Dissemination (1998-2003)
    3. Action research and reintegration of practices into livelihood systems (2003 to present).
  • Major findings of the first phase 1 and phase 2 included a drastic change in diets and reduced variety and quantity of feed available for livestock.
    • There was especially a reduction in the quality and quantity of crop residues, which was a result of the dramatic shift in cropping patterns from food to cash crops.
    • Another finding was the perceptible shift of perennial grasses by annuals.
    • The most disturbing observation was a general loss of knowledge on fodder types amongst the younger generation.
    • These shifts were largely linked to and embedded in the larger changes occurring in agriculture, as a response to policies that enabled capital and chemical-intensive green revolution to flourish and predominate over traditional agricultural practices.
  • Besides documenting indigenous knowledge systems five, different field trials were conducted to validate/assess traditional ways of utilising fodder in Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra.
    • In-depth analysis of one of these traditional practices, lopping of Acacia Nilotica trees, was conducted with the objective to measure and analyse the biomass yield from lopped branches of the tree.
      • The hypothesis was that the correct lopping does not harm the tree, but enhances its biomass production.
      • The key finding of these field trials revealed that traditional methods of lopping Acacia Nilotica trees are beneficial to the animals as they provide crucial feed, with high protein content, during the critical period of lean summer months.
      • The study also revealed that the practice of lopping does not damage the tree.
      • It enhances branching, leaf and fruit production.
      • However, there is a large variation in average fodder yield per tree, based on its age, whether it has been lopped previously or not, the soil on which it grows, rainfall, as also lopping management practices.
  • During the third phase, the emphasis was laid on the dissemination of information based on the outcomes of the previous phases and the reintegration of appropriate practices with farmers and pastoralists.
    • One of the earliest interventions made by fe/male farmers in East Godavari district was to consciously diversify their cropping pattern with multiple millets, pulses, oilseeds, vegetables, as well as other ecological farming practices.
    • This has enhanced the quantity and quality of food grains as also crop-residue and by-products available for feeding livestock and poultry.
    • Conserving traditional varieties of seeds through community seed banks and making these available to local communities, has been a core element of this intervention.
    • This strategy has subsequently been adopted by innovative farmers in all the districts where Anthra has active community-livelihood programs (nine districts in Andhra Pradesh and four districts in Maharashtra).
    • As of June 2008, there are about 600 farmers in these districts, who are actively involved in transforming their agriculture practices to mixed cropping.
  • The second major practice that has gained wide popularity was pastoralists and farmers growing traditional fodder trees and natural grasses on field bunds in their private and community lands.
    • Fodder nurseries to propagate the relevant species were established with the contribution of the local farmers.
    • Shepherds and farmers were actively involved in collecting fodder seeds and conserving them.
    • A survey carried out in the year 2007 revealed that all the 42 participants who volunteered to be a part of the fodder enhancement project now owned one or other types of livestock.
    • Prior to the practice, only 50 percent of them owned livestock.
    • There was a significant increase in the number of buffaloes and goats in the village.
  • In 2007, shepherds of the Peddagottimukkala (PGM) village in the Medak district showed interest in developing their community land with traditional fodder trees and grasses.
    • They got interested when the results of a comparative analysis on weight gain of lambs were shared by Anthra.
    • They realised that the weight gain of lambs in their village was significantly lower than the weight gain of lambs in other villages.
    • A major reason for this appeared to be the comparative non-availability of diverse fodders in PGM village as compared to other villages.
    • This particular intervention was the result of Anthra's continuous efforts of organising the community into village-level sanghams.
      • This was done with regular meetings and enabling them to access health services in terms of vaccinations and de-worming from the local government veterinary hospital.
Figure 3​. ​The average yield of randomly selected samples (kg)​ 

©SAPPLPP

3. ​Lessons learnt​ 

  • The process of documentation, validation, dissemination and practical applications were vital in the effective re-integration and revitalisation of traditional knowledge systems pertaining to fodder.
  • The methodology used ensured the complete participation and involvement of the local communities who bring in their traditional knowledge and experience.
  • The scientific and traditional validation methods have shown remarkably similar findings, especially regarding the nutritive value of specific grass and tree fodder.
  • This has helped to break the myth prevailing in the mainstream regarding the fodder value of traditional species.
    • Female/male farmers have sound traditional knowledge regarding the nutritive value of different fodders and grasses.
    • Traditional feed and fodder species are more suitable to rain fed areas compared to new fodder varieties being introduced that need irrigation facilities.
    • Documentation of traditional knowledge concerning plants, feed and fodder species has to be undertaken so that this knowledge is not lost and future generations can bank upon documented resource base.
      • This needs resources both financial and human for a considerable period of time.
    • Lopping of branches of trees undertaken in traditional ways facilitates enhanced growth of branches leading to more fodder production.
    • Forest departments can plant traditional trees/grasses that provide fodder for livestock instead of timber trees with active community participation.
    • In this experience, the tribal community has been empowered to take back control over their own knowledge and related genetic resources.
      • They have been encouraged to use it in ways that are making a positive impact on their livelihoods.
    • Government policies, as well as top-down interventions, can be counterproductive if not based on the needs and requirements of the livestock keepers as a shift towards non-food cash crops resulted in depleted fodder resources for the livestock.
    • Community-based institutions are best suited to conserve and propagate traditional species of feed and fodder. 

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropical, warm; and
  • subtropics, warm/ mod cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Innovations in common land development: ID 7683.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

6.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology allows for the engagement of community members with government, academia and civil society to revitalise and reintegrate traditional knowledge in livelihood strategies. Such syngergies lead to improved varieties of grass and fodders leading to improved livelihoods.

records.title: Confección de pinza para extracción de marcos con espátula integrada
records.description:
Descripción

  • Es una herramienta combinada y práctica compuesta de dos tenazas con funcionamiento simultáneo, que sirve para remover, agarrar y retirar los cuadros de la colmena.
  • Tiene integrado una espátula (franja metálica afilada) en la parte superior, la cual sirve para despegar o separar todas las partes móviles de la colmena (tapa, piso, marcos, alzas), así como para limpiar/raspar los marcos de la cera y el propóleo que se adhiere (Figura 1). 
Figura ​1​. ​Pinza usada para la extracción de marcos (izquierda) y espátula usada para sacar propóleo (derecha)


©​Swisscontact​

1. ​Materiales/equipo necesario para la construcción​

  • Acero de 3 mm (65 cm x 7 cm).
  • Dos tornillos de hilo de 4 mm.
  • Un resorte de 3/8“ x ¾“.
  • Cierra para metales.
  • Lima o lija para limar bordes.

2. Materia prima

  • La pinza es fabricada en base de acero galvanizado, esmaltado o aluminio (3 mm) y la espátula integrada a base de acero inoxidable o acero al carbón de calidad (3 mm), para evitar que se parta o doble a la hora de hacer palanca para mover los marcos.
  • Además se requieren otros materiales como resortes (espirales) de ⅜ “x ¾ “, tornillos y remaches (Figura 2).
Figura 2. Partes de la pinza para extracción de bastidores con espátula integrada 


©​Swisscontact​

3. Partes de la pinza para extracción de bastidores con espátula integrada

  • La pinza está compuesta por cuatro piezas principales: dos listones de acero galvanizado, un resorte de atracción y un listón de acero de alta calidad para que no se rompa ni doble (Figura 3).
Figura 3. Ilustración de la pinza para extracción de marcos con espátula integrada 


©​Swisscontact​

3.1 La pinza

  • Para cortar las diferentes partes de la pinza se debe emplear una cierra manual para cortar metales.
  • Para moldearlos se debe emplear una prensa y un martillo o maseta (si es posible calentar el acero para facilitar este manejo).
  • Finalizados los cortes se debe emplear una lima de metales para eliminar las puntas y bordes filosos (Figura 4).
Figura 4. Medidas de la pinza 

©​Swisscontact​

3.2 La espátula

  • La espátula se puede soldar o remachar a la pinza levanta marcos, o bien mantener como una herramienta por separado.
  • Los cortes se deben realizar con una sierra para cortar metales.
  • Además la espátula debe poseer una curvatura de un arco de 0,6 centímetros para levantar marcos (si se confecciona una espátula individual).
  • Un centímetro distante de la curvatura se puede hacer una perforación (3 mm) con un taladro para metales con la idea de incorporarle un saca clavos a la espátula.
  • Idealmente se debe pintar con algún color de fuerte tono para que sea fácil encontrarla si se cae entre la vegetación (Figura 5).
Figura 5. Medidas de la espátula y dos formas de sacar el propóleo

©​Swisscontact​

Figura 6. Propóleo cosechado en la espátula 

©​Swisscontact​

Figura 7. Propóleo cosechado en la espátula

©​Swisscontact​

4. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido. 

5. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Fundidor de cera de abejas a vapor artesanal: ID 8289.
  • Confección de ahumador para apicultor: ID 8295.
  • Guantes de protección para apicultor: ID 8328.
  • Confección de blusa con velo integrado para apicultores: ID 8327.

6. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

6.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta tecnología es eficiente porque el apicultor no sólo puede extraer los marcos de la colmena sin necesidad de emplear ambas manos, sino también puede extraer propóleos.

6.2 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

La confección de pinza para extracción de marcos con espátula integrada facilita al apicultor la separación de los marcos y, por tanto, es una herramienta útil.

_annotations.body:
Confección de pinza para extracción de marcos con espátula integrada

La pinza para extracción de marcos es una herramienta de gran utilidad para el apicultor, ya que permite extraer los marcos de la colmena sin necesidad de emplear ambas manos en esta labor, con lo cual se agiliza el manejo. Generalmente los marcos están pegados con propóleos entre sí. Los propóleos son sustancias resinosas que dificultan la separación y movilización de los marcos, por este motivo se hace uso de una espátula para facilitar el manejo y poder separar marcos. Además ésta herramienta permite la extracción del propóleo de raspado de los bordes superiores de los marcos e interiores de la colmena.

Esta tecnología también está disponible en: Inglés (ID10120), Francés (ID10105, coming soon)

Description: A combined tool for beekeepers featuring simultaneous-action tongs with an integrated metal spatula, enabling single-handed removal of beehive frames and propolis collection.

_annotations.field_shorter_description:
La pinza para extracción de marcos es una herramienta de gran utilidad para el apicultor, ya que permite extraer los marcos de la colmena sin necesidad de emplear ambas manos en esta labor, con lo cual se agiliza el manejo. Generalmente los marcos están pegados con propóleos entre sí. Los propóleos son sustancias resinosas que dificultan la separación y movilización de los marcos, por este motivo se hace uso de una espátula para facilitar el manejo y poder separar marcos. Además ésta herramienta permite la extracción del propóleo de raspado de los bordes superiores de los marcos e interiores de la colmena.

Esta tecnología también está disponible en: Inglés (ID10120), Francés (ID10105, coming soon)

records.title: Alimentador externo e interno para colmenas
records.description:
Descripción

  • El alimentador es un instrumento utilizado para el suministro de alimento para las abejas que puede ser usado para suplementar, incentivar o reforzar una colmena que requiera de este recurso nutricional.
  • Dependiendo del tipo de alimento que se desee suministrar a la colmena existen varios tipos de alimentadores.
  • Para suministrar alimentos energéticos en base a hidratos de carbono (miel, fructosa o azúcar) que son utilizados por las abejas para desempeñar labores de movimiento como caminar, volar, ventilar, atacar, llamar, etc. se pueden utilizar alimentadores externos o internos.
  • Las abejas también requieren incorporar a la colmena alimentos de tipo protéico, el cual ellas obtienen del polen de algunas flores, con los recursos proteicos las abejas forman sus estructuras y tejidos corporales, el polen se puede recolectar antes de las abejas mediante la utilización de una trampa de polen en la piquera.
  • Para suministrar el alimento energético se puede usar un alimentador interno, que presenta la ventaja de que mantiene la temperatura de la colmena y a la abeja le es más fácil su asimilación, por otra parte el alimentador externo permite tener una visión del consumo del alimento y por ende presumir algún tipo de problema en la colmena sin necesidad de abrir el cajón.

1. ​Alimentadores externos​

  • Entre los alimentadores externos se encuentra el alimentador de tipo Boardman en sus variados modelos (Figura 1).
  • Este alimentador se ubica en la parte externa de la colmena a un extremo de la piquera.
  • El sistema consiste en un recipiente (frasco, botella, tarro, etc.), contenedor de jarabe, cuya tapa tiene agujeros por los que se libera el alimento en la medida que las abejas lo van consumiendo.
  • Este recipiente se inserta sobre la base del alimentador en la piquera, la cual a su vez estará conectada al interior de la colmena a través de la piquera, permitiendo que las abejas recojan el alimento sin salir de la colmena.
  • Este tipo de instrumento puede ser elaborado principalmente de material plástico, zinc y madera, completamente con envases plásticos, clavos y en algunos casos haciendo uso de pegamento (cera de abeja o parafina solida) para pegar, sellar e impermeabilizar el alimentador para que no se pierda alimento y no se produzca el pillaje.
  • Una colmena bien poblada puede consumir 500 cm³ entre dos a tres días.
  • Si se realiza alimentación con este tipo de alimentador en épocas de escases es recomendable disminuir el tamaño de la piquera y comprobar que el alimentador no filtre jarabe para evitar el pillaje, la exposición del jarabe al sol no ha sido un factor que limite su uso en los lugares en Latinoamérica.

1.1 ​Materia prima

  • ​Madera, lamina de zinc galvanizado calibre 26 estándar y clavos de ½ pulgada.
  • La construcción requiere de dos listones de 1 cm x 2 cm x 17,2 cm cada uno y un tercer listón de 1 cm x 2 cm x 7,5 cm.
  • Sobre los tres listones se sitúa el soporte de la botella de 2 cm x 12 cm x 7,5 cm, este soporte en su parte más lejana a la entrada del alimentador tiene una perforación de 3,1 cm de diámetro para la inserción de la botella con la tapa perforada (Figura 2).
Figura ​1​. ​Fotos del alimentador externo de tipo Boardman


​​ ​ 
©​Swisscontact

Figura ​2​. ​Medidas de las partes necesarias a la construcción de un alimentador externo de tipo Boardman
​​

©​Swisscontact

2. ​Alimentadores internos​

  • Entre los alimentadores internos encontramos al tipo Doolittle, que consiste en una caja de madera o plástico con forma y medidas iguales a un bastidor, pero en lugar de panal tiene dos paredes que forma una cavidad al centro, donde se deposita el alimento líquido, los cuales son principalmente jarabes (Figura 3).
  • Su capacidad es de 1,5 litros aproximadamente.
  • Este tipo de alimentador permite incorporar una gran cantidad de alimento de una sola vez, además lo mantiene a la temperatura del interior de la colmena y es de fácil llenado. 

2.1 ​Materia prima

  • Madera, lámina de plywood (tipo de madera compuesta elaborado por capas de madera, llamadas chapas o chapillas de madera) y clavos de ½ pulgada.
  • La construcción del alimentador requiere de seis listones, tres para soporte del marco y tres más cortos como soporte superior para asentar el alimentador en un extremo del cajón (Figura 4).
  • Para su construcción e impermeabilización se debe sellar en su interior y/o exterior también con parafina solida o cera de abejas, para protegerla e impedir el escurrido del jarabe, además es recomendable poner un flotador para impedir que las abejas se ahoguen en el jarabe, este flotador puede ser un trozo de madera o cualquier cuerpo que flote sobre el jarabe.
  • Nota: El alimentador siempre debe ir situado en el extremo lateral de la colmena. 
Figura ​3​. ​Fotos del alimentador interno tipo Doolittle​

 
​​ ​ 
©​Swisscontact

Figura ​4​. ​Medidas para la construcción del alimentador interno tipo Doolittle


​​ ​ 
©Swisscontact

3. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido. 

4. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Banquillo individual para colmenas: ID 8326.
  • Confección de blusa con velo integrado para apicultores:  ID 8327.
  • Guantes de protección para apicultores: ID 8328.

5. Objectivos cumplidos por el proyecto

5.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Esta práctica ofrece una descripción concisa de cómo construir dos tipos de alimentadores para colmenas de manera eficiente.
