  • Sur la deuxième image, quelques temps après, le compost est prêt pour être appliqué sur le champ;
  • Avant le labour il fait l’epandage du compost dans son champ.
Figure 5a et 5b. Moussa applique le compost sur le champ

©FAO/TECA

  • Moussa dans un premier temps est en train de faire le labour de son champ.
  • Ensuite, sur la deuxième image, il est en train de semer le coton en ligne.
Figure 6a et 6b. Moussa prepare son champ et seme le coton

©FAO/TECA

  • Au niveau de la première image, Moussa est en train d’appliquer de l’urée.
  • Sur la deuxième image, Moussa a fait une bonne récolte et s’est rendu sur le marché du coton avec sa charette.
Figure 7a et 7b. Dans la première image Moussa applique de l'urée; dans la deuxième il récolte le coton

©FAO/TECA

  • Après avoir livré une grande quantité de coton à la suite d’une très bonne récolte, Moussa est en train d’être payé par le comité de commercialisation de coton. 
Figure 8. Moussa vend son récolte a la commercialisation de coton

©FAO/TECA

  • Ibrahim a une bonne récolte et il a livré sa grande quantité de coton produit.
  • Il est en train d’etre paye par le comité de commercialisation de coton.
Figure 9. Ibrahim a également eu une bonne récolte et vendu au comité

©FAO/TECA

  • Nous voyons Moussa expliquer à Ibrahim les avantages que l’on a en envoyant ses enfants à l’école.
  • Sur un panneau en face d’eux une fille et un garçon se rendent à l’école.
  • Ensuite, quelques débouchés de l’éducation des enfants sont énumérés.
  • On voit que la fille et le garçon qui vont à l’école peuvent devenir plus tard:
    • des conseillers communaux ou députés pour décider de l’avenir et du devéloppement de leur commune et de leur pays;
    • des agents de santé (infirmière, sage femme et médecin) pour soigner les vies des populations;
    • des ingénieurs agronomes pour aider les parents comme Issa, à devélopper l’agriculture et faire des producti ons de bonnes qualités et en grandes quantités dans lescommunes et dans tous le pays; et
    • des instituteurs pour sortir les milliers d’autres enfants béninois de l’illétrisme.
  • L’enfant qui s’instruit n’est pas seulement utile pour aider son père au champ et à suivre ses récoltes.
  • Il existe de milliers autres professions qu’il pourra exercer pour son bien personnel et pour celui de sa communauté et de tout le Bénin entier.
  • Selon la convention relative aux droits des enfants, les états rendent l’éducation accessible à tous les enfants.
  • C’est pour cela que le gouvernement du Bénin, avec l’aide de ses partenaires, a rendu l’éducation gratuite pour tous les enfants au niveau primaire.
  • Pour les filles, c’est jusqu’en classe de quatrième que c’est gratuit.
  • Il n’y a donc pas de raison possible que les enfants n’aillent pas à l’école.
Figure 10. Les opportunités d'emploi possibles grâce à l'éducation

©FAO/TECA

  • Moussa continue ses explications.
  • Toujours pour un enfant de producteur de coton qui va l’école, il peut aider ses parents analphabètes à maîtriser le dosage des engrais, produits chimiques et autres méthodes de fertilisation des sols pour assurer une meilleure production du coton.
  • Pour une meilleure production cotonnière et pour le bien de toute la communauté, les enfants des paysans doivent aller à l’école.
Figure 11. L'enfant éduqué pouvait enseigner à ses parents les bonnes pratiques d'agriculture

©FAO/TECA

  • Ici il s’agit d’un enfant qu’on envoie au champ.
  • L’image montre que l’enfant est malheureux et n’est pas épanoui.
  • Un enfant qui est envoyé au champ est exposé à d’énormes risques.
    • Il peut s’intoxiquer avec les produits chimiques à la moindre inattention des adultes.
    • Il peut se faire mordre par des serpents.
    • Un enfant au champ n’est pas une garantie d’une meilleure production agricole mais un grand risque de mauvaise récolte.
    • Il est source de nombreux soucis pour ses parents.
  • Il est déconseillé d’envoyer les enfants au champ pour des travaux et remplacer la main d’oeuvre.
  • Les envoyer à l’école est le meilleur investissement.
Figure 12. Envoyer les enfants à l’école est le meilleur investissement

©FAO/TECA

  • Une délégation de CmiA a rendu visite à Ibrahim et sa famille.
  • Ils sont venus expliquer à Ibrahim les avantages liés à la scolarisation des enfants, surtout dans les zones cotonnières CmiA.
  • Un membre explique comment les enfants peuvent aussi bénéficier de fournitures scolaires sans oublier les salles de classe que CmiA construit.
Figure 13. Explication de l'importance liés à la scolarisation des enfants

©FAO/TECA

  • Après les explications de Moussa et de l’équipe de CmiA, Ibrahim s’est enfin décidé à scolariser ses enfants à son tour.
  • Il les conduit lui-même pour leur inscription.
Figure 14. L'inscription des enfants à CmiA

©FAO/TECA

  • Effectivement, quelques moments plus tard après la scolarisation des enfants de Ibrahim, la délégation de CmiA est venue inaugurer les nouvelles salles de classe et a procédé à la distribution des fournitures scolaires aux élèves.
  • Il est interdit d’envoyer les enfants au champ pour des travaux et remplacer la main d’oeuvre.
  • Les envoyer à l’école est le meilleur investissement. 
Figure 15. Distribution des fournitures scolaires aux élèves

©FAO/TECA

  • Au bout de quelques années, les enfants de Ibrahim ont grandi et ont aussi fini leurs études.
  • Imorou, le fils, est devenu ingénieur agronome et sa soeur, Zoubérath, est sortie avec un Diplôme de sage-femme.
  • Ibrahim a vieilli mais est devenu plus à l’aise.
  • Tout le monde est heureux. 
Figure 16. Ibrahim et ses enfants 

©FAO/TECA

2. Les fiches techniques associées

  • La fabrication et l’utilisation du compost dans les exploitations cotonnières: ID 7897.

3. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

3.1 L'efficacité d'utilisation des ressources

La technologie combine efficacement plusieurs mesures sociales visant à donner aux enfants leurs droits à l’éducation, à l’alimentation, à la santé et à l’épanouissement nécessaire à leur développement harmonieux.

3.2 Favorable aux populations pauvres

Grâce à l'obtention de scolarité, la technologie ouvre aux enfants plusieurs opportunités pour gagner leurs vies et de prendre soins de membres de leurs familles.

Innovation: "Cotton made in Africa (CmiA) Education Project"

Description: A social innovation combining sustainable cotton production with child education support in Benin. CmiA provides school supplies and builds classrooms in cotton-producing areas, while promoting sustainable farming practices and discouraging child labor.

Criteria met: Creates improved/equitable business models by linking cotton production to social development; supports behavioral change in farming communities regarding child education; enhances inclusion and equity in rural education access.
_annotations.field_shorter_description: Depuis 2005, une culture durable du coton a vu le jour dans certains pays en Afrique au sud du Sahara. Le Bénin compte parmi ces pays. Cette forme de production cotonnière ayant le souci d’améliorer le revenu du producteur, de préserver son environnement et de prendre en charge l’aspect social de sa vie, a pris le nom de « Cotton made in Africa » (CmiA). Dans ce contexte, les acteurs du coton au Bénin ont conçu et mis en œuvre le projet Coton pour l’Education qui est une opportunité de promotion de la scolarisation des enfants dans les zones rurales. Il est un ensemble de mesures sociales visant à donner aux enfants leurs droits à l’éducation, à l’alimentation, à la santé et à l’épanouissement nécessaire à leur développement harmonieux.

records.description:
Descripción

1. Presentación del folleto

  • El folleto muestra imágenes de plagas de algodón e insectos beneficiosos, sobre los cuáles los productores de algodón deben prestar atención durante la aplicación de la gestión integrada de plagas (MIP), así cómo también la relación entre cada grupo de insectos.
  • Sirve como una herramienta para la toma de decisiones cuando se aplica el concepto de umbral como parte integrada al MIP. 
  • Al utilizar el cuadernillo, las plagas y sus respectivos insectos benéficos pueden ser fácilmente identificados por los agricultores, incluso por los que son analfabetos.
  • El tamaño original del folleto es de 7,5 cm x 10 cm por lo que cabe perfectamente en los bolsillos de los agricultores.

2. Plagas de algodón

  • Las plagas del cultivo de algodón son:
    • ácaros;
    • orugas;
    • orugas carpophages spodoptera;
    • syllepte (polillas de pasto) y otras orugas que comen plantas;
    • gusanos perforadores de algodón;
    • arrebiatados;
    • jassides o mosquito verde;
    • chinche lygus;
    • míridos;
    • mosca blanca;
    • áfidos (chinches o pulgones);
    • pupas de orugas algodoneras que se mantienen en el suelo;
    • trips.

2.1 Ácaros

Figura 1. Ácaros 


©GIZ

2.2 Orugas y gusanos

Figura 2. Orugas 


 
©GIZ

Figura 3. Gusanos perforadores de algodón 
 

©GIZ

Figura 4. Gusano (pupa) de oruga

©GIZ

2.3 Arrebiatado

Figura 5. Arrebiatado

©GIZ

2.4 Mosquito verde

Figura 6. Mosquito verde

©GIZ

2.5 Chinche lygus 

Figura 7. Chinche lygus  

©GIZ

2.6 Miridos

Figura 8. Mirido 
 

©GIZ

2.7 Moscas blancas

Figura 9. Moscas blancas 
 

©GIZ

2.8 Áfidos (pulgones)

Figura 10. Áfidos (pulgones)
 

©GIZ

2.9 Trips

Figura 11. Trips 
 

©GIZ

3. Insectos benéficos de algodón

  • Estos amigos de los agricultores cazan, atacan y matan a las plagas de algodón y otros cultivos.
  • Aprenda a identificarlos y a promover estos aliados naturales evitando los pesticidas de alto espectro que también matan a estos insectos benéficos, sobre todo al inicio de la temporada.
  • Utilice los pesticidas naturales que son eficaces y menos tóxicos tales como los pesticidas biológicos y extractos de plantas repelentes (tales como el neem, la hyptis, el ají o chili, el ricino, etc), así como aceites naturales y jabón.
  • Siembre líneas de girasol, caupí, maíz y de sorgo al interior y alrededor del campo de algodón.
  • Estas plantas protegen y nutren a los insectos útiles con polen y néctar.

3.1 Chrysoperla (crisopa)

  • Las ninfas crisopas son unos depredadores muy voraces y se alimentan de pulgones, trips, mosca blanca, mosquito verde, orugas devastadoras del algodón, ácaros y de los huevos y larvas en cápsula de las orugas devastadoras de algodón. 
  • La Figura 12 presenta el etapa adulto de la crisopa y la Figura 13 los diferentes etapas antes del imago: huevos y ninfa.
Figura 12. Crispopa adulta (imago)

©GIZ

Figura 13. El ciclo de vida de las chrysoperlas: huevo, ninfas, pupas, adultas 
 

©GIZ

3.2 Mariquitas

  • Las mariquitas (Figura 14) consumen especialmente pulgones (o hinches) pero también moscas blancas, trips y mosquitos verdes.
Figura 14. Mariquita capturando un pulgón 
 

©GIZ

Figura 15. El ciclo de vida: huevo, ninfa, pupa y un adulto que se alimenta de pulgones 
 

©GIZ

3.3 Antocóridos

  • Los antocóridos (Figura 16) son buenos para combatir: Ácaros, orugas perforadoras de algodón, pulgones y trips.
Figura 16. Antocóridos
 

©GIZ

3.4 Redúvidos

  • Los redúvidos (Figura 17) son buenos para combatir: Ácaros, orugas, orugas perforadoras de algodón, arrebiatados, chinches lygus y áfidos.
Figura 17. Redúvido cazando una oruga 
 

©GIZ

3.5 Geocoris

  • Los geocoris (Figura 18) son buenos para combatir: Ácaros, orugas perforadoras de algodón, mosquitos verdes, miridos, moscas blancas y áfidos.
Figura 18. Geocoris
 

©GIZ

3.6 Sírfidos

  • Los sírfidos (Figura 19) son buenos para combatir: Ácaros, orugas perforadoras de algodón, moscas blancas, áfidos y trips.
Figura 19. Sírfido
 

©GIZ

3.7 Hormigas

  • Las hormigas (Figura 20) son buenas para combatir: Orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras orugas filófagas y orugas perforadoras de algodón.
Figura 20. Hormiga atacando una oruga 
 

©GIZ

3.8 Arañas

  • Las arañas (Figura 21) son buenas para combatir: Orugas perforadoras de algodón, mosquitos verdes, miridos y áfidos.
Figura 21. Arañas 
 

©GIZ

3.9 Mantodea/Mantis religiosa

  • Las mantodeas (Figura 22) son buenas para combatir: Orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras orugas filófagas, orugas perforadoras de algodón y arrebiatados.
Figura 22. Mantis religiosa 

©GIZ

3.10 Libélulas

  • Las libélulas (Figura 23) son buenas para combatir: Orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras orugas filófagas, orugas perforadoras de algodón, arrebiatados y miridos.
Figura 23. Libélulas 
 

©GIZ

3.11 Tijeretas

  • Las tijeretas (Figura 24) son buenos para combatir: Orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras orugas filófagas y orugas perforadoras de algodón.
Figura 24. Tijeretas 
 

©GIZ

3.12 Nabidaes

  • Los nabidaes (Figura 25) son buenos para combatir: Orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras arugas filófagas y orugas perforadoras de algodón.  
Figura 25. Nabidae atacando un chinche
 

©GIZ

3.13 Avispas depredadoras y parasitarias

  • Las avispas depredadoras y parasitarias (Figura 26) son buenas para combatir: Mosca blanca, chinche lygus, miridos, áfidos, orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras orugas filófagas y orugas perforadoras de algodón.
Figura 26. Avispas depredadoras y parasitarias
 

©GIZ

3.14 Taquínido (mosca taquínido)

  • Los taquínidos (Figura 27) son buenos para combatir: Mosquitos verdes y orugas perforadoras de algodón.
Figura 27. Taquínido (mosca taquínido)
 

©GIZ

3.15 Avispillas trichogramma (Avispas sin aguijón)

  • Las avispillas Trichogramma (Figura 28) son buenas para combatir: Orugas carpófagos Spodopteras, polillas de pasto y otras orugas filófagas y orugas perforadoras de algodón.
Figura 28. Avispillas trichogramma

©GIZ

3.16 Carabidos

  • Los carabidos (Figura 29) son buenos para combatir: Pupas de orugas y orugas perforadoras de algodón.
Figura 29. Carabidos

©GIZ

3.17 Abejas

  • Las abejas son polinizadoras (Figura 30).
Figura 30. Abejas 
 

©GIZ

4. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.
  • Subtropical, húmedo.

5. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Cotton cultivation with laser levelling, ridge sowing, Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and compost application under drought conditions: ID 10016.
  • Management of cotton bollworns using predators ants: ID 4337.
  • Cotton culture: ID 6901.

La tecnología también está disponible en francés: ID 8668 y en inglés: ID 8677.

6. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

6.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

La tecnología aumenta el conocimiento sobre insectos benéficos y plagas. Esto permite una aplicación más eficaz del Manejo Integrado de Plagas, con impactos beneficiosos sobre el medio ambiente y la calidad de los cultivos.

records.title: Draught animal power technologies in East Africa
records.description:
Description

If left to grow, weeds will compete with crops for nutrients, moisture and light resulting in typical reductions in crop yield of 30 percent. For over 250 000 households in the Teso farming system of northern Uganda, the situation has been made even worse. HIV has reduced the number of people available for agricultural labour. Furthermore, civil disruption in the 1980s and 1990s has led to a shortage of animals for draught power. Women and children mainly undertake the toil of weeding, thereby restricting women’s involvement in other activities and keeping children away from school. Cereal crop yields (finger millet and sorghum) in the Teso farming system have stagnated at below one 500 kg per ha, despite the increasing availability of high-yielding varieties. Continuous cropping, changes in crop rotations have led to a heavy build-up of mainly annual grass weeds, especially Eleusine and Setaria and difficult perennial weeds such as Digitaria spp. and Imperata cylindrica.

1. ​Key approaches to intervention​

  • Allowing rural communities to prioritize their problems before embarking on research and/or extension (undertake a Needs Assessment).
  • Providing a range of options and allowing farmers to determine which technology best meets their needs.
  • Developing links with the private sector for post-project sustainability, including continued manufacturing involvement, production and promotion.
  • Encouraging the exchange of information between farmers (farmer-to-farmer extension).
  • Developing partnerships and training trainers (with those organizations that are likely to continue to be active for the foreseeable future).

2. ​Research findings​

  • At least 85 weed species are present in the system, of which two-thirds are annual broadleaves and one-sixth are annual grasses.
    • This weed characterization enabled rigorous testing of a number of different weeders.
  • Judged solely in terms of weed control, there was a little difference between the weeders tested on-station and on-farm.
  • DAP weeders were a practical and effective alternative to hand - hoe weeding.
    • The preferred models were the plough without mouldboard, SAARI and SG2000.
    • Of these, the favourite was the SAARI type weeder (bolted to the existing plough frame).
  • It was possible to adapt the weeders to perform ridging, planning and groundnut lifting.
  • The capital required for investment in DAP weeding is zero for those farmers (the majority) who have access to oxen and ploughs.
  • For further details see the Technical Reports by (Barton and Obou 2002) Part 1, Part 2 and (Obou and Barton 2006).

2.1 ​Impact​

  • In sorghum fields, DAP reduced the time spent hand weeding from 157 to 34 hour per hectare (although it does not increase yields). 
  • In groundnut fields, DAP reduces labour inputs and increased yields as it improves infiltration and reduces run-off of rainwater.
  • Ridging reduces labour costs to a fifth.

3. ​Promotion​

  • It is very important for farmers to be aware of this technology, how much it will cost and where they can obtain it.
    • The main issue concerned with the promotion of this technology is the production of the weeder.
    • Although initially two companies were involved in its manufacture in Uganda, by March 2005 there was only one manufacturer, SAIMMCO, located in Soroti.
    • They are manufacturing a simplified SAARI weeder design, the one identified by farmers as best meeting their needs.
    • In December 2005, the price of these weeder attachments was around USh 80 000 (Ugandan Shillings) as a bolted attachment to existing (and widely owned) plough frame, or as a standalone machine (which is more expensive – around USh 250 000/-).
    • This is considered to be affordable by many farmers.
    • However, those that are unable to find this amount can easily share the tool with neighbours.
  • As DAP weeding is a relatively rapid task, one tool can easily meet the weeding needs of five or six households.
    • Marketing of DAP equipment represents a serious challenge for the manufacturers as they have limited contacts with the agricultural community.
    • Also, decision making at SAIMMCO is controlled centrally by the Alam Group of companies (owners of SAIMMCO) that limits investment in a marketing strategy and has led to dependence on large government and NGO orders for the business.
    • A farmer-marketing agent system was established whereby prominent farmers in those communities that had received training and extension were selected as agents for manufacturers’ products.
    • The objective of this activity was to facilitate access to weeders by the farming community while at the same time assisting the manufacturer’s business development.
    • Agents are therefore intermediaries and should receive a commission on sales.
    • To date, this system has promoted DAP weeding to 3 000 farmers.
    • Hiring services for DAP weeding are arising similar to those already in existence for ploughing.
  • It has been very important to promote knowledge from this research.
    • A leaflet: Weed management with draught oxen in Teso by (OBOU 2003) presents a simple guide to the use of DAP weeding.
    • Manuals and posters have been developed in English, Ateso and Kumam by Serere Agricultural and Animal Production Research Station in Soroti, Uganda.
    • These were distributed to trainers of trainers, CBOs, NGOs (Action Aid, Self Help Development International-Uganda, SOCADIDO, Church of Uganda-Soroti Diocese, SG2000, TERUDO, Christian Children’s Fund, Tugende Omumaiso-Rural Development Programme of Hoima Catholic Diocese, Pentecostal Assemblies of God and CIDI), NAADS, farmer field schools or groups, schools and Local Governments (at sub-counties) and Government extension workers.
    • There is a high demand for these DAP extension materials both within and outside the Teso Farming System.
    • A manual outlining the use of DAP technology in cotton production (with an emphasis on mechanical weeding) was also produced (NRI/NARO 2006).
  • In addition, training has been provided to 879 NGO-based trainers and farmer trainers.
    • They should be able to train others if the necessary support can be provided through existing NGOs, NAADS service providers and local governments.
    • There is, therefore, scope to begin the process of promoting the technology in other parts of the Teso Farming System as the benefits are both clear and measurable to farmers, and adoption is likely to be relatively rapid.

3.1 ​Impact​

  • An impact assessment using a participatory farm management technique known as Participatory Budgets (PBs) was conducted in 2004.
    • The technique encourages farmers to cost all inputs and outputs and to produce a simple budget including a balance (gross margin) for a single enterprise.
    • The technique can be used to explore before and after scenarios to assess the impact of new technology or changes to the management of an enterprise.
    • Both family labour and draught animal power costs (including hire charges) were included in the budgets (at the request of participants).
    • Although the individuals whose enterprises were explored during the participatory exercise all owned oxen, DAP costs were included at the request of other members of the group who did not own oxen and need therefore to hire them to undertake ploughing and weeding operations. 
  • For each PB and each site, cash balances are higher for enterprises where DAP is used for weeding.
    • The participants attributed this to the lower costs associated with DAP weeding (when compared with hand weeding), and the higher yields that result from DAP weeded crops (improved infiltration of rainwater following mechanical weeding).
    • DAP weeding increases infiltration of rainwater but also allows more timely and efficient weeding which may also improve yields (when compared with poorly weeded fields).

4. ​Beneficiaries of this research​

  • The major beneficiaries of this research have been the farming families (2 472 households) who have been trained and have adopted DAP technology.
  • There are many benefits.
    • Reduced drudgery for women and children particularly those who formerly undertook weeding, heaping (ridging) of sweet potatoes and groundnut lifting.
    • Less withdrawal from school of children during the weeding season.
    • Expansion in the area cultivated in many cases, and enhanced food security and increased incomes.
    • Farmer adaptation has been observed in several locations with the use of a plough (minus its mouldboard) for the lifting of cassava.
      • This suggests that the research and extension process has assisted farmers to begin their own innovations with the DAP equipment.
  • The impact assessment concluded that the introduction of DAP technologies has had the following impact on livelihoods.
    • It has made women feel less oppressed and men have become involved in this task as it is mechanized.
    • It has greatly reduced drudgery.
    • It has improved food security and led to higher incomes. 
    • Women are now able to pursue more rewarding activities and are experiencing a better quality of life.
    • Children are no longer withdrawn from school during the weeding seasons (April–May and October–November).
  • It is anticipated that in the longer - term even the poorest of economically active households will benefit from mechanization as hire markets developed for DAP services (weeding, groundnut lifting and potato ridging) already exist for ploughing, and to a limited extent weeding.

5. Agro-ecological zone

  • Tropics, warm. 

6. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour saving technologies and practices: Draught Animal Power (DAP) planters and weeders: ID 7305.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: draught animal power and implements: ID 7306.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: draught Animal Powered and motorised crop processing: ID 7307.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: draught animal powered groundnut lifter: ID 7309.
  • Labour saving technologies and practices: manual and motorised cleaning of grains and pulses: ID 7310.
  • Improving the productivity of draught animal power in sub-Saharan Africa: ID 4467.
  • Development of tools for draught animals: ID 4483.

7. Objectives fulfilled  by the project 

7.1 Labour-saving technology

The technology allows for reduced drudgery, especially for women and children.

7.2 Women-friendly

Thanks to this technology, women are able to pursue more rewarding activities and experience a better quality of life.

7.3 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently uses animal-drawn implements for weeding, ridging, line planting and lifting. 

7.4 Pro poor technology

The technology allows for cultivation expansion, enhances food security and increases incomes.

records.title: Rice seed preservation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice)
records.description:
Description

This video, as a part of other video series, presents the technique of seed preservation. It is essential to preserve the seeds for sowing the following year. Women in Bangladesh are responsible for storing and preserving the seeds. They are also responsible for determining the good quality seeds prior to preserving.

This video presents the main steps to innovative and cost-effective methods for seed preservation. 

The main steps can be summarized.

  1. Select healthy pannicles.
  2. Choose and store only clean and healthy seeds. 
  3. In parallel, clean, wash and effectively dry the container as shown in the video. 
  4. Fully fill the container until the top of the container with seeds. If not available, fill the extra space with dried sand, or puffed rice. The important thing is that there is no extra space for air. 
  5. Completely seal the container to make it airtight. One method is to seal the container with clay. 
  6. Add some natural insecticides such as dried neem and tobacco leaves. This will help control insects during storage.
  7. Paint the outer and inner parts of the container with tar or used cooking oil to keep it airtight.

It is important to keep in mind that a "properly preserved seed is a good seed and the good seed is a good crop". 

Figure 1. Women in Maria village preparing the barrel for seed preservation

©RDA-Bogra/TMSS

2. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm. 

3. Related/associated technologies

  • Rice seed sorting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7205.
  • Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7210.
  • Rice seed drying (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7211.
  • Rice transplanting (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7214.
  • Rice weed management (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice): ID 7215.

4. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

4.1 Women-friendly

The technology allows for a more active role of female communities in agricultural production. 

4.2 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently uses a series of methods of storage, plant usage and other means for effective seed preservation.

4.3 Pro-poor technology

The technology, through seed preservation, leads to greater quantity and quality crop yields. This in turn provides for additional sources of food and income.

records.title: The most serious sweet potato diseases in sub-Saharan Africa
records.description:
Description

1. ​Viruses​

  • Viruses are the most damaging group of disease organisms affecting sweet potato in Africa.
  • Viruses are amongst the smallest organisms known and can only be seen using a very powerful electron microscope.
  • They are very simple organisms and can only survive and multiply inside their hosts/victims.
  • Most also need to be carried from plant to plant, usually by an insect that feeds on plant sap, such as aphids or whiteflies.
  • Once a virus enters a cell in the body of its host, it will take over part of the management of the cell’s processes, and force the cell to produce more viruses identical to itself rather than the crop yield we want.
  • These new virus particles then spread through the plant to infect more cells.

1.1 ​Common symptoms of virus infection in plants including sweet potato​

  • Diminished growth so the plants and leaves remain small (stunted).
  • Chlorosis (paleness, even whitening; aidosoikit) of the leaf tissue.
    • This chlorosis may be general or in a pattern, often either between the leaf veins in a mosaic or less well-defined mottle, or along the veins to form a chlorotic network.
  • Misshapen leaves with an uneven or curled appearance.
  • Pigmented leaves, often purple or yellow generally or in spots or rings.
  • Reduced production of sweet potato storage roots. 
  • Viruses affecting sweet potato can be spread by the use of foliar cuttings taken from infected plants.
    • They are also transmitted from plant to plant by sap-sucking aphid and whitefly insects.
Figure ​1​. ​Sweet Potato Virus Disease (SPVD) affected plant​

​​

©​FAO/TECA

2. ​Sweet Potato Feathery Mottle Virus (SPFMV) and Sweet Potato Chorotic Stunt Virus (SPCSV)​

  • Sweet Potato Feathery Mottle Virus (SPFMV) and Sweet Potato Chorotic Stunt Virus (SPCSV) are together the most important viruses affecting sweet potato in Africa.
  • By themselves, sweet potato viruses may cause only mild or no obvious symptoms.
  • However, plants can be infected by more than one type of virus.
    • When this happens, the viruses may help each other to multiply with the result that the disease is more severe than expected.
  • The combination of SPCSV and SPFMV is known as Sweet Potato Virus Disease (SPVD) and is the most important disease of sweet potato in Africa.
  • SPFMV is transmitted by a wide range of aphid species (eiliana) and is spread mainly by winged adults, even of species that do not colonise sweet potato, flying from plant to plant.
  • SPCSV is transmitted by the mobile adult form of white flies (ekwanga), especially Bemisia tabaci, as they fly from plant to plant.
  • Since it is the spread of SPCSV by white flies that synergizes SPFMV, whiteflies are also usually the driving force behind the spread of SPVD.
  • Neither disease is spread by insects over very long distances.
  • Because viruses spread quickly through the vascular system of a plant to infect the whole plant, any portions of an infected plant that are used as planting materials (vines or roots), are almost always diseased themselves.
  • This then carries the disease to the next generation of plants.
  • Thus, it is important to follow specific steps. 
    • Make sure cuttings are collected for planting new sweet potato crops from healthy plants and if possible from healthy plants in crops in which few other plants have the disease.
      • Then there is also less chance of taking cuttings from plants that have just been infected.
      • It may be better to avoid collecting cuttings from very old crops both because SPVD may have built up in these crops and because SPVD is less easy to see in old plants that in vigorously growing crops.
    • Remove and burn or feed to livestock any diseased plants as soon as they appear in young crops.
      • Plants infected when young wouldn’t have yielded much anyway.
      • The neighbouring plants will soon fill up the space and you can replant cuttings if you wish in young crops.
    • Avoid planting new crops where you grew sweet potato last season.
      • Roots and cuttings from old diseased plants surviving in the soil will produce diseased plants from which infection will easily spread to your new crop.
    • Plant your new crop away from old crops, so it is difficult for whiteflies and aphids to reach your new crop.
      • Other forms of crop hygiene are:  ensuring that the vines and leaves from harvested crops are completely destroyed (they can be fed to livestock); and that all the roots (especially the small ones which may come from diseased plants) are destroyed.
  • However, often the best and certainly the most convenient means of controlling SPVD is to plant varieties of sweet potato which have resistance to virus diseases.
  • All these management practices work better if they are done on areas as large as possible.
    • If communities can work together to manage SPVD they will all benefit.
    • The crop hygiene you do to control sweet potato viruses probably also helps control other pests and diseases.

3. ​Fungal pathogens causing diseases of the leaves and vines​

3.1 ​Alternaria​

  • The fungus survives in the soil and in plant remains.
    • The airborne spores are spread through: infected planting material; wind; splashing rain and water.
    • During the rains the increased humidity often leads to high levels of infection.
    • The disease incidence and lesion (iboconoreta) size increase in wetter, high altitude areas.
  • The disease is first observed as small, brown/grey/black oval lesions with a typical bulls’ eye appearance of concentric rings, on leaves, stems and petioles.
    • On the lower side of the leaf, blackened veins are observed.
    • As the disease progresses, the lesions become necrotic usually surrounded by a wide yellow halo.
    • Soon after the whole blade turns chlorotic and drops.
    • Vine bases and middle sections are more affected than tips.
    • Death of vines can occur.
    • The ground under affected vines is often covered with blackened leaf debris.
  • Good sanitation practices are the main management strategies for this disease.
    • Infected crop material should be destroyed and burnt.
    • Clean planting materials should be used.
    • New crops of sweet potato should not be planted in fields which have recently had a sweet potato crop grown in them.
  • Some varieties of sweet potato are more susceptible to Alternaria disease than others.
    • You could try planting different varieties to see which are more resistant.
    • In other crops fungicides are used against Alternaria diseases.
      • However there is no information about using fungicides to control the disease in sweet potato.
Figure ​2​. ​Alternaria infected sweet potato vine​ 


​​ ​ 
©​FAO/TECA

3.2 ​Root rots​

  • Several fungi and bacteria cause root rots.
  • Once rotting starts it cannot be stopped.
  • Infected plants must be destroyed to prevent further spread of the disease.
  • Planting material should not be obtained from fields where there are many rotten roots.
  • Since the fungi and bacteria that cause root rots can survive in the soil for a long time, sweet potato should be planted in rotation with other crops in order to avoid a build-up of disease.
  • Cuttings should be taken from vine sections that have not been in contact with the soil.

3.2.1. ​Black rot (Ceratocystis fimbriata)​

  • Black rot (Ceratocystis fimbriata) is a dry root caused by a fungus.
  • Sunken grayish-black lesions/areas form on the surface of the storage root.
  • A smell of alcohol like that of fermenting fruit is often present.
  • In severe infections, yellowing, wilting, stunting and death of affected plants can occur.
  • The disease can also be serious on young vines and adult plants.
  • Infected vines develop black sunken necrotic lesions or cankers at the point of attachment to the mother root.
  • Bacteria also cause root rots, disease transmission routes and management strategies are similar to those of black rot.
  • On storage roots, small brown lesions with black margins can be observed on the surface, but more frequently the rotting is internal with no signs of it outside.
  • Affected tissue becomes watery.
  • There is often a strange smell produced in infected tissues.
Figure ​3​. ​Black rot symptoms on roots​

​​​

©​FAO/TECA

Figure ​4​. ​Bacterial rot on roots​ 

©​FAO/TECA

4. Related/associated technologies

  • Production of orange-fleshed sweet potato: ID 4373.
  • Working with farmers to control sweet potato virus disease in East Africa: ID 4557.

5. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

5.1 Pro-poor technology

This technology allows for the identification and treatment of sweet potato diseases. This leads to an improvement of quality and quantity of sweet potato yield, thereby providing poor farmers with more secure sources of income and food.

1. ​Viruses​

  • Viruses are the most damaging group of disease organisms affecting sweet potato in Africa.
  • Viruses are amongst the smallest organisms known and can only be seen using a very powerful electron microscope.
  • They are very simple organisms and can only survive and multiply inside their hosts/victims.
  • Most also need to be carried from plant to plant, usually by an insect that feeds on plant sap, such as aphids or whiteflies.
  • Once a virus enters a cell in the body of its host, it will take over part of the management of the cell’s processes, and force the cell to produce more viruses identical to itself rather than the crop yield we want.
  • These new virus particles then spread through the plant to infect more cells.

1.1 ​Common symptoms of virus infection in plants including sweet potato​

  • Diminished growth so the plants and leaves remain small (stunted).

  • Pigmented leaves, often purple or yellow generally or in spots or rings.
  • Reduced production of sweet potato storage roots. 
  • Viruses affecting sweet potato can be spread by the use of foliar cuttings taken from infected plants.

records.title: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) in vegetable production: a guide for extension workers in West Africa
records.description:
Description

Vegetables are important components of daily diets in Africa and important sources of income, especially in urban and peri-urban areas. As many as twenty different types of indigenous and exotic vegetables are grown at major vegetable production sites around West Africa. These crops provide a cheap source of proteins, vitamins and other elements essential for human health and wellbeing. In West Africa, vegetables are commonly grown in the rainfed upland ecologies and in lowland ecologies such as bolilands, riverine grasslands and inland valley swamps. Agroecosystems in these various ecologies offer great opportunities for commercial production of vegetables in West Africa.

Vegetable production for urban and peri-urban areas in West Africa is popular in rainfed upland ecologies. Rainfed upland ecologies occur on hillsides, usually above rainy season, either by direct seeding or transplanting of seedlings. They are frequently intercropped with other staple food crops (e.g. rice), or planted as sole crops following the harvest of any other crop. Commercial farmers use irrigation systems that allow year-round production in upland ecologies, while smallholder farmers rely on rain and soil water to water their seasonally-grown crops. 

Bolilands are large pan-like depressions of land which are naturally flooded by rainwater and freshwater streams. The soil is often clay loam with silt deposits and usually has a large amount of humus on the surface. The vegetation is dominated by grasses. In bolilands, rice is planted either by direct seeding just before the soil is flooded in the rainy season, or by transplanting after the soil is flooded. Vegetables are planted on small mounds left on the bolilands after the rice is harvested at the end of the rainy season. 

Inland valley swamps are flooded by overflow from freshwater rivers or streams and rainwater runoff from surrounding hills. The intensity of flooding depends on the duration of the rainfall, the season and on the type of topography. The water level can be artificially controlled so vegetables can be grown on the bunds which separate the plots of rice in these swamps. 

Riverine grasslands are alluvial plains which run along the lower parts and mouths of freshwater rivers, and tend to be flooded to significant depths during the rainy season. The natural vegetation is dominated by grasses. The rice plants which are transplanted before flooding grow as floating plants in the waterlogged conditions. In the months prior to flooding, these alluvial plains are important vegetable production sites.

1. ​Vegetable agroecosystems​

  • Vegetable agroecosystems comprise a dynamic mix of biotic (living) components, abiotic (non-living) components and the interactions within and between them.
  • Any change in one component or interaction is likely to affect another component or interaction.
  • The reactions of agroecosystems to change can potentially be disastrous to farming communities, and may not be entirely predictable.
  • In order to achieve good vegetable pest management, the vital components of agroecosystems should be correctly identified, their interrelationships fully understood, and the agroecosystem treated as a functional unit.
Figure ​1​. ​Components of vegetable agroecosystems​ 


​​
Source: CTA 2010

Figure ​2​. ​Irrigation at a peri-urban vegetable site in Benin
​​ ​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​3​. ​Predatory mite (left) on a pest mite (right) called a phyoseiid ​​

​​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​4​. Aphid Lipaphis erysimi, a cabbage pest

​​

©​IITA/B.James

2. Crop types​

  • The vegetable plant is the central component of the agroecosystem. Vegetables can be grouped according to the part of the plant that is consumed and/or sold. 
  • Leafy vegetables
    • The common leafy vegetables grown in West Africa are the African garden eggplant, amaranth, cabbage and lettuce.
    • There are two common types of African garden eggplant, which are both indigenous to Africa. One is Solanum macrocarpon (Figure 5), whilst the other is S. aethiopicum. Solanum macrocarpon is grown mainly for its succulent leaves, but in some communities the bitter fruits are also eaten. S. aethiopicum is mainly cultivated for its fruits.
      • The edible parts of both S. macrocarpon and S. aethiopicum are nutritious and contain carbohydrate, cellulose and calcium, fat, protein and water. 
    • Amaranth, Amaranthus cruentus (Figure 6), is grown for its leaves which are rich in beta-carotene, calcium, iron, protein, vitamin C and water.
    • Cabbage, Brassica oleracea (Figure 7), is native to temperate regions of the world.
      • It is called the head cabbage because the immature leaves cluster up into a spherical ball or ‘head’, which is the part normally marketed and consumed.
      • The leaves contain some carbohydrates, proteins and various essential elements e.g. calcium, iron and vitamin C as well as water.
    • Lettuce, Lactuca sativa (Figure 8), is indigenous to the Mediterranean region and occurs in four groups of varieties.
      • The plant is cultivated for its succulent leaves which are used in salads.
      • Lettuce leaves contain a high proportion of water with some calcium, proteins and vitamins.
  • Fruit vegetables 
    • The most popular fruit vegetables grown in West Africa are the tomato, pepper and aubergine.
    • Tomato, Lycopersicum esculentum (Figure 9), which originates from the Andes in South America, is grown for its fruits.
      • The shape of the fruit differs according to the variety.
      • Tomato fruits can be consumed raw or cooked.
      • Tomato fruits contain a lot of water with calcium, carbohydrate, carotene, iron, niacin, riboflavin, thiamine, protein and vitamins. 
    • The sweet pepper or pepper, Capsicum annuum (Figure 10), is native to Central America.
      • It occurs in two groups of varieties.
      • Unlike most vegetables, pepper is a relatively long duration crop.
      • Both immature and fully mature fruits are marketed and consumed.
      • The fruit contains plenty of water with some carbohydrates, protein, minerals and vitamin C.
  • Root vegetables 
    • Carrot, Daucus carota (Figure 11), a crop native to Asia, is the most common root vegetable grown across West Africa.
    • It is cultivated for its swollen roots, which are rich in beta-carotene.
    • The roots also contain a large amount of water as well as carbohydrates, minerals and protein.
Figure 5. The African garden eggplant, a leafy vegetable 

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​6​. ​Amaranth, a leafy vegetable

​​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​7​. ​Cabbage, a leafy vegetable ​

​​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​8​. ​Lettuce, a leafy vegetable ​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​9​. ​Tomato, a fruit vegetable​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​10​. ​Pepper, a fruit vegetable​

​​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​11​. ​Carrot, a root vegetable​

©​IITA/B.James

3.  ​Vegetable plant production​

  • Depending on market demand and availability of water to irrigate plots, vegetables can be grown all year round.
  • The crops are grown in monocrops, intercrops and crop rotation schemes.
  • Commercial production sites are commonly located near to markets, e.g. in urban and peri-urban areas. 
    • Crop yield
      • Depending on the vegetable crop type, the leaves, fruits, and roots constitute the yield and provide both food and income to farmers.
      • Field workers and farmers need to be aware of two different types of yield in order to fully understand the purpose of crop production and pest management measures.
      • The two types of yield are maximum or potential attainable yield and actual yield. 
    • The maximum attainable yield is the yield obtained from crops grown in experimental plots and field conditions with the full use of improved technologies and inputs.
      • It is the highest yield possible from a particular variety cultivated under the ideal conditions. 
    • The actual yield is the yield obtained from crops cultivated under farmers’ conditions using the same varieties used in experimental plots.
      • Actual yields are often less than attainable yields. 
    • The difference between attainable and actual yield is due to a variety of environmental factors which include soil type, crop variety, agronomic practices, weather and pests.
      • Agricultural research, extension and training activities aim to find ways to increase actual yields towards attainable yields, for example by manipulating field and environmental factors that reduce yields.
      • The overall objective of vegetable pest management is, therefore, to prevent, reduce and maintain the effect of pests at levels where they cease to act as constraints to the achievement of higher actual yields.
      • It is in this way that pest management interventions ‘increase’ yields.

4. ​Land and seed bed preparation​

  • The most suitable sites for vegetable production are flat and sunny areas with light, well-drained soil which is rich in humus and not prone to waterlogging.
  • These conditions help to promote the establishment of good nurseries and seedling health for excellent vegetable crop growth.
  • Farmers break and loosen up the soil by ploughing, and remove stones and debris to allow sufficient aeration, moistening and drainage of the soil.
  • This promotes good root growth.
  • Removal of plant debris also helps to limit the occurrence of weeds and other pests that are carried over from the previous season.
  • Vegetables are often planted on flat land in areas that are unlikely to be waterlogged or flooded.
  • Planting on flat land is also common where the soil is rich in nutrients.
  • In areas that are likely to be waterlogged, or where the soil is poor in nutrients, farmers heap the topsoil into mounds or ridges on which they plant vegetables.
  • The mounds of soil raised above ground level are commonly referred to as "beds".

5. ​Planting​

  • Except for exotic vegetables, (e.g. beetroot, cabbage, carrot, cucumber and lettuce), most farmers produce their own vegetable seeds from their fields or they collect seeds from other farmers’ fields.
  • Large-scale farmers do not self-supply and buy certified seeds from seed companies and national seed services.
  • Vegetables are planted by direct sowing of seeds (e.g. amaranth and carrot) or by transplanting seedlings from nurseries (e.g. African garden eggplant, cabbage, lettuce and tomato).
  • In direct sowing, seeds are broadcast on seed beds and harrowed in, or sprinkled in rows and covered up with soil, and left undisturbed to germinate.
  • In transplanting, farmers select vigorous and disease-free seedlings at the right growth stage and transplant them.
  • If the crop is harvested by uprooting of whole plants (e.g. in amaranth, carrot and radish), the seedlings are usually transplanted closer to each other than when the crop will be harvested by ratooning.
  • Planting dates are usually adjusted in response to market demands e.g. in readiness for festive seasons.
  • Planting during the peak of the rainy seasons is uncommon so as to avoid flooding of vegetable beds.

6. ​Intercropping​

  • Farmers frequently intercrop vegetables on the same bed.
  • A single bed can hold as many as five different vegetables.
  • Intercrops can be economically more profitable than sole crop vegetables.
  • Intercropping increases farmers’ income per unit of land and labour and helps to maintain good soil moisture and reduce the incidence of weeds and other pests on vegetables.

7. ​Crop rotation​

  • Crop rotation enables farmers to maintain land under continuous cultivation by planting with one crop after another in successive seasons.
  • The practice also helps farmers respond to seasonal market demands for certain crops.
  • Where a rotation crop is a non-host plant of a pest that damaged a previous crop, crop rotation helps to control that pest by breaking its life cycle.
  • Good knowledge of crop susceptibility to pests is therefore essential in the use of crop rotation for pest management.
  • This is particularly the case with species of root-knot nematodes that attack a wide range of vegetables including the most economically important crops grown in many localities.
  • The wide range of host plants of the root-knot nematode makes it difficult to identify suitable crop rotation schemes for this pest, especially at sites under year-round vegetable production.

8. ​Soil fertility​

  • Soils nourish vegetables with mineral nutrients for vigorous, succulent and healthy growth.
    • However continuous production of vegetables can deplete soil nutrients at production sites.
    • Vegetable farmers use organic and mineral fertilizers to help soils to recover from nutrient losses, and in some cases, reduce pest problems.
    • Both organic (composed of decayed plant/animal material), and inorganic fertilizers (composed of chemicals and minerals), improve soil fertility by adding nutrients to the soil and are used in a number of different ways. 
  • Mulching, for example, involves mixing plant materials into the soil during land preparation or covering the bases and rows of the crops with dry grass or plastic sheets after planting.
    • Dry grass or plastic sheets serve as physical barriers between the soil and the environment so the plant residues rot into the soil and increase its organic matter content.
    • Plant foliage mixed into the soil help conserve moisture, suppress weeds and reduce the spread of plant pathogen spores onto vegetable foliage through water or soil splashes. 
  • Farmers use farmyard manure or humus from the compost of plant residues as organic fertilizers.
    • They avoid scorching the plants by first thoroughly mixing the farmyard manure with soil or water.
    • Where soils are poor, leafy vegetables such as African garden eggplant, amaranth, cabbage, and lettuce will require additional levels of nitrogen and potassium (provided by inorganic fertilizers).
    • High levels of nitrogen delay the onset of flowering and thereby favours leaf production. 

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour saving technologies and practices: Integrated Pest Management (IPM): ID 7798.
  • Vegetable cultivation with ridge sowing, farm yard manure, multi-cropping and Integrated Pest Management (IPM): 10014. 
  • Cotton cultivation with laser levelling, ridge sowing, Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and compost application under drought conditions: ID 10016. 
  • Soil fertility for sustainable vegetable production: green and animal manures in the humid forest belt: ID 4525.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

10.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently provides guidance on effective pest management in terms of land preparation, seed preparation, planting, intercropping, crop rotation, and soil fertility. This not only improves crop quality but is also beneficial to the environment.

10.2 Pro-poor technology

This technology increases farmer yields in sustainable ways that create wealth and reduce productivity risks.

Integrated Pest Management (IPM) in vegetable production: a guide for extension workers in West Africa

Indigenous and exotic vegetables are central to most nutrition, food security and poverty reduction programmes around the world. However, in most of West Africa, the economic opportunities offered by vegetables are often undermined by production and trade constraints (e.g. pest damage, inappropriate pesticide usage, absence of environmental safeguard policies and/or stringent food safety standards). Extension workers and, in some places, farmers groups and local community organizations, are working towards helping farmers to increase their yields in sustainable ways that create wealth and reduce the risks to productivity. This guide is been developed by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) and Institut National des Recherches Agricoles du Bénin (INRAB), Cotonou, Benin, with support from the CGIAR Systemwide Program on Integrated Pest Management (SP-IPM), to improve the quality and usefulness of pest management research.

1. ​Vegetable agroecosystems​

  • Vegetable agroecosystems comprise a dynamic mix of biotic (living) components, abiotic (non-living) components and the interactions within and between them.
  • Any change in one component or interaction is likely to affect another component or interaction.
  • The reactions of agroecosystems to change can potentially be disastrous to farming communities, and may not be entirely predictable.
  • In order to achieve good vegetable pest management, the vital components of agroecosystems should be correctly identified, their interrelationships fully understood, and the agroecosystem treated as a functional unit.
Figure ​1​. ​Components of vegetable agroecosystems​ 


​​
Source: CTA 2010

Figure ​2​. ​Irrigation at a peri-urban vegetable site in Benin
​​ ​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​3​. ​Predatory mite (left) on a pest mite (right) called a phyoseiid ​​

​​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​4​. Aphid Lipaphis erysimi, a cabbage pest

​​

©​IITA/B.James

2. Crop types​

  • The vegetable plant is the central component of the agroecosystem. Vegetables can be grouped according to the part of the plant that is consumed and/or sold. 
  • Leafy vegetables
    • The common leafy vegetables grown in West Africa are the African garden eggplant, amaranth, cabbage and lettuce.
    • There are two common types of African garden eggplant, which are both indigenous to Africa. One is Solanum macrocarpon (Figure 5), whilst the other is S. aethiopicum. Solanum macrocarpon is grown mainly for its succulent leaves, but in some communities the bitter fruits are also eaten. S. aethiopicum is mainly cultivated for its fruits.
      • The edible parts of both S. macrocarpon and S. aethiopicum are nutritious and contain carbohydrate, cellulose and calcium, fat, protein and water. 
    • Amaranth, Amaranthus cruentus (Figure 6), is grown for its leaves which are rich in beta-carotene, calcium, iron, protein, vitamin C and water.
    • Cabbage, Brassica oleracea (Figure 7), is native to temperate regions of the world.
      • It is called the head cabbage because the immature leaves cluster up into a spherical ball or ‘head’, which is the part normally marketed and consumed.
      • The leaves contain some carbohydrates, proteins and various essential elements e.g. calcium, iron and vitamin C as well as water.
    • Lettuce, Lactuca sativa (Figure 8), is indigenous to the Mediterranean region and occurs in four groups of varieties.
      • The plant is cultivated for its succulent leaves which are used in salads.
      • Lettuce leaves contain a high proportion of water with some calcium, proteins and vitamins.
  • Fruit vegetables 
    • The most popular fruit vegetables grown in West Africa are the tomato, pepper and aubergine.
    • Tomato, Lycopersicum esculentum (Figure 9), which originates from the Andes in South America, is grown for its fruits.
      • The shape of the fruit differs according to the variety.
      • Tomato fruits can be consumed raw or cooked.
      • Tomato fruits contain a lot of water with calcium, carbohydrate, carotene, iron, niacin, riboflavin, thiamine, protein and vitamins. 
    • The sweet pepper or pepper, Capsicum annuum (Figure 10), is native to Central America.
      • It occurs in two groups of varieties.
      • Unlike most vegetables, pepper is a relatively long duration crop.
      • Both immature and fully mature fruits are marketed and consumed.
      • The fruit contains plenty of water with some carbohydrates, protein, minerals and vitamin C.
  • Root vegetables 
    • Carrot, Daucus carota (Figure 11), a crop native to Asia, is the most common root vegetable grown across West Africa.
    • It is cultivated for its swollen roots, which are rich in beta-carotene.
    • The roots also contain a large amount of water as well as carbohydrates, minerals and protein.
Figure 5. The African garden eggplant, a leafy vegetable 

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​6​. ​Amaranth, a leafy vegetable

​​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​7​. ​Cabbage, a leafy vegetable ​

​​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​8​. ​Lettuce, a leafy vegetable ​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​9​. ​Tomato, a fruit vegetable​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​10​. ​Pepper, a fruit vegetable​

​​

©​IITA/B.James

Figure ​11​. ​Carrot, a root vegetable​

©​IITA/B.James

3.  ​Vegetable plant production​

  • Depending on market demand and availability of water to irrigate plots, vegetables can be grown all year round.
  • The crops are grown in monocrops, intercrops and crop rotation schemes.
  • Commercial production sites are commonly located near to markets, e.g. in urban and peri-urban areas. 
    • Crop yield
      • Depending on the vegetable crop type, the leaves, fruits, and roots constitute the yield and provide both food and income to farmers.
      • Field workers and farmers need to be aware of two different types of yield in order to fully understand the purpose of crop production and pest management measures.
      • The two types of yield are maximum or potential attainable yield and actual yield. 
    • The maximum attainable yield is the yield obtained from crops grown in experimental plots and field conditions with the full use of improved technologies and inputs.
      • It is the highest yield possible from a particular variety cultivated under the ideal conditions. 
    • The actual yield is the yield obtained from crops cultivated under farmers’ conditions using the same varieties used in experimental plots.
      • Actual yields are often less than attainable yields. 
    • The difference between attainable and actual yield is due to a variety of environmental factors which include soil type, crop variety, agronomic practices, weather and pests.
      • Agricultural research, extension and training activities aim to find ways to increase actual yields towards attainable yields, for example by manipulating field and environmental factors that reduce yields.
      • The overall objective of vegetable pest management is, therefore, to prevent, reduce and maintain the effect of pests at levels where they cease to act as constraints to the achievement of higher actual yields.
      • It is in this way that pest management interventions ‘increase’ yields.

4. ​Land and seed bed preparation​

  • The most suitable sites for vegetable production are flat and sunny areas with light, well-drained soil which is rich in humus and not prone to waterlogging.
  • These conditions help to promote the establishment of good nurseries and seedling health for excellent vegetable crop growth.
  • Farmers break and loosen up the soil by ploughing, and remove stones and debris to allow sufficient aeration, moistening and drainage of the soil.
  • This promotes good root growth.
  • Removal of plant debris also helps to limit the occurrence of weeds and other pests that are carried over from the previous season.
  • Vegetables are often planted on flat land in areas that are unlikely to be waterlogged or flooded.
  • Planting on flat land is also common where the soil is rich in nutrients.
  • In areas that are likely to be waterlogged, or where the soil is poor in nutrients, farmers heap the topsoil into mounds or ridges on which they plant vegetables.
  • The mounds of soil raised above ground level are commonly referred to as "beds".

5. ​Planting​

  • Except for exotic vegetables, (e.g. beetroot, cabbage, carrot, cucumber and lettuce), most farmers produce their own vegetable seeds from their fields or they collect seeds from other farmers’ fields.
  • Large-scale farmers do not self-supply and buy certified seeds from seed companies and national seed services.
  • Vegetables are planted by direct sowing of seeds (e.g. amaranth and carrot) or by transplanting seedlings from nurseries (e.g. African garden eggplant, cabbage, lettuce and tomato).
  • In direct sowing, seeds are broadcast on seed beds and harrowed in, or sprinkled in rows and covered up with soil, and left undisturbed to germinate.
  • In transplanting, farmers select vigorous and disease-free seedlings at the right growth stage and transplant them.
  • If the crop is harvested by uprooting of whole plants (e.g. in amaranth, carrot and radish), the seedlings are usually transplanted closer to each other than when the crop will be harvested by ratooning.
  • Planting dates are usually adjusted in response to market demands e.g. in readiness for festive seasons.
  • Planting during the peak of the rainy seasons is uncommon so as to avoid flooding of vegetable beds.

6. ​Intercropping​

  • Farmers frequently intercrop vegetables on the same bed.
  • A single bed can hold as many as five different vegetables.
  • Intercrops can be economically more profitable than sole crop vegetables.
  • Intercropping increases farmers’ income per unit of land and labour and helps to maintain good soil moisture and reduce the incidence of weeds and other pests on vegetables.

7. ​Crop rotation​

  • Crop rotation enables farmers to maintain land under continuous cultivation by planting with one crop after another in successive seasons.
  • The practice also helps farmers respond to seasonal market demands for certain crops.
  • Where a rotation crop is a non-host plant of a pest that damaged a previous crop, crop rotation helps to control that pest by breaking its life cycle.
  • Good knowledge of crop susceptibility to pests is therefore essential in the use of crop rotation for pest management.
  • This is particularly the case with species of root-knot nematodes that attack a wide range of vegetables including the most economically important crops grown in many localities.
  • The wide range of host plants of the root-knot nematode makes it difficult to identify suitable crop rotation schemes for this pest, especially at sites under year-round vegetable production.

8. ​Soil fertility​

  • Soils nourish vegetables with mineral nutrients for vigorous, succulent and healthy growth.
    • However continuous production of vegetables can deplete soil nutrients at production sites.
    • Vegetable farmers use organic and mineral fertilizers to help soils to recover from nutrient losses, and in some cases, reduce pest problems.
    • Both organic (composed of decayed plant/animal material), and inorganic fertilizers (composed of chemicals and minerals), improve soil fertility by adding nutrients to the soil and are used in a number of different ways. 
  • Mulching, for example, involves mixing plant materials into the soil during land preparation or covering the bases and rows of the crops with dry grass or plastic sheets after planting.
    • Dry grass or plastic sheets serve as physical barriers between the soil and the environment so the plant residues rot into the soil and increase its organic matter content.
    • Plant foliage mixed into the soil help conserve moisture, suppress weeds and reduce the spread of plant pathogen spores onto vegetable foliage through water or soil splashes. 
  • Farmers use farmyard manure or humus from the compost of plant residues as organic fertilizers.
    • They avoid scorching the plants by first thoroughly mixing the farmyard manure with soil or water.
    • Where soils are poor, leafy vegetables such as African garden eggplant, amaranth, cabbage, and lettuce will require additional levels of nitrogen and potassium (provided by inorganic fertilizers).
    • High levels of nitrogen delay the onset of flowering and thereby favours leaf production. 

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Labour saving technologies and practices: Integrated Pest Management (IPM): ID 7798.
  • Vegetable cultivation with ridge sowing, farm yard manure, multi-cropping and Integrated Pest Management (IPM): 10014. 
  • Cotton cultivation with laser levelling, ridge sowing, Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and compost application under drought conditions: ID 10016. 
  • Soil fertility for sustainable vegetable production: green and animal manures in the humid forest belt: ID 4525.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project 

10.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology efficiently provides guidance on effective pest management in terms of land preparation, seed preparation, planting, intercropping, crop rotation, and soil fertility. This not only improves crop quality but is also beneficial to the environment.

10.2 Pro-poor technology

This technology increases farmer yields in sustainable ways that create wealth and reduce productivity risks.

_annotations.field_innovation_identified: NO INNOVATION IDENTIFIED. The text is a comprehensive guide about vegetable production and IPM in West Africa, but it describes established agricultural practices and management techniques rather than introducing any new innovations. While these practices are valuable, they don't meet the criteria for innovation as they don't represent new solutions or modifications to existing processes.
_annotations.field_shorter_description: Indigenous and exotic vegetables are central to most nutrition, food security and poverty reduction programmes around the world. However, in most of West Africa, the economic opportunities offered by vegetables are often undermined by production and trade constraints (e.g. pest damage, inappropriate pesticide usage, absence of environmental safeguard policies and/or stringent food safety standards). Extension workers and, in some places, farmers groups and local community organizations, are working towards helping farmers to increase their yields in sustainable ways that create wealth and reduce the risks to productivity. This guide is been developed by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) and Institut National des Recherches Agricoles du Bénin (INRAB), Cotonou, Benin, with support from the CGIAR Systemwide Program on Integrated Pest Management (SP-IPM), to improve the quality and usefulness of pest management research.

records.title: Bonnes pratiques d’utilisation des pesticides
records.description:
La description

1. Recommandations pour une bonne utilisation des pesticides

1.1 Choix et aménagement de la parcelle à traiter

  • Sur la parcelle choisie, les lignes de semis (des sillons) doivent être orientées perpendiculairement aux vents dominants.
    • Cette disposition permet d’une part une meilleure couverture des plants par le brouillard du pesticide lors des traitements et d’autre part assure la sécurité de l’applicateur lors de son mouvement, pour qu’il ne soit pas mouillé par le produit en cours de pulvérisation.
  • Sur une pente, les lignes des semis doivent être perpendiculaires à la pente.
    • Les exploitations doivent être éloignées des cours d’eau pour éviter que les produits chimiques (les pesticides) ne souillent ces cours d’eau (Figure 1).
    • Il est recommandé que le champ se situe à au moins 2.5 km du cours d’eau. 
Figure 1. Les lignes de semis sont perpendiculaires à la pente et au sens du vent. Le champ est assez éloigné du cours d'eau

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Transport des pesticides

  • La technologie conseille le transport des produits dans un véhicule adapté à ce propos comme des bâchés, des pickups ou des camions (Figure 2). 
    • Des pictogrammes indiquant le transport des produits chimiques doivent être affichés sur le camion en cas de transport d’une grande quantité et le camion doit rouler à vitesse raisonnable pour éviter tout accident de circulation.
    • Le transport des produits dans une voiture de commerce avec les passagers et d’autres produits de consommation (produits vivriers) à bord est prohibé pour éviter les risques de contamination.
      • Ces risques peuvent couter des vies humaines.
    • Le transport peut être aussi fait sur un vélo ou une moto avec les produits disposés dans un carton et bien attachés derrière le vélo ou la moto.
Figure 2. Illustration des précautions à prendre pour le transport de pesticides

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Stockage des pesticides

  • Une fois arrivé à destination, ces produits doivent être stockés dans des magasins répondant aux normes en vigueurs et construits à cet effet (Figure 3).
    • Ces magasins doivent être construits dans des endroits isolés des habitations et bien aérés.
    • Ils doivent également se munir de deux portes et des claustras ou des aspirateurs favorisant ainsi l’aération.
    • Des pictogrammes indiquant panneaux-danger et défense de fumer doivent être affichés sur les portes (barricadées à double clés) des magasins.
  • Les produits doivent être stockés sur les planchettes et de façon à respecter la condition (premier à entrer, premier à sortir).
    • Ces précautions sont nécessaires pour éviter que les enfants s’y introduisent et pour alerter les passagers à tous risques éventuels.
    • Il est aussi déconseillé de stocker les produits dans des habitations sous le lit et à même le sol. 
Figure 3. Les pesticides doivent être stockés à l'abri, dans des bâtiments adaptés, sécurisés et signalisés

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Choix des pesticides

  • Lors du choix des produits, il faut lire attentivement les étiquettes/emballages des produits pour s’assurer du choix du produit approprié pour le traitement en question.
  • Les pictogrammes (icones/insignes) figurant sur le produit sont indicateurs des caractéristiques de chaque produit.
Figure 4. Le choix des pesticides se fait après avoir pris connaissance des étiquettes

©FAO/TECA

1.5 Port d'un équipement de protection

  • La technologie recommande aussi les équipements de protection individuelle à porter avant les traitements (Figure 5).
    • Une paire de botte
    • Un pantalon
    • Une chemise à manches longues
    • Une paire de gants aux mains
    • Un masque de protection du nez et de la bouche
    • Une paire de lunettes étanches
    • Une casquette
  • Il est vivement interdit d’effectuer les traitements le torse nu ou avec les équipements troués, fendus ou cassés car dans ces conditions les risques d’intoxication sont très élevés.
  • Il s’avère indispensable de vérifier les équipements avant de procéder au traitement.
Figure 5. L'utilisation de pesticides requiert le port d'équipements adaptés

©FAO/TECA

1.6 Respect du matériel et des conseils pratiques pour le traitement

  • La buse, l’état des piles, la moteur et la tuyauterie sont à vérifier afin d’éviter toute surprise lors du traitement (Figure 6). 
  • La préparation de la bouillie (Figure 7) doit se faire de préférence dans le champ, loin des cours d’eau, et sur un lieu enherbé selon les indications décrites dans la technologie.
  • Des matériaux appropriés (un seau ou un bol doseur; de l’eau de bonne qualité; et des produits phytosanitaires appropriés sélection conformément au traitement) doivent être disponibles sur les lieux de préparation.
  • Il est vivement conseillé de respecter les doses des liquides composant la bouillie et secouer vigoureusement le mélange pour assurer l’homogénéité de la bouillie et s’assurer de tout utiliser.
  • Avant de passer à l’application du traitement, la technologie préconise le respect des conseils pratiques à une bonne application des traitements.
    • La direction du vent en érigeant une girouette à base d’un foulard et d'un piquet, ou le déversement lent de sable fin et sec ou de cendre à une hauteur d’un mètre environ du sol (Figure 8).
  • La préparation et l’application des traitements par les mineurs, les femmes enceintes ou allaitantes, les vieillards et toutes personnes malades ou très allergiques aux produits chimiques sont déconseillées.
  • La technologie décourage les traitements en temps de très fort ensoleillement, de vents violents, ou de pluie, pour éviter le dessèchement ou le lessivage des produits des plants.
  • Il est aussi prohibé de manger, de fumer, de boire, de discuter ou de déboucher la buse par la bouche en cas d’obstruction.
Figure 6. Vérification de la buse du pulvérisateur au champ

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Préparation de la bouillie

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Test de la direction du vent

©FAO/TECA

2. Recommandations après avoir utilisé des pesticides

2.1 Nettoyage du matériel

  • Il est avantageux de procéder à la vidange tout autour du champ à dose fortement diluée avec l’eau jusqu’à rincer proprement la nourrisse sur le champ (Figure 9).
  • Il est défendu d’entretenir les appareils de traitement dans des cours d’eau pour éviter l’intoxication de ces cours d’eau.
  • Les eaux de rinçage doivent être épandues sur la zone où a lieu le traitement.
Figure 9. Nettoyage du matériel à l'eau claire dans le champ

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Gestion des emballages et contenants vides

  • Après le traitement, il s’avère indispensable de procéder à une bonne gestion/destruction des emballages vides.
  • Il est strictement prohibé d’utiliser les emballages vides pour le conditionnement des boissons de toute sorte.
  • Il faut les détruire avec les machettes et les enterrer dans un endroit caché et loin des cours d’eau (Figure 10).
  • Ne pas les laisser à la portée des enfants ou des vieillards.
Figure 10. Destruction des emballages et enfouissement en lieu sûr, éloigné des cours d'eau

©FAO/TECA

2.3 Nettoyage de son corps et vêtements

  • L’applicateur est encouragé d'observer à la lettre les étapes à suivre pour se défaire de ses habits de protection individuelle après les traitements et de prendre un bain à l’eau savonnée, loin d’un cours d’eau (Figure 11).
Figure 11. Une bonne hygiène personnelle est indispensable après traitement avec pesticides

©FAO/TECA

3. En cas d'intoxication

  • En cas d’intoxication accidentelle, veuillez apporter à la victime les premiers soins prodigués dans la technologie.
    • Éloigner la victime du lieu d’intoxication.
    • Priver la de manger et de boire jusqu’à ce qu’elle ne se sente mieux.
    • La coucher doucement sur le dos.
    • La déshabiller et la laver à l’eau savonneuse.
    • L’aider à regagner ses sens et la conduire au centre de santé le plus proche avec les références du produit source de l’intoxication.
Figure 12. Illustration des bons gestes en cas d'intoxication aux pesticides

©FAO/TECA

4. Les zones agro-écologiques

  • Les tropiques, chaud.

5. Les technologies associées/relatives

  • Réduction des risques liés à l’utilisation de pesticides: ID 8353.

6. Les objectifs atteints par le projet

6.1 Favorable aux femmes

La technologie est facile à utiliser et accessible à tous.

6.2 L’efficacité d’utilisation des ressources

Les bonnes pratiques agricoles d’utilisation des pesticides permet à une meilleure préparation et la disposition préalable de l’espace à exploiter.

6.3 La technologie favorable aux populations pauvres

Meilleure qualité de produits, nourriture plus saine.

La technologie a été conçue au Benin par le projet ‘Programme de Promotion de l’Agriculture (ProAgri, Bénin), dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre du programme COMPACI, chargé de la promotion du secteur cotonnier en Afrique. La présente technologie illustre les bonnes pratiques de gestion intégrée des pesticides. La boîte explique les étapes à suivre pour l’établissement d’une parcelle, les précautions à suivre lors du transport, le stockage, et l’utilisation des substances utilisées pour le traitement.   • La technologie décourage les traitements en temps de très fort ensoleillement, de vents violents, ou de pluie, pour éviter le dessèchement ou le lessivage des produits des plants.
  • Il est aussi prohibé de manger, de fumer, de boire, de discuter ou de déboucher la buse par la bouche en cas d’obstruction.
Figure 6. Vérification de la buse du pulvérisateur au champ

©FAO/TECA

Figure 7. Préparation de la bouillie

©FAO/TECA

Figure 8. Test de la direction du vent

©FAO/TECA
