records.title: Como estabelecer um novo pomar de caju
records.description:
Descrição

Este guia prático para a instalação de uma nova plantação de cajueiro é uma ferramenta didática destinada a apoiar os produtores de caju. O seu objetivo é capacitar os agricultores para a produção de qualidade destes frutos secos, de modo a competir no mercado nacional e internacional. Este guia prático apresenta recomendações e ilustrações, faz perguntas e dá respostas que visam garantir uma adequada condução das operações para instalar uma plantação de cajueiro. 

De seguida são apresentados os vários passos para o estabelecimento de uma plantação de cajueiros. 

1. Limpeza do campo para estabelecimento do pomar 

O campo destinado a instalação da cultura ou das árvores de fruto deve ser cuidadosamente desmatado e limpo de todos os materiais volumosos. A limpeza (desmatamento) consiste no corte da vegetação, remoção dos tocos das árvores, limpeza do solo e lavoura, se necessário (Figura 1). A melhor época para realizar esta operação é antes da estação chuvosa, de preferência entre fevereiro e maio.

Figura 1. Limpeza da vegetação, com o uso de catanas ou machetes 

©FAO/TECA

2. Colocação de estaca e abertura de covas para a plantação 

  • A colocação de estacas permite definir a localização de cada árvore. 
  • Para esta operação são necessárias varas/estacas e um cordel com comprimento conhecido (tem de ser previamente medido). 
  • A colocação das estacas é feita de maneira simples, de preferência em quadrado ou retângulo. 
  • Esta esquadria favorece a associação do cajueiro a culturas anuais (consociação), diversifica os rendimentos obtidos na exploração e reduz os custos de plantação dos cajueiros.
  • O compasso (afastamento) mínimo a utilizar é de 10 m por 10 m. 

Este compasso permite obter uma densidade de 100 plantas/hectare (ha). A instalação do pomar é esquematizada na Figura 2. 

Figura 2. Colocação das estacas, com um espaçamento de 10 m a 15 m para a plantação das futuras árvores

©FAO/TECA

Nota: Compassos maiores (10 m x 12 m ou 12 m x 15 m) são desejáveis, porque permitem a consociação do cajueiro, com culturas anuais, durante um período de tempo mais longo. 
A abertura das covas para plantação dos cajueiros deverá ser realizada nos locais onde as estacas foram cravadas (Figura 3). 

As covas devem, preferencialmente, ter uma seção transversal quadrada, com pelo menos 50 cm x 50 cm de lado e 60 cm a 80 cm de profundidade. As covas devem ser abertas imediatamente após a colocação das estacas e antes do início da época das chuvas.

Ao abrir a covas, as camadas do solo superficiais e de profundidade devem ser mantidas em separado. 

A camada superficial (mais escura) é primeira a ser utilizadas para encher a cova, sendo o restante espaço preenchido, com o solo da camada mais profunda (mais clara). 
 
Nota: A camada superficial é mais rica em nutrientes. Uma vez no fundo, nutre melhor a planta instalada 

Figura 3. Abertura da cova no local, onde as estacas são cravadas

©FAO/TECA

3. Aplicação de fertilizante ou estrume 

  • O fertilizante é necessário quando o solo é pobre em nutrientes.  Este é um suplemento que permite estimular as mudas plantadas. 
  • A aplicação é feita três ou quatro semanas antes da plantação. 
  • O solo da camada superficial é misturado com adubo, estrume ou composto e é utilizado para encher 1/3 do fundo da cova.
  • A cova é tapada com a restante terra removida na abertura (Figura 4).

Dependendo da disponibilidade por cova, o fertilizante adicionado será de:

  • 200 g a 300 g de complexo NPK, de tipo 14-10-23; 
  • 100 g a 150 g de fosfato de diamónio (20 por cento de N e 40 por cento de P); 
  • 60 g de cloreto de potássio a 60 por cento (KCl).

3.1 Informações 

  • O fertilizante ou adubo produz bons resultados.
  • O fertilizante não é a única fonte de nutrientes que pode ser usada
  • O estrume ou o composto podem ser utilizados se disponíveis, e devem sempre ser preferidos em relação ao fertilizante.
  • No momento da plantação, pode ser utilizada uma mistura de terra fina, cinzas e vários compostos orgânicos para o preenchimento das covas.  A cinza de madeira é particularmente recomendável por ser rica em potássio. 
  • Esta combinação tem um rápido impacto no desenvolvimento das mudas (plantas) jovens.
  • Dica prática: uma lata pequena de tomate de conserva cheia de fertilizante corresponde a 70 g. 
Figura 4. Fertilização no local de plantação das futuras árvores 

©FAO/TECA

4. Preenchimento das covas 

As covas devem ser cheias, de preferência, três a quatro semanas antes da colocação das plantas. A camada superficial do solo, removida na abertura da cova, é colocada no fundo da cova, que é completada com a terra que veio da camada mais profunda, de modo a formar uma ligeira cúpula (montículo) (Figura 5).

A cúpula permite o assentamento natural do solo, ao nível do buraco, com as primeiras chuvas e facilita a decomposição da matéria orgânica adicionada no preenchimento. 

4.1. Informações

  • A compactação da terra deve ser evitada aquando do preenchimento da cova.
  • A cova deve ser marcada com uma estaca no centro da cúpula. 
Figura 5. Preenchimento das covas após a fertilização, no período anterior à plantação

©FAO/TECA

5. Fornecimento de mudas (plantas) 

  • A utilização de mudas jovens de cajueiros enxertados produzidas por um viveiro reconhecido é aconselhada.
  • As mudas enxertadas podem crescer rapidamente e produzir muita fruta de boa qualidade!
  • Os porta-enxertos devem ser produzidos em viveiro com sementes selecionadas e de qualidade. 
  • Os enxertos devem provir de árvores selecionadas com boa produtividade.
  • As árvores de mudas enxertadas são resistentes e tolerantes a insetos e parasitas, produtivas após 2 anos e produzem nozes em quantidade e qualidade (Figura 6).

5.1 Informações 

Recomenda-se que seja sempre verificada a origem das sementes utilizadas pelo viveiro antes de comprar as mudas propostas. Em caso de dúvida, consulte de um técnico agrícola da zona. 

Figura 6. Muda (planta) de cajueiro (esquerda) e cajueiro adulto (direita)

©FAO/TECA

6. Preparação das mudas (plantas) antes da plantação 

  • Antes da plantação (transplantação), as mudas devem ser transferidas para um viveiro, com menos sombra.  Assim, as plantas acostumam-se às condições naturais de luz.  Estas são as condições de adaptação das mudas ao ambiente antes de serem plantadas (Figura 7). 

Durante estas, as plantas passam pelas seguintes etapas.

  • Diminuição progressiva da sombra para promover a exposição solar e preparar as mudas para o crescimento na plantação.
  • Redução gradual da quantidade de água de rega. Uma rega por dia ou a cada dois dias será suficiente.
  • As mudas devem ser preparadas quatro semanas antes da plantação.
Figura 7. Preparação das mudas antes da plantação viveiro temporário

©FAO/TECA

7. Transporte e armazenamento das mudas (plantas) 

  • As mudas são colocadas em caixas para serem transportadas em boas condições. 
  • As plantas deverão ser transportadas de preferência na véspera ou no dia da plantação, após uma boa rega. 
  • As plantas devem ser removidas do viveiro entre as 7 e as 10 horas da manhã ou entre as 4 e as 7 horas da tarde, para evitar períodos de calor excessivo.
  • As mudas podem ser transportadas em caixas de madeira, bacias ou cestos.

7.1 Informações 

  • As mudas transportadas devem ser plantadas de imediato. 
  • Caso isso não seja possível guarde-as sob sombra e regue-as bem por pouco tempo. 
Figura 8. Rega das mudas armazenadas em caixas para transporte para o campo

©FAO/TECA

8. Plantação das mudas no campo 

As mudas de cajueiro são colocadas nas covas previamente reabertas e posteriormente fechadas (Figura 9).

8.1 Etapas do processo

  • Faça uma pequena abertura no centro da cova preenchida, com terra e marcada, com a estaca.
  • Corte a base da bolsa de plástico da muda, com uma lâmina, sem danificar as raízes.
  • Coloque a planta e aconchegue o solo em redor da bolsa, depois de certificar-se de que a copa da planta fica acima da superfície do solo.
  • Retire a parte da bolsa que fica acima da borda superior da planta e, em seguida, calque o solo em redor do pé das plantas.
  • Coloque a bolsa de removida no topo da estaca, previamente cravada, que se encontra junto à planta, para torná-la mais visível.  

8.1 Informação

  • A jovem planta deve ser plantada no exato local marcado pela estaca, cuja localização marca o centro da cova anteriormente cheia.
  • A presença do saco também indica que o trabalhador não enterrou a bolsa com a terra que vinha com a muda. Permite também localizar rapidamente a planta durante as inspeções de campo. 
Figura 9. Instalação das plantas no campo

©FAO/TECA

9. Preenchimento de falhas ou retancha 

Quando as mudas (plantas) morrem ou estão doentes, é necessário proceder à sua substituição. Esta operação é chamada de retancha.

A retancha permite a substituição das plantas em falta e mantém o número inicialmente previsto de plantas para a plantação. 

A retancha deve ser realizada de preferência, um mês após a plantação das mudas ou, o mais tardar, no início da estação seguinte à instalação da plantação.

9.1 Informações

A retancha deve se realizada, o mais tardar, um ano após a instalação para permitir o desenvolvimento uniforme das árvores na plantação. 

Figura 10. Consociação do cajueiro com culturas anuais (neste caso o milho)

©FAO/TECA

10. Consociação do cajueiro com culturas anuais 

  • A consociação com culturas anuais permite aos jovens cajueiros beneficiar com a manutenção dessas culturas. 
  • A consociação permite aos produtores diversificar os seus rendimentos e reduzam reduzir os custos de produção de caju (Figura 10).
  • No entanto, nem todos os tipos de culturas anuais podem ser consociados com o cajueiro.

As culturas a serem evitadas na consociação são: 

  • a mandioca, milheto e sorgo, para evitar o abafamento das plantas jovens de cajueiro na plantação; e
  • feijão-fradinho e feijão gandu (feijão bóer em moçambique) para evitar o ataque de insetos e doenças no cajueiro. 

11. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, quente.

12. Tecnologias relacionadas/associadas 

  • Guia de colheita e processamento pós-colheita da castanha de caju: ID 2467.
  • Guia para colheita e manuseio pós-colheita da castanha de caju: ID 2476.
  • Boas práticas de colheita e pós-colheita da castanha de caju: ID 2917.

Esta tecnologia está também disponível em francês: ID 7919.

13. Objetivos cumpridos pelo projeto

13.1 Apoio às Mulheres

O guia prático é fácil de implementar e a atividade pode ser realizada por qualquer trabalhador agrícola.

13.2 A eficiência no uso dos recursos

O guia prático fornece etapas específicas a serem seguidas pelo agricultor, ajudando a decidir como limpar os campos, criar o pomar, plantar e manter as mudas.

13.3 Apoio às populações desfavorecidas

A prática permite o aumento da produtividade, a produção de alimento e cria uma fonte de rendimento adicional.

Este destina-se a munir os produtores de caju com os conhecimentos, que lhes permitam obter produções de qualidade capazes de competir no mercado nacional e internacional. O guia baseia-se nas boas práticas agrícolas fundamentais para o estabelecimento de uma exploração do sucesso, e garantir uma boa iniciação aos novos produtores ou para aqueles que querem expandir a sua produção de caju. Os seus aplicativos, a tecnologia e as ilustrações visam capacitar os produtores com os conhecimentos necessários para conduzir as operações necessárias para a instalação de uma plantação de cajueiro. Este guia prático foi elaborado como material de formação pelo projeto Iniciativa Africana para o Caju (African Cashew Initiative, GIZ) e destina-se a ser utilizado pelos técnicos (agentes) de extensão agrária, na animação de sessões de grupo para a capacitação de produtores. O guia prático também pode ser consultado por qualquer pessoa que pretenda estabelecer uma plantação de cajueiro. Este faz parte de uma série de guias que cobre a fase de estabelecimento, boas práticas de gestão, colheita e pós-colheita da produção, assim como de aspetos relacionados com a qualidade do caju.

  • As plantas deverão ser transportadas de preferência na véspera ou no dia da plantação, após uma boa rega. 
  • As plantas devem ser removidas do viveiro entre as 7 e as 10 horas da manhã ou entre as 4 e as 7 horas da tarde, para evitar períodos de calor excessivo.
  • As mudas podem ser transportadas em caixas de madeira, bacias ou cestos.

7.1 Informações 

  • As mudas transportadas devem ser plantadas de imediato. 
  • Caso isso não seja possível guarde-as sob sombra e regue-as bem por pouco tempo. 
Figura 8. Rega das mudas armazenadas em caixas para transporte para o campo

©FAO/TECA

8. Plantação das mudas no campo 

As mudas de cajueiro são colocadas nas covas previamente reabertas e posteriormente fechadas (Figura 9).

8.1 Etapas do processo

  • Faça uma pequena abertura no centro da cova preenchida, com terra e marcada, com a estaca.
  • Corte a base da bolsa de plástico da muda, com uma lâmina, sem danificar as raízes.
  • Coloque a planta e aconchegue o solo em redor da bolsa, depois de certificar-se de que a copa da planta fica acima da superfície do solo.
  • Retire a parte da bolsa que fica acima da borda superior da planta e, em seguida, calque o solo em redor do pé das plantas.
  • Coloque a bolsa de removida no topo da estaca, previamente cravada, que se encontra junto à planta, para torná-la mais visível.  

8.1 Informação

  • A jovem planta deve ser plantada no exato local marcado pela estaca, cuja localização marca o centro da cova anteriormente cheia.
  • A presença do saco também indica que o trabalhador não enterrou a bolsa com a terra que vinha com a muda. Permite também localizar rapidamente a planta durante as inspeções de campo. 
Figura 9. Instalação das plantas no campo

©FAO/TECA

9. Preenchimento de falhas ou retancha 

Quando as mudas (plantas) morrem ou estão doentes, é necessário proceder à sua substituição. Esta operação é chamada de retancha.

A retancha permite a substituição das plantas em falta e mantém o número inicialmente previsto de plantas para a plantação. 

A retancha deve ser realizada de preferência, um mês após a plantação das mudas ou, o mais tardar, no início da estação seguinte à instalação da plantação.

9.1 Informações

A retancha deve se realizada, o mais tardar, um ano após a instalação para permitir o desenvolvimento uniforme das árvores na plantação. 

Figura 10. Consociação do cajueiro com culturas anuais (neste caso o milho)

©FAO/TECA

10. Consociação do cajueiro com culturas anuais 

  • A consociação com culturas anuais permite aos jovens cajueiros beneficiar com a manutenção dessas culturas. 
  • A consociação permite aos produtores diversificar os seus rendimentos e reduzam reduzir os custos de produção de caju (Figura 10).
  • No entanto, nem todos os tipos de culturas anuais podem ser consociados com o cajueiro.

As culturas a serem evitadas na consociação são: 

  • a mandioca, milheto e sorgo, para evitar o abafamento das plantas jovens de cajueiro na plantação; e
  • feijão-fradinho e feijão gandu (feijão bóer em moçambique) para evitar o ataque de insetos e doenças no cajueiro. 

11. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, quente.

12. Tecnologias relacionadas/associadas 

  • Guia de colheita e processamento pós-colheita da castanha de caju: ID 2467.
  • Guia para colheita e manuseio pós-colheita da castanha de caju: ID 2476.
  • Boas práticas de colheita e pós-colheita da castanha de caju: ID 2917.

Esta tecnologia está também disponível em francês: ID 7919.

13. Objetivos cumpridos pelo projeto

13.1 Apoio às Mulheres

O guia prático é fácil de implementar e a atividade pode ser realizada por qualquer trabalhador agrícola.

13.2 A eficiência no uso dos recursos

O guia prático fornece etapas específicas a serem seguidas pelo agricultor, ajudando a decidir como limpar os campos, criar o pomar, plantar e manter as mudas.

13.3 Apoio às populações desfavorecidas

A prática permite o aumento da produtividade, a produção de alimento e cria uma fonte de rendimento adicional.

Este guia prático contém a informação necessária para o estabelecimento de uma nova plantação de caju e é uma ferramenta didática, destinado aos produtores de caju. O guia prático também pode ser consultado por qualquer pessoa que pretenda estabelecer uma plantação de cajueiro. Este faz parte de uma série de guias que cobre a fase de estabelecimento, boas práticas de gestão, colheita e pós-colheita da produção, assim como de aspetos relacionados com a qualidade do caju.

records.title: ​Arroz de sequeiro​
records.description:
Descrição 

1. O que é arroz de sequeiro? 

O arroz de sequeiro é um sistema de produção em que as variedades utilizadas foram especificamente desenvolvidas para se aptarem ao cultivo em terrenos bem drenados, não alagados e não saturados. O cultivo deste arroz ocorre em terreno seco, sendo a cultura irrigada do mesmo modo que o milho de regadio ou o trigo. Esta cultura com um sistema de gestão adequado, pode atingir produtividades de, pelo menos, 4 a 6 toneladas por hectare. Veja também para maiores informações. 

2. Áreas alvo 

  • “Terrenos elevados, de planaltos favoráveis para o cultivo"
    • Áreas onde a terra é plana, a precipitação com ou sem rega suplementar é suficiente para garantir o teor de água do solo próximo da capacidade de campo e onde os agricultores têm acesso a fatores de produção, como fertilizantes. 
  • Terrenos em encostas elevadas, terraços, em planícies onduladas e terras baixas de sequeiro
    • Frequentemente com solos de textura relativamente grosseira e bem drenados, de modo a que o alagamento, quando existente, apenas ocorre durante breves períodos de tempo do ciclo de desenvolvimento da cultura.
  • Planícies baixas regadas, com escassez de água
    • Áreas onde os agricultores deixaram de ter a água suficiente para manter os campos de arroz inundados durante um período substancial do ciclo de desenvolvimento da cultura. 

3. Gestão 

  • O método de cultivo usual é a sementeira direta a seco (Figura 1 e 2). 
  • O arroz de sequeiro também permite a adopção de práticas de agricultura de conservação, usadas no cultivo das terras altas, como sejam o empalhamento e a mobilização mínima.  
Figura 1. Aspecto de campo semeado com arroz de sequeiro

©IRRI

  • Este sistema cultural pode ser de sequeiro ou de regadio. 
  • A rega pode ser efetuada por inundações repentinas, irrigação por rego ou por aspersão. 
  • Ao contrário de arroz em regadio ou em terrenos alagados, a rega, quando aplicada, não implica o alagamento do solo, mas sim o aumento do teor de água do solo, na zona radicular, para níveis similares à capacidade de campo.  
Figura 2. Sementeira de arroz de sequeiro 

©IRRI

  • A gestão específica dos nutrientes no terreno (SSNM) pode ser utilizada na optimização das fertilizações (aplicação de fertilizantes). 
  • Na ausência de conhecimentos sobre SSNM, a aplicação de 70 a 90 kg/ha de N pode ser um ponto de partida para se obter uma produtividade na ordem das 4 a 6 toneladas/ha. 
  • A primeira aplicação pode ser efetuada 10 a 12 dias após a emergência, a segunda no perfilhamento e a terceira no início da formação da panícula (Figura 3). 
  • A aplicação de fósforo pode ser mais crítica para o arroz de sequeiro do que para o arroz de alagamento.
  • Os campos de arroz de sequeiro, não estão permanentemente inundados, e tendem a apresentar um maior desenvolvimento de espécies infestantes.
Figura 3. Aspecto de um campo de arroz de sequeiro na fase de maturação

©IRRI

  • O controlo das infestantes, através da aplicação do uso de um herbicida adequado, para além de mondas adicionais, manuais ou mecânicas é necessário realizar nas fases iniciais de desenvolvimento da cultura. 
  • As pragas transmitidas pelo solo, como os nematodes, afídios e fungos ocorrem mais frequentemente no arroz de sequeiro do que no arroz de regadio, especialmente nas zonas tropicais. 
  • O arroz de sequeiro deve ser cultivado em rotação com outras culturas adequadas à região.  
Figura 4. Arroz de sequeiro cultivado em rotação, com um campo de soja ao lado

©IRRI

4. Validação da prática agrícola 

  • A cultura de arroz de sequeiro foi validada por agricultores de Kaifeng, no centro-norte da China, ao longo do rio Amarelo, com produtividades demonstradas de até 5,5 toneladas/ ha, com apenas 230 mm de rega e 340 mm de precipitação, em localidades onde o arroz de alagamento normalmente consome 1 300 mm para obter produtividades de 6,5 a 9,0 toneladas/ha. 
  • Uma boa gestão da cultura do arroz de sequeiro pode atingir 75 a 80 % da produtividade do arroz de regadio, utilizando apenas se utiliza metade ou menos do volume de água. 
  • O arroz de sequeiro está a ser testado por agricultores do norte da China, numa área estimada em 200.000 ha, e ativamente pesquisado nas Filipinas, Índia, Bangladesh, Paquistão, Mianmar, Tailândia, Laos, e muitos outros países. 
  • Nas Filipinas, o arroz de sequeiro foi testado e adotado por agricultores de cerca de 10 províncias (Lampayan et ai 2012).  
    Viídeo onde os agricultores relatam a sua experiência com o cultivo do arroz de sequeiro  
  • Viídeo onde os agricultores relatam a sua experiência com o cultivo do arroz de sequeiro (link aqui). 

5. Zona agroecológica

  • Tropical, quente. 

6. Técnologias relacionadas/associadas

  • Cultura intensiva de arroz: ID 1666.
  • Rice seedbed preparation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice)-(Preparação de camas para a sementeira do Rice): ID 6973.
  • Rice seed flotation (Africa Rice Center video on rice advice)-(Flutuação da semente do arroz ): ID 7210.

Esta tecnologia está também disponível em inglês: ID 7941.

7. Objectivos atingidos pelo projecto

7.1 Eficiência na utilização de recurso

A prática permite do cultivo de variedades de arroz de sequeiro, através do uso eficiente da irrigação e a manutenção de terrenos bem drenados, não alagados e não saturados.

_annotations.body:
​Arroz de sequeiro​

Este guia prático explica onde e como cultivar o “arroz de sequeiro”. O arroz de sequeiro é um sistema de produção em que o arroz não é cultivado em condições de alagamento e na ausência de saturação de água no solo. O arroz de sequeiro necessita de menos água no terreno que o arroz de regadio convencional. O sistema de produção destina-se a ser utilizado em áreas com pouca de água rega, ou alimentadas pelas águas da chuva. A rega pode ser efetuada por alagamento ou por aspersão. A gestão de nutrientes no terreno, através da utilização de SSNM - Site-Specific Nutrient Management (www.irri.org/irrc/ssnm) pode ser utilizada para determinar a gestão optimizada dos fertilizantes. Este sistema cultural é mais propenso ao desenvolvimento de infestantes, com um maior número de espécies, sendo necessário o seu controlo. As pragas transmitidas pelo solo, como os nematodes, afídios radiculares e fungos, ocorrerem mais frequentemente no arroz de sequeiro do que no arroz de regadio, especialmente nas zonas tropicais. Recomenda-se que o arroz de sequeiro seja cultivado em rotação com outras culturas adequadas à região.

records.title: Farmer’s dairy goats’ production handbook
records.description:
Description

1. Why keep dairy goats 

1.1 ​Goat’s milk is good! Goat’s meat is tasty!​

  • Goats milk is easy to drink and is a richer food because it has more calcium, phosphorus and chlorine than cow’s milk.
  • Milk is used at home so that the family get the best milk - if there is a cow many farmers will sell the cow’s milk for cash and make sure the family gets the goat milk to drink!
  • Tasty Meat! Goat’s meat is very tasty and it is juicy and eaten often by many people
  • More and more people are learning about how good goat’s milk, cheese and yoghurt are so there is a growing market
  • Goat’s milk is better for the family as it has a “High Nutritional Content.” This means it is very high-quality food and very good for young and old.
  •  Some people cannot drink cow’s milk. They have an “allergy” to it. This is why some children are reared on goat’s milk when cow’s milk and all else has failed. Nobody is allergic to goat’s milk!
Table ​1​. ​Comparison of goat milk, cow milk and human milk content​

​​ ​

Source: FARMAFRICA,2010

1.2 ​Make more money​

  • Get cash from selling milk.
  • Get a higher price for goat milk.
  • Get kids every year (twice per year) and sell them easily when ready.
  • Kids can be twins/triplets.
  • With small farm sizes, it is a better way to earn money and feed the family.
  • In the space and using the same feed, you need to keep a cow you can keep six goats!
  • Do not need big areas to graze like cattle.
  • Farmers can pay school fees using income from the sale of milk/manure.
  • Products are fast and easy to sell.
  • Goats sell easily for meat.
  • Many people prefer goat cheese.
  • Start getting benefits quickly.
  • Uses small doses of drugs - cheap.
  • Easy to maintain.
  • Good for people who do not have a lot of money to start with.

**Goats make very good manure. Droppings are used to improve crop yields. 

1.3 ​Goats are good for the farm​

  • Less feed is needed to keep a goat than a cow.
  • Goats will eat many different plants - so easier to keep fed through the year.
  • Droppings are used as manure for organic farming.
  • Goats good at keeping bush under control - stop too much shrub growth.
  • Will live even where there is a drought. It does not need a lot of water and can go for quite a long time without water in very dry times.
Figure 1​. ​Goat waste as manure​ 


©FAO/TECA

1.4 ​Goat rearing does not require much work​

  • Goats require less labour and time per head compared to cattle.

1.5 ​Important for social events​

  • Goats are used traditionally as payment of dowry.
  • Goats are often eaten during land cases, parties, clan meetings, etc.
  • Goats are important in some rituals, they are used during circumcision ceremonies for example.
  • Goat horn and bone are used in the traditional craft industry. 
Figure 2​. ​Goats are used in social events​

​​ ​

©FAO/TECA

2. ​Housing the goat​

2.1 ​Good goat house will make keeping goats easier​

  • A good goat house should be: 
    • rainproof;
    • damp-proof;
    • well ventilated;
    • free from the direct wind;
    • free from sharp objects that might cut the goat;
    • pest and wild animal proof;
    • slats on the floor for free fall of droppings; and
    • with an area of at least 2 m per animal. 
  • If you build a goat house as the one shown then you will:
    • make sure animals do not get sick very often;
    • you can make sure that only the animals you want to breed do so;
    • make it very easy to feed;
    • stop wasting feed;
    • save the goats wasting energy and increase the amount of milk you get; and
    • keep goat’s feet dry and clean all the time. 
Figure ​3. ​Proper housing for the goat: inside​ 

​​ ©FAO/TECA

Figure ​4​. ​Proper housing for the goat: outside​ 

©FAO/TECA

2.2 ​Types of houses​

  • At the beginning of the project, it is assumed the farmer is working on a limited budget so construction of a simple house but a comfortable house for the goats is recommended.
  • The house can be built using local material.

2.2.1 ​Mud houses​

  • This is the cheapest house to build because it uses local materials.
    • posts,
    • mud,
    • rafters for floor,
    • nails, and
    • grass for thatch roof.
  • When placing mud, make holes in the wall slanting down so that, the air does not land directly on the goats.
Figure ​5​. ​Mud housing​

​​
©FAO/TECA

2.2.2 ​Offcuts houses​

  • This house costs a little more but it will last longer.
  • Materials:
    • posts,
    • off-cut planks,
    • nails,
    • iron sheets or grass for thatching, and
    • wood, rafters or planks for the floor.  
Figure ​6​. ​Off-cut housing​

©FAO/TECA

2.3 ​The house​

  • There are two main areas of the house, the sleeping area and feeding area.
  1. Sleeping area 
    • Wall right around - with a door. 
    • It must be roofed.
    • Lots of air allowed in (well ventilated).
  2. Feeding area 
    • open not roofed, goats need some sun; 
    • fence right around with a door/gate;
    • feed trough/water area;
    • a place for hanging fodder [feed racks];
    • floor with slats to let manure fall through - keeps feet and animals clean and dry; and 
    • a place to hang mineral block (placed where it cannot be rained on).
Figure 7​. ​The sleeping area of the house​

​​

©FAO/TECA

2.4 The house parts

  1. Floor
    • House should be raised 1.5 feet (or just below knee height) from the ground.
    • A slatted wooden floor is very important. This has small gaps - about half an inch wide (or the width of a side of a matchbox) between the planks or rafters.
    • Use of local materials means you can use off-cut planks, etc.
    • The floor racks made of rafters should be put where the goats feed and sleep, this stops foot rot when it is wet, keeps the house clean and dry.
  2. Feed trough
    • In the feeding area, it is built 1 m (3 feet) above the platform.
    • Should be made with rafters, it must be easy to clean troughs.
    • The floor of the trough can be made of offcuts.
    • Must be able to hold hay.
  3. Water trough
    • It should be placed 1 foot above the floor in the feeding area.
    • Hang a 5 liter can on the door to the sleeping room.
    • The door should have a small window so that goats can have access to water - day and night.
  4. Kid pen
    • Toggenburgs often give birth to twin kids so don’t make the pen small!
    • Kid pen should be for at least six kids.
    • Be half the area for the four does, e.g. 4 m2.
  5. Hay barn/store
    • To store fodder, for use during the dry season, build a store adjacent to the goat house that is roofed to avoid hay being rained on.
  6. Mineral trough
    • Should be made where the goats sleep.
    • A 1 foot square box is ideal for the purpose. A halved long ways plastic container nailed to a board, at least 1 foot wide can be useful.
    • Or just as good - hang the salt so the goat has to reach for it.
Figure ​8​. ​The floor​

​​ ​

©FAO/TECA

Figure 9​. ​The feeding trough​

​​

©FAO/TECA

Figure ​10​. ​The mineral trough​ 

©FAO/TECA


Figure ​11​. The water trough

​​ ​

©FAO/TECA

Figure ​12​. ​The ground plan​

​​ ​

©FAO/TECA

3. Feeding the dairy goat

3.1 ​What does a goat like to eat?​

  • A goat does not like to graze on the ground like a sheep or cow.
  • Goats like feeding at knee height up to head height.
  • They like to feed above the ground often standing on their hind legs and resting their forelegs up on the bush or goat house wall.
  • Goats need to be able to drink fresh water at all times.

3.2 ​Advantages of stall feeding​ 

  • It does not need a large amount of land and no grazing pastures.
  • Can use many farm products, banana leaves, maize, maize thinning, bean husks, etc.
  • Saves time and labor, do not have to take goats out of the farm for grazing or spend time looking for them.
  • Less death amongst the kids and all goats because they can be easily looked after throughout the day.
  • Easier to plan and manage to breed.
  • Keeps goats from eating crops and damaging the farm.
  • It makes collecting manure very easy.
  • It helps in controlling diseases.

3.3 What do they eat?

  • They eat a lot of different plants/feeds.
    • But they know what they want to eat.
  • They prefer some plants/feeds to others.
  • They even prefer different parts of the plant so they will eat leaves and flowers and not pods or stems, within the same plant.
  • They get bored when fed the same feed every day.
  • They can be wasteful.
    • Only eating some of the plants.
    • For example give n un-chopped feeds like napier grass they pull it out of the ground, eat the leaves only and do not eat the stem.
  • Are clean feeders, and will not eat dairy feeds which are not fresh nor dirty feed e.g. napier with mud splash from rain.
  • Do not like sticky, mouldy, wet dusty feeds.

3.4 The best way to feed goats

  • Feed only clean, fresh and dry fodder.
  • Always have fresh water for goats to drink at any time.
  • Clean the feeding trough and water bucket every day.
  • Give lots of different feeds such as grasses and legumes, tree leaves and fresh kitchen remains.
  • Give chopped mixed feeds to make sure the goats eat everything and do not waste feed.
  • Feed goats at least three times a day and at the same time every day.
  • Put some feed in the feed trough or rack or hang up some feed to be eaten overnight.
  • If you use molasses to make feed taste better do not use too much it will make feed sticky.
  • Dusty feeds and concentrates should be wetted a little.
  • Provide fresh and clean water daily.
    • There should always be water in the bucket.
  • Always give mineral lick blocks to all goats.
  • If feed too much leguminous feed such as desmodium.
  • Mix feeds with grass, hay, straw or Napier to balance.
  • Only a third of the days' feed can be lucerne.
    • Do not feed too much lucern, it can poison the goats.

3.5 Feeding different goats

  • Remember all goats must have fresh water whenever they need it. 

3.5.1 Feeding sick goats

  • Feed goats well when ill. Good feeding will give strength.
  • Small, weak, young and sick goats should be fed separately.
  • Follow the best way to feed goats carefully and handle gently. 

3.5.2 Feeding mature goats

  • Should be fed on whatever feed there is, enough to keep well and keep the animals' weight.

3.5.3 Feeding the buck

  • Feeding should be enough to keep its weight steady but not too fat.
  • A fat buck will not be active and its weight.
  • Give more feed two months before the buck has to serve the does this will improve the bucks sperm and make it more active.
  • When a buck is being used a lot to serve does, it should be separated from other goats for about two to three hours per day.
    • This will allow it time to eat as well as serve the does.
  • Lots of fresh and clean water needed all the time.
  • Must be able to lick the mineral lick at any time. 

3.5.4 Feeding does

  • Concentrates should be fed to does just before the does are served by the buck.
  • Increase feed gradually for two months up until the doe gives birth.
  • Continue feeding concentrate while she is giving milk.
  • The doe needs careful feeding in order to:
    • keep its normal weight up;
    • be fertile when served so as to get twins (Flushing);
    • carry the kid while it is pregnant;
    • give milk to its kids; and
    • give extra milk for farmers to use
  • Feeding the breeding and lactating doe.
    • One month before mating, the doe should be fed and watered very well so as she is in the best of health.
    • If she is very well she is more likely to have twins or even triplets.
    • Mineral licks hasten coming on heat.
    • Give lots of water at all times.
  • Feeding during pregnancy-First three months of pregnancy.
    • The goats need to be fed as normal and to be sure that she is healthy
  • The last two months of pregnancy.
    • The goat must be fed well with high-quality feed.
    • The foetus or kid inside does nearly all it’s growing in this period.
    • There may be twins or triplets and they will need lots of good food to grow

3.5.5 Feeding kids

  • Feeding the newborn up to three months
    • Newborn kids should suck colostrum within 24 hours and then should be with the doe and allowed as much as they need.
    • At one week, kids should be provided with small quantities of good clean feed, e. g. sweet potato vines, tree legumes leaves or natural tree leaves.
    • Kids should continue with milk for the first three weeks, and thereafter be allowed milk with fresh mixed fodder up to three to four months.
  • Feeding young stock
    • Should be fed on fresh, highly nutritious mixed fodder.
    • Give lots of water at all times.
    • Provide lots of water.
    • Mineral blocks must be given at this stage.

3.6 What kind of feed should the goat be given?

  • The dairy goat gives as much milk as it is given the right food!!
  • There are many feeds the goat likes.
  • Here are some good feeds that can be used.

3.6.1 Sweet potato vines

  • This is a very good feed that goats like very much.
  • It is a good crop to plant because it gives tubers for the family to eat and the leaves can be fed to the goats.
  • It can be planted beside river beds, steep parts of the farm and roadside edges.
  • Useful in feeding kids whose mothers die early in their life.

3.6.2 Napier

  • Plant napier along river beds, along soil terraces, road reserves, etc.
  • Where a farmer has a big farm then plant as one crop near the home to save time and work when taking to the goats.
  • Good napier needs manure and top dressing with fertilizer and needs weeding.
  • Where new fields are being planted mixed cropping with desmodium improves the quality of the fodder. 
  • If you plant Napier around your maize it stops Maize stalk borer! 
  • Cut Napier often so it is easy for the goats to eat and digest.

3.6.3 Fodder trees and legumes

  • These have lots of protein and you need only feed a little at a time.
  • These are for example Leucaena, calliandra, sesbania and desmodium.
  • The trees and legumes should be planted along the fences and terraces.
    • For example, Leucaena is good in fences.
  • Good legumes are potato vines. 
  • They do not need a lot of work once they are growing.
  • Desmodium when available should be inter-cropped with Napier.
  • Calliandra does better in high altitudes (tea zones) than leuceana.
  • Do not forget that many weeds also make good fodder.

3.6.4 Maize

  • While maize is grown for farmer’s food, there is a lot of fodder that can be used for feeding the goat which will not stop the farmer from getting a good maize yield. 
  • Thinning
    • All the extra maize seedlings that grow from the same seed hole should be thinned and dried a little before feeding to the goats.
  • Remove extra leaves
    • This should start with the leaves below the cobs as soon as the cob can be seen. 
  • Cutting the tops
    • This should start after the grains have hardened. 
  •  Stover
    • These should have sweeteners (molasses) added or sprinkle common salt after chopping. 
  • Broken grains
    • These are very nutritious especially after a heavy harvest but should be fed carefully to avoid grain overload

4. Kidding

  • This is the birth of young goats - Kids.
  • It takes five months for a goat to give birth after it has been served, by a male.

4.1 Preparation for kidding

  • There are three very important rules for kidding.
  • Rule one
    • Ensure the kidding Doe is put in a dry clean and quiet place at the time of kidding. 
  • Rule two
    • The kidding place should be under a shelter (in the house) or shade.
    • This is to protect the kid from too much sun
  • Rule three
    • The doe must have water as soon as she has given birth, so she can make sure she has enough to balance the loss of water from giving birth and to have enough milk to feed the newborn.
    • Kidding should be done where you can see what is happening easily and often.

4.2 Signs of kidding

  • Enlarged vulva.
  • The restlessness of the doe.
  • Doe seeks a quiet place away from other goats.
  • The udder is enlarged, full and firm.
  • Muscles either side of tail will become sunken and on either side of tail hollow appears.
  • Often stand or lie down and stretch her neck pointing her head skyward.
  • Will have a clear discharge from the vulva.

4.3 Kidding process

  • Keep the kid in a cool dry place away from too much heat and draught. 
  • Disinfect the navel immediately using a disinfectant e.g. dettol or tincure of iodine. 
  • Ensure kid suckles colostrum within 20 to 30 minutes after birth. 
  • Stimulate mother-kid bond by encouraging the mother to lick the kid. 
  • In case of breathing problems, help by tickling the tongue, and removing all mucus from the nostrils.

4.3.1 Helping the doe during kidding

  • Try and make sure everything is as clean as possible
  • Normally goats do not have problems giving birth or kidding but sometimes a kid may get stuck during the process of birth.
  • If you need to help then be sure that before doing so that you wash hands with Dettol, make sure nails are cut and remove any jewelry - like rings.
  • If you can get proper plastic gloves to use these to protect yourself and the goat from infections.
  • When helping kids to be delivered be gentle and make sure you understand the problem before exerting any force.
  • Be careful when pulling the kids' legs that the head is forward and down.
  • Be careful that you are dealing with one kid at a time and not holding one foot from two kids.

4.4 Care of orphans

  • Foster orphans to docile do or bottle-feed with other goat milk or milk replacers.
  • May use sweet potato vines to feed orphans.

5. Husbandry techniques

  • Once the kid is born there are a number of things to be done.

5.1 Disbudding

  • This is the removal of very young horns that have not grown.
  • It is usually done first to the second week of age.
  • It should be performed by a vet using a hot iron under general anesthesia using a drug called SAFFAN.

5.2 Castration

  • Male goats that will not be bred should be castrated early in life (in the first two months) and kept for meat.
  • It can be done by the use of rubber rings, burdizzo castrator, or open methods.

5.2.1 Rubber rings A2

  • Using an applicator insert the rubber to the testis as shown, make sure it is as high as possible.
  • Make sure the testis are in the scrotum, below the ring and release carefully.
  • This can be done on-farm after a little practice.
Figure 13. Application of the rubber ring

©FAO/TECA

5.2.2 Burdizzo B2

  • Hold the spermatic cord with your fingers right at the top, one testicle at a time
  • Clamp the Burdizzo on one cord and press the levers to snap it.
    • Repeat for the other testicle
  • Kids should continue with milk for the first three weeks, and thereafter be allowed milk with fresh mixed fodder up to three to four months.
Figure 14. Burdizzo 

©FAO/TECA

5.2.3 Open methods?

  1. It’s complete remove of testis by an operation 
  2. This is an operation that you can request your vet to perform for you in cases of trouble

5.3 Identification

  • Farmers need to be able to identify their animals so they can keep records and easily know the age, breeding and usefulness of each animal.
  • This can be done through: 
    • tattooing,
    • ear tags,
    • paint or ink,
    • branding, or
    • other marks or names?
  • Extension staff can demonstrate this to farmers interested.
  • It is useful in feeding kids whose mothers die early in their life.

5.4 Other managerial practices

  • Weaning - removing kids from its mother
    • Usually done at two to three months of age.
      • Let kids try hay and grains early in life to strengthen their stomachs.
    • When you start to wean young goats they will begin to feed on solid food.
      • So they will begin to pick up diseases such as Coccidiosis.
    • When kids start eating fodder they will suffer high worm infection so they need to be dewormed after exposure.
    • When given concentrates kids are likely to suffer Enterotoxaemia so you will need to vaccinate against these diseases.
    • Don’t stop feeding milk suddenly but this should be gradual to avoid indigestion or bloat.
  • Hoof trimming
    • Do not let hooves grow longer than shown below, cut and trim carefully.
Figure 15. Hoof trimming 

©FAO/TECA

5.5 Fodder trees and legumes

  • These have lots of protein and you need only feed a little at a time.
  • These are for example Leucaena, calliandra, sesbania and desmodium.
  • The trees and legumes, should be planted along the fences and terraces.
    • For example, Leucaena is good at fences.
  • Good legumes are potato vines.
  • They do not need a lot of work once they are growing.
  • Desmodium when available should be inter-cropped with Napier.
  • Calliandra does better in high altitudes (tea zones) than Leucaena.
  • Do not forget that many weeds also make good fodder￼.

6. Milking

6.1 Keeping milk clean

  • The most important thing to do is keep yourself, your hands and buckets, clean.
  • Also carefully clean the doe’s udder.
  • Milking shed
    • The milking shed should be cleaned after each milking and disinfected.
  • Human infectious diseases
    • People who are ill should not milk.
  • Washing hands
    • Before starting milking, the milker should wash his hands, arms with soap and hot water, or disinfectant.
    • Keep fingernails cut and clean.
  • Wash Udder
    • Before milking the udder should be washed with clean water which has disinfectant added to it.
    • Use two cloths alternatively for washing the udders.
    • Leave one in the disinfectant whilst the other is in use.
  • Cut out bacteria
    • The first drop of milk from each teat should be thrown away as it has a very high bacterial count. 

6.2 Hand milking

  • Good milking is done by the squeeze method.
  • Avoid the pulling technique as it hurts the udder and the teat and udder will get a mastitis infection.
  • The squeeze method of milking
    •  Take hold and squeeze the base of the teat with the thumb and forefinger to trap the milk in the teat.
    • Close the other three fingers squeeze downwards in turn.
    • The milk in the teats is squeezed downwards and not pulled. 
    •  Squeezing slowly downward makes the milk come out.
    • Repeat this in a rhythm and quickly-using the full hand to avoid finger and thumb striping. 
    • This should take about seven minutes.
      • So be quick so that you get as much milk as possible
  • Other important dairy goat precautions during milking
    • Always house/pen the doe and the serving buck in different pens to prevent smell in the milk.
    • Make the milking parlour far from the buck pen.
    • Wind direction should be from milking palour to the buck pen and not vice versa.
    • Always be calm, friendly to the doe and milk at the same time every day.
    • Maintain a similar milking position (back position or side position).
    • The nails on the hand of the milker should be short.
    • Measure and record your milk immediately.
    • Wash milk equipment with a hot water rinses and dry on a rack immediately after milking.
    • Avoid giving feeds with strong smells just before milking and during milking, e.g. silage, pineapple, waste, etc to avoid tainting the milk.
    • The hair on the flanks and around the udder should be trimmed regularly and the goat brushed occasionally.
    • The use of sprays/oils/soaps with smell by milker will taint the milk.
  • After milking tips
    • Irregular milking can lead to low yields and an increased chance of mastitis.
    • The kid should be allowed to suck the milked teat after milking for proper emptying of the teat canal.
    • After milking use a teat dip containing a suitable antiseptic, e.g. Tincture of iodine.
    • If possible the same person should milk always.
  • Mastitis 
    • Goats with mastitis should be milked last to prevent the spread of the infection to other goats.
    • Mastitis can reduce yields by at least 10 percent.
    • Milk from sick goats, especially goats with mastitis should not be sold but be discarded.
    • Isolate the goat with mastitis.
    • Sick animals must be treated.
  • Dry off a doe
  • If a doe has been served and is pregnant, special care is required during the fourth and the fifth months as the embryo’s gains weight rapidly.
  • The '' does" should be housed alone to avoid disturbance by the other goats.
  • The doe is dried gradually i.e milking is done normally but the amount milked at every subsequent milking is reduced gradually until finally, one stops.
  • This prevents the development of milk clots".

7. Breeding

7.1 What type of goats are available

  • Farmers keep local goats. They have been keeping these goats for many years.
    • These goats, however, do not produce enough milk for their kids and extra for human consumption.
  • Goats can be classified as dairy or meat type.
  • The local goats are mainly meat types, East African and Galla. 
  • The local goats can survive and thrive in the hot climate, low-quality forages and fodder and to some extent resistant to common diseases.
  • This makes them produce very little milk.
  • The dairy types include the following Toggenburg, Saanen, Alpine, Anglo- Nubian.
  • Dairy type goats produce a lot of milk but do not adapt very well.
  • These dairy goats are normally mated to local goats to get a goat that is “a better milk producer" than the local goats but which are easier to raise than the pure dairy types.
    • The mating of two different types of breeds of animals is called crossbreeding.

7.2 What can be done to improve the productivity of the local goats?

  • Feed them properly with different grasses and shrub browses.
  • Keep them in a properly built goat house.
  • Give them good husbandry, treatment.
  • Crossbreed them with improved goat breeds like Toggenburg.
  • Keep records to help you in knowing and managing your goats.

7.3 Why should farmers keep dairy goats 

  • Farms are becoming smaller as each new generation inherits land.
  • Goats can be kept on small pieces of land. 
  • Goats can be fed on-farm by-products. 

7.4 Why breed your goats

  • Breeding helps the farmer to have more animals.
  • With good breeding, you get more and better animals. 
  • Good breeding means a farmer has to know his animals and taking good care of them.
  • A farmer can know his / her animals by keeping records on his / her animals and the events taking place.
  • Animals of different ages need different attention.
  • Does, bucks and kids should all be given good care appropriately.

7.5 Taking good care of dairy goats

  • Well-fed and healthy parents create good offspring.
  • Both does and the buck must be well fed and cared for before becoming parents.
  • Keep does and bucks apart. 
  • Allow mating to occur at the right time. 
  •  Keep a record of dates.
  • A doeling comes into heat at four to five months of age, therefore, it must be raised apart from bucks from four months.
  • You should mate your doe when it is over 1 year old.
  • To get good results a farmer must control his goats. 
  • First mating will depend on the age and condition of the goat.
  • Mating before one year should only be allowed provided before and during pregnancy.
  • It is recommended that a doe should be bred when she reaches 75 percent to 80 percent of her mature weight.
  • For milking does, they should be bred after the third month of kidding.

7.6 When should you breed your does?

  • A goat can only be bred when she is ready. This condition is referred to as “the goat is on heat”. 
  • What are heat signs?
    • The goats become restless and mount each other.
    • Cries loudly and sometimes bleating.
    • The vulva may become swollen.
    • The goat wags the tail.
    • Frequent urination.
    • Lasts two to three days. 
  • When to mate?
    • A doe should be mated 12 to 24 hrs after you have seen her on heat.
    • Heat signs in the afternoon, the goat should be mated the next morning.
    • Heat signs in the morning should be mated in the evening.

7.7 Avoid mating goats that are related

  • When goats that are related are mated this is called inbreeding.
  • Inbreeding should be avoided in animal production. 
  • Inbreeding results in weak offspring, decreased productivity e.g milk and even death. 
  • Bucks should, therefore, be rotated or moved from their stations after one and a half years.
  • Keeping good records will help a farmer to know which animals are related and which ones are not.

8. Keeping records 

  • Keeping records
    • It helps you to know your goats.
    • Recording increases animal values and therefore sales income.
    • Recording promotes increased milk yields.
    • Recording promotes improved genetic merit.
    • It helps you to manage your animals well. 
  •  Which records to keep?
    • A farmer should keep simple records of:
      • birth dates,
      • birth weight,
      • sire and dam,
      • milk records,
      • treatment records, 
      • service dates. 
  • A good record on service date will help you calculate the expected date of birth after breeding.
  • You can know the expected date by counting five months from the date of service and take off three days. 

9. How can you know your goat is pregnant after mating?

  • Three weeks later doe not on heat.
  • Eight weeks later the vulva shows an enlargement.
  • Twelve weeks later the abdomen enlarges noticeably.
  • Abortions in goats are not common, but can be avoided by protecting the doe against difficult situations keeping the does well-fed and disease-free.
  • A pregnant doe should be dried up three months into its pregnancy. 

9.1 Signs of approaching birth

  • A few days before there will be discharge for the vulva.
  • On the day of kidding, the doe bleats, paws the bedding and becomes restless.
  • With proper feeding and management, goats normally give multiple births. 

9.2 How to identify a sick goat

  • A sick goat stands apart from the others in a group.
    • Animals about to give birth also behave like this.
  • They are restless.
  • They do not lie down and rest even when others in their group do so unless it gets very ill.
  • They hold their head down.
  • They have dull eyes and show little interest in their surroundings.
  • Often have rough coats and look weak and tired.
  • Do not like to feed. 

 10. Related/associated technology

  • Herbal de-worming for lower goat mortality: ID 7690.
  • Collective action to reduce goat mortality: a case study of interventions supported by PRADAN: ID 7904.
  • Intensive stall-fed system for rearing goats: ID 8770.
  • Goat raising in controlled areas and vaccination: ID 8937.
  • Improvement of livestock production: community based goat production: ID 4495.
  • Rearing dairy goats: ID 6925.

11. Objectives fulfilled by the project

11.1 Resource use efficiency

The technology allows for more efficient ways for goat rearing, ranging from nutritious benefits to manure production.

11.2 Pro-poor technology

The technology provides meat, milk, and increases in income. It is also not costly to use.

Farmer’s dairy goats’ production handbook

Dairy goat rearing is very beneficial for farming families, apart from the milk which is very nutritious, goat meat is also a delicacy for many households. Goats can also be used to provide manure for the farm and also earn the farmer more income. With limited capital, a farmer can start a dairy goat project and be able to reap benefits from it within a short time.

Description

1. Why keep dairy goats 

1.1 ​Goat’s milk is good! Goat’s meat is tasty!​

  • Goats milk is easy to drink and is a richer food because it has more calcium, phosphorus and chlorine than cow’s milk.
  • Milk is used at home so that the family get the best milk - if there is a cow many farmers will sell the cow’s milk for cash and make sure the family gets the goat milk to drink!
  • Tasty Meat! Goat’s meat is very tasty and it is juicy and eaten often by many people
  • More and more people are learning about how good goat’s milk, cheese and yoghurt are so there is a growing market
  • Goat’s milk is better for the family as it has a “High Nutritional Content.” This means it is very high-quality food and very good for young and old.
  •  Some people cannot drink cow’s milk. They have an “allergy” to it. This is why some children are reared on goat’s milk when cow’s milk and all else has failed. Nobody is allergic to goat’s milk!
Table ​1​. ​Comparison of goat milk, cow milk and human milk content​

​​ ​

Source: FARMAFRICA,2010

1.2 ​Make more money​

  • Get cash from selling milk.
  • Get a higher price for goat milk.
  • Get kids every year (twice per year) and sell them easily when ready.
  • Kids can be twins/triplets.
  • With small farm sizes, it is a better way to earn money and feed the family.
  • In the space and using the same feed, you need to keep a cow you can keep six goats!
  • Do not need big areas to graze like cattle.
  • Farmers can pay school fees using income from the sale of milk/manure.
  • Products are fast and easy to sell.
  • Goats sell easily for meat.
  • Many people prefer goat cheese.
  • Start getting benefits quickly.
  • Uses small doses of drugs - cheap.
  • Easy to maintain.
  • Good for people who do not have a lot of money to start with.

**Goats make very good manure. Droppings are used to improve crop yields. 

1.3 ​Goats are good for the farm​

  • Less feed is needed to keep a goat than a cow.
  • Goats will eat many different plants - so easier to keep fed through the year.
  • Droppings are used as manure for organic farming.
  • Goats good at keeping bush under control - stop too much shrub growth.
  • Will live even where there is a drought. It does not need a lot of water and can go for quite a long time without water in very dry times.

1.4 ​Goat rearing does not require much work​

  • Goats require less labour and time per head compared to cattle.

1.5 ​Important for social events​

  • Goats are used traditionally as payment of dowry.
  • Goats are often eaten during land cases, parties, clan meetings, etc.
  • Goats are important in some rituals, they are used during circumcision ceremonies for example.

2. ​Housing the goat​

2.1 ​Good goat house will make keeping goats easier​

  • A good goat house should be: 
    • rainproof;
    • damp-proof;
    • well ventilated;
    • free from the direct wind;
    • free from sharp objects that might cut the goat;
    • pest and wild animal proof;
    • slats on the floor for free fall of droppings; and
    • with an area of at least 2 m per animal. 
  • If you build a goat house as the one shown then you will:
    • make sure animals do not get sick very often;
    • you can make sure that only the animals you want to breed do so;
    • make it very easy to feed;
    • stop wasting feed;
    • save the goats wasting energy and increase the amount of milk you get; and
    • keep goat’s feet dry and clean all the time.

2.2 ​Types of houses​

  • At the beginning of the project, it is assumed the farmer is working on a limited budget so construction of a simple house but a comfortable house for the goats is recommended.
  • The house can be built using local material.

2.2.1 ​Mud houses​

  • This is the cheapest house to build because it uses local materials.
    • posts,
    • mud,
    • rafters for floor,
    • nails, and
    • grass for thatch roof.
  • When placing mud, make holes in the wall slanting down so that, the air does not land directly on the goats.

2.2.2 ​Offcuts houses​

  • This house costs a little more but it will last longer.
  • Materials:
    • posts,
    • off-cut planks,
    • nails,
    • iron sheets or grass for thatching, and
    • wood, rafters or planks for the floor.

2.3 ​The house​

  • There are two main areas of the house, the sleeping area and feeding area.
  1. Sleeping area 
    • Wall right around - with a door. 
    • It must be roofed.
    • Lots of air allowed in (well ventilated).
  2. Feeding area 
    • open not roofed, goats need some sun; 
    • fence right around with a door/gate;
    • feed trough/water area;
    • a place for hanging fodder [feed racks];
    • floor with slats to let manure fall through - keeps feet and animals clean and dry; and 
    • a place to hang mineral block (placed where it cannot be rained on).

2.4 The house parts

  1. Floor
    • House should be raised 1.5 feet (or just below knee height) from the ground.
    • A slatted wooden floor is very important. This has small gaps - about half an inch wide (or the width of a side of a matchbox) between the planks or rafters.
    • Use of local materials means you can use off-cut planks, etc.
    • The floor racks made of rafters should be put where the goats feed and sleep, this stops foot rot when it is wet, keeps the house clean and dry.
  2. Feed trough
    • In the feeding area, it is built 1 m (3 feet) above the platform.
    • Should be made with rafters, it must be easy to clean troughs.
    • The floor of the trough can be made of offcuts.
    • Must be able to hold hay.
  3. Water trough
    • It should be placed 1 foot above the floor in the feeding area.
    • Hang a 5 liter can on the door to the sleeping room.
    • The door should have a small window so that goats can have access to water - day and night.
  4. Kid pen
    • Toggenburgs often give birth to twin kids so don’t make the pen small!
    • Kid pen should be for at least six kids.
    • Be half the area for the four does, e.g. 4 m2.
  5. Hay barn/store
    • To store fodder, for use during the dry season, build a store adjacent to the goat house that is roofed to avoid hay being rained on.
  6. Mineral trough
    • Should be made where the goats sleep.
    • A 1 foot square box is ideal for the purpose. A halved long ways plastic container nailed to a board, at least 1 foot wide can be useful.
    • Or just as good - hang the salt so the goat has to reach for it.

3. Feeding the dairy goat

3.1 ​What does a goat like to eat?​

  • A goat does not like to graze on the ground like a sheep or cow.
  • Goats like feeding at knee height up to head height.
  • They like to feed above the ground often standing on their hind legs and resting their forelegs up on the bush or goat house wall.
  • Goats need to be able to drink fresh water at all times.

3.2 ​Advantages of stall feeding​ 

  • It does not need a large amount of land and no grazing pastures.
  • Can use many farm products, banana leaves, maize, maize thinning, bean husks, etc.
  • Saves time and labor, do not have to take goats out of the farm for grazing or spend time looking for them.
  • Less death amongst the kids and all goats because they can be easily looked after throughout the day.
  • Easier to plan and manage to breed.
  • Keeps goats from eating crops and damaging the farm.
  • It makes collecting manure very easy.
  • It helps in controlling diseases.

3.3 What do they eat?

  • They eat a lot of different plants/feeds.
    • But they know what they want to eat.
  • They prefer some plants/feeds to others.
  • They even prefer different parts of the plant so they will eat leaves and flowers and not pods or stems, within the same plant.
  • They get bored when fed the same feed every day.
  • They can be wasteful.
    • Only eating some of the plants.
    • For example give n un-chopped feeds like napier grass they pull it out of the ground, eat the leaves only and do not eat the stem.
  • Are clean feeders, and will not eat dairy feeds which are not fresh nor dirty feed e.g. napier with mud splash from rain.
  • Do not like sticky, mouldy, wet dusty feeds.

3.4 The best way to feed goats

  • Feed only clean, fresh and dry fodder.
  • Always have fresh water for goats to drink at any time.
  • Clean the feeding trough and water bucket every day.
  • Give lots of different feeds such as grasses and legumes, tree leaves and fresh kitchen remains.
  • Give chopped mixed feeds to make sure the goats eat everything and do not waste feed.
  • Feed goats at least three times a day and at the same time every day.
  • Put some feed in the feed trough or rack or hang up some feed to be eaten overnight.
  • If you use molasses to make feed taste better do not use too much it will make feed sticky.
  • Dusty feeds and concentrates should be wetted a little.
  • Provide fresh and clean water daily.
    • There should always be water in the bucket.
  • Always give mineral lick blocks to all goats.
  • If feed too much leguminous feed such as desmodium.
  • Mix feeds with grass, hay, straw or Napier to balance.
  • Only a third of the days' feed can be lucerne.
    • Do not feed too much lucern, it can poison the goats.

3.5 Feeding different goats

  • Remember all goats must have fresh water whenever they need it. 

3.5.1 Feeding sick goats

  • Feed goats well when ill. Good feeding will give strength.
  • Small, weak, young and sick goats should be fed separately.
  • Follow the best way to feed goats carefully and handle gently. 

3.5.2 Feeding mature goats

  • Should be fed on whatever feed there is, enough to keep well and keep the animals' weight.

3.5.3 Feeding the buck

  • Feeding should be enough to keep its weight steady but not too fat.
  • A fat buck will not be active and its weight.
  • Give more feed two months before the buck has to serve the does this will improve the bucks sperm and make it more active.
  • When a buck is being used a lot to serve does, it should be separated from other goats for about two to three hours per day.
    • This will allow it time to eat as well as serve the does.
  • Lots of fresh and clean water needed all the time.
  • Must be able to lick the mineral lick at any time. 

3.5.4 Feeding does

  • Concentrates should be fed to does just before the does are served by the buck.
  • Increase feed gradually for two months up until the doe gives birth.
  • Continue feeding concentrate while she is giving milk.
  • The doe needs careful feeding in order to:
    • keep its normal weight up;
    • be fertile when served so as to get twins (Flushing);
    • carry the kid while it is pregnant;
    • give milk to its kids; and
    • give extra milk for farmers to use
  • Feeding the breeding and lactating doe.
    • One month before mating, the doe should be fed and watered very well so as she is in the best of health.
    • If she is very well she is more likely to have twins or even triplets.
    • Mineral licks hasten coming on heat.
    • Give lots of water at all times.
  • Feeding during pregnancy-First three months of pregnancy.
    • The goats need to be fed as normal and to be sure that she is healthy
  • The last two months of pregnancy.
    • The goat must be fed well with high-quality feed.
    • The foetus or kid inside does nearly all it’s growing in this period.
    • There may be twins or triplets and they will need lots of good food to grow

3.5.5 Feeding kids

  • Feeding the newborn up to three months
    • Newborn kids should suck colostrum within 24 hours and then should be with the doe and allowed as much as they need.
    • At one week, kids should be provided with small quantities of good clean feed, e. g. sweet potato vines, tree legumes leaves or natural tree leaves.
    • Kids should continue with milk for the first three weeks, and thereafter be allowed milk with fresh mixed fodder up to three to four months.
  • Feeding young stock
    • Should be fed on fresh, highly nutritious mixed fodder.
    • Give lots of water at all times.
    • Provide lots of water.
    • Mineral blocks must be given at this stage.

3.6 What kind of feed should the goat be given?

  • The dairy goat gives as much milk as it is given the right food!!
  • There are many feeds the goat likes.
  • Here are some good feeds that can be used.

3.6.1 Sweet potato vines

  • This is a very good feed that goats like very much.
  • It is a good crop to plant because it gives tubers for the family to eat and the leaves can be fed to the goats.
  • It can be planted beside river beds, steep parts of the farm and roadside edges.
  • Useful in feeding kids whose mothers die early in their life.

3.6.2 Napier

  • Plant napier along river beds, along soil terraces, road reserves, etc.
  • Where a farmer has a big farm then plant as one crop near the home to save time and work when taking to the goats.
  • Good napier needs manure and top dressing with fertilizer and needs weeding.
  • Where new fields are being planted mixed cropping with desmodium improves the quality of the fodder. 
  • If you plant Napier around your maize it stops Maize stalk borer! 
  • Cut Napier often so it is easy for the goats to eat and digest.

3.6.3 Fodder trees and legumes

  • These have lots of protein and you need only feed a little at a time.
  • These are for example Leucaena, calliandra, sesbania and desmodium.
  • The trees and legumes should be planted along the fences and terraces.
    • For example, Leucaena is good in fences.
  • Good legumes are potato vines. 
  • They do not need a lot of work once they are growing.
  • Desmodium when available should be inter-cropped with Napier.
  • Calliandra does better in high altitudes (tea zones) than leuceana.
  • Do not forget that many weeds also make good fodder.

3.6.4 Maize

  • While maize is grown for farmer’s food, there is a lot of fodder that can be used for feeding the goat which will not stop the farmer from getting a good maize yield. 
  • Thinning
    • All the extra maize seedlings that grow from the same seed hole should be thinned and dried a little before feeding to the goats.
  • Remove extra leaves
    • This should start with the leaves below the cobs as soon as the cob can be seen. 
  • Cutting the tops
    • This should start after the grains have hardened. 
  •  Stover
    • These should have sweeteners (molasses) added or sprinkle common salt after chopping. 
  • Broken grains
    • These are very nutritious especially after a heavy harvest but should be fed carefully to avoid grain overload

4. Kidding

  • This is the birth of young goats - Kids.
  • It takes five months for a goat to give birth after it has been served, by a male.

4.1 Preparation for kidding

  • There are three very important rules for kidding.
  • Rule one
    • Ensure the kidding Doe is put in a dry clean and quiet place at the time of kidding. 
  • Rule two
    • The kidding place should be under a shelter (in the house) or shade.
    • This is to protect the kid from too much sun
  • Rule three
    • The doe must have water as soon as she has given birth, so she can make sure she has enough to balance the loss of water from giving birth and to have enough milk to feed the newborn.
    • Kidding should be done where you can see what is happening easily and often.

4.2 Signs of kidding

  • Enlarged vulva.
  • The restlessness of the doe.
  • Doe seeks a quiet place away from other goats.
  • The udder is enlarged, full and firm.
  • Muscles either side of tail will become sunken and on either side of tail hollow appears.
  • Often stand or lie down and stretch her neck pointing her head skyward.
  • Will have a clear discharge from the vulva.

4.3 Kidding process

  • Keep the kid in a cool dry place away from too much heat and draught. 
  • Disinfect the navel immediately using a disinfectant e.g. dettol or tincure of iodine. 
  • Ensure kid suckles colostrum within 20 to 30 minutes after birth. 
  • Stimulate mother-kid bond by encouraging the mother to lick the kid. 
  • In case of breathing problems, help by tickling the tongue, and removing all mucus from the nostrils.

4.3.1 Helping the doe during kidding

  • Try and make sure everything is as clean as possible
  • Normally goats do not have problems giving birth or kidding but sometimes a kid may get stuck during the process of birth.
  • If you need to help then be sure that before doing so that you wash hands with Dettol, make sure nails are cut and remove any jewelry - like rings.
  • If you can get proper plastic gloves to use these to protect yourself and the goat from infections.
  • When helping kids to be delivered be gentle and make sure you understand the problem before exerting any force.
  • Be careful when pulling the kids' legs that the head is forward and down.
  • Be careful that you are dealing with one kid at a time and not holding one foot from two kids.

4.4 Care of orphans

  • Foster orphans to docile do or bottle-feed with other goat milk or milk replacers.
  • May use sweet potato vines to feed orphans.

5. Husbandry techniques

  • Once the kid is born there are a number of things to be done.

5.1 Disbudding

  • This is the removal of very young horns that have not grown.
  • It is usually done first to the second week of age.
  • It should be performed by a vet using a hot iron under general anesthesia using a drug called SAFFAN.

5.2 Castration

  • Male goats that will not be bred should be castrated early in life (in the first two months) and kept for meat.
  • It can be done by the use of rubber rings, burdizzo castrator, or open methods.

5.2.1 Rubber rings A2

  • Using an applicator insert the rubber to the testis as shown, make sure it is as high as possible.
  • Make sure the testis are in the scrotum, below the ring and release carefully.
  • This can be done on-farm after a little practice.

5.2.2 Burdizzo B2

  • Hold the spermatic cord with your fingers right at the top, one testicle at a time
  • Clamp the Burdizzo on one cord and press the levers to snap it.
    • Repeat for the other testicle
  • Kids should continue with milk for the first three weeks, and thereafter be allowed milk with fresh mixed fodder up to three to four months.

5.2.3 Open methods?

  2. This is an operation that you can request your vet to perform for you in cases of trouble

5.3 Identification

  • Farmers need to be able to identify their animals so they can keep records and easily know the age, breeding and usefulness of each animal.
  • This can be done through: 
    • tattooing,
    • ear tags,
    • paint or ink,
    • branding, or
    • other marks or names?
  • Extension staff can demonstrate this to farmers interested.
  • It is useful in feeding kids whose mothers die early in their life.

5.4 Other managerial practices

  • Weaning - removing kids from its mother
    • Usually done at two to three months of age.
      • Let kids try hay and grains early in life to strengthen their stomachs.
    • When you start to wean young goats they will begin to feed on solid food.
      • So they will begin to pick up diseases such as Coccidiosis.
    • When kids start eating fodder they will suffer high worm infection so they need to be dewormed after exposure.
    • When given concentrates kids are likely to suffer Enterotoxaemia so you will need to vaccinate against these diseases.
    • Don’t stop feeding milk suddenly but this should be gradual to avoid indigestion or bloat.
  • Hoof trimming
    • Do not let hooves grow longer than shown below, cut and trim carefully.

  • These have lots of protein and you need only feed a little at a time.
  • These are for example Leucaena, calliandra, sesbania and desmodium.
  • The trees and legumes, should be planted along the fences and terraces.
    • For example, Leucaena is good at fences.
  • Good legumes are potato vines.
  • They do not need a lot of work once they are growing.
  • Desmodium when available should be inter-cropped with Napier.
  • Calliandra does better in high altitudes (tea zones) than Leucaena.
