_annotations.field_shorter_description: American foulbrood (AFB) is considered the most widespread and destructive infectious honeybee disease, and it can cause serious economic losses to beekeeping. The term “American” does not refer to the disease originating from the United States of America, but rather to the fact that it was first identified and studied there. American foulbrood is caused by a spore-forming bacterium, Paenibacillus larvae (P. larvae). The spores are the resistant form of this germ and can withstand a temperature of 100 °C for several minutes. In a suitable environment (e.g. in the intestine of the larvae), a single spore is able to produce 250 million new bacilli after only 24 hours. The spores can remain viable for more than 30 years in an infected hive, being able to contaminate new colonies. The long survival rate and the contagiousness of AFB are serious problems for the control of the disease. Thorough and effective sanitation measures are needed to eliminate the disease in an affected apiary.

records.title: Amoebiasis: a parasitic disease of adult honeybees
records.description:
Description

1. Introduction

Amoebiasis is caused by a protozoan called Malpighamoeba mellificae and affects adult honeybees. The symptoms of Amoebiasis are honeybees with a swollen abdomen and diarrhoea, very similar to the symptoms of nosemosis. In fact, amoebiasis and nosemosis are frequently observed together as a mixed infection.

Bees become infected by ingesting honey or pollen contaminated by the faeces of infected bees. The infection causes an inflammation of the intestines of the adult bees, which progressively become unable to work properly. The beekeeper can observe diarrhoeal faeces at the hive entrance and on the front of the hive, and honeybees that are unable to fly and with quivering and trembling wings.

The disease occurs mainly in spring and then disappears after a few months. In severe cases, amoebiasis kills the adult bees and, consequently, there are not enough bees in the hive to take care of the brood, which ultimately dies.

2. Symptoms

Symptoms of amoebiasis (Figure 1) are similar to those of nosemosis (caused by N. apis):

  • swollen abdomen;
  • inability to fly;
  • quivering wings;
  • diarrhoeal faeces smeared on honeycombs and also located at the entrance and the front of the hive.

Amoebiasis and nosemosis are frequently observed together as a mixed infection. Diagnosis is confirmed by laboratory identification of microscopic cysts in the tubules and faeces of the bees.

Figure 1. Hive entrance spotted with diarrhoeal faeces

©Flickr/D.Broberg

3. Transmission

Inside the hive, cleaning worker bees become infected when removing excrement from the hives. They pass on the infection, and the disease is transmitted through ingestion of contaminated honey and pollen.

Amoebiasis is transmitted from one hive to another by drifting bees (scouting and harvesting bees returning to the wrong hive), robbing and watering stations. The beekeeper can also transmit the disease between colonies by moving infected combs from an infected hive to a healthy one, and by using infected beekeeping equipment and tools.

Long winters, cold weather, and cool and wet summer and autumn months help spread the disease. However, amoebiasis affects a very low proportion of colonies and is rarely identified. Colonies are usually able to restore their health naturally after infection when weather conditions improve.

4. Diagnosis

It is possible to make a diagnosis in the field through the observation of the following symptoms:

  • bees with a swollen abdomen (Figure 2);
  • diarrhoeal faeces on honeycombs and at hive entrance (Figure 1);
  • bees with trembling wings, unable to fly.
Figure 2. Bee with diarrhoea

©IZSLT/Giovanni Formato

As the symptoms of amoebiasis are very similar to those of nosemosis, it is only through examination of bees in the laboratory that a final diagnosis is possible.

5. Prevention and control

Control measures for amoebiasis are similar to those for nosemosis. The adoption of GBPs can help in preventing and controlling amoebiasis (Table 1).

Table 1. Good beekeeping practices for prevention and control of amoebiasis
Recommendation Advantage or reason for the practice
Clean and disinfect regularly beekeeping equipment and hive tools (e.g. using bleach), ideally after each use. Reduces the bacteria population in the hive.
Ensure that the hives are located in a good place: sunny and dry places; avoid humidity and wind. Reduces thermal stress on the bees.
Strengthen and stimulate the colonies in autumn and spring with the administration of fortified feeding with vegetal substances or vitamin supplements specific for bees. Reduces nutritional stress on the bees.
Control other pathogens (mainly varroa) to ensure a good health status of the colony. Other pathogens, especially varroa, cause immunosuppression in bees.
Remove combs from colonies that have signs of the disease (diarrhoea). Melt the beeswax. Reduces the transmission of the disease to healthy bees.
Administer supplements to infected colonies. Reduces nutritional stress on the bees.
Do not feed bees with honey or pollen taken from unhealthy colonies. Reduces transmission of the disease to healthy bees.
Do not exchange any combs between diseased and healthy colonies. Reduces transmission of the disease to healthy bees.

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Temperate, cool
  • Temperate, cold.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Nosemosis: a fungal disease of adult honeybees: ID 8413.
  • Varroa mites (Varroatosis or Varroosis): a parasitic disease of the brood and adult honeybees: ID 8416.
  • Good beekeeping practices: ID 8409.
  • Bee viruses: ID 8419.
  • Main diseases of honey bees: ID 8412.
  • Chalkbrood: a fungal disease of the brood: ID 9002.
  • American foulbrood (AFB): a bacterial disease of the brood: ID 10018.
  • European foulbrood (EFB): a bacterial disease of the brood: ID 8418.
  • Small hive beetle (SHB): ID 10020.
  • Tropilaelaps: a parasitic disease of the brood: ID 10021.
  • Stonebrood (aspergillosis): a fungal disease of the brood and adult honeybees: ID 10031.

This technology is also available in French: ID 10006. The translation was finalized by Elsa Demoulin, Beekeeping Network North-South.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Resource-use efficiency

This practice allows for improved hive management and ensures better colony health.

records.title: Comment récolter le miel, le pollen et la propolis des mélipones
records.description:
La description

En plus du rôle pollinisateur des cultures, les mélipones produisent du miel, du pollen et de la propolis qui constituent des revenus supplémentaires pour les agriculteurs. Cette fiche technique explique comment récolter le miel, le pollen et la propolis des mélipones à l’aide d’une simple procédure.La récolte de pollen et de miel avec coques de noix de coco, est assez facile. Lorsque les pots de miel sont scellés, le miel est mûr et prêt à être récolté.  

Vérifiez le contenu de la chambre de la coque de la noix de coco avec une tige de bambou propre. Soulevez la chambre contenant les réserves de miel et de pollen et remplacez la coque retirée par une nouvelle. 

Figure 1. Vérification du contenu du pot avec une tige de bambou propre

©FAO/TECA

Figure 2. Ouverture du nid et remplacement de la chambre de stockage

S

©FAO/TECA

1.  Récolte de miel

1.1 La coque de noix de coco

 Pour récolter le miel, procédez comme suite:

  • Grattez le miel et le pollen de la coque.
    • Séparez les pots à miel des pots à pollen. Le miel peut être égoutté ou pressé à partir des pots.
    • Faites passer le miel à travers un tamis à mailles fines dans une cuve de décantation.
    • Laissez le miel décanter pendant au moins une semaine, puis mettez-le en bouteille et scellez-la.
  • Le miel peut être contaminé pendant la récolte par des spores de levures et de bactéries en suspension dans l'air. Les spores de levure germent dans des conditions de forte humidité et font fermenter le miel. Le miel devrait être pasteurisé, en particulier lorsque la teneur en humidité est supérieure à 23 pour cent.
  • La pasteurisation va tuer la levure qui provoque la fermentation. Pour la pasteurisation, placez les bouteilles de miel dans une casserole remplie d'eau et chauffez à 145⁰F (environ 62⁰C) pendant environ 30 minutes. La teneur en humidité du miel est mesurée à l'aide d'un réfractomètre.

1.2 ​La ruche en bois 

Dans les ruches en bois, les hausses sont gérées de manière à ne contenir que du miel ou du pollen.  Une fois pleines, les hausses à miel sont retirées. Les pots de miel sont coupés et retirés, et les hausses replacées au sien de la colonie. Les pots sont découpés en morceaux de plus petite taille et placés dans une presse ou laissés à égoutter. Le miel est lui aussi filtré et laissé au repos avant d’être mis en bouteille. Il sera ensuite pasteurisé selon la procédure décrite ci-dessus. 

Figure 3. Pressage des pots de miel  

©FAO/TECA

2. La récolte de pollen 

Le pollen est manuellement séparé de ses pots à l’aide d’une tige de bambou propre ou une cuillère en acier inoxydable. Le pollen propre est ensuite étalé sur des plateaux grillagés et séché à l'air libre à l'ombre pour le protéger de la lumière du soleil. L’exposition directe au soleil noircira le pollen. Cela prendra environ 3 jours à sécher à l’air libre s’il fait beau et que la température ambiante se situe entre 30 et 33°C. 

A des fins commerciales, un hygromètre est utilisé pour mesurer la teneur en humidité du pollen La valeur standard pour l'humidité du pollen ne doit pas être supérieure à 6 pour cent. Le pollen séché s’effrite lorsqu’on le presse. Le cérumen et les pots sont coupés en petits morceaux et répartis uniformément sur des plateaux grillagés et séchés à l'air. Le pollen et le cérumen séchés sont alors placés dans des sacs en plastique de qualité alimentaire et scellés sous vide (si l'équipement est disponible).

Figure 4. Les pots à miel et à pollen à l’intérieur d’une coque de noix de coco   

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Le pollen que l’on retire de ses pots

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Le pollen retiré de ses pots

©FAO/TECA

3. La récolte de propolis

La propolis est récoltée en coupant des petits morceaux de propolis de 1 cm x 1 cm autour du nid, avec une distance de 6 cm entre les eux pour minimiser les dégâts dans le nid. La procédure peut être répétée après deux semaines lorsque les espaces ouverts ont été entièrement réparés. Portez ensuite des gants en caoutchouc ou en vinyle, pour nettoyer la propolis en enlevant les débris tels que la boue, les feuilles séchées et la sciure que les abeilles mélangent à la résine. 

Figure 7. Enlèvement de la propolis/cérumen de l'intérieur de la coque de la noix de coco

©FAO/TECA

Après le nettoyage, faites sécher la propolis à l’air libre pendant environ 3 jours. La propolis séchée est moins souple et relativement plus dure que celles fraîchement récoltées. Emballez la dans des sacs en plastique propres. La propolis peut être utilisée comme matière première pour la fabrication de cosmétiques, de pommades et de composants de médicaments.

Le pollen séché et la cire peuvent être conservés dans une pièce propre, fraîche et sèche pour éviter l’apparition de moisissures. Vous pouvez stocker le miel dans un récipient en verre ou de qualité alimentaire. Veillez à ce que les couvercles soient bien fermés.  Conservez le miel, le pollen, et la propolis à l'abri de la lumière du soleil.

Figure 8. Flocons de propolis/cérumen prêts pour le séchage  

   

©FAO/TECA

4. Zones agroécologiques

  • Tropicale, chaude. 

5. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Elevage de mélipones dans des ruches en coques de noix de coco: ID 10038.
  • Use of stingless bees for pollination: ID 8254.

Cette fiche technique est disponible en espagnol: ID 8671, et en anglais: ID 8265, La traduction a été réalisée par Beekeeping Network North-South (BNNS).

6. Objectifs poursuivis à travers ce projet

  • Favorables aux femmes;
  • L'efficacité de l'utilisation des ressources ; et
  • Pratique en faveur des pauvres.

2. La récolte de pollen 

Le pollen est manuellement séparé de ses pots à l’aide d’une tige de bambou propre ou une cuillère en acier inoxydable. Le pollen propre est ensuite étalé sur des plateaux grillagés et séché à l'air libre à l'ombre pour le protéger de la lumière du soleil. L’exposition directe au soleil noircira le pollen. Cela prendra environ 3 jours à sécher à l’air libre s’il fait beau et que la température ambiante se situe entre 30 et 33°C. 

A des fins commerciales, un hygromètre est utilisé pour mesurer la teneur en humidité du pollen La valeur standard pour l'humidité du pollen ne doit pas être supérieure à 6 pour cent. Le pollen séché s’effrite lorsqu’on le presse. Le cérumen et les pots sont coupés en petits morceaux et répartis uniformément sur des plateaux grillagés et séchés à l'air. Le pollen et le cérumen séchés sont alors placés dans des sacs en plastique de qualité alimentaire et scellés sous vide (si l'équipement est disponible).

Figure 4. Les pots à miel et à pollen à l’intérieur d’une coque de noix de coco   

©FAO/TECA

Figure 5. Le pollen que l’on retire de ses pots

©FAO/TECA

Figure 6. Le pollen retiré de ses pots

©FAO/TECA

3. La récolte de propolis

La propolis est récoltée en coupant des petits morceaux de propolis de 1 cm x 1 cm autour du nid, avec une distance de 6 cm entre les eux pour minimiser les dégâts dans le nid. La procédure peut être répétée après deux semaines lorsque les espaces ouverts ont été entièrement réparés. Portez ensuite des gants en caoutchouc ou en vinyle, pour nettoyer la propolis en enlevant les débris tels que la boue, les feuilles séchées et la sciure que les abeilles mélangent à la résine. 

Figure 7. Enlèvement de la propolis/cérumen de l'intérieur de la coque de la noix de coco

©FAO/TECA

Après le nettoyage, faites sécher la propolis à l’air libre pendant environ 3 jours. La propolis séchée est moins souple et relativement plus dure que celles fraîchement récoltées. Emballez la dans des sacs en plastique propres. La propolis peut être utilisée comme matière première pour la fabrication de cosmétiques, de pommades et de composants de médicaments.

Le pollen séché et la cire peuvent être conservés dans une pièce propre, fraîche et sèche pour éviter l’apparition de moisissures. Vous pouvez stocker le miel dans un récipient en verre ou de qualité alimentaire. Veillez à ce que les couvercles soient bien fermés.  Conservez le miel, le pollen, et la propolis à l'abri de la lumière du soleil.

Figure 8. Flocons de propolis/cérumen prêts pour le séchage  

   

©FAO/TECA

4. Zones agroécologiques

  • Tropicale, chaude. 

5. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Elevage de mélipones dans des ruches en coques de noix de coco: ID 10038.
  • Use of stingless bees for pollination: ID 8254.

Cette fiche technique est disponible en espagnol: ID 8671, et en anglais: ID 8265, La traduction a été réalisée par Beekeeping Network North-South (BNNS).

6. Objectifs poursuivis à travers ce projet

  • Favorables aux femmes;
  • L'efficacité de l'utilisation des ressources ; et
  • Pratique en faveur des pauvres.

records.title: Knowledge transfer and practical learning/training model (s) in Africa
records.description:
Description

The Science and Technology Backyard (STB) model, developed by the China Agricultural University (CAU) in China in 2009, allows the scientific community to connect with the farming community to facilitate information exchange and innovation. It is a participatory approach, bringing researchers and community members into a collaborative, research context-specific environment. It addresses specific practical problems and provides a unique methodology that can effectively address some of the challenges facing the farmers and agri-food actors in rural areas.

Though the STB model has been successfully working in China, it has not been tested in African countries. Yet, projects similar to STB have been implemented in the African countries to encourage knowledge exchange between students and rural communities to enhance the uptake of innovation and the latest scientific expertise to improve sustainable agricultural production and rural livelihoods. These projects can provide essential insights, experiences, and lessons to determine which outlining conditions and factors must be considered. At the same time, facilitating exchanges between students/young researchers and rural communities in Africa using a community-based model for knowledge transfer and, training and learning.

One such community-based model includes the community-based field attachments programme (CFAPA) implemented in 2018 by the Regional Universities Forum for Capacity Building in Agriculture (RUFORUM) with the support of the FAO’s Partnerships Division. The CFAPA programme facilitates placements of students from RUFORUM member universities in the rural communities to apply and disseminate their research findings in the field and share knowledge and expertise with local farmers and rural institutions. This practice summarizes the program’s objectives, the application process, outputs, outcomes and activities while providing guidance for the successful linking up of rural communities and students/youth for knowledge exchange and transmission of innovation, which can be a part of the implementation of knowledge transfer projects and programmes to develop the capacities of the youth in Africa.

1. The Community-Based Field Attachment Award (CFAPA)

In 2018, FAO’s Partnership Division, in collaboration with Regional Universities Forum for Capacity Building in Agriculture (RUFORUM), implemented a six-month competitive grants student placement programme for graduate students from African agricultural universities - The Community-Based Field Attachment Award (CFAPA) programme. RUFORUM is a consortium of 126 African universities operating within 38 countries spanning the African continent. The consortium works to strengthen students’ capacities to contribute to sustainable agricultural development, building the resilience of sustainable small-scale agriculture, improving livelihoods, food security, and reducing rural poverty in Africa. The goal is to ensure that the next generation of agriculture specialists and scientists from Africa are innovative, understand rural realities and are committed to improving poverty levels in their countries.

The CFAPA program was designed as a graduate student placement in rural communities to apply, scale-out and disseminate students’ research findings, which can contribute to the sustainability and resilience of small-scale agriculture, improve livelihoods and reduce rural poverty.

The first pilot programme was implemented in 2018. Ten students (five male and five female) graduate students were selected to implement field projects from RUFORUM member universities from:

  • Benin
  • Uganda
  • Kenya
  • Lesotho.

The students’ project proposals covered:

  • animal health management;
  • livestock and crop production;
  • marketing; and
  • nutrition issues.

For six months, students, while based in the communities, interacted with local farmers to share their academic work, exchange knowledge and develop innovative solutions for enhancing nutrition and food security. It aimed to improve sustainable agriculture and livestock production practices, strengthening collaborations along local food-value chains for rural income generation.

With their professors’ guidance as mentors, they worked with:

  • farmers
  • traders
  • farmer associations
  • government agencies
  • ural institutions. 

Through this local engagement, students received feedback from communities on their specific research areas. Students also developed their practical skills to apply their research findings in their development-related field projects and generate innovative solutions. 

1.1 CFAPA objectives

The CFAPA program operated based on the following two main objectives:

  1. Focus on diversified and expanded partnerships and advocacy, increased public awareness, political support and resources, and enhanced capacity development and knowledge management.
  2. Provide a mechanism and model to develop the RUFORUM students’ practical skills necessary to work with agricultural development related initiatives and engage with local communities, through it to facilitate the students learning and transfer of knowledge from FAO major themes and to strengthen the knowledge exchanges between the different actors, such as FAO, academia and local communities.

1.2 CFAPA criteria and application process

The programme has a well-established set of criteria and application processes (see Fig 1 and 2).

The criteria are:

applicants must have either recently concluded their studies or submitted their Master or a Ph.D. thesis;
the proposals need to address demand or challenge from the local communities;
support for the implementation of the projects from local organizations or communities be included in the proposal;
a letter of support from the student’s University is needed.

All applications are submitted online through the RUFORUM information management system (RIMS). Students had to submit:

  • a field project proposal;
  • a timeline for implementation;
  • the goal(s), objectives and methodology.

The proposals must demonstrate:

  • the student’s work with a rural community, show clearly what they want to achieve and how.
  • Present acceptance of their project by the target local community, thus ensuring that it reflects the community’s needs.
  • Identify a university supervisor to guide his/her work in the rural community and provide advice,

The RUFORUM personnel responsible for the programme provides overall coordination and supervision. Figures 1 and 2 below illustrate the CFAPA criteria and application process.

Figure 1. CFAPA criteria

©RUFORUM/FAO

Figure 2. CFAPA application process

©RUFORUM/FAO

In the first pilot programme, in 2018, the Community-Based Field Attachment Award programme (CFAPA) received 34 applications. Grants are awarded on a competitive basis by the RUFORUM Technical Committee. 

The application process was open to all RUFORUM previously funded students. This fund targets students who received scholarships from RUFORUM for their graduate studies and therefore were eligible for the call. Ten applications were successful under this CFAPA call.

To ensure the quality and feasibility of the proposals, Criteria for selection and ranking by the Technical Committee depended on several factors:

  • clear articulation of the purpose of the project proposals;
  • timeline for implementation, goal(s), objectives and methodology,
  • realistic timeline and achievable objectives;
  • clearly identified benefits for the rural community where the project will take place.

Preparation of proposals ensured students ‘ownership’ of their work with the rural community, show a clear idea of what they want to achieve and how. Students had to produce proof of acceptance of their project by the target local community, with the local community leaders, University supervisors, extension services and local governments, ensuring that the project reflects the community needs (see Annex I – case studies). Students had a budget of around 1 000 USD per month to cover their living, transportation costs and costs for fieldwork (i.e., organization of workshops, preparation of training materials, tools for technology demonstrations, etc.). The proper allocation of the budget was determinant for the full participation of students.

1.3 CFAPA outputs

By the end of the RUFORUM programme CFAPA student awardees were expected to have achieved the following deliverables which are showcased in Table 1 below.

Table 1. CFAPA Student awardee, the seven deliverables
CFAPA Student Awardee Deliverables
Deliverable 1

Monthly progress reports to the host institution/university supervisor.

To support the process of monitoring progress and provide a basis for RUFORUM to continuously engage with each student awardee and address specific contextual issues.
Deliverable 2 Provide a brief biodata with an outline of the career record of the student awardee - for RUFORUM.
Deliverable 3 FAO Newsletter at the end of the second month.
Deliverable 4 A one-page write-up of their experiences for the RUFORUM/FAO newsletters.
Deliverable 5 A policy brief generated from the implementation of activities during the CFAPA - submitted to the University and RUFORUM.
Deliverable 6

Submit at the end of the six months a CFAPA final report to RUFORUM. (Highlighting the field experiences and potential areas for further research and action and the CFAPA outcome). 

The reports should include evidence of:

  • that students were liaising both with their university supervisors and RUFORUM;
  • submission of monthly reports);
  • consultation on both technical and logistical matters during the project;
  • guidance and follow up from their supervisors;
  • methods and means to communicate the research results to local communities.
Deliverable 7

Produce ten-minute videos prepared by each student on the:

  • activities delivered under the community-based field placements; and
  • impacts on the local community.

Source: RUFORUM 2020

To disseminate their research results and promote innovative approaches, students targeted a wide range of stakeholders from rural communities, including:

  • farmers;
  • agricultural traders;
  • farmer associations;
  • community health institutions;
  • veterinary and extension services; and
  • rural community leaders, with a particular emphasis on women, youth and small-scale farmers.

Students organized a series of dissemination and outreach actions:

  • interactive workshops and training;
  • presentations; and
  • radio-shows.

These actions disseminated knowledge and encouraged dialogue at the rural community level to use  innovative methods to improve food security and nutrition, enhance sustainable food and agriculture practices and reduce rural poverty.

1.4 CFAPA outcomes

The CFAPA initiative implementation outcomes describe and evaluates the outcomes set for each of the three levels: the students, the rural community and FAO. Table 2 below highlights the outcomes and uses color scoring for the evaluation. The scoring is an average derived from:

  • the students’ information in their final reports;
  • their follow-up questionnaires; and
  • questionnaire feedback from RUFORUM.

In general, the outcomes fall between good and excellent. It is worth highlighting that the outcomes related to FAO scored well by both students and RUFORUM, indicating that there is still an opportunity to further increase the thematic coverage of the FAO topics and increase partnerships. On the other hand, the students have highlighted that policy support was fair. These scores are indicative but are excellent learning lessons for revising the follow-up CFAPA outcomes and processes.

Table 2. CFAPA initiative implementation outcomes
CFAPA initiative implementation outcomes Excellent Good Fair
Student outcomes        
Strengthen students’ practical skills in the application of their research results in the implementation of development-related projects and initiatives. It is necessary for the dissemination of good agricultural practices and innovative approaches to engage with local communities. Student feedback x    
RUFORUM feedback x    
Enhance students’ knowledge of prevailing traditional agricultural practices in rural areas and identified themes for future research reflecting rural community needs. Student feedback x    
RUFORUM feedback   x  
Strengthen students’ skills to communicate research results and develop practical field solutions applicable to address local issues related to food security, nutrition, sustainable agriculture, and rural poverty reduction.  Student feedback x    
RUFORUM feedback   x  
Enhance students’ capacity development, knowledge management, and transferable skills, such as networking, advocacy communication, leadership, teamwork, and entrepreneurship skills. In particular, students noted that the field attachment helped them build networks with various stakeholders for potential future exchanges, dissemination or employment opportunities. Student feedback   x  
RUFORUM feedback x    
Enhance the visibility and relevance of universities/academic community and strengthened knowledge exchanges on approaches for improving sustainable rural livelihoods between academia, farmers and other stakeholders, including local farmer organizations, traders, veterinary services and extension workers, rural community leaders, amongst others. RUFORUM feedback   x  

Source: RUFORUM 2020

1.5 CFAPA successes

The programme’s successful outcomes were highlighted in the individual student’s final reports and feedback from RUFORUM. Table 3 and 4 shows a summary of the key successes they noted. 

Table 3. CFAPA successes based on students and RUFORUM feedbacks
CFAPA successes based on students and RUFORUM feedbacks                    
Students feedback RUFORUM feedback
Students Farmers Students Farmers
Learned how to chair meetings, demonstrations and put in practice their research. Programmed raised farmers awareness of issues The selection process was smooth, The communities were appreciative of the student’s projects
Were able to reach out easily to local government officials and mobilize farmers to attend workshops and meetings. Farmers learned faster through demonstration and visuals. No issues encountered during the selection
Improved their costing and budgeting skills and learned  about grant management Communities expressed clearly the issues to the students with face to face contact. RUFORUM has a robust student evaluation system Appreciated the role that’s students played in disseminating technologies and innovations and management practices
Keen to continue with the proposed evaluation tool and follow up An increase in women’s involvement, as workshop and meeting attendance, was greatly comprised of female communities. Good communication between the supervisors and the students.
Excellent communication and engagement between students and supervisors.

Source: RUFORUM 2020

In its feedback, RUFORUM stated that the 2018 CFAPA programme’s overall feedback was good and has provided many reflection points:

  • Firstly, on the benefit that working with the students at the community level can deliver.
  • Second, the need to reconsider some design aspects within the CFAPA model to allow for greater infusion and integration of the fellow at the community level for a longer time;
  • The perception that communities have of the universities is beginning to shift positively.

The CFAPA programme’s ten student awardees also encountered challenges during their six-month practice. These were derived and synthesized directly from the students’ experiences, highlighted in their final reports and from the questionnaires sent to them to fill out. It also includes feedback from RUFORUM staff.

Table 4. Challenges of the CFAPA programme – student feedback
CFAPA challenges encountered
Participation
  • Lack of attendance.
  • Inadequate environment - rural village noise, disruption, remote access, etc.
Finance
  • Low budget – unable to provide villages with tools to advance the training into practices.
  • Financial difficulties - the grant was only issued to students at the end of the study.
  • Village expectations of handouts.
  • Lack of University Human Resources support.
In the field
  • Limited assistance in training and communication between researchers and farmers.
  • Working with farmers where extension services were poor was difficult for students.
  • Expectations were too high for some community members, which hindered their full participation in the training.
  • Low access to the internet.
Time frame
  • The six month period is insufficient to fully implement all the recommendations the students may have proposed to the villages.
  • Studies and research time management was difficult.

Source: RUFORUM 2020

2. Recommendations or lessons learned for improving and scaling-up knowledge transfer and practical training models in Africa

The CFAPA programme can provide instrumental and valuable insight into tailoring knowledge transfer and training models to develop practical skills for the African context.

While far from being a full-fledged model, insights from partners like RUFORUM can be precious in leveraging academia and other local stakeholders in the region to further develop this initiative.

From the application process to the on-the-ground activities, specific steps will need to be followed to successfully implement Africa’s model.
To increase the likelihood of this model’s success, the inclusion of the recommendations proposed by the CFAPA students in their final reports and questionnaires (Figure 5) should be considered.

2.1 Summary of key recommendations

For the successful implementation of the model scale-up in Africa, key recommendations from students included:

  • improved financial provision, through an appropriate funding modality - private Sector/University, partnerships with government – University…);
  • language and cultural awareness;
  • context-specific adaptation of tools and demonstrations;
  • increased supervision and follow-up by supervisors and professors;
  • the establishment of monitoring and evaluation procedures;
  • incentives for long-term students based in rural areas; and
  • increased FAO involvement through the development of a mentorship scheme or a results communication follows up. 

2.2 RUFORUM key recommendations

Based on the 2018 programme’s student feedback and their 2019 questionnaire feedback, there is a need to identify ways to address the programme’s issues and challenges to be up-scaled into the STB model. RUFORUM provided recommendations and actions to take going forward.

  • Enhance the role played by the Community Based Supervisors/Extension workers.
  • Extend the period to one year of implementation, with the first six months being probationary and assess their performance. For the remaining six months, the fellow receives a contract as a Community Based Agricultural Advisor (Village Based Agricultural Advisor).
  • Internally at the RUFORUM Secretariat is to readjust the budget framework to support the community-based supervisor.
  • Increase the budget beyond the current amount to instead fund fewer studentsrather  than many for more significant impact.
  • Strengthen orientation of the CFAPA grantees and catalyze experience and lesson learning, including face to face meeting sessions.

2.2.1 RUFORFUM detailed suggestions

As a result of the experience and lessons learned from the pilot programme’s implementation and its general key recommendations, RUFORUM provided more specific and detailed suggestions regarding incentives, measures and financial guidance for students, reduction of cultural barriers, and increased FAO role.

Increase financial support

What incentives need to be put in place to increase university and government financial support for Africa model implementation.
  • Continuous reports/ sensitization about benefits-protracted effort to inform people about the model to integrate in programmes at individual and community levels.
  • Scholarships to support the field attachments and activities during the second and third year.
  • Co-funding / counterpart resource for the model by key actors.
  • echnical assistance with counterpart funding to promote adoption of the model.
  • Existence of University or other government institution programmes where the model could be anchored, such as extension services.
Measures Key measures that can provide students with financial guidance in using the finances and resources available.
  • Integrate general project management training as part of CFAPA project orientation, which should include financial management in projects. This will not only be important for the success of the CFAPA but also build the capacity of the students to be better financial managers.
  • As already integrated into the CFAPAs, quarterly financial reporting should be integrated where the project managers, for example, at RUFORUM review students’ financial reports and provide feedback.
  • Include a contractual clause that “all expenditures must be those included in the work plan approved by the funder. Any other expenditure not included in the plan must be approved before incurred” or a “No Objection” requirement for expenditure.
Overcoming cultural barriers How can cultural and language barriers be reduced when students interact with other cultural /language university professors and students.
  • Provide basic culture and language orientation to African students participating in the projects. This could be done through co-current language and culture lessons when they are having their technical training.
  • African students participating in the project should be integrated at the host universities in the countries of assignments. This will enable African students to interact with other students and shorten the cultural emersion time in the University.
  • Organize a culture week/days when students showcase their cultures to allow better appreciation and integration.
  • Establish (if not present) a culture and psycho-social support office with staff and activities to help students adapt to the culture and language and reduce missing home thoughts.
Incentives for students Incentives for students to remain in their rural areas for an extended period.
  • Allow students to identify and work on a problem of their technical interest or careers they want to pursue after their studies. This will motivate them to gain more knowledge about the problem and identify the solutions which make them experts in the field.
  • Allow students to work in communities where they come from, especially for students who have grown up in rural areas because it motivates them to contribute to their community.
  • Provide basic necessities such as accommodation, local transportation, food and funds for meetings such as food for participants, etc.
  • Place the students in farming families to act as demonstration nodes for other farmers in the community.
How FAO’s involvement can be increased in its role in the STB Africa model.
  • FAO could focus on full knowledge documentation and publication of outputs from the model in a non-academic form such as policy briefs, newsletters as advocacy tools for model integration at national agricultural innovation systems
  • Since FAO has leverage at national and continental levels, it will help mobilize policy-makers to integrate the model and its outputs into a national agricultural innovation system.
  • FAO can provide technical support to the overall implementation of the programme’s field level activities in Africa.
  • Through enhanced partnerships and collaboration with the South-South and Triangular Cooperation Division.
  • FAO could further broker partnerships with development partners to implement field-based pilots of models in Africa within the same time of the CAU’s Africa-STB Master Programme that could inform and support the setting up of the STBs.
Follow-up measures Following the completion of the three years, RUFORUM recommended the need for follow-up measures.
  • Work with central and local governments to integrate the model in their programmes based on the initiatives’ outputs and outcomes.
  • Monitoring, evaluation of the impact of the project on all the beneficiaries, including students (skills gained and their sustainability). communities (change caused by the work of students and how to sustain it beyond the three years), universities (difference it is making on the proficiency of professors to effectively work with communities and supervise students in community setting, and how this model is being integrated into the university student training, research and outreach agenda).
  • Document the project’s outputs and outcomes and widely publicize within the participating institutions for adoption and with policy-makers for integration into a National Agricultural Innovation System. 

Engage in resource mobilization to scale-out and scale-up the knowledge transfer and learning/training modules in Africa.

2.3 Summary of African knowledge transfer and learning/training model implementation

For the African knowledge transfer and learning/training module implementation success, Table 5 summarizes the consideration and recommendations drawn from the pilot project for each step in the updated design plan of the transfer model to Africa, including the students’ recommendations.

Table 5. The updated design plan of the transfer model to Africa
Talent training processes Student recommendations from the CFAPA programme RUFORUM recommendations from the CFAPA programme Outcomes
STEP 1- Selection criteria of candidates

Key criteria for applicants:

  • hold a Bachelors’ degree;
  • hold a Major in agronomy;
  • are 30 years old or less;
  • hold African nationality; and
  • be willing to work in Africa.

Criteria from the CFAPA programme should also be taken into consideration (see Table 2)
  • When applying to the programme, proper documentation, dissemination planning, and uptake evaluation should be mandatory.
  • Transport costs, research funding from both tutors, and the cost of living for African students in Africa need to be calculated.
  • Provide an initial sum from the grant (e.g., 30-40 percent) to facilitate travel and preparation.
  • Establish a reimbursement procedure (e.g., two installments).
  • Ensure the grant is sufficient enough to cover all necessary expenses. Values need to be revised according to the student’s placement.
  • Provide incentives for increased university and government support, which is lacking in a number of African countries.

Widen the program to include studying adoption techniques and uptake information disseminated to the communities after the end of the programme.
  • Build capacity among university graduates and senior academics, guiding the Master’s fellows in conceptualizing non-technical projects. This could be achieved through a joint orientation of the CFAPA fellows in the subsequent roll-outs. Currently, RUFORUM has considered a remote engagement but with funding available with a physical orientation.
  • RUFORUM has taken into account that the six-month period is insufficient to fully implement all the recommendations the students’ may have proposed to the villages. RUFORUM has considered that the CFAPA if restructured, could be extended to one year or at least two years depending on funds availability.

RUFORUM recognized that financial difficulties were encountered since the grant was only issued to students at the end of the study. By design of the CFAPA, these are awarded at the end of the research projects. In reference to CFAPA itself, the delays sometimes arise because of delay of submission of workplans and budgets due to students’ limited capacity to prepare quality work plans and budgets. RUFORUM suggests that this could be solved by initiating this process early enough to allow them to learn and train them on work planning and budgeting as part of orientation.
  • Tailored technology for farmers
  • Push the change of agricultural development
  • Empowerment of smallholder farmers
  • Trained high-level talent for Africa.
STEP 2- First year

The first year comprises of learning at the CAU:

  • six months of theory learning at CAU; and
  • six months staying in an STB.
  • Tools for demonstrations need to be locally adapted (e.g., costs of transport, materials, etc.).
  • Particular attention to languages and cultural differences will also need to be taken into account.
  • Create incentives and attractive conditions for students to be based in rural areas for extended periods of time.
  • RUFORUM recognized that there was limited assistance in training and communication between researchers and farmers and the students and academic staff. It has now instituted a process to strengthen students’ communication capacity and write development reports through the technical backstopping of its knowledge management and communication officers.
  • Working with farmers where extension service was poor and difficult for students, RUFORUM recommended that students always consult with the local extension service before working with farmers. Farmers tend to have a more trusting relationship with extension workers.
  • Regarding the issue of high expectations that hindered participation, RUFORUM is considering restructuring the engagement model with the farmers to re-orient the level of engagement.
  
STEP 3- Second and third years

Activities conducted in the second and third years are listed below.

  • Conduct technology innovation and knowledge transfer in Africa.
  • Living in rural areas.
  • Co-supervision of the students.
  • Local supervisors help the students to finish the experiment and training.
  • The Chinese supervisor should go to Africa regularly.
  • Cooperation with Chinese or international enterprises
  • Supervisors from CN and Africa help students finish their thesis.
  • Village eagerness to learn, flexibility and open-mindedness.
  • Need more training, more sensitization and more assistance with training (e.g., supervisor attendance, professor follow-ups).
  • Students expressed a determination to follow up and go back to give further training and presentations to the villages. A monitoring and evaluation procedure should be installed either locally or remotely.
  • Improve university human resources support by informing and involving them in the programme.
  • Increase FAO involvement through the development of a mentorship scheme or establishing results- communication follow-up.
  • RUFORUM recognized village lack of attendance, which was exacerbated by the proliferation of development based organizations, especially those operating emergency programmes that pay hefty sitting allowances for participants.
  • RUFORUM is proposing a Community Based Agricultural Advisors (Village Based Agricultural Advisors) with a unique budget framework to strengthen greater integration at the community to enhance mobilization for knowledge for uptake is an alternative direction.
    • Additionally, RUFORUM is exploring the creation of a possible window of CFAPA fellows after their attachment to Community Agricultural Based Advisors to reinvigorate the strained agricultural extension delivery systems in many of the African agricultural communities. The CFAPA fellows would work for additional six months with a relatively raised stipend value as a formal short-term employment contract.  
  • RUFORUM also recognized that there were no adequate environments for training, arising from the places where the students tended to organize the sessions. It has advised students to host the trainings in farmer homesteads and taking into consideration the work calendar of farmers as well as gender considerations.
  • RUFORUM acknowledged the issues of low budget. In the current framework of the CFAPA, the budget is aligned to taking care of the dissemination materials. However, the farmers require more inputs and consideration for purposes of facilitating uptake of technologies, innovations and management practices.
  • For example, if the student is disseminating bean varieties for example, the farmers require to go beyond the experimental/demonstration seed but to receive the actual seeds which they can plant.
  • The current budgets do not accommodate this kind of costs.
  

Source: RUFORUM 2020

Annex I. CFAPA case studies

Annex I. includes summary descriptions of the ten CFAPA students’ case studies, taken from the students’ project reports.

List of the ten approved CFAPA projects.

  1. Gastrointestinal parasites (GIPs) in Angora goats and their control methods
  2. Increasing farmers and traders’ awareness about aflatoxin contamination and its control strategies for enhanced groundnut productivity in eastern Uganda
  3. Disseminating the MSc findings by sensitizing the cattle keeping communities of Gweri County in Soroti on Fascioliasis outbreaks in cattle and demonstrate some control measures.
  4. Promoting utilization of millet-sesame-soy complimentary food composite to prevent undernutrition amongst children 6-23 months old in Amuru and Nwoya districts rural Benin
  5. Improvement of traditional, complementary foods to meet minimum nutrients requirement for children aged six months to five years
  6. The promotion of the consumption of sorghum porridge dual fortified with moringa leaf powder and baobab fruit pulp among under five-year-old children in rural Benin
  7. Stakeholder engagement and sensitization on best practices to maximize on rabbit production in central Kenya through effective treatment and control of coccidiosis
  8. Farmer’s training on different control measures and prevalence of gastrointestinal parasites of Merino sheep in Lesotho
  9. Sustainable multiplication of improved common bean seed in favour of smallholder farmers of Buhimba and Kiziranfumbi sub-county Hoima district, Uganda
  10. Increasing commercialization and profitability of indigenous chicken production through innovation platforms in Omoro district, Northern Uganda

Case study 1 – Uganda

Increasing commercialization and profitability of indigenous chicken production through innovation platforms in Omoro district, Northern Uganda

Aryemo Irene Penninah, a Gulu University student in Uganda, wrote her Master’s thesis on “Commercialization and profitability of indigenous chicken production.” She was awarded a CFAPA grant to disseminate her research findings and train local chicken innovation platform members in the Omoro district.  Ms. Penninah chose her research area based on the selection of her Masters - ‘Master of Science in Agri-enterprises Development.’

During her university research, she learned about several issues that have had a negative impact on the commercialization of chicken production in the area, including poor management of chickens that lead to high mortality rates, lack of understanding amongst farmers how food value chains function and limited relations between different actors along local agri-food value chains.

To increase commercialization and profitability of chicken production, Ms. Penninah trained local farmers on:

  • strategies to increase flock size;
  • enhance chicken management practices;
  • explain about production and marketing activities to increase farmers’ incomes;
  • organize activities to inform rural communities how to keep the innovation platform alive through the facilitation of business to business linkages amongst different actors along the chicken production value chain.

Ms. Penninah disseminated her research results to the rural community by:

  • mobilizing farmers using innovation platforms;
  • undertaking trainings; and
  • a copy of her research findings and recommendations were given to the agricultural officer, veterinary officer and the community development officer for the Bobi and Lalogi sub-counties.
Table 6. The success of research uptake by the rural community
Situation before uptake Situation after uptake

Poor management of chicken that lead to high mortality rates.

The majority of the farmers were not vaccinating their indigenous chickens hence many were dying due to New Castle Disease, Fowl typhoid and fowl pox.
  • Overall, increased commercialization and profitability of chicken production, enhanced chicken management practices and increased farmers’ incomes through facilitation of business to business linkages amongst different actors along the chicken production value chain.
  • After the training and formation of vaccination groups to lower the cost of vaccination, there was an increase in the number of people vaccinating their chickens, as reported by the veterinary officer.

Lack of understanding amongst farmers how food value chains function.

Most farmers were selling their chickens individually at giveaway prices because of their vulnerability and low bargaining power.
  • Through the training and innovation platforms, farmers formed marketing groups to sell their chickens in large numbers and at a good price. However, this requires commitment and patience and it is a process, so the adoption process is a bit slow.

Poor record-keeping and limited relations between different actors along local agri-food value chains in Uganda.

None of the farmers were keeping records of expenses and income from the indigenous chicken sales. They never took it as a business venture but rather something to give them emergency funds.
  • After training on record-keeping, Ms. Penninah asked farmers to keep simple records that were easy to understand and they were able to track expenses and income. She was able to view record books for some of them and provide guidance.

Source: RUFORUM 2020

Figure 3. A training session in Lalogi sub-county

©RUFORUM/FAO

Case study 2 – Benin

The promotion of the consumption of sorghum porridge dual fortified with moringa leaf powder and baobab fruit pulp among under five-year-old children in rural Benin

Student Marius Affonfere of the University of Abomey-Calavi, Benin, through the CFAPA award program, trained mothers on dual fortification of under five-year-olds on preparing sorghum porridge with moringa leaf powder and baobab fruit pulp. This was to prevent child malnourishment. He identified his research area through literature review and experience from local populations and nutrition stakeholders. He also trained resource persons of key nutrition institutions on sorghum porridge's dual fortification with moringa leaf powder and baobab fruit pulp. Home follow-up visits were also conducted to analyze child response to porridge consumption.

In sum, his dissemination methods were the following:

  • meeting with the under five-year-old children mothers;
  • culinary demonstrations with the under five-year-old children mothers;
  • meeting with resource persons; an
  • home visit follow-ups of the under five-year old children for 15 days.
Table 7. The success of research uptake by the rural community
Situation before uptake Situation after uptake

Poor practices.

The rural populations did not apply the dual food fortification with moringa leaf powder and baobab fruit pulp.

 After the training and culinary demonstrations, mothers produced the dual fortified fermented sorghum ogi porridge. 92 percent of the targeted mothers successfully applied the flow diagram for processing fermented sorghum ogi porridge dually fortified with moringa leaf powder and baobab fruit pulp.

Low consumption

The under five-year-old children did not consume the sorghum ogi porridge dual food fortified with moringa leaf powder and baobab fruit pulp.

 85 percent of the under-five-years old children consumed the dual food fortified porridge at least once a day during the fifteen (15) days of the home visit follow-up.

Poor training

The nutrition agents were not trained on the dual food fortification using moringa leaf powder and baobab fruit pulp

 Thirty resource persons from Nutritional Recuperation Center, Social Promotion Center, GiZ, PMASN, i.e. «Programme Multisectoriel de l’Alimentation, de la Santé et de la Nutrition», BORNEfondern, Territorial Agency of Agricultural Development (ATDA) were sensitized about the health benefit of the dual food fortified fermented sorghum ogi porridge. They were also trained on how to fortify porridge with moringa leaf powder and baobab fruit pulp.

Source: RUFORUM 2020

Following the end of the CFAPA programme, Mr. Affonfere continued research through his ongoing Ph.D. thesis. He also had the opportunity to work in the same area of his CFAPA implementation location. He visited the program beneficiaries on how they applied the information they received through this program. Click here to watch the video.

Case study 3 – Benin

Promoting utilization of millet-sesame-soy complimentary food composite to prevent undernutrition amongst children 6-23 months old in Amuru and Nwoya districts rural Benin

Prossy Nassanga, a Gulu University student in Uganda, conducted training in the Amuru and Nwoya districts (Benin) on the dangers of not adhering to the recommended complementary feeding practices, how to make complimentary food from millet, sesame and soy composite. Ms. Prossy identified her research area based on the fact that the two districts had the highest rates of undernutrition in Acholi sub-region according to the food and nutrition security status assessment report by WFP, 2012.

The results were first disseminated to the district officials in Amuru and Nwoya. Later these were distributed to selected leaders at the sub-county level. After this, the community members’ mobilization from villages was chosen randomly through their local leaders. Meetings were organized to give information on the study, followed by training on infant and young child feeding practices and the dangers of not adhering to recommended complementary feeding practices. The participants were briefed about the available option of using locally available foodstuff such as millet, sesame and soy to design complementary foods at the household level. This was followed by hands-on training on preparing complementary food using millet, sesame and soybeans as ingredients. Lastly, there was a follow-up evaluation of the exercise.

The meetings were attended mostly by women (86.8 percent). 97.4 percent of the respondents liked the idea of the University of working with the community and identified some community challenges for research.

Table 8. The success of research uptake by the rural community
Situation before uptake Situation after uptake
People did not know that they could use the foods that are produced in their households and blend them into different combinations to produce nutritious composite formulae for their children. People appreciated the use of locally available foods to produce nutritious foods for their children.
People in the community did not appreciate cheap and affordable foods as nutritious foods. For instance, for silverfish, some people thought that it was for poor people. People in the community appreciated the cheap and affordable foods as nutritious foods for their children. For instance, silverfish, simsim, and millet among other foods.
The community did not know that some foods needed special treatment like roasting to remove certain anti-nutritional factors and also improve the bioavailability of certain nutrients. Additionally, there were knowledge and practice gaps in complementary feeding. The community appreciated certain processing technologies like roasting to improve the bioavailability of nutrients and remove certain anti-nutritional factors. There was an improvement in the knowledge and practices regarding complementary feeding.

Source: RUFORUM 2020

Following the CFAPA programme end, Ms. Prossy met a few of the caregivers that were trained and asked them about the progress in the use of the product. Some reported using the product once in a while. Others reported not using the product because of the difficulties accessing soya, which is one of the ingredients. Ms.  Prossy did this follow up because she wanted to know if the communities were integrating this Millet-Sesame-Soy composite into their household nutrition to prevent child undernutrition. If not so, she wanted to know what the challenges were and what would be the possible options to address them.

Figure 4. Participants attending one of the training in Kalang Village Koch Goma sub-county, Nwoya district

©RUFORUM/FAO

Case study 4 – Kenya

Stakeholders engagement and sensitization on best practices to maximize rabbit production in central Kenya through effective treatment and control of coccidiosis

Student Kennedy Ogolla received a CFAPA award to train rabbit farmers on best rabbit management practices (feeding, housing, and breeding) to promote Kenya's rabbit production. Mr. Ogolla identified his research area because he developed an interest while doing his undergraduate studies. He guided farmers on management practices from housing, breeding, feeding, cleaning and maintain hygiene, biosecurity and biosafety. Farmers were also informed about the most common rabbit diseases and how to prevent or treat them. Farmers responded positively, were open-minded, and expressed appreciation for new knowledge and skillset. It was noted that farmers were best taught through demonstrations and visual aids.

Mr. Ogolla summarized his results in easy to understand training manuals and held training sessions with farmers in the rural areas in Kiambu and Nyeri counties. He also organized on-farm demonstrations in selected model farms where he trained the farmers on the best rabbit production practices. He also held a stakeholder forum at the University of Nairobi where he facilitated farmers' attendance and presented his results. Mr Ogolla further prepared a summarized copy of his study results. He printed his published peer-reviewed papers, which he shared with local leaders and representatives of the rabbit farmers for their easy access.

Table 9. The success of research uptake by the rural community
Situation before uptake Situation after uptake
Farmers were using an herbal concoction of aloe Vera and other plants to treat coccidiosis. Farmers adopted the use of conventional drugs such as ESB3, Amprolium and Biotrim to treat coccidiosis.
Farmers were waiting until the rabbits presented symptoms before treating them instead of introducing prevention measures. Farmers had very limited knowledge of biosafety, biosecurity and hygienic practices, which are key in preventing rabbit diseases. Farmers started focusing on prevention measures and instituted strict biosecurity and biosafety measures. Some even appropriately constructed designed rabbit houses.
Stocking rates were low. Most farmers were producing for subsistence consumption and didn’t view it as an income-generating enterprise. Stocking numbers increased, the production commercialized increased by most farmers who organized themselves in groups to access and meet the market's higher demands.

Source: RUFORUM 2020

Following the CFAPA programme's end, Mr Ogolla made follow-up on the model farms to see how they were faring. He also visited farmers who invited him to offer advice and even provided structure designs for other rabbit farmers.

Two other case studies – example provided by RUFORUM

1. Gastrointestinal parasites (GIPs) in Angora goats and their control methods.
Table 10. The success of research uptake by the rural community
Situation before uptake Situation after uptake
High gastrointestinal parasites prevalence in small ruminants in Lesotho owing to poor management of goats and sheep by smallholder farmers Adoption of management practices for the control of gastrointestinal parasites, in particular, integrated parasite management, as part of holistic management strategies.

Source: RUFORUM 2020

2. Sustainable multiplication of improved common bean seed in favour of smallholder farmers of Buhimba and Kiziranfumbi sub-county Hoima district, Uganda.
Table 11. The success of research uptake by the rural community
Situation before uptake Situation after uptake
Poor common bean seed production for smallholder farmers in South Africa. Adoption and multiplication of improved beans aimed at climate change adaptation improved farmers’ perception and awareness levels about climate change and the adoption of improved and drought-tolerant seed varieties.

Source: RUFORUM 2020

RUFORUM has pointed out that CFAPA fellows explored all possible avenues to get the message of their projects to the communities beyond those they directly worked with during their research project phase. They highlighted that while raising awareness was the first step to the empowerment of rural subsistence communities. It is persistence and continued investment into these processes that would lead to significant technology uptake.

RUFORUM wants to further pursue down this avenue and seek to move beyond dissemination to catalyzing the adoption of the technologies, innovations, and management practices.

RUFORUM specified that for all the case studies, follow-up activities for the 2018 CFAPA program were undertaken, such as:

  • Routine reporting for every CFAPA grantee mid-stream of the implementation.
  • Reporting at the end of the CFAPA period.
  • Field-based supervision by University supervisors.
  • Visits to the field sites where implementation took place (this was marginal but was much appreciated and recognized as a practice that the RUFORUM needs to increase).

Annex II. Scaling and comparisons of various models

In addition to including CFAPA recommendations for successful future scaling, this work also undertook comparative literature of different models (Table 6.).

For the successful implementation of the model scale-up in Africa, specific recommendations include:

  • improved financial provision;
  • language and cultural awareness;
  • context-specific adaptation of tools and demonstrations;
  • increased supervision and follow-up by supervisors and professors;
  • the establishment of monitoring and evaluation procedures;
  • incentives creation for long-term students base in rural areas;
  • increased FAO involvement through the development of a mentorship scheme or results communication follows up.

4. Validation of the practice

The practice was validated and applied in different African countries (Uganda, Kenya, Lesotho, Benin). The output products, which consisted of student findings and rural community feedback, provided proper validation of the practice.

5. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

The necessary conditions are highlighted in the criteria sections of this document.

Limiting factors included costs and some obstacles in communication with rural communities.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Women-friendly

The practice empowers smallholder farmers, especially women and contributes to education, gender equality.

8.2 Resource use efficiency

CFAPAs facilitate knowledge sharing and efficient usage of technologies and practices.

8.3 Pro-poor technology

Through the use of new agricultural techniques and an increase in knowledge sharing, rural communities are able to increase their yields, thus guaranteeing a higher food source and source of income generation. The practice is also adaptable in different countries and contexts.

_annotations.body:
Knowledge transfer and practical learning/training model (s) in Africa

In Africa, agricultural Gross Domestic Product (GDP) accounts for more than 20 percent of the total GDP. The farmers’ income is mainly from the farming industry, and it accounts for more than 80 percent of total household income. However, despite Africa’s plentiful agricultural resources, the continent still faces serious food security issues. In many African countries, government and infrastructure tend to be weak and poor. Many rural communities also do not have access to electricity (internet, landlines, etc.), making knowledge transfer difficult when using digital resources. 



Description

The Science and Technology Backyard (STB) model, developed by the China Agricultural University (CAU) in China in 2009, allows the scientific community to connect with the farming community to facilitate information exchange and innovation. It is a participatory approach, bringing researchers and community members into a collaborative, research context-specific environment. It addresses specific practical problems and provides a unique methodology that can effectively address some of the challenges facing the farmers and agri-food actors in rural areas.

Though the STB model has been successfully working in China, it has not been tested in African countries. Yet, projects similar to STB have been implemented in the African countries to encourage knowledge exchange between students and rural communities to enhance the uptake of innovation and the latest scientific expertise to improve sustainable agricultural production and rural livelihoods. These projects can provide essential insights, experiences, and lessons to determine which outlining conditions and factors must be considered. At the same time, facilitating exchanges between students/young researchers and rural communities in Africa using a community-based model for knowledge transfer and, training and learning.

One such community-based model includes the community-based field attachments programme (CFAPA) implemented in 2018 by the Regional Universities Forum for Capacity Building in Agriculture (RUFORUM) with the support of the FAO’s Partnerships Division. The CFAPA programme facilitates placements of students from RUFORUM member universities in the rural communities to apply and disseminate their research findings in the field and share knowledge and expertise with local farmers and rural institutions. This practice summarizes the program’s objectives, the application process, outputs, outcomes and activities while providing guidance for the successful linking up of rural communities and students/youth for knowledge exchange and transmission of innovation, which can be a part of the implementation of knowledge transfer projects and programmes to develop the capacities of the youth in Africa.

1. The Community-Based Field Attachment Award (CFAPA)

In 2018, FAO’s Partnership Division, in collaboration with Regional Universities Forum for Capacity Building in Agriculture (RUFORUM), implemented a six-month competitive grants student placement programme for graduate students from African agricultural universities - The Community-Based Field Attachment Award (CFAPA) programme. RUFORUM is a consortium of 126 African universities operating within 38 countries spanning the African continent. The consortium works to strengthen students’ capacities to contribute to sustainable agricultural development, building the resilience of sustainable small-scale agriculture, improving livelihoods, food security, and reducing rural poverty in Africa. The goal is to ensure that the next generation of agriculture specialists and scientists from Africa are innovative, understand rural realities and are committed to improving poverty levels in their countries.

The CFAPA program was designed as a graduate student placement in rural communities to apply, scale-out and disseminate students’ research findings, which can contribute to the sustainability and resilience of small-scale agriculture, improve livelihoods and reduce rural poverty.

The first pilot programme was implemented in 2018. Ten students (five male and five female) graduate students were selected to implement field projects from RUFORUM member universities from:

  • Benin
  • Uganda
  • Kenya
  • Lesotho.

The students’ project proposals covered:

  • animal health management;
  • livestock and crop production;
  • marketing; and
  • nutrition issues.

For six months, students, while based in the communities, interacted with local farmers to share their academic work, exchange knowledge and develop innovative solutions for enhancing nutrition and food security. It aimed to improve sustainable agriculture and livestock production practices, strengthening collaborations along local food-value chains for rural income generation.

With their professors’ guidance as mentors, they worked with:

  • farmers
  • traders
  • farmer associations
  • government agencies
  • ural institutions. 

Through this local engagement, students received feedback from communities on their specific research areas. Students also developed their practical skills to apply their research findings in their development-related field projects and generate innovative solutions. 

1.1 CFAPA objectives

The CFAPA program operated based on the following two main objectives:

  1. Focus on diversified and expanded partnerships and advocacy, increased public awareness, political support and resources, and enhanced capacity development and knowledge management.
  2. Provide a mechanism and model to develop the RUFORUM students’ practical skills necessary to work with agricultural development related initiatives and engage with local communities, through it to facilitate the students learning and transfer of knowledge from FAO major themes and to strengthen the knowledge exchanges between the different actors, such as FAO, academia and local communities.

1.2 CFAPA criteria and application process

The programme has a well-established set of criteria and application processes (see Fig 1 and 2).

The criteria are:

applicants must have either recently concluded their studies or submitted their Master or a Ph.D. thesis;
the proposals need to address demand or challenge from the local communities;
support for the implementation of the projects from local organizations or communities be included in the proposal;
a letter of support from the student’s University is needed.

All applications are submitted online through the RUFORUM information management system (RIMS). Students had to submit:

  • a field project proposal;
  • a timeline for implementation;
  • the goal(s), objectives and methodology.

The proposals must demonstrate:

  • the student’s work with a rural community, show clearly what they want to achieve and how.
  • Present acceptance of their project by the target local community, thus ensuring that it reflects the community’s needs.
  • Identify a university supervisor to guide his/her work in the rural community and provide advice,

The RUFORUM personnel responsible for the programme provides overall coordination and supervision. Figures 1 and 2 below illustrate the CFAPA criteria and application process.

Figure 1. CFAPA criteria

©RUFORUM/FAO

Figure 2. CFAPA application process

©RUFORUM/FAO

In the first pilot programme, in 2018, the Community-Based Field Attachment Award programme (CFAPA) received 34 applications. Grants are awarded on a competitive basis by the RUFORUM Technical Committee. 

The application process was open to all RUFORUM previously funded students. This fund targets students who received scholarships from RUFORUM for their graduate studies and therefore were eligible for the call. Ten applications were successful under this CFAPA call.

To ensure the quality and feasibility of the proposals, Criteria for selection and ranking by the Technical Committee depended on several factors:

  • clear articulation of the purpose of the project proposals;
  • timeline for implementation, goal(s), objectives and methodology,
  • realistic timeline and achievable objectives;
  • clearly identified benefits for the rural community where the project will take place.

Preparation of proposals ensured students ‘ownership’ of their work with the rural community, show a clear idea of what they want to achieve and how. Students had to produce proof of acceptance of their project by the target local community, with the local community leaders, University supervisors, extension services and local governments, ensuring that the project reflects the community needs (see Annex I – case studies). Students had a budget of around 1 000 USD per month to cover their living, transportation costs and costs for fieldwork (i.e., organization of workshops, preparation of training materials, tools for technology demonstrations, etc.). The proper allocation of the budget was determinant for the full participation of students.

1.3 CFAPA outputs

By the end of the RUFORUM programme CFAPA student awardees were expected to have achieved the following deliverables which are showcased in Table 1 below.

Table 1. CFAPA Student awardee, the seven deliverables
CFAPA Student Awardee Deliverables
Deliverable 1

Monthly progress reports to the host institution/university supervisor.

To support the process of monitoring progress and provide a basis for RUFORUM to continuously engage with each student awardee and address specific contextual issues.
Deliverable 2 Provide a brief biodata with an outline of the career record of the student awardee - for RUFORUM.
Deliverable 3 FAO Newsletter at the end of the second month.
Deliverable 4 A one-page write-up of their experiences for the RUFORUM/FAO newsletters.
Deliverable 5 A policy brief generated from the implementation of activities during the CFAPA - submitted to the University and RUFORUM.
Deliverable 6

Submit at the end of the six months a CFAPA final report to RUFORUM. (Highlighting the field experiences and potential areas for further research and action and the CFAPA outcome). 

The reports should include evidence of:

  • that students were liaising both with their university supervisors and RUFORUM;
  • submission of monthly reports);
  • consultation on both technical and logistical matters during the project;
  • guidance and follow up from their supervisors;
  • methods and means to communicate the research results to local communities.
Deliverable 7

Produce ten-minute videos prepared by each student on the:

  • activities delivered under the community-based field placements; and
  • impacts on the local community.

Source: RUFORUM 2020

To disseminate their research results and promote innovative approaches, students targeted a wide range of stakeholders from rural communities, including:

  • farmers;
  • agricultural traders;
  • farmer associations;
  • community health institutions;
  • veterinary and extension services; and
  • rural community leaders, with a particular emphasis on women, youth and small-scale farmers.

Students organized a series of dissemination and outreach actions:

  • interactive workshops and training;
  • presentations; and
  • radio-shows.

These actions disseminated knowledge and encouraged dialogue at the rural community level to use  innovative methods to improve food security and nutrition, enhance sustainable food and agriculture practices and reduce rural poverty.

1.4 CFAPA outcomes

The CFAPA initiative implementation outcomes describe and evaluates the outcomes set for each of the three levels: the students, the rural community and FAO. Table 2 below highlights the outcomes and uses color scoring for the evaluation. The scoring is an average derived from:

  • the students’ information in their final reports;
  • their follow-up questionnaires; and
  • questionnaire feedback from RUFORUM.

In general, the outcomes fall between good and excellent. It is worth highlighting that the outcomes related to FAO scored well by both students and RUFORUM, indicating that there is still an opportunity to further increase the thematic coverage of the FAO topics and increase partnerships. On the other hand, the students have highlighted that policy support was fair. These scores are indicative but are excellent learning lessons for revising the follow-up CFAPA outcomes and processes.

1.5 CFAPA successes

The programme’s successful outcomes were highlighted in the individual student’s final reports and feedback from RUFORUM. Table 3 and 4 shows a summary of the key successes they noted.
