Farmer managed natural regeneration (FMNR)

Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) is both a technical practice and community development approach used to support local communities to restore their natural environment through the systematic pruning and management of remnant vegetation in agricultural, pastoral and communal land. The practice involves thinning the shoots from tree stumps or wild saplings to rapidly foster their growth into mature trees. Increased tree cover provides numerous benefits such as improved soil fertility, wind breaks, increased firewood and climate change mitigation. Secondary benefits include increased crop yields and animal fodder as a result of improved soil fertility. This practice is often used as part of a community development approach whereby community members set environmental regeneration goals and use FMNR as an early restoration intervention because it is simple and low cost. This then provides a foundation to build additional restoration activities upon.



Description

Figure 1. A farmer practising FMNR in Malawi


 
©World Vision Australia/Sarah McKenzie

1. FMNR in practice

FMNR has been promoted by many entities including development organizations, research institutions, governments, community groups, and passionate individuals. The FMNR Hub at World Vision Australia was established in 2012 to synthesize the learnings from all these stakeholders and to co-develop effective ways of promoting FMNR with communities. Decades of FMNR training, awareness raising, and advocacy has led to the refinement of how to best spread this practice at a local level. This process is contextualized depending on the country, but it is always a highly participatory approach. This means people are at the centre of every decision. FMNR is more than just the regeneration of trees. It is about ensuring all community members can have access to this practice, apply it for their own needs and experience the rich benefits which come from increased tree cover in their environment. 

Some people may wish to regenerate the forest they use for firewood. Alternatively, farming families may wish to restore trees on their agricultural land to improve soil fertility. Community members use these goals to develop their own plan for how they want FMNR to look in their environment. As well as encouraging community members to develop their own plan, they are also supported to become FMNR champions and train others in their region. Encouraging community-ownership of this practice it ensures sustainability beyond the end of an FMNR training session or an FMNR project. 

Wherever possible FMNR can be bolstered by teaching community members advocacy skills, so they can encourage their lawmakers to adopt policies that protect trees and the environment. The practices of FMNR can also be supported by encouraging community members to take-up complimentary Natural Resource Management practices, such as Assisted Natural Regeneration, to amplify the benefits of regeneration. Because FMNR can increase crop yields or generate new tree-based products, it can also provide communities with additional livelihood opportunities, such as developing local value chains, so they can profit from these new resources. 

At the heart of all FMNR is the mindset shift that occurs when community members can see that they have the capacity and the resources to re-green their environment and provide a better world for future generations. 

1.1 Technical practice

The technical components comprise the pruning and tree management part of FMNR. In the scientific community this technical component is what most people are referring to when they talk about FMNR. In the development sector, FMNR is seen as a more holistic community development approach to support people to take up this pruning practice.  The pruning practice involves the following steps:

  1. Select: FMNR practitioners identify the number and species of trees and shrubs to be regenerated and/or actively managed in a landscape. FMNR is traditionally used to regenerate indigenous species, but the same principles can be applied to exotics.
  2. Prune: FMNR practitioners selectively remove the stems and side branches of regenerating indigenous tree stumps and shrubs to maximize growth and regeneration by directing resources and nutrients to a few selected stems and side branches.
  3. Manage: FMNR practitioners manage pruned stumps and shrubs by periodically returning to selectively remove new stems and side branches, and by protecting those that remain from potential threats including livestock, fire, humans, and competing vegetation or weeds by adopting, for example, improved grazeland and livestock management practices, social fencing, live fencing and/or fire breaks.
  4. Utilize: FMNR practitioners utilize stems harvested through the pruning process for planned purposes including firewood, fodder or mulch with the understanding that shoots regenerating following harvesting of stems will be actively managed to expedite their recovery. As trees grow, practitioners may also utilize wild foods, traditional medicines, dyes, gums and other non-timber forest products, depending on the species. In some instances, the entire tree may be felled and utilized by the FMNR practitioner. Many FMNR trees provide secondary benefits for the community such as increased soil fertility, wind breaks and erosion control.

While FMNR is commonly used to restore trees on land that has been cleared of vegetation, it can also be used to manage areas of dense bushland which have formed as a result of poor land management practices. These areas effectively become ‘green deserts’ of limited use to either wildlife or livestock. On rangeland this is called bush encroachment. On such sites, the focus of FMNR is on better management of existing trees, shrubs and even grassland. The same process of species surveying, prioritization and selection still applies; land users can choose which trees and shrubs they would like to manage, and what management needs to occur to help them reach their desired goals. This might involve clearing out an invasive species to allow for indigenous trees to grow. 

Vast areas of land in Africa have been cleared and/or burnt at some point and abandoned, and are now overrun by bush encroachment. Through FMNR, these lands can be rapidly recovered for forestry and agroforestry purposes. In Nakuru and Baringo counties in Kenya, milk production from the same area and with the same number of cows increased by 200 to 500 percent once this scrub encroachment had been thinned and pruned (Njiru 2014 Pers. Comm.). Consequently, land values have increased as areas once considered worthless have become sought after. 

The initial thinning of the vegetation in these areas ultimately leads to greater biomass and carbon sequestration as trees can grow taller with reduced competition and the thinned canopy allows grass and ground cover to grow.

Figure 2. The pruning practice of FMNR

©World Vision Australia/Nick Ralph

1.2 Community approach

As discussed, pruning is only one part of the FMNR approach. For maximum impact, FMNR projects are designed to deeply involve the community and other significant stakeholders at every stage of the FMNR adoption process. A crucial part of this process is understanding the social dimensions within the community – including power dynamics and inequalities. This includes identifying leaders, as well as knowing who may face discrimination and inequality. Taking time to understand these dimensions means that the FMNR project will be as inclusive as possible. This could include simple modifications such as organizing childcare, so women can attend an FMNR training, finding ways for landless community members to practice on communal land or doing an assessment for how training venues and locations can be accessible for people with a disability. The main practitioners of FMNR are land users (farmers, pastoralists, forest users) and their families, but the practice can be done by anyone who desires to regenerate trees in their area. This engagement process is always contextualized, but in general it involves the following components:

  1. Connect: Community members come together to analyse, discuss and connect the root causes and consequences of deforestation and landscape degradation in their community. Once the connection has been made, FMNR is introduced as a potential solution.
  2. Plan: Community members engage in a participatory visioning process to identify common goals and agree on tangible actions to drive and enable the scale-up of FMNR on communal and privately owned/managed land. These plans can vary in formality and may be developed and refined over the years.
    Objectives will vary according to the context. For example, in the Republic of Niger, major issues facing farming households addressed by FMNR include low soil fertility, drought, destructive winds at sowing time, low yields, periodic total crop failure and fuel wood shortage. In Timor Leste, fuel wood shortage is not as big an issue as flooding, landslides and low soil fertility. And in pastoral zones in East Africa, lack of fodder is a major issue. Typical FMNR projects working with farming families primarily seek to improve livelihoods. The main objective of an FMNR conservation project might be to restore biodiversity and ecosystem health and function. In countries where there are conflicts over scarce natural resources FMNR may be employed as a peace-building tool.
  3. Enable: Community members are trained in the technical knowledge and skills to adopt and promote the practice of FMNR on landscapes. This component also includes the identification, training and follow up of FMNR Champions who actively work to enhance the spread and adoption of FMNR in their communities.

Beyond these recommended components, it must be recognized that all development interventions are ‘journeys’ involving individuals, communities, development partners, local government and the interactions between them. In Niger, at the beginning of the FMNR journey, much energy was spent respectfully and persistently combating negative attitudes towards trees and destructive practices. FMNR proponents also came up against outright opposition to change, a colonial legacy, and the sheer struggle for survival in a degraded landscape scarcely able to meet the subsistence needs of a growing population. The journey involved tentative steps forward and major setbacks before eventual success when restoration was achieved. 

By investing the time to ensure that this practice is owned by the community it has a far greater success rate and is therefore more likely to be continued after a project is finished. This community-ownership has ensured greater outcomes for carbon mitigation and sequestration – and livelihoods.

Figure 3. An FMNR youth group in Uganda

©World Vision Australia/Sarah McKenzie

2. Mindset change

Central to FMNR is the mindset transformation that occurs as individuals and communities meaningfully engage with the FMNR process and adopt the practice. Through this process of mindset transformation, individuals and communities experience a positive shift in their attitudes and agency toward addressing the causes and consequences of environmental degradation. The result is a transformation from hopelessness and apathy to optimism and empowerment for a more prosperous and sustainable future.

3. Enabling factors

These components are not a required part of an FMNR programme, but they have been shown to increase the likelihood that FMNR will be adopted and owned by the community. 

3.1 Livelihoods

Livelihood support could include introducing complimentary income-generating activities or supporting community members to sell the new products, such as firewood, they may have from FMNR activities. Implementing complementary economic activities, such as beekeeping within regenerated areas, can improve FMNR adoption and sustainability by increasing perceived value of trees, as well as income to households. These livelihood activities can also be used to bolster short-term fluctuations in household resource availability and income, which may otherwise undermine the success of FMNR by placing increased pressure on the use and cutting of trees. As well as introducing additional income-generating activities, some communities may benefit from support to help them decide how and when to sell the new products they have due to FMNR. This value-chain support could involve supporting famers to pool their firewood to sell as a collective or to invest in equipment to process grains to on sell at a higher price.

Figure 4. Farmer in Uganda with increased bean yields from practicing FMNR

©World Vision Uganda

3.2 Natural resource management

Implementing FMNR with other complementary landscape management approaches can help create the enabling conditions required to accelerate the natural regeneration of trees on landscapes and provide more benefits for communities. Common complementary landscape management approaches include supplementary tree planting or reseeding on denuded or bare areas that lack sufficient regenerants such as living rootstocks and/or wild seeds (also known as enrichment planting), and the installation of small-scale physical structures for rainwater harvesting and soil and water conservation infrastructure (e.g. terraces, trenches, check-dams, sand dams or weirs). A key driver of deforestation is over-cutting of vegetation for fuelwood. The introduction of FMNR, and the protection of trees, may be perceived by some as a threat to their fuelwood supply. Reducing fuelwood demand, such as by facilitating adoption of fuel-efficient cook stoves, can facilitate FMNR adoption by reducing this demand. When integrated as a component of a broader natural resource management (NRM) approach, FMNR becomes a foundational practice upon which others may be layered to enhance NRM outcomes.   

3.3 Advocacy

Building awareness and understanding of FMNR as a low-cost, scalable approach to address landscape restoration and build climate resilience enhances its adoption and helps to create an enabling environment at the community and/or sub-national level(s). This could include a law which enshrines the protection of regenerated trees or a national policy which designates that 5 percent of all private land must have tree cover. In communities where these laws already exist, an FMNR project simply needs to ensure that all community members are aware of these laws and policies. In a community where they don’t exist the community may need to be supported with advocacy training so they can petition their local government for greater environmental protection laws to support the adoption of FMNR and the future protection of trees.

4. Validation of the practice

FMNR has been practiced in at least 27 countries: Somalia, Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Uganda, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Lesotho, Kingdom of Eswatini, Democratic Republic of Congo, South Sudan, Chad, Niger, Mali, Burundi, Ghana, Senegal, India, Myanmar, Indonesia, Timor-Leste, Haiti, Mongolia, South Africa and Sri Lanka.

It is important to note that FMNR, which is a form of coppicing or pollarding has been in existence in one form or other for centuries in various parts of the world where land users have integrated management of naturally occurring trees into agricultural, pastoral and forest contexts. Historical examples include agroforestry parklands in the West African Sahel on both agricultural and pastoral land, Quesungual in Honduras which involves pollarding trees on agricultural land and coppice tree management in forests spanning at least two centuries in England and at least 700 years in Japan.

FMNR as a distinct practice has been tested in a wide range of eco-zones, ranging from very Dry (hyper-arid regions in Somaliland, through the semi-arid tropics in the Sahel) to humid (sub-tropics in humid regions of Africa and Central America and the Caribbean), and tropical regions (e.g the Philippines). records.title: Saguna Regenerative Technique (SRT), a no-till, conservation agriculture method of rice-based farming
records.description:
Description

Saguna Regenerative Technique (SRT) quickly rejuvenates the soil by enhancing percent organic carbon, by enhanced earthworm and microbial activity, by improved drainage, water infiltration and aerobic condition at rhizosphere, all of it together considerably increases yield at lower cost of production. 

Figure 1. Healthy soil for healthy food and healthy environment

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

1. Protocol of SRT

  • Bed making: the permanent raised beds are used unchanged for the next 20 years or more. The dimensions: centre to centre 136 cm, top width of the bed 100 cm, the furrow channel between beds 36 cm. Height of the bed 20 cm.
  • Direction: along the slope.
  • Seed Sowing: date of sowing for different crops including rice are to be sown as per the local agroclimatic traditions. Until an automatic seed dibbling machine is developed / located, the operation is to be performed manually with the help of SRT Frame. The iron frame is designed to make holes at 25 x 25 cm but can be changed to multiples of 25 cm as per the crop requirement. E.g. Sweet corn to be planted at 25 x 50 cm. 
  • Pre emergence selective weedicide application: this is important to prevent weed growth in the first month of plantation. The selective pre emergence weedicide is to be applied within 24 hours after seed planting on a moist land walking backwards. 
  • Post emergence selective weedicide application: if for some reason the aggressive weed is noticed after crop emergence these set of selective weedicides can be sprayed.
  • Gap filling and fertilizer application: this is to be performed between 15 and 25 days after emergence of the crop.
  • Pest management: due to SRT the organic carbon of the soil starts rising which helps the crop to keep the insects at a distance. But we strongly recommend use of IPM practices which involves different types of insect pest traps.
  • Nutrition booster spray: this spray enhances crop immunity and yield considerably. This can be applied between 50 and 60 days after germination. This consists of mainly the micronutrients and can also have major nutrients in a small quantity.
  • Harvesting: as of today harvesting is done either manually or by reaper. But a modified combined harvester can solve the problem of stubble burning and can motivate the large farmers.
  • Roots for the land: roots of the previous crop are to be kept undisturbed in-situ. Our philosophy is, “the fruit and the grain is for human being, the leaves and straw for the animals and the roots with stubble for the land”.
  • Once the roots of the harvested crop start sprouting again after five to seven days it is to be sprayed by systemic general purpose weedicide which stops the competition for the next crop and the stubbles are converted into organic carbon, the precious source for next crop.
  • Crop rotation: the easy possibility of relay crops is one of the important advantages of SRT. If irrigation is available three crops can be taken very easily. Crop rotation is a must in SRT.

1.1 Preparation of permanent raised beds

In this method we make the permanent raised beds. They are used over and again to grow various rotation crops without tillage or land preparation for the next crop.

Figure 2. The permanent raised beds made by the farmer will be used for growing crops for 20 year or more without any tillage

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Farmer Mr Hitendra Bagmare

1.2 Vigorous uniformity

The aerobic condition at the rhizosphere triggers positive chain reaction for healthy root and plant growth and reduced risk and drudgery to the farmer.

Figure 3. Excellent germination and vigorous root and uniform plant growth of the seedling

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Farmer Mr Hitendra Bagmare

2. Impact on soil structure and water infiltration

With increase in organic carbon, in-situ decomposing of organic matter, capillary formation by drying roots and earthworms, enhanced aerobic condition in the deeper layer of soil, quickly builds a healthy soil. Improved water drainage makes the crop climate smart and climate resilient. 

2.1 Presence of earthworms in the paddy field in many types of soils.

With the traditional method where ploughing and puddling is performed the survival and performance of earthworms was impossible. But with No Till SRT method all the 3 000 farmers in all six agroclimatic zones are dancing with happiness after noticing naturally presence of earthworms.

Figure 4. Different types of soils showing earthworms

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

2.2 Improved soil structure and well drained condition leads to climate smart farming

Increased organic carbon enhanced earthworm activity and higher microflora improve soil aggregation and water drainage which helped all 100 percent SRT farmers during floods in past two years. The same resilience was also noticed in drought conditions. 

Figure 5. Side-by-side SRT and traditional rice plots affected by flood

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

3. Crop rotation

Crop rotation ensures biodiversity of microflora and in turn the soil health. This also ensures the crop resilience and higher income to the farmers. As the small farmers depend for their home food consumption on their own land, the rotation comes in very handy, ensuring the food security.

3.1 Crop rotation and subsistence farming

A one hectare tribal farmer is able to provide 25 different food items to his family on their food plate due to SRT while he was able to provide only four items by traditional method.

Figure 6. The happy and content tribal farmer with 25 different food items from his one hectare SRT farm

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

3.2 Problem of residue burning on farm lands

Organic residue burning on farms is practised either to get rid of the bulk of residue and quickly making it convenient for next crop sowing or to sterilize the land for seed sowing. Both problems are taken care in SRT method by avoiding burning of crop residue.

Figure 7. Wheat after rice without burning of crop residue by SRT

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

4. Happiness and dignity to a smallholder farmer is possible

Small farmers are giving up and their next generation is rapidly losing interest in farming. SRT brought an unparalleled change and made every farmer happy and confident for the first time in their life, soon after their adoption to the SRT. Now their next generation after experiencing dignity to the farming even they are joining and taking over the farming profession.  

4.1 Farmer happiness index

The survey of 160 farmers was conducted by visiting them and asking a set of 20 questions, collecting replies in smiles and was analysed by statistical tool.

Figure 8. The SRT farmer happiness index

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

4.2 The no till science became a movement

The technique was developed to solve my own problems of farming. Our success story was taken to other farmers at our individual level from 2012. The successful farmers are now spreading the technique to other needy farmers in their respective area. Now the ball is about to get rolling which requires intervention by large organizations.

Figure 9. SRT Happy and confident farmers

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

5. Validation of the practice

  • The technique initially was tested in two districts of Maharashtra, India with 30 rice farmers in 2013. It has gradually grown to 3 000 farmers with 25 different crops in 26 districts of Maharashtra having six agroclimatic zones.
  • Initially the technique was used only for rice based farming system under rainfed condition with rainfall +/- 1 500 mm to 3 000 mm. It is now been accepted by POCRA, Project on Climate Resilient Agriculture, World Bank for drought prone 16 districts of Maharashtra for resolving soil and water issues of the region for crops such as cotton, soybean, pigeon pea, maize, sorghum, pearl millet, green gram, chickpea, etc.
  • It is accepted for “The Vision of Antyodaya” documentation of the best practices of sustainable development by ISRN, Indian Social Responsibility Network, Ministry of Culture, Govt of India.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

The most important basic necessity for successful implementation of SRT is that the farmer should be motivated and ready for change for self upliftment. SRT is working out very well with all types of soil texture, soil PH, water quality, even saline soils in coastal area with respective crops of the area. The technique involves minimum inputs and is “too good to be true” is one of the problem we have noticed for even trying out the technique on a small area by a new farmer.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Zero/minimum tillage in rice-wheat system: ID 7715.
  • Introduction to conservation agriculture: principles and benefits: ID 7413.
  • No-till technology: a no-till system with crop residue management for medium scale wheat and barley farming: ID 7507.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

SRT saves 50 percent labor especially in rice due to avoiding of transplanting operation (a drudgery to the labor). The transplanting operation in knee deep mud is carried out by both men and women.

9.2 Women-friendly

The traditional rice cultivation which involves many small tasks to be carried out by women such as preparation of food for laborers, uprooting the seedling, weeding, cleaning the bullock barn and so on. All these tasks in case of small holder farmer have become zero with SRT which has brought high comfort level to the women. The technique is so easy, light and manageable that she can easily and effectively take care of the farm with or without help of a man. Thus she has become happy, independent and confident.

9.3 Resource use efficiency

  • Land: with availability of small amount of irrigation a SRT farmer is easily able to take three crops making the land efficiency 300 percent.
  • Water: the increase water holding capacity has reduced water requirement by 40 to 50 percent. Also in case of rice no puddling for transplanting can save 40 percent water.
  • Soil: SRT quickly stops soil erosion; during puddling of traditional method 20% fertile silt is washed away with water which is completely saved in SRT.
  • Energy inputs: 100 percent saving of fossil fuel required for tillage operations which is almost 90% requirement of small holder farmer.

9.4 Pro-poor technology

The technology reduces the dependence of the small holder farmers on tractor and implements, excess labors and optimum rain/water and yet get the high productivity. This has improved their livelihood because they can easily spend on the education of their young ones, celebrate social functions luxuriously, have sufficient time at hand for future planning, all of which build their confidence.

Saguna Regenerative Technique (SRT), a no-till, conservation agriculture method of rice-based farming

Conservation Agriculture (CA), No-till method of farming which is climate smart, increases organic carbon of the soil, essentially are generative agricultural practice, considerably increases productivity of the land and adds to the amazing happiness & confidence of the farmer." The Saguna Regenerative Technique (SRT) cultivation method was evolved in 2011 at Saguna Baug, Neral, Dist. Raigad, Maharashtra, India.

The permanent raised beds used in this method facilitates ample of oxygen supply to the root zone area while maintaining optimum moisture condition there. SRT is being used for 25 to 30 different crops such as cereals, vegetables, pulses, oilseeds, millets, cotton, maize, etc. Absence of puddling and transplanting of rice makes it possible for “Not dependent on high amount of water, availability of tractor or plough and skilled labour during specific period of transplanting“.



Description

Saguna Regenerative Technique (SRT) quickly rejuvenates the soil by enhancing percent organic carbon, by enhanced earthworm and microbial activity, by improved drainage, water infiltration and aerobic condition at rhizosphere, all of it together considerably increases yield at lower cost of production. 

Figure 1. Healthy soil for healthy food and healthy environment

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

1. Protocol of SRT

  • Bed making: the permanent raised beds are used unchanged for the next 20 years or more. The dimensions: centre to centre 136 cm, top width of the bed 100 cm, the furrow channel between beds 36 cm. Height of the bed 20 cm.
  • Direction: along the slope.
  • Seed Sowing: date of sowing for different crops including rice are to be sown as per the local agroclimatic traditions. Until an automatic seed dibbling machine is developed / located, the operation is to be performed manually with the help of SRT Frame. The iron frame is designed to make holes at 25 x 25 cm but can be changed to multiples of 25 cm as per the crop requirement. E.g. Sweet corn to be planted at 25 x 50 cm. 
  • Pre emergence selective weedicide application: this is important to prevent weed growth in the first month of plantation. The selective pre emergence weedicide is to be applied within 24 hours after seed planting on a moist land walking backwards. 
  • Post emergence selective weedicide application: if for some reason the aggressive weed is noticed after crop emergence these set of selective weedicides can be sprayed.
  • Gap filling and fertilizer application: this is to be performed between 15 and 25 days after emergence of the crop.
  • Pest management: due to SRT the organic carbon of the soil starts rising which helps the crop to keep the insects at a distance. But we strongly recommend use of IPM practices which involves different types of insect pest traps.
  • Nutrition booster spray: this spray enhances crop immunity and yield considerably. This can be applied between 50 and 60 days after germination. This consists of mainly the micronutrients and can also have major nutrients in a small quantity.
  • Harvesting: as of today harvesting is done either manually or by reaper. But a modified combined harvester can solve the problem of stubble burning and can motivate the large farmers.
  • Roots for the land: roots of the previous crop are to be kept undisturbed in-situ. Our philosophy is, “the fruit and the grain is for human being, the leaves and straw for the animals and the roots with stubble for the land”.
  • Once the roots of the harvested crop start sprouting again after five to seven days it is to be sprayed by systemic general purpose weedicide which stops the competition for the next crop and the stubbles are converted into organic carbon, the precious source for next crop.
  • Crop rotation: the easy possibility of relay crops is one of the important advantages of SRT. If irrigation is available three crops can be taken very easily. Crop rotation is a must in SRT.

1.1 Preparation of permanent raised beds

In this method we make the permanent raised beds. They are used over and again to grow various rotation crops without tillage or land preparation for the next crop.

Figure 2. The permanent raised beds made by the farmer will be used for growing crops for 20 year or more without any tillage

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Farmer Mr Hitendra Bagmare

1.2 Vigorous uniformity

The aerobic condition at the rhizosphere triggers positive chain reaction for healthy root and plant growth and reduced risk and drudgery to the farmer.

Figure 3. Excellent germination and vigorous root and uniform plant growth of the seedling

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Farmer Mr Hitendra Bagmare

2. Impact on soil structure and water infiltration

With increase in organic carbon, in-situ decomposing of organic matter, capillary formation by drying roots and earthworms, enhanced aerobic condition in the deeper layer of soil, quickly builds a healthy soil. Improved water drainage makes the crop climate smart and climate resilient. 

2.1 Presence of earthworms in the paddy field in many types of soils.

With the traditional method where ploughing and puddling is performed the survival and performance of earthworms was impossible. But with No Till SRT method all the 3 000 farmers in all six agroclimatic zones are dancing with happiness after noticing naturally presence of earthworms.

Figure 4. Different types of soils showing earthworms

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

2.2 Improved soil structure and well drained condition leads to climate smart farming

Increased organic carbon enhanced earthworm activity and higher microflora improve soil aggregation and water drainage which helped all 100 percent SRT farmers during floods in past two years. The same resilience was also noticed in drought conditions. 

Figure 5. Side-by-side SRT and traditional rice plots affected by flood

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

3. Crop rotation

Crop rotation ensures biodiversity of microflora and in turn the soil health. This also ensures the crop resilience and higher income to the farmers. As the small farmers depend for their home food consumption on their own land, the rotation comes in very handy, ensuring the food security.

3.1 Crop rotation and subsistence farming

A one hectare tribal farmer is able to provide 25 different food items to his family on their food plate due to SRT while he was able to provide only four items by traditional method.

Figure 6. The happy and content tribal farmer with 25 different food items from his one hectare SRT farm

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

3.2 Problem of residue burning on farm lands

Organic residue burning on farms is practised either to get rid of the bulk of residue and quickly making it convenient for next crop sowing or to sterilize the land for seed sowing. Both problems are taken care in SRT method by avoiding burning of crop residue.

Figure 7. Wheat after rice without burning of crop residue by SRT

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

4. Happiness and dignity to a smallholder farmer is possible

Small farmers are giving up and their next generation is rapidly losing interest in farming. SRT brought an unparalleled change and made every farmer happy and confident for the first time in their life, soon after their adoption to the SRT. Now their next generation after experiencing dignity to the farming even they are joining and taking over the farming profession.  

4.1 Farmer happiness index

The survey of 160 farmers was conducted by visiting them and asking a set of 20 questions, collecting replies in smiles and was analysed by statistical tool.

Figure 8. The SRT farmer happiness index

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

4.2 The no till science became a movement

The technique was developed to solve my own problems of farming. Our success story was taken to other farmers at our individual level from 2012. The successful farmers are now spreading the technique to other needy farmers in their respective area. Now the ball is about to get rolling which requires intervention by large organizations.

Figure 9. SRT Happy and confident farmers

©Saguna Rural Foundation/Mr Anil Nivalkar

5. Validation of the practice

  • The technique initially was tested in two districts of Maharashtra, India with 30 rice farmers in 2013. It has gradually grown to 3 000 farmers with 25 different crops in 26 districts of Maharashtra having six agroclimatic zones.
  • Initially the technique was used only for rice based farming system under rainfed condition with rainfall +/- 1 500 mm to 3 000 mm. It is now been accepted by POCRA, Project on Climate Resilient Agriculture, World Bank for drought prone 16 districts of Maharashtra for resolving soil and water issues of the region for crops such as cotton, soybean, pigeon pea, maize, sorghum, pearl millet, green gram, chickpea, etc.
  • It is accepted for “The Vision of Antyodaya” documentation of the best practices of sustainable development by ISRN, Indian Social Responsibility Network, Ministry of Culture, Govt of India.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

The most important basic necessity for successful implementation of SRT is that the farmer should be motivated and ready for change for self upliftment. SRT is working out very well with all types of soil texture, soil PH, water quality, even saline soils in coastal area with respective crops of the area. The technique involves minimum inputs and is “too good to be true” is one of the problem we have noticed for even trying out the technique on a small area by a new farmer.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Zero/minimum tillage in rice-wheat system: ID 7715.
  • Introduction to conservation agriculture: principles and benefits: ID 7413.
  • No-till technology: a no-till system with crop residue management for medium scale wheat and barley farming: ID 7507.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

SRT saves 50 percent labor especially in rice due to avoiding of transplanting operation (a drudgery to the labor). The transplanting operation in knee deep mud is carried out by both men and women.

9.2 Women-friendly

The traditional rice cultivation which involves many small tasks to be carried out by women such as preparation of food for laborers, uprooting the seedling, weeding, cleaning the bullock barn and so on. All these tasks in case of small holder farmer have become zero with SRT which has brought high comfort level to the women. The technique is so easy, light and manageable that she can easily and effectively take care of the farm with or without help of a man. Thus she has become happy, independent and confident.

9.3 Resource use efficiency

  • Land: with availability of small amount of irrigation a SRT farmer is easily able to take three crops making the land efficiency 300 percent.
  • Water: the increase water holding capacity has reduced water requirement by 40 to 50 percent. Also in case of rice no puddling for transplanting can save 40 percent water.
  • Soil: SRT quickly stops soil erosion; during puddling of traditional method 20% fertile silt is washed away with water which is completely saved in SRT.
  • Energy inputs: 100 percent saving of fossil fuel required for tillage operations which is almost 90% requirement of small holder farmer.

9.4 Pro-poor technology

The technology reduces the dependence of the small holder farmers on tractor and implements, excess labors and optimum rain/water and yet get the high productivity. This has improved their livelihood because they can easily spend on the education of their young ones, celebrate social functions luxuriously, have sufficient time at hand for future planning, all of which build their confidence.

_annotations.body:
How to make a traditional African hive with two openings

Rwanda's climate and rich and varied melliferous flora are favourable for the development of beekeeping.  This document explains how to make a traditional hive model composed of elongated cyclinder made with the stems of Pennisetum (Urubingo), bamboo or papyrus. This hive model is very suitable to promote among smallholder producers that wish to take up beekeeping because it is well adapted to the local environment and it is easy to make and manage. In addition, this hive model requires little financial investment because it is made with locally available materials.

How to make a topbar hive in Nkoko (Raphia vinifera)

Raphia palm is a natural material widely available in Central and West Africa that can be used to produce all type of hives. records.title: Smallholder Horticulture Empowerment and Promotion (SHEP) approach as an innovative agriculture extension method
records.description:
Description

SHEP Approach has four essential steps and are as following; sharing goal with farmers, raising farmers’ awareness, facilitating farmers by decision-making, and developing farmers’ skills. 

Figure 1. Training participants from various African countries visiting Kenyan farmers

©JICA

1. Sharing goal with farmers

SHEP regards sharing its goal and vision with the beneficiary farmers as the crucial first step because it is the farmers themselves, after all, who make the most effort to materialize economically viable farming business throughout the training course. Through this step, farmers can feel ownership on the project activities.

1.1 Sensitization workshop

The sensitization workshop aims at sharing the SHEP vision and goal with the farmers to help farmers become self-reliant with entrepreneurial aspirations.

Figure 2. Farmers and extension officers participating in the sensitization workshop

©JICA

2. Raising farmers’ awareness

Raising farmers’ awareness on opportunities and potential of horticultural farming is extremely important. Without awareness the farmers are less likely to get motivated to make a commitment to change their farming practices for the better.

2.1 Market survey

The main purpose of SHEP’s farmer-initiated market survey is to encourage farmers to have hands-on experiences of understanding how markets operate and what markets want from them. At the same time, by conducting market surveys, farmers will be able to build a relation with various market players, such as wholesalers, retailers, middlemen, etc., and widen their interpersonal networks which can contribute to creating a win-win situation with the market stakeholders. Through this exercise, farmers can feel competence since they can discover new things by themselves.

The markets in which the market survey is conducted can be both at formal and informal, and/or domestic and international markets. However, it is recommended to start in a nearby local market. The location of the markets should be determined through discussions with the farmer group. In addition, the market can be on the side of a highway bus stops, schools, supermarkets, organizations, companies, or anywhere farmers can do business.

The market surveys should be conducted by farmers on a regular basis with a questionnaire form in hand. The questionnaire contains about 10 questions to be asked, such as consumers’ preference, marketing challenges, market prices, required quality and quantity of produce, seasonal fluctuations of prices and traded quantity, and mode and terms of payments.

The SHEP implementers, government extension officers and/or private extension staff, are encouraged to assist farmers make realistic decisions throughout the process of market survey.

Figure 3. Farmers conducting market survey with a tomato retailer at the local market

©JICA

3. Facilitating farmers with decision-making

With the awareness and new knowledge which farmers gained from the surveys, they are able to make informed decisions to make a change. This process involves farmers selecting target crops and making a plan such as Crop Calendar so that they will be able to better adapt their production to market and strategically and timely supply their target crops to the specific markets of their choice.

3.1 Target crop selection

Target Crop Selection is conducted so that the farmer groups can collectively identify the specific types of crops that are demanded by the market. The farmers agree to produce and market the identified crops as a group. Through these activities, farmers can feel autonomy because they decide their future by their own.

The farmer groups select the target horticultural crops based on their finding during the market survey. The decisions are based on group consensus and various collective actions for facilitating efficient production and marketing will be discussed and agreed by the farmer group members. The SHEP implementers give useful advice and suggestions, particularly in the area of agro-ecological suitability of specific crops, so that the farmers can make a well-rounded decision in choosing the target crops. Their role is not to make decisions for the farmers, rather, to help farmers to make the right decisions by providing appropriate guidance and expert knowledge on agriculture.

Crop Calendar enables the farmer group to plan future action as a group in terms of both production and marketing activities of the target crops. A crop calendar is a concrete annual plan for what crops to grow at what time, in what quantity and quality, and so forth written as monthly activities which facilitate the groups’ farming business. The SHEP implementers ensure that the plan is realistic and attainable considering the current capacity of the farmer group.

Figure 4. Women's and men's groups making a Crop Calendar/business plan in Egypt

©JICA

4. Developing farmers’ skills

As the last step, the SHEP implementers provide technical solutions to the farmers, i.e. give in-field trainings for the target crops the farmers selected, so that they can produce the crops as they have planned in the Crop Calendar/business plan.

4.1 In-field training

In-field trainings are designed to disseminate skills and knowledge necessary for the practical production of the target crops which the farmers have chosen. It is a demand-driven training. Since farmers are aware of the importance of techniques through above steps, adoption rate on techniques by farmers is very high. Then farmers can feel more competent/confident.

Figure 5. Encouraging farmers to weed with simple tools

©JICA

5. Validation of the practice

Up to March 2020, SHEP Approach is practised by approximately 180 000 farmers in more than 20 countries. Beyond Africa, the approach is implemented also in Middle-East (Egypt and Palestine) and Nepal.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

SHEP Approach can be worked not only in areas where horticultural crops are cultivated, but also where there are small-scale farmers who are willing/trying to practice farming as a business. Therefore, this approach can be applied to other crops, livestock, etc. The SHEP Approach is a simple method that is easily accepted by all farmers, so it does not depend on the farmer's characteristics/abilities (age, education level, yeas of farming experience etc.) and their assets (size of landholding, location and fertility of farmland etc.). For example, farmers living far from markets can negotiate with buyers who come to their community.

  • At least, minimum water resource are necessary to cultivate horticulture crop.

SHEP Approach encourages working farmer as a group, but also individual farmers can practice the approach.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Ten ways to improve milk marketing: ID 8240.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The farmer group, who realized the benefits of joint shipping through the implementation of the SHEP Approach, became accustomed to jointly carrying out labor-intensive agricultural activities, such as harvesting and weeding. Therefore, the labor-intensive agricultural work that had been carried out individually has been reduced and the work efficiency has been improved.

9.2 Women-friendly

SHEP encourages farmer to jointly engage in farming between husband and wife as a business unit. In case it is necessary, Gender Awareness Training is organized to recognize roles and responsibilities between men and women for the better farming activities. Through SHEP Approach, the relationship between husband and wife is changed from manager and labour to management partner.

9.3 Pro-poor technology

Since farmers decide to engage in SHEP Approach by themselves, most of the farmers keep practising SHEP’s essential activities even after the terminal of the project. Regarding cultivation technics which are employed in SHEP Approach, they are not the advanced one since smallholder farmers and extension officers can implement with their own knowledge and resource.  Farmers have kept to conduct market survey before sowing seeds even after the project intervention.  At the same time, many of the beneficial countries (more than 20) has started to implement by their own as a normal extension services.

Smallholder Horticulture Empowerment and Promotion (SHEP) approach as an innovative agriculture extension method

Smallholder Horticulture Empowerment and Promotion (SHEP) Approach is an extension and advisory approach, aiming to help farmers to access and benefit from markets by changing their mindset from “Grow and Sell” to “Grow to Sell”.  

It was developed through the technical cooperation project in Kenya and managed to double the income of the targeted smallholder farmers. In the SHEP Approach, farmers visit an adjacent market and conduct market survey to see for themselves and better understand the market’s functioning. Based on this experience, they then develop a crop calendar or a business plan according to the identified market demands. Having seen and understood what the price, required quality, timing and volume of production is, the target farmers were able to better adapt their farming and production to the market demands. They moved thus to “Farming as Business” by establishing relations with market actors and filling the information gap regarding quality, price etc. As a result, their livelihoods improved. Another key feature of the SHEP Approach is motivating farmers through Self Determination Theory which boosts adoption rate of good practices. The SHEP Approach proves that it is possible to improve farmers’ livelihoods by tapping into local human and technical resources, without advanced technology.

The SHEP implementers give useful advice and suggestions, particularly in the area of agro-ecological suitability of specific crops, so that the farmers can make a well-rounded decision in choosing the target crops. Their role is not to make decisions for the farmers, rather, to help farmers to make the right decisions by providing appropriate guidance and expert knowledge on agriculture.

Crop Calendar enables the farmer group to plan future action as a group in terms of both production and marketing activities of the target crops. A crop calendar is a concrete annual plan for what crops to grow at what time, in what quantity and quality, and so forth written as monthly activities which facilitate the groups’ farming business. The SHEP implementers ensure that the plan is realistic and attainable considering the current capacity of the farmer group.

Figure 4. Women's and men's groups making a Crop Calendar/business plan in Egypt

©JICA

4. Developing farmers’ skills

As the last step, the SHEP implementers provide technical solutions to the farmers, i.e. give in-field trainings for the target crops the farmers selected, so that they can produce the crops as they have planned in the Crop Calendar/business plan.

4.1 In-field training

In-field trainings are designed to disseminate skills and knowledge necessary for the practical production of the target crops which the farmers have chosen. It is a demand-driven training. Since farmers are aware of the importance of techniques through above steps, adoption rate on techniques by farmers is very high. Then farmers can feel more competent/confident.

Figure 5. Encouraging farmers to weed with simple tools

©JICA

5. Validation of the practice

Up to March 2020, SHEP Approach is practised by approximately 180 000 farmers in more than 20 countries. Beyond Africa, the approach is implemented also in Middle-East (Egypt and Palestine) and Nepal.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

SHEP Approach can be worked not only in areas where horticultural crops are cultivated, but also where there are small-scale farmers who are willing/trying to practice farming as a business. Therefore, this approach can be applied to other crops, livestock, etc. The SHEP Approach is a simple method that is easily accepted by all farmers, so it does not depend on the farmer's characteristics/abilities (age, education level, yeas of farming experience etc.) and their assets (size of landholding, location and fertility of farmland etc.). For example, farmers living far from markets can negotiate with buyers who come to their community.

  • At least, minimum water resource are necessary to cultivate horticulture crop.

SHEP Approach encourages working farmer as a group, but also individual farmers can practice the approach.

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Ten ways to improve milk marketing: ID 8240.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The farmer group, who realized the benefits of joint shipping through the implementation of the SHEP Approach, became accustomed to jointly carrying out labor-intensive agricultural activities, such as harvesting and weeding. Therefore, the labor-intensive agricultural work that had been carried out individually has been reduced and the work efficiency has been improved.

9.2 Women-friendly

SHEP encourages farmer to jointly engage in farming between husband and wife as a business unit. In case it is necessary, Gender Awareness Training is organized to recognize roles and responsibilities between men and women for the better farming activities. Through SHEP Approach, the relationship between husband and wife is changed from manager and labour to management partner.

9.3 Pro-poor technology

Since farmers decide to engage in SHEP Approach by themselves, most of the farmers keep practising SHEP’s essential activities even after the terminal of the project. Regarding cultivation technics which are employed in SHEP Approach, they are not the advanced one since smallholder farmers and extension officers can implement with their own knowledge and resource.  Farmers have kept to conduct market survey before sowing seeds even after the project intervention.  At the same time, many of the beneficial countries (more than 20) has started to implement by their own as a normal extension services.

field_extracted_original_innovat.value: Smallholder Horticulture Empowerment and Promotion (SHEP) approach as an innovative agriculture extension method

_annotations.field_innovation_identified: SHEP Approach: An innovative agricultural extension methodology that transforms smallholder farmers' mindset from "Grow and Sell" to "Grow to Sell" through market surveys, business planning, and skill development. It's an innovation because it creates improved business models, supports behavioral change, and enhances inclusion through strong grassroots participation, leading to doubled farmer incomes.
_annotations.field_shorter_description:
Smallholder Horticulture Empowerment and Promotion (SHEP) Approach is an extension and advisory approach, aiming to help farmers to access and benefit from markets by changing their mindset from “Grow and Sell” to “Grow to Sell”.  

It was developed through the technical cooperation project in Kenya and managed to double the income of the targeted smallholder farmers. In the SHEP Approach, farmers visit an adjacent market and conduct market survey to see for themselves and better understand the market’s functioning. Based on this experience, they then develop a crop calendar or a business plan according to the identified market demands. Having seen and understood what the price, required quality, timing and volume of production is, the target farmers were able to better adapt their farming and production to the market demands. They moved thus to “Farming as Business” by establishing relations with market actors and filling the information gap regarding quality, price etc. As a result, their livelihoods improved. Another key feature of the SHEP Approach is motivating farmers through Self Determination Theory which boosts adoption rate of good practices. The SHEP Approach proves that it is possible to improve farmers’ livelihoods by tapping into local human and technical resources, without advanced technology.

records.title: Pathe Pathshala: a peoples' vocational school on move
records.description:
Description

Different agencies like universities and government run institutes fail to attract livestock keepers to training as they train them in cities with languages other than those of farmers. Women livestock keepers refuse to attend such training programmes, as they have to leave their children and old dependents at home.

To overcome these difficulties the concept of the moving school, at the peoples’ place, in peoples’ time with peoples’ language came to mind. In practical, I see that “Democratization of knowledge and skills” happen through these “Pathe Pathshala” classes and lead to sustainable development.

Who are the main stakeholders and how Pathe Pathshala interacts with them?

  • The main stakeholders of the project are the small livestock keepers, small and marginal farmers, pastoralists, school dropouts, unemployed high school pass outs in tribal area and the women who keep livestock.
  • Small livestock keepers:
    • The small livestock keepers who keep cattle, sheep, goat, pig and poultry for earning their livelihood are the main stakeholders.
    • These small livestock keepers are spread throughout the state of Odisha.
  • Pastoralists:
    • There are groups of livestock keepers who move from place to place for grazing animals.
    • They remain away in forests and grasslands while migration.
    • They need Pathe Pathshala more frequently.
  • School dropouts & unemployed high school pass outs:
    • These groups of youth are mostly present in the tribal area of the state.
    • As they are brought up in village ecosystem; they can be good healers and livestock feed making entrepreneurs.
  • Women at grass-root:
    • Women folk are the real livestock keepers who are resilient enough to look after the livestock grazing, livestock health management and feed making.
  • We interact with the stakeholders directly in “Pathe Pathshala”. Back home, they are connected through tele-vet programme.
  • During the period of the project a robust system of interaction through “Pathe Pathshala” are made.
    • They are conveyed the knowledge and skills through storytelling, healing rhymes, practical demonstrations and herbarium show.
    • The farmers, pastoralists, youth and women are provided with study material in their language.
    • They are provided with telephone numbers of “Pathe Pathshala” so that they are connected with the tele-vet programmes by which interactions will be strengthened further.
    • The process of learning will continue.

What are the main challenges?

  1. I peruse my passion for reaching people and diffusing knowledge through Pathe Pathshala. Till now I am doing this voluntarily by spending the logistics costs from own, as a token of love to give back to the society from where I have come from. To enhance and ramify the work, funds crunch are the first challenges I meet. Although I receive local hospitality and partial logistics from friends, well-wishers, mentors still funds are the main challenge.
  2. Instilling the sense of confidence and belief among the small livestock keepers, pastoralists, unemployed youth and women in regard to the herbal healing of their own animals by themselves, in their own situations is the other main challenge. They do not easily believe, unless they see the fruits.
  3. The other challenges are the difficulties in diffusion of skills and knowledge to the poor farmers, unemployed youth and women livestock keepers who are not formally educated much. The methodology to be employed in diffusing the knowledge and skill should be convincing, easily understandable, use of simple words in local language, people-friendly and above all in storytelling, rhyming with audio visuals.
  4. To tell them that, wherever they go for earning their livelihood, they are not alone, they are with their knowledge and skills imparted to them. To instill this much of confidence in them, the knowledge and skills are imparted through storytelling, healing rhymes, herbarium show and practical demonstrations.
  5. Another challenge is the existing poverty that hinders them in leading a happy life. It becomes really challenging to show them the way, potentiality lying in the knowledge and skill that comes to fruition in shape of employment, income generation and happy living. In future the same challenges are anticipated.
Figure 1.  Pathe Pathshala with tribal women of baliguda, Odisha state, India on treating of goats with herbs

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/Pathe Pathshala

1.  Pathe Pathshala - the roadside class

  • Most of the Pathe Pathshala are conducted in peoples’ environment, without light, in open air system without microphone etc.
    • Teachings are in storytelling, rhymes.
  • Herbal Parliament:
Figure 2. Livestock Herbal Parliament of women

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/Pathe Pathshala

  • Herbal recipe preparation training:
Figure 3. Women learn to prepare herbal recipe for their livestock

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/Pathe Pathshala

  • Women Self Help Group: Learn and Practice: 
Figure 4. Women participate in reproducing their training and practice

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/Pathe Pathshala

  •  School dropouts:
Figure 5. Unemployed youth are trained on low cost livestock healing

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/Pathe Pathshala

2. Validation of the practice

  • The classes have been conducted since 2008 and more than 1000 classes have been conducted.

3. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

  • Logistic support, reading and skill materials.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

5. Related/associated technologies 

  • Building life skills for youth: ID 7655.
  • Farmer field schools on integrated plant nutrient systems: ID 7527.
  • Módulos pecuarios escolares: ID 6005.
  • Huertos escolares: ID 7219.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1. Women-friendly 

The concept of Pathe Pathshala offers particularly women the opportunity to expand their knowledge in the field of sustainable livestock management and to actively participate in the design process.

6.2 Pro-poor technology 

This moving school shows stakeholders low-input based, climate-resilient, thus cost-effective forms of sustainable livestock production.

Pathe Pathshala - A Peoples’ Vocational School on Move; at people’s place, in peoples’ time with peoples’ language for low-input based, climate-resilient, herbal healing of livestock. Many times, pastoralists who are on move are benefited by Pathe Pathshala - the moving school. records.title: Herbal preparations for control of foot and mouth disease in cattle
records.description:
Description

1. Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD)

FMD is an infectious viral disease that affects cloven-hoofed animals. Symptoms of FMD are ulcers in mouth and cleft of hooves, drooping saliva and difficulties in walking.

2. Herbal treatment 

2.1 Ingredients

Ingredients required for the treatment:

  • manjal (Turmeric) 200 g (freshly harvested rhizome is preferred);
  • coconut kernel extract (from 1 coconut);
  • sotrukatralai (Aloe vera) – 200 g;
  • palm jaggery 200 g;
  • common salt 100 g;
  • garlic 100 g;
  • pepper 50 g;
  • cumin 50 g;
  • fenugreek 50 g.

2.2 Preparation and application

  • The above ingredients viz. turmeric, sotrukatralai (Aloe vera), garlic, grated coconut are ground well through grinder.
  • Mix the ingredients using sufficient water (sprinkle water to moist the ingredients).
  • Collect the mixture in a vessel.
  • Make powder of pepper, cumin, fenugreek.
  • Mix together thoroughly and add sufficient water to make it about 1 litre.
  • Filter the solution and apply orally.

2.3 Dose and application

  • Use 100 ml at a time for adult animals or 50 ml for young ones or sheep or goats.
  • Before giving the treatment, the animals are to be fed with banana (two for cows and one for ruminants) soaked in sesame oil (gingelly oil) 50 ml.
  • This treatment can be continued for two to three days depending upon the severity of disease.

For treatment of wounds in the foot region:

  • A special wound healing thaila can be prepared by using the following ingredients:
    • Mix 500 ml of coconut oil and 500 ml Datura leaf extract together.
    • Boil the mixture in a vessel for one hour till it gets oily texture.
    • Turn off the fire.
    • Add 5 g mayilthutham (copper sulphate) and stir well.
    • Store the thaila in a bottle.

The thaila can be used for all types of wounds including maggot wounds in animals (can be stored up to six months).

Datura                                                   Turmeric                                                Copper sulphate                                                Aloe vera

Animals can also be fed with gruel prepared by boiling with ragi, wheat and bajra flour each 100 g to 200 g and mixed together (total 500 g) with sufficient water in a vessel.

Figure 1. Preparation of mathan thailam by participants of NRLM training, Guwahati, Assam

©SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

3. Animal health camp

SEVA in association with NGOs and women self-help group members organized village level training programme for livestock keepers on herbal treatment for animals which include practical demonstration and organizing animal health camps using herbal preparations. We have received good feedback from the livestock keepers on the effectiveness of our preparations for disease of animals including FMD.

Figure 2. Women prepare herbal preparations for FMD in Erode District, Tamil Nadu 

© SEVA/P. Vivekanandan

Mr. Jayaraman, (62), a herbal healer in Vandipalayam village, Vilupuram District has treated 60 cows affected by FMD during September 2011 in his village (using SEVA formula), Figure 3. All animals recovered after two days of treatment.

Figure 3. Mr. Jayaraman herbal healer in Vandipalayam village, Tamil Nadu

© Pitchandikulam Forests /Parvathi

4. Validation of the practice 

During 2013 there was an outbreak of FMD in many districts of Tamil Nadu. SEVA team members visited Erode district, and we administered herbal preparations for more than 500 animals (dairy cows) and they recovered after our herbal treatment. Dairy farmers in Karnataka, Haryana, Punjab contacted us, and we communicated our method of herbal preparations for FMD. Later they reported that the treatment was effective for FMD in buffaloes and not effective for cross-breed dairy cows (Holstein Friesian).

Table 1. A list of farmers who treated their animals for FMD using SEVA herbal formula
Sl.No. Name of farmer Place/state/region Particulars of treatment
1.

Pankaj Seth

 Amritsar, Punjab During Feb. 2018 he treated 8 adult dairy animals (local desi cattle and cross-breed cows) successfully.
2.

Dinesh

 Thalal, Hariyana During March 2017 he treated 12 murrah buffaloes successfully.
3.

Pavan

Kari, Rupa, District

Dadri, Hariyana

 During March 2017 he treated four murrah buffaloes successfully. Not effective for HF cows.
4.

Jaibir

 Dadri, Hariyana All five buffaloes recovered.

Source: SEVA 2021

5. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

This treatment is effective for local and desi breeds of cattle, buffaloes, sheep and goats. It is not effective for Holstein Fersian cows. 

6. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

7. Related/associated technologies

  • Goat raising in controlled areas and vaccination: ID 8937.
  • Mitigating diseases and saving valuable assets - poultry vaccinators delivering services to the poorest: ID 7682. 
  • Genetically marked vaccines for improved control or eradication of Rinderpest and antigenically related diseases: ID 4517.
  • Herbal masala bolus for digestive problems for animals: ID 10062.
  • Worm control in sheep: ID 6926.

8. Objectives fulfilled by the project

8.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

It is a low-cost technology and livestock keepers can reduce economic loss for the animals affected by FMD by both preventive and timely treatment.  

8.2 Women-friendly

SEVA has trained officers of National Rural Livelihood Mission (NRLM), community livestock volunteers and women in the method of preparing herbal recipes. It is simple to follow. 

8.3 Resource use efficiency

Locally available medicinal plants and materials are utilized for the preparation of herbal recipes and Mathan thailam.

8.4 Pro-poor technology

It is a low-cost technology and trained livestock keepers/women who can prepare herbal recipes and special oil for FMD. Also administered as preventive treatment when rainy season starts.

INNOVATION TITLE: Traditional Herbal Treatment Protocol for FMD

DESCRIPTION: A validated, documented traditional medicine protocol using locally available herbs and materials to treat Foot and Mouth Disease in livestock, particularly effective for indigenous cattle breeds and buffaloes.

_annotations.field_shorter_description: Dairy farmers or livestock keepers who keep small ruminants can get affected when an outbreak of Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) occurs in their region. It usually occurs during rainy season (July to October) and during summer (February to June). The disease cause mortality of young ruminants; general vigour and health of adult animals are affected as well. The consequences of this disease lead to economic loss for the livestock keepers. SEVA has organized herbal health camps for animals for treatment of FMD in selected villages in Tamil Nadu. After the treatment the local farmers gave good feedback of animal recovery from FMD. There was increase in the milk yield and fat content in the milk after the treatment. This method of herbal healing practices was earlier documented from local healers by SEVA in association with Honey Bee Network supported by National Innovation Foundation. Selected best practices are included in our training programme for farmers on the method of preparation and administration of herbal recipes for specific conditions of animals.

records.title: Reducing input costs for Paddy, Sugarcane, Groundnut, Turmeric and Banana by using herbal pesticides
records.description:
Description

Three preparation methods are commonly used by farmers; Amirtha Karaisal, Panchagavya, and herbal pesticide.

1. Preparation and application of Amirtha Karaisal (Nectar solution)

1.1 Ingredients

Ingredients needed:

  • cow dung: 2 kg
  • cow urine: 2 litres
  • jaggery: 200 g, (jaggery is obtained by heating the crushed sugarcane juice)
  • Water: 20 litres.

1.2 Preparation steps

  • Take a plastic container of 30 litre capacity and dissolve the cow dung in water.
  • Make the jaggery into a powder
  • Mix the jaggery powder with the cow urine (made into a thick solution by adding 20 litres of water).
  • Stir the mixture thoroughly and close the container.
  • This has to be kept for two days, and then it is ready for use.

1.3 Application options

  1. Apply the Amirtha Karaisal by mixing it with irrigation water (20 litres for one acre (0.4 ha)), the application can be done at 15 to 30 days interval.
  2. Add the Amirtha karaisal to a half-kg of each of the following microbial cultures: Rhizobium, Azospirillum, Azotobacter, Trichoderma viride. Take 20 litres of Amirtha karisal and mixed with microbial culture. Keep it for 12 hours, then mix it with irrigation water and apply. The application of the microbial culture mixed with Amirtha karisal is done seven times for turmeric, six times for banana, two times for paddy.

1.4 Benefits

This organic method of manure application reduces  the quantity of chemical or inorganic fertilizer  and thus reduces the cost of cultivation.   This method is practised now by more than 10 000 farmers for many crops in states of Tamil Nadu, Kerala & Karnataka in India.

2. Preparation and application of Panchagavya

2.1 Ingredients

Ingredients needed:

  • cow dung: 5 kg
  • cow urine: 2 litres
  • milk: 2 litres
  • curd: 2 litres
  • ghee (clarified butter): 500 ml
  • sugarcane juice: 2 litres.

2.2 Preparation steps

  • The cow dung should be mixed with the Ghee in a plastic bucket (about 15 litres capacity) and kept for three days.
  • Cover it with a piece of cloth and put it in a shaded area.
  • On the 4th day, the other ingredients are added into the bucket and stirred well. They are kept for 18 days and allowed for fermentation.
  • During the time of fermentation, the slurry has to be stirred clockwise and anti-clockwise using a wooden stick.
Figure 1. Mr. Chellamuthu, Karukkampalayam village, erode district, Tamil Nadu, who sells Herbal pesticide and Panchagavya

©SEVA / Vivekanandan

2.3 Application options

  • Panchagavya can be sprayed at a 2 to 3 percent concentration or mixed with irrigation water.
  • Use 3 to 5 litres for spray per 1 acre of land (0.4 ha) or 50 litres for mixing it with irrigation water.
  • Banana rhizome material (seed material) and seedlings of paddy or vegetables are dipped in panchagavya solution for few minutes before planting.
  • For 1 000 planting material about 2 litre panchagavya is sufficient.

2.4 Benefits

In Tamil Nadu more than 5 000 farmers practised this technique and are able to reduce the chemical fertilizer inputs for crops like paddy, vegetables, banana etc.

3. Preparation and application of Herbal pesticide

3.1 Ingredients

Local name of plant species (Tamil) Scientific name of the plant Quantity in Kg
Leaves of Nochi Vitex negundo 2
Leaves of Peenarichangu Clerodendrum  inerme 2
Leaf Petals of Sotrukatralai Aloe vera 2
Seeds of Vembu Azadirechta indica 2
Leaves of Erukku Calotropis gigantea 2

3.2 Preparation steps

  • The above ingredients are procured fresh and ground separately by sprinkling some drops of water by using a motorized wet grinder.
  • Then they are mixed together and kept as such for two days.
  • Then it is ready for spraying.
Figure 2. Grinder used for preparation of herbal pesticide

©SEVA/ Vivekanandan  

3.3 Application options

  • Mix 200 to 500 ml of plant extract in 10 litres of water (sprayer tank capacity) and spray as foliar spray for crops depending upon type and stage of crop.
  • This formulation has been validated for its effectiveness for control of pests of paddy and brinjal by Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Coimbatore.

4. Crop-wise application of the organic pesticides

The following table shows the

Table 1. Crop-wise application of the organic pesticides
Crop Organic pesticides Time of spray /application
Paddy Green manure

Before sowing of paddy raise green manure crops and plough in situ on 45th day.

Remark: Daincha, Sunhemp, legumes, millets are sown together.
Organic manure Apply  100 kg of organic oil cake (mixture of groundnut cake, neem cake, pongamia cake etc.) as basal dose in 0.40 ha.
Amirtha Karaisal 15th, 30th day of planting.
Panchagavya 30th, 60th day of planting.
Herbal pesticides 45th, 75th day of planting.
Sugarcane Green manure Before planting of setts, raise green manure crops and plough in situ on 45th day.
Organic manure Apply 10 tractor loads of farmyard manure in the soil for 0.40 ha.
Amirtha Karaisal 10th, 20th, 30th, 40th, 50th, 60th, 70th, 80th, 90th, 100th day of planting.
Panchagavya 60th, 120th day of planting.
Herbal pesticides 75th day of planting.
Banana Green manure Before planting of setts, raise green manure crops and plough in situ on 45th day.
Amirtha Karaisal 30th, 40th, 50th, 60th, 70th, 80th day of planting.
Panchagavya 30th, 60th, 90th day of planting and continued at 30 days interval till emergence of fruit bunch.
Herbal pesticides 45th, 75th, 105th day of planting and continued at 30 days interval till emergence of fruit bunch.
Groundnut Green manure Before planting of setts, raise green manure crops and plough in situ on 45th day.
