Turmeric Green manure Before planting of seeds, raise green manure crops and plough in situ on 45th day.
Organic manure Apply 10 tractor loads of farmyard manure in the soil for 0.40 ha.
Amirtha Karaisal 30th, 40th, 50th day of planting and continued at 10 days interval by mixing in irrigation water.
Panchagavya 60th, 120th day of planting.
Herbal pesticides 75th, 90th day of planting.
Figure 3. Turmeric grown organically by Mr Chellamuthu

©SEVA/ Vivekanandan

5. Organic paddy cultivation using sustainable farming practices by Mr. Thangaraj

Mr. P. Thangaraj (60) studied up to SSLC. He had been employed as a bus conductor and he retired voluntarily three years ago. Then he continued his main family profession of farming in 1.2 ha of lands in Noyyal village, Karur District, Tamil Nadu. He cultivates paddy and coconut using one open well as irrigation source.  He says that he earns more income by cultivation of paddy crop (white Ponni variety with 140 days duration) in 0.4 ha using sustainable farming practices. His practices are given below: Paddy nursery is raised and “white Ponni” variety is sown. He applies basal dose of mixture of neem cake (5 kg) and groundnut cake (2 kg) before sowing. He also raises sanappu (sunhemp Crotalaria juncea) green manure plant and ploughed in-situ. Then 15 to 20 days old seedlings are plucked and planted in the main field at 1’ x 3/4’ spacing. The main field is also raised with sanappu (sunhemp) and after 45 days of sowing (attains flowering stage) it is ploughed in-situ and incorporated in the soil. He applies basal dressing of manure using neem cake and groundnut cake 25 kg each before planting. After 20 days of planting the following sprays are given:  

  • 20 days after planting: Herbal Pesticide spray.
  • 35 days after planting: “Panchagavya” spray.
  • 60 days after planting: Herbal Pesticide + Panchagavya spray.
  • 75 days after planting: Panchagavya spray.
  • 90 days after planting: Herbal Pesticide spray.

With this method he stopped applying Diammonium Phosphates (DAP) and urea each about 50 kg as basal and topdressing respectively. His harvest was about 81/2 Pothi (2 210 kg) of paddy in 0.4 ha. The harvested paddy is then transported to a nearby rice mill for parboiling and polishing. It yields about 1 050 kg of rice and 1 000 kg of bran. It is valued at Rs. 76 800. There is good demand for his organic rice as it fetches Rs. 60 per kg from local customers. He says that he is not using DAP, urea each about 50 kg while the other farmers apply as fertilizer as basal and top dressing and Mr. Thangaraj saves Rs. 2 000. He also does not use any chemical pesticide, and it saves Rs. 1 000 per spray. Instead, he spends about only Rs. 750/ for spraying organic liquid formulations. He gets a net income of Rs. 50 000 or more from 0.4 ha of lands.

Figure 4. Organic paddy cultivation by Mr. Thangaraj in Velliampalayam village, Karur district.

©SEVA/Vivekanandan

Figure 5. Liquid manure being mixed with irrigation water

©SEVA/Vivekanandan

Figure 6. Preparation of Panchagavya by Mr. Muthuvel, Ellapalayam village, Erode district.

©SEVA/Vivekanandan

Figure 7. Green manure being raised in coconut garden by Mr. Thangaraj in Velliampalayam village, Karur district.

©SEVA/Vivekanandan

Figure 8. Turmeric fungal disease being controlled by using panchagavya and azospirillum by Mr. Muthuvel, Ellapalayam village, Erode district.

©SEVA/Vivekanandan

6. Validation of the practice

This practice of spraying herbal pesticide and Panchagavya, Amirtha Karaisal initially followed by Mr. Chellamuthu. By seeing the effectiveness of these practices now more than 500 farmers adopted them in Erode district, Tamil Nadu and they continue for more than five years. Now farmers in other districts are also adopting these practices in many districts especially Coimbatore, Tiruppur, Dindigul, Karur, Namakkal districts. These practices are found effective in the plain areas of Tamil Nadu with tropical climate where average rainfall is 800 to 1 000 mm per annum. Farmers follow when they raise crops viz. paddy, sugarcane, turmeric, groundnut, vegetables, maize etc. during North East Monsoon period (October to December) and also during summer season (March – June).

7. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Availability of plant ingredients for preparation of herbal pesticide is important. However few farmers who unable to prepare the herbal pesticide, purchase it from Mr. Chellamuthu who sells it at Rs. 150/- per litre. These practices are found effective in the plain areas of Tamil Nadu with tropical climate where average rainfall is 800 to 1 000 mm per annum.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Green manuring in sugarcane production for soil improvement and water efficiency: ID 8768.
  • Soil fertility for sustainable vegetable production: green and animal manures in the humid forest belt in Ghana: ID 5425.
  • Nutrient management in organic agriculture: ID 8368.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

It reduces the cost of cultivation for crops by reducing the the quantum of application of chemical fertilizers and pesticides.

10.2 Women-friendly

Women labourers are involved in collection and preparation of herbal pesticide, Panchagavya, Amirthakarisal  for different crops. It provides employment of women labourers in this method.

10.3 Resource use efficiency

Plant ingredients are available locally and harvested only leaves or seeds. In addition cow products (cow dung, cow urine, cow milk, cow ghee, cow curd are utilized and they are available easily in all villages.)

10.4 Pro-poor technology

Marginal farmers or tenant farmers need not spend much amount for purchase of chemical fertilizers and pesticides. They prepare simple herbal pesticides and organic liquid fertilizers for their field crops. Therefore these methods of preparation are user friendly and eco-friendly.

records.description:
Description

1. Step by step description

1.1 Cutting

  • Cut up scraps to create mulch and incorporate them into the soil
  • Cut up the scraps from the plant’s leftover from the previous harvest to make mulch. The smaller these pieces are cut up, the faster its decomposition and biocide effect will be.

1.2 Mulch incorporation

  • Incorporate this mulch into the soil. This can be done using a rotavator or using non-mechanized gardening tools.
  • Create grooves in the soil and incorporate remaining mulch and guano.

1.3 Grooves creation

  • After it has been incorporated, create grooves about 20 cm deep over the planting row.
Figure 1. The soil should look like this once the grooves have been put in.

©Sociedad Española de Agricultura Ecológica. Cultivo ecológico del tomate y del pimiento.

Figure 2. The depth of the planting rows (20 cm) is about the same length as a fork. The picture is for scale.

©https://www.mathsisfun.com/measure/metric-length.html

  • Introduce any leftover remains into the grooves and mix it with guano (approximately 2.5 to 5 kg per m2).
  • It is recommended that farmers incorporate larger amounts of guano depending on the population of nematodes in the soil (for more nematodes, more organic matter is recommended).

1.4 Grooves filling

  • Fill in the grooves and lay irrigation tubes, covering them with plastic sheet.
  • Use the mounds of dirt next to the grooves to fill them in, incorporating this soil in with the organic matter. The ground will look flatter at this point, although you should still be able to tell where the grooves are (the area where you mixed guano into the soil). This is important because this will be the part of the soil that you later cover with plastic.
  • Immediately after filling the grooves in, we lay the irrigation tubes down on the soil and cover each mound with a plastic sheet, making sure to bury the edges of the plastic sheet with approximately 5 cm of soil to ensure that there is no loss of humidity, gases or temperature.
  • The soil should now be watered for the first time and following this first day should be watered every four to six days (if the soil has a high sand content and does not retain moisture as well, then it should be every four days).
Figure 3. Soil covering

©https://aghealth.ucdavis.edu/news/how-sustainable-agriculture-relates-farm-worker-safety

  • Keep the soil covered for 30 days, followed by 10 days of ventilation before planting crops.
  • The soil should remain covered by this transparent plastic for at least 30 days, and then should be uncovered for ventilation for 10 days before planting crops. It is important to repair any tears in the plastic while it is covering the soil.
Figure 4. The pictures below illustrate what the soil should look like after biosolarization is complete

©Fundación Ingenio              
 
You can test whether the soil is ready by doing a small seed germination test. You can plant a few number of lettuce or tomato seeds in the soil and if all the seeds germinate this means the soil is ready, but if some of them fail then the planting should be postponed.

2. Validation of the practice

There are many organic growers that use this methodology in South-Eastern Spain (in the Region of Murcia), where the climate is warm and dry. Although we have used the example of biosolarization for tomato cultivation, this technique can be implemented in growing many types of vegetables. This practice must be properly timed in order to reap the maximum benefits. In our region our most productive crop growing season, when the ground is most active and temperatures are ideal, is in the winter. Therefore, we carry out biosolarization in the summer. This practice is carried out by family farmers who have access to irrigation systems.

3. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Farmers need to have enough sunshine and high enough temperatures that the soil will generate enough heat to disinfect. They need to make sure the plastic adequately covers the ground, not letting any heat or gases escape. This also means frequently checking for holes or tears in the plastic and repairing them with tape, especially if there are many animals in the area. Lastly, this process requires an adequate supply of leftover crop scraps and manure.

As previously stated, as with any practice it may require some trial and error to figure out the quantities of organic matter to incorporate, the frequency with which to water the soil, and to know when the soil is ready for planting. We generally recommend that this process be carried out in the warmest spring, summer and autumn months.

We recommend that farmers keep in mind that this technique does not permeate to lower levels of the soil, so deeper rooted organisms residing past about 20 cm may be to be manually removed.

The best plastics for the plastic sheets are transparent, 1 to 3 mm thick (thinner plastic is recommended for smaller areas), and if possible, UV-inhibited. It is important to repair any tears in the plastic. More durable plastic sheets may be reused if taken care of.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Solarization: reducing insect damage from cowpeas: ID 4425.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

This technology is labour-saving because it ultimately prevents men and women (whoever is farming) from having to spend time removing weeds from crops, and even boosts efficiency because it prevents crop loss due to pests and fungi.

6.2 Women-friendly

This technology is women-friendly because it does not require heavy lifting and can be done at their convenience, so long as it's in the proper season.

6.3 Resource use efficiency

This technology uses resources efficiently in that it recycles leftover scraps from the previous harvest as well as dung, and the only energy that it uses is solar-powered.

6.4 Pro-poor technology

This technology should be accessible to most populations, as long as those have access to leftover crop scraps, dung, plastic sheets and irrigation materials.

Biosolarization (Example: tomato plants)

Biosolarization provides a sustainable, organic method to soil disinfection and control of nematodes, phytoparasitic fungi and weeds in preparation for crop planting. The high temperatures that are produced during the decomposition process in addition to solar radiation create an effect that controls pathogenic microorganisms in the soil. In applying and incorporating organic matter into the soil, there is a series of microbiological changes that are produced. There is a proliferation of microorganisms that feed off of and obtain energy from the decomposing material, which facilitates its growth and accelerates the process. The organic material decomposition stimulates the development of both beneficial and pathological organisms in the soil, which reproduce and die. They thereby generate organic products (like amonia, nitrate, hydrogen sulphide, etc.) that help control soil pathogens. These products primarily produce a nematicidal effect on egg incubation and on the mobility of these species. records.title: Farm cart technology for smallholder farmers
records.description:
Description

Small-scale agriculture is the cultivation of crops and livestock on a small piece of land without the use of sophisticated and costly technologies. Though the size of these farms may vary, farming on family plots of land, traditional lands, and smallholdings on the outskirts of urban areas fall is considered small-scale agriculture. Farm cart for small-scale farmers is an idea to expose small-scale farmers to the simplest and highly productive technology on a farm. Farm cart technology helps in reducing the labour needed by providing farmers with a tractor-like machine which can help in transporting, plowing, pulling of farm harvests, fertilizing, water pumping, mowing, planting, and other related activities. The farm cart technology has the similar advantages to heavy machines like tractors and Power tillers, and it is cost-effective. With this technology, smallholder farmers can improve productivity. The project is under development, and it aims to make sure small-scale farmers are equipped with a well-improved Farm cart machine.

1. Farm cart technology project 

Figure 1. Farm cart technology during first modification

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Anna Aido Sanga

2. Ploughing

  • The farm cart technology is there to perform all the basic farm works including ploughing.

2.1 Ploughing system and design

  • The farm cart machine, based on its power, is designed to plough a land sine of 0.4 m at once.
  • Its design is based on the four oxen combined to give an efficient land cultivation.
Figure 2. Farm cart machine during farm works

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Musa Gese Doto

2.2 Tractive power

  • The farm cart machine has a power of about 17 HP which is enough to perform farm works based on the traction and soil calculations.
Figure 3. Rear tyre traction on soil

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Musa Gese Doto

3. Post harvesting of crops

  • The farm cart technology can be used to process harvested crops like maize, sorghum, millet and ground nuts.

3.1 Maize sheller system 

  • The farm cart runs a simple designed maize sheller machine with the capacity to shell 50 bags of maize per hour.
Figure 4. Maize sheller machine operated by farm cart 

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Anna Aido Sanga

3.2 Cargo (pulling)

  • The farm cart has a powerful joint that is connected to the trailer which can pull up to 700 kg (0.5 t).
Figure 5. Farm cart with a joint for connecting a trailer for pulling

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Musa Gese Doto

4. Gender balance

  • The farm cart technology is women-friendly and so contributes to achieve gender balance, that female can participate in farm works and do excellent than their male counterpart.

4.1 Female participation in farm works

  • Female empowering is an important factor for farm cart technology to be successful as it values women efforts in agricultural production, specifically in rural areas.
Figure 6. Female participation

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Musa Gese Doto

4.2 Operation comfortability during farm works

  • The farm cart technology is designed to give all favourable conditions for women/female during the farm works.
Figure 7. The farm cart is easily managed by women too

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Musa Gese Doto

5. Engine setup, operation, maintenance and repair

5.1 Engine setup

  • The engine setup is simple and does not need any extra technique and skills to know how to fix it. Its operation is just like other motorcycle engines which are easily accessible.
  • The engine is placed on the right hand of the operator to simplify the operation and fix any problem that can occur to engine components or brake failure.
  • Fewer components make the setting to be user-friendly.
Figure 8. Engine set up

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Musa Gese Doto

5.2 Operation, maintenance and repair

  • The engine operating system is very easy though it engages the transmission manually.
  • The gearing are in the form of 5-4-3-2-1-N engaged by right hand using a nob.
  • For maintenance and repair the engine can be disassembled without any complication and re-fix again to proceed with operation or farm works.
Figure 9. Engine

©Sokoine University of Agriculture/Anna Aido Sanga

6. Validation of the practice

The technology is firstly tested by Sokoine University of Agriculture farms in Morogoro, Tanzania. Currently, the machines are available at SUGECO and Sokoine University of Agriculture (SUA), Morogoro Tanzania under the Agro-mechanization Unit where effective research, modification, and development is taking place. The farmer can contact the innovator through email musadoto260@gmail.com or call +255769763285 also can contact the SUGECO office through info@sugeco.or.tz. The project is planning to make these machines available in at least two to three regions in Tanzania before the beginning of 2022.

NOTE: Farm cart technology is still on the prototype level. This is due to fund resources constraints, it needs more development to attain all the desired functions to perform.

7. Agro-ecological zones 

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Temperate, cool.

8. Related/associated technologies 

  • Farmer field schools on integrated plant nutrient systems: ID 7527.
  • Direct seeding equipment for tractors (conservation agriculture): ID 7417.
  • Animal traction and single-axle tractor drawn planters in conservation agriculture: ID 7416.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: small-scale motorised transport: ID 7316.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: single axle tractors: ID 7315.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: motorised single-axle mowers and reapers for harvesting cereals: ID 7314.
  • Labour-saving technologies and practices: manual and motorised threshers: ID 7313.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The work requires short time (approximately 45 minutes) to cultivate an area which could be cultivated in two days by using hand hoes or oxen. Labour is saved because instead of using six people to cultivate one acre by hand hoe, by applying farm cart technology only one person with either gender can operate alone during farm works.

9.2 Women-friendly

The design of farm cart technology is 100 percent women-friendly, as it gives women with a comfortable environment during operation. Despite the affordable price of the technology but the same women with a minimum of one day training about the services and maintenance can perform well without need of foreign exchange or distant expert (as in figures 6 and 7 above).

9.3 Resource use efficiency 

Farm cart machine consumes Petrol fuel with the rate of 2.1 litres per 100 km without full loading, and 2.1 litres for 56 km at full loading. It costs USD 2 of petrol to travel a distance of 100 km, and the same cost to cultivate an area of 2.5 Acres. The technology is resources efficiency compared to large machines like tractors and power tillers.

9.4 Pro-poor technology

Hiring or owning tractors and power tiller is expensive as they need technical experts for services and maintenance. Sometimes the foreign exchange is needed but with this technology as the local solution all the basic knowledge used to design the machine is locally and therefore the resources are available even in rural area which makes it easier for them to adopt. The existing technologies which are said to be poor must not ignore because they give an ordinary remark to the adaptation.

records.title: Improvised hive security against honey theft using hive casing
records.description:
Description

Construction of the hive casing can be done following the steps below.

1. Materials

  • 1 inch angular iron (x 2; each is 18 feet long, approximately 36 feet = 12 m long);
  • electrodes; and
  • oxy acetylene flames.

Price of the materials:

  • Length (x2) of 1 inch angular iron is sold for N2400 x 2 = USD 6 x 2.
  • Labour N1600 = USD 4.
  • Padlock and key N800 = USD 2.
  • Total = USD 18.

2. Methods

  • Cut the angular iron to get parts for the casing, for example, a length of 86 cm, width of 46 cm, and depth of 30 cm.
  • Assemble the parts together and braze the metal parts, take care to cover your eyes in the process.
  • Make sure that the brazing was done well for firmness.

Note: The material mentioned above is the Nigerian standard measurement from the manufacturer, thus the length may vary according to different countries.

3. Installation

  • The installation is done by cementing the iron casing permanently on the ground within your apiary so that it becomes impossible to move it around.
  • This will prevent the thieves from stealing the iron casing itself and also disallow them of having access to the hive.
  • Also, it will give the hive the stamina to withstand breeze or animals.

4. Hives

4.1 Hive burnt by the thieves

Improvised hive security against honey theft using hive casing

The vandalism of hives and theft of honey in Nigeria is a perennial problem that has led to the loss of investments and gains by beekeepers and discouraged consumers as well. Beekeepers find it difficult to securely situate their apiaries as they describe it as simply 'no-go' areas for placing hives. As most beekeepers only keep an estimated five percent of their hives on their own land close to them where they can reach on a daily basis, the direct control of their commercial enterprise is reliant on availability of safe sites in areas out of their direct control and most time very far from them. Continual theft and property damage drives businesses into the ground. Producing locally in Nigeria is becoming commercially unviable, as beekeepers battle to find safe sites that equally have a good forage area for bees and devoid of pollutants around the foraging zones. Thus, there is a need for an effective, simple, cost-effective and labour-saving security system for the hives.

  • electrodes; and
  • oxy acetylene flames.

  • Labour N1600 = USD 4.
  • Padlock and key N800 = USD 2.

records.title: Using IoT (Internet of Things) in measuring water quality parameters in fish farming
records.description:
Description

1. IoT processes

A microcontroller is a mini computer that is embedded on a semi-conductor circuit chip. A microcontroller contains a CPU (central processing unit) along with memory and programmable input/output peripherals. Below is an Arduino, a small device with a microcontroller that is able to execute data gathered from sensors.

Figure 1. Microcontroller

©RARICO/Mary Adeline Imanirakiza

2. Data gathering

Data is gathered from sensors that track the condition of physical things. In fish farming, we use a pH sensor to know the acidity or alkalinity of the water. In case, one of the two increased, fishes can be harmed. We also use a temperature sensor, which is used to know the thermal condition of water. Another important sensor is the dissolved oxygen sensor, which measures oxygen that has dissolved in water. Fishes need oxygen for respiration, in the absence of adequate oxygen, fishes suffer and may die.

1.1  Device configuration

All sensors and other hardware are configured together to make harmony in data gathering. On the picture below, Temperature and pH sensors are connected on a breadboard. Data that are gathered are sent to a microcontroller. 

Figure 2. Image showing the water parameters kits used before using IoT

©RARICO/Bizimana J.Bosco

3. Water quality parameters kits

  • A thermometer is used to measure the pond temperature.
  • An oxygen meter is used to measure oxygen in the pond.
  • Finally, a pH meter which is used to measure the alkalinity and acidity of the water.

These are the existing tools that are already being used in fish farming.

Figure 3. Tilapia and catfish

©RARICO/Bizimana J. Bosco.

Table 1. Requirement of water quality parameters in Tilapia and catfish

Abbreviations: ppm: parts per million, L/min: Litre per minute, [ ] stand for concentration.

3.1 Working principle

The Arduino ATMega is connected to four sensors namely temperature, water level, pH and turbidity as per the circuit design shown in Figure 2. The Arduino checks if the water level is between 25oC to 30oC. If it is less than 25oC, the water is too cold for the fish therefore heater switches on. If it is above 30oC the water is too warm therefore the fan switches on. Similarly, the water level is set to be checked for the top 10 to 20 cm of the tank so that it is always maintained and does not get too low. If the water level is less than 200 mm then the pump switches on and when it reaches 200 the pump switches off. For pH of the water 6.5 to 8 is suitable for the fish therefore a change of less 6.5 or greater than 8 will cause the pump to switch on automatically to pump water out in separate tank. Then water pumped in to fill tank from storage tank. For turbidity the measurement is in ntu and if it is less than 2000 ntu the water is still in acceptable turbidity but if it is above the water is too murky therefore the pump gets switched on and dirty water pumped out while the tank is filled with the clear water from the storage tank. 

To send data to cloud the Arduino is connected to the ESP 8266, the Wi-Fi is connected to the things speak. So to write data to the cloud the Arduino sends to the ESP 8266 and that sends to the things speak channel, using the API key. The things speak after every 16 seconds updates data.

The controller monitors temperature, pH and turbidity through sensor readings and automate switching on/off heater and pump based on sensor readings. The system is connected to internet through Wi-Fi and sensor readings are also sent to the cloud database. Furthermore, the cloud data can be viewed by fish farmers on their mobile and in web application.

3.1.1 Measuring temperature

The DS18B20 is a waterproof temperature sensor that can work from -10oC to +85oC with an accuracy of 0.5 degrees. This sensor is a 1-wire bus ie. it has single bus to control the device. Therefore the 1-Wire interface is enabled using the 1-wire library. To read the sensor values and convert it to degrees such as, Celsius the Dallas Temperature library is used. This library retrieves temperature reading and understood in degrees Celsius using begin (request temperatures) and get Temperature.

3.1.2 Measuring pH 

For using the 425oC analogue pH sensor it has to be first calibrated. The calibration is to convert 10bit analogue value to 0-5 voltage (V) accurately. Since pH is 0-14 the pH is mapped with 5 volts such that, pH 7 is 2.5 V, pH14 is 5 and 0 is 0V. The calibration will identify the uncertainty in the readings because pH 7 may not give a reading of exactly 2.5 V in actual conversion. The output should be 2.5 as the short circuit represents a pH of 7. Figure 4 shows the implementation for reading pH value.

3.1.3 Measuring turbidity

The turbidity sensor is a 10 bit analogue sensor shown in Figure 5, similar to the pH sensor the 10 bit value has to be converted to voltage and also calibrated. To convert the 10 bit analogue reading i.e., 0-1023 to voltage reading between 0-5V Turbidity is inversely proportional to the voltage, means lower voltage higher turbidity and vice versa. 

ntu=-1120.4 x voltage2 + 5742.3 x voltage. This equation converts voltage to turbidity in ntu units.

The actuators are two water pumps, water heater, fan and feeder. If water level is below 100 mm, relay switches on motor and water is pumped in until it reached 200 mm and relay turns off motor.

Similarly, temperature above or below threshold will switch off fan or heater, respectively. For the tilapia fish the ideal is 25oC to 30oC and when it goes below the relay switches on the heater. For turbidity, 3000 above pumps water out to another water tank. For the fish feeder the time is set and fish is fed during the day by rotating and opening lid automatically.

The API key is very important to keep securely as anyone who has access to the key can use it to write and read the data. There are two keys one for read and one for write. The write key is used to connect the microcontroller to the cloud and upload data via Wi-Fi. Along with the key the update channel URL is used to continually update data onto cloud via internet. The results can be seen on the channel’s dashboard where the data is represented as a line graph for each parameter. Water, feeds and materials of IoT are needed to install this technology.

4. Importance of water quality in aquaculture

Fish perform all their functions in water. Because fish are totally dependent upon water to breathe, feed and grow, excrete wastes, maintain a salt balance, and reproduce, understanding the physical and chemical qualities of water is critical to successful aquaculture. To a great extent water determines the success or failure of an aquaculture operation.

Very high (greater than 9.5) or very low (less than 4.5) pH values are unsuitable for most aquatic organisms. Young fish and immature stages of aquatic insects are extremely sensitive to pH levels below 5 and may die at these low pH values.

High pH levels (9 to 14) can harm fish by denaturing cellular membranes. Changes in pH can also affect aquatic life indirectly by altering other aspects of water chemistry. Low pH levels accelerate the release of metals from rocks or sediments in the stream. These metals can affect a fish's metabolism and the fish's ability to take water in.

Table 2. The effects of pH on warm-water pond fish

Tilapia and catfish need a temperature ranging between 20oC and 35oC.

4.1 Dissolved oxygen

The amount of dissolved oxygen is critical in fish farming and other forms of aquaculture. Dissolved oxygen in aquaculture, the volume of oxygen contained in water, is often the most critical parameter in the health and well-being of your livestock. In general, most fish species will grow and thrive within a dissolved oxygen range of 5 to 12 mg per L (ppm). However, if levels drop below 4 mg per L they may stop feeding, become stressed and begin to die. This series of events can start a chain reaction in a pond aquaculture system that could prove detrimental.

Oxygen depletion usually occurs in the summer months because warmer water holds less oxygen than cooler water. For example, water with a temperature of 32ºC can hold up to 7.3 mg per L of oxygen, while 7ºC water can hold 12.1 mg per L. As water temperatures rise, oxygen levels decrease. Higher temperatures also increase the metabolic rate of fish, resulting in the need for more oxygen in your fish farming operation.

Figure 4. Data centre

©RARICO/Mary Adeline Imanirakiza

5.  Data storage/cloud

The cloud is a virtual storage of data and computing power, without direct active management by the user. A data store can be programmed and it is the back-end of a system. It consists of a database and the authentications of the users. Users are allowed to view data that has been assigned to them or when they have access permissions.

Figure 5.  How data are collected, processed and transferred to fish farmers

©RARICO/Jean Bosco BIZIMANA

Figure 6. Device configuration/picture

©RARICO/Mary Adeline Imanirakiza

4.2 Gateway and data sending

An Internet of Things (IoT) gateway is a physical device or software program that serves as the connection point between the cloud and controllers, sensors and intelligent devices. All data moving to the cloud, or vice versa, goes through the gateway, which can be either a dedicated hardware appliance or software program. An example is a GSM, which is a standard-based Low Power Wide Area technology. A GSM sends data to the data centres via the internet.

5. Validation of the practice

The practice has been tested at Mulindi, Ndera Sector, Gasabo District in Kigali at fish farm of Cooperative COPAMAGA.

The pH, temperature and oxygen were measured using sensors and every five minutes we received the data from a device that were inserted in fishponds, canals and water sources at the farm.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Minimum requirements for water to be used in fish farming are:

  • Oxygen ≥4
  • Temperature ≥20oC
  • CaCO3 ≥20 ppm
  • pH ≥ 6.5
  • NH4 ≥ 0.01
  • CO2 ≤ 0.01
  • Water flow >300 L per min (for catfish only).

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Make a living through fish farming: ID 7357.
  • Small-scale freshwater fish farming: ID 6958.
  • Management of fish in the pond: ID 7235.
  • Selection of site and water quality testing for fishpond: ID 4376.
  • Fishpond layout and construction: ID 4384.
  • Management strategies for new or lightly exploited fisheries: ID 4583.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The pond culture is controlled automatically and does not require any labour.

9.2 Women-friendly

Traditional methods are unreliable and also a hazardous and unhygienic because farmers especially have to physically be present in the aquaculture area during feeding time and measure the parameters. Therefore, this project is proposed to overcome these challenges to automate the monitoring process involved in fish farming in small and medium scale fisheries.

9.3 Pro-poor technology

The system is further developed to change the speed by itself, by analyzing the data fed and predict how much food the feed dispenser should release next time. Using previous data about fish speed, water temperature and other parameters a probability diagram is made which shows the relation of each parameter to the other and according to that the feeder system will predict the next feed amount. The review of existing systems shows that there is a need for a smart system comprising of all functionalities for complete monitoring and automation of aquaculture in small and medium scale fisheries. Therefore, a smart aquaculture system is proposed and implemented for effective fish production.

The cloud is a virtual storage of data and computing power, without direct active management by the user. A data store can be programmed and it is the back-end of a system. It consists of a database and the authentications of the users. Users are allowed to view data that has been assigned to them or when they have access permissions.

Figure 5.  How data are collected, processed and transferred to fish farmers

©RARICO/Jean Bosco BIZIMANA

Figure 6. Device configuration/picture

©RARICO/Mary Adeline Imanirakiza

4.2 Gateway and data sending

An Internet of Things (IoT) gateway is a physical device or software program that serves as the connection point between the cloud and controllers, sensors and intelligent devices. All data moving to the cloud, or vice versa, goes through the gateway, which can be either a dedicated hardware appliance or software program. An example is a GSM, which is a standard-based Low Power Wide Area technology. A GSM sends data to the data centres via the internet.

5. Validation of the practice

The practice has been tested at Mulindi, Ndera Sector, Gasabo District in Kigali at fish farm of Cooperative COPAMAGA.

The pH, temperature and oxygen were measured using sensors and every five minutes we received the data from a device that were inserted in fishponds, canals and water sources at the farm.

6. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Minimum requirements for water to be used in fish farming are:

  • Oxygen ≥4
  • Temperature ≥20oC
  • CaCO3 ≥20 ppm
  • pH ≥ 6.5
  • NH4 ≥ 0.01
  • CO2 ≤ 0.01
  • Water flow >300 L per min (for catfish only).

7. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

8. Related/associated technologies

  • Make a living through fish farming: ID 7357.
  • Small-scale freshwater fish farming: ID 6958.
  • Management of fish in the pond: ID 7235.
  • Selection of site and water quality testing for fishpond: ID 4376.
  • Fishpond layout and construction: ID 4384.
  • Management strategies for new or lightly exploited fisheries: ID 4583.

9. Objectives fulfilled by the project

9.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

The pond culture is controlled automatically and does not require any labour.

9.2 Women-friendly

Traditional methods are unreliable and also a hazardous and unhygienic because farmers especially have to physically be present in the aquaculture area during feeding time and measure the parameters. Therefore, this project is proposed to overcome these challenges to automate the monitoring process involved in fish farming in small and medium scale fisheries.

9.3 Pro-poor technology

The system is further developed to change the speed by itself, by analyzing the data fed and predict how much food the feed dispenser should release next time. Using previous data about fish speed, water temperature and other parameters a probability diagram is made which shows the relation of each parameter to the other and according to that the feeder system will predict the next feed amount. The review of existing systems shows that there is a need for a smart system comprising of all functionalities for complete monitoring and automation of aquaculture in small and medium scale fisheries. Therefore, a smart aquaculture system is proposed and implemented for effective fish production.

records.title: Small fish-based fish chutney production
records.description:
Description

The fish Chutney is based on a traditional "achar" or pickle recipe, which is commonly served with rice, vegetables and resembles various savory condiments served in many cuisines. Jat Puti fish is one of the common small indigenous variety selected for producing this chutney as the basic ingredient, as it is a rich source of micro nutrients and widely available in open water fisheries. The recipe has further been extended by including garlic, onion, chilly, iodized salt and soybean oil to make it a mass rich in nutrients essentially needed by the PLW.

Figure 1. A bottle of fish pickle

©SKSS Limited/Abdul Haye Chowdhury

1. Basic ingredient and the source of nutrients

The Chutney is made of cheap small fish, namely Jat Puti (puntius sophore) as the base ingredient added with garlic, onion, chili, iodized salt and soya bean oil for taste and to make it popular, and also for their preservation properties. The recipe contains all source of iron, calcium, zink, vitamin 12, and essential fatty acid from the edible oil that provides the energy part of the chutney.

2. Description of the procedures of preparing the Chutney

The standard procedure of Chutney making is as following:

  • Wash dried fish several times in water to clean (The eyes and head from the small fish should not be removed during cleaning). Then the dried fish was stained in a strainer and was kept for drying.
  • Put oil in a pan and heat it. Add the dried fish to the pan.
  • Fish stirred continuously on a low flame for about 10 to 15 minutes until their color becomes light brown.
  • Transfer the lightly fried dried fish to a bowl.    
  • In the Pan, continue to heat the oil and add onion and garlic for 15 minutes on a low flame until they become brown, and stir continuously.
  • Keep the fried dry fish, onion and garlic to cool. Grind the fried dry fish to make a thick powder.
  • Grind the onion and garlic separately from the fish to make a thick powder.
  • Combine the fried dried fish powder, and the onion and garlic powder in the grinder and grinded to a slightly coarse powder. Add salt to the mixture.
  • After cooling, store the fish powder in an airtight plastic container with mustard oil.

Before finalizing the recipe, tasting trails can be undertaken with the target community as taste can be varied from community to community. Considering taste of the community minor change has made after conducting acceptability trail.

Figure 2. Fish drying before preparing fish pickle

©SKSS Ltd

The main ingredient of fish chutney is dry fish, fish from small indigenous species (SIS). Dry fish produced by contract producer following standard protocol provided by the experts. After completing the preparation steps, one can add 5 g dried bay leaf powder, 8 g ginger powder and 1 g black pepper powder was added to the mixture.

Table 1. List of the ingredients of the final production in percentage

One Bottle = 280 Gram

“Mache bhate Bengali” Fish and rice make a Bengali Fish most commonly eaten animal-source food across all income groups because the small indigenous fish are highly nutritious.

3. Quality control

For ensuring the quality control, the product ensured the quality certification provided by Bangladesh Standard and Testing institute (BSTI) who are the sole authority of Government of Bangladesh to ensure such types of products. SKSSS fIsh pickle also get the approval of the authority by ensuring all terms and condition of BSTI.

4. Bottling and selling

The fish chutney bottled by 280 g each and sold at BDT 280 (USD 3.2) when its unit gross cost of production is BDT 240 (USD 2.82).

4.1 Benefits

The benefits of chutney are tremendous:

  • It addresses the challenge to meet the nutritional deficit of the first 1000 days of life, which is a critical period for the mother and child to protect the under-five child stunted.
  • This is a cheap portion as a product and in the ingredients, but highly effective to meet the nutritional needs with resources easily available locally and the processing is too simple. One tablespoon (30 g of Chutney) contains 44 g of raw fish which is ample to meet the nutrition needs compromising iron, calcium, zink, vitamin B12 and essential fatty acid.
  • Only four bottles of chutney per month can provide PLW sufficient micro nutrient.
  • Quality bottling can preserve over the year.
  • The product can be scaled for industrial production to reach maximum number of PLWs.
  • The production is easy and women can be engaged in the production activities.
Figure 3. Production and packaging

©SKSS Limited/Rakibl Hasan Rana

5. The norms of business

This product was produced based on Social Business compliances - no profit, no loss basis in Bangladesh. Meantime the product has got the certification from Bangladesh Standard Testing Institution for marketing the product in open market.

6. Validation of the practice

Primarily it was followed the traditional method and in Bangladesh making chutney was a household skill, which later was taken at industrial level of production. Prior to the certification, its test and choices were validated through acceptability trail at the community level consumers.

  • Over the 25 villages under six Union of South Sunamganj and Derai Upazila of Sunamganj District (100 pregnant and 50 lactating women (PLW) and 150 Under-two year’s children= 300 HH)
  • The field work was conducted during the month of August- September, 2014. In Sunamganj August- September are the rainy season and thus this two month relatively high food insecurity in Bangladesh, thus the food security ‘picture’ that emerges from the study is related to the seasonal factors of food access and availability during this time period
  • HIS (Helvetas Swiss Interco operation) conducts different phases of the shiree project; conducted in September 2009-August 2012 in about 1 000 HHs (phase 1), September 2013-December 2015 in 2 500 HHs (phase 2) and April 2014-December 2015 in about 5 000 HHs (phase 3).

Women’s Chutney distribution was started on September 2014 for 12 months continuation up to September 2015. Before starting the fish chutney distribution, WorldFish had conducted a baseline survey to identify the nutrition condition of selected pregnant and lactating women. It was found that among all the participants, 72 percent were suffering from anemia (Hb <120 g/L). Besides these, they had some other problems like weakness, dizziness, drowsiness, nausea, less appetite etc. After nine months of fish consumption, WorldFish conducted a qualitative survey to identify their improvement, and it was found that after consuming fish chutney regularly, the majority of the participants are recovered from these problems. In September 2015, the end line survey shows that the number of anemia participants decreased by 28 percent in a year.

7. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

The minimum requirement for the successful implementation of the production is availability of SIS. It would not be a problem due to abundance of SIS from open water fisheries and these species are cheaper than any varieties consumed by the local community. Small fish (Puti & kachki not available all time) is a limiting factor. During rainy season abundance of puti & kachki high with low price.

8. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

9. Related/associated technologies

  • Fish powder: ID 8731.
  • Fish and their by-products: ID 8717.
  • Preservation of fish and meat: ID 6961.

10. Objectives fulfilled by the project

10.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

As the production has been mechanized it has reduced the workload and time, and women have got free from any stress full work like grinding by physical labour.

10.2 Women-friendly

Totally women friendly and dominated by women engagement at every stage of the process. We can say the product is by the women, with the women and for the women – from its resource collection, processing to use.

10.3 Resource use efficiency

Most efficient in using the resources. The technology is using the neglected underused fish to use and using the whole fish for production wasting nothing of the body mass including the head, bone, tail etc.

10.4 Pro-poor technology

Largely pro-poor. The product is reachable by the poor with minimum cost but with maximum benefit being particularly suitable for the first 1 000 days of life of poor families in rural Bangladesh who usually predominantly suffer from nutrition deficit due to lack of food.

records.title: Treating mastitis in cows, with low-cost and climate resilient, herbal regimen
records.description:
Description

1. Mastitis disease

Milk is secreted from the udder of the mother cow. Due to infections, the udder becomes swollen leading to blood coming out with the milk.

1.1 Symptoms

  • Udder is swollen.
  • Udder is reddened and inflamed.
  • The colour of milk becomes red.
  • Texture of milk looks silky.
  • Milking becomes painful.
  • Milk yield is reduced and may be stopped.

1.2 Causes

  • Bacterial infection of udder and also milk canal.
  • Unhygienic condition of cow shed.

2. Herbal treatment

Mastitis can be treated effectively using betel leaves (Piper betel) and castor oil prepared from castor seed (Ricinus communis). The two components are mixed and offered to treat mastitis.

Scientifically, castor oil contains ricinoleic acid, methyl ricinoleate, ricinolein. And betel leaves contain piperine and piperidene. These biomolecules prevent and controls infection and mastitis is controlled.

2.1 The remedy

  • Ten betel leaves.
  • 100 ml Castor oil.

Ten Green betel leaves are pounded to make its paste and then mixed with 100 ml of castor oil.

Two third of the mixture is offered to the animal orally and the other one third is applied directly to the udder.

Figure 1. Betel leaves

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/Photo from public domain

Figure 2. Castor oil heals wound and infection

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/Photo from public domain

Women cow-keepers find it easier to prepare the herbal regimen and do the practice by themselves.

3. Validation of the practice

This practice has been validated in the hands of 500 farmers in India successfully.

4. Agro-ecological zones

  • Tropics, warm.
  • Tropics, cool/cold/very cold.
  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Eight golden rules for sustainable development of dairy: ID 8652.
  • Rearing dairy goats: ID 6925.
  • Farmers dairy goat production handbook: ID 6939.
  • Tsetse and trypanosomiasis control measures: restricted application of insecticide to livestock: ID 4514.

6. Objectives fulfilled by the project

6.1 Labour-saving technology (LST)

This practice is low-cost and does not require many inputs. The preparation is simple and not labor-intensive.

6.2 Women-friendly

The process of preparation is simple and women-friendly.

6.3 Resource use efficiency

This practice uses local biomass and herbs.

6.4 Pro-poor technology

Poor farmers can save money by applying this practice instead of buying antibiotics.

Treating mastitis in cows, with low-cost and climate resilient, herbal regimen

Mastitis is an inflammation of one or more quarters of the udder (dairy herds) usually caused by bacterial infection. Several types of bacteria cause distinctly different mastitis infections. As a consequence, the udder is inflamed, swollen, and blood may come out with milk which yields to reduction in milk yields. The mastitis is caused by bacterial infection that can be treated by antibiotics, however, poor cow-keepers cannot afford or sometimes do not have access to. Additional, the use of antibiotics lead to residual antibiotics in milk and can lead to anti-microbial resistance on the long run. An alternative treatment which is not synthetic in nature can be used. This treatment can be made of betel leaves and castor oil. The mixed paste is offered orally as well as applied on the udder. This practice is effective, low-cost and climate resilient.

records.title: Herbal treatment of chronic diarrhoea in cattle and small ruminants
records.description:
Description

1. Diarrhoea

Unhygienic food and water causes diarrhoea. Organisms, such as bacteria, enter the body, replicate in intestine and cause diarrhoea. It is associated with foul smell and shooting loose motion. Diarrhoea causes loss of water and salts from the body of the animals which make them dull, inactive and lying low. Diarrhoea can be treated with an easy yet effective practice. For this Harida/Chebulic myroban (Terminalia Chebula) is used along with yogurt or curd from cow milk or goat milk. Terminalia chebula contains chebulin, chebulic acid and yogurt contains RNAase enzyme. Both elements help stop the activities of the organism and stop diarrhoea.

1.1 Symptoms

  • Watery, shooting, foul smelling diarrhoea.
  • Undigested food materials come out with stool.
  • The animal looses water, salts from the body and becomes thirsty.

1.2 Causes

  • Under digestion.
  • Contaminated food and fodder.
  • Excess eating of proteinous diet.
  • Excess eating of newly sprouted green grass in rainy season.
  • Grass and crop plants sprayed with pesticides.
  • Contaminated drinking water.

2. Remedy

Curd from cow milk or goat milk cures diarrhoea due to its antimicrobial effect.

2.1 For an adult cow

  • Harida or chebula powder: 100 to 150 g.
  • Yogurt or cow curd: 50 ml.

Herbal treatment of chronic diarrhoea in cattle and small ruminants

Chronic diarrhoea in grazing animals is common in tropical livestock. Infection by bacteria and virus lead to diarrhoea. Use of antibiotics is costly and has residual effects through milk and meat. The traditional use of Chebulic myrobalan (Terminali chebula) along with curd from cow or goat milk is an effective way. Description

1. Diarrhoea

Unhygienic food and water causes diarrhoea. Organisms, such as bacteria, enter the body, replicate in intestine and cause diarrhoea. It is associated with foul smell and shooting loose motion. Diarrhoea causes loss of water and salts from the body of the animals which make them dull, inactive and lying low. Diarrhoea can be treated with an easy yet effective practice. For this Harida/Chebulic myroban (Terminalia Chebula) is used along with yogurt or curd from cow milk or goat milk. Terminalia chebula contains chebulin, chebulic acid and yogurt contains RNAase enzyme. Both elements help stop the activities of the organism and stop diarrhoea.

records.title: Treating anoestrus cases in cattle and small ruminants
records.description:
Description

1. Oestrus

A heifer or an adult cow, female sheep and goat comes to heat or oestrus for breeding. If a heifer, cow, sheep or goat does not come to heat, then there is a problem due to lack of hormones, and as a consequence they cannot become mothers. This condition of not coming to heat is called as anoestrus.

1.1 Symptoms

  • Heifers and cows do not come to heat or anoestrus.
  • The animal does not allow mounting by bulls.
  • There is no sign of frequent unrest and belowing as in case of heat.
  • Cow even if conceives, aborts.
  • There is absence of full and complete heat.

1.2 Causes

  • Lack of balanced, nutritious food which help produce hormone that induces heat.
  • Defect in hormone secretion.
  • Defect in the uterine and allied organs.

2. Remedy

Herbally the cases of anoestrus in animals is treated with seeds of nutmeg. Nutmeg (Myristica fragrans) seeds are also used as spices for food.

Scientifically nut meg contains myristic acid, elemicin, safrole, trimyristin, macelignan and other phytohormones like molecules which help in bringing heifers and cows to heat.

One nutmeg seed (Myristica fragrans) locally called Jaiphal is grounded to powder and mixed with 20 to 25 g of jaggery. A bolus from the mixture is prepared and offered to the cow. After a month (21 to30 days), the animal comes to heat. If not, the process can be repeated.

records.title: Pregnancy testing in livestock by bio-indicator method
records.description:
Description

1. Pregnancy test in livestock

Generally trained vets do pregnancy testing in cows. They physically check by par rectal examination. In an early stage of conceive like in 15 days post conceive, physical testing cannot give the right diagnosis.

In the absence of modern pregnancy tests in rural areas, one can easily monitor the germination of pulse by soaking them in cows's urine. This method is easily available and cost-effective.

A pregnant cow’s urine contains some hormones like progesterone and others, which inhibit germination. Presence of these germination inhibition factors are detected by pulses like mung (Paseolus mungo) after soaking in urine.

The test can be done when there is no clear-cut symptom of pregnancy of cows.

2. Alternative testing method

Alternative testing methods are needed for the following reasons:

  • Lack of modern tests in rural to detect pregnancy in early days.
  • Non-availability of trained vets in remote field situations.

3. Method and application

The urine of the tested cows is collected in a cup. In another cup, a normal tap water is collected. One hundred green pulses are soaked in the cup containing urine and another hundred are soaked in the cup containing normal water. Pulses are soaked for six to seven hours or overnight. In the next day, seeds soaked in urine and soaked in water are revived and are allowed to germinate over 12 to 20 hours. Then germinated seeds are counted. The seeds soaked in water, must give 90 to 100 percent germination. If the percentage is much lower, then there is something wrong with the seeds. In the case of urine soaked seeds, the germinations are counted. If it is zero or less than 10, the cow is pregnant. If it is more than 10 then the cow is not pregnant.

This practice is simple, low-cost and can detect early pregnancy.

Figure 1. Gram seeds

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/ Pathe Pathshala

Figure 2. Germination of seeds after soaking in urine

©Innovate Orissa Initiative/ Pathe Pathshala

4. Validation of the practice

This practice was applied by 500 livestock keepers in India.

records.title: Couvain plâtré: Une maladie fongique du couvain
records.description:
La description

1. Introduction

Le couvain plâtré est une maladie fongique causée par le champignon Ascosphaera apis, qui affecte l'intestin du couvain. Les larves d'abeilles s'infectent en ingérant des spores d'Ascosphaera apis avec de la nourriture. Les spores germent dans les intestins, ce qui entraîne la mort des larves, généralement après operculation. Chaque larve morte produit des milliards de spores et, si elles ne sont pas éliminées par les abeilles ouvrières, elles peuvent rester infectieuses pendant plusieurs années dans la ruche. Le couvain situé sur les bords des cadres (généralement le couvain de faux-bourdons) est le plus touché car c'est là qu'il est le plus difficile de contrôler la température.

2. Symptômes

La maladie est transmise par l'ingestion d'aliments infectés contenant des spores fongiques. Les larves peuvent être touchées à différents stades de leur vie, plus fréquemment au troisième ou quatrième jour de leur vie. Elles meurent ensuite au cours des deux premiers jours qui suivent l'operculation, de sorte que les abeilles doivent désoperculer les cellules pour éliminer les larves mortes. Le couvain plâtré produit une momification et/ou une calcification des larves (figure 1). Tout d'abord, les larves apparaissent molles et prennent la forme hexagonale de la cellule. Ensuite, elles se dessèchent et deviennent dures. La plupart des larves affectées restent blanches mais certaines deviennent grises ou noires (figure 2). La présence de petits cailloux (le couvain plâtré) sur le plancher ou à l'entrée de la ruche est typique.

Figure 1. Momification des larves à l'intérieur des cellules

©www.beeinformed.org/Rob Snyder 

Figure 2. Les larves affectées par le couvain restent blanches mais certaines deviennent grises ou noires

©ASL VT/Massimo Palazzetti

L'Ascosphaera apis se développe mieux dans les larves situées en bordure du couvain, où il est plus froid. Ce phénomène se produit surtout pendant la croissance de la colonie au printemps, lorsqu'il n'y a pas assez d'abeilles adultes pour assurer un contrôle adéquat de la température du nid sur toute la zone de couvain. Les colonies moins peuplées et plus faibles sont plus sensibles car les abeilles ne sont pas capables de garder tout le couvain au chaud. Les larves de faux-bourdons sont généralement les plus touchées en raison de leur emplacement sur les bords du couvain. De basses températures, une humidité élevée dans le rucher et une mauvaise ventilation des ruches contribuent à aggraver la maladie.

3. Transmission

À l'intérieur de la ruche, cette maladie est transmise par les aliments infectés qui contiennent les spores fongiques. Ces spores sont très infectieuses et peuvent facilement se propager d'une ruche à l'autre par le pillage et la dérive ainsi que par les points d’eau.

En outre, l'apiculteur peut facilement propager la maladie entre les ruches et entre les ruchers en utilisant du matériel contaminé et en transférant du pollen contaminé vers des ruches saines. Les spores du couvain plâtré peuvent rester contagieuses jusqu'à 15 ans, voire plus, dans le matériel apicole et dans le sol.

Éviter toute activité entraînant une perte de chaleur dans les colonies peut contribuer à prévenir la maladie du couvain plâtré. Parmi les activités qui provoquent des pertes de chaleur, on peut citer:

  • des inspections trop nombreuses et/ou trop longues des ruches pendant l'hiver ou les jours froids;
  • les divisions de colonies pour l'essaimage artificiel;
  • l'agrandissement du nid avec interposition de rayons munis de feuilles de cire entre les rayons de couvain, en particulier pendant les périodes défavorables à la construction des rayons de cire, comme au début du printemps, en automne ou en hiver, lorsque les abeilles ne trouvent pas suffisamment de ressources alimentaires.

Le couvain plâtré peut apparaître dans les ruches après un traitement antibiotique en raison d'un manque de compétition microbienne.

4. Diagnostic

L'apiculteur peut observer des abeilles momifiées dures, blanches à gris-noir, ratatinées dans les rayons de couvain et dans et autour de la ruche.

5. Contrôle

De nombreux médicaments ont été testés mais la persistance des spores rend l'éradication de la maladie impossible. La meilleure solution semble être l'administration de sirop de saccharose (1 pour 1), acidifié avec du jus de citron, du vinaigre ou de la poudre d'acide ascorbique, jusqu'à atteindre un pH de 4. La prévention peut également être assurée par l'application de bonnes pratiques apicoles (BPA) dans le rucher. Le tableau 1 donne un aperçu des bonnes pratiques à adopter pour maintenir des colonies saines et prévenir les maladies du couvain.

Tableau 1. Bonnes pratiques apicoles pour la gestion de la maladie du couvain plâtré
Recommandation Avantages et raisons d’adopter cette pratique
Placez vos ruches dans des endroits appropriés, correctement exposés au soleil et en évitant les zones humides ; évitez d’exposer le trou de vol aux vents dominants. Réduit l'humidité et le stress thermique des abeilles.
Sélectionnez des reines résistantes. Réduit le nombre de ruches touchées par le couvain plâtré.
Veillez à ce que la ruche dispose à tout moment de réserves alimentaires suffisantes et fournissez une alimentation artificielle si nécessaire. Réduit le stress nutritionnel dans les colonies.

La maladie du couvain plâtré provoque fréquemment des pertes au printemps mais l'évolution de la maladie est généralement bénigne. Les colonies touchées peuvent se rétablir par elles-mêmes, surtout si elles augmentent leur population. Cela se produit notamment dans des conditions environnementales favorables, comme les jours ensoleillés au printemps et au début de l'été, avec la présence de ressources nutritionnelles abondantes.

6. Les zones agroecologiques

  • Multiple.

7. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Nosemosis: a fungal disease of adult honeybees: ID 8413.
  • Bonnes pratiques apicoles: ID 8674.
  • Les virus des abeilles: ID 8786.
  • Les principales maladies des abeilles: ID 8714.
  • Loque américaine: la plus grave maladie bactérienne du couvain: ID 10114.
  • Amibiase: une maladie parasitaire des abeilles adultes: ID 10006.
  • Small hive beetle (SHB): ID 10020.
  • Couvain pétrifié (aspergillose): Une maladie fongique du couvain et des abeilles adultes: ID 10130.
  • Tropilaelapsose: Une maladie parasitaire du couvain: ID 10132.

Cette fiche technique est disponible en anglais: ID 9002.

8. Les objectifs atteints par le project

8.1 L’efficacité d'utilisation des ressources

Implementation of the practices and measures recommended above allows for improved management of bees and ensures better colony health.

Le couvain plâtré produit une momification et/ou une calcification des larves (figure 1). Tout d'abord, les larves apparaissent molles et prennent la forme hexagonale de la cellule. Ensuite, elles se dessèchent et deviennent dures. La plupart des larves affectées restent blanches mais certaines deviennent grises ou noires (figure 2). La présence de petits cailloux (le couvain plâtré) sur le plancher ou à l'entrée de la ruche est typique.

Figure 1. Momification des larves à l'intérieur des cellules

©www.beeinformed.org/Rob Snyder 

Figure 2. Les larves affectées par le couvain restent blanches mais certaines deviennent grises ou noires

©ASL VT/Massimo Palazzetti

L'Ascosphaera apis se développe mieux dans les larves situées en bordure du couvain, où il est plus froid. Ce phénomène se produit surtout pendant la croissance de la colonie au printemps, lorsqu'il n'y a pas assez d'abeilles adultes pour assurer un contrôle adéquat de la température du nid sur toute la zone de couvain. Les colonies moins peuplées et plus faibles sont plus sensibles car les abeilles ne sont pas capables de garder tout le couvain au chaud. Les larves de faux-bourdons sont généralement les plus touchées en raison de leur emplacement sur les bords du couvain. De basses températures, une humidité élevée dans le rucher et une mauvaise ventilation des ruches contribuent à aggraver la maladie.

3. Transmission

À l'intérieur de la ruche, cette maladie est transmise par les aliments infectés qui contiennent les spores fongiques. Ces spores sont très infectieuses et peuvent facilement se propager d'une ruche à l'autre par le pillage et la dérive ainsi que par les points d’eau.

En outre, l'apiculteur peut facilement propager la maladie entre les ruches et entre les ruchers en utilisant du matériel contaminé et en transférant du pollen contaminé vers des ruches saines. Les spores du couvain plâtré peuvent rester contagieuses jusqu'à 15 ans, voire plus, dans le matériel apicole et dans le sol.

Éviter toute activité entraînant une perte de chaleur dans les colonies peut contribuer à prévenir la maladie du couvain plâtré. Parmi les activités qui provoquent des pertes de chaleur, on peut citer:

  • des inspections trop nombreuses et/ou trop longues des ruches pendant l'hiver ou les jours froids;
  • les divisions de colonies pour l'essaimage artificiel;
  • l'agrandissement du nid avec interposition de rayons munis de feuilles de cire entre les rayons de couvain, en particulier pendant les périodes défavorables à la construction des rayons de cire, comme au début du printemps, en automne ou en hiver, lorsque les abeilles ne trouvent pas suffisamment de ressources alimentaires.

Le couvain plâtré peut apparaître dans les ruches après un traitement antibiotique en raison d'un manque de compétition microbienne.

4. Diagnostic

L'apiculteur peut observer des abeilles momifiées dures, blanches à gris-noir, ratatinées dans les rayons de couvain et dans et autour de la ruche.

5. Contrôle

De nombreux médicaments ont été testés mais la persistance des spores rend l'éradication de la maladie impossible. La meilleure solution semble être l'administration de sirop de saccharose (1 pour 1), acidifié avec du jus de citron, du vinaigre ou de la poudre d'acide ascorbique, jusqu'à atteindre un pH de 4. La prévention peut également être assurée par l'application de bonnes pratiques apicoles (BPA) dans le rucher. Le tableau 1 donne un aperçu des bonnes pratiques à adopter pour maintenir des colonies saines et prévenir les maladies du couvain.

Tableau 1. Bonnes pratiques apicoles pour la gestion de la maladie du couvain plâtré
Recommandation Avantages et raisons d’adopter cette pratique
Placez vos ruches dans des endroits appropriés, correctement exposés au soleil et en évitant les zones humides ; évitez d’exposer le trou de vol aux vents dominants. Réduit l'humidité et le stress thermique des abeilles.
Sélectionnez des reines résistantes. Réduit le nombre de ruches touchées par le couvain plâtré.
Veillez à ce que la ruche dispose à tout moment de réserves alimentaires suffisantes et fournissez une alimentation artificielle si nécessaire. Réduit le stress nutritionnel dans les colonies.

La maladie du couvain plâtré provoque fréquemment des pertes au printemps mais l'évolution de la maladie est généralement bénigne. Les colonies touchées peuvent se rétablir par elles-mêmes, surtout si elles augmentent leur population. Cela se produit notamment dans des conditions environnementales favorables, comme les jours ensoleillés au printemps et au début de l'été, avec la présence de ressources nutritionnelles abondantes.

6. Les zones agroecologiques

  • Multiple.

  • Small hive beetle (SHB): ID 10020.

Cette maladie du couvain est présente dans le monde entier, en particulier pendant la croissance de la colonie au printemps, lorsqu'il n'y a pas assez d'abeilles adultes dans la ruche pour maintenir au chaud le couvain en expansion rapide. records.title: Couvain pétrifié (aspergillose): Une maladie fongique du couvain et des abeilles adultes
records.description:
La description

1. Introduction

Le couvain pétrifié est une maladie fongique causée par différentes espèces de champignons appartenant au genre Aspergillus. Elle affecte les abeilles adultes et le couvain (larves et pupes). Les principales espèces de champignons responsables de cette maladie chez les abeilles domestiques sont Aspergillus flavus et, moins fréquemment, Aspergillus fumigatus et Aspergillus niger. La maladie se transmet par voie alimentaire ou par un contact direct. Des larves momifiées vertes peuvent être observées dans les rayons du couvain ainsi que sur le plancher ou la planche de vol. Les larves momifiées ressemblent à de petites pierres blanches, jaunes ou vertes et sont difficiles à écraser, contrairement aux larves affectées par le couvain plâtré, lesquelles ressemblent à une éponge.

La température idéale pour le développement des champignons se situe entre 33° C et 37° C, mais ils peuvent aussi se multiplier à des températures comprises entre 7° C et 40° C. L'exposition à des températures supérieures à 60° C pendant au moins 30 minutes peut dévitaliser à la fois les spores et les hyphes, ces longues structures filamenteuses et ramifiées des champignons.

2. Symptômes

Chez les larves d'abeilles, l'infection donne naissance à un anneau caractéristique près de la tête des larves infectées. Tout d’abord, les larves mortes ont une apparence blanche et molle. Ensuite, elles moisissent et se recouvrent souvent d'une sorte de feutre constitué de spores fongiques. Ce feutre peut présenter différentes couleurs, selon l'espèce d'Aspergillus impliquée: vert jaunâtre dans le cas d'A. Flavus; gris-vert dans le cas d'A. fumigatus; et noir dans le cas d'A. niger. Lorsque les larves meurent, ce qui se produit dans les cellules operculées, leur corps se durcit et ressemble à une petite pierre, difficile à écraser; d'où le nom de «couvain pétrifié». Les larves momifiées sont difficiles à retirer des cellules du couvain, même avec des pincettes.

Les abeilles adultes retirent les larves mortes des cellules: on peut ainsi trouver des larves momifiées vertes sur le plancher ou le trou de vol de la ruche.

Dans de rares cas, l'infection peut également affecter des abeilles adultes, par ingestion d'aliments contaminés par ce champignon. Les abeilles infectées apparaîtront initialement excitées et agitées; la phase suivante est la paralysie, l'incapacité de voler puis la mort, laquelle se produit généralement loin de la ruche.

Bien qu’on ait observé la mort de colonies entières d'abeilles affectées par ce champignon, cette maladie est généralement passagère et a tendance à être surmontée naturellement.

3. Transmission

La maladie est transmise par des aliments (miel et pollen) contenant des spores fongiques ou par contact direct entre les abeilles.

La maladie peut se propager des ruches malades aux ruches saines par la dérive des abeilles infectées, le pillage par des abeilles en bonne santé des ruches infectées ou l'essaimage. L'apiculteur peut également transmettre la maladie en utilisant des outils infectés ou en déplaçant les rayons des colonies malades vers des colonies saines.

4. Diagnostic

L'un des premiers signes de la maladie est un couvain présentant une structure tachetée et irrégulière (quantité élevée de cellules vides, mélangées avec des cellules contenant des œufs, des larves et des nymphes de tous âges).

Les larves apparaissent d'abord ridées, de couleur crème et perdent leur segmentation. Elles changent ensuite de couleur, passant du gris au verdâtre. Enfin, les larves se momifient, adhérant aux parois cellulaires, ce qui les rend difficiles à éliminer (Figure 1). La momie peut être recouverte d'un feutre blanc grisâtre ou bien jaune verdâtre, gris-vert ou noir, selon l'espèce fongique de la maladie.

Figure 1. Les larves affectées par le couvain pétrifié se momifient, adhérant aux parois cellulaires, ce qui les rend difficiles à éliminer

©http://kathykeatleygarvey.com//Kathy Garvey

En ce qui concerne les abeilles adultes, il arrive d’en trouver, paralysées, sur les rayons infectés. Le corps de ces abeilles mortes devient dur. En cas d'humidité élevée, leur corps peut se recouvrir d'un feutre fongique gris-blanc, typique de l'infection.

L'identification positive du champignon requiert un laboratoire spécialisé capable d’effectuer son identification biomoléculaire ou sa culture: Aspergillus spp. peut être cultivé sur du dextrose de pomme de terre ou sur des géloses de Sabouraud au dextrose.

De nombreuses espèces d'Aspergillus peuvent produire des aflatoxines, lesquelles sont cancérigènes pour l'homme lorsqu'elles sont ingérées par voie orale (par exemple via des produits de la ruche contaminés, en particulier le pollen). C’est pour cette raison que, dans de nombreux pays, la maladie du couvain pétrifié doit être signalée aux autorités sanitaires compétentes dès qu’elle est diagnostiquée. Des mesures doivent être prises pour protéger la santé des apiculteurs et des consommateurs.

5. Prévention

Les apiculteurs doivent détruire les rayons moisis et gravement infectés qui contiennent du couvain touché par la maladie ; que ce soit pour la consommation humaine ou à destination de colonies saines, ils ne peuvent utiliser aucun des produits récoltés à partir de colonies malades (par exemple, miel, pollen, gelée royale, cire et propolis).

L'adoption des bonnes pratiques apicoles (BPA) est le moyen le plus efficace pour prévenir la maladie. Le tableau 1 présente une liste de bonnes pratiques qui peuvent aider à maintenir des colonies saines et à prévenir la maladie.

Tableau 1. Bonnes pratiques apicoles pour la prévention du couvain pétrifié
Recommandation Avantages et raisons pour adopter cette pratique
Choisissez un bon emplacement pour le rucher, de préférence avec une bonne exposition au soleil, en évitant les zones humides. Rend difficile le développement des champignons.

Veillez à une bonne conduite de la ruche en:

  • favorisant la ventilation de la ruche grâce à une ouverture dans le toit, ou trou d’aération (également en hiver);
  • empêchant l'eau de pénétrer dans la ruche;
  • réduisant le nombre de rayons pour une bonne préparation de l’hivernage;
  • retirant les rayons non peuplés en hiver et donc en ne laissant que des rayons peuplés.
 L'humidité est un environnement favorable pour le développement des champignons.
Remplacez au moins un tiers des rayons à couvain chaque année. Réduit la population microbienne (champignons inclus) dans la ruche.
Assurez-vous que les colonies aient suffisamment de nourriture pendant les périodes de disette. Fournissez une alimentation supplémentaire si nécessaire. Éviter le stress nutritionnel réduit le risque d’infection.
Ne conservez que les colonies fortes dans le rucher. Les colonies plus faibles mais qui sont saines doivent être réunies à une colonie plus forte. Les colonies faibles peuvent être plus exposées aux maladies que les colonies saines.
Veillez à un bon équilibre entre les abeilles adultes et le couvain, surtout au printemps. Au printemps, la taille du couvain à nourrir augmente. Le manque d'abeilles adultes provoque un stress nutritionnel.
Ne nourrissez pas les abeilles avec du pollen moisi et ne gardez pas de couvain sur des rayons moisis. Bien souvent, ces rayons moisis se trouvent sur les cadres de rive qui, en hiver, restent inutilisés à l'intérieur des ruches (en position latérale / externe). Les rayons moisis ont généralement une couleur blanchâtre, opaque, ou verdâtre. Ils sont fortement contaminés par les champignons.

6. Contrôle

Des recherches supplémentaires sont nécessaires pour déterminer les mesures de contrôle appropriées à adopter. Le remplacement de la reine peut s’avérer très utile. À ce jour, il n'existe aucun traitement homologué pour lutter contre cette infection chez les abeilles, bien que, expérimentalement, on ait observé que les huiles essentielles de cannelle (Cinnamomum zeylanicum), de Litsea cubeba et de géranium (Pelargonium graveolens), ainsi que leurs mélanges, sont capables de contenir le développement de ce champignon. La sélection génétique des abeilles pour leur résistance au couvain pétrifié constitue une piste intéressante à approfondir car on a observé des prédispositions génétiques différentes d'une colonie à l'autre.

7. Impact du couvain pétrifié sur la santé humaine

Les champignons responsables du couvain pétrifié se trouvent partout dans le sol et sont capables d'induire des maladies chez les insectes, les oiseaux, les mammifères et aussi chez les humains, ce qui en fait une maladie zoonotique (maladie qui peut être transmise des animaux vers l’être humain).

Chez l'homme, ce champignon peut provoquer des maladies respiratoires, telles que des infections pulmonaires (aspergillose broncho-pulmonaire et aspergillome, ou aspergillose pulmonaire chronique) ou une bronchite allergique, en cas d'inhalation. Elle peut également provoquer des infections des yeux, du pharynx, de la peau et des plaies ouvertes en cas de contact direct avec le couvain, des abeilles ou des rayons infectés.

En outre, la multiplication de champignons appartenant au genre Aspergillus peut être responsable de la production de mycotoxines spécifiques qui peuvent être dangereuses lorsqu'elles sont transmises par voie orale aux animaux et aux humains. Dans le cas du couvain pétrifié, les mycotoxines peuvent être transmises à l'homme par la consommation de pollen.

8. Les zones agroecologiques

  • Multiple.

9. Les fiches techniques associées

  • Tropilaelapsose: Une maladie parasitaire du couvain: ID 10132.
  • Couvain pétrifié (aspergillose): Une maladie fongique du couvain et des abeilles adultes: ID 10130.
  • Nosemosis: a fungal disease of adult honeybees: ID 8413.
  • Bonnes pratiques apicoles: ID 8674.
  • Les virus des abeilles: ID 8786.
  • Les principales maladies des abeilles: ID 8714.
  • Loque américaine: la plus grave maladie bactérienne du couvain: ID 10114.
  • Amibiase: une maladie parasitaire des abeilles adultes: ID 10006.
  • Amoebiasis: a parasitic disease of adult honeybees: ID 10019.
  • Small hive beetle (SHB): ID 10020.

10. Les objectifs atteints par le project

10.1 L’efficacité d'utilisation des ressources

Implementation of the practices and measures recommended above allows for improved beehive management and ensures better colony health.

10.2 La technologie favorable aux populations pauvres

The practice allows poor and vulnerable households to be more aware of the possible transmission of the fungi to other animals and humans, and to learn how to avoid it. Through this awareness, poor households can prevent transmission, and so prevent detrimental effects on their health and bee health. Through increased colony health, yield loss caused by disease can also be limited.
