_annotations.field_shorter_description:
Le miel est un aliment pur et naturel que les abeilles conservent dans la ruche, dans les alvéoles. Pour extraire le miel des rayons de cire dans de bonnes conditions d’hygiène, il existe différentes méthodes : l’extraction par égouttage (par gravité) ou par pressage pour les apiculteurs utilisant des ruches à rayons fixes ou des ruches à barrettes ou bien l’extraction par centrifugation pour les apiculteurs utilisant des ruches à cadres.

Cette fiche présente un modèle de pressoir développé par M. Fobasso, apiculteur camerounais expérimenté, qui permet d’extraire le miel de plusieurs ruches en même temps. La fiche explique comment fabriquer le pressoir et comment extraire le miel par pressage avec l’extracteur.

Cette fiche technique est aussi disponible en: Anglais (ID10140)

records.title: Honey extracted by pressing: wooden honey press from Cameroon
records.description:
Description

1.       Principle of extraction of honey by pressing

The extraction of honey using a press is used all over the world, mainly by beekeepers using fixed-comb hives (African straw hive, trunk hive, terracotta canary hive or hives made with other local materials) or movable comb hives or topbar hives such as the La Grande hive, the Fonge hive (model with topbars) or the Kenyan topbar hive. Combs collected from natural hives in the wild can also be extracted with this method.

During harvesting in the apiary, honeycombs are placed in a bucket with a lid, preferably airtight to prevent the honey from:

-        capturing atmospheric moisture [1];

-        capturing unwanted odors;

-        being contaminated with impurities such as dust;

-        attracting bees and other insects.

The combs harvested for extraction must be (i) operculated (capped) for at least 80% or even better if they are completely operculated, (ii) should not be black (old brood combs) and (iii) should not show any traces of mold (or green rot on the surface), as shown in Figure 1. The moldy parts will be cut off and discarded.

[1] As a reminder, honey is a hygroscopic product, meaning that it absorbs moisture from the environment, which can affect its preservation. Honey with too high a humidity, will ferment over time, and can no longer be consumed/marketed.

Figure 1. Combs containing traces of mold - © MMH

Combs that are not capped for at least 80% should be left to the colony to feed the brood. Should such a comb be removed by accident, then the uncapped part of the comb containing unripe honey will be cut from the capped part of the comb using a sharp knife and placed in a separate bucket for family consumption. Combs containing brood should under no circumstances be removed and harvested. If you have inadvertently harvested a comb containing a little brood, cut the brood. The part with brood is either discarded or consumed directly. Indeed, brood is a very nutritious food and rich in proteins, but should be removed from the hive with moderation not to weaken the colony.

The buckets used should be food grade. Do not use buckets that have contained paint, chemicals, gasoline, oil, etc. Even if they have been thoroughly washed, they keep odors and traces of products that can contaminate the honey.

The rest of the manipulations take place in a honey house, private or collective. If you do not have access to a honey house, you can work in a room of the house. It must be clean and have mosquito nets on the windows. If you do not have mosquito nets and/or if the windows and doors are not tightly closed, the smell of honey will attract bees and other insects. The place is at risk of being invaded and you won’t be able to continue to work. The room must be away as far as possible from bad odors (toilet, cattle stable, smoke from the kitchen, etc.) and, may not be used as a storage room for chemicals (pesticides, cleaning products, gasoline, etc.) or food coated with preservatives. These may contaminate the honey during extraction.

Arrived at the honey house, wash your hands and make sure all utensils are clean. The honey and wax combs are cut into pieces in the bucket with a knife and then crushed or grinded, using a large wooden spoon. There are manual or electric grinders available on the international market, but they are quite expensive. The crushed combs are poured either directly in the rack of the press or in a bag arranged in the press. The bag is of loosely woven canvas material (fabrics, nylon or plastic) that will let honey through and retain most of the wax.

The advantage of the honey pressing system over dripping is that it is faster. As a reminder, dripping is a honey extraction method that consists of letting the honey drip (drain) from the honeycombs previously broken into small pieces (or crushed) and arranged on a filter or sieve above a bucket. In the case of pressing, honey is less in contact with the air. Therefore, it does not have time to capture moisture from the air and is not oxidized by the oxygen contained in the air (loss of flavor). The honey is filtered directly at the exit of the press and stored in airtight containers: food grade plastic buckets or stainless-steel settling tanks. Pressing honey retains its aromas better because it is less oxidized.

2.       Description of the press developed by Mr. Fobasso

It is a manual hydraulic press using a car jack. It has a capacity of about 30 liters. Honey is in contact only with the wooden parts of the press.

Figure 2 presents an annotated picture of the press.   Specific parts of the press are then described in detail to present a clear overview of the main parts of the press.

Figure 2. Photo of the hydraulic press – © PROCEFFA/Jospeh Dinga

2.1        Description and role of each piece of the press

- The rectangular iron bar is a rectangular metal tube. It is fixed with nuts on the 2 threaded rods and must withstand the pressure that the hydraulic jack will apply on the crushed honeycombs (Figure 3, (A)).

- The two metal threaded rods are positioned along the sides of the press chamber and the wooden collection tray (Figure 3, (A)). They are fixed at the base by an inverted U-profile metal piece placed under the tray (Figure 3, (B)) and held in place by the flat inverted V rods (Figure 3, (C)). Their role is to position and fix the rectangular iron bar above, so that the jack can be blocked and apply pressure on the wax and honeycombs in the press cage.

- The iron inverted V-shaped rods (Figure 3, (C)): their role is to support and reinforce the stability and position of the threaded rods at the base of the wooden collection tray. A ring or tube that holds the threaded rod is attached. The inverted V-shaped rods are fixed to the collection tray, on both sides, by bolds and nuts.

Figure 3. (A) the rectangular metal bar is fixed on the threaded rods, (B) inverted U-profile metal piece under the collection tray, and (C) flat inverted V-shaped rods - © MMH/Elsa Demoulin

- The wooden press cage (Figure 4, (D)) consists of 28 wooden bars about 50 cm long and 3 cm wide. These are spaced 4 to 5 millimeters apart. The bars are held in place by two rectangular metal structures to which each bar is fixed with a flat-headed screw (inner side of the cage) and a nut (outer side of the cage). The sides of the cage measure about 25 cm wide (30 cm with the metal structures protruding) and 50 cm high.

- The rectangular wooden collection tray (Figure 4, (E)) is used to collect honey during the pressing operation. Its dimensions are about 40 cm by 50 cm with an edge high of 10 cm.

- The legs of the structure are 40 cm high (Figure 4, (E) and (F)). They must be strong enough to support the weight of a volume of 30 liters of crushed combs as well as the pressure that will be applied by the jack to the bag filled with crushed honeycombs.

Figure 4. (D) wooden press cage, (E) collection tray for honey, and (F) the legs of the press are fixed to the wooden collection tray – © Joseph Dinga (4D) and Elsa Demoulin (4 E and F)

- The dripping or drainage hole (Figure 5) is used to evacuate the honey, pressed by the jack and filtered through the wooden cage, which has been accumulated in the tray during the pressing operation. A clean and dry food grade bucket is placed on the ground under the hole in order to collect the honey. It is equipped with a lid to block the honey in the tray if necessary.

Figure 5. Drainage hole with lid – © MMH/Elsa Demoulin

2.2        Other essential parts and their use: the jack and wedges

- Pieces of wood, also called wedges or blocks (Figure 6 (B)) are distributed in the press cage on the canvas bag containing the honeycombs in order to apply regular pressure on the entire surface of the bag.

- The hydraulic jack (Figure 6 (A)) is then arranged on these wedges and abutted on top against the rectangular metal piece.

Figure 6. (A) hydraulic jack and (B) wooden wedges/blocks – © Joseph Dinga

3.       Some tips before starting

Check that you have all the parts of the press clean and available.

Place a food grade bucket under the drainage hole of the press. Place a fine mesh filter on the bucket to rid the honey of the smallest debris that will pass through the press cage (Figure 7).

Figure 7. (A) different fine mesh filters: canvas on the left and stainless-steel on the right and (B) metal filter arranged on a food grade bucket – © MMH/Elsa Demoulin

Remove the cap from the drain hole if you want the honey to flow directly into the bucket during the pressing operation. Otherwise, you can wait until you have a certain amount of honey in the tray before opening the lid.

You are now ready to start pressing operations.

4.       How to use the press

1) The cut and crushed honey combs are poured into a fine-meshed bag, which is itself already placed in the press cage of the press. By pouring them, the honey will already begin to flow through the bag, this is why this operation must be carried out directly with the bag inside the press.  Close the bag.

2) The wooden wedges/blocks are distributed on the closed canvas bag, in order to apply regular pressure on the entire surface of the bag.

3) The hydraulic jack is then placed on top of the wedges and held in place at the top by the rectangular iron bar. The jack is then operated manually to compress the contents of the press cage by raising and lowering the handle of the jack. The jack will go down into the cage, little by little. As the pressure on the combs increases, the honey starts flowing through the wooden bars of the press cage onto the collection tray. Wooden wedges are regularly added under the jack to ensure that all the honey is removed from the combs.

5.       Advantages and disadvantages of this handmade press

5.1        The advantages of the press

  • It is made with quality wood available locally. The wood comes from sustainably managed forests where trees are cut down at the recommended age and season. It is solid wood that does not rot and has no smell. It is of course easier and cheaper to make this type of press in regions rich in wood and forests.

  • It is cheaper than similar imported presses.

  • It is easy to use and if the legs are strong enough, it can press up to 60 liters of honeycombs at once.

  • In general, users confirm its ease of use. It is easy to clean after use.

  • It can be dismantled and is easy to transport. Once installed, beekeepers not disassemble it anymore.

  • This model is interesting because, metal parts are not in contact with honey, which is why it is not necessary to use stainless metal, unlike many honey press models that consist of a central metal rod.

Figure 8. Two dismantled presses – © Joseph Dinga

5.2        The disadvantages of the press

Of course, it can always be improved.

  • One of the disadvantages for some beekeepers is that it requires the purchase of a jack, not always easy to find and which increases the price of the press. The jack can possibly be replaced by large bricks added little by little during the pressing operation. It will be less efficient and less fast because, the beekeeper will have to wait and come back later (1 hour later for example) to add pressure by adding new bricks.

  • The manufacturing of this press requires either good carpentry skills or working with well-equipped carpenters to obtain the best result (strength and precision).

  • The structure can be solidified by attaching two flat crossed metal bars to the legs as illustrated in Figure 9 below and to the 4 sides.

Figure 9. Illustration of the reinforcement of the legs of the press with crossed metal bars – © Elsa Demoulin, 2019

5.3        Feedback

The press has been used in schools in Cameroon. Users are very satisfied with the press and confirm the need for reinforcement of the legs of the structure.

6.       Presentation of Mr. Fobasso

The honey press model presented here is a model developed by Mr. Fobasso Etienne, beekeeper since the 1990s in Cameroon. He studied beekeeping in Cameroon but also at the University of Tor Vergata in Italy, in the year 2000. He owns an apiary of more than 2 000 hives of different models.

Skilled in carpentry, Mr. Fobasso made his first press in 2002 inspired by models found in beekeeping books. He then improved his model from year to year after his return from the training in Italy. It is one of the first wooden presses developed in Cameroon. It is currently used throughout the country.

- Pieces of wood, also called wedges or blocks (Figure 6 (B)) are distributed in the press cage on the canvas bag containing the honeycombs in order to apply regular pressure on the entire surface of the bag.

- The hydraulic jack (Figure 6 (A)) is then arranged on these wedges and abutted on top against the rectangular metal piece.

Figure 6. (A) hydraulic jack and (B) wooden wedges/blocks – © Joseph Dinga

3.       Some tips before starting

Check that you have all the parts of the press clean and available.

Place a food grade bucket under the drainage hole of the press. Place a fine mesh filter on the bucket to rid the honey of the smallest debris that will pass through the press cage (Figure 7).

Figure 7. (A) different fine mesh filters: canvas on the left and stainless-steel on the right and (B) metal filter arranged on a food grade bucket – © MMH/Elsa Demoulin

Remove the cap from the drain hole if you want the honey to flow directly into the bucket during the pressing operation. Otherwise, you can wait until you have a certain amount of honey in the tray before opening the lid.

You are now ready to start pressing operations.

4.       How to use the press

1) The cut and crushed honey combs are poured into a fine-meshed bag, which is itself already placed in the press cage of the press. By pouring them, the honey will already begin to flow through the bag, this is why this operation must be carried out directly with the bag inside the press.  Close the bag.

2) The wooden wedges/blocks are distributed on the closed canvas bag, in order to apply regular pressure on the entire surface of the bag.

3) The hydraulic jack is then placed on top of the wedges and held in place at the top by the rectangular iron bar. The jack is then operated manually to compress the contents of the press cage by raising and lowering the handle of the jack. The jack will go down into the cage, little by little. As the pressure on the combs increases, the honey starts flowing through the wooden bars of the press cage onto the collection tray. Wooden wedges are regularly added under the jack to ensure that all the honey is removed from the combs.

5.       Advantages and disadvantages of this handmade press

5.1        The advantages of the press

  • It is made with quality wood available locally. The wood comes from sustainably managed forests where trees are cut down at the recommended age and season. It is solid wood that does not rot and has no smell. It is of course easier and cheaper to make this type of press in regions rich in wood and forests.

  • It is cheaper than similar imported presses.

  • It is easy to use and if the legs are strong enough, it can press up to 60 liters of honeycombs at once.

  • In general, users confirm its ease of use. It is easy to clean after use.

  • It can be dismantled and is easy to transport. Once installed, beekeepers not disassemble it anymore.

  • This model is interesting because, metal parts are not in contact with honey, which is why it is not necessary to use stainless metal, unlike many honey press models that consist of a central metal rod.

Figure 8. Two dismantled presses – © Joseph Dinga

5.2        The disadvantages of the press

Of course, it can always be improved.

  • One of the disadvantages for some beekeepers is that it requires the purchase of a jack, not always easy to find and which increases the price of the press. The jack can possibly be replaced by large bricks added little by little during the pressing operation. It will be less efficient and less fast because, the beekeeper will have to wait and come back later (1 hour later for example) to add pressure by adding new bricks.

  • The manufacturing of this press requires either good carpentry skills or working with well-equipped carpenters to obtain the best result (strength and precision).

  • The structure can be solidified by attaching two flat crossed metal bars to the legs as illustrated in Figure 9 below and to the 4 sides.

Figure 9. Illustration of the reinforcement of the legs of the press with crossed metal bars – © Elsa Demoulin, 2019

5.3        Feedback

The press has been used in schools in Cameroon. Users are very satisfied with the press and confirm the need for reinforcement of the legs of the structure.

6.       Presentation of Mr. Fobasso

The honey press model presented here is a model developed by Mr. Fobasso Etienne, beekeeper since the 1990s in Cameroon. He studied beekeeping in Cameroon but also at the University of Tor Vergata in Italy, in the year 2000. He owns an apiary of more than 2 000 hives of different models.

Skilled in carpentry, Mr. Fobasso made his first press in 2002 inspired by models found in beekeeping books. He then improved his model from year to year after his return from the training in Italy. It is one of the first wooden presses developed in Cameroon. It is currently used throughout the country.

_annotations.field_innovation_identified:
TITLE: Wooden Hydraulic Honey Press by Fobasso

DESCRIPTION: A locally-developed manual honey extraction press using a car jack and locally-sourced wood, designed for fixed-comb and topbar hives. The innovation eliminates metal contact with honey and costs less than imported models.

INNOVATION CRITERIA: This is a modified solution developed with grassroots participation that solves accessibility and cost issues in honey extraction, while being adapted to local contexts. It represents both technological and social innovation in beekeeping practices in Cameroon.
_annotations.field_shorter_description:
Honey is a pure and natural food that bees store in the honey combs inside the hive. There are different methods to hygienically extract honey from wax combs. For beekeepers using fixed comb hives or topbar hives, honey can be extracted using the dripping method (gravity) or the honey press. Beekeepers using frame hives usually extract honey using the centrifugal extractor.

This sheet presents a honey press model developed by Mr. Fobasso, an experienced beekeeper from Cameroon. The honey press allows honey to be extracted from several hives at the same time. We explain how to make the press and how to use it.

This technical description is also available in: French (ID10134)

records.title: Extraction du miel par pressage - Pressoir à miel de Goma (RDC)
records.description:
Figure 1. Pressoir à miel développé par RACOD en RDC © MMH

1.       Introduction

Jusqu’il y a peu, Recherche et Action pour la Conservation et le Développement (RACOD) copiait des modèles de pressoir à miel importés et les fabriquait localement. Le modèle de pressoir à miel présenté ici (Figure 1) est le résultat d’un processus de test (méthode de « recherche-action »): importation de modèles, tentatives de copie d'adaptation des modèles importés aux besoins locaux et enfin mise au point du premier modèle fabriqué localement. Ce modèle a ensuite été testé avec succès et utilisé dans la miellerie de RACOD à Goma (République Démocratique du Congo) pendant un an. Il est aujourd'hui utilisé par les apiculteurs de la région et poursuivra naturellement son évolution en fonction des besoins et des conditions locales.

Le modèle de presse à miel utilisé au Cameroun (ID10134) était l'un des modèles qui a été importé et étudié pour la production locale. Cependant, les apiculteurs locaux ont préféré se tourner vers un modèle de presse à miel uniquement en bois, sans aucune pièce en fer ; la menuiserie étant une compétence disponible localement. Avec l'aide de l'expert belge Daniel Isorez, et en collaboration avec un atelier de menuiserie à Goma, la fabrication locale a été initiée et le résultat est présenté ici.

2.       L’objectif

Fabriquer localement le matériel apicole plutôt que de l'importer (matériel souvent excessivement cher), augmente potentiellement l'accès au matériel pour les apiculteurs disposant de moyens modestes. Favoriser localement la production de matériel apicole améliore donc non seulement l'accès des apiculteurs au matériel localement et à moindre coût, mais offre également aux apiculteurs la possibilité de travailler avec les artisans locaux, et donc d’apporter plus facilement des améliorations au matériel en fonction de leurs propres besoins.

3.       Présentation du pressoir

Cette presse est composée de 4 pièces en bois sec (Figure 2) et d'un seau en plastique. Les 4 pièces de la presse sont :

  1. un bras de levier
  2. une jambe de force et une presse circulaire
  3. un montant principal et sa partie basale (ou table)
  4. une plaque secondaire ajourée

Évidemment, les dimensions de la presse présentées dans cette fiche dépendent de la taille du seau utilisé. Dans ce cas, cette presse est basée sur un type de seau en plastique couramment disponible à Goma.

Figure 2. Le pressoir de Goma. Vue de haut : à gauche, en position de pressage, à droite, la presse est relevée ©RACOD

Les quatre pièces de bois sont les suivantes :

3.1      Bras de levier (Figure 3)

Il s’agit d’une pièce de bois qui s’articule grâce à une cheville avec le montant principal. En son milieu, le bras de levier s’articule avec la jambe de force au bout de laquelle se trouve la presse, pièce de bois ronde qui rentre dans le seau et fait pression sur les rayons de miel broyés.

Figure 3. Le bras de levier : vue de haut ©RACOD

3.2      Jambe de force et presse (Figures 4 et 5)

La jambe de force est une barre de bois sous laquelle est fixée une plaque de bois circulaire faisant office de presse, qui pénètre dans le seau et dont le diamètre (ici 245 mm) dépend du diamètre intérieur de la base du seau. Il est souhaitable que cette jambe de force soit fixée au bras de levier.

Figure 4. Dimensions de la jambe de force et la presse : vue latérale ©RACOD

Figure 5. Dimensions de la jambe de force et la presse : vue du haut ©RACOD

 

3.3      Montant principal et table (Figure 6)

Le montant principal est une pièce en bois reliant le bras de levier et la table (ou base de la presse). Il est fixé à la base avec des clous ou des vis. Il doit pouvoir supporter la pression exercée sur le bras de levier.

La base du pressoir, également appelée table, sert de support au seau et permet de recevoir le miel s'écoulant des trous du seau avant d'atteindre le filtre (en l'occurrence un double tamis) par l’ouverture d'écoulement. La table a un rebord de 40 mm de haut afin de contenir le miel qui s’écoule du seau troué et qui est ainsi dirigé vers le seau de stockage.

Figure 6. Dimensions du montant principal et de la table ©RACOD

3.4      Plaque secondaire (Figures 7 et 8)

La plaque secondaire est utilisée comme cale et placée dans le fond du seau pour empêcher la cire de coller à la surface du seau et de boucher les trous. La plaque secondaire est constituée de lattes de bois de 20 mm de large.

La plaque secondaire est réalisée comme illustrée sur les figures 7 et 8. Le socle est composé de quatre lattes espacées de 30 mm et de 10 mm entre la deuxième et la troisième lattes. Ensuite, des lattes de 20 mm de large sont posées perpendiculairement au-dessus du socle, espacées de 5 mm, et maintenues en place à l'aide de clous.

Figure 7. Plaque secondaire : vue de profil ©RACOD

Figure 8. Plaque secondaire : vue de haut ©RACOD

De plus, les éléments suivants sont nécessaires :

  • une base : sert de support à la presse. L'apiculteur peut utiliser une simple table.
  • un seau : un récipient en plastique qui contient les rayons de miel à presser. Le seau utilisé ici permet de travailler environ 7 rayons qui sont broyés au préalable. Ce seau est percé de trous d'environ 6 mm Ø qui serviront de voie de sortie du miel lors du pressage. Les trous sont répartis en quatre lignes circulaires, ils sont distants de 40 mm. Avec le modèle de seau utilisé, cela implique un total de 104 trous. Le nombre de trous nécessaire dépend de la fluidité du miel. L'utilisateur peut facilement adapter ce nombre.

4.       Utilisation de la presse

Pour commencer le pressage, placez les rayons de miel, préalablement coupés en petits morceaux ou broyés, au-dessus de la plaque secondaire dans le seau. Abaissez la presse circulaire dans le seau à l'aide du bras de levier et appliquez une pression.

Le miel sort par les trous du seau et s'écoule sur la table ; guidé par le rebord de cette table, il s’écoule ensuite par simple gravité par l’ouverture d’écoulement, à travers le système de filtrage, et termine sa course dans le seau de stockage.

5.       Fabrication de la presse

5.1 Outils nécessaires

Les outils nécessaires sont : marteau, équerre, scie, ciseaux à bois, perceuse et mètre.

5.2 Matériaux

Cette presse est réalisée avec des planches en bois sec de Grevillea robusta (chêne soyeux d'Australie ou chêne gris), de 4 cm d'épaisseur et de 10 cm de largeur. Les différentes pièces sont assemblées à l'aide de clous.

5.3 Fabrication étape par étape

Pour fabriquer la presse, suivez 4 étapes :

1) Rabotez les pièces de bois pour qu'elles soient lisses.

2) Couper les pièces de bois aux dimensions requises.

3) Assemblez les différents éléments des 4 composants en bois de la presse.

4) Percez le seau en faisant des trous de Ø 6 à 8 mm pour permettre au miel de s'écouler hors du seau lors du pressage. Dans le seau utilisé ici, 104 trous ont été faits, espacés de 40 mm, disposés en quatre lignes circulaires. Le nombre de trous peut être augmenté en fonction de la fluidité du miel.

6.       Avantages et inconvénients par rapport à d’autres modèles de pressoir

6.1       Avantages:

  • Le matériel de fabrication est disponible localement.
  • Coût de fabrication et ou d’achat abordable par les apiculteurs.
  • Facile à fabriquer localement.
  • Facile à utiliser. 

6.2       Inconvénients:

  • La capacité de pressage dépend de la force physique appliquée au bras de levier, mais la structure légère du pressoir nécessite de maîtriser cette force pour ne pas endommager le pressoir lui-même.
  • Parfois le miel déborde de la presse circulaire en bois fixée à la jambe de force (Figure 2).

7.       Remarques de apiculteurs

En collaboration avec les apiculteurs, RACOD a engagé le processus d'extension de ce pressoir. L'utilisation du pressoir va de pair avec un changement de mentalité autour des ventes de miel brut. Les apiculteurs n'investiront dans la fabrication et l'achat de la presse que s'ils comprennent les avantages de la vente de miel filtré et s'il existe des opportunités de marché pour le miel filtré. Le miel filtré (produit avec cette presse) est vendu plus cher et la presse permet aussi de commercialiser la cire (qui est séparée du miel lors du pressage).

8.        Défauts identifiés et quelques solutions

8.1       Défauts

  • Les clous utilisés sont ordinaires et non recommandés dans le cadre de l’hygiène alimentaire. Les clous communs sont à éviter, ils s’oxydent au contact du miel. Il est donc important d’utiliser des vis et/ou clous en inox ou encore d’assembler les pièces par des chevilles en bois.
  • À force de pressage, le bras de levier peut se briser.
  • Obstruction partielle des trous du seau lors du pressage.

8.2       Quelques solutions

  • Remplacement de clous par des chevilles en bois.
  • Le bras de levier peut être remplacé par un tube métallique ou un tuyau galvanisé, étant donné qu’il n’entre normalement pas en contact avec le miel
  • Augmenter le nombre de trous afin d’éviter le débordement du miel lors du pressage.

9.       Conseils d’utilisation (Figure 9)

  • Lavage, nettoyage et séchage obligatoire avant et après usage, le pressoir est gardé à l’abri de la poussière et est séché dans la miellerie.
  • S’assurer que tout le matériel est bien sec avant utilisation (dépourvu de toute trace d’eau).
  • Couper les rayons de miel en petits morceaux pour faciliter le pressage.
  • Appliquer progressivement la force physique sur le levier.

Figures 9. Utilisation du pressoir © Delphin Musafiri

10.       Conclusions

Dans le but de trouver une solution durable au problème d'approvisionnement en matériel apicole, les expérimentations et des améliorations seront faites au fil du temps. La collaboration entre les acteurs du développement de la filière apicole s'est avérée porteuse de résultats positifs en matière d'essais d'équipements, de transfert de connaissances et d’apport de compétences d'expertise locale, nationale et internationale.

11.       Présentation de RACOD

RACOD ASBL (Recherche et Action pour la Conservation et le Développement) est une association congolaise à but non lucratif. RACOD prône des alternatives résilientes pour les habitants des aires protégées de l'Est de la République Démocratique du Congo afin d'augmenter leurs revenus et ainsi contribuer à la préservation d'écosystèmes fragiles, en l'occurrence le Parc National des Virunga.

Depuis 2015, RACOD, a adopté la méthodologie « recherche-action » comme approche stratégique pour agir sur le terrain, méthode basée sur les résultats d'un diagnostic participatif.

Soucieux de la conservation des écosystèmes, RACOD a invité les apiculteurs à s'organiser en NEBA (Noyau Écologique de Base) afin de mieux accompagner les apiculteurs pratiquant les méthodes traditionnelles et à accompagner le développement de l'apiculture. Ces NEBA s'appuient sur les ruchers-pédagogiques mis en place par le RACOD.

Des démarches de recherche-action ont été mises en place, l'objectif étant d’amener les apiculteurs/trices à tester et à s’approprier les modèles de matériel apicole qu’ils jugent adaptés à leurs pratiques et objectifs apicoles, selon différents critères (rentabilité, efficacité, appropriation par des artisans locaux, etc.).

 

Cette fiche technique a été documentée par Delphin MUSAFIRI avec la collaboration de Deo KUJIRAKWINJA, coordinateur de RACOD et de Daniel ISOREZ, expert apicole belge.

En collaboration avec les apiculteurs, RACOD a engagé le processus d'extension de ce pressoir. L'utilisation du pressoir va de pair avec un changement de mentalité autour des ventes de miel brut. Les apiculteurs n'investiront dans la fabrication et l'achat de la presse que s'ils comprennent les avantages de la vente de miel filtré et s'il existe des opportunités de marché pour le miel filtré. Le miel filtré (produit avec cette presse) est vendu plus cher et la presse permet aussi de commercialiser la cire (qui est séparée du miel lors du pressage).

8.        Défauts identifiés et quelques solutions

8.1       Défauts

  • Les clous utilisés sont ordinaires et non recommandés dans le cadre de l’hygiène alimentaire. Les clous communs sont à éviter, ils s’oxydent au contact du miel. Il est donc important d’utiliser des vis et/ou clous en inox ou encore d’assembler les pièces par des chevilles en bois.
  • À force de pressage, le bras de levier peut se briser.
  • Obstruction partielle des trous du seau lors du pressage.

8.2       Quelques solutions

  • Remplacement de clous par des chevilles en bois.
  • Le bras de levier peut être remplacé par un tube métallique ou un tuyau galvanisé, étant donné qu’il n’entre normalement pas en contact avec le miel
  • Augmenter le nombre de trous afin d’éviter le débordement du miel lors du pressage.

9.       Conseils d’utilisation (Figure 9)

  • Lavage, nettoyage et séchage obligatoire avant et après usage, le pressoir est gardé à l’abri de la poussière et est séché dans la miellerie.
  • S’assurer que tout le matériel est bien sec avant utilisation (dépourvu de toute trace d’eau).
  • Couper les rayons de miel en petits morceaux pour faciliter le pressage.
  • Appliquer progressivement la force physique sur le levier.

10.       Conclusions

Dans le but de trouver une solution durable au problème d'approvisionnement en matériel apicole, les expérimentations et des améliorations seront faites au fil du temps. La collaboration entre les acteurs du développement de la filière apicole s'est avérée porteuse de résultats positifs en matière d'essais d'équipements, de transfert de connaissances et d’apport de compétences d'expertise locale, nationale et internationale.

11.       Présentation de RACOD

RACOD ASBL (Recherche et Action pour la Conservation et le Développement) est une association congolaise à but non lucratif. RACOD prône des alternatives résilientes pour les habitants des aires protégées de l'Est de la République Démocratique du Congo afin d'augmenter leurs revenus et ainsi contribuer à la préservation d'écosystèmes fragiles, en l'occurrence le Parc National des Virunga.

Depuis 2015, RACOD, a adopté la méthodologie « recherche-action » comme approche stratégique pour agir sur le terrain, méthode basée sur les résultats d'un diagnostic participatif.

Soucieux de la conservation des écosystèmes, RACOD a invité les apiculteurs à s'organiser en NEBA (Noyau Écologique de Base) afin de mieux accompagner les apiculteurs pratiquant les méthodes traditionnelles et à accompagner le développement de l'apiculture. Ces NEBA s'appuient sur les ruchers-pédagogiques mis en place par le RACOD.

Des démarches de recherche-action ont été mises en place, l'objectif étant d’amener les apiculteurs/trices à tester et à s’approprier les modèles de matériel apicole qu’ils jugent adaptés à leurs pratiques et objectifs apicoles, selon différents critères (rentabilité, efficacité, appropriation par des artisans locaux, etc.).

 

Cette fiche technique a été documentée par Delphin MUSAFIRI avec la collaboration de Deo KUJIRAKWINJA, coordinateur de RACOD et de Daniel ISOREZ, expert apicole belge.

records.title: Honey extracted by pressing - wooden honey press of Goma (DRC)
records.description:
Figure 1. Honey press developed by RACOD in DRC © MMH

1.       Introduction

Until recently, Research and Action for Conservation and Development (RACOD) copied imported honey press models and manufactured them locally. The honey press model presented here (Figure 1) is the result of a long process of testing imported models, attempts to copy and adapt the imported models to local needs and finally the fine tuning of the first locally made model. This model was subsequently successfully tested and used in RACOD's honeyhouse in Goma (Democratic Republic of Congo) for a year. It is now being used by beekeepers in the area and will naturally continue its evolution according to local needs and conditions.

The Cameroonian honey press model (ID10140) was one of the models that was imported and studied for local production. However, the preference of local beekeepers went to a honey press model made solely of wood, without any pieces in iron, as carpentry is the locally available skill. With the help of the Belgian expert Daniel Isorez, and in collaboration with a carpentry workshop in Goma, the local manufacturing was initiated and  the result t is presented here.

2.       The objective

Locally manufacturing beekeeping equipment rather than importing (often excessively expensive equipment), potentially increases access of beekeepers with modest means to equipment.  Promoting the production of beekeeping equipment locally therefore not only improves access of beekeepers to equipment locally and at a lower cost, but it also offers beekeepers the opportunity to work together with the local craftsmen, to make improvements to equipment regarding their own needs.

3.       Presentation of the honey press

This press consists of 4 pieces made of dry wood (Figure 2) and a plastic bucket.  The 4 pieces of the press are:

  1. a lever arm
  2. a support leg and circular press
  3. a support/junction pillar and its basal part/table
  4. an openwork secondary plate

Obviously, the dimensions of the press presented in this sheet depend on the size of the bucket used. In this case, this press is based on a type of plastic bucket commonly available in Goma.

Figure 2. The press of Goma. Top view: on the left, in the pressing position; on the right, the press is raised up ©RACOD

The four pieces of wood are as following:

3.1      Lever arm (Figure 3)

It is a piece of wood with a dowel at one end and a support pillar at the other end. The support leg with at the end the press (a round piece of wood that fits into the bucket and puts pressure on the crushed honeycombs) is attached to the lever arm.

Figure 3. The lever arm: top view ©RACOD

3.2      Piston and piston base (Figures 4 and 5)

The piston is a wooden bar under which is fixed a circular wooden plate acting as a piston base, which penetrates the bucket and whose diameter (here 245 mm) depends on the inner diameter of the base of the bucket. It is desirable that this piston is attached to the lever arm.

Figure 4. Dimensions of the piston and piston base: side view ©RACOD
Figure 5. Dimensions of the piston and the piston base: top view ©RACOD

3.3      Support pillar and base (Figure 6)

The support pillar is a wooden piece connecting the lever arm and the base of the press. It is fixed to the base with nails.  It should be able to support the pressure applied on the lever arm.

The base of the press, also called the table, serves as a support for the bucket and allows to receive the honey flowing from the holes in the bucket before reaching the filter (in this case a double sieve) through the dripping hole. The base has an edge of 40 mm high to maintain the honey flowing on the base.

Figure 6. Dimensions of the junction pillar and the table ©RACOD

3.4      Bucket base (Figures 7 and 8)

The bucket base is used as a wedge and placed on the bottom of the bucket to prevent the wax from sticking to the surface of the bucket, and thus sealing the holes. The bucket base consists of wooden slats of 20 mm wide.

The bucket base is made as illustrated in Figures 7 and 8. The base is composed of four slats spaced 30 mm apart and 10 mm between the second and third slat. Next, slats of 20 mm wide are placed perpendicularly on top of the base, spaced 5 mm apart, and are kept in place using nails.

Figure 7. Bucket base: profile view ©RACOD

Figure 8. Bucket base: top view ©RACOD

In addition, the following elements are required:

  • the base: serves as a support for the press. The beekeeper can use a simple table.
  • bucket: a plastic container that contains the honeycombs to be pressed. The bucket used here allows to work about 7 combs that will be crushed beforehand. This bucket is perforated with holes of about 6 mm Ø which will serve as the exit route of the honey during pressing. The holes are divided into four circular lines, they are 40 mm apart. With the bucket model used, this implies a total of 104 holes. The necessary number of holes depends on the fluidity of honey. The user can easily adapt this number.

4.       How to use the press

To start the pressing, place the honeycombs, previously cut into small pieces or crushed, on top of the bucket base in the bucket. Lower the press into the bucket using the lever arm and apply pressure.

The honey comes out of the holes of the bucket and flows onto the base and through the dripping hole onto the filtering system.

5.       How to make the press

5.1        Necessary tools

The necessary tools are: hammer, try square, saw, wood scissors, drill and meter.

5.2        Materials

This press is made with dry Grevillea robusta (commonly known as the southern silky oak or Australian silver oak) wood planks, 4 cm thick and 10 cm wide. The different pieces are assembled using nails.

5.3        Step-by-step explanations of manufacturing

To manufacture the press, follow 4 steps:

1) Plane the wooden pieces so that they are smooth.

2) Cut the pieces of wood to the required dimensions.

3) Assemble the different elements of the 4 wooden components of the press.

4) Perforate the bucket making holes of 6 to 8 mm Ø to allow the honey to flow out of the bucket during pressing. In the bucket used here, 104 holes were made, 40 mm apart, arranged in four circular lines. The number of holes can be increased depending on the fluidity of the honey.

6.       Advantages and disadvantages compared to other press models

6.1        Advantages:

  • Manufacturing equipment is available locally.
  • Affordable manufacturing and/or purchasing cost for beekeepers.
  • Easy to manufacture locally.
  • Easy to use.

6.2        Disadvantages:

  • The pressing capacity depends on the physical force applied to the lever arm, but the light structure of the press requires controlling this force so as not to damage the press itself.
  • Sometimes the honey overflows with the wooden circular press attached to the support leg (Figure2).

7.       Feedback from beekeepers using the press

In collaboration with beekeepers, RACOD has started the extension process for this press. The use of the press goes hand in hand with a mentality change around the sales of raw honey. Beekeepers will only invest in the manufacturing and purchase of the press if they understand the benefits of selling filtered honey and if there are market opportunities for filtered honey. Filtered honey (produced with this press) is sold at a higher price and the press makes it possible to market the wax too, as the 2 end products of the press are honey and wax.

8.       Defects identified and some solutions

8.1        Defects

  • The nails used are regular nails and not recommended for food hygiene. The regular nails must be avoided; they oxidize when in contact with honey. It is therefore important to use stainless steel nails or to assemble the parts with wooden dowels.
  • By pressing, the lever arm can break.
  • Partial obstruction of the bucket holes during pressing.

8.2        Some solutions

  • Replacement of nails by wooden dowels.
  • The lever arm can be replaced with a metal tube or galvanized pipe, since it does not normally come into contact with honey.
  • Increase the number of holes in order to prevent the overflow of honey during pressing.

9.        Directions for use (Figure 9)

  • Washing, cleaning and drying of the press are mandatory before and after use, the press is kept away from dust and is dried in the honeyhouse.
  • Ensure that all equipment is completely dry before use.
  • Cut the honeycombs into small pieces to facilitate pressing.
  • Gradually apply physical force to the lever arm.
Figures 9. Use of the press © Delphin Musafiri

10.       Conclusions

With the aim of finding long lasting solution to the problem of beekeeping equipment supply, experiments and improvements will be made over time. Collaboration between stakeholders in the development of the beekeeping value chain has shown to bring positive results when it comes to the testing of equipment and the transfer of knowledge and skills of local, national and international expertise.

11.       Introducing RACOD

RACOD ASBL (Research and Action for Conservation and Development) is a Congolese non-profit association. RACOD advocates resilient alternatives for residents of protected areas in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo in order to increase their income and thus contribute to the preservation of fragile ecosystems, in this case Virunga National Park.

Since 2015, RACOD, has adopted the “research-action” methodology as a strategic approach to act in the field, based on the results of a participatory diagnosis.

RACOD is concerned about the conservation of ecosystems and in order to better support beekeepers practicing traditional methods, invited beekeepers to organize themselves in NEBAs (“Noyau Écologique de Base” in French, Basic Ecological Core) and to support the development of beekeeping. These NEBAs are based on the apiaries-pedagogical set up by RACOD.

Research-action processes have been implemented, the objective being to get beekeepers to test and appropriate the models of beekeeping equipment that they consider adapted to their beekeeping practices and objectives, according to different criteria (profitability, efficiency, appropriation by local artisans, etc.).

This technical sheet has been documented by Delphin MUSAFIRI with the collaboration of Deo KUJIRAKWINJA, coordinator of RACOD and Daniel ISOREZ, Belgian beekeeping expert.

records.title: Nutrition-sensitive fish production in homestead ponds within rice landscapes, Bangladesh
records.description:
Description

Many seasonal floodplains and flooded rice fields in Asia contain an abundance of small indigenous fish during flood periods [1]. Easily processed and consumed whole (in its entirety – including head, eyes, bones in addition to flesh) these small fish are rich sources of micronutrients including calcium, zinc, iron, and vitamin A [2]. Processed small fish are easily consumed by children under two years of age, providing key nutrients to combat stunting and other forms of malnutrition [3].

These micronutrient-rich, small indigenous fish species (SIS) can be produced via polyculture in ponds and pond connected rice-fields with other fish such as carps and tilapia. This polyculture practice was developed in Bangladesh, focusing on the incorporation of Mola, a micronutrient-rich Small Indigenous Species (SIS) of fish, into homestead ponds.

The steps outlined below focus on the addition of SIS to an existing homestead pond. The steps were developed through research and trials with Mola in Bangladesh. Some modifications may be needed to adapt the practice for other SIS.

Figure 1. Nutrition-sensitive homestead pond of a farmer in Sadar Upazila, Dinajpur District, Bangladesh © WorldFish/Utpal Chakraborty

Figure 2. The micronutrient-rich small fish Mola © WorldFish/Utpal Chakraborty

1. Sourcing, collection, and transportation of live small indigenous fish species (SIS)

A source for obtaining SIS must be identified. These species are rarely available in hatcheries, nurseries, or other aquaculture suppliers, and often must be collected from the wild. Attention must be paid to regulations for wild collection, and to prevent depletion of the natural population. This may require formal assessments of the natural population, especially during wet months. However, once the homestead culture system is established, many SIS breed and self-recruit within a short period. This homestead SIS supply can replace collection from the wild. Farmers may keep some of the SIS stock in the homestead pond from one production season to the next to continue production and may sell some stock to new farmers who wish to stock their ponds.

For Mola, guidelines have been developed on the sourcing, collection, and transport methods. This included developing a method of “acclimatization” critical to reduce mortality during transport from the sources for stocking, including over long distances. Like fry/fingerlings in nursery ponds, the acclimatization of Mola include application of feed and frequent netting and release of the fish in the same pond. For collection of bulk amount from the source (e.g. culture pond) ‘acclimatization’ is carrying out by stocking mola in a pond separately from other species of fish by frequent netting and adding supplementary feed.

Regarding the transport of live Mola from source [4], various types of containers and transportation devices can be used. It includes:

  • open tank system, such as placing fish and water in a pick-up bed lined with a polythene sheet to transport up to 50 km distance,
  • closed tank system, such as containers with oxygen cylinders to transport long distances >50 km, and
  • aluminium containers set up in bicycle, rickshaw van or motorized vehicle used for short distance transport.

Figure 3. Transport of live Mola in different distances using aluminum containers © WorldFish/Utpal Chakraborty 

Figures 4. Open tank system in pick-up van © WorldFish/Utpal Chakraborty                             

Figure 5. Closed tank system with oxygen cylinder © WorldFish/Utpal Chakraborty

2. Stocking live SIS into the homestead pond

Pre-stocking management often includes draining of the pond, removal of vegetation, removal of bottom mud, dike repairing, removal of predatory fish and aquatic animals, application of lime, filling the pond with water, application of organic and inorganic fertilizers and testing of natural feed.

Stocking procedure of carp, tilapia and other species for polyculture begins with identifying species of fish that are readily produced and a good source of income, such as carps and tilapia. Although the optimum stocking densities may vary under local conditions to get good production, the usual carp-tilapia-mola polyculture in homestead ponds use the following stocking density (Table below):

Some farmers do polyculture of Mola in small homestead ponds connected to rice fields to get higher fish production. For this, dikes in rice fields are raised to protect from flooding and escape of fish. When stocked in ponds connected to rice fields, fish can move to rice field areas and eat insects, weeds and other natural feeds available in the rice fields.

Post-stocking management often includes application of feed, fertilization, monitoring growth performance and health status of fish and maintaining the water supply in pond.

3. Facilitating breeding in the pond

SIS breeding biology can differ from species to species. A good understanding of the breeding basics for the species in use is important to ensure production in the pond.

For Mola, there is a self-recruitment, breeding within the pond, two or three peak periods for breeding, but largely asynchronous breeding and a presence of mature mola found throughout the production season. Mola fry take about three or four months to mature.

Figure 6. Adult and juvenile Mola with carp observed during netting in carp-mola polyculture pond of farmer in Dhulia Beel community in Sadar Upazila, Nilphamari District, Bangladesh © WorldFish/Manos Kumar Saha

Adding small indigenous fish species (SIS) like Mola to homestead ponds fill production and supply gaps of fish to the household. Often there is a gap period (three to four months) between harvesting and stocking of carp and other species of fish in ponds. During this gap period, SIS such as Mola broodstock remain in the pond, continue breeding, and improve the efficiency of conversion of pond resources to fish production.

Small size grader nets can be used to separate mola and other SIS from the larger fish, and also to save the floating eggs/larvae/very small fish and avoid stress, ensuring continued good production and follow-on harvests.

Figure 9. Use of grader net by members of fishing team to separate mola and other SIS from large fish and to avoid stress during harvesting.

The homestead pond fish culture approach is particularly important for women’s empowerment in the production practice [6].

5. Conserving and transporting SIS broodstock from homestead ponds

Broodstock of Mola and other SIS can be conserved in the pond as stock for continuing production starting right from the beginning of the production season in the following years. There is no need to restock the ponds every year, provided the pond is perennial (i.e., it contains water year-round).

Due to regular netting in the ponds for partial harvests, the broodstock available in the ponds are “acclimatized” and less vulnerable to stress during netting. The ponds thus become a very good source of broodstock (or seed) to propagate in other ponds. This SIS can be collected and transported live, even long distances, for stocking in new ponds.  

If the pond dries up, the SIS broodstock can be conserved for a short period by transferring it to a ditch or depression within the pond.

6. Nutrition education

To ensure the nutritional benefits of the SIS are received, it is important to raise awareness on nutrition-sensitive methods for processing, cooking, and consuming SIS. Children under 2 years of age, pregnant or lactating mothers, and adolescent girls of poor and very poor households suffering from micronutrient-based malnutrition can especially benefit from nutrition-sensitive SIS preparation.

The importance of preparing SIS 1) whole/entirely, without removing any part, 2) with other ingredients to enhance micronutrient bioavailability, and 3) in a way that is safe and palatable for young children to eat, can be shared among household members, village caretaker groups, and/or disseminated more broadly to communities through governmental and non-governmental agencies.

Figures 10 and 11.  Mola processing for preparation of a recipe called “Kitchuri” (mixed with mola paste, other ingredients like red spinach, onion, pulses and others) useful even by minor children in a community in Parbatipur Upazila, Dinajpur District, Bangladesh © WorldFish /Utpal Chakraborty

Figure 12. Mola after processing, cooked mola and children eating “Kitchuri” mixed with mola paste, other ingredients like red spinach, onion, pulses and others © WorldFish /Manos Kumar Saha

7. Validation of the practice

Nutrition-sensitive homestead ponds have been implemented by farmers in Bangladesh since 2010 with 1500 households located in Rangpur and Dinajpur Districts in North-West region Bangladesh under the IFAD funded Small Fish and Nutrition Project of WorldFish. Afterwards, the practice was promoted to thousands of farmers located throughout the country under CSISA-BD, BANA, CRS, Ecopond, CALIP and CREL projects of WorldFish, Winrock International, DoF and NGOs.

Under the Blue Gold funded project of WorldFish, around 4000 women in Khulna and Patuakhali Districts in southern Bangladesh adopted SIS based nutrition-sensitive fish culture using the ‘Ecopond’ approach [5].  In recent years, under the EU and FCDO funded Suchana program, more than 60,000 women of poor and very poor well-being categories in Sylhet and Moulvibazar Districts in North-East Bangladesh adopted this nutrition-sensitive ‘carp-tilapia-Mola polyculture’ in small homestead ponds.  

Department of Fisheries in Bangladesh built on the successful practice to establish a “Mola village” in Northwestern Bangladesh as part of a dissemination program. Following the success of the practice in Bangladesh, it has been adapted for use in Cambodia, Myanmar, Nepal, and Assam and Odisha in India.

The practice has been carried out primarily in rainfed rice agroecosystems, both lowland and upland areas. Many of the areas are experience periodic flooding and/or drought. The most productive growing period for SIS tends to be during the wet season, when natural signals are present to induce reproduction. The homestead pond practice has been carried out under individual management initiated with support from government extension services and/or non-governmental technical support. The practice most often targets small-scale landholders, but can also be conducted by other groups, such as landless and/or women’s groups under a collective management scheme (e.g. low land rice fields/floodplains). The practice was trialed in community approaches with ponds or other small water bodies managed by community-based organizations (e.g. rice-fields in low land areas/floodplains) during wet months.

8. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

Pond area is usually between 200 m2 and 2000 m2, but may be larger. Water depth is usually 1.5 to 2.0 m and ideally should be present throughout the year.

The minimum necessary conditions include pond holds water for at least 5-6 months (seasonal) with access to a source of mola to obtain as live for stocking. A perennial pond is more useful to get good production. Finally, best results are obtained from ponds with sandy loam or loamy soil. 

The knowledge about the wild mola source at the initial stage of promotion, the integration of mola and other SIS with carp and overall management with major emphasis on regular harvesting are important to get success. 

Limiting factors to nutrition-sensitive homestead pond success includes; complete flooding of the pond, less interest of farmers to do the regular harvests of SIS required for successful production, less interest to stock SIS or Mola at the initial stage of pond establishment, or insufficient conservation of SIS stock to continue sufficient production in following years. 

9. Agro-ecological zones

  • Subtropics, warm/mod cool
  • Tropics, warm.

Initially the Nutrition-sensitive fish culture with the SIS ‘Mola’ introduced in the northwest region, the area with seasonal ponds and pond connected rice fields, later it has been disseminated throughout Bangladesh covering all the regions including the Hill Tracts in ponds with fresh waters. 

10. Related/Associated Technologies

  • Rice-fish Culture System (RFC): ID 8732.
  • Fish pond layout and construction: ID 4384.
  • Management of flood control, drainage and irrigation (FCDI) sluice gates: ID 4479.
  • Small fish-based fish chutney production: ID 10072.
  • Complex Rice Systems, Indonesia: ID 10104.

INNOVATION: Nutrition-sensitive fish polyculture in homestead ponds

DESCRIPTION: Integration of micronutrient-rich small indigenous fish species (particularly Mola) with carp and tilapia in homestead ponds, combined with nutrition education and gender-sensitive approaches.

REASONING: This is a social and technological innovation that modifies existing aquaculture practices to address micronutrient malnutrition, particularly focusing on vulnerable groups. It meets criteria of being a modified solution used in a new context, enhancing inclusion and equity, and supporting behavioral change through nutrition education.
