_annotations.body:
Shexian dryland stone terraced system

Shexian dryland stone terraced system is a rain-fed agricultural system in the mountains, developed by the local ancestors through adapting to and transforming the harsh natural environment and inherited from generation to generation. The dryland terrace system has outstanding soil and water conservation abilities. This practice explains the process of building stone terraced fields includes constructing stone shelters (known as Shi’anzi), piling stone ridges and backfilling soil in three phases.



Description

1. Background

Shexian has an elevation between 350 to 1150 m above sea level, with a slope gradient up to 66°at its steepest, featured by landform such as mountains, hills and valleys. The bedrock is mostly limestone and thus easily eroded. Soluble substances within have mostly been dissolved and eroded by water, with merely 5 percent left to form soil. The soil-retention capacity of the bedrock under soil is relatively low and soil is easily washed away, causing the soil layer to be thin and discontinuous. Along with the large amount of cracks present in the bedrock, signs of seepage are serious.

Shexian dryland stone terraced system is located in WangJinZhuang of Jingdian Town, Zhang Jia Zhaung of Gengle town and Guanfang Township in the southeast of Shexian County, involving 46 administrative villages. The total land area of the heritage site is 204.35 square kilometers, of dryland stone terraced  area is 27.68 square kilometers (about 2768 hectares).

Figure 1. Shexian dryland stone terraced system 3D topographic map.

©FAO/GIAHS

Therefore, the nature environment of Shexian can be characterized as “high mountains and steep slopes, more mountainous than flat land, more rock than soil, arid and dry”. In order to reduce the loss of soil and water and gain as much arable land as possible, the locals constructed large numbers of stone terraced fields along the steep mountains (Figure 1).

Figure 2. Stone terraced fields in Shexian.

©FAO/GIAHS

2. Structure and function

The Shexian dryland stone terraced system is jointly comprised of forests and shrubs in the mountain peaks, the stone terraced fields that wind up the mountains, the villages and rivers/river beaches in the valleys, Figure 3.

Figure 3. Spatial structure and important functions of the system.

©FAO/GIAHS

Benefits of the stone terraced fields:

  • maintain soil and water, achieve the cycling of nutrients and other materials, provide abundant agricultural products and protect germplasm resources.
  • effectively reduce soil erosion and maintain soil moisture levels, thus playing a key role in conserving the natural environment.
  • Various grains, cash crops and economic tree species are cultivated in stone terraced fields, not only providing locals with a diverse range of foods, but also significantly improving the biodiversity of the dryland terrace system.

3. Important ecological functions

3.1 Soil and water conservation

The Shexian dryland stone terraced system has outstanding soil and water conservation capabilities. Forests and shrubs on the mountain peaks are able to capture precipitation, protecting the soil from rain splashes and surface runoff, thus effectively reducing soil erosion. Precipitation captured by forests and shrubs seeps into the soil and increases soil moisture content. The terraced fields located on the mountainsides are usually constructed in 30-50° reverse-slopes according to the terrain, and are able to effectively reduce soil erosion caused by rain wash, thus enhancing the ability of the terraces to store water and retain soil.

The borders of the terraced fields are protected by two layers of stone ridges, and are planted with trees of Chinese prickly ash at a certain density. The roots of the Chinese prickly ash coil around the gaps in the stone ridges, forming an “iron fence” that holds the stone ridges in place, thus effectively reducing soil erosion. Economic tree species such as the Chinese prickly ash, black jujube and walnut that are cultivated in the terraced fields can also retain rainwater and prevent soil erosion caused by rain, and their fallen branches and leaves can also reduce surface runoff. Layers of rock can be found below the terraced fields, from bottom to top respectively large rocks, medium rocks and small rocks. Under vertical pressure, the soil is closely compact with the rock. The gaps between the rocks can also store moisture, thus considerably conserving soil and water (Figure 4).

Figure 4. Illustration of soil and water conservation capabilities of stone terraced fields.

©FAO/GIAHS

3.2 Nutrient cycling

The dryland terrace system of Shexian has important nutrient cycling functions. Local farmers regularly feed the straw (stalks and stems of crops) to donkeys and return the organic fertilizer made from the fermentation of a mixture of straw and donkey manure to the fields. At the same time, some straw is returned directly to the field (Figure 5). According to surveys, the utilization of digested straw, fermented straw and straw directly incorporated, in proportional terms, is roughly 50 percent, 20 percent and 30 percent.

Figure 5. Illustration of nutrient cycling in the heritage system.

©FAO/GIAHS

Long-term returning of straw to the land can significantly enhance the soil fertility and improve the soil structure, not only ingeniously solving the problems of nutrient conversion and soil fertilization, but also realizing nutrient cycling within the terraced fields. Furthermore, planting economic tree species such as Chinese prickly ash and black jujube in the stone terraced fields increases soil fertility as their fallen leaves and branches are converted to organic material by microorganisms.

4. Water and soil resource utilization

4.1 Dryland terrace construction

The process of building stone terraced fields includes constructing stone shelters (known as Shi’anzi), piling stone ridges and backfilling soil in three phases, which is an epitome of how locals fully utilize soil and stone resources.

Phase 1: Constructing stone shelters

Before constructing stone terraced fields, a stone shelter (shi’anzi) on the slope must firstly be built in the selected region, in order to provide those constructing the terrace places to rest and shelter from rain (Figure 6) After the construction of the terraces, the stone shelter would be left in its original location, and become an important venue for the storage of production inputs such as farming tools and for farmers to rest during farm breaks. Stone shelters are usually squarish, approximately 2 m in height and width. They are built by piling trimmed stones, which takes about ten days.

Figure 6. A stone shelter (Shi’anzi)

©FAO/GIAHS

Phase 2: Building stone ridges

After the construction of the stone shelter, the gravel in the foundations of the terraces is first dug out and placed aside, and then the construction of stone ridges begins. Stone ridges are built from overlapping vertical blocks, with larger rocks at the bottom and smaller rocks at the top, forming an interlayer mosaic structure (Figure 7). Stacking of the stone layers in the plots and construction of the stone ridges are carried out at the same time, similarly following the “large rocks at the bottom, gravel on the top” principle, and leaving space at the top for soil backfill.

Figure 7. Side view (Left) and top view (Right) of stone ridges.

©FAO/GIAHS

Phase 3: Backfilling soil

After the construction of stone ridges is complete, soil would be backfilled onto the uppermost stone layer of the plot. As the soil is scarce locally, people would collect soil from the slopes or from neighbouring regions with flatter terrain using shoulder poles, and deposit it on the gravels enclosed by the stone ridges, eventually forming an arable plot (Figure 8).

Figure 8. Cross-section of the enclosed plot.

©FAO/GIAHS

5. Dryland terrace maintenance

5.1 Planting Chinese prickly Ash trees along the stone ridges

Through long-term agricultural production, local farmers discovered that planting Chinese prickly ash trees along the stone ridges, thus forming a “green fence” around the terraces, plays an important role in the maintenance of the terraces. The extension and coiling of the root systems of Chinese prickly ash trees not only significantly increases the structural stability of the stone ridges, but also conserves and accumulates soil, and reduces the loss of soil and water (Figure 9).

Figure 9. Planting Chinese prickly ash trees along the stone ridges.

©FAO/GIAHS

5.2 Pruning vines from stone ridges

Local farmers prune the vines growing along the stone ridges biennially to prevent them from competing with crops for water and nutrients. They dig a ditch 50 cm to 1 m deep along the inside of stone ridges, and clear the vines before filling the ditch with soil and gravels.

5.3 “Suspended Arch Mosaic” structure

Stone terraced fields are divided into relatively narrow plots, and stone ridges are prone to collapse during tillage. Furthermore, floods occur frequently from July to August, and it is common for stone ridges to be washed away by the deluge. In order to repair damaged stone ridges, locals creatively invented the “suspended arch mosaic” structure.

When repairing damaged stone ridges, a suspended arch is first set up. A stone ridge is then built on the arch. As the situation requires, one has the option of backfilling gravels and soil under the arch, or leave it empty as a field storage space or a resting space for people and livestock (Table 1, Figure 10).

Table 1: Suspended Arch Mosaic structure construction phases
Clearing the area Clearing the area surrounding the collapsed stone ridge, collecting rocks.
Digging to foundations Clearing the soil from the two sides of the collapsed area, exposing the bottom of the stone ridge.
Building the arch Building an arch using small rocks as a scaffold.
Closing the arch Placing square-shaped rocks into the middle of the arch.
Building the top of the arch Restoring the stone ridge to its original height.
Backfilling Backfilling gravels and soil under the arch.
 
Figure 10. Suspended arch mosaic structure construction phases content:
1: Clearing the Area 2: Digging to Foundations

Figure 11. Suspended arch mosaic structure construction phases content:
3: Building the Arch 4: Closing the Arch

Figure 12. Suspended arch mosaic structure construction phases content:
5: Building the Top of the Arch 6: Backfilling

©FAO/GIAHS

The “suspended arch mosaic” structure is a representative of the techniques used to restore stone terraced fields. It not only ensures the firmness of the stone ridge, but also fully utilizes local rock resources. The “suspended arch mosaic” structure is also used in the construction of stone arch bridges (Figure 13).

Figure 13. Arch bridge of “Suspended Arch Mosaic” structure.

©FAO/GIAHS

6. Rainfall harvest and storage

Water used in agricultural production and daily life originates entirely from precipitation, while rainfall is typically concentrated in the summer. In order to solve the conflict between uneven rainfall throughout the year and the water need for production and daily life, the locals have always paid attention to the harvest and storage of rainwater. They employ traditional farming methods that conserve water and soil, and construct a series of facilities to collect rain and store water. Shexian has four water conservancy construction projects with four big canals which provide water to some parts of terraces. But the pools, tanks and cellars are bigger sources of water for terraces. People use them to collect water in summer and use water in autumn and winter. Soil is also the key storage space for water, which directly stores atmospheric precipitation in terraces ensuring water needs of crops.

6.1 Water cellars

Water cellars have a long history, and are known as “family heirlooms” (chuanjiabao). Some are built in villagers’ courtyards (Figure 14) while some are built in wider areas of streets and alleys. Normally, locations with a low-lying terrain are chosen for water cellars. Rocks are firstly used to build an underground space to store water, and then suitable locations on the surface are chosen to build a narrow opening for water inflow and a wide opening for water extraction. When using water cellars, pails are lowered with ropes into the wide openings and rainwater that has been left to settle is drawn.

Figure 14. Composition of a water cellar (Inflow opening, extraction opening, pail).

©FAO/GIAHS

6.2 Wells

As the local annual precipitation varies greatly seasonally, groundwater is the water resource that local residents rely upon when there is a shortfall of rain. As welldrilling activities are carried out, wells gradually appeared next to the main streets of the villages, providing public water resources to the villagers (Figure 15).

Figure 15. A well in a village.

©FAO/GIAHS

6.3 Water pools

Water pools are divided into ancient pools and modern pools. It is unclear when ancient pools were built, but they are mostly found outside the villages or in open spaces of the villages, and used to collect rainwater, providing villages with water for washing, production and consumption (both by people and livestock). Some ancient pools were converted to modern pools after the 1970s, mainly used for sowing during droughts.

6.4 Water tanks

There are two types of water tanks in the heritage site: one is built in villagers’ yards, mainly used to store running water and rain/snow, providing water for daily life, akin to a water cellar with a larger capacity; the other is a large-capacity tank collectively built by one or more villages, situated on the mountainside or the mountain summit (Figure 16), capable of storing larger amounts of water and providing a convenient water source during agricultural production.

Figure 16. Water tanks on the mountainside.

©FAO/GIAHS

6.5 Reservoirs

Reservoirs are the central part of the ecological water network in moutainous areas. Reservoirs were built using government funds in recent years, and serve such functions as guarding against floods and storing water.

Figure 17. Moon lake reservoir in Wangjinzhuang Village.

©FAO/GIAHS

7.  The farming system

records.title: Traditional Gudeuljang Irrigated rice terraces in Cheongsando
records.description:
Description

1. Background

The Cheongsando Island area is located south of the Korean Peninsula, and is affiliated with Wando County of Jeollanam-do. The Gudeuljangnon paddy system was born out of the natural environment of the island being disadvantageous for paddy agriculture due to steep slopes, sandy soil with rocks and rapid drainage, and a scarcity of water for paddy farming. To overcome these limitations, the “Gudeuljang” structure, used in the traditional Korean home-heating system called Ondol, was applied to build the irrigation system for the rice paddies.

Figure 1: Distribution of Cheongsando Island Gudeuljangnon.

©FAO/GIAHS

2. Working principle

Gudeuljangnon, made from stacked stones, prevent soil loss and improve the soil's ability to purify water. The water that flows through gaps between the stones and in the waterways provides an environment for reptiles, amphibians, and crustaceans such as the longtail tadpole shrimp. The waterway connects the upper forest area, where water remains for an extended period, with the lower village area, forming an ecological cycle that allows increased biological species diversity.

In terms of land use, Cheongsando Gudeuljangnon is made by using an agricultural technology that is different from that of typical terraced paddies. Even small plots of land were maximized in Cheongsando Island, if irrigation was possible, by stacking stones. A continuous irrigation and drainage system was applied, where water used in the upper-level paddies could be recycled in the lower-level paddies. On the edges of the paddies, 2 to 3 aqueducts were constructed to control irrigation and drainage. These irrigation techniques reflected the wisdom of the residents of Cheongsando, who used the fields in all seasons, alternating between dry fields and rice paddies depending on weather conditions. Gudeuljangnon requires more refined and frequent ploughing than typical rice paddies.

Figure 2: Structure of the stone walls of Gudeuljangnon

©FAO/GIAHS

Figure 3: Agricultural landscape of Gudeuljangnon

©FAO/GIAHS

2.1  Construction techniques for Cheongsando Island Gudeuljangnon

Gudeuljangnon are constructed of four layers. The lower walls of Gudeuljangnon are constructed by mixing and stacking up stones of various sizes (20-50cm in diameter). The heights of the stone walls differ depending on the elevation of the terrain. On average, the walls are 100-150cm high, but can range from 70 to 300cm. The aqueducts are constructed by laying a large flat flagstone (Gudeul) above the lower stone walls, taking into consideration the water flow and the crops on the upper and lower paddies. The size of the aqueducts differs depending on the location of the Gudeuljangnon, and the average diameter is 30-50cm. The sizes are generally larger upstream than downstream.

Figure 4: Structure of the lower stone wall in Gudeuljangnon

©FAO/GIAHS

The upper part of the lower Gudeuljangnon stone wall is composed of different soil layers. The very bottom, which contacts the wall, is covered with approximately 15-20 cm of red mud. The mud layer prevents water loss and allows the water be retained for maximum amount of time possible. The roots of the crops do not reach the mud layer; a 20 to 30cm thick soil layer is placed above the mud layer for cultivation. Because this soil layer is thin, with the thickness differing for each Gudeuljangnon, intricate farming techniques are required.

Figure 5: Cross section of Gudeuljangnon

©FAO/GIAHS

Figure 6: Structure of the Gudeuljangnon

©FAO/GIAHS

The aqueducts of Gudeuljangnon were approximately 50-200 cm deep, and there were approximately 2 to 3 per plot on average. The aqueducts had the basic function of irrigating and draining the water needed for agriculture. Furthermore, unnecessary water was kept out and excess water was directed through the bottom, such that the lower aqueducts functioned in drainage. The drainage aqueducts as sluices finally released the water from both the upper and lower aqueducts. The average number and size of the aqueducts differed depending on the lots the location and number of aqueducts were determined based on the water flow. Normally, as water was more abundant upstream than downstream, aqueducts were larger and more abundant upstream.

Figure 7: (left) Yangji-ri village Gudeuljangnon, (middle) Yangji-ri village drainage aqueduc, (right) Inner structure of the aqueducts

©FAO/GIAHS

Figure 8: Cross-sectional view of the Gudeuljangnon

©FAO/GIAHS

2.2 Soil and water conservation

The Cheongsando Island Gudeuljangnon was constructed using the stone-stacking method for the lower part of the structure. The terrace paddies built by this method prevent soil erosion on the slopes and increase soil fertility. Furthermore, due to the geographic characteristics of the island, the runoff coefficient is high, but Gudeuljangnon cultivation creates an environment where the water resource can remain in the soil for an extended time. The ecological cycle is strengthened in this manner and can support a habitat for amphibians, reptiles, and other taxa.

The agricultural water retained in the Gudeuljangnon is combined with compost to promote microbiological reactions, preventing hardening of the soil. Furthermore, due to the surrounding forests and artificially created pools, a biologically self-sustainable environment is created. The water that enters the Gudeuljangnon continuously flows to the lower paddies, and is combined with microorganisms, strengthening the capacity for purification of the paddies.

Figure 9: Gudeuljangnon self-purification

©FAO/GIAHS

2.3 Edge effect of Gudeuljangnon for enriching biodiversity

Gudeuljangnon paddies are manmade areas of arable land that trace the mountain valleys. The upper forest area, the Gudeuljangnon, and the lower village area are connected in an ecological cycle, increasing biological diversity. This signifies a connection of the ecological cycle with the forested hills that were separate before the formation of the Gudeuljangnon. The constructed Gudeuljangnon contain gaps in the lower structure that allow rodents, arthropods, amphibians and reptiles, and the surrounding forest ecotone to be connected as an eco-corridor, and to increase the biological diversity in the Gudeuljangnon.

Figure 10: Schematic diagram of the Edge effect and  Sectional view diagram of the Edge effect

©FAO/GIAHS

2.4 Structure of the food chain near Gudeuljangnon

The food chain surrounding the Gudeuljangnon includes arthropods that live in the gaps between stones in the lower part of the rice paddy, amphibians and reptiles that live on the rice paddies with water, and birds of prey (common buzzard, Buteobuteoand Japanese Sparrowhawk, Accipitergularis, both endangered bird species level 2), forming a hierarchical structure. Of particular note, the longtail tadpole shrimp an environmental indicator species living in clean environments, is found in the Gudeuljangnon.

The longtail tadpole shrimp is an endangered species (level 2) that consumes organic material in the soil and is effective in removing weeds and suppressing pests. This species can be seen by the naked eye between April and September in Sangseo-ri village. The outstanding ecology of Sangseo-ri village has been recognized and this area was designated as a Nature Eco-Village the by the Ministry of Environment in 2010.

Figure 11: Longtail tadpole shrimp

©FAO/GIAHS

3. Universal use of Gudeuljangnon

Unlike typical terrace rice paddies, Gudeuljangnon paddies, in which aqueducts are used for irrigation management, allowed for versatile use of the land. In years with low precipitation, the rice paddies were converted into dry fields; when two crops were planted in a year, water was irrigated in the paddies to grow rice during summer, and after the rice harvest, the field was used to grow garlic, onions, and ferns. The current agricultural production on Cheongsando Island is still highest for rice, and previous staples such as tubers and condiment vegetables are now cultivated for income.

3.1 Crop diversity of the Gudeuljangnon rice paddies and fields

Traditionally, rice, barley, millet, and cotton plants have been cultivated in Cheongsando Island. A type of brown rice is grown in Gudeuljangnon that has 8 times the content of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), than that of normal brown rice, and 4 times the GABA content of black rice. This rice can help promote the growth and development of adolescents, and can strengthen the immune system. On Cheongsando Island, tubers (sweet potatoes and potatoes) and garlic have been cultivated. Presently, produce such as garlic, onions, legumes, and spring cabbages are cultivated in dry fields for income, and not as staple foods. The farmhouse population of Cheongsando Island has been decreasing each year, and the number of households participating in both agriculture and fisheries has been increasing through increased abalone farms. Recently, canola and green barley have been planted as landscaping and decorative crops.

Figure 12:

©FAO/GIAHS

3.2 Flexible use as paddies and dry fields

The Cheongsando Island Gudeuljangnon was devised as an underground drainage culvert system to manage water for agriculture, due to rapid drainage rates of sandy soil with high rock content. However, the rapid drainage of water was actually advantageous in the conversion of Gudeuljangnon between rice paddies and dry fields. Gudeuljangnon were traditionally used as versatile fields that met both the water requirements of rice paddies and the drainage requirements of dry fields. When there was a severe drought on Cheongsando Island, creating difficulties for rice farming, buckwheat was planted instead or the paddies were converted into dry fields to grow potatoes. If a Gudeuljangnon is drained and converted into a dry field, the conditions of the soil for crop growth are poor immediately after conversion. However, the intermediate products of the degradation of organic substances accumulated during the irrigation period were quickly degraded, and for the next one to two years, there was an increase in ammonia supply-an advantageous condition for crops. Furthermore, conversion of rice paddies into dry fields could lead to a decline in soil-borne diseases and pests. Black rot in legumes or snow mold in wheat is more common under repeated cultivation, and if the fields are irrigated and rice is cultivated, these diseases decline. The Gudeuljangnon, with high drainage and conversion between rice paddies and fields, also helped prevent the growth of weeds.

4. Difference between normal terraces and Gudeuljangnon

At first glance, Gudeuljangnon appear to be similar to typical terraced fields, but they have a significantly different irrigation system. Gudeuljangnon maximize the usable area of the land by constructing the paddies above stacked rocks of various sizes, to increase the agricultural productivity of Cheongsando Island, which has scarce arable land. In normal terraces, water and drainage flow on the surface, but in Gudeuljangnon, underground aqueducts are used at upper and lower levels. It is unique that a large flagstone (Gudeul) is used to control water flow by damming water as required for cultivation or releasing it to the paddy below. 5. Farming methods and tools

5.1  Traditional fertilization for soil resource management

The building of arable land by Gudeuljangnon did not overcome all of the limitations of the soil. Cheongsando Island Gudeuljangnon has a thin soil layer, and drainage between the supporting stone structures is higher than that in rice paddies on the peninsula. Therefore, loss of nutrients, and hardening and drying of soil are high. To overcome these limitations, traditional fertilization and management have been continuously used.

Traditional fertilization of Gudeuljangnon was achieved by composting grass and barley left after feeding cattle in the neighbouring forest, in a mixture with human manure. In the past, when rice production was low, rice straw was used to make thatched straw roofs that are used in the traditional funerals called Chobun. Therefore, previously, the residents of Cheongsando Island spent most of their time going to the nearby mountains to collect grass and plants. The methods of cutting grass and plants were similar to those used in other regions. However, to improve soils with a high level of nutrient loss, compost was used continuously throughout the year. Another mode of fertilization management in udeuljangnon was to use the silk tree (scientific name: Albizia julibrissin Durazz). The residents of Cheongsando Island collected the young leaves of the silk tree, called "Umsun," to mix with grass and use as fertilizer. Because the silk tree leaves have antiseptic properties, this helped to prevent disease and pests in the Gudeuljangnon.

5.2  Adaptability of Gudeuljangnon ploughing techniques

Gudeuljangnon agriculture was characterized by labour-intensive agriculture and a refined ploughing technique, because the bottom of the Gudeuljangnon was composed of stone on top of which a 15 to 20cm mud layer and a 15 to 25cm layer of cultivatable soil was laid. The plough could not be dug in deeply. Therefore, the ploughing practices maintained an egg-sized depth, and the bastion on the plough was adjusted depending on the condition of the soil. If the bastion was raised, the ploughing could go deeper, and if it was lowered, the ploughing would be more shallow. If the bastion was not adjusted correctly, it could break hitting rocks and so have to be refined to not damage the mud layer. Furthermore, the shape (Topography-adaptation) of the Gudeuljangnon is irregular, necessitating a labour-intensive ploughing technique. As the paddies were made following the slope in a terraced shape, if the corners could not be ploughed, a pick or shovel was used to manually plough the corner.

©FAO/GIAHS

5.3  Traditional cropping system of Gudeuljangnon

The traditional cropping system of Cheongsando Island, based on rice cultivation, is classified as either one-crop-a-year, or as two-crops-a-year, where rice cultivation is followed by barley cultivation. The one-crop–a-year system which is more common towards the slope of the mountain, requires 7 ploughing cycles and 2 harrowings of the land. In the two-crop-a-year systems, the soil is softer than that in one-crop-a-year areas, because barley is planted and 4 ploughing and 2 harrowing cycles are required.

The order of steps in the one-crop-a-year system is as follows:

  1. Ploughing the land sitting over the winter (also called “Baemitanda”);
  2. Ploughing the levee (“Geoseulinda”);
  3. Adding compost in the ditch, and breaking large soil masses with the plough (“Gunggeullinda”); and
  4. Ploughing the levees again to turn the grass over.

The subsequent wet-ploughing steps included the following:

  1. Irrigating and harrowing;
  2. Creating ditches and levees by ploughing;
  3. Using the plough (“Junggari”) to create levees using the soil; and
  4. Ploughing the irrigated field cleanly using the plough (“Mujaenggi”), and harrowing on the day of seedling transplantation.

The steps for the 2-crop-a-year system are as follows:

  1. On the first day of “Baemittagi,” using the first plough to cut the rice and to turn over the roots of the barley;
  2. Adding compost to the harrowed field ditches;
  3. Ploughing when making the levees; and
  4. Harrowing thorough “Mujaenggi hitting”.
Figure 16: The order of steps in Traditional cropping system

©FAO/GIAHS

Consequently, the number of ploughing cycles is much higher and the variety is wider, compared to typical ploughing in agricultural communities (3-4). Furthermore, as the rice is not planted in deep soil, but rather in artificially constructed Gudeuljangnon, intricate ploughing techniques are required. In particular, controlling the depth of ploughing is an intricate technique that only the owner of the field can know. Steps 1 to 4 are called "dry ploughing" because water is not added, and the subsequent steps are called "wet ploughing," with the addition of water.

6. Validation of the practice

The residents have constructed and maintained Gudeuljangnon as the principal means of livelihood. The Gudeuljangnon surveyed thus far cover approximately 57 lots and 4.9 ha, in Buheung-ri Village, Yangji-ri Village, and Sangseo-ri Village. Gudeuljangnon have been found in other areas of the island, but due to the decline and aging of the Island’s population, damaged and fallow Gudeuljangnon paddies have been increasing in number. To resolve these problems, the residents of Cheongsando Island have declared the island to have a vision of an "Environmentally Friendly Organic Agriculture Island," and have formed a citizens' association for the conservation and application of Gudeuljangnon.

7. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

The ancestor of Cheongsando Island repeated the endless process of gathering and stacking stones to build the Gudeuljangnon. Therefore, a continuous stream of labour-intensive work was supplied. For this reason, the residents of Cheongsando Island used family- and village-level cooperative labour to build arable land. Cheongsando Island residents say that it requires at least a few months, or up to one to two years to create a small Gudeuljangnon. Cooperative labour was also critical to cultivate and maintain the Gudeuljangnon, and to manage the artificially created Bo that were constructed to supply and distribute water. A few plots were grouped to select a Bojagin, and the people managed the irrigation. The Bojagin system is a cooperative irrigation-management system that manages the use of water, critical for rice paddy cultivation, through mutual agreement and convention. In addition, the Soeondu system, in which the cattle necessary for cultivation were shared, was a method for cooperatively utilizing the tools required for agriculture.

  • Temperate, cool,
  • Temperate, cold.

Traditional Gudeuljang Irrigated rice terraces in Cheongsando

Gudeuljangnon are rice paddies created by re-engineering the natural environment to increase rice production in areas with disadvantageous soil and water conditions in Cheongsando Island. The main characteristics of Cheongsando Island Gudeuljangnon are culverts constructed by stacking stones; these culverts are used as aqueducts of underground irrigation and drainage systems so as to preserve effective surface of paddies. The Cheongsando Island residents call these paddies constructed on stone walls, “Gudeuljangnon,” because the techniques and forms of stone stacking used to construct them is similar to the Gudeuljang, a flagstone used for Ondol-the traditional Korean home heating system. This practice describes the construction of Gudeuljangnon.



Description

1. Background

The Cheongsando Island area is located south of the Korean Peninsula, and is affiliated with Wando County of Jeollanam-do. The Gudeuljangnon paddy system was born out of the natural environment of the island being disadvantageous for paddy agriculture due to steep slopes, sandy soil with rocks and rapid drainage, and a scarcity of water for paddy farming. To overcome these limitations, the “Gudeuljang” structure, used in the traditional Korean home-heating system called Ondol, was applied to build the irrigation system for the rice paddies.

Figure 1: Distribution of Cheongsando Island Gudeuljangnon.

©FAO/GIAHS

2. Working principle

Gudeuljangnon, made from stacked stones, prevent soil loss and improve the soil's ability to purify water. The water that flows through gaps between the stones and in the waterways provides an environment for reptiles, amphibians, and crustaceans such as the longtail tadpole shrimp. The waterway connects the upper forest area, where water remains for an extended period, with the lower village area, forming an ecological cycle that allows increased biological species diversity.

In terms of land use, Cheongsando Gudeuljangnon is made by using an agricultural technology that is different from that of typical terraced paddies. Even small plots of land were maximized in Cheongsando Island, if irrigation was possible, by stacking stones. A continuous irrigation and drainage system was applied, where water used in the upper-level paddies could be recycled in the lower-level paddies. On the edges of the paddies, 2 to 3 aqueducts were constructed to control irrigation and drainage. These irrigation techniques reflected the wisdom of the residents of Cheongsando, who used the fields in all seasons, alternating between dry fields and rice paddies depending on weather conditions. Gudeuljangnon requires more refined and frequent ploughing than typical rice paddies.

Figure 2: Structure of the stone walls of Gudeuljangnon

©FAO/GIAHS

Figure 3: Agricultural landscape of Gudeuljangnon

©FAO/GIAHS

2.1  Construction techniques for Cheongsando Island Gudeuljangnon

Gudeuljangnon are constructed of four layers. The lower walls of Gudeuljangnon are constructed by mixing and stacking up stones of various sizes (20-50cm in diameter). The heights of the stone walls differ depending on the elevation of the terrain. On average, the walls are 100-150cm high, but can range from 70 to 300cm. The aqueducts are constructed by laying a large flat flagstone (Gudeul) above the lower stone walls, taking into consideration the water flow and the crops on the upper and lower paddies. The size of the aqueducts differs depending on the location of the Gudeuljangnon, and the average diameter is 30-50cm. The sizes are generally larger upstream than downstream.

Figure 4: Structure of the lower stone wall in Gudeuljangnon

©FAO/GIAHS

The upper part of the lower Gudeuljangnon stone wall is composed of different soil layers. The very bottom, which contacts the wall, is covered with approximately 15-20 cm of red mud. The mud layer prevents water loss and allows the water be retained for maximum amount of time possible. The roots of the crops do not reach the mud layer; a 20 to 30cm thick soil layer is placed above the mud layer for cultivation. Because this soil layer is thin, with the thickness differing for each Gudeuljangnon, intricate farming techniques are required.

Figure 5: Cross section of Gudeuljangnon

©FAO/GIAHS

Figure 6: Structure of the Gudeuljangnon

©FAO/GIAHS

The aqueducts of Gudeuljangnon were approximately 50-200 cm deep, and there were approximately 2 to 3 per plot on average. The aqueducts had the basic function of irrigating and draining the water needed for agriculture. Furthermore, unnecessary water was kept out and excess water was directed through the bottom, such that the lower aqueducts functioned in drainage. The drainage aqueducts as sluices finally released the water from both the upper and lower aqueducts. The average number and size of the aqueducts differed depending on the lots the location and number of aqueducts were determined based on the water flow. Normally, as water was more abundant upstream than downstream, aqueducts were larger and more abundant upstream.

Figure 7: (left) Yangji-ri village Gudeuljangnon, (middle) Yangji-ri village drainage aqueduc, (right) Inner structure of the aqueducts

©FAO/GIAHS

Figure 8: Cross-sectional view of the Gudeuljangnon

©FAO/GIAHS

2.2 Soil and water conservation

The Cheongsando Island Gudeuljangnon was constructed using the stone-stacking method for the lower part of the structure. The terrace paddies built by this method prevent soil erosion on the slopes and increase soil fertility. Furthermore, due to the geographic characteristics of the island, the runoff coefficient is high, but Gudeuljangnon cultivation creates an environment where the water resource can remain in the soil for an extended time. The ecological cycle is strengthened in this manner and can support a habitat for amphibians, reptiles, and other taxa.

The agricultural water retained in the Gudeuljangnon is combined with compost to promote microbiological reactions, preventing hardening of the soil. Furthermore, due to the surrounding forests and artificially created pools, a biologically self-sustainable environment is created. The water that enters the Gudeuljangnon continuously flows to the lower paddies, and is combined with microorganisms, strengthening the capacity for purification of the paddies.

Figure 9: Gudeuljangnon self-purification

©FAO/GIAHS

2.3 Edge effect of Gudeuljangnon for enriching biodiversity

Gudeuljangnon paddies are manmade areas of arable land that trace the mountain valleys. The upper forest area, the Gudeuljangnon, and the lower village area are connected in an ecological cycle, increasing biological diversity. This signifies a connection of the ecological cycle with the forested hills that were separate before the formation of the Gudeuljangnon. The constructed Gudeuljangnon contain gaps in the lower structure that allow rodents, arthropods, amphibians and reptiles, and the surrounding forest ecotone to be connected as an eco-corridor, and to increase the biological diversity in the Gudeuljangnon.

Figure 10: Schematic diagram of the Edge effect and  Sectional view diagram of the Edge effect

©FAO/GIAHS

2.4 Structure of the food chain near Gudeuljangnon

The food chain surrounding the Gudeuljangnon includes arthropods that live in the gaps between stones in the lower part of the rice paddy, amphibians and reptiles that live on the rice paddies with water, and birds of prey (common buzzard, Buteobuteoand Japanese Sparrowhawk, Accipitergularis, both endangered bird species level 2), forming a hierarchical structure. Of particular note, the longtail tadpole shrimp an environmental indicator species living in clean environments, is found in the Gudeuljangnon.

The longtail tadpole shrimp is an endangered species (level 2) that consumes organic material in the soil and is effective in removing weeds and suppressing pests. This species can be seen by the naked eye between April and September in Sangseo-ri village. The outstanding ecology of Sangseo-ri village has been recognized and this area was designated as a Nature Eco-Village the by the Ministry of Environment in 2010.

Figure 11: Longtail tadpole shrimp

©FAO/GIAHS

3. Universal use of Gudeuljangnon

Unlike typical terrace rice paddies, Gudeuljangnon paddies, in which aqueducts are used for irrigation management, allowed for versatile use of the land. In years with low precipitation, the rice paddies were converted into dry fields; when two crops were planted in a year, water was irrigated in the paddies to grow rice during summer, and after the rice harvest, the field was used to grow garlic, onions, and ferns. The current agricultural production on Cheongsando Island is still highest for rice, and previous staples such as tubers and condiment vegetables are now cultivated for income.

3.1 Crop diversity of the Gudeuljangnon rice paddies and fields

Traditionally, rice, barley, millet, and cotton plants have been cultivated in Cheongsando Island. A type of brown rice is grown in Gudeuljangnon that has 8 times the content of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), than that of normal brown rice, and 4 times the GABA content of black rice. This rice can help promote the growth and development of adolescents, and can strengthen the immune system. On Cheongsando Island, tubers (sweet potatoes and potatoes) and garlic have been cultivated. Presently, produce such as garlic, onions, legumes, and spring cabbages are cultivated in dry fields for income, and not as staple foods. The farmhouse population of Cheongsando Island has been decreasing each year, and the number of households participating in both agriculture and fisheries has been increasing through increased abalone farms. Recently, canola and green barley have been planted as landscaping and decorative crops.

Figure 12:

©FAO/GIAHS

The Cheongsando Island Gudeuljangnon was devised as an underground drainage culvert system to manage water for agriculture, due to rapid drainage rates of sandy soil with high rock content. INNOVATION TITLE: Gudeuljangnon Terraced Rice System

DESCRIPTION: A traditional agricultural engineering innovation combining stone-stacking techniques and underground aqueducts to create productive rice paddies on disadvantaged terrain, enabling water management, soil conservation, and flexible land use between wet and dry farming.

CRITERIA MET: It's an existing solution used in a different context, adapting the Korean Ondol heating system's stone-stacking technique (Gudeuljang) to create a novel agricultural system.

records.title: Varroa mite control: efficient approach for organic acid treatments through colony structural adjustment with creation of artificial swarms, China
records.description:
Description

Varroa mite infestation represents one of the greatest threats to honey bee health, honey production, and pollination services. The varroa mite (or simply “varroa”) feeds on the brood and adults of western (European) honey bees (A. mellifera) (figure 1), which could reduce overall colony vigor as well as transmit and enhance diseases, such as honey bee viruses. Varroa is the most damaging honeybee pest and a major factor responsible for colony losses worldwide. When honeybee colonies are untreated or treated ineffectively, colonies may gradually depopulate up to fail, and beekeepers can incur major economic losses. In addition, colonies with high varroa mite levels are a source of mites that can spread to other colonies, even in other apiaries, through drifting, robbing, and absconding activity of bees. Therefore, several approaches are developed for varroa mite control, such as the use of oxalic acid and formic acid. However, these chemicals may result toxic for honey bees (e.g. especially formic acid for honey bee queens, in case of high temperatures) or may give poor efficacy if there is much brood present, for they won’t kill mites in the brood. 1. Advantage of the approach

The approach here presented consists in bringing hives in a broodless state, where no sealed brood is present, through the creation of artificial swarms. This strategy allows for increasing the number of hives in the apiary and may have a minimal impact on honeybee production if the intervention on the hives is performed before or after honey flow period.

Equipment needed:

  • grafting tool
  • queen cell cup
  • queen cage
  • syringe or spray bottle
  • organic acid (oxalic acid or formic acid).

The practical step-by-step guide of how to implement the practice is provided below.

2.1 New queen rearing

Select a colony with perfect performance, graft 1-day larvae into artificial queen cell cups, and place the frame with transferred larvae into a strong queenless colony (queen bank) for queen rearing. After 8 days, put the matching cages over the queen cell (figure 2).

For the target colony, all frames with capped brood (with a certain amount of nurse bees, figure 3) and sufficient nutriment (pollen and honey) are moved to the new hive. Make sure the brood frames are surrounded with honey and pollen reserves. Meanwhile, a caged virgin queen from the queen bank is introduced into the newly established colony. The queen is easily accepted by the young workers, so the queen can be removed from the cage when it is accepted on the next day. The newly established colony with all sealed brood should be moved to a nearby apiary to avoid cross-infection. Treat the new colony with a chemical after 13 days, when all the brood has developed into adult bees.

The mother hive with bloodless frames can now be treated with chemicals. Then offer frames with pollen and honey for colony maintenance (the food storage will be refilled quickly because of a large number of foragers) and add new frames with foundation in the hive to create space for development.

Figure 3. Broodless frame (left) and frame with capped brood cells (right). ©IAR of CAAS, BBC of ASAC/Yu Fang

Treat the two hives with chemicals.   • Avoid chemical treatment during the honey flow or when the honey super is on the hive, to reduce the risk of chemical contamination of the honey with the acaricide compounds.
  • Treat all the colonies in the same apiary at the same time, to avoid re-infestation of the treated hives by untreated ones.

3. Validation of the practice

The main pollination areas of Apis mellifera (e.g. Beijing and Henan Provinces) follow this procedure.

Basic equipment for queen rearing; some level of expertise in queen rearing and creation of artificial splits of colonies are needed.

records.title: How to harvest royal jelly, China
records.description:
Description

Royal jelly is not only a natural health substance for human beings, it is also a lucrative hive product for beekeepers. The method for efficient royal jelly production described here requires: good queens (highly recommend high royal jelly producing bee, selective breeding in China), large and strong colony throughout the bee season (the more populous the colony, the better for royal jelly production), sufficient food supply (including honey and pollen), agreeable temperature (20-30°C), efficient tools for royal jelly production, and experienced beekeepers.

The method consists of grafting one day old worker larvae into plastic queen cell cups (queen cell bases) that are inserted into a strong colony for the worker bees to raise the queens. After two days, the artificial queen cells are removed from the hive and the royal jelly is removed from the queen cells.

1. The tools required for royal jelly production

1.1 Grafting pen

This is a tool used to transfer worker larvae from cells in a comb to queen cell bases. A grafting pen is composed of a soft tongue made of bull horn, a plastic tube, and a spring loaded plunger (Figure 1-A). Compared to the grafting needles made of metal, grafting pens are more convenient to use and increase the survival of grafted larvae.

1.2 Royal jelly scraping bar

The royal jelly scraping bar is used to remove the royal jelly from the queen cells. It is composed of a royal jelly scraping tongue and a handle (Figure 1-B). The scraping tongue is made of a flexible plastic or rubber sheet of high tenacity, with a flat shovel- like shape. The width of the scraping tongue piece is the same as that of the longitudinal section of a queen cell. The handle is made of rigid plastic approximately 100 mm in length.

1.3 Tweezers and queen cell wax cleaner

Stainless steel tweezers are used to remove the larva from a queen cell. The queen cell wax cleaner is used for scraping residual wax from the inner wall of a queen cell after royal jelly collection. It has a metal piece that has a similar shape to that of a royal jelly scraping tongue and a rotatable handle sleeve (Figure 1-C).

1.4. Queen cell base bar

The queen cell base bar (Figure 1-D) is made of non-toxic plastic and consists of many queen cell cups. A common queen cell base bar has two rows of cups. The worker larvae will be grafted into the queen cell bases and inserted into a hive. The bees will finish building the queen cell and raise the queen cell larva inside it.

Figure 1. A. grafting pen B. Royal jelly scraping bar C. Queen cell wax cleaner D. Queen cell base bar

©IAR of CAAS, BBC of ASAC/Yu Fang

1.5 Royal jelly production frame

Queen cell base bars can be installed in a royal jelly production frame (figure 4) made of fir tree wood. The size of the periphery of a royal jelly production frame is the same as that of a comb frame. A royal jelly production frame consists of a long beam (width: 13 mm, thickness: 20 mm), 2 sidebars (width: 13 mm, thickness: 10 mm), 5 inner plates attached to the queen cell base bars (width: 13 mm, thickness: 5 mm), and a bottom thicker plate (width: 13 mm, thickness: 10 mm).

1.6 Stainless steel queen cell cutting blade

Before collection of royal jelly, a stainless steel queen cell cutting blade is used to cut off the protruding part of a queen cell built by workers above the plastic queen cup (figure 5).

2. The procedure for producing royal jelly by artificially grafting larvae

The procedure for producing royal jelly by artificially grafting larvae consists of four steps: larva preparation, grafting larvae, harvesting and cleaning queen cells.

2.1 larva preparation

Insert an empty comb and the queen inside a queen excluder (a grid frame with the seam width 4.2 mm that worker could go through freely but the queen could not. figure 2) and insert the frame in the hive. The queen is now forced to to lay eggs on the frame inside of excluder for about 12 h. Generally, most of the cells of the frame contain newly laid eggs, which contributes to the following step of larva grafting. Due to checking whether the cells have egg or not is skipped, the efficiency and success rate of grafting will be improved ultimately.

Move the frame to super hive when the eggs are ready. Make sure the queen keeping away from the frame, and will not lay eggs on that any more. Three days later, the hatched larvae will be grafted to plastic queen cells.

Figure 2. Frame in queen excluder: the queen will fill the frame with eggs

©IAR of CAAS, BBC of ASAC/Yu Fang

2.2 Grafting of larvae

The grafting process consists of grafting 1-day old eggs from the frame that was placed inside the queen excluder into the cups on the queen cell base bar. These are the steps to follow:

  1. Place the assembled frame into a colony for cleaning by the honey bees for 12–24 h.
  2. Put the royal jelly production frame on the comb, then rotate the queen cell bar so that the opening of queen cells faces upward. This will make it easier to insert the larva into the cup.
  3. Insert the tongue of a grafting pen along the inner wall of a worker cell until it slides underneath the body of a larva, lift the larva together with the royal jelly.
  4. Transfer the larva to a plastic queen cell. Insert the grafting pen until the tongue rests on the bottom of a queen cell, and gently press the spring-loaded plunger to force the larva and royal jelly off the tongue (figure 3).
  5. Turn the openings of queen cells downward after each queen cell on the bar is loaded with a larva.
  6. Insert the royal jelly production frame into a royal jelly production colony as soon as possible after all queen cells are loaded with larvae. Generally, a colony with 8–10 combs can support one or two royal jelly production frames (each frame contains 128 queen cells), and a colony with more than 10 combs can have two or three royal jelly production frames.
  7. Inspect the acceptance of queen cells. Open the hive 3–5 h after the royal jelly production frame was inserted into the royal jelly production colony, to check the acceptance of queen cells. If a larva in a queen cell has been accepted, it will be surrounded by nurse bees, and the queen cell will have fresh royal jelly secreted by workers. If the larva was damaged during the transfer or rejection of a larva happens, the larvae will have been removed by workers. In order to increase the production, supplementary grafting will be required to fill the removed cells using the previous larva frame.

Note: the grafting of larvae is the most important step during the process of producing royal jelly. The grafting action has to be gentle and fast and should be completed in a single lift-and-insert operation to avoid damaging the larvae. Otherwise, the larva should be discarded and a new larva, grafted. The best larvae age for the grafting is 12–18 h after hatching. Larvae at this age have a curvy body, a shovel-like shape, and are bathed in royal jelly (Figure 3).

Figure 3. Larva grafting. 1-day-old larvae are grafted into plastic queen cells mounted on bars; the bars are put into a strong colony, nurse bees then feed the larvae in the queen cells with royal jelly.

©IAR of CAAS, BBC of ASAC/Yu Fang

2.3 Harvesting royal jelly

  1.  Retrieve the royal jelly production frame from the hive 68–72 h after larvae grafting. Gently shake the frame and use a bee brush to remove the nursing bees (figure 4).
  2. Cut off the protruding part of a queen cell with a stainless steel queen cell cutting blade, and remove the larvae from the queen cells using tweezers (figure 5).
  3. Collect royal jelly from the queen cells with a royal jelly scraping bar, and transfer the royal jelly into a royal jelly bottle for storage (figure 6).
  4. Immediately freeze the bottle or place it temporarily in a thermos flask with ice.
Figure 4. The bars for royal jelly production are removed from the colony after about three days.

©IAR of CAAS, BBC of ASAC/Yu Fang

Figure 5. The protruding part of a queen cells are cut off, larvae are removed from the queen cups.

©IAR of CAAS, BBC of ASAC/Yu Fang

Figure 6. Royal jelly is collected with scraping bar and packed

©IAR of CAAS, BBC of ASAC/Yu Fang

2.4 Cleaning queen cells

  1. Clean the queen cells with a queen cell wax cleaner to remove residual wax on the inner wall and rim of plastic queen cell (figure 7).
  2. Assemble the queen cell base bar for the next round of larva grafting.
Figure 7. Remove residual wax on the inner wall and rim of plastic queen cell.

©IAR of CAAS, BBC of ASAC/Yu Fang

In order to maintain hygiene, it is important to sterilize all the tools or containers before use and wear gloves when collecting. Generally, the harvested royal jelly could be put in buckets for wholesale, or divided in bottles for retail, but no matter which way to trade, they are necessary to be stored in freezer as soon as possible.

Furthermore, the discarded queen larvae rich in source of proteins, vitamins and minerals, which could be exploited as nourishment or senior food, please refer to the specific method information sheet on honeybee drone larvae (https://www.fao.org/teca/en/technologies/8775).

3. Validation of the practice

The main producing areas of royal jelly follow this procedure, such as Beijing, Henan and Zhejiang Provinces.

4. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

The practices described here uses Chinese bees selected for royal jelly production that can produce a high amount of queen cells. The quantity of cells must be adapted (reduced) when using other queen lines.

The agreeable temperature (20-30°C) and sufficient food supply (nectar and pollen plants surrounding) are required, which support the colonies developing well.

Royal jelly producers should have a reliable cold storage facility available to store the royal jelly, as royal jelly spoils very quickly at room temperature.

5. Related/associated technologies

  • Honey extracted by pressing: wooden honey press from Cameroon
  • How to make a Kenyan topbar hive
  • How to make the hive "Ruche Fonge"
  • How to make the "La grande" topbar hive
  • Harvesting honey from giant honey bees
  • Beekeeping in Africa: honey and bee wax extraction

  1.  Retrieve the royal jelly production frame from the hive 68–72 h after larvae grafting. Gently shake the frame and use a bee brush to remove the nursing bees (figure 4).
  2. Cut off the protruding part of a queen cell with a stainless steel queen cell cutting blade, and remove the larvae from the queen cells using tweezers (figure 5).
  3. Collect royal jelly from the queen cells with a royal jelly scraping bar, and transfer the royal jelly into a royal jelly bottle for storage (figure 6).
  4. Immediately freeze the bottle or place it temporarily in a thermos flask with ice.
Figure 4. The bars for royal jelly production are removed from the colony after about three days.

©IAR of CAAS, BBC of ASAC/Yu Fang

Figure 5. The protruding part of a queen cells are cut off, larvae are removed from the queen cups.

©IAR of CAAS, BBC of ASAC/Yu Fang

Figure 6. Royal jelly is collected with scraping bar and packed

©IAR of CAAS, BBC of ASAC/Yu Fang

2.4 Cleaning queen cells

  1. Clean the queen cells with a queen cell wax cleaner to remove residual wax on the inner wall and rim of plastic queen cell (figure 7).
  2. Assemble the queen cell base bar for the next round of larva grafting.
Figure 7. Remove residual wax on the inner wall and rim of plastic queen cell.

©IAR of CAAS, BBC of ASAC/Yu Fang

In order to maintain hygiene, it is important to sterilize all the tools or containers before use and wear gloves when collecting. Generally, the harvested royal jelly could be put in buckets for wholesale, or divided in bottles for retail, but no matter which way to trade, they are necessary to be stored in freezer as soon as possible.

Furthermore, the discarded queen larvae rich in source of proteins, vitamins and minerals, which could be exploited as nourishment or senior food, please refer to the specific method information sheet on honeybee drone larvae (https://www.fao.org/teca/en/technologies/8775).

3. Validation of the practice

The main producing areas of royal jelly follow this procedure, such as Beijing, Henan and Zhejiang Provinces.

4. Minimum requirements for the successful implementation of the practice

The practices described here uses Chinese bees selected for royal jelly production that can produce a high amount of queen cells. The quantity of cells must be adapted (reduced) when using other queen lines.

The agreeable temperature (20-30°C) and sufficient food supply (nectar and pollen plants surrounding) are required, which support the colonies developing well.

Royal jelly producers should have a reliable cold storage facility available to store the royal jelly, as royal jelly spoils very quickly at room temperature.

records.description:
La description

1. Introduction 

La grande fausse teigne et la petite fausse teigne sont des papillons de nuit de la famille des Pyralidae qui constituent sous leur forme larvaire un danger certain pour les colonies d’abeilles.

On distingue deux types de fausse teigne : la petite fausse teigne (Achorea grisella) et la grande, plus fréquente (Galleria mellonella). Privilégiant les climats chauds et des altitudes inférieures à 1000 mètres, la fausse teigne apprécie l’humidité et les espaces confinés. La grande et la petite teigne procèdent de la même manière et provoquent les mêmes dégâts. Attention cependant avec la petite teigne : il faut redoubler d’attention car sa petite taille la rend difficilement détectable.

Figure 1: Grande teigne (Galleria mellonella)

© Linnaeus, 1758

Figure 2: Petite teigne (Achroea grisella)

© Fabricius, 1794

Source: www.apisavoir.ch/la fausse teigne

On retrouve la fausse teigne sur tous les continents :

Figure 3: Répartition géographique de la fausse teigne

Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5492075/

2. La fausse teigne (grande et petite fausse teigne) : c’est quoi?

La grande teigne a une longueur de 20-25 mm et une envergure de 30 à 41 mm.

Quant à la petite teigne, elle peut atteindre 14 mm et une envergure de 23 à 28 mm.

Après une ponte (nocturne) de grappes d’œufs dans les alvéoles de la ruche, l’éclosion a lieu après 5 à 8 jours à 24-27° C, ou 10 à 15 jours si la température dépasse les 35°C, mais elle s’interrompt sous -9°C.

Les petites larves subissent de nombreuses mues (de 8 à 9 mues) lors des différents stades larvaires, par conséquent elles grossissent rapidement (les 10 premiers jours, si les conditions sont favorables, une larve peut doubler son poids) avant de devenir papillon.

Figure 4: Cycle biologique de la grande fausse teigne

© d’après S. Boucher, 2016

3. Les menaces pour la ruche

Comme tous les êtres vivants, l’abeille est exposée aux agressions les plus diverses: molécules chimiques qui se trouvent dans les insecticides et herbicides, virus, spores de champignons, bactéries, acariens, hyménoptères, oiseaux, et papillons de nuit: la grande et la petite teigne (Galleria mellonella et Achroia grisella).

Les larves de la fausse teigne s’enfouissent dans les rayons de cire des ruches, dans les cellules non operculées. Elles creusent leur réseau de galeries tapissées de soie dans tous les rayons. Les abeilles ne peuvent pas retirer cette soie, les cellules abîmées ne sont pas réparées et deviennent impropres à la ponte et au stockage du nectar. En grandissant, les larves de la fausse teigne établissent des ponts de soie entre les rayons, ce qui entrave la circulation des abeilles. La ruche devient une vaste toile d’araignée.

4. La fausse teigne: son action et ses dégâts

  • D’une manière générale, les larves de la fausse teigne attaquent seulement les colonies faibles qui arrivent difficilement à se défendre. Il peut arriver cependant qu’elles attaquent même les colonies fortes à cause de leur multiplication très rapide et du fait que les larves de la grande teigne dévorent le couvain operculé à l’abri des contre-attaques des ouvrières.
  • Les dégâts qu’elles engendrent sont très importants durant les températures favorables (le printemps, l’été et début de l’automne).
  • Les larves sont dotées d’un fort appétit, elles dévorent la cire, se nourrissent de pollen et creusent des galeries jusque dans le bois des ruches et des cadres.
  • La larve creuse un réseau de galeries pour trouver sa nourriture. Elle tapisse ses tunnels avec de la soie qui lui sert de protection contre les abeilles ouvrières. Les alvéoles abimées sont irréparables et le cadre tout entier finit par être irrécupérable. La larve passe alors aux cadres voisins en établissant des ponts de soie qui entravent le passage des abeilles.
  • Les larves de la petite fausse teigne sont également à l’origine du couvain tubulaire (ou couvain chauve).
  • Les galeries qu’elles creusent dans la cire réduisent l’espace disponible pour la larve d’abeille: la cellule de la larve dépasse alors du reste du couvain et, en conséquence, ne sera pas operculée.
  • Les teignes adultes et leurs larves transmettent les agents pathogènes de maladies graves pour les abeilles, telle que la loque américaine.
Figure 5: Les différents dégâts du papillon dans une ruche et sur des cadres entreposés. a, b) cocons de fausse teigne ; c) les larves creusent des galeries dans les cadres, d) cadre tapissé de soie

© INRAA/Kabli N, 2014

5. Les conditions favorables à la fausse teigne

Les cycles de vie, et donc le développement général de la fausse teigne dépend des conditions climatiques et environnementales et est en particulier lié à la température du milieu, l’aération le niveau de luminosité. La reproduction et le développement rapide de la fausse teigne sont favorisés lorsque la température se situe entre 28 et 30°C. Au-dessous de 28ºC et au-dessus de 30ºC, son développement est ralenti. Les niveaux d'éclairage et la ventilation jouent également un rôle non négligeable: le manque de lumière et/ou de ventilation accélèrent le développement de la fausse teigne.

Une colonie forte, saine et hygiénique n’est en générale pas confrontée à ce problème.

6. Comment lutter contre la fausse teigne?

  • Il existe différents moyens de lutter contre la fausse teigne et de limiter les dégâts qu’elle cause:
  • Bien entretenir le rucher afin de rendre les colonies d’abeilles fortes (denses) et à même de neutraliser la fausse teigne.
  • Selon le cas, incinérer ou traiter par le froid les cadres infectés des ruches abandonnées car ils peuvent constituer des lieux propices à la propagation de la fausse teigne. Dans le cas d’infestation importante, il est préconisé en général l’élimination immédiate des cadres par incinération. Si toutefois l’incinération n’est pas une option pour l’apiculteur, il est conseillé de traiter les cadres en question par flammes (chalumeau) une fois la cire brulée. Ainsi, les cadres désinfectés peuvent être réutilisés après une inspection rigoureuse. D’autre part si l’infestation est modérée, mettre les cadres infectés dans un sac en plastique et procéder à leur congélation pendant 48 heures à une température avoisinant les -7°C. Après congélation, racler avec un couteau les matières fécales, toiles et larves de la fausse teigne.
  • Quant aux colonies faibles, les renforcer en les réunissant dans une même ruche.

Pour protéger les cadres stockés de la fausse teigne, les méthodes suivantes se sont avérées efficaces:

  • Le courant d’air : Les larves de fausse teigne détestent les courants d’air. Pour en créer, on utilise l’effet cheminée : cette méthode consiste à empiler les hausses en colonne (Figure 10).
  • Congélation : Mettre les cadres au congélateur de -20°C à -28°C pendant 48 heures (Figure 16).
  • La chaleur. Si la chaleur peut être contrôlée, mettre les cadres à 47°C pendant 1h30 (attention la cire fond à 62°C).
  • La gestion des cadres non utilisés : ne pas entreposer les cadres plus d'une saison sans les placer dans une ruche afin qu’ils soient nettoyés par abeilles.
  • Le soufre (anhydride sulfureux) : les hausses sont empilées pour former une colonne, fermée en bas. La languette de soufre est placée dans un récipient, plat de préférence (assiette, couvercle en métal, etc.), lui-même posé sur le haut des cadres de la hausse au sommet de la colonne. On rajoute ensuite une hausse vide au-dessus. On allume la mèche de soufre et on ferme le haut de la colonne (avec par exemple un toit de ruche). Laisser agir une journée. Le soufre n'élimine pas les œufs de la fausse teigne, donc il faudra faire un second traitement deux semaines après le premier (certains conseillent toutes les deux semaines) pour éliminer les éventuelles larves écloses des œufs. Attention, les vapeurs de soufre sont agressives pour les éléments métalliques des hausses et des cadres lorsqu’ils sont exposés longtemps et/ou à répétition (Figures 11). Cependant, le soufre étant volatile et n’étant pas soluble dans les graisses, il ne présente pas de risque de contamination pour les abeilles, la cire ou le miel.
  • Acide acétique: Les hausses sont empilées pour former une colonne, fermée en bas. Une éponge imbibée d'acide acétique est mise dans un récipient, plat de préférence (assiette en verre, couvercle plastique, etc.), lui-même posé sur le haut des cadres de la hausse au sommet de la colonne. On rajoute ensuite une hausse vide au-dessus et on ferme le haut de la colonne (avec par exemple un toit de ruche). Laisser agir une journée. Cela élimine la totalité de la fausse teigne (œufs, larves, adultes). (Figure 12).
  • Bacillus thuringiensis : bactérie que l’on utilise souvent en agriculture. Elle sécrète une toxine qui s’attaque aux larves de fausse teigne. Inoffensive pour les abeilles, l’homme et les animaux. Le traitement est assez long à appliquer et onéreux.
  • Nourriture pour la volaille : les larves font le bonheur du poulailler. Avant de gratter ou de brûler vos cadres atteints, confiez-les aux poules qui se chargeront du nettoyage (Figure 10).
  • Désinfecter vos hausses, cadres et corps de ruche : à la flamme du chalumeau (Figure 9), ou par trempage dans de l’eau de javel diluée. Une solution efficace peut être préparée en versant 1 volume d’eau de javel disponible en commerce [2,6% Chlore Actif (CA)] dans 9 volumes d’eau froide. On laisse tremper pendant 20 à 30 minutes, puis, on rince à l’eau claire et on sèche au soleil et au courant d’air.

Conseil

  • L’utilisation d’un cérificateur solaire est une bonne pratique tout au long de la saison apicole. Il réglera le problème de stockage des vieux cadres à fondre. Ne recyclez pas en cire gaufrée la vieille cire du corps de ruche. Celle-ci renferme trop souvent des traces de molécules chimiques. Utilisez-la en encaustique ou comme bougies.

À éviter

  • L’utilisation de boules ''antimites'' pour protéger les hausses stockées ! En effet, la matière active particulièrement toxique - paradichlorobenzène (PDCB) - est liposoluble, donc capable de migrer dans la cire et ensuite dans le miel. Très cancérigène pour l’homme.
  • En règle générale : éviter de stocker sans traitements les cadres de ruches dans lesquels se trouve du pollen pour empêcher la croissance des larves de la fausse teigne, celles-ci se nourrissent des restes du pollen et des résidus (cocons).
Figure 6.  Stockage des hausses en colonne en créant un courant d’air.

©INRAA

Figure 7. Les languettes de soufre

Source : https://maiabeille.blogspot.com

Figure 8. Traitement à base de Bacillus thuringiensis  

Source : http://www.ruchewarre.net/viewtopic.php   

Figure 9. Désinfection des hausses au chalumeau

©INRAA/Kabli N

Figure 10. Nettoyage des cadres par les poules

©INRAA

Figure 11. Diffuseur de soufre

©Marc Reynes

Figure 12. Réfrigération des hausses

©INRAA

7. Validation de la technologie/pratique

Cette fiche technique a été développée dans le cadre du projet PRIMA « Sustainable mixte cropping-beekeeping system in the Mediterranean basin (PLANT-B) » Par l'Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique d’Algérie -INRAA.

8. Exigences minimales pour une mise en œuvre réussie

Cette pratique est applicable à l’apiculture utilisant des ruches à cadres.

9. Zones agro-écologiques

  • Tempéré, frais.

10. Technologies associées

  • Les principales maladies des abeilles: ID 8714.
  • Varroas (varroa): ID 8712.
  • Mesures de biosécurité dans l'apiculture concernant les principales maladies des abeilles: ID 10101.
  • Loque américaine : la plus grave maladie bactérienne du couvain: ID 10114.
  • Amibiase : une maladie parasitaire des abeilles adultes: ID 10006.

La grande fausse teigne est un papillon de nuit causant de nombreux dégâts à la ruche et aux colonies d‘abeilles (Apis mellifera), en particulier aux colonies faibles et exposées à un climat chaud et humide. Les larves de la fausse teigne causent des dommages en envahissant les cellules des rayons de cire, en creusant des tunnels dans les cadres, qu’ils soient utilisés dans une ruche ou en stock, et en créant des toiles de soie qui empêchent les abeilles de circuler normalement dans la ruche. Elles peuvent transmettre en outre, des agents pathogènes de maladies graves pour les abeilles. Les ravages causés par la fausse teigne sont souvent sous-estimés alors que ses larves dévorent tout sur leur passage: cire, réserves de nourriture, stocks de pollen, bois, polystyrène et le couvain.

Cela élimine la totalité de la fausse teigne (œufs, larves, adultes). (Figure 12).
  • Bacillus thuringiensis : bactérie que l’on utilise souvent en agriculture. Elle sécrète une toxine qui s’attaque aux larves de fausse teigne. Inoffensive pour les abeilles, l’homme et les animaux. Le traitement est assez long à appliquer et onéreux.
  • Nourriture pour la volaille : les larves font le bonheur du poulailler. Avant de gratter ou de brûler vos cadres atteints, confiez-les aux poules qui se chargeront du nettoyage (Figure 10).
  • Désinfecter vos hausses, cadres et corps de ruche : à la flamme du chalumeau (Figure 9), ou par trempage dans de l’eau de javel diluée. Une solution efficace peut être préparée en versant 1 volume d’eau de javel disponible en commerce [2,6% Chlore Actif (CA)] dans 9 volumes d’eau froide. On laisse tremper pendant 20 à 30 minutes, puis, on rince à l’eau claire et on sèche au soleil et au courant d’air.

Conseil

  • L’utilisation d’un cérificateur solaire est une bonne pratique tout au long de la saison apicole. Il réglera le problème de stockage des vieux cadres à fondre. Ne recyclez pas en cire gaufrée la vieille cire du corps de ruche. Celle-ci renferme trop souvent des traces de molécules chimiques. Utilisez-la en encaustique ou comme bougies.

À éviter

  • L’utilisation de boules ''antimites'' pour protéger les hausses stockées ! En effet, la matière active particulièrement toxique - paradichlorobenzène (PDCB) - est liposoluble, donc capable de migrer dans la cire et ensuite dans le miel. Très cancérigène pour l’homme.
  • En règle générale : éviter de stocker sans traitements les cadres de ruches dans lesquels se trouve du pollen pour empêcher la croissance des larves de la fausse teigne, celles-ci se nourrissent des restes du pollen et des résidus (cocons).

Source : https://maiabeille.blogspot.com

Figure 8. Traitement à base de Bacillus thuringiensis  

Source : http://www.ruchewarre.net/viewtopic.php   

Figure 9. Désinfection des hausses au chalumeau

©INRAA/Kabli N

Figure 10. Nettoyage des cadres par les poules

©INRAA

Figure 11. Diffuseur de soufre

©Marc Reynes

Figure 12. Réfrigération des hausses

©INRAA

Cette pratique est applicable à l’apiculture utilisant des ruches à cadres.
