records.title: Pests and diseases of tamarillo
records.description:
Description

1. Tamarillo diseases

1.1 Whiteflies

Identification: Whiteflies are tiny yellow bodied sap-sucking insects, with white wings. Affected plant turns yellow and die. They are also known to be vector of several viruses on tamarillo e.g., cucumber mosaic virus.

Treatment/management:

  • Use pest free materials.
  • Destroy alternative hosts.
  • Ensure proper weeding.
  • Protect seedlings by using aerated mesh.
  • Use traps/pheromones like Roller Trap, Entrap or Monitrap. See https://realipm.com/.
  • Apply chemical treatment of Cyhalothrin at 14-day intervals.
Figure 1. Whiteflies.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.2 Mosaic virus

Cause: Potyviruses, e.g., tamarillo mosaic virus, potato virus, potato aucuba mosaic virus, alfalfa mosaic virus, tomato spotted wilt virus.

Identification: Characterized by Patches of yellow-green, mosaic patterned mottling and leaf deformation, with reduced fruit quality. Leaves have reduced size and patches of dark green tissue alternating with yellowing.

Treatment/management:

  • Remove trees showing virus symptoms to protect other stands from becoming infected.
  • Use virus free, certified nursery materials.
  • Avoid intercropping with alternative hosts.
  • Use resistant root stocks.
  • Avoid intercropping with alternative hosts like pawpaw, tomato or potato, among others.
  • Control vectors, e.g., aphids, whiteflies, thrips and grasshoppers by using insecticides with the following active ingredients: Lambdacyhalothrin, Acetamiprid, etc.
Figure 2. Mosaic virus.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.3 Anthracnose disease

Causes: Glomerella cingulata or Colletotricum spp.

Identification: Mostly affects the fruit, causing dark or brownish concentric necrotic lesions.

Treatment/management:

  • Use resistant varieties.
  • Ensure proper and timely weeding.
  • Intercrop with non-hosts of anthracnose to avoid inoculum build up.
  • Use disease germplasm from certified sources.
  • Apply a preventive fungicide programme from early onset of fruiting due to latent infection e.g., copper-based products.
Figure 3. Anthracnose disease.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.4 Scale insects

Identification: Scale insects are immobile and look like small bumps. They are sapsucking pests that attach themselves to the twigs, leaves, branches and fruits of the host. They exude wax for protection. They withdraw sap, and some species can transmit viruses.

Treatment/management:

  • Use natural enemies like parasitic wasps and predators, e.g., beetles, bugs, lacewings and mites
  • Prune heavily infested branches to open canopy and expose them to heat and parasites
  • Use pesticide baits (insecticides mixed with an attractant)
  • Apply neem oil, horticultural oils (e.g.., Bonide horticultural oil or Monterey horticultural oil) or insecticidal soap.
  • Use systemic insecticides.
Figure 4. Scale insects.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.5 Blight

Cause: Alternaria spp.

Identification: Initial infection occurs in older leaves, with concentric dark brown spots, which turn yellow with time and finally fall off. Lesions increase with severity.

Treatment/Management:

  • Crop rotation with non-host plants
  • Use resistant varieties
  • Ensure proper weeding
  • Use disease free germplasm
  • Use foliar fungicide with active ingredients, like Metalaxyl-M, Mancozeb, Difenoconazole among others recommended by PCPB.
Figure 5. Blight.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.6 Powdery mildew

Causes: several species of fungi from order Erysiphales with the most common genera being Erysiphe.

Identification: Characterized by fungus growing on surface and producing spores, which appear white on the surface of the leaves and stems.

Treatment/management:

  • The orchard should have adequate sunlight and good air circulation to revent growth of the fungus by controlling humidity.
  • Control watering to reduce humidity and inhibit growth of the fungi.
  • Allow proper spacing.
  • Prune when necessary to reduce shaded leaves.
  • Remove infected plants to prevent inoculum sources.
  • In severe cases, chemical control can be applied using sulphur- and copper-based fungicides, e.g., with active ingredients like copper hydroxide, propineb and Cymoxanil.
  • Use biopesticides like neem oil, etc.
Figure 6. Powdery mildew.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.7 Mealybugs

Identification: Characterized by white, waxy-bodied, cotton-like insects. They produce a sugary substance which attracts ants to feed on.

Treatment/management:

  • Avoid alternative hosts, e.g., pawpaw, mango, etc.
  • Prune heavily infested branches.
  • Use clean farm tools to avoid transferring mealybugs.
  • Encourage natural enemies, e.g., parasitoids.
Figure 7. Mealybugs.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.8 Aphids

Identification: They are characterized by tiny, brown, reddish brown to blackish brown bodies. They suck fluid from leaves and young shoots. Heavy infestation leads to leaves curling and
yellowing. They produce honeydew, which attracts ants.

Treatment/management:

  • Practice orchard hygiene, e.g., proper weeding.
  • Undertake crop rotation with nonhost plants.
  • Use predators, e.g., lacewings, parasitic wasps, etc.
  • Use biopesticides, e.g., the insect pathogenic fungus Metarhizium anisopliae ICIPE 62.
  • Use effective pesticides with the following active ingredients: Lambdacyhalothrin or Thiamethoxam, among others recommended by PCPB.
Figure 8. Aphids.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.9 Diamondback moth caterpillars

Identification: Diamondback moth caterpillars are green in colour with chewing mouth parts. They feed on leaves, stems and all plant parts.

Treatment/management:

  • Crop rotation.
  • Practice orchard hygiene.
Figure 9. Diamondback moth caterpillars.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

2. Related/associated technologies

  • Managing Fall Armyworm: ID 10160.​
  • Major pest and disease identification and management guide for mango: ID 10161.
  • Step by step conversion to organic agriculture: ID 8364.
  • Weed management in organic agriculture: ID 8375.
  • Crop planning and management in organic agriculture: ID 8367.
  • Risk reduction while manipulating pesticides: ID 8348.

  • Ensure proper weeding
  • Use disease free germplasm

Identification: Diamondback moth caterpillars are green in colour with chewing mouth parts. They feed on leaves, stems and all plant parts.

records.title: Pest and diseases of avocado
records.description:
Description

1. Avocado diseases

1.1 Aphids

Identification: They are tiny soft-bodied insects that attack fruit trees by sucking the fluid from young leaves. They are brown, reddish-brown to blackish-brown or greyish-green to blackish-green, and covered with a light powdery dusting. Infested leaves curl, stunt and turn yellow. Wilting can occur due to excess sap withdrawal. Aphids produce honeydew, a sugary substance that attracts ants and facilitates growth of sooty mould, which reduces photosynthesis activity in leaves.

Treatment/management:

  • Timely weeding.
  • Orchard hygiene and sanitation is required.
  • Use natural enemies, e.g., parasitic wasps or lace beetles, among others.
  • Use resistant varieties.
  • Use contact and systemic insecticides with the following active ingredients: Imidacloprid, Acephate, among others.
  • Alternate various chemicals within a crop season to avoid the building up of resistance.
  • Mix the chemicals with Integra or any other sticker, penetrant and spreader to enhance their effectiveness.
  • You can use Jambo Clean to clear sooty mould or any other effective product available in the market.
Figure 1. Aphids.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.2 Stem end rot

Causes: Lasiodiplodi theobromae, Dothiorella sp., Phomopsis sp., Botryosphaeria.

Identification: Dark brown to black rot begins at stem ends and continues toward the other ends. Stem end rot may cause symptoms similar to those of anthracnose disease. The rate of
rot development depends on storage temperature and transport.

Treatment/management:

  • Avoid injuring fruit, as wounds provide an entry point for pathogens.
  • Reduce time between harvesting and consumption.
  • Apply fungicide to manage the disease in the field.
  • Treat the fruit with a fungicide after harvest.
Figure 2. Stem end rot.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.3 Avocado scab disease

Cause: Sphaceloma perseae.

Identification: Avocado scab disease causes lesions, which appear as small dark spots slightly raised on fruits. It gives a corky appearance to the surface of the fruit.

Treatment/management:

  • Proper orchard sanitation, e.g., timely weeding, pruning, sterilizing pruning tools, and removing plant debris and rotten fruits, among others.
  • Ensure proper watering and pruning.
  • Apply a fungicide spray programme with the following active ingredients: Benomyl, Metiram, Propineb or Thiabendazole, among others at preflowering and after harvest.
Figure 3. Avocado scab disease.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.4 Whiteflies

Identification: Characterized by twowinged, white-bodied insects. They suck sap from leaves causing them to turn yellow and fall off following heavy infestation.

Treatment/management:

  • Ensure proper weeding.
  • Avoid alternative hosts.
  • Use traps like Roller Trap or Entrap, among others.
  • Use effective recommended pesticides, e.g., Pyrethroid.
Figure 4. Whiteflies.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.5 Fruit flies

Identification: Fruit flies are two-winged insects, which puncture the surfaces of fruits, leaving holes and causing black lesions. They also puncture twigs and branches, and lay eggs, which hatch into maggots.

Treatment/management:

  • Prune the orchard to improve aeration.
  • Harvest mature and not overripe fruits, which attract fruit flies.
  • Preserve natural enemies, e.g., beetles, ants, parasitic wasps and birds.
Figure 5. Fruit flies.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.6 Stem borers

Identification: Stem borers are larvae that burrow into avocado stems and feed on internal tissue. They can girdle young seedlings and cause older stands to stunt and produce less fruit.

Treatment/Management:

  • Cut off infested branches.
  • Introduce parasitic wasps.
  • Plant repellent plants like Mexican marigold, which produce chemicals that repel stem borers.
Figure 6. Stem borers.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.7 Cercospora spot disease

Cause: Pseudocercospora purpurea.

Identification: Characterized by irregular dark brown lesions, which eventually harden and crack. Leaves display brown spots surrounded by yellow halos. The twigs and pedicles may show
dark brown lesions, which can cause premature fruit fall.

Treatment/management:

  • Proper sanitation to avoid insect pests.
  • Avoid intercropping with alternative hosts.
  • Prune dead branches and remove any fallen fruit.
  • Disinfect farm tools before use.
  • Apply chemicals, e.g., Captan, Thiophanate-methyl, Dithiorcarbamates, copper hydroxide.
Figure 7. Cercospora spot disease.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.8 Thrips

Causes: Selenothrips spp., Heliothrips spp.

Identification: Thrips are small slender insects that feed by sucking sap from leaves, flowers fruits and branches. Infested fruits show silver, brown discolouration. Scabby or leathery
brown scars appear as fruits enlarge, sometimes stunting fruits.

Treatment/management:

  • Prune trees to allow light to penetrate into the orchard.
  • Conserve natural enemies and avoid persistent use of pesticide.
  • Use lambda-cyhalothrin-based products, e.g., Duduthrin; Imidachloprid-based insecticides, e.g., Tata Mida 200SL or Confidor; horticultural oil, Pyrethrin, Alonze, Profile, Defender, Fenthion, Carbaryl, Decamethion, Malathion, Omethoate, Diazinon, among others recommended by PCPB.
Figure 8. Thrips.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.9 Anthracnose

Cause: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides.

Identification: Characterized by occurrence of brown spots, and premature fruit drop. Symptoms develop on flowers, fruits, leaves or twigs. After harvest, the lesions on fruit become
darker, larger and sunken. The lesions eventually spread on fruit surfaces and in the pulp. The fruit rots, and decay advances.

Treatment/Management:

  • Practice orchard hygiene.
  • Remove dead parts.
  • Ensure proper pruning.
  • Use resistant varieties e.g., Hass rather than Fuerte.
  • Use chemical control with copperbased fungicidess e.g., with active ingredients like Mancozeb, sulphur, copper hydroxide, Benomyl, Metiram, Propineb, Thiabendazole or Triforine
  • Apply treatment on fruit using Tecto 500 SC, for example, as a postharvest treatment.
Figure 9. Anthracnose.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.10 Mites

Cause: Oligonychus perseae.

Identification: Mites cause development of circular chlorotic brown spots under the leaves and fruit surface. The colonies cause a silk webbing.

Treatment/management:

  • Apply fertilizers.
  • Ensure proper pruning.
  • Water regularly to avoid plant stress.
  • Apply horticultural oil.
  • Use the predatory mite like Phytoseiulus persimilis.
Figure 10. Mites.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.11 Avocado root rot

Cause: Phytophthora cinnamom.

Identification: The fungus thrives best in soils with excess moisture. It is characterized by yellowing and falling of leaves; wilting and dieback of shoots; and little new leaf growth. Trunks can show water soak cankers and blackened roots, which rot and die with time.

Treatment/management:

  • Use disease free germplasm.
  • Avoid alternate hosts, which include grevillea, acacia, eucalyptus, casuarina, etc.
  • Remove and destroy diseased trees in the orchard.
  • Avoid moving soil or water from infested areas.
  • Sterilize farm tools before and after use.
  • Ensure proper drainage and avoid excess moisture in soil.
  • Seeds obtained from soil should be treated in hot water (50°C for 20 mins).
  • Drench the soil with Trichoderma to limit spread.
  • Practice mulching and ensure good soil health.
  • Use resistant varieties, e.g., Puebla.
  • Use fungicides with the following active ingredients: Mancozeb, sulphur, copper hydroxide, Metalaxyl-M, Oxathiapiprolin, S-Isomer or Fosetylaluminium, among others around canopy areas as a soil drench at monthly intervals.
Figure 11. Avocado root rot.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.12 Mealybugs

Identification: Characterized by white, creamy-coloured insects with waxy bodies. They produce a sugary substance, which attracts ants and growth of sooty mould.

Treatment/management:

  • Proper aeration of orchards by pruning.
  • Reduce inoculum sources by pruning heavily infested branches.
  • Avoid alternative hosts.
Figure 12. Mealybugs.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.13 Red rust

Identification: Also called algae spot, it is characterized by tiny, rust-coloured spots on leaves. It is caused by parasitic algae, Cephaleuros spp.

Treatment/management:

  • Ensure proper pruning.
  • Sterilize pruning materials.
  • Use copper-based fungicides.
Figure 13. Red rust.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.14 Avocado lace bugs

Identification: Avocado lace bugs are small sap-sucking insects that suck sap from leaves, causing chlorotic blotches on leaves, which eventually dry out after heavy infestation. Lace bugs  restrict their feeding to the undersides of leaves and insert their needle-like mouthparts into leaf tissue cells causing curling. Dead areas appear salt damaged. Heavy feeding causes leaf drop.

Treatment/management:

  • Apply insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, neem oil or Pyrethrin.
Figure 14. Avocado lace bugs.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.15 Heart-shaped scale insects

Identification: They are small heartshaped parasites. Adults are immobile and feed on phloem sap through their piercing-sucking mouth parts. They excrete honeydew, on which sooty mould can develop. They cause leaves to yellow and eventually drop off.

Treatment/management:

  • Encourage natural enemies, e.g., parasitoids.
  • Use pesticides like Buprofezin during crawlers’ active stage.
Figure 15. Heart-shaped scale insects.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

2. Related/associated technologies

  • Managing Fall Armyworm: ID 10160.​
  • Major pest and disease identification and management guide for mango: ID 10161.
  • Major pest and disease identification and management guide for tamarillo: ID 10162.
  • Bacterial Black Spot (BBS) identification and control for mango farmers: ID 8470.
  • Anthracnose control for mango farmers: ID 8466.
  • Fruit fly control for mango farmers: ID 8471.
  • Video on how to prune a mango tree: ID 8237.
  • Step by step conversion to organic agriculture: ID 8364.
  • Weed management in organic agriculture: ID 8375.
  • Crop planning and management in organic agriculture: ID 8367.
  • Risk reduction while manipulating pesticides: ID 8348.

records.title: Pests and diseases of Grevillea robusta
records.description:
Description

1. Grevillea robusta diseases

1.1 Botryosphaeria canker

Cause: commonly caused by fungi from family Botryosphaeriaceae.

Identification: Characterized by dark sunken lesions followed by gum exudate around the lesions.

Treatment/management:

  • Remove infected trees.
  • Use proper pruning techniques to avoid unnecessary wounding, which can provide an entry point for pathogens.
  • Promote tree vigour by timely weeding and pruning.
  • Ensure proper site matching to avoid a stressful environment for trees.
  • Use disease-free seeds and seedlings.
  • Pruning tools should be disinfected, and wounds sprayed with fungicides
  • to reduce chances of infection.
Figure 1. Botryosphaeria canker.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.2 Termites

Cause: Genus Macrotermes.

Identification: Termites are small or medium-sized, whitish or colourless insects with short antennae. They have strong biting mouthparts and live in social groups. They are considered to be of economic importance, but some can cause considerable damage. Furthermore, they cause ring debarking destructing vascular bundles.

Treatment/management:

  • Use tolerant tree species, e.g., Melia volkensii as an option for agroforestry in termite prone areas, or incorporate indigenous tree species of desired qualities in Arid and Semi-arid lands (ASALS).
  • Use termite baits (Novaluron, Hexaflumuron).
  • Use botanicals, e.g., Melauleuca spp., Tagetes erecta, garlic oil, Aframomum meleguata, Azadirachta indica, among others Pests and diseases of Grevillea robusta.
  • You can use bacteria, e.g., B. thuringiensis.
  • Apply termiticides regulated by PCPB, e.g., pyrethroids like Permethrin that repel termites from the treatment barrier, and those that kill by lethal contact, e.g., Fipronil or Imidacloprid.

Pests and diseases of Grevillea robusta

Increasing demand for tree products has led to wide production of exotic and native tree species in forest and agroforestry plans. Pests and diseases incidences are at the same time a growing continental crisis. Diseases spread is accelerated by climate change dynamics and implications are concerning African farmers already challenged by weak intervention capacity, fragmented ecosystems, and porous borders. Impacts may also trigger loss of biodiversity, food crisis and constrain agroforestry adaptations strategies. Field observations in parts of Rwanda and Kenya where mango, tamarillo, avocado and grevillea production is prominent, pest and disease incidence is reducing benefits of these production systems. This practice is therefore intended to provide vital information to help smallholders, extension and rural advisory services identify and mange pest and disease incidence before causing total crop failure. Major pest and diseases found in mango are highlighted and possible management plans to reduce spread and losses are indicated as part of wider strategies to dealing with pest and disease break-outs.



Description

1. Grevillea robusta diseases

1.1 Botryosphaeria canker

Cause: commonly caused by fungi from family Botryosphaeriaceae.

Identification: Characterized by dark sunken lesions followed by gum exudate around the lesions.

Treatment/management:

  • Remove infected trees.
  • Use proper pruning techniques to avoid unnecessary wounding, which can provide an entry point for pathogens.
  • Promote tree vigour by timely weeding and pruning.
  • Ensure proper site matching to avoid a stressful environment for trees.
  • Use disease-free seeds and seedlings.
  • Pruning tools should be disinfected, and wounds sprayed with fungicides
  • to reduce chances of infection.
Figure 1. Botryosphaeria canker.

©CIFOR-ICRAF

1.2 Termites

Cause: Genus Macrotermes.

Identification: Termites are small or medium-sized, whitish or colourless insects with short antennae. They have strong biting mouthparts and live in social groups. They are considered to be of economic importance, but some can cause considerable damage. Furthermore, they cause ring debarking destructing vascular bundles.

Treatment/management:

  • Use tolerant tree species, e.g., Melia volkensii as an option for agroforestry in termite prone areas, or incorporate indigenous tree species of desired qualities in Arid and Semi-arid lands (ASALS).
  • Use termite baits (Novaluron, Hexaflumuron).
  • Use botanicals, e.g., Melauleuca spp., Tagetes erecta, garlic oil, Aframomum meleguata, Azadirachta indica, among others Pests and diseases of Grevillea robusta.
  • You can use bacteria, e.g., B. thuringiensis.
  • Apply termiticides regulated by PCPB, e.g., pyrethroids like Permethrin that repel termites from the treatment barrier, and those that kill by lethal contact, e.g., Fipronil or Imidacloprid.

records.title: Growing wild loquat, Uapaca kirkiana
records.description:
Description

Uapaca kirkiana is an indigenous fruit that is widely consumed and traded informally in southern Africa, north of the Limpopo River. The species’ natural range of distribution spans eastern Angola, southern DRC, Burundi, Tanzania, Zambia, Malawi, Mozambique and Zimbabwe (Fig. 1) in a series of disjunct populations. In this expansive area, the species is known by a variety of local names: msuku (Bemba, Chewa, Nyanja); mushuku, muzhanje, (Shona); nkusu, mkusu (Kiswahili); chilundu, muhaka (Lozi); kabofa (Lunda); umhobohobo (Ndebele); mpotopoto (Nyanja) and by its common name, wild loquat. Wild loquat trees are predominantly dioecious, i.e. there are male and female trees, although rare hermaphrodites (both female and male flowers on the same tree) have been observed (Ngulube et al. 1998). The sex ratio in undisturbed natural and planted stands raised from unselected seedlings is 1:1, meaning that both sexes occur in equal numbers. On farmland, however, there is a preponderance of female trees as male trees are removed selectively.

Figure 1. Natural range of distribution of wild loquat

Source: Chawafambira et al. (2020)

1. Flowering

Onset and time of flowering in wild loquat depends on locality. The flowering period is between September and April throughout the natural range of distribution (2°S–20°48’S). There is a south-to-north time lag in flowering, with trees in the southern range flowering and maturing first and progressively moving to the centre and finally the northern ones last. In Malawi for example, flowering occurs between January and May with a peak between February and March when the proportion of trees flowering is highest. Male trees flower earlier than female trees (Seyani 1996; Ngulube et al. 1998). Bud development takes about 16 days for male flowers and about twice as long for female flowers (Ngulube et al. 1998). During anthesis, female flowers remain open for 10 to 14 days, whereas male flowers wither within three to seven days of anthesis. Abortion of male flowers is low but very high for the female inflorescences, where nearly half may abort (Ngulube et al. 1998).

1.1 Pollination agents

Many insects frequent both male and female flowers. Potential pollinators of wild loquat include honeybees (Apis mellifera), beetles (Dothera bennigseni, Chelomenes lunata, Alcidodes denticulatus and Mitracamenta sp) (Ngulube et al. 1998).

1.2 A simple guide to growing wild loquat, Uapaca kirkiana Pollination agents

Many insects frequent both male and female flowers. Potential pollinators of wild loquat include honeybees (Apis mellifera), beetles (Dothera bennigseni, Chelomenes lunata, Alcidodes denticulatus and Mitracamenta sp) (Ngulube et al. 1998). Fruiting: Fruit set occurs between January and April, and fruits ripen from September to February depending on locality. In the Copperbelt province of Zambia, for example, fruits mature between August and November (Mwamba 1995), while in southern Malawi and Zimbabwe, fruits ripen from October to February (Seyani 1996). Fruits are globose in shape and are yellow to brown in colour when ripe. Big fruits with a brown colour are those most preferred by consumers (Kadzere et al. 2006). The edible part of the fruit (mesocarp) constitutes 25 to 50 percent of the fruit weight.

1.3 Nutritional composition

Fruits are rich in carbohydrates, energy, fibre, minerals, proteins and vitamins. The fruit is also an excellent source of vitamin C as well as iron and potassium. Use: Wild loquat fruits are primarily consumed as fresh fruit. Depending on locality, different communities also process wild loquat fruits in a variety of ways to produce a wide range of products such as juice or squashes, jam, wine, sweet beer, porridge and cakes. A study in Zimbabwe found that household income from the sale of wild loquat fruit ranges from USD 10 to USD 260 with an average of USD 66.91 (Chadzimura 2016) per harvesting season, a sizeable amount considering the low investment. Akinnifesi et al. (2007) reported a slightly lower average of USD 50 per season. This average yearly income is enough to buy up to five 50-kg bags (0.25 tonnes) of a staple food (maize). One market in Harare, Zimbabwe, was estimated to trade as much as 20 metric tonnes of wild loquat in a week (Karaan et al. 2005).

2. Propagation

Wild loquat can be propagated by seeds as well as by vegetative methods. Vegetative propagation by grafting air layering (Mkonda et al. 2001; Akinnifesi et al. 2006; Mwang’ingo and Lulandala 2011), tissue culture (Mng’omba 2007) and stem cuttings have all been evaluated for wild loquat with varying degrees of success. Grafting and air layering (marcotting) are recommended, as they are cheap and do not require investments in high-technology equipment. Trees raised from seeds take a long time (+10 years) to first fruiting (Akinnifesi et al. 2008). Because wild loquat is an outcrossing species, trees raised from seeds do not produce true-to-type fruits, whereas grafted and air-layered trees (marcots) only take about 4 years to first fruiting (Mng’omba et al. 2008).

2.1 Propagation through seeds

The process of raising seedlings to establish wild loquat trees is the same as raising seedlings for grafting as rootstocks.

  • Select healthy female trees that have the preferred fruits and other desirable attributes.
  • Collect ripe fruits. Avoid collecting fruits that have fallen on the ground.
  • Fruits should not be stored in sacks or covered containers, as heating will kill the seed within a short time.
  • Seed extraction involves removal of the fruit skin and separation of the seed from the pulp (de-pulping). Clean the seeds with water and air dry them. Do not sun dry seed.
  • Sow seed immediately after extracting it from the ripened fruit as the seed has a very short shelf life.
  • Although fresh seed germinates readily, scarification, manual nicking or soaking seed in water for 24 hours at room temperature will improve germination.
  • Germination is epigeal and will take two to six weeks.

2.1 Growing media

A good growing medium is critical to producing healthy seedlings. A medium comprising 75 percent forest soil and 25 percent composted sawdust is best for producing healthy seedlings (Mhango et al. 2008). Such a medium (forest soil and composted sawdust) has high porosity and good infiltration (Mhango 2000). Forest soil collected from U. kirkiana tree stands is preferred as it contains naturally occurring ectomycorrhizal which improves wild loquat growth by enhancing nutrient and water uptake by the seedlings. The fungus may also lengthen the life of host tree roots, protecting the roots system against soil-borne pathogens (Sileshi et al. 2007; Ramachela 2013). Amending the growing medium with an NPK fertilizer may also improve the quality (large root collar diameter and height) of the seedlings (Mhango et al. 2008). Depending on management, seedlings take between one and two years to reach the right size for planting or grafting (Figure 2). Suckers should be removed (de-suckering) frequently on seedlings grown for grafting (rootstocks) to promote apical dominance and fast growth.

Figure 2. A rootstock of Uapaca kirkiana ready for grafting

©ICRAF

3. Propagation by grafting

Rootstocks of U. kirkiana need to attain pencil-size thickness before grafting. Graft uptake in wild loquat can be as high as 80 percent and both the wedge and the whip grafting methods will produce successful grafts (Mhango and Akinnifesi 2001). The best time to graft Uapaca kirkiana seedlings is at the onset of the summer rains. In Malawi, for example, this is the period between November and December. Grafting success is mainly influenced by the skill of the person grafting, time of the year the scion is collected and the interval between time of scion collection and grafting. When collecting scions observe the following:

  • Scions should be taken from the upper part of the tree.
  • Scion length should be about 10–20 cm.
  • Scion diameter should preferably be of the same size as rootstock i.e. roughly pencil thickness.
  • Scion should have 2 to 4 buds.

3.1 Wedge or cleft graft

Wedge grafting, also known as cleft grafting, is a method of propagating trees by physically joining a small healthy branch, known as a scion, to another tree called the rootstock.

  • Select the preferred, disease-free, mature, healthy, fruit-bearing (i.e. female) wild loquat tree.
  • Select a branch (scion) with a healthy growing tip. Use a sharp knife or pruning shears to cut the scion. A smooth, clean cut is needed for best results.
  • Make a 45-degree angle cut on both sides of the base of the scion using a sharp grafting knife (Figure 3).
  • Make a clean cut horizontally on the rootstock using a knife.
  • Make a wedge-shaped cut down the centre of the rootstock, leaving about a 2.5 cm V-shaped cut or groove in the rootstock.
  • Using a clefting tool, pull back to separate the wedge and insert the scion into the wedge.
Figure 3. Wedge or cleft grafting

©ICRAF

Figure 4. Whip grafting

©ICRAF

Ensure that the bark of the scion matches the bark of the rootstock so that the cambium of scion and rootstock align.

  • Tie grafting tape around the union. You can use a grafting wax or gel if available.
  • Cover the scion with a plastic bag to reduce water loss by transpiration Whip grafting: Rootstocks are raised as described above.
  • Select and collect the scion as described above.
  • Make a slanting 45-degree cut through the bottom end of the scion (Figure 4).
  • On the rootstock, make a 45-degree angled a smooth and straight diagonal cut upwards. This slanting straight-plane cut should be about 5 cm long.
  • Join the cut side of the scion onto the cut side of the rootstock to match.
  • Ensure the cambium of both scion and rootstock align.
  • Tie grafting tape around the union. You can apply a grafting wax or gel if available.
  • Cover the scion with a plastic bag to reduce water loss by transpiration.

3.2 Caring for the grafted plants

Grafted plants should be kept in the shade and watered daily. Keep the grafted plants in a humid environment (RH>70 precent) and maintain good care until the grafting union heals. Remove all shoots growing below the union. Once the union heals, remove the grafting tape.

3.3 Incompatibility

Grafting may fail because of incompatibility between the scion and the rootstock, poor grafting technique, grafting at the wrong physiological stage or poor care in the nursery, which can also cause problems. Most of the observed incompatibility in wild loquat manifests as larger rootstock diameter compared with the scion (Figure 5).

Figure 5. Grafting incompatibility in U. kirkiana manifests as a slow-growing scion on a fast- growing rootstock

©ICRAF

4. Propagation by air layering

Time of setting air layers or marcots is critical to enhancing rooting. The best time to set marcots is at the onset of the rains, and in Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe, this is the period between November and December (Mhango and Akinnifesi 2001; Mhango et al. 2000). In Tanzania, one study (Mwang’ingo and Lulandala 2011) indicated the period soon after the end of the summer rains (June) as the best time. In Malawi, rooting of initiated air layers averaged 63 percent (Mhango et al. 2000; Akinnifesi et al. 2006) while in Tanzania rooting of 83 percent was realized in June-initiated air layers treated with 50 mg L–1 of indole-3-butyric acid (IBA) (Mwang’ingo and Lulandala 2011). Air layers set in April (autumn) and June (winter) in Malawi had respectively 5 percent and 15 percent rooting success (Mhango et al. 2000). The media used to root marcots varies. One can use composted sawdust, peat moss or just soil rich in organic matter. An ideal medium consists of 100 percent peat moss with a pH of 6. Application of the plant hormone IBA to marcots of Uapaca kirkiana enhanced rooting in Tanzania (Mwang’ingo and Lulandala 2011) but had no effect in Malawi (Akinnifesi et al. 2004).

4.1 Setting marcots

  • Select healthy disease-free branches from a superior or desired fruit-bearing (female) wild loquat tree.
  • Select branches that are accessible.
  • Girdle the branch, i.e. remove the bark and cambium on a length of at least 10 cm.
  • Wrap the medium (soil or sawdust or peat moss) around the ringbarked area with cloth or plastic (Figure 6a).
Figure 6a. Marcots are set on selected healthy branches and covered in plastic to minimize water loss

©ICRAF

  • Use of the plastic alleviates the problem of daily watering as the plastic retains moisture.
  • Adventitious roots will develop at the distal cut surface.
  • Detach the marcots from the parent tree once they have formed sufficient roots to survive on their own. Appearance of brown roots is a good indicator (Figure 6b).
Figure 6b. Well-developed brown roots are a good indicator that the rooted branch can be detached

©ICRAF

  • Remove 50 percent of the leaves from the marcots to reduce transpiration before the tree is fully established.
  • Plant the delicate marcots in a well-drained potting mix and keep them in the shade (Figure 6c).
Figure 6c. Detached rooted branch is delicately established in a pot and kept n the shade

©ICRAF

5. Propagation by cuttings and tissue culture

Propagation of wild loquat using stem cuttings and tissue culture has been undertaken with limited success. The utility of these methods is therefore still very low.

6. Field establishment and tree management

6.1 Soil

Wild loquat is naturally adapted to soils that are typically infertile sand or gravel, free draining and acidic. Trees can, however, be grown successfully on other soil types including
ferrallitic latosols (pH 5.2), Ferric Lixisols (46 percent sand, 46 percent clay and 8 percent silt) and Gleyic Luvisols (5 percent clay). Because of its preference for relatively poor soils, a fruit orchard of wild loquat should not compete with other tree crops for the best soils.

6.2 Rainfall and temperature

Wild loquat naturally grows from about 500 to 2 000 m a.s.l. with rainfall of 500–1 400 mm per annum. Some seed sources from semi-arid and dry subhumid areas could have drought tolerance, while material from higher latitude (southern Zimbabwe and Mozambique) and high altitude may have frost tolerance. Seed sources from Tanzania and northern Zambia (lower latitude) is susceptible to frost, and therefore should not be planted on frost-prone sites.

6.3 Tree planting

Planting holes of 60 cm x 60 cm x 60 cm should be dug for transplanting. The holes should be filled with compost and soil collected from under a Uapaca kirkiana stand if available. Such soil has ectomycorrhizal material, which is important for wild loquat establishment and growth.

6.4 Fertilization

Early studies indicated that application of mineral fertilizer and manure appears not to improve early growth and survival of U. kirkiana (Akinnifesi et al. 2008). The poor response to fertilization was attributed to the species’ adaptation to infertile soils. While tree growth may not be affected by fertilizer application, the effect on fruit yield is not yet clear.

6.5 Spacing

When planted with close spacing, wild loquat trees have a straight stem and will self-prune. Preliminary studies have shown improved fruit productivity and quality following canopy opening through thinning applications (Mwamba 1995). The suggested spacing of 3.5 x 3.5 m (Ngulube et al. 1996) appears to be too close. Based on the tree’s architecture, a spacing of at least 6 x 6 m will be suitable depending on the site, with wider spacing being used on high-potential sites where tree size is likely to be bigger.

6.6 Pruning and training

Pruning is the judicious removal of tree parts such as shoots and leaves, or the nipping away of terminal parts to maintain a desired tree structure and size. Training is a practice in which tree growth is directed into a desired shape and form. Responses to pruning and training in wild loquat are not yet known.

6.7 Growth and fruit yields

Fruit yields vary, but yields of 6 000 fruits per tree per annum have been recorded in the wild (Figure 7) while 14-year-old grafted trees at Makoka produced 5 300 fruits (Nyoka et al. 2020). Mature fruit weigh between 5 g and 50 g, with the amount of pulp ranging from 0.2 to 30 g. Fruit load is related to tree size. Reducing the number of fruits (fruit thinning) improves the size of the remaining fruits and reduces their seed weight (Mng’omba et al. 2014). Marcots tend to produce higher fruit yield compared with grafted trees (Akinnifesi et al. 2009). Marcots also have better crown architecture (crown spread and number of branches) compared with grafted trees.

6.8 Pests and diseases

Insect pests of wild loquat include leaf chewers, shoot borers and sapsuckers. The following pests have been identified as potential pests: Bunaea alcinoe, Leptoglossus membraceus and white scales, Cercoplastes uapacae, Ledapis spp, Microsyagrus rosae and Euphoria spp (Ngulube et al. 1996; Meke 1998). These pests damage leaves, flowers, fruits and growing points of the trees. Pest populations are known to be highest in the ho dry season before the onset of the rains and are lowest in the cool dry season. Insect pests that feed on fruits include Carpohilus fumatus, Deudorix sp, Drosophila enanasse and Ceratitis cosyrae (Ngulube et al. 1996). Baboons (Papio cynocephalus) and monkeys (Cercopithecus spp) are major animal pests of wild loquat. Major diseases of U. kirkiana include necrosis linked with Pestalotiopsis versicolour, Speg leaf spots caused by Cercospora species, mildew and sooty moulds caused by Cladosporium cladosporioides (Meke 1998).

Figure 7. Grafted wild loquat tree with a good fruit load at Makoka, Malawi.

©ICRAF

Parasitic plants that attack wild loquat include Agelanthus subulatus, Phragmanthera cornetii, Tapinanthus dependeus and Viscum congdonii. Manual control by removing affected branches is ineffective (Ngulube et al. 1996).

7. Related/associated technologies

  • ​Propagating and planting trees​: ID 6960
  • Vegetative tree propagation in agroforestry: ID 7794.
  • Establishing a tree nursery: ID 7808.

  • Germination is epigeal and will take two to six weeks.

2.1 Growing media

A good growing medium is critical to producing healthy seedlings. A medium comprising 75 percent forest soil and 25 percent composted sawdust is best for producing healthy seedlings (Mhango et al. 2008). Such a medium (forest soil and composted sawdust) has high porosity and good infiltration (Mhango 2000). Forest soil collected from U. kirkiana tree stands is preferred as it contains naturally occurring ectomycorrhizal which improves wild loquat growth by enhancing nutrient and water uptake by the seedlings. The fungus may also lengthen the life of host tree roots, protecting the roots system against soil-borne pathogens (Sileshi et al. 2007; Ramachela 2013). Amending the growing medium with an NPK fertilizer may also improve the quality (large root collar diameter and height) of the seedlings (Mhango et al. 2008). Depending on management, seedlings take between one and two years to reach the right size for planting or grafting (Figure 2). Suckers should be removed (de-suckering) frequently on seedlings grown for grafting (rootstocks) to promote apical dominance and fast growth.

Figure 2. A rootstock of Uapaca kirkiana ready for grafting

©ICRAF

3. Propagation by grafting

Rootstocks of U. kirkiana need to attain pencil-size thickness before grafting. Graft uptake in wild loquat can be as high as 80 percent and both the wedge and the whip grafting methods will produce successful grafts (Mhango and Akinnifesi 2001). The best time to graft Uapaca kirkiana seedlings is at the onset of the summer rains. In Malawi, for example, this is the period between November and December. Grafting success is mainly influenced by the skill of the person grafting, time of the year the scion is collected and the interval between time of scion collection and grafting. When collecting scions observe the following:

  • Scions should be taken from the upper part of the tree.
  • Scion length should be about 10–20 cm.
  • Scion diameter should preferably be of the same size as rootstock i.e. roughly pencil thickness.
  • Scion should have 2 to 4 buds.

3.1 Wedge or cleft graft

Wedge grafting, also known as cleft grafting, is a method of propagating trees by physically joining a small healthy branch, known as a scion, to another tree called the rootstock.

  • Select the preferred, disease-free, mature, healthy, fruit-bearing (i.e. female) wild loquat tree.
  • Select a branch (scion) with a healthy growing tip. Use a sharp knife or pruning shears to cut the scion. A smooth, clean cut is needed for best results.
  • Make a 45-degree angle cut on both sides of the base of the scion using a sharp grafting knife (Figure 3).
  • Make a clean cut horizontally on the rootstock using a knife.
  • Make a wedge-shaped cut down the centre of the rootstock, leaving about a 2.5 cm V-shaped cut or groove in the rootstock.
  • Using a clefting tool, pull back to separate the wedge and insert the scion into the wedge.
Figure 3. Wedge or cleft grafting

©ICRAF

Figure 4. Whip grafting

©ICRAF

Ensure that the bark of the scion matches the bark of the rootstock so that the cambium of scion and rootstock align.

  • Tie grafting tape around the union. You can use a grafting wax or gel if available.
  • Cover the scion with a plastic bag to reduce water loss by transpiration Whip grafting: Rootstocks are raised as described above.
  • Select and collect the scion as described above.
  • Make a slanting 45-degree cut through the bottom end of the scion (Figure 4).
  • On the rootstock, make a 45-degree angled a smooth and straight diagonal cut upwards. This slanting straight-plane cut should be about 5 cm long.
  • Join the cut side of the scion onto the cut side of the rootstock to match.
  • Ensure the cambium of both scion and rootstock align.
  • Tie grafting tape around the union. You can apply a grafting wax or gel if available.
  • Cover the scion with a plastic bag to reduce water loss by transpiration.

3.2 Caring for the grafted plants

Grafted plants should be kept in the shade and watered daily. Keep the grafted plants in a humid environment (RH>70 precent) and maintain good care until the grafting union heals. Remove all shoots growing below the union. Once the union heals, remove the grafting tape.

3.3 Incompatibility

Grafting may fail because of incompatibility between the scion and the rootstock, poor grafting technique, grafting at the wrong physiological stage or poor care in the nursery, which can also cause problems. Most of the observed incompatibility in wild loquat manifests as larger rootstock diameter compared with the scion (Figure 5).

Figure 5. Grafting incompatibility in U. kirkiana manifests as a slow-growing scion on a fast- growing rootstock

©ICRAF

4. Propagation by air layering

Time of setting air layers or marcots is critical to enhancing rooting. The best time to set marcots is at the onset of the rains, and in Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe, this is the period between November and December (Mhango and Akinnifesi 2001; Mhango et al. 2000). In Tanzania, one study (Mwang’ingo and Lulandala 2011) indicated the period soon after the end of the summer rains (June) as the best time. In Malawi, rooting of initiated air layers averaged 63 percent (Mhango et al. 2000; Akinnifesi et al. 2006) while in Tanzania rooting of 83 percent was realized in June-initiated air layers treated with 50 mg L–1 of indole-3-butyric acid (IBA) (Mwang’ingo and Lulandala 2011). Air layers set in April (autumn) and June (winter) in Malawi had respectively 5 percent and 15 percent rooting success (Mhango et al. 2000). The media used to root marcots varies. One can use composted sawdust, peat moss or just soil rich in organic matter. An ideal medium consists of 100 percent peat moss with a pH of 6. Application of the plant hormone IBA to marcots of Uapaca kirkiana enhanced rooting in Tanzania (Mwang’ingo and Lulandala 2011) but had no effect in Malawi (Akinnifesi et al. 2004).

4.1 Setting marcots

  • Select healthy disease-free branches from a superior or desired fruit-bearing (female) wild loquat tree.
  • Select branches that are accessible.
  • Girdle the branch, i.e. remove the bark and cambium on a length of at least 10 cm.
  • Wrap the medium (soil or sawdust or peat moss) around the ringbarked area with cloth or plastic (Figure 6a).
Figure 6a. Marcots are set on selected healthy branches and covered in plastic to minimize water loss

©ICRAF

  • Use of the plastic alleviates the problem of daily watering as the plastic retains moisture.
  • Adventitious roots will develop at the distal cut surface.
  • Detach the marcots from the parent tree once they have formed sufficient roots to survive on their own. Appearance of brown roots is a good indicator (Figure 6b).
Figure 6b. Well-developed brown roots are a good indicator that the rooted branch can be detached

©ICRAF

  • Remove 50 percent of the leaves from the marcots to reduce transpiration before the tree is fully established.
  • Plant the delicate marcots in a well-drained potting mix and keep them in the shade (Figure 6c).
Figure 6c. Detached rooted branch is delicately established in a pot and kept n the shade

©ICRAF

5. Propagation by cuttings and tissue culture

Propagation of wild loquat using stem cuttings and tissue culture has been undertaken with limited success. The utility of these methods is therefore still very low.

6. Field establishment and tree management

6.1 Soil

Wild loquat is naturally adapted to soils that are typically infertile sand or gravel, free draining and acidic. Trees can, however, be grown successfully on other soil types including
ferrallitic latosols (pH 5.2), Ferric Lixisols (46 percent sand, 46 percent clay and 8 percent silt) and Gleyic Luvisols (5 percent clay). Because of its preference for relatively poor soils, a fruit orchard of wild loquat should not compete with other tree crops for the best soils.

6.2 Rainfall and temperature

Wild loquat naturally grows from about 500 to 2 000 m a.s.l. with rainfall of 500–1 400 mm per annum. Some seed sources from semi-arid and dry subhumid areas could have drought tolerance, while material from higher latitude (southern Zimbabwe and Mozambique) and high altitude may have frost tolerance. Seed sources from Tanzania and northern Zambia (lower latitude) is susceptible to frost, and therefore should not be planted on frost-prone sites.

6.3 Tree planting

Planting holes of 60 cm x 60 cm x 60 cm should be dug for transplanting. The holes should be filled with compost and soil collected from under a Uapaca kirkiana stand if available. Such soil has ectomycorrhizal material, which is important for wild loquat establishment and growth.

6.4 Fertilization

Early studies indicated that application of mineral fertilizer and manure appears not to improve early growth and survival of U. kirkiana (Akinnifesi et al. 2008). The poor response to fertilization was attributed to the species’ adaptation to infertile soils. While tree growth may not be affected by fertilizer application, the effect on fruit yield is not yet clear.

6.5 Spacing

When planted with close spacing, wild loquat trees have a straight stem and will self-prune. Preliminary studies have shown improved fruit productivity and quality following canopy opening through thinning applications (Mwamba 1995). The suggested spacing of 3.5 x 3.5 m (Ngulube et al. 1996) appears to be too close. Based on the tree’s architecture, a spacing of at least 6 x 6 m will be suitable depending on the site, with wider spacing being used on high-potential sites where tree size is likely to be bigger.

6.6 Pruning and training

Pruning is the judicious removal of tree parts such as shoots and leaves, or the nipping away of terminal parts to maintain a desired tree structure and size. Training is a practice in which tree growth is directed into a desired shape and form. Responses to pruning and training in wild loquat are not yet known.

6.7 Growth and fruit yields

Fruit yields vary, but yields of 6 000 fruits per tree per annum have been recorded in the wild (Figure 7) while 14-year-old grafted trees at Makoka produced 5 300 fruits (Nyoka et al. 2020). Mature fruit weigh between 5 g and 50 g, with the amount of pulp ranging from 0.2 to 30 g. Fruit load is related to tree size. Reducing the number of fruits (fruit thinning) improves the size of the remaining fruits and reduces their seed weight (Mng’omba et al. 2014). Marcots tend to produce higher fruit yield compared with grafted trees (Akinnifesi et al. 2009). Marcots also have better crown architecture (crown spread and number of branches) compared with grafted trees.

6.8 Pests and diseases

Insect pests of wild loquat include leaf chewers, shoot borers and sapsuckers. The following pests have been identified as potential pests: Bunaea alcinoe, Leptoglossus membraceus and white scales, Cercoplastes uapacae, Ledapis spp, Microsyagrus rosae and Euphoria spp (Ngulube et al. 1996; Meke 1998). These pests damage leaves, flowers, fruits and growing points of the trees. Pest populations are known to be highest in the ho dry season before the onset of the rains and are lowest in the cool dry season. Insect pests that feed on fruits include Carpohilus fumatus, Deudorix sp, Drosophila enanasse and Ceratitis cosyrae (Ngulube et al. 1996). Baboons (Papio cynocephalus) and monkeys (Cercopithecus spp) are major animal pests of wild loquat. Major diseases of U. kirkiana include necrosis linked with Pestalotiopsis versicolour, Speg leaf spots caused by Cercospora species, mildew and sooty moulds caused by Cladosporium cladosporioides (Meke 1998).

Figure 7. Grafted wild loquat tree with a good fruit load at Makoka, Malawi.

©ICRAF

Parasitic plants that attack wild loquat include Agelanthus subulatus, Phragmanthera cornetii, Tapinanthus dependeus and Viscum congdonii. Manual control by removing affected branches is ineffective (Ngulube et al. 1996).

7. Related/associated technologies

  • ​Propagating and planting trees​: ID 6960
  • Vegetative tree propagation in agroforestry: ID 7794.
  • Establishing a tree nursery: ID 7808.

INNOVATION IDENTIFIED:
Vegetative propagation techniques for wild loquat (U. kirkiana)
Description: Grafting and air layering methods reduce fruiting time from 10+ to 4 years, maintain desired traits, and increase yields compared to traditional seed propagation. This meets criteria of "modified process that helps solve a problem" by addressing long maturation times and inconsistent fruit quality in indigenous fruit tree cultivation.
_annotations.field_shorter_description:
Uapaca kirkiana, commonly known as wild loquat, is a native fruit tree found in various regions of Southern Africa, including eastern Angola, southern DRC, Burundi, Tanzania, Zambia, Malawi, Mozambique, and Zimbabwe. This species goes by different local names in the region, such as msuku, mushuku, nkusu, and others. It exhibits dioecious characteristics, meaning it has separate male and female trees, although hermaphrodites have been observed rarely.

The flowering of wild loquat varies with location, occurring between September and April. Male trees typically flower earlier than female trees. Insects like honeybees and beetles serve as potential pollinators. Fruits ripen from January to April, depending on the area, with larger, brown-colored fruits being preferred by consumers. These fruits are rich in carbohydrates, energy, fibre, minerals, proteins, and vitamins, particularly vitamin C, iron, and potassium. The soil and climate requirements for wild loquat are adaptable, and tree planting and management techniques, including spacing and pruning, can influence growth and fruit yields. Insect pests and diseases, as well as parasitic plants, can affect wild loquat cultivation, but their impact varies by location. Further research and technology adoption can enhance the cultivation and utilization of this valuable indigenous fruit tree in southern Africa.

records.title: Ocho reglas de oro para el desarrollo sustentable de lácteos
records.description:
Descripción

1. Reglas de oro para la cría de terneras 

1.1 Garantizar un saludable medio para el nacimiento de terneros 

  • Los terneros deben nacer bajo condiciones higiénicas. 
  • Las vacas que van a parir deben ser provistas de un área seca y limpia en la que puedan parir. 
  • El cordón umbilical de las terneras debe ser limpiados inmediatamente después del parto con un rociador que contenga una solución yodada al 7 por ciento (Figura 1).
Figura 1. Rociar el cordón umbilical con solución yodada

©FAO/TECA

1.2 Asegurar la primera alimentación con leche del ternero recién nacido

  • Los terneros deben tomar calostro de alta calidad (Figura 2). 
  • Cada ternero debería recibir cuatro litros de calostro dentro de las primeras seis horas de nacido. 
  • También puede seguir siendo alimentado con calostro durante los días siguientes.
Figura 2. Darles de tomar a las terneras calostro de alta calidad

©FAO/TECA

1.3 Asegurar la alimentación concentrada para las terneras jóvenes

  • Las terneras pueden ser destetadas a los tres meses de edad, la leche puede ser reemplazada por agua y concentrado para terneras (kg/dia) (Figura 3). 
  • Después de los tres meses, se les debe empezar a dar concentrado a una razón de 1 kg por día y deben tener libre acceso a agua (tanto como lo que necesiten). El nivel de concentrado debe incrementarse de acuerdo al crecimiento de las terneras. 
Figura 3. Proveer a las terneras destetadas con concentrado para terneras

©FAO/TECA

1.4 Proveer agua limpia y buena ventilación

  • Las terneras deben ser provistas siempre con agua adecuada y limpia para beber. El cobertizo para terneras debe ser provista con buena ventilación (Figura 4). 
  • Se debe identificar cada ternera con un arete plástico.
  • Se debe mantener un registro constante de cada ternera (registros médicos, registros de alimentación, peso).
Figura 4. Cobertizos ventilados

©FAO/TECA

Figura 5. Identificación de las terneras con aretes plásticos

©FAO/TECA

2. Reglas de oro para la crianza de las terneras destetadas 

2.1 Requerimiento de alimentación: Alimentación adecuada con forraje y alimento concentrado

  • Las terneras destetadas deben ser alimentadas con una dieta balanceada (que depende del peso corporal, la raza, etc.) en base a forraje de calidad (Figura 6) y concentrado que depende de la edad de las terneras. 
  • El concentrado debe contener por lo menos 16 a 18 por ciento de proteína. 
  • Se debe proveer al ganado con agua limpia para beber. 
Figura 6. Forraje y alimento concentrado de calidad

©FAO/TECA

2.2 Buen manejo de terneras

  • Las terneras bien criadas mostrarán signos de estar en celo entre los primeros 10 a 12 meses de vida, y podrán estar aptas para parir entre los 24 a 27 meses de edad. 

3. Reglas de oro para la alimentación de vacas lecheras 

3.1 Requerimiento de agua y alimento para las vacas lecheras

  • Las vacas lecheras tienen un alto requerimiento de agua. Los productores deben proveer a su ganado con agua limpia para beber de manera separada y no como parte de ningún concentrado (Figura 7).
  • La alimentación con forraje es en relación con el peso de la vaca y el rendimiento de leche producida. 
  • Los productores deben proveer suficiente forraje de calidad y complementarlo con alimento concentrado. Se puede usar adicionalmente forraje seco. 
  • Se debe secar el forraje dejándolo bajo el sol durante un día antes de ser cortado (Figura 8). Esto reduce su humedad y promueve que la vaca coma más de este forraje seco, y así produzca más leche. 
Figura 7. Provisión separada de agua limpia para beber

©FAO/TECA

Figura 8. Secar el forraje en el sol para reducir el nivel de humedad

©FAO/TECA

3.2 Detectar la condición alimenticia de las vacas 

  • Si existe alguna sospecha de una dieta desbalanceada en el ganado lechero, monitorear de cerca la consistencia de sus desechos (estiércol), posible reducción de ingesta de alimentos, cambios en el rendimiento de producción de leche y su composición, y la proporción de vacas que están rumiando. 
  • Aproximadamente 60 por ciento de las vacas lecheras que están descansando deberían estar rumiando. 
  • Las vacas potencialmente más rendidoras son más suceptibles a otras restricciones de la propia granja como insuficiente alimento de calidad, ansiedad y estrés, pobre salud animal y una limitada capacidad de gestión por parte del productor.
  • Además, los productores necesitan desarrollar capacidades para identificar cuando las vacas se encuentran en celo. Esto requiere observación continua incluyendo observaciones nocturnas (Figura 9). 
Figura 9. Productores necesitan identificar cuando las vacas se encuentran en celo

©FAO/TECA

4. Reglas de oro para la reproducción en vacas adultas 

4.1 Salud de las vacas para la reproducción

  • Las vacas lecheras necesitan estar bien alimentadas para reproducirse. Si las vacas estan muy flacas o en sobre peso, tendrán una baja fertilidad.
  • El periodo voluntario de espera, o días entre el parto y la nueva reproducción no debería ser mayor de 50 a 60 días. 
  • Se debe observar si hay señales de estar en celo, en caso que todavía no estén preñadas. 

4.2 Desempeño reproductivo

  • Las mejores tasas de concepción se obtienen a través de la inseminación (manual o artificial) realizada dentro de las 4 a 12 horas inmediatas depués de las primeras señales de estar en celo (Figura 10).
  • Podría ser necesario sacrificar vacas adicionales en caso que más del 15 por ciento del ganado tenga más de 16 meses entre cada parto. 
  • Es importante mantener registro de las inseminaciones y apareamientos naturales para asegurar un buen desempeño reproductivo del ganado y para saber cuando es necesario buscar ayuda veterinaria. 
  • Los productores tienen que identificar mensualmente las vacas no preñadas, que tengan más de 80 días de su último parto pero no que muestren ningún signo de estar en celo. 
  • Se debe pedir asistencia veterinaria para revisarlas y detectar posibles anomalías. 
Figura 10. Realizar la inseminación entre las 4-12 horas después de la primera señal de celo

©FAO/TECA

5. Reglas de oro para el cuidado de la salud del ganado 

5.1 Plan de prevención contra las enfermedades

  • Desarrolle un plan de prevención contra las enfermedades que incluya una buena higiene, aislamiento del ganado enfermo y un programa de vacunas regulares. 
  • Aprenda a identificar rápidamente los animales enfermos asintomáticos a través de su apariencia física y su comportamiento. 
  • Provea a las vacas con una cama suave, como un área de descanso de tierra o arena o tapetes de hule, para mejorar la comodidad de las vacas y reducir a su vez los problemas en sus extremidades (Figura 11). 
  • Desarrolle por escrito un programa de salud del ganado que contenga acciones de manejo de la salud del ganado para prevenir y controlar enfermedades y desórdenes específicos para cada región. 
Figura 11. Camas suaves para vacas

©FAO/TECA

5.2 Habilidades de crianza para cuidar animales enfermos

  • Si un animal está visiblemente enfermo, entonces debe ser movido a un cobertizo aislado para evitar que infecte o contagie al ganado restante (Figura 12). 
  • La cojera puede ser un problema común en vacas viviendo bajo cobertizos. Se debe identificar su causa, ya que puede ser respuesta a un trauma o a una dieta desbalanceada (Figura 13). 
  • No se debe usar drogas antiguas que estén pasadas de la fecha de expiración para tratar a los animales enfermos. 
Figura 12. Aislar animales enfermos 

©FAO/TECA

Figura 13. La cojera cómo signo de un trauma o de una dieta desbalanceada

©FAO/TECA

6. Reglas de oro para el manejo de animales bajo estrés por calor 

6.1 Consecuencias del estrés por calor

  • Vacas con altas temperaturas corporales pierden el apetito. Vacas muy sedientas pierden el apetito.
  • El estrés por calor puede reducir el tiempo del ciclo de las vacas, en el que muestran signos de estar en celo. 
  • El estrés por calor reduce la fertilidad de las vacas y si se hace severo, puede incluso acabar con la vida del feto que se está desarrollando en la vaca preñada.  

6.2 Estrategias para enfrentar el estrés por calor

  • Es mejor alimentar vacas durante la noche, cuando el ambiente es más fresco, así cómo también durante el día. 
  • Agua adicional siempre es escencial en días calientes o durante el verano para contrarrestar el calor corporal. 
  • Cobertizos con techos y muros bajos (que obstruyen el viento) reducen la ventilación natural, por lo que deberían ser evitados (Figura 14). 
  • Rocie con agua a las vacas con altas temperaturas corporales, incluso con una manguera por algunos minutos, seguido de ubicarlos cerca de un ventilador (o mejor aún, un ambiente natural ventilado natural). Esto refrescará a las vacas con altas temperaturas. 
  • El agua debe ser rociado sobre el lomo de las vacas, suficiente como para cubrir toda la vaca (Figura 15). 
Figura 14. Techos y muros bajos reducen la ventilación

©FAO/TECA

Figura 15. Rociar con agua a las vacas con altas temperaturas corporales 

©FAO/TECA

7. Reglas de oro para el mantenimiento del ganado vacuno lechero 

7.1 Importancia del mantenimiento del ganado para su salud

  • El ganado necesita de 12 a 14 horas de descanso imperturbado por día, preferible en establos que sean cómodos. 
  • Si se cuenta con pasadizos y establos de descanso bien diseñados, superficies cómodas para echarse, y suelos no resbaladizos; las vacas sufren menos de cojera, se pueden comportar de manera más normal y sufrir de menos estrés, tener rendimientos más altos en la producción de leche y una vida productiva más larga.

7.2 Desventajas de un mal manejo

  • No es conveniente que las vacas estén cubiertas hasta las extremidades de estiércol fresco o seco. 
  • No es conveniente que las vacas estén forzadas a descansar en suelos duros y sucios (Figura 16). 
  • No es conveniente mantener a las vacas atadas al concreto todo el día todos los días. 
  • No es conveniente que las cuerdas usadas para atar a las vacas sean demasiado cortas que le dificulten el pararse y echarse. 
  • Se les debe proveer una porción del alimento diario en un campo o patio exterior para promover el movimiento de las vacas en el espacio abierto. 
Figura 16. Suelos duros y sucios no son conveniente para el buen manejo del ganado

©FAO/TECA

8. Reglas de oro para la producción de leche de calidad 

8.1 Impactos negativos de una calidad pobre de leche

  • Una calidad pobre de leche reduce la vida útil (tiempo de caducidad) de la leche líquida (pasteurizada o ultrapasteurizada) y es cada vez más importante para los pequeños productores de leche. 
  • El punto más importante en la producción de leche es la higiene tanto durante el proceso de ordeñar las vacas así como al manipular y transportar la leche del cobertizo del ganado al centro de recolección lechero (Figura 17). 
Figura 17. Higiene para producir leche de calidad

©FAO/TECA

8.2 Importancia del correcto ordeño y manipulación adecuada al ordeñar en la calidad de la leche

  • El personal para el ordeño debe tener las manos y la vestimenta siempre limpia, no estar enfermo y es preferible que use siempre guantes (Figura 18). 
  • Los utensilios para ordeñar deben ser limpiados a profundidad con agua y con jabón, seguido de agua caliente, saneados y ser colgados de cabeza para que escurran y sequen completamente ante de ser usados nuevamente para ordeñar.
  • Cada vaca lechera debe contar con su propio material de limpieza para limpiar sus ubres antes de ser ordeñadas (Figura 19).
  • Debe ser lavado con jabón y agua corriente, esterilizado y colgarlo para dejarlo secar en el sol antes de ser nuevamente usado para la siguiente vez que la vaca sea ordeñada.
  • Las ubres de las vacas deben ser desinfectadas (insertadas o rociadas) en solución yodada al 7 por ciento después de ser ordeñadas (Figura 20).
  • El veterinario local o la cooperativa lechera podría proveerle de esta solución yodada. 
  • El CMT (Prueba de Mastitis California) debe ser realizada en cada vaca lechera una vez por mes hasta que el ganado alcance un nivel bajo de mastitis (Figura 21).
  • Luego puede ser realizado cada tres meses (Figure 21). 
Figura 18. Uso de guantes y ropa limpia y adecuada

©FAO/TECA

Figura 19. Uso de materiales independientes para la limpieza de ubres antes de ser ordeñadas

©FAO/TECA

Figura 20. Desinfectar la ubre de la vaca en 7 por ciento de solución yodada después de ordeñar

©FAO/TECA

Figura 21. Realizar la Prueba de Mastitis California en cada vaca lechera

©FAO/TECA

9. Validación de la práctica

  • La información presentada en esta práctica fue tomada directamente del documento: 8 reglas de oro para el desarrollo sostenible de la lechería.
  • Estas reglas de oro fueron desarrolladas por la Oficina Regional de la FAO para Asia y el Pacífico, junto con la Subdivisión de Sistemas de Producción Ganadera (AGAS), la División de Producción y Sanidad Animal de la FAO, en el marco del Proyecto de Desarrollo Lechero para Pequeños Productores en Bangladesh, Myanmar y Tailandia (SDDP).

10. Zonas agroecológicas

  • Tropical, cálido.

11. Tecnologías relacionadas y asociadas

  • Services for marketing animals and milk: ID 8248.
  • Producing animals and milk for market: ID ​8249.

Esta tecnología también está disponible en inglés: ID 8652.

12. Objetivos cumplidos por el proyecto

12.1 Eficiencia en el uso de recursos

Estas reglas conducen a muchos resultados positivos, como un aumento en la calidad de producción de leche, sostenibilidad, salud y alimentación nutritiva del ganado.

12.2 Atiende a las necesidades de la mujer

Esta tecnología no requiere mucho esfuerzo físico, por lo que cualquier persona puede realizarla. Especialmente las mujeres se benefician de una buena producción de leche, que pueden manejar ellas mismas o utilizar en los alimentos.

12.3 Tecnología a favor de los pobres

A través de la aplicación de estas reglas de oro los productores son capaces de mejorar la gestión en salud, crianza y alimentación del ganado vacuno lechero, por lo cual los agricultores generan una producción de leche saludable y sostenible.
